STROKE — CLOT OR BLEED, AND THE CLOCK IS THE TREATMENT The two look identical at the door. A CT scan before anything else is what separates them.

entries.h: TWO THINGS THAT LOOK THE SAME
entries.t: Ischemic : a clot blocks it · 87% of strokes Hemorrhagic : it bursts · 13% — worse odds 💡 CT scan first. Thrombolytics into a bleed are fatal.

B — Balance lost suddenly E — Eyes — vision loss or double F — Face droops on one side A — Arm drifts down when both are raised S — Speech slurred or nonsense T — Time — note when she was last normal 💡 Last known well is the number the whole plan hangs on.

4.5 h — IV alteplase, from last known well 24 h — mechanical thrombectomy, selected cases < 25 min — to the CT scanner from arrival NPO — until a swallow screen is passed Do not treat a BP of 180 in an ischemic stroke — that pressure is perfusing the brain.
LEFT stroke vs RIGHT stroke
LEFT stroke right RIGHT stroke left
LEFT stroke aphasia RIGHT stroke intact
LEFT stroke cautious RIGHT stroke impulsive

LEFT stroke rare RIGHT stroke ignores left side 🚨 THE RIGHT-SIDED STROKE IS THE FALL RISK Impulsive, denies the deficit, does not see her left side. Approach from the unaffected side; bed rails up. Presentation update · original course graphic wording retained · October 2026

The tests you perform with your hands, a tuning fork or a cuff — not the ones that come back from the lab. For each one: what you are testing for , how to do it , what a positive looks like , and the part that catches people out. Most tests include an illustration; select a picture to enlarge it. Pictures are study aids; use the written steps and supervised clinical training. Search a test, a sign, or what it is for
🧭 Body system 🎓 Class 📚 Module 🔢 Test name A–Z

Everything NUR 125 NUR 175 NUR 198 NUR 234 NUR 235 NUR 258 🧠 Neuro 👁 Eyes & ears 🫀 Heart & vessels 🫁 Lungs 🍽 Abdomen & GI 🦴 Bones, joints & nerves 🧪 Endocrine & metabolic 🚰 Kidney & urinary 🤰 Maternity 🧸 Newborn & child 🩹 Skin & wounds 🗣 Mental health
NUR 258 NUR 198 · M2 Fluid & Electrolytes M5 Endocrine 🧪 Endocrine & metabolic 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Low calcium (and low magnesium). It is one of the two bedside signs of neuromuscular irritability.
Have her sit with her face relaxed. Tap lightly over the facial nerve , just in front of the earlobe and below the zygomatic arch. Watch the same side of her face.
Twitching of the lip, nose or whole side of the face on the side you tapped.
Chvostek is the cheek ; Trousseau is the tourniquet . Both mean calcium is low - a positive sign after a thyroidectomy means the parathyroids were bruised or removed. Read the full page →

entries.h: 🧪 Trousseau's sign Carpal spasm / cuff sign
entries.t: NUR 258 NUR 198 · M2 Fluid & Electrolytes M5 Endocrine 🧪 Endocrine & metabolic 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Low calcium. It is the more specific of the two calcium signs.
Put a blood-pressure cuff on her upper arm. Inflate it about 20 mmHg above her systolic pressure. Leave it up for 3 minutes and watch her hand.
Carpal spasm - the wrist and knuckles flex, the finger joints straighten, and the thumb draws across the palm with the fingers held together.
It is uncomfortable and she needs to know it is coming. Have calcium gluconate available if the calcium is known to be low; laryngospasm is the emergency at the far end of this. Read the full page →
NUR 258 M6 Diabetes 🧪 Endocrine & metabolic 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Protective sensation in the diabetic foot - whether she would feel a stone in her shoe before it became an ulcer.

Show her the filament on her arm first so she knows the sensation. Ask her to close her eyes. Press the 10 g monofilament perpendicular to the sole until it buckles , hold about 1 second. Test several sites on each foot; avoid callus and ulcer.
Any site she cannot feel means loss of protective sensation .

A foot that cannot feel is a foot that gets injured silently. This test is why the teaching is to look at the feet daily and check the water with a hand or a thermometer, not a foot . Read the full page →
NUR 258 M8 Neuro infection 🧠 Neuro 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Meningeal irritation - meningitis or subarachnoid blood.
Lay her flat. Flex one hip to 90 degrees with the knee bent. Then try to straighten the knee .
Pain and resistance that stop you extending the knee.
Kernig is the knee . Both meningeal signs can be absent in a very young, very old or immunosuppressed client - a negative sign does not rule meningitis out. Read the full page →
NUR 258 M8 Neuro infection 🧠 Neuro 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Meningeal irritation - meningitis, the same thing Kernig is looking for.
Lay her flat with no pillow. Put a hand behind her head and flex the neck towards her chest. Watch her hips and knees.
Her hips and knees flex up involuntarily - she pulls her legs up as you bend her neck.
Brudzinski is the brain end - the neck. Nuchal rigidity, photophobia and headache travel with it. Read the full page →
NUR 125 Neuro assessment 🧠 Neuro 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Upper motor neuron integrity - the corticospinal tract.
Use the handle of the reflex hammer, not a sharp point. Stroke up the lateral edge of the sole from heel to ball, then across the ball towards the big toe.
The great toe dorsiflexes up and the other toes fan out .

The catch is age. That response is normal until about age 2 . After that it is an abnormal finding and points to an upper motor neuron lesion. Normal in an adult is all the toes curling down. Read the full page →
NUR 125 Neuro assessment 🧠 Neuro 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Proprioception and the vestibular system - can she stay upright without her eyes helping?
Have her stand with feet together and arms at her sides, eyes open , for 20 seconds. Then ask her to close her eyes and hold it for another 20. Stand beside her ready to catch her.
Marked swaying or loss of balance once the eyes close.
It is a fall risk test you perform - never leave her unguarded. Swaying with the eyes open too points to the cerebellum rather than proprioception. Read the full page →
NUR 258 M7 Neuro 🧠 Neuro 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Level of consciousness, scored so that a change is measurable rather than a matter of opinion.
Score three things: eye opening (1-4), verbal response (1-5), best motor response (1-6). Use the best response she gives. Add them: the range is 3 to 15 .
A total of 8 or less means she cannot protect her airway and intubation is anticipated. A drop of 2 points is reportable.
There is no zero - the lowest possible score is 3, not 0. And the trend matters more than any single number. Read the full page →
NUR 125 Neuro assessment 🧠 Neuro 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Cranial nerves II and III, and rising intracranial pressure.
Dim the lights. Bring the penlight in from the side , not straight at her. Check size, shape, equality, the direct and consensual response, and accommodation.
A newly unequal, sluggish or fixed dilated pupil.

A fixed dilated pupil on one side is cranial nerve III being compressed - in raised ICP that is herniation and it is an emergency. Some people have unequal pupils normally, so the word that matters is new . Read the full page →
NUR 258 M7 Neuro 🧠 Neuro
Whether a sudden change could be a stroke - fast enough to get her to imaging while treatment is still possible.

B alance - sudden loss of balance or coordination? E yes - sudden vision loss or change in one or both eyes? F ace - ask her to smile. Does one side droop? A rms - raise both arms. Does one drift down? S peech - repeat a simple sentence. Slurred, or the wrong words? T ime - call it now, and find out when she was last known well .
Any one new finding is a positive screen and a stroke alert.

The time that matters is when she was last known well , not when she was found. Check the glucose - low blood sugar mimics a stroke exactly. Nothing by mouth, aspirin included, until she has had a swallow screen and the CT has ruled out a bleed. Read the full page →
NUR 258 M7 Neuro 🧠 Neuro
How severe a stroke is, scored so the next person can tell whether she is getting better or worse.

Score the eleven items in order: level of consciousness, gaze, visual fields, facial palsy, arm and leg motor, limb ataxia, sensation, language, speech (dysarthria) and neglect. Score what she actually does , on her first attempt - not what you think she could do. Add the items for a total from 0 to 42 . Repeat it on the schedule set by the stroke protocol, especially around thrombolytics.
0 is no measurable deficit and 42 is the maximum. Higher means a bigger stroke - your module notes treat 10 or higher as severe. A rising score is a worsening stroke and is reported now.

It measures how much damage, not what kind - it cannot tell a clot from a bleed, which is why the CT comes first. It leans heavily on language and limb strength, so a posterior (brainstem or cerebellar) stroke can score low and still be dangerous. Read the full page →

entries.h: 🧠 Pronator drift With motor strength 0 to 5
entries.t: NUR 258 NUR 125 · Neuro assessment M7 Neuro 🧠 Neuro
Subtle one-sided weakness from an upper motor neuron problem - the stroke or rising pressure on the opposite side of the brain.

Have her hold both arms straight out in front, palms up . Ask her to close her eyes and hold the position for about 10 seconds. Watch each arm, then grade grip and leg strength on both sides: 5 full power against resistance, 4 some resistance, 3 against gravity only, 2 with gravity removed, 1 a flicker, 0 nothing.
One arm drifts down and the palm turns inward (pronates). Any new difference between the two sides.

The eyes are closed so she cannot correct the drift by watching her arm. The weak arm is on the opposite side from the brain lesion. Compare left with right, and now with the last check - the change matters more than the number. Read the full page →

entries.h: 🧠 Deep tendon reflex grading DTRs 0 to 4+ and ankle clonus
entries.t: NUR 234 NUR 198 · M2 Fluid & Electrolytes Antepartum 🧠 Neuro
How irritable or how depressed the nervous system is - preeclampsia, magnesium sulfate toxicity, and calcium, magnesium and potassium problems.

Let the limb hang relaxed - for the patellar reflex, have her sit with her legs dangling. Strike the tendon briskly with the hammer and compare both sides. Grade it: 0 absent, 1+ diminished, 2+ normal, 3+ brisker than normal, 4+ very brisk with clonus. For clonus, support the knee, dorsiflex the foot sharply and hold it there.

Clonus is a rhythmic beating of the foot while you hold it up. 3+ or 4+ with clonus in preeclampsia means a seizure is getting closer. Diminished or absent reflexes on magnesium sulfate are usually the earliest sign of toxicity .

On magnesium, reflexes often go first but they are one check in a panel: respirations under 12, urine output under 30 mL/hr, level of consciousness, SpO2 and lung sounds, and serum magnesium when ordered. Any of them failing means stop the infusion and notify - calcium gluconate is the antidote. With an epidural the legs may not respond, so use the biceps reflex. Low calcium or magnesium makes reflexes brisk; high magnesium, high calcium or low potassium makes them weak. Read the full page →

entries.h: 🧠 Cushing's triad Late sign of rising ICP
entries.t: NUR 258 M7 Neuro 🧠 Neuro
Brain herniation - pressure inside the skull high enough to compress the brainstem.

Trend the blood pressure, pulse and respirations against her own baseline , not against normal ranges. Work out the pulse pressure - systolic minus diastolic - every time. Check level of consciousness and pupils alongside the vital signs.
All three together: rising systolic with a widening pulse pressure , bradycardia , and irregular respirations such as Cheyne-Stokes.

Cushing’s triad is late - it is never the answer to the earliest sign. The earliest sign of rising pressure is a change in level of consciousness . By the time all three appear she is herniating, so this is an emergency, not a trend to watch. Read the full page →

entries.h: 🧠 Battle's sign, raccoon eyes and the halo test Basilar skull fracture
entries.t: NUR 258 M8 Neuro trauma 🧠 Neuro
A fracture through the base of the skull - a tear in the dura that lets cerebrospinal fluid leak out and bacteria in.

Look for bruising around both eyes without a direct blow to them (raccoon eyes). Look behind the ears , over the mastoid bone (Battle’s sign). Look for clear drainage from the nose or ear . Drip any drainage onto white gauze , or test it for glucose .
The halo test: a central spot of blood with a clear or yellow ring spreading around it. Drainage that tests positive for glucose is CSF - nasal mucus has none.

Never pack the nose or ear, never pass a nasogastric tube or suction through the nose - it can go through the fracture into the brain. Let it drain onto a loose dressing. Battle’s sign can take a day or more to appear, so a clean look on arrival does not clear her. Read the full page →

entries.h: 🧠 Bedside swallow screen Before anything by mouth
entries.t: NUR 258 M7 Neuro 🧠 Neuro
Whether she can swallow safely, or will aspirate - after a stroke, or with a weak cough, a wet voice or an absent gag.

Keep her NPO - water and oral medicines included - until the screen is done. She must be alert and sitting fully upright . Follow your facility’s screen: listen to her voice and cough, then give a small, measured amount of water and watch the swallow. Watch and listen for a minute afterwards, not just during the sip.
Coughing, choking, a wet or gurgly voice , drooling, or water leaking from the mouth. Any one is a fail.

A failed screen means she stays NPO, medicines included , and gets a speech-language pathology referral. A present gag reflex does not prove a safe swallow, and some people aspirate silently without coughing. Read the full page →

entries.h: 🧠 Numeric pain scale 0 to 10, with PQRST
entries.t: NUR 125 Pain 🧠 Neuro
How much it hurts, in her own words - for anyone able to self-report.

Ask her to rate it: 0 is no pain, 10 is the worst pain imaginable . P - what provokes it, and what makes it better? Q - quality: sharp, dull, burning, crushing? R - region, and does it radiate? S - severity, the number. T - timing: when it started, constant or coming and going.
1-3 mild, 4-6 moderate, 7-10 severe. What matters most is whether it is above her acceptable level.

Pain is what she says it is - believe her number , not your impression of how she looks. Vital signs are not a pain scale; chronic pain often comes with normal ones. Reassess after every intervention , and a sleeping patient is not proof the pain is controlled. Read the full page →
NUR 125 Pain 🧠 Neuro
Sedation from opioids - which climbs before the respiratory rate falls.

Check it with the respiratory rate before and after every opioid dose. Talk to her, and wake her if she is asleep. Score it: S asleep but easy to wake, 1 awake and alert, 2 slightly drowsy but easily roused. 3 frequently drowsy and drifting off mid-sentence. 4 minimal or no response to voice or touch.
3 or 4 is unacceptable. At 3, hold or reduce the opioid and watch her closely. At 4, stop the opioid , stay with her, and prepare naloxone and call.

Sedation is the smoke detector; apnea is the fire. Drifting off in the middle of a conversation is the warning - do not wait for the respiratory rate to drop. S only counts if she is easy to wake. Read the full page →
NUR 258 M1 Sensory 👁 Eyes & ears 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Which side hears differently. It cannot tell you the type of loss.
Strike a tuning fork and place the base on the midline of the forehead or the top of the head. Ask: where do you hear it?
Normal is equally in both ears . Lateralizing to an ear suggests conductive loss in that ear ; lateralizing away suggests sensorineural loss in the other.
Conductive goes to the bad ear, sensorineural goes away from it. An unequal Weber is not a diagnosis - Rinne is the next step. Read the full page →
NUR 258 M1 Sensory 👁 Eyes & ears 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Which type of hearing loss - it compares air conduction with bone conduction.

Strike a tuning fork and hold the base on the mastoid bone behind the ear (bone conduction). When she says the sound has gone, move the tines beside the ear canal (air conduction). Ask whether she can hear it again, and for how long.
Normal is AC > BC , about twice as long - a positive Rinne. BC > AC is a negative Rinne and means conductive loss.
Sensorineural loss is also a positive Rinne, because both routes drop together and air is still the better one. So positive does not mean normal. Read the full page →
NUR 125 Head-to-toe 👁 Eyes & ears 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Gross hearing, one ear at a time, with no equipment.
Stand about 2 feet behind her so she cannot lip-read. Occlude the ear you are not testing. Whisper a set of letters and numbers after a full exhalation and ask her to repeat them.
She repeats fewer than half correctly in that ear.
Standing behind her is the whole point - in front, she reads your lips and passes a test she should fail. Read the full page →
NUR 125 Head-to-toe 👁 Eyes & ears 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Distance visual acuity.
Stand her 20 feet from the chart. Test each eye separately, then both, with her glasses on if she wears them. Record the smallest line she reads more than half of.
20/200 means she must be at 20 feet to read what a person with normal sight reads at 200 feet - the bigger the bottom number, the worse the vision.
Corrected 20/200 or worse in the better eye is the usual threshold for legal blindness . Read the full page →
NUR 258 M1 Sensory 👁 Eyes & ears 🔍 Enlarge illustration
The macula - central vision.
Hold the grid at normal reading distance, wearing reading glasses. Cover one eye and stare at the central dot . Ask what the surrounding lines look like. Repeat for the other eye.
Lines look wavy, bent or broken , or there is a blank patch in the middle.
This is the one clients do at home , and it is how wet macular degeneration gets caught early enough for anti-VEGF injections to matter. Read the full page →
NUR 258 M1 Sensory 👁 Eyes & ears 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Intraocular pressure - screening for glaucoma.
Anesthetic drop first for applanation; the puff-of-air version needs none. She sits still and looks straight ahead while the instrument touches or puffs the cornea.
Dr. Halecka gives normal as 12-20 mmHg with anything over 22 suspicious. (The textbook says 10-21 - use hers on the exam.)
Hold the timolol the morning of the test , or you measure a pressure that has already been treated. Read the full page →
NUR 125 Head-to-toe 👁 Eyes & ears 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Peripheral vision - gross visual field loss.

Sit about 2 feet away, at eye level. She covers one eye; you cover your opposite one. Bring a wiggling finger in from the periphery and ask her to say when she sees it, comparing her field with yours.
She sees the finger noticeably later than you do in one quadrant.
Peripheral loss is the pattern in open-angle glaucoma , and she will not have noticed it herself - that is why it gets screened for. Read the full page →
NUR 235 NUR 258 · M1 Sensory Assessment 👁 Eyes & ears
Anything blocking light from reaching the retina - congenital cataract in a baby, retinoblastoma in a young child, cataract in an adult.
Darken the room. Hold the ophthalmoscope at about arm’s length and look through it at both pupils . Compare the color and brightness of the glow in the two eyes.
A white pupil (leukocoria), an absent or dark reflex, or two eyes that do not match.

A white pupil in a young child is retinoblastoma until proven otherwise - parents often notice it first in a flash photograph, where one eye glows red and the other white. Never reassure; refer urgently. A dulled red reflex in an adult points to cataract. Read the full page →
NUR 125 NUR 198 · M2 Acid-Base / ABG Procedures 🫀 Heart & vessels 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Whether the ulnar artery alone can supply the hand - done before a radial ABG or arterial line.
Ask her to make a fist. Press on both the radial and ulnar arteries until the hand blanches. Have her open the hand - it should look pale. Release the ulnar side only and keep timing.
Color returns within about 5-7 seconds - that is a positive (pass) and the radial stick is safe. Color that stays pale beyond ~7-15 seconds means do not use that wrist.
The wording trips people up: the result you want is the one that lets you proceed. If collateral flow fails, the hand is living on the radial artery alone and puncturing it risks the whole hand.
NUR 258 NUR 198 · M7-8 Cardiovascular M13 Vascular 🫀 Heart & vessels 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Historically used to suggest a DVT.
Straighten the leg and dorsiflex the foot . Ask about calf pain.
Calf pain on dorsiflexion.

It is unreliable and is no longer recommended. It misses about half of real clots and is positive in plenty of people without one - and the maneuver itself is a theoretical embolization risk. Know it because it appears as a distractor ; the answer is a venous duplex ultrasound . Read the full page →
NUR 125 NUR 198 · M7-8 Cardiovascular Vital signs 🫀 Heart & vessels 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Peripheral perfusion.
Hold the hand at about heart level. Press the nail bed until it blanches, then release. Count.
Normal is under 3 seconds . Longer suggests poor perfusion, dehydration or shock.
Cold hands, dark nail polish and a cold room all slow it, so read it alongside the rest of the picture rather than on its own. Read the full page →
NUR 125 NUR 198 · M2 Fluid & Electrolytes Vital signs 🫀 Heart & vessels 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Volume status and fall risk - whether her pressure holds when she stands.
Measure BP and pulse lying , after she has been flat a few minutes. Sit her up, wait 1-3 minutes , measure again. Stand her, wait 1-3 minutes, measure again. Stay with her.
A fall of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic , or a rise in pulse of 20 , with symptoms.
The waiting is the test. Taking the standing pressure immediately misses the drop, and the client who says "I feel dizzy" mid-test needs sitting down, not finishing. Read the full page →
NUR 258 NUR 198 · M7-8 Cardiovascular M13 Cardiac 🫀 Heart & vessels 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Right-sided filling pressure - fluid overload, right heart failure, tamponade.
Position the head of the bed at 30-45 degrees . Turn her head slightly away. Use tangential lighting and look at the internal jugular pulsation in the neck.
Visible distension more than about 3-4 cm above the sternal angle at 45 degrees.

The angle is the test. Flat, everyone has distended neck veins; sitting fully upright, almost nobody does. JVD + muffled heart sounds + hypotension is Beck triad - cardiac tamponade. Read the full page →
NUR 258 NUR 198 · M7-8 Cardiovascular M13 Cardiac 🫀 Heart & vessels 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Cardiac tamponade, and severe asthma or COPD.
Inflate the cuff above systolic and deflate slowly. Note the pressure where Korotkoff sounds are heard only on expiration . Keep deflating to where they are heard through the whole cycle. Subtract.
A drop of more than 10 mmHg in systolic pressure on inspiration.
The name is misleading - it is an exaggeration of something normal, not a reversal. Read the full page →
NUR 258 NUR 198 · M7-8 Cardiovascular M13 Vascular 🫀 Heart & vessels 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Arterial supply to the leg - peripheral arterial disease.
Take the highest ankle systolic pressure with a Doppler. Take the highest brachial systolic pressure. Divide ankle by brachial.
Normal 1.0-1.4 . Under 0.9 is arterial disease; under 0.4 is severe and limb-threatening.
A falsely high value (over 1.4) happens with calcified, non-compressible vessels in long-standing diabetes - a high number there is not reassurance. Read the full page →
NUR 125 NUR 198 · M7-8 Cardiovascular Vital signs 🫀 Heart & vessels
The strength of the arterial pulse - perfusion to a limb, and volume status.

Use the pads of two or three fingers, never your thumb. Feel the same pulse on both sides at once and compare - except the carotids, one at a time. Grade it: 0 absent, 1+ weak or thready, 2+ normal, 3+ full, 4+ bounding. If you cannot feel it, find it with a Doppler and mark the spot.
A new difference between the two sides , a weak thready pulse, or a pulse you could feel before and cannot now.

Do not chart absent until a Doppler has failed to find it - chart it as Doppler-only if that is all you have. Some facilities and pages use a 0 to 3+ scale where 3+ is bounding, so check which one your charting uses. Read the full page →
NUR 125 NUR 198 · M2 Fluid & Electrolytes Head-to-toe 🫀 Heart & vessels
Fluid in the tissues - fluid overload, heart failure, kidney or liver disease.

Press a fingertip firmly over a bony area - shin, ankle, top of the foot - for a few seconds. Let go and watch how deep the dent is and how long it takes to fill. In anyone in bed, check the sacrum too.
1+ about 2 mm, rebounds at once. 2+ 3-4 mm, about 15 seconds. 3+ 5-6 mm, about 30 seconds. 4+ 8 mm or more, 1-2 minutes.

Edema goes where gravity takes it - the ankles when she is up, the sacrum when she is in bed, so a clear ankle does not mean a dry patient. Daily weight is the better fluid measure: 1 kg is about 1 L. Read the full page →

entries.h: 🫀 Heart sound auscultation All People Enjoy Time Magazine
entries.t: NUR 125 NUR 198 · M7-8 Cardiovascular Head-to-toe 🫀 Heart & vessels
Rate, rhythm, the two normal heart sounds, and anything added - extra sounds, murmurs, or sounds gone quiet.

Listen on bare skin, with the diaphragm first and then the bell. A ortic - 2nd intercostal space, right sternal border. P ulmonic - 2nd intercostal space, left sternal border. E rb’s point - 3rd intercostal space, left sternal border. T ricuspid - 4th intercostal space, left sternal border. M itral (apical) - 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line.
A murmur , an extra sound (S3 or S4), an irregular rhythm, or heart sounds that have become muffled .

S1 is loudest at the apex , S2 at the base . An S3 is normal in children but means heart failure in an older adult. S1–S4 mnemonics (“Ken-TUC-ky”, “TEN-nes-see”) → The mitral point is where you count the apical pulse for a full minute before digoxin. Read the full page →
NUR 258 NUR 198 · M7-8 Cardiovascular M13 Cardiac 🫀 Heart & vessels
Cardiac tamponade - fluid or blood in the pericardial sac squeezing the heart so it cannot fill.
Take her blood pressure. Look at the neck veins with the head of the bed at about 45 degrees. Listen to the heart sounds. Check for pulsus paradoxus while the cuff is on.
All three: hypotension , distended neck veins (JVD), and muffled, distant heart sounds .

Think of it after chest trauma , cardiac surgery or pericarditis. After heart surgery, chest tube drainage that suddenly stops can mean the blood is collecting around the heart instead. This is an emergency - the fix is pericardiocentesis, not fluids and waiting. Read the full page →
NUR 258 M13 Shock 🫀 Heart & vessels
Whether a patient with an infection is at high risk of a bad outcome - a bedside screen that needs no lab.
One point for a respiratory rate of 22 or more . One point for altered mentation - anything new, even mild confusion. One point for a systolic pressure of 100 or less .
2 or more out of 3 is a positive screen - escalate, and expect lactate, blood cultures and antibiotics.

It flags risk; it does not diagnose sepsis, and a low score does not rule it out . In an older adult new confusion may be the only sign, often with no fever at all. Cultures go before the first antibiotic, but never hold the antibiotic for them. Read the full page →
NUR 125 NUR 198 · M5 Respiratory Head-to-toe 🫁 Lungs 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Whether the lung underneath is solid, normal, or full of air or fluid.
Place the ulnar edge or ball of your hands on her back. Ask her to say "ninety-nine" each time you move. Compare side to side, top to bottom, in a ladder.
Increased over consolidation such as pneumonia; decreased over pleural effusion, pneumothorax or emphysema.
Always compare left with right at the same level. Absolute vibration varies hugely between people; the asymmetry is the finding. Read the full page →

entries.h: 🫁 Egophony, bronchophony, whispered pectoriloquy The voice sounds
entries.t: NUR 125 NUR 198 · M5 Respiratory Head-to-toe 🫁 Lungs 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Consolidation - solid lung transmits voice better than air-filled lung.
Egophony: she says "eeee" while you listen. Bronchophony: she says "ninety-nine" while you listen. Whispered pectoriloquy: she whispers "one-two-three" while you listen.
Egophony: the "eeee" sounds like "ayyy" . The other two: the words become unusually loud and clear instead of muffled.
All three say the same thing - consolidation . Egophony is the memorable one: E turns to A . Read the full page →
NUR 258 NUR 198 · M5 Respiratory Respiratory 🫁 Lungs 🔍 Enlarge illustration
How obstructed her airways are right now - asthma monitoring at home.
Stand or sit upright, pointer at zero. Deep breath in, tight seal on the mouthpiece. Blow out as hard and fast as possible. Do it three times and record the best , not the average.
Compared with her own personal best : green 80-100%, yellow 50-79%, red under 50%.
Her personal best, not a chart, is the reference. Red zone means rescue inhaler and get help - it is not a "watch and see". Read the full page →
NUR 125 NUR 198 · M5 Respiratory Head-to-toe 🫁 Lungs
Air moving through the lungs, and anything in the way - fluid, narrowing, secretions or inflamed pleura.

Sit her upright and listen on bare skin with the diaphragm. Ask her to breathe slowly and deeply through an open mouth . Zig-zag down the chest, comparing side to side at each level, one full breath per spot. Listen front, back and sides - the lower lobes are mostly heard from the back and the sides.

Crackles - popping, fluid in the alveoli. Wheezes - musical, narrowed airways. Rhonchi - low and snoring, secretions that may clear with a cough. Friction rub - grating, does not clear with coughing. Stridor - high-pitched crowing on inspiration, an upper airway emergency.
A silent chest in someone having an asthma attack is not improvement - it means almost no air is moving. Stridor is the one you act on before you finish the assessment. Read the full page →
NUR 125 NUR 198 · M2 Acid-Base / ABG Vital signs 🫁 Lungs
The rhythm and depth of breathing as well as the rate - acidosis, brain injury, and the end of life.
Count for a full minute without telling her you are counting. Watch the depth and the rhythm , not just the number. Note any pauses and time them.

Kussmaul - deep, rapid and regular: metabolic acidosis such as DKA. Cheyne-Stokes - breaths that build up, fade, then stop for a while: heart failure, brain injury, the end of life. Biot - irregular clusters with pauses: brainstem injury.

Kussmaul breathing is compensation - the lungs blowing off CO2 to correct the acid - so you treat the cause, not the breathing. Cheyne-Stokes at the end of life is expected; explain it to the family before they see it. Read the full page →
NUR 258 NUR 198 · M11-12 GI M-GI 🍽 Abdomen & GI 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Peritoneal irritation - peritonitis, a ruptured appendix.
Press slowly and deeply over the area. Release quickly. Ask when it hurt more.
Pain is worse on release than on pressure.

Do it last in the abdominal exam - it hurts, and it guards the rest of the assessment. Order for the abdomen is inspect, auscultate, percuss, palpate : listening comes before touching, because touching changes the bowel sounds. Read the full page →
NUR 258 NUR 198 · M11-12 GI M-GI 🍽 Abdomen & GI 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Appendicitis.
Find the point one third of the way from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus . Palpate gently there.
Sharp localized tenderness at that point, often after pain that started around the umbilicus and migrated .
Sudden relief of the pain is not good news - it can mean the appendix has ruptured, and peritonitis follows. No heat, no enemas, no laxatives. Read the full page →
NUR 258 NUR 198 · M11-12 GI M-GI 🍽 Abdomen & GI 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Appendicitis, when the picture is not obvious.
Rovsing: press on the left lower quadrant. Psoas: she lies on her left side; you extend her right hip. Obturator: flex her right hip and knee, then internally rotate the hip.
Rovsing: pain felt in the right lower quadrant. Psoas and obturator: right lower quadrant pain on the movement.
Rovsing is the counter-intuitive one - you press on the opposite side and it hurts where the appendix is. Read the full page →
NUR 258 NUR 198 · M10 Hepatobiliary M-GI 🍽 Abdomen & GI 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Acute cholecystitis.
Press under the right costal margin at the mid-clavicular line. Ask her to take a deep breath in .
She stops the breath partway because it hurts - an inspiratory arrest.
Do not confuse it with Murphy’s punch (CVA tenderness), which is the kidney. Same name, different organ, different place. Read the full page →
NUR 258 NUR 198 · M10 Hepatobiliary M-GI 🍽 Abdomen & GI 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Retroperitoneal bleeding - most often severe hemorrhagic pancreatitis.
Inspect the abdomen with good light. Look around the umbilicus and at both flanks .
Cullen: bruising around the umbilicus. Grey Turner: bruising along the flanks.
These are late and ominous . They are inspection findings - you get them by looking, which is why inspection comes first. Read the full page →
NUR 258 NUR 198 · M10 Hepatobiliary M-GI 🍽 Abdomen & GI 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Ascites - free fluid in the abdomen.

Fluid wave: she (or a second person) presses the ulnar edge of a hand down the midline; you tap one flank and feel the other. Shifting dullness: percuss from resonant to dull with her supine, mark it, roll her to one side and percuss again.
Fluid wave: a distinct impulse reaches your other hand. Shifting dullness: the dull border moves when she rolls.
The midline hand stops the impulse travelling through fat rather than fluid - without it the test fools you. Ascites belongs with cirrhosis : low albumin, high portal pressure. Read the full page →
NUR 125 NUR 198 · M11-12 GI Head-to-toe 🍽 Abdomen & GI
Whether the gut is moving - ileus after surgery, obstruction, and when it is safe to feed.

Inspect, then auscultate before you touch - the abdomen is the one exam where listening comes before palpating. Turn off NG suction while you listen. Rest the diaphragm lightly in all four quadrants . If you hear nothing, keep listening for a full 5 minutes before you call them absent.
Chart them as active, hypoactive, hyperactive or absent . Absent after surgery suggests a paralytic ileus; high-pitched, tinkling sounds can mean an obstruction.

Pressing or percussing first sets the bowel off and gives a false reading. Never chart just "present". Absent sounds, a distended belly and no flatus after surgery is a report , not a recheck later. Read the full page →

entries.h: 🚰 CVA tenderness Murphy's punch / kidney punch
entries.t: NUR 258 NUR 198 · M9 Renal Renal 🚰 Kidney & urinary 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Kidney inflammation - pyelonephritis or a stone.
She sits up. Place one palm flat over the costovertebral angle - where the twelfth rib meets the spine. Strike the back of that hand once with the ulnar side of your fist.
Sharp pain over the kidney, rather than the thud she should feel.
One firm tap, not repeated blows. Flank pain + fever + a positive urine culture is pyelonephritis , not a simple UTI. Read the full page →
NUR 125 NUR 198 · M9 Renal Procedures 🚰 Kidney & urinary 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Whether she is emptying her bladder - retention, and BPH.
Ask her to void normally, and measure it if you can. Within about 10 minutes , scan the bladder (or catheterize if ordered).
More than about 100 mL left behind suggests incomplete emptying; large volumes mean retention.
Do it straight after she voids - wait too long and the kidneys have refilled the bladder, and you measure new urine as if it were residual. Read the full page →
NUR 258 NUR 198 · M13 Musculoskeletal Musculoskeletal 🦴 Bones, joints & nerves 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Carpal tunnel syndrome - median nerve compression.
Have her press the backs of both hands together with the wrists fully flexed, fingers pointing down. Hold for 60 seconds .
Numbness or tingling in the thumb, index, middle and half the ring finger - the median nerve distribution.
The little finger is not median territory. Numbness there points somewhere else, usually the ulnar nerve. Read the full page →
NUR 258 NUR 198 · M13 Musculoskeletal Musculoskeletal 🦴 Bones, joints & nerves 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Carpal tunnel syndrome - the same nerve, a different provocation.
Tap lightly over the median nerve on the palmar side of the wrist, at the carpal tunnel.
Tingling or an electric shock shooting into the median-nerve fingers.
Phalen bends it, Tinel taps it. Both point at the same nerve, and neither is a diagnosis on its own - nerve conduction studies settle it. Read the full page →
NUR 258 NUR 198 · M13 Musculoskeletal Musculoskeletal 🦴 Bones, joints & nerves 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Sciatic nerve root irritation - a herniated lumbar disc.
She lies flat. Keep the knee straight and slowly raise the leg by the heel.
Radiating pain down the back of the leg below the knee between about 30 and 70 degrees .
Back pain alone is not a positive. It has to radiate down the leg , which is what separates a nerve root from a muscle strain. Read the full page →
NUR 258 NUR 198 · M13 Musculoskeletal Musculoskeletal 🦴 Bones, joints & nerves 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Compartment syndrome in a limb - after a fracture, a cast, or a crush injury.

Check the limb distal to the injury for each in turn: Pain out of proportion, and pain on passive stretch Pressure - the compartment feels tight and full Paraesthesia , then Pallor , then Paralysis , and last Pulselessness
Pain out of proportion to the injury, and pain when you passively stretch the muscles, are the earliest findings.

Do not wait for a lost pulse. Pulselessness is last and by then the muscle is dying. Elevate no higher than the heart and never ice it - both reduce perfusion further. A cast gets bivalved. Read the full page →
NUR 235 Musculoskeletal 🦴 Bones, joints & nerves 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Hip abductor weakness, and developmental dysplasia of the hip in an older child.
Ask her to stand on one leg. Watch the opposite side of the pelvis.
The pelvis drops on the side of the lifted leg - the standing hip cannot hold it level.
Watch the hip that is off the ground, not the one bearing weight. It is the standing side that is weak. Read the full page →

entries.h: 🦴 Gower's sign Climbing up the legs
entries.t: NUR 235 Musculoskeletal 🦴 Bones, joints & nerves
Weakness of the muscles around the hips and thighs - Duchenne muscular dystrophy in a young boy.
Sit the child on the floor. Ask him to stand up without using furniture or a hand . Watch how he gets there.
He rolls onto all fours , pushes up, puts his hands on his knees and walks them up his thighs to stand - climbing up his own legs.

Classic in boys aged about 3 to 5 , often with big, firm calves (pseudohypertrophy). It shows proximal weakness rather than proving Duchenne, which is confirmed by tests. As the disease progresses, breathing and the heart are what you watch. Read the full page →

entries.h: 🦴 Adam's forward bend test Scoliosis screen
entries.t: NUR 235 Musculoskeletal 🦴 Bones, joints & nerves
Scoliosis - a sideways curve of the spine with rotation, screened in early adolescence at the growth spurt.

Have her stand with her back exposed - in underwear or a gown open at the back - feet together and knees straight. Look from behind first: are the shoulders, shoulder blades and hips level? Ask her to bend forward at the waist with arms hanging down. Look along the back from behind for any asymmetry.
A rib hump - one side of the rib cage rides higher than the other as she bends - and uneven shoulders, scapulae or hips.

The screen does not diagnose - an X-ray and the Cobb angle do. Idiopathic scoliosis is usually painless , so real back pain needs a look for another cause. Bracing works only while she is still growing, which is exactly when body image makes wearing it hardest. Read the full page →

entries.h: 🦴 Morse Fall Scale Fall risk score
entries.t: NUR 125 Safety & mobility 🦴 Bones, joints & nerves
Her risk of falling in hospital, so prevention starts before the fall rather than after.

Score six items: a fall history , a secondary diagnosis , an ambulatory aid , an IV or saline lock , gait , and mental status . Mental status asks whether she knows her own limits, not whether she is oriented. Score on admission, after any fall, after a change in her condition, and on transfer.
Totals run from 0 to 125 ; higher means higher risk. 45 or more is a common high-risk cutoff, but your facility sets its own.

Learn what the items are, not one cutoff - they vary by hospital. The score only matters if it changes care: gait belt, bed in the lowest position with brakes on, call light in reach, non-skid socks, and toileting on a schedule. Read the full page →
NUR 234 Antepartum 🤰 Maternity 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Fetal lie, presentation, position and engagement by feel, before you place the monitor.

Have her empty her bladder and lie supine with knees slightly bent, a wedge under the right hip. 1. Fundal grip - what is in the top? Buttocks are soft and irregular; the head is hard and round. 2. Umbilical grip - which side is the smooth firm back, which is the knobbly small parts? 3. Pawlik grip - grasp just above the symphysis: what is presenting, and does it move? 4. Pelvic grip - fingers down towards the pelvis: is it engaged?
You end up able to say where the fetal back is - and that is where the fetal heart is best heard.
Bladder empty first, and do not leave her flat for long - supine hypotension. Maneuver 4 is the only one where you face her feet . Read the full page →
NUR 234 Intrapartum 🤰 Maternity 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Whether the membranes have actually ruptured.
Nitrazine: touch the paper to the fluid in the vagina. Fern: smear fluid on a slide, let it air-dry, look under the microscope.
Nitrazine turns blue (pH 6.5-7.5) - amniotic fluid is alkaline, urine is acidic. Fern shows a fern-leaf crystal pattern .

Blood, semen and bacterial vaginosis all raise the pH and give a false positive nitrazine. Ferning is the more specific of the two. Once membranes rupture, the first things to check are the fetal heart rate and the color of the fluid - and the risk is cord prolapse. Read the full page →
NUR 234 Antepartum 🤰 Maternity 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Fetal growth and dating between about 18 and 36 weeks.
Empty bladder, lie supine. Measure in centimeters from the top of the symphysis pubis over the curve of the abdomen to the top of the fundus .
From about 18-36 weeks the measurement in centimeters roughly equals the weeks of gestation , give or take 2.

A fundal height well ahead suggests multiples, polyhydramnios or a big baby; well behind suggests growth restriction or oligohydramnios. Postpartum the fundus should be firm, midline, and descend about a fingerbreadth a day - boggy means massage . Read the full page →
NUR 234 Antepartum 🤰 Maternity 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Fetal wellbeing - does the heart rate accelerate when the baby moves?
Semi-Fowler with a left tilt; external monitors on. Record for 20-40 minutes .
Reactive (the result you want): 2 or more accelerations of 15 bpm above baseline lasting 15 seconds, in 20 minutes. Non-reactive means further testing.

The vocabulary is backwards from most tests: reactive is good, non-reactive is the worry . A sleeping fetus is the commonest reason for non-reactive, so the test gets extended or the baby stimulated. Read the full page →

entries.h: 🤰 Hegar's, Goodell's and Chadwick's signs Probable signs of pregnancy
entries.t: NUR 234 Antepartum 🤰 Maternity
The changes an examiner can find in early pregnancy, from about 6 to 8 weeks.
Hegar - on bimanual exam, the lower uterine segment feels soft. Goodell - the cervix feels soft. Chadwick - on speculum exam, the cervix, vagina and vulva look bluish-purple .
All three are probable signs - things the examiner finds. None of them confirms a pregnancy on its own.

Hegar is the lower uterine segment , Goodell is the cervix , Chadwick is the color . Presumptive is what she feels, probable is what you find, positive is the fetus itself - heart tones, an ultrasound image, or movement the examiner feels. A positive pregnancy test is only probable . Read the full page →

entries.h: 🤰 Bishop score Cervical readiness for induction
entries.t: NUR 234 Intrapartum 🤰 Maternity
Whether the cervix is ripe enough for an induction to be likely to succeed.

Score five findings from the vaginal exam: dilation , effacement , station , cervical consistency and cervical position . Dilation, effacement and station score 0 to 3; consistency and position score 0 to 2. Add them for a total out of 13 .
8 or more is a favorable cervix - induction is likely to succeed. A low score means the cervix is ripened first.

Inducing an unripe cervix usually fails and ends in cesarean, which is why ripening with a prostaglandin or a balloon comes first. Oxytocin waits at least 4 hours after misoprostol, and the dinoprostone insert comes out before it starts. Read the full page →
NUR 234 Postpartum 🤰 Maternity
The whole postpartum check, in an order that does not miss anything.

B reasts - soft, filling or engorged? Nipples intact? U terus - firm and midline, about 1 cm lower each day. B ladder - emptying fully? First void within 6-8 hours. B owels - bowel sounds, flatus, first bowel movement. L ochia - amount, color, clots, odor. E pisiotomy or perineum - REEDA. H omans, now the legs - one-sided calf pain, warmth or swelling. E motional - mood, bonding, support.
A boggy or displaced uterus, heavy bleeding, a fever after the first 24 hours, one swollen painful calf, or a mood that is getting worse rather than better.

The H no longer means doing Homans sign - it is unreliable and is no longer recommended. Look for one-sided pain, warmth, swelling and redness instead. A uterus pushed up and to the right is a full bladder. Read the full page →

entries.h: 🤰 Postpartum fundus and lochia check Fundal massage
entries.t: NUR 234 Postpartum 🤰 Maternity
Whether the uterus is contracting hard enough to clamp the bleeding vessels - postpartum hemorrhage.

Have her empty her bladder if she can, then lie flat with knees bent. Put one hand just above the pubic bone to support the lower uterus. With the other, feel for the top of the fundus and note its firmness , position , and how many fingerbreadths it is above or below the umbilicus. Check the pad and underneath her : scant is a stain under 2.5 cm, light under 10 cm, moderate under 15 cm, heavy is a pad saturated in an hour.
A boggy fundus: massage it until it firms and have her empty her bladder. Call for help early - uterotonics per order and notifying the provider go alongside, not after everything else.

Always support the lower segment while you massage, or you risk inverting the uterus. A firm fundus that is still bleeding is not atony - assess for trauma (a laceration or hematoma), retained tissue or a clotting problem, and massage will not fix it. Blood pools under her buttocks while the pad looks clean. Read the full page →
NUR 234 Postpartum 🤰 Maternity
How an episiotomy, a perineal tear or a cesarean incision is healing - and early infection.

For the perineum, help her into a side-lying position, lift the upper buttock and use a good light. R edness, E dema, E cchymosis, D ischarge, A pproximation - are the edges together? Score each 0 to 3 for a total of 0 to 15 if your unit uses the numbers.
Spreading redness, discharge or pus, or edges coming apart. Mild edema with no discharge is expected.

Severe perineal pain with a firm fundus and little visible bleeding is a hematoma , not ordinary soreness - look for a bulging bluish mass and report it. Fever after the first 24 hours points to infection. Read the full page →
NUR 234 Newborn 🧸 Newborn & child 🔍 Enlarge illustration
How the newborn is adapting, at 1 and 5 minutes .
Score 0, 1 or 2 for each of five: Appearance (color), Pulse , Grimace (reflex irritability), Activity (tone), Respiration . Add them - the range is 0 to 10 .
7-10 reassuring; 4-6 moderately abnormal; 0-3 low. It describes her status and her response to what has been done.

Apgar does not decide whether to resuscitate - you do not wait a minute to start. Breathing, tone and heart rate decide it: apneic, gasping or a heart rate under 100 means positive-pressure ventilation, whatever the score. Acrocyanosis (blue hands and feet) is normal and still costs a color point. Read the full page →
NUR 235 Newborn 🧸 Newborn & child 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Developmental dysplasia of the hip in a newborn.

Baby relaxed and supine, hips and knees flexed. Ortolani: abduct the hips and lift the femur forward - you are trying to relocate a dislocated hip. Barlow: adduct and press gently back - you are trying to dislocate a loose one.
A palpable clunk in either direction. Also look for asymmetric thigh skin folds and unequal knee height (Galeazzi).
Ortolani puts it in , Barlow pushes it out . Do it gently and only by someone trained - repeated forceful testing damages the joint. Treatment is a Pavlik harness . Read the full page →

entries.h: 🧸 Newborn reflexes Moro, rooting, grasp, tonic neck, stepping, Babinski
entries.t: NUR 235 Newborn 🧸 Newborn & child 🔍 Enlarge illustration
An intact newborn nervous system - and their disappearance on schedule is just as important.

Moro: a sudden controlled drop of the head - arms abduct then embrace. Gone by 4-6 months . Rooting: stroke the cheek - head turns towards it. Gone by 3-4 months . Palmar grasp: press the palm - fingers curl. Gone by 3-4 months . Tonic neck (fencing): turn the head - same-side arm extends. Gone by 3-4 months . Stepping: hold upright with feet touching - stepping motion. Gone by 4 weeks .
Present when they should be, and gone when they should be.

A reflex that persists past its age is as abnormal as one that never appeared - it suggests a neurological problem. An asymmetric Moro points to a fractured clavicle or brachial plexus injury. Read the full page →
NUR 234 Newborn 🧸 Newborn & child 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Gestational age from physical and neuromuscular maturity, when dates are uncertain.

Score six neuromuscular items (posture, square window, arm recoil, popliteal angle, scarf sign, heel to ear). Score six physical items (skin, lanugo, plantar surface, breast, eye/ear, genitals). Add and read the age off the maturity chart.
A gestational age in weeks, which is then plotted against weight to classify the baby SGA, AGA or LGA.
Do it within the first 12 hours or so - the neuromuscular findings change as the baby recovers from birth. Read the full page →
NUR 235 Assessment 🧸 Newborn & child 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Age-appropriate baselines - the numbers move a long way between a newborn and a teenager.

Count respirations first , while the child is quiet, for a full minute . Then apical pulse for a full minute in a child under 2. Do the blood pressure and temperature last - they are the most upsetting. Use a cuff covering about two thirds of the upper arm .
Compared against the range for that age , not the adult range.
Least invasive first, most invasive last, and keep the child on the parent’s lap where you can. A crying child’s respiratory rate and heart rate are not usable. Read the full page →
NUR 235 Assessment 🧸 Newborn & child
Pain in a child who cannot tell you - infants, toddlers, and any child who is nonverbal or cognitively impaired.
Watch the child for a few minutes, longer if asleep. Score five behaviors 0 to 2 each: F ace, L egs, A ctivity, C ry, C onsolability. Add them for a total from 0 to 10 .
0 relaxed and comfortable, 1-3 mild discomfort, 4-6 moderate pain, 7-10 severe pain.

The choice between FLACC and FACES is decided by whether the child can self-report , not by how much pain you think there is. Your course gives FLACC as the scale for under 3s. Behavior and physiology count as evidence - children under-report to avoid injections. Read the full page →

entries.h: 🧸 Wong-Baker FACES scale Self-report for young children
entries.t: NUR 235 NUR 125 · Pain Assessment 🧸 Newborn & child
How much it hurts, reported by the child - usually from about 3 years old.

Point to each face and use the words: no hurt , hurts a little bit, a little more, even more, a whole lot, hurts worst . Ask the child to point to the face that shows how much they hurt. Record the number under that face - 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 or 10 .
The face the child picks is the score. Treat and reassess as you would a numeric score.

The child picks the face - you do not match a face to the child’s expression. The faces show how much it hurts, not how happy or sad they feel. It also works for adults who struggle with numbers. Read the full page →

entries.h: 🧸 NIPS and CRIES Newborn pain scales
entries.t: NUR 235 Assessment 🧸 Newborn & child
Pain in a newborn, scored by what you observe.

NIPS (Neonatal Infant Pain Scale): facial expression, cry, breathing pattern, arms, legs and state of arousal. Cry scores 0 to 2, the rest 0 or 1, for a total of 0 to 7 . CRIES , for pain after surgery: C rying, R equires oxygen, I ncreased vital signs, E xpression, S leeplessness. Each 0 to 2, for a total of 0 to 10 . Score before and after anything painful, and after treating it.
NIPS above 3 suggests pain. CRIES above 4 suggests pain that needs treating.

A very premature or very sick baby may not have the energy to show pain, so a low score is not proof of comfort . Comfort measures count: swaddling, skin-to-skin, non-nutritive sucking and oral sucrose for procedures. Read the full page →
NUR 125 NUR 198 · M2 Fluid & Electrolytes Head-to-toe 🩹 Skin & wounds 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Hydration - though it is a rough guide, not proof.
Pinch a fold of skin over the sternum or forehead in an adult, or the abdomen in a child. Release and watch it.
Skin that stays tented instead of falling straight back.

Use the sternum , not the back of the hand - the hand loses elasticity with age and gives a false positive in every older adult. Read it with mucous membranes, urine output and weight. Read the full page →
NUR 125 NUR 198 · M3 Periop & Integument Pressure injury 🩹 Skin & wounds 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Risk of developing a pressure injury.
Score six areas: sensory perception, moisture, activity, mobility, nutrition, and friction/shear . Five of them score 1-4; friction/shear scores 1-3.
Total 6 to 23 . Lower is worse - 18 or under is generally the point at which prevention starts.

The scale that runs the opposite way to most: a low Braden is the client at risk. It is a prompt to act - turning schedule, surface, moisture, nutrition - not just a number to chart. Read the full page →

entries.h: 🩹 Rule of Nines Lund-Browder for children
entries.t: NUR 258 NUR 198 · M3 Periop & Integument M4 Burns 🩹 Skin & wounds 🔍 Enlarge illustration
How much body surface is burned - which drives the fluid resuscitation.

Count only partial and full thickness burns, never superficial ones. Adult: head 9, each arm 9, each leg 18, front torso 18, back torso 18, perineum 1. Use the client’s palm ≈ 1% for scattered patches.
A percentage that feeds the Parkland formula : 4 mL x kg x %TBSA, half in the first 8 hours from the time of the burn , the rest over 16.
The clock starts at the injury , not at arrival. A child’s head is proportionally much bigger, which is why children get the Lund-Browder chart instead. Read the full page →

entries.h: 🩹 Blanch test Press on redness or a rash
entries.t: NUR 125 NUR 258 · M8 Neuro infection Pressure injury 🩹 Skin & wounds
Whether redness is just pressure that will fade, or damage already done - and whether a rash is bleeding into the skin.
Press a fingertip, or the side of a clear glass , on the red area for a few seconds. Release and watch whether the color comes back. Compare with the surrounding skin and with the other side.

Redness that stays red when pressed over a bony area is a Stage 1 pressure injury . A rash that does not fade under the glass is petechial or purpuric bleeding - with a fever, think meningococcal disease.

A non-blanching rash with fever is a medical emergency ; escalate immediately. Blanching is hard to see on darker skin, so also feel for warmth, coolness, firmness or bogginess and ask about pain. Take the pressure off a reddened area now - stage 1 is reversible. Read the full page →
NUR 125 NUR 175 · Cognitive assessment Mental status 🗣 Mental health 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Cognitive screening - a possible dementia, and a baseline to compare against later.
Mini-Cog: name 3 words , draw a clock showing a set time, then recall the 3 words. MMSE: 30 questions covering orientation, registration, attention, recall, language and copying.
Mini-Cog: failing recall with an abnormal clock suggests impairment. MMSE: out of 30 , with lower scores suggesting more impairment.

These screen - they do not diagnose. And they are confounded by delirium, depression, deafness, pain and language , all of which need excluding first. Delirium is acute and fluctuates; dementia is gradual and progressive. Read the full page →
NUR 125 NUR 175 · Substance use Mental status 🗣 Mental health 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Problem drinking, in four questions.
C - have you felt you should cut down ? A - have people annoyed you by criticizing your drinking? G - have you felt guilty about your drinking? E - have you had a morning drink, an eye-opener ?
Two or more yes answers is a positive screen.

Ask it matter-of-factly and without judgment, or you get a polite answer instead of a true one. A positive screen means asking when the last drink was - withdrawal peaks at 24-48 hours and delirium tremens is a medical emergency. Read the full page →
NUR 175 Psychopharmacology 🗣 Mental health 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Tardive dyskinesia - the involuntary movements that antipsychotics can cause, and that may be permanent.

Have her sit still, feet flat, hands unsupported on her knees, and watch before you ask anything. Ask her to open her mouth and look at the tongue at rest, then stick it out twice. Ask her to tap thumb to each finger, and watch the face and legs while she does it. Have her stand, walk a few paces, turn and come back - movements often show up on walking. Score each of seven body areas 0 to 4, plus the questions about her own awareness of them.
Any score of 2 or more in a single area, or 1 in two areas, is a positive screen worth reporting.

Do it at baseline and then regularly - the whole point is catching it early. Tardive dyskinesia can be permanent once established , unlike the acute reactions. Involuntary tongue and lip movements are usually the first thing to appear. Read the full page →
NUR 175 Substance use 🗣 Mental health 🔍 Enlarge illustration
How severe alcohol withdrawal is right now, and whether she needs medicating.

Score ten items: nausea, tremor, sweats, anxiety, agitation, tactile, auditory and visual disturbance, headache, and orientation. Each is 0 to 7 except orientation, which is 0 to 4. Reassess on a schedule - typically hourly while the score is high. Medicate by protocol against the score rather than on a fixed clock.
Under 8 is mild. 8-15 is moderate and usually needs medication. Over 15 is severe , with a real risk of seizures and delirium tremens.

Withdrawal peaks at 24-72 hours and delirium tremens is a medical emergency . Ask when the last drink was, not just whether she drinks. A rising score is more important than any single number. Read the full page →
NUR 175 Crisis & safety 🗣 Mental health 🔍 Enlarge illustration
Whether she is thinking about suicide, and how close she is to acting on it.

Ask directly : are you thinking about killing yourself? Asking does not plant the idea. If yes: do you have a plan ? Ask what it is. Do you have the means to carry it out, and access to them right now? Have you set a time ? Ask about past attempts - a previous attempt is the strongest single predictor. Ask what has stopped her so far, and who she would tell.
A specific plan, available means and a set time is the highest risk combination and needs immediate one-to-one observation and a provider now.

A sudden calm after a period of deep depression is a warning sign, not an improvement - she may have decided. Energy returning before mood lifts is the dangerous window. Never promise to keep it secret. Read the full page →
NUR 175 Assessment 🗣 Mental health 🔍 Enlarge illustration
A structured snapshot of how she is thinking, feeling and behaving at this moment.

Appearance and behavior - grooming, eye contact, psychomotor activity. Speech - rate, volume, whether it is pressured or slowed. Mood (what she tells you) and affect (what you observe) - note if they do not match. Thought process - logical, tangential, flight of ideas, loose associations. Thought content - delusions, obsessions, and always suicidal or homicidal ideation. Perception - hallucinations; ask what they are hearing and whether voices tell her to do anything. Cognition - orientation, memory, attention. Ins
Any command hallucination , delusion of persecution, or expressed intent to harm is reported immediately.
Mood is reported, affect is observed. That distinction is asked constantly. Describe what you actually saw and heard in her own words rather than summarizing it as 'appropriate'. Read the full page →

entries.h: 🗣 Confusion Assessment Method CAM - delirium screen
entries.t: NUR 125 NUR 175 · Cognitive assessment Mental status 🗣 Mental health
Delirium - an acute, fluctuating change in attention and thinking that is a medical problem until proven otherwise.

1 - acute onset and fluctuating course: is this a change from her baseline, and does it come and go? 2 - inattention: can she hold a thread, or is she easily distracted? 3 - disorganized thinking: rambling, illogical, jumping between ideas? 4 - altered level of consciousness: anything other than alert - drowsy, stuporous or hypervigilant.
1 and 2, plus either 3 or 4 .

Attention is compulsory - you cannot have delirium with normal attention. Ask the family: is this how she usually is? Delirium is acute and often reversible; dementia is gradual. Look for the cause - infection, drugs, dehydration, low oxygen. Read the full page →

entries.h: 🗣 PHQ-9 and GAD-7 Depression and anxiety screens
entries.t: NUR 175 Assessment 🗣 Mental health
How severe depression (PHQ-9) or anxiety (GAD-7) symptoms have been over the last two weeks .

She answers each item herself: not at all (0), several days (1), more than half the days (2), nearly every day (3). PHQ-9 has nine items, total 0 to 27 . GAD-7 has seven, total 0 to 21 . Read item 9 of the PHQ-9 yourself every time - thoughts of being better off dead or of self-harm.
PHQ-9: 5 mild, 10 moderate, 15 moderately severe, 20 severe. GAD-7: 5 mild, 10 moderate, 15 severe. 10 or more on either usually means further evaluation.

Any answer other than "not at all" on item 9 means you ask about suicide directly, today - whatever the total. A screen is not a diagnosis; a low score with a worrying presentation still gets followed up. Read the full page →
NUR 234 Postpartum 🗣 Mental health
Depression during pregnancy and after the birth.

She fills in ten questions herself, about how she has felt over the past seven days . Each item scores 0 to 3, for a total from 0 to 30 . Screen across pregnancy and postpartum - before discharge, and again at follow-up.
13 or higher means depression is likely. Many practices refer at a lower cutoff, around 9 to 10.

The last item asks about thoughts of self-harm - any positive answer is acted on now, whatever the total. Baby blues peak around days 3-5 and resolve by about two weeks; still low or unable to function beyond that is depression, not blues. Read the full page → Nothing matches that. Try a shorter word — calcium rather than low calcium sign , or hip rather than hip dysplasia test .

Peripheral Vascular Disease I · what it is and how it looks & feels NG-045 CARDIO ADHD-friendly visual edition PVD = any disease of the blood vessels OUTSIDE the heart — almost always the legs. It splits into two opposite problems : arteries can't get oxygen IN (PAD), or veins can't get blood back OUT (chronic venous insufficiency). Page 1 teaches the difference. Get that one contrast right and most of the exam falls over. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🩸 ARTERIES = blood IN Cool · pale · hairless · no pulse · ulcer on the TOES · pain when walking . 🫙 VEINS = blood OUT Warm · brown · swollen · pulse present · ulcer at the ANKLE · aches at end of day . ↕️ The trap = position Arterial DANGLE ⬇️ · Venous ELEVATE ⬆️ . Opposite answers, same-looking question. 🚨 6 P's = emergency Sudden cold, pulseless, painful leg = acute arterial occlusion . Limb is on a clock. 🧭
STEP 1 · TWO PIPES One leg, two plumbing systems. Arteries deliver, veins drain — and each one fails in its own signature way.

entries.h: 🧭 One leg, two circuits — arteries deliver, veins drain
entries.t: Every sign in this whole topic comes from asking one question: is the problem getting blood IN, or getting blood OUT?

Arterial problem Reduced delivery of oxygenated blood. Venous problem Impaired return allows blood to pool. Different tissue effects Assess the pattern before choosing care. Arterial clues Coolness, diminished pulses, exertional pain and distal tissue injury. Venous clues Edema, skin changes and gaiter-region ulceration; pulses may remain palpable. Care planning Skin protection and risk reduction apply to both. Compression requires assessment of arterial circulation. 🧠 “A = Away, V = Vacuum.” A rteries carry blood

entries.h: 🚧 ARTERIAL patho: the pipe narrows, the muscle starves
entries.t: Answer first: plaque narrows the artery → oxygen supply can't rise when demand rises → pain with activity . Supply vs demand: at rest the trickle is just enough. Start walking, the calf muscle demands more O₂, supply can't rise → cramping pain that stops when they stop. That's intermittent claudication . 🧠 “Claudication = the limping clock.” Claudicare is Latin for to limp . It shows up at the same distance every time — that reproducible distance is the tell.

entries.h: 🚪 VENOUS patho: the valves quit, blood pools
entries.t: Answer first: incompetent valves let blood fall backward → pressure builds in the leg veins → fluid and iron leak into the tissue. The brown stain is hemosiderin — iron left behind when pooled red cells break down. It is permanent , and it is the fingerprint of a venous leg. 🧠 “Rusty ankles = venous.” Blood sat still in the ankle so long it rusted the skin brown. Rust doesn't wash off — neither does hemosiderin staining.

entries.h: 📚 Word check — PVD, PAD, CVI, and the two “-scleroses”
entries.t: Term What it actually means Use it when… PVD peripheral vascular disease The umbrella — any disease of vessels outside the heart, arterial or venous. The question doesn't specify which side. PAD peripheral arterial disease The arterial half. Narrowed arteries → ischemia. Claudication, absent pulses, toe ulcers. CVI chronic venous insufficiency The venous half. Failed valves → pooling. Ankle edema, brown skin, medial ankle ulcer. Arteriosclerosis Hardening & loss of elasticity of the artery wall — the general aging
STEP 2 · SPOT IT The single most tested contrast in vascular nursing. Read the leg, then read the ulcer, then check the position that helps.

entries.h: ⭐ THE BIG SIDE-BY-SIDE — arterial leg vs venous leg
entries.t: 🧠 “ARTERIAL falls DOWN the leg to the TOES. VENOUS pools at the ANKLE.” Arterial damage shows up at the furthest, coldest, bumpiest spots — toe tips, heel, outer ankle . Venous damage shows up where the blood puddles — the inner ankle . And the fix is always the opposite of where the problem is: starving foot → drop it down. Flooded ankle → lift it up.

entries.h: ⭐ The same nine rows, in table form — memorize this grid
entries.t: Assess 🩸 ARTERIAL (PAD) 🫙 VENOUS (CVI) Pain Intermittent claudication — cramping with walking, gone with rest. Advanced: rest pain at night, relieved by hanging the leg down. Dull, heavy ache — worse with standing and by evening, relieved by elevating. Pulses Weak, thready or ABSENT distal to the block. Present (may be hard to palpate through edema). Temperature Cool / cold foot. Warm leg. Color Pale when elevated ( elevation pallor ), dusky red when dependent ( dependent rubor ). Ruddy / brown — hemosiderin staini

entries.h: 😖 Claudication vs rest pain — the arterial timeline
entries.t: 🚶 Stage 1 · No symptoms — plaque is there, flow is still enough ▼ 🦵 Stage 2 · Intermittent claudication — cramping calf pain at a reproducible distance , gone in minutes of rest ▼ 🌙 Stage 3 · REST PAIN — burning pain in the forefoot/toes at night; client hangs the leg off the bed to relieve it ▼ 🖤 Stage 4 · Tissue loss — ulcer, necrosis, gangrene = critical limb ischemia Why the night? Lying flat removes the gravity assist and cardiac output falls in sleep — the foot loses its last bit of perfusion. Hanging the leg

entries.h: 🔬 The position test at the bedside: pallor ⬆️ / rubor ⬇️
entries.t: Normal color returns in about 10 s and normal veins refill in about 15 s after lowering. Marked delay points to arterial disease. 🧠 “Up = white, down = red, both = arterial.” A venous leg goes the other way — elevating it makes it feel better and look less swollen.

entries.h: ⚠️ Look-alikes that get confused with a venous leg
entries.t: DVT — sudden , one-sided calf pain, swelling, warmth and redness in a leg that was fine yesterday. CVI is chronic and gradual ; DVT is acute . SEE NG-223 Cellulitis — hot, sharply demarcated red skin with fever and rising WBC. Venous stasis skin is brown and chronic, not febrile. Heart-failure edema — bilateral , symmetric, comes with weight gain, crackles and JVD. Venous insufficiency edema is often one leg worse and has skin staining. Lymphedema — non-pitting, firm, involves the toes and foot dorsum , no brown st
STEP 3 · WHEN TO ESCALATE Chronic PVD is managed. A limb that goes cold, white and pulseless is an emergency measured in hours.

entries.h: 🚨 ACUTE ARTERIAL OCCLUSION — the 6 P's · time is tissue
entries.t: 1 🛑 Stop and stay with the client — assess both legs, compare, mark where you found (or lost) the pulse with a pen. 2 📞 Notify the provider / rapid response IMMEDIATELY — this is a limb-threat, not a next-round finding. 3 ⬇️ Keep the limb DEPENDENT (below heart level) and at rest — never elevate an acutely ischemic leg. 4 🧣 Keep it comfortably warm with a light blanket — never apply a heating pad, hot water bottle, or ice . 5 🍽️ Keep NPO and get IV access — anticipate anticoagulation, thrombolytics, embolectomy or

entries.h: ❌ NEVER — the four that fail students
entries.t: Never apply heat (heating pad, hot soak) to an ischemic or neuropathic limb — the skin can't feel it and can't dissipate it. Burn on a foot that can't heal. Never elevate a leg with arterial disease for comfort — elevation is the venous answer. Arterial legs go down . Never apply compression stockings or wraps to an arterial leg — squeezing a starving limb finishes the job. Compression is the venous answer, and only after arterial supply is confirmed adequate. Never let the client cut their own corns, calluses or t

entries.h: ✅ What the nurse actually assesses, every shift
entries.t: 💓 Bilateral pulses — palpate, compare sides, mark the spot; if you can't feel it, get a Doppler before you chart “absent.” 🎨 Color, temperature, cap refill ( <3 s normal), hair distribution, nail thickness. 👣 Inspect the feet daily — including between the toes and the heels. 📏 Measure calf circumference at the same marked point each time. 🚶 Ask the distance : “how far can you walk before the cramp starts?” A shrinking distance = disease progressing. 🧠 “The 6 T's of a foot check” — T emperature, T one (pulse), T int
Risk factors that build plaque and the complications when it ruptures → page 2 . ABI, antiplatelets, statins, revascularization → page 3 . ⬇️ DANGLE stays true on every page

Why valves fail and where venous ulcers come from → page 2 . Compression, positioning and vein procedures → page 3 . Acute clot → NG-223 DVT . ⬆️ ELEVATE stays true on every page PVD set 1 · Patho & Signs 2 · Causes & Complications → 3 · Treatments → ＋ DVT → ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🩸 Arterial Cool, pale, hairless, pulseless · toe/heel/lateral ulcer, round & punched out · pain when walking · DANGLE ⬇️ 🫙 Venous Warm, brown, swollen, pulse present · medial ankle ulcer, irregular & weepy · pain when standing · ELEVATE ⬆️ 🕳️ Ulcer shortcut A rterial = A way & down (toes, outer). V enous = in the middle (medial malleolus). 🚨 6 P's Pain · Pallor · Pulselessness · Paresthesia · Paralysis · Poikilothermia = call NOW, keep the leg down & warm.

Q1: A client's leg ulcer sits over the medial malleolus , is shallow with irregular edges and drains heavily. Arterial or venous — and how do you position the leg? Show answer VENOUS. Elevate the leg above the level of the heart, and compression stockings are appropriate once arterial supply is confirmed adequate. Q2: A round, deep, “punched-out” ulcer on the tip of the great toe with a pale dry base and scant drainage. Which one, and what position? Show answer ARTERIAL. Keep the leg dependent — dangle it.
