Deep Vein Thrombosis — a CLOT in a deep vein · plus Raynaud's & Buerger's NG-223 CARDIO ADHD-friendly visual edition A clot in a deep vein is not dangerous where it sits — it is dangerous where it GOES. Blood from a leg vein travels to the right heart and straight into the lungs. That is why the calf you find swollen today is a pulmonary embolism tomorrow, and why you never massage or vigorously palpate a calf you suspect of clotting . Related PVD 1 · Patho & Signs PVD 2 · Causes & Complications PVD 3 · Treatments

🐄 COWS C alf pain & cramping · O ne-sided swelling · W arm & red · S OB + chest pain = PE! 🌀 Virchow's triad Stasis · Vessel injury · Hypercoagulability. Every risk factor is one of these three. 🚫 NEVER massage No rubbing, no vigorous palpation, no Homans' maneuver — you can launch the clot into the lungs. 🧪 WEPT W arfarin → PT /INR → vitamin K · H eparin → a PTT → protamine sulfate. 🌀
STEP 1 · VIRCHOW'S TRIAD Three conditions make blood clot where it shouldn't. Every risk factor you'll ever be asked about slots into one of them.

entries.h: 🌀 VIRCHOW'S TRIAD — the three-legged stool every DVT stands on

entries.t: Venous stasis or injury Reduced flow and clotting risk favor thrombosis. Deep venous thrombus A clot forms within a deep vein. Possible embolization A fragment may travel to the pulmonary circulation. Recognize Unilateral swelling, pain or warmth may occur; signs are not diagnostic. Assess Clinical probability and ordered testing guide diagnosis. Manage Prescribed anticoagulation, bleeding monitoring and appropriate mobility planning. 🧠 “SHIP” — Stasis · Hypercoagulability · Injury to the Pipe. Picture the classic

entries.h: ⚠️ Risk factors, sorted by which leg of the triad
entries.t: Triad leg Who's at risk 🧍 STASIS Post-op & immobile clients · bed rest · casts and splints · paralysis/stroke · long car rides and flights · prolonged sitting · heart failure · obesity · pregnancy (the uterus compresses pelvic veins) 🩹 INJURY Orthopedic surgery — especially hip and knee replacement · major trauma and fractures · central lines and IV catheters · smoking 🧬 HYPERCOAG Cancer (and chemotherapy) · dehydration · pregnancy and postpartum · estrogen therapy / oral contraceptives , especially in a smoker ove

entries.h: 🫙 Deep vs superficial — why only one of them scares you
entries.t: Superficial thrombophlebitis — clot in a surface vein. You can see and feel a red, tender, cord-like vein just under the skin. Uncomfortable, usually treated with warm compresses, elevation and anti-inflammatories. DVT — deep vein thrombosis — clot in a deep vein (calf, popliteal, femoral, iliac). You cannot see it. It sits in a high-volume vein with a straight path to the lungs. That path is the whole point: leg vein → inferior vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → PE . 🧠 “Superficial you
STEP 2 · SPOT IT Four letters for the leg. One line for the lungs. And one thing your hands must never do.

entries.h: 🐄 COWS — the DVT sign set, and the S that changes everything
entries.t: C CALF PAIN & CRAMPING — aching, tightness or a “charley horse” that doesn't ease. Often worse with walking or dorsiflexion , and tender along the vein. O ONE-SIDED SWELLING (unilateral) — this is the money sign. Measure calf circumference at the same marked point on both legs and compare. Two swollen legs points at the heart; one swollen leg points at a vein. W WARM & RED — blood pooling behind the clot makes the skin warm, red/erythematous and shiny-tight . May come with a low-grade fever. S SOB & CHEST PAIN = PE

entries.h: 🚫 NEVER massage or vigorously palpate a calf you suspect has a clot
entries.t: Why: the thrombus is only loosely attached. Pressure, kneading or forceful dorsiflexion can dislodge it into the circulation , and a venous clot goes straight to the lungs . Homans' sign (calf pain on forced dorsiflexion) is no longer used — it is unreliable, it misses most DVTs, and the maneuver itself risks dislodging the clot. Inspect and measure instead. Do NOT apply SCDs to a leg with a known acute DVT unless the provider specifically orders it. SCDs are a prevention device. Gentle inspection, gentle circumfer

entries.h: 🔬 Confirming it — what actually diagnoses a DVT
entries.t: Venous duplex ultrasound — the first-line, non-invasive test . Shows the clot and whether the vein compresses. D-dimer — a fibrin breakdown product. A normal D-dimer helps rule OUT a clot; an elevated one does not rule it IN (it rises with surgery, trauma, infection, pregnancy, cancer). Wells score — a clinical probability tool that decides whether the client goes straight to ultrasound. For suspected PE: CT pulmonary angiography is the standard confirming study. ABG may show hypoxemia with a low CO₂ from blowing o

entries.h: 🚨 PE — what it looks like when the clot arrives
entries.t: 😮‍💨 SUDDEN shortness of breath — the hallmark. Abrupt, not gradual. 💥 Sharp, pleuritic chest pain — worse on deep breath. 💓 Tachycardia and tachypnea ; low SpO₂ despite effort. 😰 Anxiety, restlessness, a sense of impending doom — take this seriously, it is a real early sign of hypoxia. 🩸 Cough, sometimes with blood-streaked sputum (hemoptysis) . 📉 Hypotension, cyanosis, syncope = massive PE, obstructive shock. 🧠 “Sudden + Short of breath + Sharp chest pain + Scared = PE.” Four S's. In a post-op client with a swolle

entries.h: 🚨 PE ESCALATION — priority actions in order
entries.t: 1 STAY with the client and sit them UP — high Fowler's. It maximizes lung expansion immediately and costs nothing. ▼ 2 Apply OXYGEN and put on continuous pulse oximetry. Hypoxia is what's killing them right now. ▼ 3 CALL — provider / rapid response. Use the call light or a colleague so you never leave the client alone. ▼ 4 Vital signs, cardiac monitor, IV access. Establish or confirm a patent IV — the treatment is going to be intravenous. ▼ 5 Anticipate: IV heparin, CT pulmonary angiography , ABG, D-dimer, ECG, and
STEP 3 · STOP THE NEXT ONE Anticoagulants don't dissolve the clot — they stop it from growing while the body breaks it down. Prevention is where nursing wins.

entries.h: 💊 Anticoagulant comparison — which lab watches which drug
entries.t: Drug Route & speed Monitoring Nursing key points Heparin unfractionated IV drip or SC. Immediate onset — this is the one you start in an emergency. aPTT (some facilities use anti-Xa). Therapeutic ≈ 1.5–2.5× the control value. Also follow PLATELETS. Antidote protamine sulfate . Watch for HIT — heparin-induced thrombocytopenia: platelets fall (classically >50% drop) and the client paradoxically clots . Stop the heparin and notify. Never rub SC injection sites. LMWH enoxaparin, dalteparin SC, weight-based, more predic

entries.h: 🩸 Bleeding precautions — the same teaching for every anticoagulant
entries.t: 🪥 Soft toothbrush, electric razor , no flossing with force. 🚽 Report black tarry stools, pink/red urine, coffee-ground emesis, bleeding gums, nosebleeds, unusual bruising , or a headache/confusion after a fall. 💊 No NSAIDs or aspirin unless the provider ordered them; check every OTC and herbal product. 🪪 Wear medical-alert identification and tell every dentist and surgeon. 🩹 Hold pressure longer after venipunctures and injections; avoid IM injections when possible. 🤕 Fall precautions — a head strike on an anticoagu

🚶 Early ambulation after surgery — the single most effective prevention. 🦵 SCDs / intermittent pneumatic compression and graduated compression (TED) stockings for immobile clients. Check skin under them; make sure they aren't rolled or bunched. 💉 Prophylactic anticoagulation — low-dose SC heparin or LMWH for at-risk hospitalized and post-op clients. 💧 Hydration — dehydrated blood is thick blood. 🦶 Ankle pumps, calf exercises and position changes for anyone on bed rest. ❌ No pillows under the knees, no leg crossing,

🦶 C — Calf exercise & isometrics 💧 H — Hydration thin the blood 🚶 A — Ambulation keep moving 🪑 N — No long sitting car · airplane · bed rest 🧦 T — TED & SCDs after the clot is resolved Two nuances the exam cares about: Elevate the affected leg to promote venous return and reduce swelling — the same rule as every venous problem. entries.h: 🕸️ When drugs aren't enough: the IVC filter
entries.t: What it is: a small mesh basket placed in the inferior vena cava to catch clots traveling from the legs before they reach the lungs. Who gets one: clients who cannot take anticoagulants (active bleeding, recent neurosurgery) or who keep throwing clots despite therapeutic anticoagulation. What it does NOT do: it does not dissolve clots and it does not prevent new ones from forming — it is a net, not a treatment. 🧠 “A pool skimmer, not a filter for the water.” It catches what floats by; it doesn't clean the pool. Ant

entries.h: 🎨 Also on this card: Raynaud's vs Buerger's
entries.t: 🤍 RAYNAUD'S · “R = Ring finger” 🖤 BUERGER'S · “B = Black fingers & toes” Spasm of small arteries in the fingers (and toes), triggered by COLD and STRESS . Buerger's disease (thromboangiitis obliterans) — inflammation and clotting of small and medium arteries and veins in the hands and feet . Classic color sequence: WHITE (spasm, no blood) → BLUE (deoxygenated) → RED (blood rushes back). Numbness, tingling, throbbing. Tissue actually dies: intense pain, claudication of the arch of the foot, cold sensitivity, ulcers,

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🐄 COWS C alf pain · O ne-sided swelling · W arm & red · S OB + chest pain = PE, call now . 🌀 Triad Stasis · vessel Injury · Hypercoagulability. Post-op ortho client in bed = all three. 🚫 Hands off No massage, no vigorous palpation, no Homans'. Look, measure, report. 🧪 WEPT W arfarin → PT/ INR 2.0–3.0 → vitamin K · H eparin → a PTT 1.5–2.5× → protamine · DOAC → no routine lab.

Infective & noninfective inflammation of the heart's INNER lining & valves NG-229 CARDIO ADHD-friendly visual edition Inflammation INside the heart — bacteria (or, less often, sterile clot/inflammation with no bacteria) seed the endocardium and valves, growing a vegetation that keeps valves from closing fully. Less cardiac output = less oxygen OUT to the body, plus pieces of that vegetation can break off and embolize to the brain, lungs, and fingertips. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🦠 Bugs on the valve Infective (bacteria — "mold on the valve") vs. noninfective (inflammation, no bacteria). 🩸 Blood cultures BEFORE antibiotics Draw multiple sets from different sites first — don't let the first antibiotic dose sterilize the culture. 🖐️ Four classic exam signs Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, splinter hemorrhages, Roth spots. 🦷 Protect the at-risk valve Antibiotic prophylaxis before dental/procedures; gentle oral care, no flossing. 🧨
STEP 1 · BUGS FIND A DOOR A valve gets damaged or exposed, bacteria land on it, and a vegetation grows — the whole disease follows from that one event.

entries.h: 🫀 A heart valve with vegetation growth
entries.t: EXAM TIP Infective endocarditis = bacteria seed a valve (often one already scarred or abnormal), forming a sticky vegetation of fibrin, platelets, and bacteria. The leaflets can't close fully → regurgitation → the vegetation keeps growing and keeps shedding infected emboli.

Organisms enter blood A bloodstream infection can seed susceptible tissue. Vegetations form Infection commonly affects valves. Valve or embolic injury Regurgitation, heart failure or emboli may result. Recognize Fever, a new or changing murmur, embolic signs or unexplained systemic illness. Investigate Blood cultures and echocardiography help establish the diagnosis. Care Prolonged prescribed antimicrobials, response monitoring and sometimes surgery. 🧠 "Mold on the valve." Picture the vegetation exactly like fuzzy

💉 Dirty needles — IV drug use 🦷 Dental visits without antibiotic prophylaxis in an at-risk client 🔪 Heart surgery — valve replacement & CABG 🤒 Untreated strep throat 🧠 "Four doors bacteria walk through." Needles, teeth, surgery, and an ignored strep infection — every route is a break in a barrier that lets bacteria reach the bloodstream and then the valve.

🦠 Infective 🧊 Noninfective Bacteria present — "mold on the valve" No bacteria — sterile inflammation/clot only Needs antibiotics Treat the underlying cause (e.g., lupus, cancer) 🧠 Say the word: Endo (inside) + card (heart) + itis (inflammation) = inflammation INSIDE the heart — the lining & valves, not the sac around it (that's pericarditis, NG-066 ) and not just the muscle (myocarditis). 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT IT One mnemonic for the systemic picture, four unmistakable fingertip-and-eye findings, and the culture rule that changes the whole plan.

C — C lots in the heart & brain — risk for stroke/CVA; monitor for agitation, change in level of consciousness L — L ung fluid — crackles O — O verheated — fever T — T oo little oxygen — low cardiac output Plus: clubbing fingers , new or changing heart murmur , fatigue, and the four classic peripheral findings below. 🧠 A CLOT is exactly what's forming — on the valve, and sometimes flying to the brain. The mnemonic is the pathophysiology.

entries.h: Four classic findings of infective endocarditis
entries.t: Tap an illustration to enlarge it. Compare the location, shape, and tenderness . These are original teaching illustrations; the photo links show clinical examples.
Fingertip pad A raised, tender red-purple nodule on the fleshy pad of a finger or toe. Compare clinical photos ↗
Palm or sole Flat, painless red or brown spots. Look at the fleshy areas along the sides of the palm. Compare clinical photos ↗
Under the nail Thin red-brown streaks run in the direction of nail growth. Trauma can cause these too. Compare clinical photos ↗

Retina On funduscopic exam, look for a retinal hemorrhage with a pale center. The larger pale area where vessels branch is the optic disc. Compare clinical photos ↗ 🧠 Osler = Ouch. A tender bump on a pad. Janeway = painless palm. Splinters follow the nail; Roth spots are seen in the retina. These are clues, not a diagnosis on their own.

Draw blood cultures from multiple sites before the first dose of antibiotics. Giving antibiotics first can sterilize the blood and make it impossible to identify the organism — which is exactly what guides therapy. 🩸 Multiple sets, different venipuncture sites, before treatment starts 🫀 Echocardiogram — visualizes the vegetation directly 🧫 Elevated WBC, inflammatory markers 🧠 "Culture first, cure second." If a question shows antibiotics being hung before cultures are drawn, that's the error to catch.

Pieces of the vegetation can break off and travel to the brain. New agitation or a change in level of consciousness in an endocarditis client is a stroke until ruled out. 🧠 The C in CLOT is not abstract — it's a real embolus that can lodge in the brain within minutes. 🩺
STEP 3 · CLEAR THE INFECTION, PROTECT THE VALVE Antibiotics do the heavy lifting; teaching and prophylaxis keep it from happening again.

💉 IV antibiotics — organism-specific, typically a prolonged course; started only after cultures are drawn 🔪 Valve repair or replacement for severe damage, large/embolizing vegetations, or heart failure from valve destruction 🧠 "Bugs out, then rebuild." Kill the infection first — surgery on an actively infected valve is reserved for those who need it urgently (large vegetations, heart failure, uncontrolled infection).

entries.h: 🩸 The PICC — what the family needs to hear
entries.t: The course teaching for endocarditis is 2–6 weeks of IV antibiotics . A peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) can provide access for the prescribed course if it remains needed, functioning and free of complications. ⏳ Several weeks with proper care is the correct parent-teaching answer. No routine site rotation every 3 days. A dressing change does not mean replacing the catheter. An arm board is not routinely required. Protect the line from pulling and follow the child’s activity restrictions. An operating

🪥 Brush 2x /day with a soft toothbrush NO flossing — can introduce bacteria into the bloodstream 🦷 Routine dental care is still important — just done with antibiotic prophylaxis, not skipped 🧠 "Brush soft, skip the string." Any break in the gum line is a door bacteria can walk through straight to a damaged valve.

entries.h: 🦷 Dental & procedure prophylaxis for at-risk clients
entries.t: Clients with a history of endocarditis , a prosthetic heart valve , certain congenital heart disease , or a cardiac transplant with valve regurgitation need prophylactic antibiotics before dental work or other procedures that can cause bacteremia. 📣 Tell every provider — dentist, surgeon, even routine procedures — about the history of endocarditis 🪪 Consider a medical alert card/bracelet 🧠 "Announce it before they touch you." The single biggest prevention failure is the client not mentioning their history — make th

1 🩸 Cultures before antibiotics — never reverse the order 2 🧠 Monitor — new agitation or altered LOC = possible embolic stroke 3 📣 Let all providers know of history of endocarditis 4 🦷 Dental visits/surgery in an at-risk client require prophylaxis 5 💊 Antibiotic adherence — the full prolonged course, every dose 🧠 "CLOT" gets you the signs; this ladder gets you the actions. Say both out loud and you have the whole page. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🦠 Vegetation on the valve Fibrin + platelets + bacteria stop the leaflets from closing 🩸 Cultures BEFORE antibiotics Never sterilize the sample before you identify the bug 🖐️ Osler = ouch, Janeway = no way Splinters under nails, Roth spots in the eye 🦷 Prophylax the at-risk valve Prosthetic valve or prior endocarditis + dental work = antibiotics first

Q1: What must happen before the first dose of antibiotics is given? Show answer Blood cultures — multiple sets from different sites — must be drawn first, or the organism may never be identified. Q2: How do you tell Osler nodes apart from Janeway lesions? Show answer Osler nodes are painful/tender nodules on the finger or toe pads. Janeway lesions are painless flat macules on the palms or soles. Q3: What does the CLOT mnemonic stand for? Show answer Clots in the heart & brain (stroke risk) · Lung fluid (crackles) ·

entries.h: Cholesterol Lowering Agents · NG-242 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Cardio · Pharmacology

Statins · Ezetimibe · Sequestrants · Fibrates · Niacin · PCSK9 NG-242 Cardio · Pharm ADHD-friendly visual edition Indication: high cholesterol — hypercholesterolemia · hyperlipidemia · dyslipidemia (different names for the same thing). Every drug on this page is aiming at one target: the plaque from NG-145 . Lower the LDL, calm the artery wall, and thicken the fibrous cap so it doesn't rupture . Statins are the backbone. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

💊 “-statin” Blocks the liver enzyme that MAKES cholesterol. First-line, biggest LDL drop. 💪 Muscle pain = REPORT New muscle aches/cramps/tenderness without injury → call the HCP. Rhabdo risk. 🍊 NO grapefruit It blocks the enzyme that clears the statin → drug piles up → more myopathy. 🌙 Take at NIGHT Cholesterol is made mostly while she sleeps — dose the short-acting statins at dinner/bedtime. 💊
STEP 1 · SIX DIFFERENT ATTACKS Each class hits cholesterol at a different address: the liver factory, the gut doorway, the bloodstream, or the liver's recycling receptors.

Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, so the liver makes less cholesterol and puts out more LDL receptors, clearing LDL from the blood. Ezetimibe blocks cholesterol absorption (NPC1L1) at the small-intestine lining. Bile acid sequestrants bind bile acids in the gut so they leave in stool; the liver uses cholesterol to replace them. Main effect: lower LDL. PCSK9 antibodies (evolocumab, alirocumab) stop PCSK9 from destroying liver LDL receptors, so more receptors clear LDL. Fibrates activate PPAR-alpha and mainly lower

atorvastatin · simvastatin · lovastatin · rosuvastatin · pravastatin MOA: it reduces new cholesterol production in the liver — technically by blocking the enzyme the liver needs to make cholesterol: HMG-CoA reductase . Less cholesterol made inside → the liver puts out more LDL receptors → it pulls LDL out of the blood .

Step 1: the statin inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, an early step in cholesterol synthesis. Step 2: with less cholesterol inside, liver cells put more LDL receptors on their surface. Step 3: the receptors bind LDL in the blood and take it into the cell, so blood LDL falls. It reduces synthesis; it does not stop all cholesterol production. Not a dosing guide. ⬇️ Biggest LDL drop of any oral class — the reason it's first-line 🛡️ Also stabilizes the plaque cap and lowers inflammation — benefit beyond the number ( NG-145 )

💊 “-statin” (lovastatin, simvastatin…) 🍄 NYSTATIN Cholesterol-lowering — blocks HMG-CoA reductase in the liver ANTIFUNGAL — treats yeast infections (oral thrush, candidiasis, diaper rash) Oral tablet, usually once daily Often a swish-and-swallow or swish-and-spit suspension, or a topical powder/cream Watch: muscle pain, liver enzymes Watch: it must contact the fungus — hold it in the mouth, don't eat/drink right after EXAM TIP NYstatin = NO cholesterol. It's for YEAST. 🧠 “NY = New York yeast — a bagel.” NY statin b

entries.h: 🗂️ The other five classes, cleanly separated

entries.t: ezetimibe MOA: blocks cholesterol absorption at the small-intestine brush border — dietary and biliary cholesterol never gets in. Use: usually added on to a statin when LDL isn't at goal, or used alone if she can't tolerate statins. Modest LDL lowering on its own. Watch: generally well tolerated — GI upset/diarrhea; rare myalgia (more likely when combined with a statin); can raise liver enzymes when combined.

entries.h: 💊 BILE ACID SEQUESTRANTS — the bile sponge
entries.t: cholestyramine · colestipol · colesevelam MOA: bind bile acids in the gut so they're excreted in stool . The liver must then use up cholesterol to make new bile → blood LDL falls. Same trick as the soluble fiber in oatmeal. Big advantage: not absorbed systemically — it works entirely inside the gut. Watch: CONSTIPATION (the classic), bloating, gas. May RAISE triglycerides — a poor choice if TGs are already high. HUGE NURSING POINT It binds other drugs and the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, K . Give other medications

gemfibrozil · fenofibrate MOA: speed the breakdown and clearance of triglyceride-rich particles (they activate the pathway that boosts lipoprotein lipase). Best at: lowering TRIGLYCERIDES — the go-to for very high TGs, including preventing pancreatitis . Modest HDL rise, little LDL effect. Watch: GALLSTONES (cholelithiasis), GI upset, ↑ liver enzymes, and myopathy — the risk climbs sharply when combined with a statin (gemfibrozil is the worst offender). Use with caution in kidney disease.

entries.h: 💊 NIACIN (nicotinic acid, vitamin B₃) — the HDL raiser
entries.t: niacin · extended-release niacin MOA: reduces the liver's release of VLDL → ↓LDL and ↓triglycerides , and it raises HDL more than any other agent . Watch — the one everybody tests: FLUSHING — hot, red, itchy face and neck. It's prostaglandin-mediated and harmless but miserable. 💊 Take aspirin about 30 minutes before the dose (if the provider approves) to blunt flushing 🍺 Avoid alcohol and hot drinks around the dose — they intensify flushing ⏳ Extended-release forms flush less; flushing fades over weeks of consisten

entries.h: 💉 PCSK9 INHIBITORS — the injectable heavy hitters
entries.t: alirocumab · evolocumab MOA: monoclonal antibodies that block PCSK9 , the protein that destroys LDL receptors. Block it → the liver keeps far more LDL receptors → it vacuums LDL out of the blood. Very large LDL reductions. Use: familial hypercholesterolemia , or established atherosclerotic disease when a maximally tolerated statin (± ezetimibe) isn't enough, or true statin intolerance. Route: SUBCUTANEOUS injection every 2–4 weeks — not a pill. Teach self-injection, site rotation, refrigerate and let the pen reach

entries.h: 🧪 Target vs bad — the bar scale

entries.t: Atherogenic particles LDL-containing particles contribute to plaque. Treatment lowers exposure Drug mechanisms target synthesis, absorption or clearance. Risk reduction Long-term therapy helps reduce cardiovascular events. Statins Reduce hepatic cholesterol synthesis and increase LDL clearance. Monitor Adherence, response, interactions and unexplained muscle symptoms. Whole plan Nutrition, activity, smoking cessation and other risk treatment remain important. EXAM TIP Clients with known heart disease or diabetes ar

Lipid panel — baseline, then to check response (often re-checked weeks to months after a change) ALT & AST — baseline liver function before starting a statin; re-check if she has symptoms CK (creatine kinase) — drawn when she reports muscle pain, to look for myopathy/rhabdo Creatinine / BUN — kidney function, especially with rhabdo risk or fibrates A1c / glucose — statins and niacin can nudge glucose up Uric acid — niacin can precipitate gout 🧠 “Muscle pain → CK. Yellow eyes → ALT/AST.” The complaint tells you whic

entries.h: 🍽️ Diet still does half the work
entries.t: 🥣 Soluble fiber (oats, beans, barley, psyllium) — binds bile, same mechanism as sequestrants 🐟 Fatty fish & omega-3s — help triglycerides 🥑 Swap saturated & trans fats for unsaturated (olive oil, nuts, avocado) 🍬 Cut refined sugar & alcohol — the biggest drivers of high triglycerides 🏃 Exercise — the most reliable way to raise HDL 🚭 Smoking cessation — smoking lowers HDL directly 🧠 “Sugar makes triglycerides; fat makes LDL; movement makes HDL.” Three sentences, three numbers, three behaviors. ⚠️
STEP 3 · THE STATIN ADVERSE EFFECTS ATI, HESI and Kaplan all ask the exact same question about statins — and the answer is always the muscles.

entries.h: 💪 Muscle pain without injury = REPORT IT
entries.t: Answer first: new muscle aches, cramps, spasms, tenderness or weakness that she cannot explain by exercise or injury → notify the HCP . This is the single most tested statin fact. 🧠 “Sore muscles → dark pee → sick kidneys.” Three beats, in that order. Rhabdo isn't “muscle pain,” it's muscle dissolving — and the kidney is downstream of the mess.

🧪 Baseline liver enzymes (ALT/AST) before starting; re-check if she develops symptoms 💩 Report clay-colored stools — the classic source cue 💛 Jaundice (yellow skin/sclera), dark urine , RUQ pain , unusual fatigue, loss of appetite, nausea 🍺 Limit alcohol — adds liver insult ⚠️ Use caution/avoid in active liver disease Serious statin liver injury is uncommon , but the teaching point is constant: symptoms get reported, not waited out. 🧠 “Clay stool, dark pool, feeling cruel.” Pale stools + dark urine + fatigue = live

entries.h: 🍊 Grapefruit — and the St. John's wort correction
entries.t: Answer first: No grapefruit or grapefruit juice with simvastatin, lovastatin or atorvastatin. Why: grapefruit inhibits the CYP3A4 enzyme that clears these statins → the drug builds up → higher myopathy/rhabdo risk Not all statins: pravastatin and rosuvastatin aren't metabolized by CYP3A4, so grapefruit is far less of an issue with them — but teach the rule as written on her bottle SOURCE CHECK St. John's wort is also on the avoid list — but for the opposite reason : it induces CYP3A4 and can make the statin less ef

entries.h: ⚠️ The rest of the statin cautions
entries.t: Caution What to do about it Pregnancy & breastfeeding Standard nursing teaching is to avoid statins in pregnancy and to use reliable contraception; a client planning pregnancy should talk to her provider before stopping or continuing. Cholesterol is needed for fetal development. New-onset diabetes / ↑ A1c A small, real effect. It does not outweigh the cardiovascular benefit — monitor glucose, don't stop the statin on your own. Alcohol & liver disease Limit alcohol; caution in active hepatic disease. Kidney disease
STEP 4 · WHAT SHE TAKES HOME Timing, expectations, and the three exam questions that are really the same question.

entries.h: 🌙 Why statins are taken at night
entries.t: 🌙 The liver makes most of its cholesterol overnight — HMG-CoA reductase activity peaks in the night/early morning hours 💊 So the short-acting statins — simvastatin, lovastatin, fluvastatin — are taken in the evening (dinner or bedtime) so the drug level peaks when the enzyme is busiest 🍽️ Lovastatin is specifically taken with the evening meal — food improves its absorption ☀️ Long-acting statins — atorvastatin and rosuvastatin — can be taken at any time of day , because their effect lasts a full 24 hours ⏰ The best

entries.h: 📝 The exam questions — all three are the same question
entries.t: Source Question Answer ATI “Patient on lovastatin — when would the nurse notify the HCP?” Muscle aches & cramps HESI “Which teaching is essential?” “Report muscle pain & tenderness without injury” Kaplan “Which statement shows understanding?” “Report NEW muscle tenderness to the HCP” NCLEX wording to recognize: “muscle cramps” · “muscle spasms” · “muscle aches” · “muscle tenderness” · “weakness” · “dark urine.” Any of them = report. 🧠 Three testing companies, one answer: THE MUSCLES. If a statin appears in a questi

entries.h: ✅ Teaching checklist — say it in her words
entries.t: 💊 Take it every day, even feeling fine — high cholesterol has no symptoms 🌙 Evening dose for short-acting statins; any time for atorvastatin/rosuvastatin 💪 Call for new muscle pain, weakness or dark urine 💛 Call for yellow skin/eyes, clay-colored stools, RUQ pain, unusual fatigue 🍊 No grapefruit · avoid St. John's wort · limit alcohol 🤰 Tell the provider if she's pregnant or planning to be 🥗 Keep the diet & exercise going — the drug does not replace them 🧪 Keep lab appointments — lipids, liver enzymes, CK if sympto

💊 Sequestrants: “Take your other pills 1 hour before or 4 hours after this one, and expect constipation — fluids and fiber.” 💊 Niacin: “Your face may flush and burn. Take aspirin ~ 30 min before if approved, skip alcohol and hot drinks, and it fades over time.” 💊 Fibrates: “Report right-upper-belly pain — gallstones. And tell me about any muscle pain, especially since you're also on a statin.” 💊 Ezetimibe: “Usually easy to tolerate — but muscle pain still gets reported.” 💉 PCSK9: “It's a shot every 2–4 weeks. Keep

SAY IT OUT LOUD 💊 Statin = block the liver enzyme HMG-CoA reductase. Biggest LDL drop + stabilizes the plaque cap. 💪 Muscle pain → HCP Myalgia → myopathy → rhabdo → dark cola urine + AKI. Check CK . 🧪 200 · 150 · 100 · 40 Total ≤200 · Trigs ≤150 · LDL ≤100 · HDL ≥40 🗂️ Match drug to number LDL→statin · TG→fibrate · HDL→niacin · huge LDL→PCSK9 SubQ

Q1: How does a statin lower cholesterol? Show answer It prevents cholesterol production in the liver by blocking the enzyme the liver needs — HMG-CoA reductase. Less made inside → more LDL receptors → LDL pulled out of the blood. Q2: The client on lovastatin reports new leg aches with no injury. Action? Show answer Notify the HCP. Muscle pain/tenderness/cramps without injury can signal myopathy and possible rhabdomyolysis — expect a CK level, and ask about dark, cola-colored urine and weakness. Q3: Why no grapefrui
Sickle cell clogs vessels. Thalassemia and G6PD deficiency lose red cells. Hemophilia cannot form a clot. All four are inherited, and each has one intervention that matters most.
🖼️ Open readable diagram & course labels

Autosomal recessive. Two genes = disease; one gene = trait , usually symptom-free Symptoms do not appear before about 6 months , because fetal hemoglobin protects Infection is the leading cause of death in young children — the spleen is damaged early, so penicillin prophylaxis and full vaccination are essential Acute chest syndrome — chest pain, fever, hypoxia, new infiltrate. A leading cause of death; a medical emergency Splenic sequestration — sudden splenic enlargement, rapid drop in hemoglobin, shock

The body cannot build enough hemoglobin. An inherited (autosomal recessive) gene slows or stops one of the globin chains — usually beta . The red cells come out small, pale and fragile (microcytic, hypochromic) and break down early. So the child is transfused — and the iron in all that blood becomes the danger. Most common in families of Mediterranean (Greek, Italian), Middle Eastern , South and Southeast Asian and African descent.

Thalassemia minor (trait) — one gene. Mild anemia with small cells, often no symptoms. Easily mistaken for iron deficiency , so iron is not given unless a deficiency is proven. Thalassemia intermedia — moderate anemia; transfusions only some of the time. Thalassemia major (Cooley anemia) — two genes. Severe anemia that appears in the second half of the first year , as fetal hemoglobin falls. Needs lifelong transfusions. The most severe alpha -thalassemia causes hydrops fetalis before birth.

entries.h: 👀 What you see in thalassemia major
entries.t: Pallor , fatigue, irritability, poor feeding, failure to thrive Enlarged spleen and liver (hepatosplenomegaly) from all the cell breakdown; jaundice The marrow overworks and expands: frontal bossing (prominent forehead), prominent cheekbones and upper jaw , and thin bones that fracture easily Bronze or grayish skin as iron builds up Delayed growth and late puberty Diagnosis: CBC (low Hgb, small pale cells, target cells) and hemoglobin electrophoresis , which names the type.

Regular red-cell transfusions , about every 3–4 weeks, to keep hemoglobin near 9.5–10 g/dL . That lets the child grow normally and quiets the overworking marrow. Iron chelation to remove the extra iron: deferoxamine as a slow subcutaneous (or IV) infusion over 8–12 hours, usually overnight, 5–7 nights a week , or the oral drugs deferasirox or deferiprone. Folic acid to support red-cell production. Splenectomy if the spleen is destroying too many cells — then pneumococcal, Hib and meningococcal vaccines, daily penic

T — Transfusion dependent H — Hepatosplenomegaly A — Anemia , severe L — Low MCV : small, pale (microcytic, hypochromic) cells A — Abnormal face : frontal bossing, prominent cheekbones and upper jaw (“chipmunk” face) S — Skeletal changes and fragile bones S — Stunted growth E — Elevated fetal hemoglobin (HbF) on electrophoresis M — Mediterranean (and Middle Eastern, Asian) family origin I — Iron overload from the transfusions A — Amenorrhea and other endocrine problems (late puberty, diabetes, hypothyroidism) from

Transfusion safety: two-person check, baseline vital signs, stay with the child for the first 15 minutes, and watch for reactions. Watch for iron overload and heart problems: ferritin, heart rate and rhythm, fatigue, swelling. Teach home chelation: the overnight pump, rotating sites, keeping it going most nights. Deferoxamine needs yearly hearing and eye checks . After splenectomy: infection precautions and an urgent call for any fever. Support body image (facial bone changes, short stature), school and normal acti

The red cells are missing their shield. G6PD (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase) is the enzyme that protects red cells from oxidant stress . Without enough of it, the cells look and work normally — until something oxidizing comes along. Then they break apart ( acute hemolysis ), usually 1 to 3 days after the exposure. Most days the child is well. The whole job is avoiding the triggers. X-linked recessive , so it is mostly boys , carried by mothers. Most common in families of African , Mediterranean , Middle Eastern

Pallor , fatigue, fast heart rate — a sudden drop in hemoglobin. Jaundice (yellow skin and sclera). Dark, tea- or cola-colored urine (hemoglobin in the urine). Back or abdominal pain, sometimes fever. Labs: low Hgb and Hct, high reticulocyte count , high indirect bilirubin; Heinz bodies and “bite cells” on the smear. Diagnosis: a G6PD enzyme assay. It can read falsely normal during a crisis (the young cells have more enzyme), so it may be repeated a few weeks later. Never give a sulfa drug, an antimalarial or aspir

Give the family a written list of drugs and foods to avoid , and teach them to tell every provider, dentist and pharmacist. A medical alert ID helps. Read labels on over-the-counter products for aspirin (salicylates); use acetaminophen for fever and pain unless told otherwise. No fava beans; no mothballs in the house. Treat infections early — illness alone can set off hemolysis. Report dark urine, yellow eyes or skin, pallor or unusual tiredness right away. Genetic counseling: a carrier mother passes it to each son

A missing clotting factor — factor VIII in hemophilia A, factor IX in B. X-linked recessive , so it affects boys, carried by mothers. Lab Result aPTT Prolonged PT Normal Platelet count Normal — the platelets are fine, the factor is missing Bleeding time Normal

The hallmark. Warm, swollen, painful joint with reduced movement. Repeated bleeds destroy the joint permanently. Treatment: RICE + factor R est — immobilize; do not move it I ce C ompression E levate above the level of the heart Give the missing factor — this is the definitive treatment No aspirin, no NSAIDs. Acetaminophen is the safe analgesic. No IM injections, no rectal temperatures, no contact sports.

Swimming and cycling with a helmet are encouraged; contact sports are not Soft toothbrush ; electric razor when older Medical alert identification Dental work needs factor cover Teach parents to recognize a joint bleed early — a tingling or warmth before visible swelling

Immune thrombocytopenic purpura — platelets destroyed after a viral illness. Low platelets , petechiae and bruising, often in an otherwise well child. Usually self-limiting. Hemophilia = normal platelets, missing factor. ITP = low platelets.

Sickle crisis = oxygen, hydration, analgesia, warmth. Never cold, never aspirin Sickle symptoms start after 6 months Hemophilia has NORMAL platelets — only the factor is missing Joint bleed → immobilize, ice, elevate, give factor Acetaminophen only — no aspirin or NSAIDs in either condition Sources. Written from CDC , HealthyChildren.org (AAP) , MedlinePlus and OpenStax A&P 2e (CC BY 4.0).
Sort them by which way blood shunts. Left-to-right floods the lungs; right-to-left makes a blue baby.

Structural connection An opening links chambers or great vessels. Pressure gradient The gradient influences shunt direction and volume. Circulatory effect Pulmonary flow, chamber workload or oxygenation changes. ASD and VSD Openings in atrial or ventricular septa can create left-to-right flow after birth. PDA Persistent connection between aorta and pulmonary artery changes flow after birth. AV septal defect Septal and atrioventricular valve anatomy are affected.

Outflow narrowing A valve or vessel limits forward flow. Upstream pressure The pumping chamber works against a greater load. Downstream effects Perfusion may fall when obstruction is severe. Aortic stenosis Obstruction at the aortic valve increases left-ventricular workload. Pulmonary stenosis Obstruction at the pulmonary valve increases right-ventricular workload. Coarctation Aortic narrowing can cause upper/lower limb pressure or pulse differences.

Right ventricular outflow obstruction Limits blood reaching the lungs. VSD with overriding aorta Allows flow across the septal opening into the aortic outflow. Right ventricular hypertrophy Develops from the pressure load. Physiology The severity of outflow obstruction strongly influences cyanosis. Hypercyanotic episode Increased right-to-left flow can cause sudden worsening cyanosis and distress. Response Calm and position the child as instructed and activate the urgent congenital-heart care plan. Ask which way th

A narrowing of the aorta. The classic finding is a blood pressure difference : High blood pressure and bounding pulses in the ARMS Low blood pressure and weak or absent pulses in the LEGS Cool lower extremities; leg pain on exertion in older children Always compare upper and lower limb pulses and pressures in a child with hypertension. Coarctation is a fixable cause that is missed by only checking an arm. 🧒 Coarctation of the aorta Picture, memory hook and nursing care →
P ulmonary stenosis R ight ventricular hypertrophy O verriding aorta V SD 🧒 Tetralogy of Fallot Picture, memory hook and nursing care →

Sudden deep cyanosis, usually triggered by crying, feeding or straining — anything that drops systemic resistance and sends more blood right-to-left. Put the infant in the KNEE-CHEST position immediately. Older children squat instinctively - it does the same thing. Why it works: flexing the hips raises systemic vascular resistance, which pushes blood back through the pulmonary artery to be oxygenated. Then: calm the child, oxygen, morphine if ordered, IV fluids .

It looks like feeding trouble, not like adult heart failure. Sweating with feeds ; tiring after a few minutes Poor weight gain — often the earliest sign Tachypnea and tachycardia at rest Hepatomegaly — the pediatric equivalent of peripheral edema Periorbital edema rather than ankle swelling Ankle edema is an adult sign. In a baby, look at the liver and the weight chart. 🧒 Pediatric heart failure Picture, memory hook and nursing care →

entries.h: 🍽️ Feeding a baby in heart failure
entries.t: Small, frequent feeds ; limit each to about 30 minutes — longer burns more calories than it delivers Higher-calorie formula Feed at the first hunger cue , before crying exhausts them Cluster care to allow long rests Daily weights — the best measure of both nutrition and fluid

Count the apical pulse for a full minute before every dose Hold and report: <90–110 in an infant, <70 in a child Early toxicity in a child is usually vomiting and bradycardia — not the visual changes adults get Watch potassium — low potassium worsens digoxin toxicity Never repeat a dose that was vomited, and never mix digoxin into a bottle of formula - if the feed is not finished, the dose is unknown.

Fever for 5 or more days plus red eyes, strawberry tongue , cracked lips, rash, and swollen red hands and feet that later peel. It inflames coronary arteries and causes aneurysms , so treatment is IVIG plus aspirin — the one situation where a child is deliberately given aspirin. After IVIG, live vaccines must be delayed about 11 months - the antibodies block the immune response. 🧒 Kawasaki disease Picture, memory hook and nursing care →

Left-to-right = failure. Right-to-left = blue. Tet spell → knee-chest immediately Coarctation: arms high, legs low — compare both Infant heart failure = sweating with feeds, poor weight gain, hepatomegaly Apical pulse for a full minute before digoxin Kawasaki is the exception where aspirin is given Sources. Synchronized or not · what each device is for · living with one NG-405 Cardiovascular ADHD-friendly visual edition The whole topic turns on one distinction: cardioversion is synchronized, defibrillation is not . Synchronized means the shock waits for the R wave. If there is no R wave to wait for, you cannot synchronize. Cardioversion SYNCHRONIZED · low energy · a pulse is present Defibrillation NOT synchronized · high energy · V-fib or pulseless V-tach Pacemaker Too slow — it makes the heart beat ICD Too fast and l

Synchronized cardioversion An unstable tachyarrhythmia with a pulse may need synchronized cardioversion. The device times delivery to the R wave. Confirm synchronization; sedate when feasible. Defibrillation Use unsynchronized shock for ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia. Sustained polymorphic VT also requires immediate defibrillation. Pacemaker Provides pacing impulses when needed. Used for selected slow rhythms or conduction disorders; some devices also resynchronize ventricular contrac

Doing it safely Confirm the rhythm and check for a pulse before choosing the mode. Turn the sync button ON for cardioversion, OFF for defibrillation. Check it every single time — some machines reset to off after each shock. “All clear” — look at the bed, look at yourself, look around, then shock. Nobody touching anything. Remove oxygen from the immediate area; remove nitroglycerin patches. Pads go at least 2.5 cm from a pacemaker or ICD , or use anterior-posterior placement. Resume compressions immediately after a

Living with a device — the teaching Carry the device card at all times and wear medical identification. Take your own pulse daily and report a rate below the set rate. No MRI unless the device is certified MRI-conditional. Tell every provider, including the dentist. Airport security: show the card, ask for a hand search, do not linger in the archway. Mobile phone on the opposite ear , and not carried in a breast pocket over the device. Microwaves, hair dryers and electric blankets are fine. Keep away from strong ma

Cardioversion SYNCHRONIZED · low energy · a pulse is present Defibrillation NOT synchronized · high energy · V-fib or pulseless V-tach Pacemaker Too slow — it makes the heart beat ICD Too fast and lethal — it shocks the heart back What is the difference between cardioversion and defibrillation? Show answer Cardioversion is synchronized to the R wave and used when there is a pulse. Defibrillation is unsynchronized, for V-fib and pulseless V-tach. Why can V-fib not be cardioverted? Show answer There is no organized R

entries.t: Skip to the study guide CARDIAC VALVE DISORDERS · NUR 198 M8 / EXAM 3 · BIO 280 M10
Narrow gate. Wet lungs. Diastolic rumble. The mitral valve cannot open fully, restricting blood flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle during diastole.

Sit upright, assess breathing and oxygen saturation, and obtain urgent help. Give oxygen and prescribed treatment under the emergency protocol. Severe breathlessness, falling oxygen saturation or pink frothy sputum can signal pulmonary edema. New stroke symptoms also need emergency escalation. [4]
Original Study Hub infographic + memory scene

Narrowing raises left-atrial and pulmonary venous pressure. Pulmonary congestion can follow; severe chronic disease can progress to pulmonary hypertension and right-sided failure. Rheumatic disease is the classic cause; calcification is another cause in older adults. [1] [2]
Exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, fatigue and palpitations. Atrial enlargement favors atrial fibrillation and embolic stroke. A faster rate shortens filling time and may worsen symptoms. [3]

Classic finding: an opening snap followed by a low-pitched diastolic rumble . Listen with the bell at the apex, with the patient lying on the left side. The snap may disappear with heavy calcification. Doppler echocardiography confirms and grades the narrowing. [2]

Trend breathing, oxygen saturation, lung sounds, pulse/rhythm, blood pressure, activity tolerance, intake/output and daily weight. Reassess after prescribed therapy. Escalate new respiratory distress or neurologic deficits; do not wait for a textbook murmur. [4]

Diuretics relieve congestion; prescribed rate control allows more filling time. Anticoagulation is used for indications such as atrial fibrillation or atrial thrombus. In rheumatic mitral stenosis with AF, warfarin is used rather than a DOAC. [2] Medicines do not open the narrowed valve. Suitable patients may need balloon commissurotomy or valve surgery. [1]

Look for easier breathing, improving oxygenation and congestion, controlled rate, and better activity tolerance. After diuretics, follow ordered renal-function and electrolyte testing; after anticoagulants, monitor for bleeding and follow the monitoring plan. [4]

entries.h: Match each picture to the fact
entries.t: Narrow jeweled gate: the mitral valve has trouble opening. Waiting blood cells: restricted left-atrium → left-ventricle filling. Wet lung clouds: pressure backs up into pulmonary circulation. Snapped latch + low drum: opening snap + diastolic rumble. Upright patient and nurse: assess and escalate acute breathing distress. The “wet lungs” cue describes a possible complication; early disease can be asymptomatic. Stenosis means impaired opening; regurgitation means impaired closing. [3]

entries.h: Read the original handout with these qualifications
entries.t: Lung sounds: the handout’s “clear lung sounds” line is not a rule. Pulmonary congestion and crackles can occur; right-sided failure may develop later. [2] Medication and INR notes: the handout combines several valve conditions and replacement-valve teaching. Do not apply every drug, lifelong-treatment statement or INR target to every person with mitral stenosis. Check the valve type, indication and prescribed plan. Dental care: antibiotic prophylaxis is for selected high-risk conditions and procedures, not all nati

entries.t: Diastole —blood is passing through the narrowed mitral valve while the ventricle fills.

entries.h: Why does a valve problem cause shortness of breath?
entries.t: Left-atrial pressure rises and backs up toward the lungs, producing pulmonary congestion.

entries.h: What comes first with sudden severe dyspnea?
entries.t: Position upright, assess breathing and oxygenation, and get urgent help. Follow the emergency oxygen and treatment protocol.

When the body's temperature vital sign drops too far NG-041 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition Hypothermia is a core body temperature below 95°F (35°C) — well under the typical adult range from NG-079 Vital Signs . The body becomes like a popsicle : organs slow down, can't compensate for heat loss, and the cold, irritated heart muscle can throw a deadly arrhythmia. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🧊 <95°F (35°C) the definition — cross-ref NG-079 's ~98.6°F typical baseline. 🚨 Cold heart = irritable heart Anticipate V-Fib — attach the monitor, anticipate defibrillation. 🖐️ Handle gently Rough movement can trigger a lethal arrhythmia in a hypothermic heart. 🌡️ Warm the trunk first Core before extremities — prevents "afterdrop." 🧊
STEP 1 · WHY THE BODY SHUTS DOWN One number defines it, one mechanism explains everything else that happens after.

entries.h: 🌡️ The definition — and why the heart is the danger
entries.t: Hypothermia = core temp below 95°F (35°C) . Below that line, organs — including the myocardium (heart muscle) — cool down and become unable to compensate for ongoing heat loss.

Cold exposure Heat loss exceeds heat production. Hypothermia Core temperature falls and organ function slows. Frostbite Tissue freezes and develops local injury. Hypothermia care Handle gently, prevent further heat loss and use the appropriate rewarming pathway. Frostbite care Protect tissue, avoid rubbing and prevent refreezing after thawing. Assess Mental status, breathing, circulation and the extent of injury. Stage cutoffs vary slightly by source/protocol — treat as typical teaching bands, not one hard rule. 🧠

entries.h: 🚨 Why the heart is the emergency
entries.t: The nearly-frozen myocardium becomes irritated , which can trigger deadly arrhythmias — especially Ventricular Fibrillation (V-Fib) . 🧠 NCLEX priority: attach cardiac monitor 1st , anticipate defibrillation 2nd .

👴 Older adults reduced thermoregulation 👶 Infants large SA:mass ratio 🏚️ Homeless / outdoor exposure 🍺 Intoxicated vasodilation + impaired judgment 🩸 Trauma / burns 🦋 Hypothyroid 🧠 "Old, young, drunk, hurt." Four groups that can't compensate for cold as well as a healthy adult. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT IT Heart and lungs both tell on a cooling body — and the findings get quieter, not louder, as it worsens.

💓 Pulses : weak and thready — from the cold heart muscle 🫁 Wheezing may be heard — indicates bronchospasm 🫁 Crackles at the lung bases — indicates pulmonary edema from fluid buildup SEE ALSO NG-082 Assessment Locations — where to listen for these lung/heart findings. 🧠 "Quiet, not loud." As hypothermia worsens, vital signs typically slow and weaken — don't expect a loud, obvious presentation.

Stage Approx. temp Typical presentation Mild 90–95°F (32–35°C) Shivering, tachycardia, tachypnea, mild confusion Moderate 82–90°F (28–32°C) Shivering stops, decreased LOC, bradycardia, bradypnea, arrhythmia risk rises Severe <82°F (<28°C) Unresponsive, high risk of V-Fib/asystole; pulses may be very hard to detect These bands are commonly taught but vary by textbook/protocol — verify against your program's source. 🧠 "Not dead until warm and dead." A profoundly hypothermic client can look clinically dead but may sti
Do not move a hypothermic client roughly or abruptly — jostling a cold, irritable heart can precipitate V-Fib. 🧠 "Gentle hands, cold heart."

Rewarming the extremities before the core can push cold, acidotic peripheral blood back toward the heart, dropping core temperature further and worsening arrhythmia risk. 🧠 "Trunk first, limbs later." 🩺
STEP 3 · REWARM SAFELY Airway and circulation first, then rewarm from the inside out — three tiers depending on severity.

1 🫁 Airway — anticipate mechanical ventilation if severe 2 🫀 Circulation — attach cardiac monitor, anticipate defibrillation 🧠 1st = monitor, 2nd = defib-ready. A cold, irritable heart needs continuous monitoring before anything else once airway is secured.
For mild hypothermia: Remove wet/cold clothing Cover with warm blankets — head & trunk Warm, dry environment

For moderate–severe hypothermia: Warmed IV fluids via 2 large-bore IVs Warm, humidified oxygen More invasive core-warming measures for severe cases, per facility protocol 🧠 "2 big lines, warm inside." Two large-bore IVs of warmed fluid is the classic active internal intervention.

entries.h: 🌡️ Passive vs active rewarming — side by side
entries.t: 🧠 "Blankets for mild, lines for the sick." Passive external rewarming is enough for mild cases; moderate-to-severe cases need active internal warming plus continuous cardiac monitoring.

NG-079 Vital Signs — the ~98.6°F typical baseline this condition drops well below. › NG-082 Assessment Locations — where to auscultate the wheezing/crackles and palpate the weak, thready pulses described above. › NG-190 Head-to-Toe Assessment — temperature's place inside the full systematic exam. › ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧊 <95°F (35°C) the definition of hypothermia 🚨 V-Fib risk cold, irritated myocardium — monitor 1st, defib-ready 2nd 🫁 Wheezing + basilar crackles bronchospasm + pulmonary edema 🌡️ Trunk before limbs avoid afterdrop when rewarming

Q1: What core temperature defines hypothermia? Show answer Below 95°F (35°C) — well under the typical adult vital sign baseline (~98.6°F) from NG-079 . Q2: What is the priority arrhythmia risk in hypothermia, and what are the first two nursing actions? Show answer Ventricular fibrillation (V-Fib) from the cold, irritated myocardium — attach the cardiac monitor first, anticipate defibrillation second. Therapeutic Patient Positions & Their Indications NG-072 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition Every position is a tool, not a default. The nurse picks a position to ensure comfort and safety while preventing complications related to the client's condition, treatment, or procedure. Pick the wrong one and you can drop a blood pressure, aspirate a patient, or blow a fresh surgical line. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

⬇️ Trendelenburg Head down, feet up — for shock / hypotension & central line work. ⬆️ Semi/High-Fowler's Head up 30–90° — for SOB, cardiac issues, NG tube feeding. 🤰 Sims' Semi-prone, top knee to chest — for enemas & perineal exams. 🚨 Aspiration risk Never feed a patient flat — HOB up 30–45° during & after meals/tube feeds. 🛏️
STEP 1 · THE PURPOSE Positioning is never random — every position serves comfort, safety, a procedure, or a physiologic goal.

To ensure client comfort and safety while preventing complications related to the client's condition, treatment, or procedure. 🫁 Respiratory support — upright positions ease breathing & maximize lung expansion. ❤️ Hemodynamic support — head-down positions increase venous return in shock. 🩹 Post-procedure protection — the right position protects a fresh surgical site or line. 🛡️ Skin integrity — repositioning at least every 2 hours prevents pressure injury. 🚽 Access for a procedure — enemas, pelvic exams, and childb

entries.h: 🦴 Body alignment matters in every position
entries.t: Whatever position you choose, keep the spine neutral, support joints in slight flexion , and use pillows/wedges to prevent foot drop , shoulder subluxation, and skin shear. 🧠 Alignment first, position second. A "correct" position with a dangling foot or twisted neck is still a bad position.

Bedbound clients: reposition at least every 2 hours . Chair-bound: shift weight every 15 minutes , full reposition every 1 hour . 🧠 "2 in bed, 1 in the chair." Bed = every 2 hours; chair = every 1 hour (with small shifts every 15 min). 🧍
STEP 2 · KNOW EACH ONE Seven named positions — picture each one, memorize the one-line indication.

Assess the goal Comfort, respiratory support, procedure access or protection. Choose the position Account for diagnosis, precautions and mobility. Reassess tolerance Check symptoms, pressure areas, alignment and circulation. Respiratory care Upright positioning may ease breathing when appropriate. Pressure prevention Reposition and offload using an individualized schedule. Procedure-specific care Follow instructions for the procedure and patient condition. Indication: Abdominal, facial & extremity surgeries; the de

Indication: Drainage of the mouth after oral/neck surgery; allows full extension of hip & knee joints. 🧠 Prone = face-down on the ground. Good for drainage — gravity pulls secretions out of the mouth.
Indication: GI issues, rectal surgery, and pressure-injury prevention (alternate sides). 🧠 Right lateral = right side down. Name the side that's touching the mattress.
Indication: Administering enemas, perineal exams, and comfort in pregnancy. 🧠 Sims' = "S" for enema. Upper knee climbs toward the chest, upper arm flexes at the elbow.

Indication: Cardiac issues, shortness of breath (SOB), or NG tube feeding — gravity keeps the diaphragm free & secretions out of the airway. 🧠 Low → high: Semi-Fowler's 30–40° → Fowler's 45–60° → High-Fowler's 90° . Higher angle = more respiratory/cardiac relief.

Indication: Hypotension/shock (increases venous return), GYN & abdominal hernia surgery, central line placement/removal, and treatment of venous air embolism (traps air away from the pulmonary outflow tract). 🧠 Trendelenburg = treat the pressure that's TOO LOW. Feet up sends blood back to the heart and brain.

Indication: Promotes perfusion during surgery in obese patients; helps prevent aspiration. 🧠 Reverse = the opposite problem. Same tilted-bed idea as Trendelenburg, flipped — head high instead of head low.
Indication: Gynecological procedures & childbirth — most commonly seen in OB. 🧠 Lithotomy = "L" for labor and delivery. Stirrups + legs up = the classic OB/GYN table position.

Position Correct use Common wrong-answer trap Trendelenburg Hypotension/shock, GYN & hernia surgery, central line access NOT for a patient with increased ICP or respiratory distress — head-down worsens both Semi/High-Fowler's SOB, cardiac patients, tube feeding NOT flat — never feed or run a tube feeding with HOB flat Sims' Enemas, perineal exams, pregnancy comfort Confused with plain lateral — Sims' specifically flexes the upper leg and arm Prone Oral secretion drainage, full hip/knee extension Avoid in late pregn
STEP 3 · SAFE POSITIONING Assess before you move, support what you place, and reassess after.

Assess hemodynamic stability (a hypotensive patient can drop further with rapid position changes — reposition slowly). Assess lines, drains, and dressings before and after the move. Assess skin at every position change for redness/breakdown. Check for orders/contraindications (spinal precautions, recent surgery, ICP). 🧠 CHECK before you ACT. Robo's study map: Step → Check → Act — assess first, every time.

🛏️ Pillows/wedges under joints to maintain neutral alignment. 🦶 Footboards or high-top sneakers to prevent foot drop . 🌀 Trochanter rolls to prevent hip external rotation (supine). 🎈 Pressure-redistribution mattress for high pressure-injury risk. 🧠 Support the gaps. Anywhere there's an empty space between the body and the bed, put a pillow there.

entries.h: 🚨 The one you must never forget
entries.t: Never leave a patient flat during or right after a tube feeding or oral meal — keep HOB elevated 30–45° for at least 30–60 minutes after to prevent aspiration. 🧠 "Flat feeds fail." Flat + feeding tube = aspiration pneumonia risk.

Positioning covers bed mobility — how a client lies. Once they're moving out of bed, body mechanics, gait belts, and assistive devices take over. See the companion page for safe transfers, ambulation, and fall prevention. ➡️ See NG-167 — Ambulation (Body Mechanics & Mobility) for logrolling, transfers, and the wide-base-of-support principles that protect both nurse and patient during a position change. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD ⬇️ Trendelenburg Shock, GYN/hernia surgery, central lines ⬆️ Fowler's SOB, cardiac, NG feeding — never flat while feeding 🤰 Sims' Enemas, perineal exam, pregnancy comfort 🦵 Lithotomy OB/GYN procedures — stirrups, hips flexed

Q1: A hypotensive post-op patient needs a BP boost fast — which position? Show answer Trendelenburg — head down, feet up increases venous return to the heart. Q2: A patient with SOB and a new NG tube feeding — which position and why? Show answer Semi- or high-Fowler's (30–90°) — eases breathing and prevents aspiration during the feed. Q3: What's the difference between lateral and Sims' position? Show answer Lateral is simple side-lying; Sims' is semi-prone with the upper leg flexed toward the chest and upper arm fl

Standard Precautions · Transmission-Based Precautions · Donning & Doffing NG-073 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition Every barrier you put on — gloves, gown, mask, goggles — exists to stop germs moving between a contaminated surface and a clean one. Standard precautions apply to every patient, every time ; transmission-based precautions stack an extra barrier on top when you know (or suspect) contact, droplet, or airborne spread. The doffing order — not donning — is the single highest-yield NCLEX point in thi

🧤 Standard = ALWAYS Blood, body fluids, secretions, excretions, mucous membranes, non-intact skin — on every single patient. 🥽 Gloves come off FIRST Doffing order is reversed and gloves — the dirtiest item — are always removed first. 😷 N95 = Airborne Measles, TB, Varicella (chickenpox/shingles) need an N95 & negative-pressure room. 🧼 Hand hygiene = LAST The final step of doffing, every single time, no exceptions. 🧤
STEP 1 · THE FLOOR EVERYONE STANDS ON The baseline layer of protection used on every patient, every encounter — regardless of diagnosis or infection status.

entries.h: 🦠 Why this whole topic exists: nosocomial infection
entries.t: Sterile & aseptic technique exist to drastically reduce (and ideally eliminate) the chance of bacteria entering a wound, catheter site, or sterile body cavity — cutting the risk of a nosocomial infection , also called a healthcare-associated infection (HAI) : "nosocomial" literally means "hospital-acquired."

Source and route Identify how organisms can spread. Appropriate barrier Hand hygiene, equipment practices and PPE reduce transfer. Reliable technique Correct use matters as much as equipment selection. Standard precautions Apply to all patient care based on anticipated exposure. Transmission-based precautions Add contact, droplet or airborne measures when indicated. Aseptic practice Protect key sites and sterile fields from contamination. 🧠 "Standard is the floor, transmission is the extra wall." You never drop sta

Touching blood , body fluids, secretions, excretions Touching contaminated items or surfaces Touching mucous membranes Touching non-intact skin 🧠 "If it's wet and it's not yours, glove up." Any body substance that isn't sweat = standard-precaution glove indication.

Use during procedures & patient-care activities when contact of your clothing or exposed skin with blood, body fluids, secretions, or excretions is anticipated — think splash, spray, or heavy contact, not just a quick vitals check. 🧠 Gown = protects your clothes ; gloves = protect your hands . Different barrier, different job.

Wear a surgical mask within 3 feet (<3 ft) of a patient when respiratory secretions or splash to the face are anticipated — this is a standard-precaution mask, distinct from the N95 respirator reserved for airborne precautions (Step 2). 🧠 "3 feet, surgical. Airborne, N95." Distance-based splash protection is a different tool from a fit-tested airborne respirator — don't mix them up on the exam. 🚧
STEP 2 · ADD THE RIGHT WALL Three categories, three barriers, three sets of diseases — contact, droplet, and airborne each protect against a different way germs travel.

entries.h: 🚧 Contact vs. Droplet vs. Airborne — side by side
entries.t: Type Extra barrier How it spreads Example diseases 🤲 Contact Gown + gloves for touching patient/environment Direct or indirect touch — skin, equipment, surfaces MRSA, VRE, C. diff, wounds, scabies 💧 Droplet Surgical mask, < 3 ft or entering room Large respiratory droplets — cough, sneeze, talking Flu, strep, pertussis, mumps, rubella 🌬️ Airborne N95 respirator + negative-pressure room Tiny particles that float & travel on air currents Measles, TB, Varicella (chickenpox/shingles) 🧠 Barrier scales with particle size.

S carlet fever, Strep pharyngitis P ertussis (whooping cough), Parvovirus B19 (5th disease) I nfluenza (also contact) D iphtheria (pharyngeal) E piglottitis (H. influenzae type b) R ubella (German measles) M umps, Meningitis (meningococcal), Mycoplasma pneumonia A de N ovirus (also contact) 🧠 "SPIDERMAN swings 3 feet, then stops." Droplets are heavy — they can't hang in the air like Spider-Man's web across a whole room. Mask up within 3 feet, no negative pressure room needed.

M easles T uberculosis (TB) V aricella — chickenpox and disseminated herpes zoster/shingles (airborne + contact) 🧠 MTV plays on air. All three float on air currents across a whole room — door stays closed, negative-pressure room, fit-tested N95 .

M ultidrug-resistant organisms — MRSA, VRE R espiratory infections — RSV, parainfluenza S kin infections — impetigo, lice, scabies, herpes simplex W ounds with excessive drainage / staph E nteric — C. diff , norovirus, rotavirus (soap & water only — sanitizer does NOT kill C. diff spores) E ye infections — conjunctivitis 🧠 "MRS WEE has an accident" — she picked up a resistant bug, has a runny nose, a rash, a weepy wound, and can't make it to the bathroom. Everything on this list is something your hands or gown can

entries.h: 🧻 Special case: C. diff needs soap & water, not sanitizer
entries.t: EXAM TRAP Alcohol-based hand sanitizer does not kill Clostridioides difficile spores. For diarrheal illnesses of unknown origin or confirmed C. diff , norovirus , or rotavirus — wash with soap and water every time. Also remember Hepatitis A is spread through stool, so diapered or incontinent patients need the same enteric-contact awareness. 🧠 "Spores laugh at sanitizer." Friction + running water physically washes spores away; alcohol gel just isn't strong enough to destroy them. 🥽
STEP 3 · THE ORDER THAT'S TESTED Putting PPE ON is forgiving. Taking it OFF is not — the doffing order is the single highest-yield fact in this topic.

1 🥼 Gown — tie in back 2 😷 Mask or respirator — mold to nose, check seal 3 🥽 Goggles or face shield 4 🧤 Gloves — pull cuffs over gown sleeves 🧠 "Gown-Mask-Goggles-Gloves = GMGG, biggest to hands." You build the barrier from your core outward — gloves go on last so the cuff seals over the gown sleeve.

entries.h: 🥽 Doffing (taking OFF) — most contaminated FIRST, hand hygiene LAST
entries.t: 🧤 Gloves first — they touched the patient directly and are the most contaminated item on your body 🥽 Goggles / face shield next — grab by the strap/ear pieces only, never the front 🥼 Gown next — unfasten at the neck, pull down and away rolling it inside-out, contaminated side stays inward 😷 Mask / respirator last of the PPE — touch only the ties/loops, never the front panel 🧼 Hand hygiene — the true final step of every doffing sequence 📍 Order is one question, where is another. Everything comes off at the doorway o

entries.h: 🚨 NCLEX trap: why gloves come off first
entries.t: Gloves are the single most contaminated surface on your body after patient contact — leaving them on while you touch your goggles, gown ties, or mask would transfer pathogens straight to those "cleaner" surfaces. Removing them first protects everything you touch next. 🧠 If an NCLEX question asks "what do you remove first?" and gloves are an option — gloves win, every time.

Peel gloves off touching only the outside-to-outside , then tuck the second glove inside the first Discard PPE in the designated receptacle before leaving the room Perform hand hygiene immediately after the last item comes off 🧠 "Glove in a glove." The classic peel-and-tuck keeps the contaminated outer surface balled up inside, away from your bare skin. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧤 Standard precautions = every patient, every time — gloves, gown, mask as indicated 🚧 Contact / Droplet / Airborne = gown+gloves / mask <3ft / N95 + negative pressure 🧠 SPIDERMAN · MTV · MRS WEE = droplet · airborne · contact disease mnemonics 🥽 Doffing: gloves first, wash last = the #1 tested fact in this topic

Q1: What is the very first item removed when doffing PPE? Show answer Gloves — they're the most contaminated item and removing them first prevents transferring pathogens to your goggles, gown, or mask. Q2: A patient has active TB. What PPE and room setup are required? Show answer Airborne precautions — a fit-tested N95 respirator and a negative-pressure isolation room with the door closed (MTV: Measles, TB, Varicella). Q3: A patient has C. diff diarrhea. Is alcohol-based hand sanitizer enough? Show answer No — sani
