Surgical Asepsis · Sterile Field Setup · Sterile Gloving NG-074 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition Sterile technique is performed to drastically reduce — and ideally eliminate — the chance of bacteria entering a wound, catheter site, or sterile body cavity , cutting the risk of a nosocomial (hospital-acquired) infection . Four rules protect the entire field: the 1-inch border is contaminated , anything below waist level is contaminated , reaching over the field contaminates it, and wet = contaminated. Steril

📏 1-inch border = dirty Everything inside a sterile field is sterile except the outer 1-inch edge. ⬇️ Below the waist = dirty Anything under waist level or out of your direct sightline is contaminated. 💧 Wet = contaminated Moisture wicks bacteria through a barrier — strike-through means contamination. 🙅 Never reach over the field Reaching across a sterile field contaminates it — go around instead. 🧾
STEP 1 · PURPOSE, SUPPLIES, ASSESS Know why you're doing this, gather everything within reach, and screen the patient before you ever open a kit.

entries.h: 🎯 Purpose & when sterile technique is used
entries.t: Surgical procedures, catheter insertion/changes, chest tube care, cervical checks, and any time you're working on a body part that wouldn't normally contact bacteria — a sterile body cavity, a fresh wound bed, the bloodstream. Surgical asepsis ("sterile technique") aims to eliminate organisms entirely — a much higher bar than the "reduce" goal of medical/clean asepsis (see the Asepsis & Handwashing page). 🧠 "If it doesn't normally meet germs, it gets sterile technique." Skin meets germs all day — a fine needle aspi

Sterile kit (pre-packaged, unexpired) Running water and soap Sterile gloves — sometimes packaged inside the kit A clean, dry surface for setup Clean paper towels 🧠 Check the expiration date before you even open the outer wrapper — an expired kit is treated as non-sterile.

Confirm the need for the procedure Assess the site for existing infection Screen for latex, iodine, or adhesive allergies Assess pain level — give analgesia 30–45 min before the procedure for comfort 🧠 "LIA before you begin" — L atex, I odine, A dhesive. Ask about all three before you open a single package.

Risk for infection Risk for impaired tissue integrity Risk for pain Risk for hypersensitivity reaction — think latex/iodine/adhesive 🧠 Same four risks apply to nearly every sterile procedure — infection, tissue damage, pain, and allergy — build your care plan around these before you even touch the kit. 🧤
STEP 2 · FIELD SETUP & STERILE GLOVING Four rules govern the entire field. Break one, and the whole field — or your glove — is contaminated.

entries.h: 📏 The four rules of a sterile field

entries.t: Source and route Identify how organisms can spread. Appropriate barrier Hand hygiene, equipment practices and PPE reduce transfer. Reliable technique Correct use matters as much as equipment selection. Standard precautions Apply to all patient care based on anticipated exposure. Transmission-based precautions Add contact, droplet or airborne measures when indicated. Aseptic practice Protect key sites and sterile fields from contamination. 📏 The outer 1-inch border of any sterile drape or package is always contamina

entries.h: 🧾 Setting up the sterile field — step by step
entries.t: 1 🧼 Check the expiration date on the package and perform hand hygiene 2 📦 Open the kit using the special flap so the first flap opens away from you 3 🤏 Pinch the remaining flaps on their outside corners only and pull them back gently 4 🚫 Do not touch the inside — everything inside is sterile except the 1-inch border 5 🗑️ Throw the outer wrapper away 6 🧤 Get sterile gloves ready on a clean, dry surface next to the field 🧠 "Flap away, pinch the corners, hands stay out." The whole setup is really one rule repeated: yo

1 🧼 Wash hands the same thorough way as before; dry with a clean paper towel 2 📦 Open the glove wrapper so the gloves lie in front of you — do not touch them yet 3 ✋ With your dominant hand, grab the other glove by the folded wrist cuff only 4 🧤 Slide that glove on, leaving the cuff folded — don't let the outside touch your skin 5 🤲 Slide the fingers of your gloved hand under the cuff of the second glove to lift it — glove that hand keeping fingers flat, thumb away from skin 6 🔄 Reach under both cuffs and unroll th

entries.h: 🚨 Break in technique — what to do
entries.t: If a gloved hand touches anything outside the sterile field — a rail, your own skin, an unsterile surface — remove the gloves, wash hands again, and redo the entire gloving sequence with a brand-new pair. Once gloved, touch only your sterile supplies. 🧠 There is no "just this once." Any break in sterile technique means starting the gloving sequence completely over — there's no partial fix. 📋
STEP 3 · DOCUMENT & TEACH The procedure isn't done when the field comes down — document it and prep the patient to protect the site themselves.

Date and time of the procedure Type of procedure performed Fluid/exudate from the site — color, amount, odor Follow hospital policy for dating, timing & initialing dressings, specimens, or catheter sites Document the client's tolerance of the procedure 🧠 "CTFO" — C olor, amount ( T otal), odor, F luid type — describe drainage the same four ways every time.

Practice good personal hygiene Ask for analgesia before pain becomes unbearable — don't wait it out Know the signs & symptoms of infection and when to notify the HCP 🧠 Teach the same infection red flags every time: increasing redness, warmth, swelling, pain, purulent drainage, or fever — call the HCP if any appear.

🌡️ Fever >100.3°F 🔴 Increasing redness around the site 🥵 Warmth & swelling 🤕 Increasing pain not resolving 🧪 Purulent drainage foul odor 🧠 Any one of these after a sterile procedure is enough to notify the HCP — don't wait for all of them to appear together. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 📏 1-inch border = always contaminated, even on a sterile drape ⬇️ Below waist / out of sight = contaminated 💧 Wet = contaminated strike-through wicks bacteria through the barrier 🔄 Any break = start over new gloves, rewash, redo the whole sequence

Q1: How much of a sterile drape's border is considered contaminated? Show answer The outer 1 inch — everything inside that border is sterile, the border itself is not. Q2: A nurse's sterile glove brushes the bed rail. What now? Show answer Remove the gloves, wash hands again, and redo the entire sterile gloving sequence with a new pair — there's no partial fix for a break in technique. Q3: Why is a wet sterile drape considered contaminated? Show answer Moisture allows bacteria to wick through the barrier by capilla

entries.h: Vital Signs · NG-079 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Fundamentals of Nursing

Temp · Pulse · Respirations · BP · SpO2 — and Pain, the "extra" vital sign NG-079 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition Vital signs are the baseline data every assessment starts with — one number, one set of locations, one reason it moves. This page is the foundation card for the whole Nursing Core batch: NG-082 Assessment Locations zooms into exactly where you find these, and NG-190 Head-to-Toe puts them inside the full physical exam. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🖐️ 5 vitals, 1 baseline Temp · Pulse · Respirations · BP · SpO2 — all measured, all compared to the client's own trend. 🚨 SpO2 <85% Severe hypoxia — this is an emergency, not a "recheck it" number. ⏱️ Irregular pulse? Count apical for a full 60 seconds — never estimate an irregular rhythm. 😖 Pain = 5th/6th vital Ask every time, 0–10 scale — it's subjective, and it's still data. 🌡️
STEP 1 · KNOW THE BASELINE One number, one set of locations, one reason it moves — learn all three together and the rest of nursing school gets easier.

entries.h: 🫀 Where these vitals live on the body
entries.t: Pulses can be palpated at seven classic sites; the apical pulse and lung sounds are auscultated , not palpated. Full landmark detail lives on NG-082 Assessment Locations — this is the quick map.

Observe and ask History and appearance provide context. Examine and measure Use the correct technique and equipment. Interpret and reassess Compare with baseline and the clinical picture. Vital signs Temperature, pulse, breathing, pressure and oxygenation need context. Head-to-toe Use a consistent sequence while prioritizing urgent findings. Focused assessment Investigate the specific symptom or change in greater detail. SEE ALSO NG-082 Assessment Locations — exact landmark technique for every point above, plus hea

Vital Sign Typical adult reference range Common sites What moves it How we classify it 💓 Pulse 60–100 bpm Radial, carotid, brachial, femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial, apical Exercise, cardiac output changes, fluid volume shifts Absent, weak, normal, increased, bounding 🩸 BP < 120 /< 80 mmHg Brachial (standard), radial, popliteal, posterior tibial Acid–base balance, activity, fluid volume shifts Normal, hypotensive, hypertensive (staged) 🫁 Respirations 12–20 breaths/min Anterior & posterior chest

~98.6°F / 37°C is the commonly-cited average — real "normal" is a range , roughly 97.8–99.1°F , and it shifts with time of day, age, and site measured. Febrile = has a fever Afebrile = no fever Sites, most → least invasive-accurate: rectal ≈ temporal > oral > axillary 🧠 Cross-ref: hypothermia is core temp <95°F (35°C) — full pathophysiology on NG-041 Hypothermia.

60–100 bpm at rest. Always note rate, rhythm, AND quality — three data points, one vital sign. 0 = absent 1+ = weak / thready 2+ = normal 3+ = increased / full 4+ = bounding 🧠 Irregular rhythm? Count the apical pulse for a full 60 seconds — never a 15-second count ×4.

12–20 breaths/min, counted for a full minute without the client knowing (they'll change their pattern if they notice you counting). Eupnea = normal, unlabored Tachypnea = fast, > 20 Bradypnea = slow, < 12 Apnea = absent breathing 🧠 "Count the chest, not the story." Keep your fingers on the pulse site while you covertly watch the chest rise — the client relaxes their breathing when they think you're still counting pulse.

Systole = max contraction of the left ventricle (top number). Diastole = pressure of the resting ventricles (bottom number). 🧠 "Systole = Squeeze." Both start with S — the squeeze makes the top number.

95–100% is the typical adult reference range. Below that, hypoxia is commonly taught in tiers: 🧠 "85 = call for backup." Under 85% is severe hypoxia — that's an emergency escalation, not a "recheck in an hour."

Pain is assessed at every vitals check using a 0–10 numeric scale (or a validated behavioral/faces scale for nonverbal clients). It's subjective — the client's report is the data Ask location, quality, timing, aggravating/relieving factors Reassess after every intervention 🧠 "Pain is what the patient says it is." Never substitute your own judgment of how much pain "looks right." 🔎
STEP 2 · READ THE CLUES Individual numbers matter less than the pattern they make together — a fast pulse plus a rigid belly tells a very different story than a fast pulse alone.
🧠 "HF = Heavy Fluid." Crackles at the lung bases = think fluid overload / heart failure. SEE ALSO NG-082 Assessment Locations — exact anterior/posterior auscultation sequence & ladder pattern.

Value Resp. acidosis Resp. alkalosis pH ↓ low ↑ high pCO2 ↑ high ↓ low HCO3 normal (acute) normal (acute) Respiratory problems move pH and pCO2 in opposite directions; verify the full ROME/Tic-Tac-Toe method your program teaches.
🔥 Fever (febrile) — above the client's typical baseline 🧊 Hypothermia — core temp <95°F (35°C) SEE ALSO NG-041 Hypothermia — full stages, rewarming priorities, at-risk populations.

Category Typical range (mmHg) Hypotension < 90/60 Normal < 120/80 Elevated 120–129 /< 80 Hypertension (staged) ≥ 130/80 , higher stage ≥ 140/90 Category cutoffs are updated periodically by clinical guidelines — verify the current version your program/facility uses.

A pulse can be the "right number" and still be abnormal — rate is only 1 of 3 things you must chart : rate, rhythm, quality. 🧠 "Number's fine, pattern's not." A rate of 88 with a thready, irregular, weak quality is NOT a normal finding — always chart all three. 🩺
STEP 3 · ACT ON IT Vital signs exist to trigger an action — know what each red-flag pattern means you do next.

entries.h: 🚨 Airway → Breathing → Circulation — the universal priority order
entries.t: 1 🫁 Airway — is it open/patent? Position, suction, anticipate advanced airway if needed 2 💨 Breathing — rate, effort, SpO2, adventitious sounds 3 🫀 Circulation — pulse, BP, cap refill, cardiac monitor if unstable 🧠 ABC never changes. Whatever the diagnosis, the priority framework for an unstable vital sign pattern is always Airway → Breathing → Circulation.
SpO2 <85% — severe hypoxia New irregular pulse — get a full apical minute + notify Temp <95°F — hypothermia protocol Rigid, board-like abdomen + fever + tachycardia — think peritonitis

A single normal-range vital sign doesn't rule out deterioration — always compare to the client's own trend , not just the textbook range. 🧠 "Trend beats snapshot." A BP of 110/70 is reassuring for most people — but it's a red flag if their baseline is 160/95.

entries.h: 🗺️ Where this page fits in the batch
entries.t: NG-082 Assessment Locations — precise pulse points, lung/heart/bowel auscultation landmarks. › NG-190 Head-to-Toe Assessment — the full systematic exam sequence, using this page's normal ranges as its baseline. › NG-041 Hypothermia — deep dive on the temperature vital sign gone dangerously low. › ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🌡️ 98.6°F / 37°C typical average temp — real range ~97.8–99.1°F 💓 60–100 bpm rate + rhythm + quality, every time 🫁 12–20/min count a full minute, don't let them notice 🌬️ 95–100% SpO2 <85% = severe hypoxia, escalate now

Q1: A client's pulse is irregular. How should the nurse count it? Show answer Count the apical pulse for a full 60 seconds — never estimate an irregular rhythm from a partial count. Q2: SpO2 reads 83%. What tier of hypoxia is this and what's the priority? Show answer Severe hypoxia (typically taught as <85%) — this is an emergency; assess airway/breathing immediately and escalate, don't just recheck later. Q3: What three things must be charted for a pulse, not just the number? Show answer Rate, rhythm, and quality

entries.h: Assessment Locations · NG-082 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Fundamentals of Nursing

Exactly where to put your fingers and your stethoscope NG-082 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition Every vital sign from NG-079 has a physical spot on the body where you actually collect it. This page is the landmark map — pulse points, lung auscultation ladder, heart's five listening points, and the abdomen's four quadrants. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

💓 7 pulse points Radial, brachial, carotid, femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial. ⚠️ Never both carotids at once Bilateral pressure can slow heart rate or drop cerebral blood flow. 🫀 "All People Enjoy Time Magazine" Aortic → Pulmonic → Erb's → Tricuspid → Mitral, top to bottom. 🩻 IAPP for the belly Inspect → Auscultate → Percuss → Palpate (auscultate BEFORE touching). 💓
STEP 1 · FIND THE BEAT Same seven sites you saw on NG-079 — here's the exact anatomy and the one you never press on both sides at once.

Observe and ask History and appearance provide context. Examine and measure Use the correct technique and equipment. Interpret and reassess Compare with baseline and the clinical picture. Vital signs Temperature, pulse, breathing, pressure and oxygenation need context. Head-to-toe Use a consistent sequence while prioritizing urgent findings. Focused assessment Investigate the specific symptom or change in greater detail. 🧠 "CBR-FPD-T" top to bottom: Carotid, Brachial, Radial, Femoral, Popliteal, Dorsalis pedis, Tib
Never palpate both carotid pulses at the same time — bilateral compression can slow the heart rate (vagal response) or reduce blood flow to the brain. 🧠 "One side of the neck at a time — always."

entries.h: ✅ Circulation checks — distal to the pulse
entries.t: Capillary refill : press nail bed, should return <3 sec Skin turgor : pinch skin, should return <3 sec Temperature should be equal bilaterally in all extremities SEE ALSO NG-190 Head-to-Toe — where these fit in the full exam sequence. 🫁
STEP 2 · WALK THE LADDER A systematic zig-zag down the chest, comparing side to side at every stop — never straight down one side then the other.

Start top-right, above the clavicle — listen for a full inhale + exhale Move to the opposite side , same spot — compare quality, depth, extra sounds Move down one interspace at a time, comparing side-to-side every stop Continue through the 6th ICS at the midaxillary line (armpit) — this covers the lower lobes Flip to posterior: client leans forward, hands in lap to separate the scapulae for a clean listen 🧠 "HF = Heavy Fluid." The lung bases are the best place to catch crackles from fluid overload / heart failure.

Use the ulnar and palmar surfaces of your hands against the chest wall while the client says "ninety-nine" — vibration should feel equal bilaterally. 🧠 Increased fremitus = consolidation (e.g., pneumonia). Decreased = air/fluid blocking transmission (e.g., pneumothorax, effusion).
Correct client language for shortness of breath: "It's hard for me to breathe and I feel short winded all the time." Dys-PNEA = Difficult breathing — a PRIORITY symptom.

Ensure the airway is open Monitor O2 saturation Place client in High Fowler's Evaluate effectiveness of respiratory effort after intervening 🧠 Most important objective data confirming hypoxia: ABGs (arterial blood gases) — not just the SpO2 number.

Bluish discoloration from hypoxia is checked at: Nailbeds — peripheral cyanosis Conjunctiva — central/mucosal cyanosis, more reliable in darker skin tones Earlobes 🧠 Also watch for: clubbing of the fingernail beds (chronic hypoxia), vertigo /dizziness, and increased pulse rate as signs of longer-term hypoxia. 🫀
STEP 3 · THE OTHER TWO STOPS Five points for the heart, four quadrants for the belly — and one order you can't mix up.

entries.h: 🫀 Heart auscultation — 5 points, "All People Enjoy Time Magazine"
entries.t: 🧠 "All People Enjoy Time Magazine" — A ortic, P ulmonic, E rb's point, T ricuspid, M itral, top to bottom down the left sternal border, ending at the apex (mitral/apical — the same spot you count the apical pulse from NG-079 ).

entries.h: 🎵 Heart sounds — S1, S2, S3, S4
entries.t: S1 “lub” — the mitral and tricuspid (AV) valves closing at the start of systole. Loudest at the apex. S2 “dub” — the aortic and pulmonic (semilunar) valves closing at the end of systole. Loudest at the base. S3 — an extra sound just after S2, early diastole: blood rushing into a volume-overloaded ventricle. Heart failure or fluid overload in an older adult ; can be normal in children, young adults and late pregnancy. S4 — an extra sound just before S1, late diastole: the atria pushing blood into a stiff ventricle.
Listen for sounds in all four quadrants . If absent, listen for a full 5 minutes before charting "absent." 🧠 Chart as active, hyperactive, or hypoactive — never just "present."

entries.h: 🚨 The order you can't mix up: IAPP
entries.t: 1️⃣ Inspect ▼ 2️⃣ Auscultate ▼ 3️⃣ Percuss ▼ 4️⃣ Palpate The abdomen is the ONE exception to the usual inspect→palpate→percuss→auscultate order — palpating or percussing first can artificially stimulate bowel sounds and give a false reading. 🧠 "Look, Listen, THEN Touch" for the belly — auscultate before you ever press on it.

Belly should be flat , non-pulsating , and even/symmetric . Ask about pain with palpation — a rigid, board-like abdomen with fever and tachycardia is peritonitis until proven otherwise and is a priority to report. SEE ALSO NG-190 Head-to-Toe Assessment — where heart, lung, and abdominal auscultation fit into the full systematic exam sequence. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 💓 7 pulse points never both carotids at once 🫁 6th ICS midaxillary lowest stop on the ladder = lower lobes 🎵 S3 “Ken-TUC-ky” · S4 “TEN-nes-see” S3 = too much volume (heart failure) · S4 = a stiff ventricle. 🩻 Auscultate before palpate only true for the abdomen

Q1: Why should you never palpate both carotid pulses at once? Show answer Bilateral pressure can slow the heart rate via a vagal response or reduce cerebral blood flow. Q2: Where is the best place to auscultate for fluid overload in the lungs? Show answer The posterior lung bases — listen for crackles ("HF = Heavy Fluid"). Q3: What's the correct order of abdominal assessment, and why is it different from other systems? Show answer Inspect, Auscultate, Percuss, Palpate — auscultate before touching so you don't artif
FROM YOUR SAVED SET

entries.h: Diet Types · NG-084 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Fundamentals of Nursing

Diet Progression & Special Therapeutic Diets NG-084 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition Diets are ordered along a texture ladder — NPO to regular — and layered with disease-specific restrictions like renal, cardiac, or diabetic diets. Know both axes: how solid the food is, and what it's restricting. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🚫 NPO Nothing by mouth — not even ice chips. Pre-op cutoff often midnight. 🥤 Clear → Full → Soft → Regular The texture progression after NPO, step by step. 🧂 Cardiac diet Low sodium — under 2g/day . 🚨 CHF + fluid restriction Educate — the heart can't pump forward, fluid backs up into the lungs. 🥣
STEP 1 · TEXTURE LADDER Post-op and GI-recovery diets advance one texture step at a time — never skip a rung.

Assess requirements Age, illness, activity and healing affect needs. Match the plan Food texture, nutrients and route fit the person. Monitor outcomes Weight, intake, function and relevant labs guide changes. Diet types A prescribed diet targets a particular need; restrictions should have a clear purpose. Swallowing Texture and liquid changes require assessment and instructions. Collaboration Include preferences, access, culture and dietitian input. 🧠 "See it, sip it, sneak it in, chew it." Clear (see through it) →

No food or water, not even ice chips. Classic use: before surgery, often ordered as NPO after midnight . 🧠 "N-P-Zero." NPO status means zero intake — ice chips still count as intake and are not automatically allowed.
Any liquid you can see through : clear juice (apple, not orange), gelatin/Jell-O, broth, water, clear sports drinks, black coffee/tea. 🧠 If you can read a newspaper through it, it's clear.
Everything in clear liquid plus liquid dairy (milk, custard, ice cream) and all other juices (with pulp okay). 🧠 "Full = clear + dairy." One-word difference from clear liquid: dairy is now allowed.

Pureed: clear + full liquid, plus pureed meats, eggs, and fruits — anything that can go in a blender. Mechanical soft: clear + full liquid, plus chopped, diced, or ground food. 🧠 Pureed = blender. Mechanical soft = knife. Same base diet, different processing tool.
Easy-to-digest foods that are low in fiber — a bridge between mechanical soft and a full regular diet. 🧠 Soft = gentle on a healing gut, not just gentle to chew. 🩺
STEP 2 · MATCH THE DIET TO THE DISEASE These restrict or emphasize specific nutrients based on a diagnosis — layered on top of, not instead of, the texture diet.

No added salt, less than 2 g of sodium/day . Often paired with a low-cholesterol diet (less than 300 mg cholesterol/day) for cardiovascular disease. Used for heart failure, hypertension, and coronary artery disease — excess sodium pulls in fluid, raising blood pressure and cardiac workload. 🧠 "Salt holds water, water raises pressure." Every gram of sodium the patient skips is a little less fluid the heart has to move.

Typically restricts sodium, potassium, phosphorus, and sometimes protein and fluid , depending on the stage of kidney disease and dialysis status. Exact restrictions vary by lab values and nephrology orders — always individualized. ➡️ See the Renal batch pages (electrolyte imbalances, AKI/CKD) for the lab values and pathophysiology behind each restriction. 🧠 Renal diet = the kidneys can't clear it, so the plate has to. Failing kidneys can't excrete potassium/phosphorus/fluid — diet does the filtering job the kidney

A balance of protein and carbohydrates , no added sugar (soda, refined pasta, white bread). Modern practice favors a consistent-carbohydrate approach — same amount of carbs at each meal/snack, timed with insulin — over a strict "diabetic diet" of banned foods. 🧠 Consistency > restriction. The goal isn't zero carbs, it's predictable carbs the insulin dose can match.

Minimizes undigested material reaching the colon — used for IBD flares, diverticulitis, bowel rest, or before/after bowel surgery . Restricts raw fruits/veggies, whole grains, nuts, and seeds. 🧠 Low-residue = "give the gut a break." Less bulk moving through an inflamed or healing bowel.

Ordered after a swallow evaluation (often with speech-language pathology); texture is modified for both food and liquids to reduce aspiration risk. Food levels (general concept): pureed → mechanically altered/ground → soft & bite-sized → regular, with each step requiring less oral processing. Liquid thickness levels (general concept): thin → nectar-thick → honey-thick → pudding-thick, from least to most viscous. Exact level names and numbering vary by facility and by the framework used (e.g., IDDSI) — always follow
STEP 3 · INTAKE, MONITORING & TEACHING Diet orders only work if intake is actually monitored and the patient understands why.

Weigh at the same time every day , same scale, same clothing — usually first thing in the morning after the first void. All liquid intake/output measured in mL . 1 oz = 30 mL — the conversion you'll use constantly. 🧠 Same time, same scale, same clothes. Any variable you change makes the trend meaningless.

Restriction: heart failure and other conditions where fluid backs up into the lungs/body — educate the patient on why , don't just enforce it silently. Encouragement: some clients need more than the recommended intake — offer favorite (diet-appropriate) drinks and keep the pitcher full and fresh. 🧠 Same intervention, opposite direction — always check the order before assuming "more fluids is always better."

Age: decreased metabolism, decreased thirst mechanism, increased fiber need in older adults. Financial constraints — fixed income, cost of protein. Religion — restricts certain foods (pork, seafood) or requires fasting periods. Appetite — illness, eating disorders, or bad past experiences with "hospital food." Environment — hospital smells/sights are not always conducive to eating. Disease & medications — a newly diagnosed diabetic may dislike the options offered; some meds suppress appetite. 🧠 Nutrition isn't just

Explain the reason for every diet restriction — adherence improves when the patient understands the "why," e.g., low-sodium prevents fluid overload in heart failure. Confirm understanding of any fluid restriction and how to track it at home. For dysphagia diets, reinforce that thickened liquids and modified textures are a safety measure, not a punishment. Coordinate with dietitian/speech-language pathology for complex or combined therapeutic diets. 🧠 "Bland but explained." A low-sodium tray tastes worse — patients

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🚫 NPO Nothing at all — not even ice chips 🥤 Clear vs Full Full liquid = clear liquid + dairy 🧂 Cardiac diet Low sodium, < 2g/day 🩸 Renal diet Restricts Na, K, phosphorus ± protein/fluid

Q1: What's the difference between clear liquid and full liquid diets? Show answer Clear liquid is anything you can see through (broth, clear juice, gelatin, water). Full liquid is clear liquid plus liquid dairy and all other juices. Q2: A heart failure patient is on a low-sodium diet — how much sodium per day, and why? Show answer Less than 2 g/day. Sodium holds fluid, and in heart failure the heart can't pump that extra fluid forward, so it backs up into the lungs/body. Q3: What nutrients does a renal diet typical

entries.h: Pain Management Detailed · NG-086 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Fundamentals of Nursing

Detailed: Pathophysiology, Assessment & Multimodal Treatment NG-086 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition Pain is whatever the patient says it is — the 5th vital sign, and the single most reported symptom in healthcare. Assess it, believe it, and treat it with the smallest effective combination of pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic tools. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🎯 Pain = subjective Believe the patient's number, not your own guess. 🪜 WHO ladder Non-opioid → weak opioid → strong opioid, adding not replacing. 🔤 PQRST / OLDCART Structured pain history — don't skip the assessment for the med. 🚨 Respiratory depression #1 opioid safety priority — assess RR before & after every dose. 🧠
STEP 1 · HOW PAIN WORKS Nociception is the whole pathway from tissue injury to the brain's perception of pain.

Assess the experience Location, quality, severity, context and functional effects. Select treatment Combine appropriate non-drug and medication approaches. Reassess Measure benefit, function and adverse effects. Opioids Monitor sedation and breathing as well as pain relief. PCA Only the patient should press the patient-controlled dose button unless a specifically authorized protocol applies. Other formulations Fentanyl patches have delayed effects and specific eligibility and heat precautions. Nociceptors are pain

entries.h: ⭐ COX-1 vs. COX-2 — why it matters for NSAIDs
entries.t: COX-1 COX-2 "Housekeeping" enzyme — protects gut lining, supports platelet function Induced by inflammation — drives pain, fever, swelling Blocking it → GI ulcers/bleeding risk Blocking it → reduces pain/fever/inflammation 🧠 COX-1 protects, COX-2 provokes. Non-selective NSAIDs block both — that's why they can cause GI upset while also relieving pain. See NG-256 NSAIDs for drug-level detail.

Endorphins and enkephalins are the body's own opioids — they inhibit substance P (a neurotransmitter that amplifies pain signals), naturally decreasing pain sensation. 🧠 "Endorphins are the body's built-in morphine." Exercise, laughter, and touch can boost this system — part of why nonpharmacologic care genuinely reduces pain, not just distracts from it.

entries.h: 📈 Acute vs. chronic pain — different bodies, different exam answers
entries.t: Acute pain Chronic pain Sudden onset, specific to an injury; lasts seconds up to 6 months Persistent, often malignant or non-malignant, lasts longer than 6 months ↑ cardiac output, impaired insulin response, immune suppression, ↑ cortisol, ↑ fluid retention Immune suppression, depression, disability, fatigue, anger, inability to perform ADLs Visible physiologic signs (↑ HR, ↑ RR, diaphoresis, grimacing) Often NO visible signs — normal vitals do not rule out chronic pain 🧠 NCLEX trap: A calm patient with normal vita
STEP 2 · ASK BEFORE YOU TREAT A structured history plus the right scale for the right patient — assessment always comes before the medication.

Letter What it means P Provocation/Palliation — aggravating & alleviating factors: what makes it worse? What makes it better? Q Quality — dull, sharp, stabbing, burning? R Region/Radiation — where is the pain? Does it radiate? S Severity — rate on a 0–10 scale T Timing — when did it start? What was happening at onset? Duration? 🧠 "Please Quit Radiating, Send Timely help." Many programs also teach OLDCART (Onset, Location, Duration, Characteristics, Aggravating/Alleviating, Radiation, Treatment) — same core question

0 None 1-3 Mild 4-6 Mod 7-9 Severe 10 Worst Gold standard when the patient can self-report — always use the patient's own number over a nurse's visual guess. 🧠 Pain is whatever the patient says it is, at the intensity they say it is.

Wong-Baker FACES scale — young children or anyone who can't use numbers; picks a face from smiling to crying. FLACC scale — infants, nonverbal, or cognitively impaired patients. Scores F ace, L egs, A ctivity, C ry, C onsolability, 0–2 each (0–10 total). CPOT / behavioral pain scales — sedated or intubated ICU patients; observe facial expression, body movement, muscle tension, ventilator compliance. 🧠 "Can't talk? Watch, don't guess." Nonverbal patients still feel pain — behavior is the vital sign when words aren't

entries.h: ⭐ Factors that influence how pain is expressed
entries.t: Past experience with pain shapes current perception and coping. Anxiety and depression both decrease the pain threshold — psych distress makes pain feel worse. Age and gender influence reporting and treatment bias. Culture — different cultures teach different "appropriate" pain responses; stoicism does not mean absence of pain. 🧠 Never assume — ask. A stoic patient from a culture that discourages outward pain expression can still be in severe pain; the number they give you is still the truth. 💊
STEP 3 · MULTIMODAL & STEPPED The WHO pain ladder steps therapy up with severity — and nonpharmacologic care belongs at every step, not just the mild ones.

entries.h: 🪜 WHO analgesic ladder — match the drug class to the severity
entries.t: 1 Mild pain (1–3): non-opioids — acetaminophen and/or NSAIDs (± adjuvant) 2 Moderate pain (4–6): weak/mild opioids (e.g., tramadol, codeine combinations) ± non-opioid 3 Severe pain (7–10): strong opioids (e.g., morphine, hydromorphone, fentanyl, oxycodone) ± non-opioid Multimodal analgesia = combining drug classes with different mechanisms (e.g., an NSAID + an opioid + a nonpharmacologic measure) to get better relief at lower opioid doses — fewer side effects, less respiratory depression risk. 🧠 The ladder adds, it

entries.h: 💊 Pharmacologic categories — see the dedicated pages for drug detail
entries.t: Non-opioids: NSAIDs (ketorolac, ibuprofen) for mild pain; acetaminophen can be given with NSAIDs and carries a hepatotoxicity risk at high/chronic doses. Opioids: tramadol, codeine (Tylenol #3), meperidine, oxycodone, fentanyl, morphine, hydromorphone. Adjuvants/routes: topical agents, local anesthesia, intraspinal (epidural/intrathecal) analgesia. Delivery methods: routine around-the-clock dosing for constant pain; PRN for breakthrough pain; PCA (patient-controlled analgesia) pump for self-titrated IV opioid dosin

entries.h: ✅ Nonpharmacologic interventions — real tools, not "just distraction"
entries.t: Cutaneous stimulation: TENS unit, massage Thermal therapy: heat and cold application Cognitive-behavioral: distraction, relaxation, guided imagery, hypnosis Music therapy Complementary: acupuncture 🧠 Nonpharm ≠ optional extra. These work through real physiologic pathways (e.g., gate-control theory, endorphin release) and should be layered in at every rung of the ladder, not reserved for "mild" pain only.

entries.h: 🚨 Opioid safety priorities — assess before AND after every dose
entries.t: Priority Why Respiratory rate Hold and notify provider if RR < 12/min — respiratory depression is the #1 life-threatening opioid adverse effect. Sedation level Increasing sedation precedes respiratory depression — a rising sedation score is an earlier warning sign than the RR itself. Bowel function Opioid-induced constipation is nearly universal — prophylactic bowel regimen, not PRN. Naloxone Opioid antagonist reversal agent — know where it is and keep it available for any patient on IV/high-dose opioids. 🧠 "Sedati

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🎯 Pain = subjective Trust the patient's number over your own guess 🪜 WHO ladder Mild → weak opioid → strong opioid, always adding non-opioid + nonpharm 🧒 FLACC / FACES Use behavior scales for nonverbal or pediatric patients 🚨 RR < 12 Hold the opioid dose, notify the provider, have naloxone ready

Q1: What does PQRST stand for in a pain assessment? Show answer Provocation/Palliation, Quality, Region/Radiation, Severity, Timing. Q2: A calm patient with normal vital signs rates their chronic pain 8/10 — what should the nurse do? Show answer Believe the reported number and treat accordingly — chronic pain often shows no visible physiologic signs, unlike acute pain. Q3: Which scale is used for a nonverbal, cognitively impaired patient? Show answer The FLACC scale (Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability) or ano

entries.h: Ethical Key Terms · NG-133 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Legal & Ethics Series

The 6 ethical principles every legal/ethics NCLEX question is built on NG-133 NURSING CORE Series: Legal & Ethics 1 of 5 ADHD-friendly visual edition Every ethics/legal NCLEX question — informed consent, restraints, refusing treatment, AMA discharge, advance directives — is secretly testing one of six words : autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice, fidelity, and veracity . Learn these six cold first — the rest of this series (Tort Law, Informed Consent, Advance Directives, AMA & Mandatory Reporting) is just

🅰️ Autonomy Competent client's right to choose — even if the nurse disagrees. 🤝 Fidelity Keep the promise — follow through on what you said you'd do. 🗣️ Veracity Tell the truth — report the error even with zero harm done. ⚖️ Justice Fair & equitable care for every client, every time. 📖
STEP 1 · KNOW THE WORDS Six pillars hold up every ethical decision a nurse makes — memorize the word, the one-line gloss, and one real example each.

entries.h: 🏛️ The six pillars of nursing ethics

entries.t: Information The responsible clinician explains benefits, risks and alternatives. Understanding and choice The person decides voluntarily with appropriate capacity support. Documentation and follow-through Record the decision and respect the care plan. Nursing role Advocate, identify unanswered questions and follow policy for witnessing consent. Advance directives Clarify preferences and the designated decision-maker under applicable law. Ethics Autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence and justice guide deliberation. 🧠

The client's right to make their own healthcare decisions , as long as they are a competent adult who has been informed of the risks. Example: Respecting a competent client's right to refuse a treatment — even a Jehovah's Witness refusing a life-saving blood transfusion, or a client signing out AMA. 🧠 NCLEX trap: the nurse's job is to educate on the risks, not to override the choice. Ignoring a competent refusal = a violation of autonomy (and can become battery — see Tort Law, page 2 of this series).

Doing and promoting good for the client — actively acting in their best interest, not just avoiding harm. Example: Calling a client's family to tell them their loved one is "critically ill and we are caring for their needs" so the family isn't left in the dark. 🧠 Beneficence = doing the good thing. Nonmaleficence (next card) is its quieter twin — not doing the bad thing.

= "first, do no harm" To avoid causing harm to the client, intentionally or through carelessness. Example: Double-checking a drug dosage with another nurse before giving a high-alert medication. 🧠 "Mal" = bad (think "malicious"). Non-mal-eficence = actively steering away from the bad outcome.

Treating clients fairly and equally — resources, time, and care distributed equitably regardless of race, gender, religion, culture, insurance status, or ability to pay. Example: Providing the same standard of care to every client on the unit, not just the ones who tip better or complain loudest. 🧠 Justice ≠ identical. True justice is equitable — the client who needs more gets more; the point is no one is shorted because of who they are .

Staying loyal to the client and following through on your responsibilities and promises — even the small ones. Example: Client reports 8/10 pain ; the nurse states she will return with pain medication — and does . 🧠 Fidelity = "I do what I said I'd do." Every broken small promise ("I'll be right back") chips away at trust — and is a fidelity violation, even if nothing bad happens medically.

To tell the truth — full, accurate information, even when it's uncomfortable. Example: A medication error occurs with NO adverse effect on the client — the nurse still reports it , and still tells the client/family it happened. 🧠 Veracity is tested by the "no harm done" trap. If the stem says "no harm resulted," students often think "so don't bother reporting." Wrong — veracity says report it anyway.

Not always grouped with the classic 6, but shows up constantly on ethics questions: to protect the client's rights, health, and safety — speaking up on their behalf. Example: Reporting a critical change in the client's condition to the HCP right away. Example: Relaying a client's wish (e.g., about code status or a treatment refusal) to the care team when they cannot speak for themselves. 🧠 Advocacy is the action arm of autonomy + beneficence combined — you protect the client's right to choose (autonomy) and their w
STEP 2 · MATCH THE SCENARIO NCLEX never says the word "autonomy" out loud — it gives you the scenario and makes you name the principle.

Scenario Principle tested Client reports 8/10 pain; nurse promises to return with pain meds — and does Fidelity 🤝 Nurse calls family: "he is critically ill and we are caring for his needs" Beneficence 💙 Nurse double-checks a drug dosage with a coworker before giving it Nonmaleficence 🚫 A medication error happens with zero adverse effect — nurse reports it anyway Veracity 🗣️ Nurse provides the same quality of care regardless of race, gender, religion, or culture Justice ⚖️ Nurse respects a competent client's decisio
🧠 Every fidelity question has this exact shape: promise made → promise kept. If the nurse promises and does NOT follow through, that's a fidelity violation — same principle, opposite direction. ⚖️
STEP 3 · PRIORITIZE The hardest ethics questions pit two good principles against each other — you have to know which one wins, and why.

entries.h: 🪢 The classic tug-of-war: Autonomy vs. Beneficence
entries.t: If the client is competent, informed, and adult , their right to choose (even to refuse) outranks what the nurse or family thinks is "best." The nurse's job shifts to educate, document, and support — not override. 🧠 "Competent wins." The single fastest way to answer an autonomy-vs-beneficence question: ask "is this client competent?" If yes — autonomy wins almost every time.

entries.h: 🚧 When autonomy does NOT automatically win
entries.t: 🧒 Client is a minor without emancipated status 🧠 Client lacks decision-making capacity — unconscious, severely impaired, actively intoxicated 🚨 True emergency , life/limb at risk, no surrogate reachable ⚠️ Client is a danger to self or others (may trigger a legal hold — varies by state ) 📋 Mandatory reporting laws override confidentiality/autonomy (abuse, certain communicable diseases) 🧠 These five exceptions come back in full on page 4 (Advance Directives) and page 5 (AMA & Mandatory Reporting) of this series.

entries.h: 🔀 Nonmaleficence vs. Beneficence — the subtle one
entries.t: Nonmaleficence (avoid harm) is usually the floor ; beneficence (do good) is the ceiling . A nurse must always clear the floor, and should reach for the ceiling when possible — but never sacrifice "do no harm" chasing "do more good." Example: Restraining an agitated client "for their own good" (beneficence reasoning) without meeting the legal criteria can cross into harm — false imprisonment (see Tort Law, next page). 🧠 "First, do no harm" outranks "do more good." If an intervention risks harm, that's a nonmaleficen
STEP 4 · DON'T GET FOOLED These six words are the connective tissue for the rest of this legal & ethics series — here's where they trip students up.

If a competent client refuses treatment and the nurse personally disagrees with the choice, the correct action is still to respect autonomy — document the refusal, ensure the client is informed, and notify the HCP. Overriding it can become battery . 🧠 The nurse's opinion is not a legal override. Feelings ≠ authority.

entries.h: ⭐ Trap: "no harm was done, so why report it?"
entries.t: A med error with zero adverse effect must still be reported — that's veracity , not overkill. Reporting also protects the next client and feeds facility safety data. 🧠 "No harm" changes the outcome, not the obligation to be honest.

entries.h: ✅ Foundation: the ANA Code of Ethics
entries.t: The American Nurses Association (ANA) establishes the ethical standards for the entire nursing profession — every one of these six terms traces back to that Code. 🧠 If a question asks "who sets nursing's ethical standards," the answer is the ANA — not a hospital's individual policy. 🔗 Where this goes next: Autonomy violated by force = NG-172 · Tort Law (battery, false imprisonment). Autonomy exercised through a signature = NG-192 · Informed Consent . Autonomy exercised in advance = NG-212 · Advance Directives . Aut

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🅰️ Autonomy Competent client's choice — nurse educates, doesn't override 💙🚫 Beneficence / Nonmaleficence Do good / avoid harm — nonmaleficence is the floor ⚖️ Justice Equitable care, regardless of who the client is 🤝🗣️ Fidelity / Veracity Keep the promise · tell the truth, even with no harm done

Q1: A client with 8/10 pain is told by the nurse "I'll be back with your medication," and the nurse returns as promised. Which principle? Show answer Fidelity — following through on a promise/responsibility. Q2: A medication error occurs but causes zero harm. Should the nurse report it? Show answer Yes — veracity requires honesty regardless of outcome. Q3: A competent adult refuses a blood transfusion the nurse believes is life-saving. What wins? Show answer Autonomy — for a competent, informed adult, their choice

entries.h: Ambulation (Body Mechanics & Mobility) · NG-167 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Fundamentals of Nursing

Body Mechanics, Mobility & Fall Prevention NG-167 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition Coordinated effort to maintain balance, posture, and body alignment while lifting, moving, and ambulating clients — protecting both the patient and the nurse's own spine. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🦴 Wide base, bent knees Feet apart, knees flexed, load close to the body — never the back. 🎗️ Gait belt = default Use it for any client with fall risk or weakness before ambulating. 🦯 Cane on the STRONG side Advance cane + weak leg together, then the strong leg. 🚨 #1 hospital injury Falls — assess fall risk before every transfer/ambulation. 🦴
STEP 1 · PROTECT THE SPINE Purpose: the safe, coordinated practice of maintaining balance, posture, and alignment while lifting, moving, and ambulating clients.

entries.h: 🏋️ The five rules of safe lifting

entries.t: Assess ability Strength, balance, cognition and weight-bearing status. Fit the device Height and technique should match the person. Practice the sequence Move safely through walking, turns and transfers. Cane Often used on the stronger side; follow individualized instruction. Crutches Support weight through the hands, not the axillae. Walker Keep the frame stable and avoid stepping too far ahead of support. 🦶 Wide base of support — feet shoulder-width apart. 🦵 Bend at the knees , not the waist — squat, don't stoop.

Arrange for help before moving a client — never solo a heavy or unpredictable transfer. Encourage the client to assist when able. Avoid twisting — keep back, neck, pelvis, and feet aligned and facing the same direction. Position yourself close to the client or object. 🧠 Close and squared-up. The nearer you are, and the more your whole body faces the load, the less shear on your spine.

Uncoordinated lifts — no count-of-three teamwork Manual lifting without equipment Lifting while tired Repetitive lifting, transferring, repositioning Prolonged standing 🧠 The team lift. The person bearing the brunt of the load calls the count of three — everyone moves together, not one person straining alone.

entries.h: 🔁 Moving a client in bed — slide, don't drag
entries.t: Slide the client toward you using a pull/draw sheet instead of dragging skin across linen — dragging causes shear and friction injury to fragile skin. 🧠 Sheet, not skin. The pull sheet takes the friction so the patient's skin doesn't have to. 🚶
STEP 2 · GAIT, ROM & TOOLS Know what normal gait and range of motion look like — then match the right assistive device to the client.

entries.h: 🩺 Mobility assessment — what to ask & observe
entries.t: Daily activity & endurance: "What does your day look like? What makes you tired?" Exercise goals and mobility problems: pain, SOB, or discomfort with movement? Physical/mental alterations and external factors affecting ambulation. Range of motion (ROM): the full movement potential of a joint — flexion & extension. Active ROM Passive ROM Patient moves the limb themselves, no assistance Therapist/equipment moves the joint — no effort from the patient 🧠 Active = "I move it," Passive = "you move it."

Normal Abnormal Head erect, spine straight, arms swing in alternation with legs; one leg in stance while the other swings Ataxia, Parkinsonian gait, scissor gait, steppage gait, spastic hemiparesis Straight line ear–shoulder–hip in alignment Abnormal spinal curvature (scoliosis), can't maintain alignment independently Full ROM, no joint deformity Limited ROM, swelling, heat, tenderness, crepitation, deformity Voluntary, controlled, coordinated movement Tremors, tics, chorea, dystonia, fasciculations 🧠 Watch the who

Age & developmental level Attitudes & family values Neuromuscular / joint disorders Trauma to the musculoskeletal system Mental health & medications (sedation, weakness) Lifestyle, stress, environment 🧠 Mobility isn't just "can they walk" — it's biology, environment, and psychology all together.

entries.h: 🦯 Assistive devices — match the tool to the deficit
entries.t: Device Best for / key point Cane 🦯 Mild weakness/balance issues on one side. Held on the strong side; advance with the weak leg. Walker 🚶 Greater instability; needs more support & upper-body strength. All 4 legs contact the floor before stepping — never "walk" it by only advancing 2 legs at a time unless it's a rolling walker with wheels . Crutches 🩼 Non-weight-bearing or partial weight-bearing on one leg. Weight goes through the hands/palms , never the axillae — axillary pressure risks nerve damage (crutch palsy)
STEP 3 · PREVENT THE #1 INJURY Falls are the leading cause of hospital-acquired injury — assess risk before every transfer.

entries.h: 🚨 Fall risk assessment — before you move anyone
entries.t: History of falls, gait/balance problems, or use of an assistive device Medications: sedatives, opioids, antihypertensives, diuretics (orthostatic hypotension risk) Cognitive status: confusion, dementia, impulsivity Sensory deficits: vision, hearing, peripheral neuropathy Environment: clutter, poor lighting, wet floors, improper footwear, tubing/lines underfoot 🧠 Assess before you ambulate, not after they fall. Most inpatient fall-risk tools (e.g., Morse Fall Scale) score history, mental status, gait, and IV/meds —

Gait belt on any client identified as fall risk Bed in lowest position , brakes locked, call light within reach Non-skid footwear before every ambulation Clear the path — cords, tubing, clutter out of the way Orthostatic check: sit → dangle → stand, pausing at each step 🧠 "Sit, dangle, stand" — never rush a first mobilization. Orthostatic hypotension causes a huge share of first-time-up-out-of-bed falls.

entries.h: ⚠️ Signs of activity intolerance — stop and reassess
entries.t: Significantly increased pulse, respirations, or BP; SOB/dyspnea; weakness; pallor; confusion; vertigo; pain. 🧠 If any of these appear during ambulation, stop, sit the patient down, and reassess vitals before continuing.

Ambulation starts with safe bed mobility . Before a client stands, they need to be positioned and moved correctly in bed — logrolling, using a pull sheet, and choosing the right position to sit up from. ➡️ See NG-072 — Positioning for the named bed positions (Fowler's, lateral, Sims', etc.) that set up a safe transfer to standing. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🦴 Bend knees, not waist Wide base, load close, use legs to lift 🦯 Cane = strong side Advance cane + weak leg together 🩼 Crutches = weight on hands Never the armpits — nerve damage risk 🚨 Sit, dangle, stand Check orthostatics before first ambulation

Q1: What are the core body mechanics rules for lifting a client? Show answer Wide base of support, bend at the knees not the waist, keep the load close to the body, use arms/legs not the back, and tighten the abdomen/glutes before moving. Q2: Where should crutch weight be borne, and why? Show answer On the hands/palms — weight on the axillae can cause nerve compression ("crutch palsy"). Q3: Which side does a cane go on, and how does the patient step? Show answer The strong side. The cane and the weak leg advance to

entries.h: Med Math Memory Tricks · NG-171 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Fundamentals of Nursing

Memory Tricks for Dosage Calculation NG-171 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition Three formulas run almost every med-math question you'll ever see : D/H×Q for tablets & liquids, mL/hr for pumps, and gtt/min for gravity tubing. Learn the formula, learn where the numbers plug in, and always convert your units first. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🎯 D/H × Q Desired ÷ Have × Quantity = amount to give. 💧 gtt/min (mL × drop factor) ÷ min — gravity/manual tubing. 🖥️ mL/hr mL ÷ hr — what you program into a pump. 🔁 Convert FIRST Same units before you plug into any formula, or the whole answer is wrong. 🧮
STEP 1 · KNOW THE THREE Almost every dosage-calc question on the NCLEX is one of these three formulas wearing a different costume.

entries.h: 💊 The master formula: D/H × Q — "Desired over Have, times Quantity"
entries.t: USE FOR tablets, capsules, and oral/IM liquids — anything where the drug comes in a fixed strength and you need to figure out how many units to give.

Read the order Identify the prescribed amount and route. Read the supply Identify concentration and available volume. Calculate and verify Cancel units and check whether the result is reasonable. Dose volume Desired dose divided by concentration gives the required volume. Infusion rate Volume divided by time gives mL/hour when units are aligned. Safety checks Use kilograms when required, leading zeros and no unnecessary trailing zeros. 🧠 "What you WANT, over what you'VE GOT, times what it comes IN." D = the order,

Formula mL/hr = Volume (mL) ÷ Time (hr) USE FOR anything running on an electronic infusion pump — you program the rate directly in mL per hour. 🧠 "Pump = per hour." If it has a screen and buttons, it wants mL/hr .

Formula gtt/min = (mL/hr × drop factor) ÷ 60 USE FOR manual/gravity tubing with no pump — you count drops falling in the drip chamber per minute. 🧠 "No pump = count the drops." Drop factor (gtt/mL) is printed right on the IV tubing package.

entries.h: ⚖️ Weight-based dosing — same D/H×Q, plus one extra step
entries.t: Many pediatric doses, and adult doses ordered as "per kilogram," use mg/kg or mcg/kg/min . You must find the total dose before you can use D/H×Q. Step 1 Weight (kg) × ordered dose (mg/kg) = total dose Step 2 If divided doses: total dose ÷ number of doses/day = dose per administration Step 3 Now plug that number into D/H × Q like any other order. 🧠 "Weight first, formula second." A weight-based order is never the final number to give — it's the D you still have to run through D/H×Q.

entries.h: 📐 Body Surface Area (BSA) — the formula behind chemo & some pediatric dosing
entries.t: Some high-alert doses (chemotherapy, certain pediatric meds) are ordered per m² of body surface area instead of per kilogram, because BSA correlates better with organ function and drug clearance. Mosteller formula BSA (m²) = √[ height (cm) × weight (kg) ÷ 3600 ] Then Total dose = BSA (m²) × ordered dose (mg/m²) 🧠 BSA math is high-stakes — verify with a second RN. These are exactly the calculations where facilities require an independent double-check before the drug leaves the Pyxis. ✍️
STEP 2 · PLUG IN NUMBERS The same five formulas, now with numbers plugged in step by step. All example numbers below are made up for practicing the math only — not real drug orders.

EXAMPLE PROBLEM · not a real order Ordered (D) 500 mg Have (H) 250 mg per tablet Quantity (Q) 1 tablet Plug in 500 ÷ 250 × 1 = 2 tablets 🧠 If D and H are already the same unit, the math is just a simple ratio.

EXAMPLE PROBLEM · not a real order Ordered (D) 750 mg Have (H) 250 mg per 5 mL Quantity (Q) 5 mL Plug in 750 ÷ 250 × 5 = 15 mL 🧠 Q is whatever volume H is measured in — here H is "per 5 mL," so Q = 5 mL, not 1.

EXAMPLE PROBLEM · not a real order Step 1 154 lb ÷ 2.2 = 70 kg Step 2 70 kg × 5 mg/kg/day = 350 mg/day Step 3 350 mg ÷ 2 doses = 175 mg/dose q12h 🧠 Weight goes to kg before anything else touches it. Skipping the lb→kg conversion is the single most common weight-based math error.

entries.h: 🖥️💧 Worked example — pump (mL/hr) vs. gravity tubing (gtt/min)
entries.t: EXAMPLE PROBLEM · not a real order Ordered 1000 mL over 8 hr, drop factor 15 gtt/mL Pump 1000 ÷ 8 = 125 mL/hr Gravity Step 1 1000 ÷ 8 = 125 mL/hr Gravity Step 2 (125 × 15) ÷ 60 = 31.25 Pump: 125 mL/hr · Gravity: round to 31 gtt/min 🧠 Same order, two different final answers depending on the equipment. Round gtt/min to a whole drop — you cannot count a quarter of a drop falling in the chamber.

entries.h: ⚡ Shortcut: skip step 2 for common drop factors
entries.t: Because 60 minutes is always the denominator, common drop factors simplify to one quick division of mL/hr: Drop factor Tubing type Shortcut from mL/hr 10 gtt/mL Macrodrip gtt/min = mL/hr ÷ 6 15 gtt/mL Macrodrip gtt/min = mL/hr ÷ 4 20 gtt/mL Macrodrip gtt/min = mL/hr ÷ 3 60 gtt/mL Microdrip gtt/min = mL/hr (1:1) 🧠 Microdrip = 60, and 60 makes gtt/min and mL/hr the SAME NUMBER. Microdrip tubing (60 gtt/mL) is used for peds, critical care, and any fluid needing very precise, small-volume control — the exact drop facto
STEP 3 · SAME UNITS FIRST Every formula above only works if D and H are already in the same unit — convert before you calculate, not after.

entries.h: 🪜 The metric staircase — mcg ⇄ mg ⇄ g, and mL ⇄ L
entries.t: Same rule for volume: 1 L = 1000 mL . And for weight: 1 kg = 2.2 lb — lb → kg, divide by 2.2; kg → lb, multiply by 2.2. 🧠 "Small word, small step; big jump, big multiply." Kilo → milli → micro is always ×1000 each step down. Confusing mcg and mg is a 1000-fold overdose — always double-check the abbreviation before you calculate.

A misread or miswritten unit — mcg mistaken for mg — is a 1000× dosing error . High-alert IV drips are especially at risk because they're often dosed in mcg/kg/min . 🧠 "Micro is minuscule." mcg is always the smallest, most cautious unit in the room — if a number in mcg looks small, that's normal, not a mistake.

Calculating a weight-based dose using pounds instead of kilograms gives an answer that's roughly 2.2× too high . Always convert weight to kg before multiplying by mg/kg. 🧠 Weight-based order? Kilos or it doesn't count. If the chart shows lb, convert first — every single time.

entries.h: ⚠️ NCLEX trap: pump formula vs. gravity formula
entries.t: Using gtt/min math when the fluid is actually running through an electronic pump (or vice versa) gives a nonsense rate. Pump screens want mL/hr; gravity tubing needs a drop count. 🧠 "Buttons = mL/hr. No buttons = count drops." Look at the equipment before you pick the formula.

Using 15 gtt/mL math on 60 gtt/mL microdrip tubing (or the reverse) throws the whole answer off. The drop factor is printed on the tubing package — never assume it. 🧠 Read the box before you do the math. Different tubing, different formula — every time.

entries.h: 🚨 High-alert meds: math isn't the only safety check
entries.t: Insulin, heparin, IV opioids, chemotherapy, and other high-alert drugs typically require an independent double-check by a second RN before administration — regardless of how confident you are in your own calculation. Correct math does not replace a required double-check. 🧠 "High alert, second set of eyes." Facility policy, not your certainty, decides when a double-check is required — always verify the policy for the specific drug. ⚡
SAY IT OUT LOUD 🎯 D/H × Q Desired ÷ Have × Quantity = amount to give 💧 gtt/min (mL/hr × drop factor) ÷ 60 🖥️ mL/hr Volume (mL) ÷ Time (hr) 🔁 Convert first kg/g/mg/mcg ×1000 down, ÷1000 up · lb÷2.2=kg

Q1: What's the master oral/IM dosage formula? Show answer D/H × Q — Desired dose ÷ Have (dose on hand) × Quantity (the form that dose comes in). Q2: An electronic pump is infusing fluid — which formula do you use, mL/hr or gtt/min? Show answer mL/hr = Volume (mL) ÷ Time (hr). gtt/min is only for gravity/manual tubing with no pump. Q3: Before calculating a weight-based dose given in pounds, what must you do first? Show answer Convert pounds to kilograms (lb ÷ 2.2 = kg) before multiplying by the mg/kg order — skippin
FROM YOUR SAVED SET

entries.h: Tort Law · NG-172 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Legal & Ethics Series

Negligence, malpractice, and the intentional torts that show up on every NCLEX legal question NG-172 NURSING CORE Series: Legal & Ethics 2 of 5 ADHD-friendly visual edition A tort is a wrongful act or violation of someone's rights that creates legal liability. Nursing torts split into two families: unintentional (negligence, malpractice — you didn't mean to cause harm, but you did) and intentional (assault, battery, false imprisonment, defamation — willful acts that violate a client's rights). The burden of proof a

🧾 Burden of proof Sits with the accuser — not the nurse. 🪜 4 elements of negligence Duty → Breach → Causation → Damages — all 4 required. 🆚 A before B Assault (threat) always comes before Battery (actual harmful contact). 🔒 No consent = Battery Any procedure or treatment given without consent is battery. 🧾
STEP 1 · DEFINE THE TERM One umbrella word — tort — covers everything from an honest mistake to a deliberate violation.

entries.h: ⚖️ Tort = a wrongful act that creates legal liability

entries.t: Recognize the issue Consent, privacy, safety or a possible legal duty. Use the correct pathway Follow applicable law and organizational policy. Document objectively Record findings, communication and actions. Leaving against advice Assess capacity, explain risks and alternatives, and support a safer plan. Reporting Mandatory duties differ by location and circumstance; use the required reporting process. Civil concepts Assault, battery, negligence and confidentiality breaches describe different issues. 🧠 "Innocent u

Civil Criminal Crime against an individual Crime against the state Most nursing torts land here More serious — can involve licensure loss, jail 🧠 Most malpractice suits are civil — but abuse, patient abandonment with harm, or falsifying records can escalate to criminal .

Used to determine the standard of care in every negligence/malpractice case: "What would a reasonable, prudent nurse — with similar training and experience, in a similar setting — have done in this same situation?" 🧠 It's not "what would a perfect nurse do" — it's what a reasonably careful peer would do. This test comes back on the Informed Consent page too. ⚖️
STEP 2 · UNINTENTIONAL TORTS Same family, different license — malpractice is negligence committed by a licensed professional.

entries.h: 🪜 The 4 elements of negligence — ALL FOUR must be present
entries.t: Example: A nurse doesn't wash hands before inserting a Foley catheter ( breach — a duty existed) and the client develops a catheter-associated UTI ( causation + damages ). All four elements present = negligence. 🧠 "DBCD — Don't Break the Client's Duty." Duty → Breach → Causation → Damages. Miss any one link and there's no negligence claim, no matter how careless the nurse was.

The failure to provide adequate care that another reasonable, prudent nurse would provide in a similar situation. Example: A nurse identifies an absent peripheral pulse in a client's casted extremity in the early morning — but doesn't report it to the HCP until the early afternoon. The delay is the breach. 🧠 Withholding informed consent can itself be negligence — if a provider doesn't obtain proper consent, that provider can be found negligent.

entries.h: 🩺 Malpractice — negligence with a license attached
entries.t: Illegal, improper, or negligent actions by a licensed professional — practice that falls below the accepted standard of care. Example: An RN fails to check the dosage printed on a medication vial, and the client is harmed as a result. 🧠 Malpractice = negligence + a license. Every malpractice case is negligence, but not every negligence case is malpractice — malpractice specifically requires the person to be a licensed professional acting within their scope.

Desertion of a client by anyone who has already assumed responsibility for their care — for example, leaving an assignment or ending a nurse-client relationship without properly transferring care or giving adequate notice. 🧠 Once a nurse accepts an assignment (duty exists), walking away without a proper hand-off is abandonment — even if the intent was reasonable (e.g., leaving because the assignment felt unsafe). Always notify the charge nurse/supervisor first. 🚨
STEP 3 · WILLFUL ACTS These are deliberate — no accident excuse. Assault and battery are the two NCLEX loves most.

entries.h: 🆚 Assault (the threat) vs. Battery (the act) — A comes before B
entries.t: 🧠 "A & B, in order — Assault before Battery." The threat (A) doesn't require contact; the act (B) does. Both can happen in one scenario: threatening an NG tube (assault) then inserting it anyway over refusal (battery).

Using physical restraints, seclusion, or a chemical restraint to keep someone against their will — without a valid order/indication. Example: Using restraints on a competent client just to prevent them from leaving the facility. Chemically restraining a competent client able to make their own decisions is both false imprisonment and assault/battery. 🧠 A restraint used for the wrong reason (convenience, punishment, "they might leave AMA") is false imprisonment — see page 5 for the correct AMA process.

entries.h: 📚 Defamation of character — Libel vs. Slander
entries.t: Making false, rude, or insulting remarks that harm a client's (or coworker's) reputation. Libel Slander Written Spoken 🧠 "LIBEL lives in the LIBRARY" — both start with L, and a library holds written words. Example: break-room gossip about a coworker's alleged affair with a client = slander (spoken).

Violating a client's confidentiality rights — including HIPAA violations. Example: Discussing a client's diagnosis where others can overhear, or accessing a chart with no professional reason to. 🧠 Confidentiality violations sit at the intersection of tort law and HIPAA — same act, two different legal exposures. 🎯
STEP 4 · DON'T GET FOOLED The exam loves to mix these terms up on purpose — here's how to keep them straight.

entries.h: 🔀 Side-by-side: the pairs students swap by mistake
entries.t: Term Definition Key distinguisher Negligence Failure to provide the care a reasonable, prudent peer would Anyone with a duty of care Malpractice Negligence committed by a licensed professional , below standard of care Requires a license Assault Threat of harm No contact required Battery Unconsented harmful/offensive contact Contact did occur False imprisonment Restricting freedom without valid cause Restraints/seclusion misused Libel Defamation Written Slander Defamation Spoken

entries.h: 🚨 Highest-yield fact: treatment without consent = battery
entries.t: This single fact links Tort Law directly to the next page in this series. Any invasive procedure, medication, or treatment given without valid consent — even if medically appropriate — is legally battery. 🧠 See NG-192 · Informed Consent for exactly how consent is obtained, witnessed, and withdrawn.

In any tort claim, the accuser must prove all required elements. A nurse is not required to prove they did nothing wrong — the plaintiff must prove the nurse did. 🧠 This is why thorough, honest documentation matters so much — it's the nurse's best defense if an accusation is ever made. 🔗 Series link: These terms are built on the six ethical principles from NG-133 · Ethical Key Terms (battery = a violation of autonomy; false imprisonment = a violation of autonomy done under a false banner of beneficence). Restraint

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧾 Burden of proof On the accuser, not the nurse 🪜 4 elements Duty → Breach → Causation → Damages 🆚 Assault → Battery Threat, then act — in that order 🔒 No consent = Battery, every time

Show answer Breach (skipped standard technique) and causation/damages (the UTI resulted) — plus duty, since a nurse-client relationship existed. All four elements are present. Q2: A nurse says "I'll restrain you if you get up again" but never actually restrains the client. What tort is this? Show answer Assault — the threat of harm, without any actual contact. Q3: A com

entries.h: Delegation · 5 Rights · NG-180 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Fundamentals of Nursing

The 5 Rights of Delegation NG-180 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition Delegation transfers the task, never the responsibility. The RN is still accountable for choosing to delegate correctly and for supervising the outcome — which is exactly why assessment, evaluation, teaching, and any task requiring nursing judgment can never be delegated to a UAP. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

✋ 5 Rights Task · Circumstance · Person · Direction/Communication · Supervision. ✅ UAP CAN Stable vitals, ADLs, ambulation, positioning, I&O on a stable client. ❌ RN ONLY Assessment, evaluation, teaching, IV push — never delegated. 🛡️ Still accountable The RN can be liable for negligent supervision — delegation ≠ off the hook. ✋
STEP 1 · BEFORE YOU DELEGATE Every one of these five has to be true before a task leaves the RN's hands.

Assess the situation Patient stability and the task’s complexity. Choose the delegatee Match competence and scope to the task. Communicate and supervise State expectations, follow up and evaluate outcomes. Five rights Task, circumstance, person, direction/communication and supervision/evaluation. Retained judgment The nurse remains responsible for appropriate delegation and follow-up. Feedback Set clear escalation thresholds and reporting expectations. 🧠 "TCP-DS" — T ask · C ircumstance · P erson · D irection · S u

Right Task — the task is stable, routine, standardized, and does not require nursing judgment. Right Circumstance — the client's condition is stable and predictable for this task, right here, right now. Do not delegate a task for an unstable client — even a normally-delegable task like vital signs becomes RN-only if the client is unstable. 🧠 Stable task + stable client = safe to hand off. Either one being unstable cancels the delegation.

Only delegate tasks allowed by state Nurse Practice Act and workplace/facility policy , to someone whose knowledge, skill, and experience matches the task. Assess the assistant's competency to perform the task safely before delegating. "Right Person" applies at every level — RN → LPN/LVN, and RN/LPN → UAP/CNA. 🧠 Scope of practice isn't optional. "I thought they could do it" is not a defense — verify competency first.

Give a clear, concise description of the task, the goal, the expected time frame, and exactly when to report back . 🧠 "Task + Time frame + Tell me." Every delegated order needs all three, or the AP doesn't know when something is wrong.

Follow up, and evaluate the outcome of the delegated task. Always reassess tasks you have delegated — supervision doesn't end when you walk away. 🧠 Delegate, don't disappear. The RN checks the work and the outcome, every time. 🧩
STEP 2 · SCOPE OF PRACTICE Delegation flows downhill from RN → LPN/LVN → UAP/CNA — and the higher-judgment tasks stop at the top.
🧠 "Judgment doesn't roll downhill." The higher the level of clinical judgment a task requires, the closer it stays to the RN.

entries.h: ✅ CAN delegate to UAP/CNA — stable, routine, predictable tasks
entries.t: 🩺 Vital signs stable client 🚶 Ambulation stable client 🛁 ADLs bathing, grooming, feeding, toileting 🔄 Position changes turning, repositioning 📋 Record I & O recording only ⚖️ Weighing routine daily weight 🧠 "SAP" = Stable, no Assessment, Predictable. If a task is routine and doesn't require interpreting data, it's usually delegable to a UAP.

entries.h: ❌ CANNOT delegate to UAP/CNA — RN judgment tasks
entries.t: 🧠 Assessment initial or ongoing 📊 Evaluation interpreting labs, vitals trends, pain 🗣️ Teaching any patient education 💉 IV push meds RN only 🩸 Blood products transfusions 🧪 Central line drugs chemo, TPN 🧠 "ATE-B" never leaves the RN — A ssess · T each · E valuate · B lood/high-risk meds. Say it like "eat a B" — the RN always eats that whole plate alone.

✅ LPN/LVN CAN ❌ LPN/LVN CANNOT Reinforce/secondary teaching (not initial teaching) Initial, first, or primary assessment Follow-up assessment (not initial/primary) First/initial patient teaching Administer PO, SQ, IM medications IV push medications Maintain IVs; calculate & monitor IV flow rates Titrate (change) an IV drip rate Administer IVPB (piggyback) medications Independent evaluation of outcomes Monitor an ongoing blood transfusion Initiate/administer a blood transfusion CAUTION IV push scope for LPN/LVN vari
STEP 3 · SUPERVISE & PROTECT You can delegate a task — you cannot delegate the responsibility for the outcome.

entries.h: 🚨 Keywords that mean "do NOT delegate — RN territory"
entries.t: 🆕 New admission ⚡ Sudden change in status 🥇 First time doing anything 🏥 Post-op / returning from a procedure 📉 Unstable vitals, labs, blood sugar 🧾 Discharge teaching 🧠 "New, First, Sudden, Unstable" = RN. Any client who is new to the unit, newly changed, or newly unstable needs the RN's own eyes first.

entries.h: 🚦 Stable vs. unstable — the same task, two different answers
entries.t: 🧠 Vital signs on Monday ≠ vital signs on the day of a code. A task being "usually delegable" never overrides an unstable client in front of you right now.
🧠 Delegation is a loop, not a handoff. The RN's job doesn't stop until the outcome has been evaluated and reassessed.

The RN (or LPN/LVN) may be legally liable if negligent in supervising the UAP/CNA — even though the UAP performed the task itself. Delegating the task transfers the action , not the accountability. Failing to check competency, give clear direction, or follow up = negligent supervision. 🧠 "You picked them, you own the pick." If the delegation decision itself was unsafe, the licensed nurse who made it is accountable.

entries.h: 📝 ATI-style scenario: delegating vital signs to an AP
entries.t: An RN delegates routine vital signs to an assistive personnel (AP). Which actions should the nurse plan to take? Confirm the client is stable and the task is appropriate to delegate right now. Confirm the AP has the skill/competency to perform vital signs correctly. Communicate the specific time frame for when the AP should report results back to the RN. Tell the AP what values require an immediate report (e.g., outside expected parameters). Follow up — review the results and reassess the client as needed. 🧠 Vitals

SAY IT OUT LOUD ✋ TCP-DS Task · Circumstance · Person · Direction · Supervision ✅ UAP stable vitals, ADLs, ambulation, positioning, I&O ❌ RN only assessment, evaluation, teaching, IV push, unstable client ⚖️ Still liable negligent supervision = RN/LPN accountability

Q2: A newly admitted client needs vital signs — can this be delegated to a UAP? Show answer No — a new admission requires the RN's initial assessment; "new admission" is a keyword that keeps the task with the RN.
