The full systematic exam, top to bottom, in order NG-190 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition This is the master reference page for the batch — the sequence that ties everything together. It leans on NG-079 Vital Signs for normal ranges and NG-082 Assessment Locations for exact pulse/auscultation landmarks, so you're not re-learning them here — just placing them in the walk-through. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🧾 Consent → privacy → hands Always before you touch the client. 🚶 Head → neck → chest → abdomen → extremities One direction, never skip around. 🩻 IAPP for the belly only Inspect → Auscultate → Percuss → Palpate. 📌 Not all programs teach DTR/CN/breast Check your school manual & state practice act. 🧾
STEP 1 · PREP Six things happen before your hands ever touch the client — every single time.

1 👋 Introduce yourself 2 🚪 Provide privacy 3 🧼 Wash hands 4 📝 Obtain consent 5 ⚠️ Assess for allergies 6 🧠 Obtain a psychosocial assessment 🧠 "I Prep With A Plan" — Introduce, Privacy, Wash hands, Allergies, Psychosocial, (consent tucked in with intro). Do this before the first vital sign.

Vital Typical adult reference range BP < 120 /< 80 mmHg (typical normal; staged hypertension begins ≥ 130/80 ) Pulse 60–100 bpm RR 12–20 breaths/min Temp ~ 98.6°F / 37°C SpO2 > 95% FULL DETAIL NG-079 Vital Signs — hedged reference ranges, classification tiers, and why "normal" varies by source. 🚶
STEP 2 · THE WALK-THROUGH Same direction every time — head/neck, chest, abdomen, extremities/circulation. Consistency is what lets you spot when something's off.

Observe and ask History and appearance provide context. Examine and measure Use the correct technique and equipment. Interpret and reassess Compare with baseline and the clinical picture. Vital signs Temperature, pulse, breathing, pressure and oxygenation need context. Head-to-toe Use a consistent sequence while prioritizing urgent findings. Focused assessment Investigate the specific symptom or change in greater detail. 🧠 "HEN-CAB-E" — Head, Eyes/ENT, Neck, Chest, Abdomen, Breast, Extremities. Same order, every cl

Hair — clean, well-kept? Cranial nerves assessed (if in program scope) Eyes — PERRLA , sclera white, conjunctiva pink/moist, no debris/drainage Nares — check patency, occlude one nostril at a time Mouth — oral mucosa pink & moist, no caries/redness/lesions; tongue midline Jaw/neck — palpate for swollen or painful lymph nodes 🧠 PERRLA = Pupils Equal, Round, Reactive to Light & Accommodation.

Heart : 5-point auscultation (Aortic → Pulmonic → Erb's → Tricuspid → Mitral) Lungs : RR should be even & unlabored ; auscultate anterior + posterior ladder Breast (if in scope) : check for lumps, drainage, nipple size/color changes FULL DETAIL NG-082 Assessment Locations — the exact 5 heart points and lung auscultation ladder.

Shape : flat, non-pulsating, even Bowel sounds : active in all 4 quadrants; if absent, listen 5 min before charting "absent" Order : Inspect → Auscultate → Percuss → Palpate Ask about pain on palpation FULL DETAIL NG-082 Assessment Locations — the four-quadrant map.

Peripheral pulses : radial, brachial, femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis, posterior tibialis (never palpate both carotids at once) Capillary refill : <3 sec Skin turgor : returns <3 sec ; skin warm, dry, intact Temperature equal in all extremities ROM in all joints + DTRs (if in program scope) FULL DETAIL NG-082 Assessment Locations — every pulse landmark, illustrated. 📌 Program note: not every nursing program teaches DTRs, cranial nerve exams, or breast exams as part of the routine head-to-toe — check your school'
STEP 3 · KNOW THE DIFFERENCE Same eight stops — here's what "normal" looks like next to what should make you stop and reassess.

System Normal finding Red flag Eyes PERRLA, sclera white Unequal/nonreactive pupils Neck No swollen/painful nodes Tender, enlarged lymph nodes Lungs Even, unlabored RR 12–20 Crackles, wheezes, rhonchi, labored breathing Heart Regular rate & rhythm at all 5 points New murmur, irregular rhythm Abdomen Flat, non-pulsating, active bowel sounds x4 Rigid/board-like, absent sounds x5min, pulsating mass Pulses 2+ bilateral, equal Absent, markedly unequal, thready/weak Skin Warm, dry, intact; cap refill & turgor <3s Cool/cl

entries.h: 🚨 Priority combo: rigid belly + fever + tachycardia
entries.t: Board-like abdomen, fever >100.3°F, rebound tenderness, restlessness, tachycardia/tachypnea = suspected peritonitis — report to the HCP as a priority.
Jumping around the body (e.g., checking a pulse, then eyes, then coming back to the chest) increases the chance of missing a finding . Stick to head-to-toe order every time.

entries.h: 🩻 IAPP — the one order that flips for the abdomen
entries.t: Touching the belly before listening can stir up bowel sounds and give a false reading — so auscultation jumps ahead of percussion and palpation for this one system only.

entries.h: Informed Consent · NG-192 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Legal & Ethics Series

Voluntary · Informed · Competent — and the one distinction NCLEX tests every single time NG-192 NURSING CORE Series: Legal & Ethics 3 of 5 ADHD-friendly visual edition Informed consent is required before any invasive procedure or surgery. It's the paperwork proof of autonomy (page 1) — and skipping it is legally battery (page 2). The single most-tested fact on this whole topic: the provider obtains consent — the nurse witnesses the signature and confirms the client actually understands. 📄 Simple Nursing original —

✅ 3 requirements Voluntary · Informed · Competent — all 3 or it's not valid. ✍️ Provider obtains Nurse witnesses the signature & checks understanding. ☎️ Emergency + can't consent Telephone consent, witnessed by 2 authorized people. 🔓 Withdraw anytime Client can revoke consent at any point, even after signing. ✅
STEP 1 · WHAT MAKES IT VALID Miss any one of these three and the "signed" consent isn't legally valid.

Information The responsible clinician explains benefits, risks and alternatives. Understanding and choice The person decides voluntarily with appropriate capacity support. Documentation and follow-through Record the decision and respect the care plan. Nursing role Advocate, identify unanswered questions and follow policy for witnessing consent. Advance directives Clarify preferences and the designated decision-maker under applicable law. Ethics Autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence and justice guide deliberation. 🧠

Given freely, without coercion, pressure, or undue influence — from staff, family, or anyone else. 🧠 A client who signs only because a family member is standing over them insisting has not given truly voluntary consent.

The provider must disclose: the diagnosis , the nature and purpose of the treatment, the risks and benefits , and the alternatives — including the alternative of no treatment at all . 🧠 If any of these pieces is missing, the consent is not truly "informed" — even with a signature on the form.

The client must be a legal adult (or emancipated minor), alert and oriented , and not impaired by sedating medications, illicit substances, or acute intoxication at the time of signing. 🧠 Pre-op sedation is the classic trap: once meds are given, that client can no longer legally sign — consent must be obtained before sedation. 👥
STEP 2 · IDENTIFY THE RIGHT SIGNER When the client can't sign for themselves, the law has a specific order of who steps in.

entries.h: ❌ Who generally cannot consent for themselves
entries.t: 🧒 Minors — unless legally emancipated (state-dependent) 😵 Clients who are unconscious or have severely impaired cognition 💉 Clients who are sedated or acutely intoxicated ⚖️ Clients under a court-appointed guardianship for decision-making 🧠 In these cases, consent shifts to a legal guardian, healthcare proxy/durable power of attorney for healthcare, or — in a true emergency — the emergency-treatment doctrine.

entries.h: 🚨 Involuntary psychiatric admission ≠ loss of consent rights
entries.t: Clients admitted involuntarily still have the right to informed consent for their general medical treatment. An involuntary hold addresses safety — it does not strip away every other legal right. 🧠 Classic ATI trap: students assume "involuntary" means "no rights." Wrong — see page 5 (AMA & Mandatory Reporting) for the full right-to-refuse discussion.

entries.h: 🌳 Decision tree: client can't sign — now what?
entries.t: 🧠 Telephone consent for an emergent surgery must be witnessed by 2 authorized individuals (commonly two staff on separate extensions/lines) — a single witness is not enough. 🩺
STEP 3 · THE #1 NCLEX DISTINCTION The provider explains and obtains; the nurse verifies and witnesses. Confusing these two is the most common wrong answer.

entries.h: 🚫 The provider obtains consent — the nurse is NOT the one explaining risks/benefits
entries.t: 🧠 "Provider persuades, nurse notices." If a question asks who should explain surgical risks, the answer is almost never "the nurse" — it's the surgeon/provider performing the procedure.

entries.h: 🔄 Client can withdraw consent at any time
entries.t: Consent isn't a one-way door. If the client expresses doubt, asks a new question, or says they've changed their mind — even minutes before the procedure — the nurse must stop, notify the provider, and hold the procedure . 🧠 A signed form does not lock a client in. "I don't want this anymore" always overrides a signature.

An ethics committee is a healthcare team that provides guidance during an ethical dilemma — it gives recommendations , and does NOT impose a decision on the care team or family. The ANA (American Nurses Association) sets the ethical standards for the whole nursing profession — first covered on page 1 of this series. 🧠 If a stem asks "who makes the final call in an ethical dilemma," it's never the ethics committee — they advise, the care team/family/client still decide. 🎯
STEP 4 · DON'T GET FOOLED Real exam-style stems, straight from the source material.

"A nurse applies restraints without a prescription on a client who threatens to leave AMA. Select all that apply — which are intentional torts?" Correct: Battery, False imprisonment. Not correct: Malpractice and Negligence are unintentional torts, and HIPAA is a federal privacy law, not itself an intentional tort category. 🧠 Sort by the word first — "intentional" rules out negligence and malpractice immediately.

"Two nurses overhear a coworker say she believes a married HCP is in a relationship with a client." This is slander — a spoken, harmful (and unverified) statement about someone's reputation. 🧠 Say it out loud = slander. Write it down = libel.

"Client needs emergency surgery but cannot sign the operative consent form due to sedation. Priority action?" Obtain telephone consent from a family member , witnessed by 2 authorized individuals . 🧠 "Cannot sign" ≠ "skip consent." The team pivots to the next legally valid pathway — it doesn't disappear. 🔗 Series link: Skipping this whole process is NG-172 · Tort Law 's definition of battery. The right being protected here is NG-133 · Ethical Key Terms 's autonomy. Advance consent for future incapacity is covered n

SAY IT OUT LOUD ✅ VIC Voluntary · Informed · Competent = valid consent ✍️ Provider obtains Nurse witnesses signature, checks understanding ☎️ 2 witnesses For telephone/emergency consent 🔄 Withdraw anytime A signature never locks a client in

Q1: Who is legally responsible for explaining the risks and benefits of a surgical procedure? Show answer The provider/HCP performing the procedure — not the nurse. The nurse witnesses the signature and verifies understanding. Q2: What are the 3 requirements for valid consent? Show answer Voluntary, Informed, and Competent (capacity). Q3: A client who was involuntarily admitted for psychiatric treatment needs an appendectomy. Do they still have the right to informed consent? Show answer Yes — involuntary admission

entries.h: Advance Directives · NG-212 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Legal & Ethics Series

Living wills, durable power of attorney for healthcare, code status, and the PSDA NG-212 NURSING CORE Series: Legal & Ethics 4 of 5 ADHD-friendly visual edition Advance directives are legal documents that spell out a client's wishes for medical care before they become unable to speak for themselves — think a client with a GCS < 7 or aphasia from an intracerebral hemorrhage. This is autonomy (page 1) exercised in advance, so it survives even after the client can no longer voice a choice. 📄 Simple Nursing original —

📜 2 main types Living Will (treatment wishes) + DPOA-HC (a person to decide). 👥 2 witnesses Not the treating nurse/HCP, not the named proxy. ❓ No AD found? Default is FULL treatment / full code. 📋 PSDA Facilities MUST ask every admitted client about advance directives. 📜
STEP 1 · TWO MAIN TYPES One document says what you want; the other says who decides for you.

entries.h: 📜 From client wishes to the chart

entries.t: Information The responsible clinician explains benefits, risks and alternatives. Understanding and choice The person decides voluntarily with appropriate capacity support. Documentation and follow-through Record the decision and respect the care plan. Nursing role Advocate, identify unanswered questions and follow policy for witnessing consent. Advance directives Clarify preferences and the designated decision-maker under applicable law. Ethics Autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence and justice guide deliberation. 🧠

A document, separate from a final will , that describes the kind of treatment wanted if the client becomes incapacitated or unable to communicate — e.g., whether they want life-sustaining measures like a ventilator or tube feeding. 🧠 It's about what — the treatments themselves.

entries.h: 🖋️ Durable Power of Attorney for Healthcare (DPOA-HC)
entries.t: Assigns another person — a health care proxy / surrogate — to make medical decisions for the client if they become incapacitated. NCLEX TIP There are many types of general Power of Attorney — always clarify it's specifically the healthcare POA that's needed. 🧠 It's about who — the decision-maker, not the decisions themselves.

✅ Commonly does NOT need to be notarized — can typically be completed right in the healthcare setting ✅ Commonly requires 2 witnesses ❌ Witnesses cannot be the nurses or HCPs directly involved in that client's care ❌ Witnesses cannot be individuals named as the healthcare proxy Exact witness count and notarization requirements are set by state law and vary — always verify the specific state's requirements rather than assuming one universal rule. 🧠 The witness has to be neutral — not treating, not benefiting from th

entries.h: 🚨 Portable orders: POLST / MOLST & DNR bracelet
entries.t: POLST (Physician's Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment) — actual medical orders, signed by a provider, that summarize the client's wishes and travel with them across care settings (home, EMS, hospital). Terminology varies by state — some regions use MOLST or another name. A DNR bracelet is a portable, visible way to communicate code status outside the hospital record. 🧠 A living will is a wish ; a POLST is a standing medical order — that's why POLST can be acted on immediately by EMS. 🚦
STEP 2 · KNOW THE LADDER From everything to nothing — know exactly what each order does and does not include.
🧠 DNR/DNI/AND are NOT "do not treat." Comfort measures, oxygen by nasal cannula, IV fluids, and symptom-relief medications can still be given — those are not considered resuscitative efforts.

Default is full treatment / full code . The law requires the facility to give written information outlining the client's rights and options for stating their wishes. 🧠 Silence defaults to "do everything," not "do nothing."

A federal law that protects and ensures client rights in determining end-of-life care. It requires facilities to ask every admitted client whether they already have an advance directive. 🧠 The PSDA is a process requirement (ask on admission), not a guarantee every client will have one. 🩺
STEP 3 · FACILITATE, DON'T STALL CARE When code status is unclear, the nurse verifies without abandoning the client.

entries.h: 🌳 Client's condition is worsening — code status unclear. What now?
entries.t: 🧠 Two things happen in parallel, not in sequence. The nurse does NOT stop caring for the client while the chart is searched — assessment and verification happen at the same time.

The nurse's role is to open the door for advance care planning discussions, provide facility information, answer process questions, and notify the provider or ethics resources as needed — not to pressure a client toward a specific choice. 🧠 This mirrors the informed consent rule from page 3: the nurse supports the process, the client (or their legal decision-maker) makes the actual choice.

entries.h: 🗺️ Where the ethics of dying live on this site
entries.t: 🔗 The euthanasia, DNR ethics, grief, and end-of-life communication angle is covered in depth on the Mental Health batch's NG-065 · Death & Dying and NG-222 · Death, Dying, Grief & Loss pages — this page focuses on the legal document itself. 🎯
STEP 4 · DON'T GET FOOLED These exact questions have appeared on Kaplan, HESI, and Saunders-style review material.

entries.h: 🚨 "My living will is secured in a safety-deposit box"
entries.t: This is the most concerning statement a client can make — an advance directive that no one can access in an emergency is functionally useless. The correct nursing response is to encourage a copy in the chart and with family/proxies. 🧠 A perfect document with zero accessibility = zero protection.

entries.h: ⭐ Newly diagnosed with mild Alzheimer's — priority teaching
entries.t: Encourage the client to complete an advance directive BEFORE cognitive abilities decline further — this is one of the most frequently missed NCLEX questions on this topic. 🧠 Capacity to complete an AD requires being competent at the time of signing — waiting until symptoms progress may mean it's too late.

entries.h: ✅ Timing matters — plan early, not in crisis
entries.t: Advance care planning conversations are ideally started at a calm, non-emergent time — not in the middle of an acute decline, when stress and impaired capacity make truly informed decisions harder. 🧠 If the exam gives you a chance to teach proactively, that's usually the better answer than waiting. 🔗 Series link: Advance directives are the future-tense version of NG-192 · Informed Consent , and both protect the NG-133 · Ethical Key Terms principle of autonomy. When no AD exists and a client wants to leave AMA inste

SAY IT OUT LOUD 📝 Living Will The "what" — treatments wanted/not wanted 🖋️ DPOA-HC The "who" — names a healthcare proxy 👥 2 witnesses Not the treating nurse, not the proxy ❓ No AD found = default to full treatment

Q1: What's the difference between a Living Will and a Durable Power of Attorney for Healthcare? Show answer A Living Will states WHAT treatments are wanted/not wanted; a DPOA-HC names WHO will make decisions if the client becomes incapacitated. Q2: Can the treating nurse witness a client's advance directive? Show answer No — witnesses cannot be nurses/HCPs directly involved in that client's care, or anyone named as the healthcare proxy. Q3: A client's condition is worsening and the code status is unclear. What shou

entries.h: Asepsis & Handwashing · NG-214 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Fundamentals of Nursing Course

Medical vs. Surgical Asepsis · Handwashing Technique · Hand Hygiene Moments NG-214 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition Asepsis is the absence of disease-causing organisms. Handwashing is the single best way to prevent the spread of germs — full stop. Everything else in infection control (gloves, gowns, sterile fields) is layered on top of this one habit. Two flavors exist: medical asepsis "clean technique" reduces organisms; surgical asepsis "sterile technique" eliminates them. Clean / low-organism zone Conta

🧼 Reduce vs. Eliminate Medical asepsis reduces organisms; surgical asepsis eliminates them entirely. ⏱️ 15 sec – 2 min Soap + water + friction, every time hands are visibly soiled. 🙅 Never on the floor The floor is always contaminated — nothing sterile or clean ever touches it. ➡️ Clean to dirty, never back Move from clean areas/tasks to dirty ones — never reverse the direction. 🧼
STEP 1 · TWO LEVELS OF "CLEAN" Same goal — keep organisms away from the patient — but two very different bars for how clean is clean enough.

Source and route Identify how organisms can spread. Appropriate barrier Hand hygiene, equipment practices and PPE reduce transfer. Reliable technique Correct use matters as much as equipment selection. Standard precautions Apply to all patient care based on anticipated exposure. Transmission-based precautions Add contact, droplet or airborne measures when indicated. Aseptic practice Protect key sites and sterile fields from contamination. 🧼 Medical / clean 🧫 Surgical / sterile Reduces number of organisms Eliminates

😷 Cover coughs into your shoulder or elbow , not your hands — otherwise wash immediately after 💅 No acrylic or gel nails — bacteria hide underneath where handwashing can't reach 💍 Keep jewelry minimal — any surface that can harbor bacteria will grow it 🚫 Never place anything on the floor — the floor is always contaminated 🛏️ Never shake linens when changing a bed — this launches organisms into the air ➡️ Move from clean areas to dirty areas , never the reverse 💦 Avoid splashing when emptying body fluids — pour clos
STEP 2 · SOAP + WATER + FRICTION The single most effective infection-control action a nurse performs, done correctly, every time.

Good hand hygiene requires soap, water, and friction — the physical rubbing is what actually lifts organisms off the skin, not just the soap itself. 🧠 "0:15 to 2:00 — sing it twice." The classic teaching trick: humming "Happy Birthday" twice through covers about 20 seconds, comfortably inside the required range.

Hands are visibly soiled After caring for a patient with C. diff , norovirus, or rotavirus Before eating, after using the restroom 🧠 "Soap beats spores." Alcohol sanitizer cannot destroy C. diff spores — only mechanical washing with soap, water, and friction removes them.

entries.h: 🧴 When alcohol-based hand sanitizer is okay
entries.t: Use alcohol-based hand sanitizer only when hands are not visibly soiled , and only as an occasional substitute between actual soap-and-water washes — not as a full replacement for it. 🧠 "Sanitizer is a bridge, not a destination." It fills the gaps between real washes; it never fully replaces them.

💅 Acrylic / gel nails bacteria hide beneath 💍 Excess jewelry rings, bracelets 🧴 Sanitizer only when hands are soiled 🛏️ Shaking linens launches organisms airborne 🪑 Items on the floor always contaminated 🧠 Every item on this list creates a hiding spot or a launch pad for organisms — undoing the work good handwashing just did. ⏰
STEP 3 · THE KEY MOMENTS Hand hygiene isn't random — it's tied to specific moments around every patient contact.

Wash before seeing a client, after seeing a client, before putting on gloves, and when changing gloves — those four moments form the backbone of every patient encounter. The WHO "5 Moments for Hand Hygiene" is the standard framework taught worldwide: 1) before touching a patient, 2) before a clean/aseptic task, 3) after body fluid exposure risk, 4) after touching a patient, 5) after touching a patient's surroundings. 🧠 "Before you, before clean, after risk, after you, after their space." Four of the five moments br

Gloves are not a substitute for hand hygiene. Wash before putting gloves on and after taking them off — and every time you change gloves between tasks or patients. 🧠 "Gloves protect the glove, not skip the wash." A puncture, a tiny tear, or contamination on removal all still reach bare skin without hand hygiene bookending the glove.

entries.h: 🚨 NCLEX trap: "just changed gloves" ≠ clean hands
entries.t: Changing gloves without hand hygiene in between is a classic exam distractor — the correct sequence is always remove gloves → wash/sanitize hands → don new gloves , never glove-to-glove. 🧠 If an answer choice skips the hand hygiene step between glove changes, it's wrong — no exceptions. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧼 Medical = reduce Surgical = eliminate — different goal, different bar ⏱️ 15 sec – 2 min soap + water + friction is what actually removes organisms 🧴 Sanitizer only if hands aren't soiled never for C. diff, norovirus, rotavirus ⏰ WHO's 5 Moments before patient · before clean task · after fluid risk · after patient · after surroundings

Q1: What's the difference between medical and surgical asepsis? Show answer Medical (clean) asepsis reduces the number of organisms; surgical (sterile) asepsis aims to eliminate them entirely. Q2: How long should a proper handwash last? Show answer At least 15 seconds, up to 2 minutes for heavily soiled or high-risk hands — soap, water, and friction together are what remove organisms. Q3: A nurse's hands aren't visibly soiled between two clean tasks on the same patient. Is alcohol-based sanitizer acceptable? Show a

entries.h: AMA & Mandatory Reporting · NG-220 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Legal & Ethics Series

The right to refuse and leave — and the legal duty to speak up for someone who can't NG-220 NURSING CORE Series: Legal & Ethics 5 of 5 ADHD-friendly visual edition Two forces, same series: a competent client's autonomy lets them leave against medical advice — and the nurse's duty to protect the vulnerable requires mandatory reporting when someone can't protect themselves. This is the final page — the exact edge cases where the six ethical principles from page 1 collide in real practice. 📄 Simple Nursing original —

🚪 Competent = can leave Right to refuse/leave AMA if the client has capacity. 🚫 Never call security AMA discharge is a documentation process, not a restraint. 🛡️ Protect first Mandatory reporting starts with removing the client from immediate harm. 📋 Assess, THEN report Report suspected abuse only after a full assessment/history. 🚪
STEP 1 · THE RIGHT TO REFUSE A competent client can walk out — the nurse's job is to inform, document, and never obstruct.

entries.h: ✅ Right to refuse — even if involuntarily admitted

entries.t: Recognize the issue Consent, privacy, safety or a possible legal duty. Use the correct pathway Follow applicable law and organizational policy. Document objectively Record findings, communication and actions. Leaving against advice Assess capacity, explain risks and alternatives, and support a safer plan. Reporting Mandatory duties differ by location and circumstance; use the required reporting process. Civil concepts Assault, battery, negligence and confidentiality breaches describe different issues. Clients have

🧠 "INDS-SR" won't roll off the tongue, so picture it as a checklist you read left to right: inform → notify → no security → discuss → sign → remove lines. Step 3 is the single most-tested step — calling security to physically stop a competent client can itself become false imprisonment.

entries.h: ⭐ Assessing the risk before they walk out
entries.t: Was the client properly educated on why staying matters? Are they competent to make this decision right now? Do they have a legal hold in place? 🧠 Three quick questions, asked in order, decide the whole scenario.

entries.h: 🔄 If the client refuses to sign the AMA form
entries.t: The nurse still documents the refusal to sign — a client cannot be forced to sign anything, but the discharge (and the fact that risks were explained) is still documented in the chart. 🧠 Refusing to sign the AMA form does not equal being forced to stay. 🔒
STEP 2 · CAPACITY CHECK The right to leave only applies to someone who can actually understand the choice they're making.

🍺 Acutely intoxicated — e.g., drinking heavily for 12 hours and unable to walk safely 🗣️ Actively psychotic with command hallucinations to harm self or others (e.g., voices telling them to hurt someone) 👑 Severe impairment of reality testing that removes capacity to understand the decision (e.g., a client who believes they are a historical figure) ⚖️ Client is under an active legal/involuntary hold for danger to self or others (specific hold names/timeframes vary by state) 🧠 The common thread isn't the diagnosis —

entries.h: 🏥 Voluntary psychiatric admission, wants to leave
entries.t: A client admitted voluntarily for an anxiety disorder demands release. Initial nursing action: notify the client's primary HCP — the client generally retains the right to leave unless they meet criteria for an emergency hold. 🧠 Voluntary admission ≠ locked in. The HCP evaluates whether a hold is legally justified; the nurse doesn't unilaterally block the door.

"You don't have to take the medication if you don't want to" is the most therapeutic nursing response to a competent client's refusal. 🧠 Respecting the refusal — not arguing, bargaining, or threatening — is the correct action. 🚨
STEP 3 · PROTECT THE VULNERABLE When someone can't advocate for themselves, the law requires the nurse to.
🧠 "PICS" — Protect · Interview (separately) · Collect (evidence) · Safety plan. Do them in that order — safety always comes before evidence-gathering.

entries.h: ⚠️ Report only after a full assessment
entries.t: Suspected abuse is reported only after a detailed assessment and full history — not on a hunch alone. Once that threshold of reasonable suspicion is met, reporting is mandatory , not optional. 🧠 "Report only after assessment" ≠ "wait and see." A completed assessment that raises suspicion still legally obligates the report.

🧒 Suspected child abuse or neglect 👴 Suspected elder or dependent-adult abuse/neglect 🦠 Certain communicable diseases to public health authorities 🔫 Gunshot or stab wounds , in jurisdictions that require it 🧠 Exact reportable conditions and timeframes are set by state law and facility policy — always verify locally rather than assuming one national rule.

entries.h: 🗺️ Related page in the Mental Health batch
entries.t: 🔗 Full signs/symptoms of physical, emotional, sexual abuse and neglect across the lifespan are covered on the Mental Health batch's NG-139 · Abuse & Neglect page — this page focuses on the nurse's legal reporting duty. 🎯
STEP 4 · DON'T GET FOOLED This closes out the whole 5-page series — every trap here reaches back to an earlier page.

Calling security to physically prevent a competent client from leaving is never the correct AMA response — it risks false imprisonment (see page 2, Tort Law). 🧠 The nurse's tools here are words and documentation, not force.

entries.h: ⭐ Trap: family overrides a competent client
entries.t: A family member's wishes do not override a competent client's own informed refusal — this is autonomy (page 1) at its strongest test. 🧠 If the stem pits family against a competent client, the client's voice wins.

entries.h: ✅ The full-circle idea of this series
entries.t: Ethical principles (page 1) → become legal exposure when violated (page 2, Tort Law) → get formalized through signed process (page 3, Informed Consent) → extend into the future (page 4, Advance Directives) → and hit their real-world limits here, where competence, refusal, and duty to protect all meet. 🧠 Every legal/ethics question on this exam is really just asking: "is this client competent, and whose right is being protected?" 🔗 Series link: Start over from NG-133 · Ethical Key Terms , or review NG-172 · Tort Law

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🚪 Competent = can leave Even if involuntarily admitted, except true emergencies 🚫 Never call security Risk of false imprisonment 🛡️ PICS Protect → Interview separately → Collect → Safety plan 📋 Full assessment first Then reporting is mandatory, not optional

Q1: A competent client wants to leave AMA and staff are worried. What should the nurse NOT do? Show answer Call security to physically stop them — this risks false imprisonment. Instead: inform of risks, notify the provider, discuss risks, get the AMA form signed (or document refusal), and remove lines/tubes. Q2: An intoxicated client who cannot walk wants to leave. Can they sign out AMA? Show answer No — acute intoxication that impairs capacity means they cannot legally/safely be allowed to sign out AMA at that ti
Protecting a patient who cannot protect themselves, and caring well when cure is no longer the goal.

entries.h: 🚨 Neutropenia — the number that changes everything

entries.t: Treatment or disease effects Blood counts, energy and organ function may change. Prevent and detect complications Infection and symptom burden need active assessment. Support quality of life Care goals guide treatment choices and comfort measures. Neutropenia A reduced neutrophil count can blunt infection signs; follow the oncology fever plan. Infection prevention Hand hygiene, line care and avoiding infectious exposure are central. Palliative care Can accompany disease-directed treatment and addresses symptoms, co

Hand hygiene — the single most effective measure, by a wide margin Private room; positive-pressure room if available No fresh flowers, no potted plants, no standing water — all harbor organisms Dedicated equipment; meticulous line and catheter care Screen staff and visitors for any infection Daily oral care with a soft brush; inspect for mucositis

No rectal temperatures, suppositories or enemas - they break mucosa and seed bacteria No urinary catheter unless genuinely necessary No live vaccines for the patient or household contacts No intramuscular injections if platelets are also low

Avoid crowds and anyone unwell No raw fruit or vegetables , no undercooked meat or eggs, no unpasteurized dairy No gardening, no cleaning litter trays or cages Take temperature daily and know the number to call Report fever, chills, sore throat, cough, burning on urination, or any new pain

Palliative care Hospice When Any time , from diagnosis Prognosis usually 6 months or less Alongside treatment? Yes — curative treatment continues Curative treatment has stopped Goal Comfort, dignity, quality of life Palliative care is not giving up, and it does not require stopping treatment. That misconception is the point of many questions.

entries.h: 🚨 Pain at the end of life
entries.t: There is no maximum opioid dose when titrating to comfort. Doses that would be unsafe in other contexts are appropriate here. Fear of respiratory depression is not a reason to under-treat a dying patient's pain. Relieving suffering is the goal of care. Give analgesia around the clock , not only on request — steady levels control pain far better than chasing it.

The best response almost always stays, listens and reflects rather than reassuring, redirecting or explaining. Do Do not “Tell me more about that.” “Everything will be fine.” Sit down. Allow silence. Change the subject “This sounds frightening.” “Don’t think like that.” Ask what matters most to them Speak only to the family

Fever + ANC < 500 = emergency No rectal anything in neutropenia Hand hygiene beats every other precaution Palliative can start at diagnosis ; hospice comes later No opioid ceiling at end of life Sources. Written from MedlinePlus , NINDS , CDC and OpenStax A&P 2e (CC BY 4.0).
The two axes that answer most pediatric questions: what stage they are in, and what they fear.

entries.h: ⭐ Erikson, play and what they need
entries.t: Stage Age Erikson Play Fears most Infant 0–18 mo Trust vs mistrust Solitary Separation from carer Toddler 18 mo–3 y Autonomy vs shame Parallel — beside, not with Separation ; loss of routine Preschool 3–6 y Initiative vs guilt Associative Bodily harm / mutilation School age 6–12 y Industry vs inferiority Cooperative , team games Loss of control; not measuring up Adolescent 12–18 y Identity vs role confusion Peer group Being different ; body image Match the intervention to the fear and most questions answer themselv

entries.h: 🧠 The two responses that keep reappearing
entries.t: Toddler having a tantrum → ignore the behavior, keep them safe. Attention reinforces it. Toddler resisting care → offer two acceptable choices , never an open question. “Pink cup or blue cup?” not “Will you take your medicine?”

Age Motor Social / language 2 months Lifts head when prone Social smile 4 months Rolls front to back Laughs, coos 6 months Sits with support ; rolls both ways Babbles; stranger anxiety begins 9 months Sits alone, crawls, pincer grasp “Mama/dada” nonspecific 12 months Walks ; birth weight TRIPLES 1–3 words; waves bye 15 months Walks well 3–5 words 2 years Runs, kicks a ball 2-word phrases ; ~50% intelligible 3 years Tricycle 3-word sentences ; ~75% intelligible 4 years Hops, dresses self ~100% intelligible 5 years S

Words per phrase roughly equals age in years at 2 and 3 Intelligibility: 2 y = 50%, 3 y = 75%, 4 y = 100% Weight doubles at 6 months, triples at 12 Posterior fontanelle closes by 2–3 months ; anterior by 12–18 months A sunken fontanelle means dehydration. A bulging fontanelle means raised intracranial pressure.

Unintentional injury is the leading cause of death in children past infancy — and the type changes predictably with what they can newly do. Age Main risk Teach Infant Suffocation, falls, choking Back to sleep , empty crib, rear-facing car seat Toddler Drowning, poisoning, falls, burns Locked cupboards, stair gates, never alone near water, pot handles turned in Preschool Road traffic, burns, drowning Supervision, road safety, swimming lessons School age Bicycles, sport, pedestrian Helmets , booster seat until the be

No honey before 12 months — infant botulism No cow’s milk before 12 months Choking foods to avoid under 4: nuts, whole grapes, hot dogs, popcorn, hard candy Rear-facing car seat in the back until at least 2 years Solids from about 6 months , iron-fortified cereal first, one new food every 4–7 days
FLACC — non-verbal, under 3 FACES — about 3 and older Numeric 0–10 — about 8 and older Children under-report pain to avoid injections. Behavior and physiology count as evidence.

Toddler = parallel play, limited choices, autonomy Preschooler thinks illness is a punishment — say it is not Adolescent = confidentiality Weight doubles at 6 months, triples at 12 Sunken = dehydrated. Bulging = raised ICP. Ignore the tantrum; keep them safe 📌
FROM YOUR SAVED SET

Live vs inactivated is the distinction that decides who can be vaccinated, and it drives almost every question on the topic. 💉 Also on this topic: Childhood Immunizations (NG-342) — which vaccines are live, who cannot have them, and true contraindications versus myths. This page carries the schedule and ages.

Vaccine exposure Presents an antigen or instructions for making one. Immune response The body develops targeted defenses. Memory response Later exposure can be controlled more effectively. Schedule Age, medical conditions and prior doses determine what is due. Contraindications Different products have different restrictions; live vaccines require particular assessment. Documentation Record product, dose, route, site and follow-up according to policy. This one distinction answers most immunization questions. Live va

Immunocompromised — chemotherapy, high-dose steroids, HIV with low CD4, transplant Pregnant Recently had IVIG or a blood product — wait about 11 months; the antibodies block the response Severe febrile illness — postpone until recovered A mild cold with a low fever is NOT a reason to postpone. Withholding vaccines for minor illness is the single commonest missed opportunity.

Age Given Birth Hepatitis B 2 months DTaP, IPV, Hib, PCV, RV, HepB 4 months DTaP, IPV, Hib, PCV, RV 6 months DTaP, PCV, RV, HepB, influenza annually from 6 months 12–15 months MMR, Varicella , Hib, PCV, HepA 4–6 years DTaP, IPV, MMR, Varicella boosters 11–12 years Tdap, HPV, MenACWY — the adolescent set 16 years MenACWY booster — a second dose, not a repeat of nothing 16–23 years MenB — shared decision, not routine for everyone Every year Influenza, from 6 months onward for life Every 10 years Td or Tdap booster, f

Anaphylaxis to a previous dose or a vaccine component Severe egg allergy — care with some influenza formulations Encephalopathy within 7 days of a pertussis-containing vaccine → use DT instead of DTaP Live vaccines in the situations above Not contraindications: mild illness, low fever, current antibiotics, family history of reactions, prematurity (vaccinate by chronological age), or breastfeeding.

🚨 The dose that gets missed is the one at 16. MenACWY is given at 11–12 and again at 16 . An 18-year-old who had “their meningitis shot” at twelve and nothing since is not up to date , and that is exactly how the question is written.

entries.h: 💉 HPV: the hinge is the 15th birthday
entries.t: Series started Doses Timing Before the 15th birthday 2 0, then 6–12 months At 15 through 26 3 0, 1–2 months, 6 months Immunocompromised, 9–26 3 3 doses whatever the starting age It is the age at the first dose that sets the number of doses, not the age now. Someone who started at 13 and finishes at 16 still needs only two .

MenACWY — the 16-year booster; many schools require it for dormitory living MenB — 16–23, shared clinical decision-making . Not routine for everyone, and that wording is the answer HPV catch-up through age 26 — starting now means the 3-dose schedule Influenza every year, and Td/Tdap every 10 years from here on Check MMR, varicella and hepatitis B series are actually complete

A healthy 18-year-old, up to date, moving into a campus dormitory. The answer is meningococcal — crowded residential living is the classic risk setting. The other options are ruled out by age group alone , which is the fastest way through this question: Option Who it is actually for Meningococcal The answer — adolescents, and dormitory residents Pneumococcal polysaccharide 65+ , or younger adults with chronic conditions Rotavirus Infants only — the series cannot even be started after 15 weeks Herpes zoster 50+ A na
An 18-year-old comes to the campus clinic before moving into a dorm. Records show the full childhood series, MenACWY at 12 , and one HPV dose at 16 . What does she need?

MenACWY booster — the 16-year dose was never given. Two more HPV doses — she started at 16, so she is on the 3-dose schedule and has had one. Influenza if not had this season, and MenB offered as a shared decision. Nothing is restarted. Schedule details checked against the CDC child & adolescent and adult immunization schedules and the CDC HPV vaccination recommendations.

entries.h: 🩸 Tetanus after a wound — which product, by age
entries.t: ⭐ The answer is chosen by age, not by the wound. The cut-off is the 7th birthday — the same cut-off that separates DTaP from Td and Tdap in the routine schedule. Everything else in the question is a distractor built on that one line. Age For wound prophylaxis Why not the others Under 7 DT (or DTaP if the child is also due routine doses) Full-strength pediatric formulation. Tdap is not licensed under 10 , and the adult Td is not the childhood product. 7 and older Td — the adult tetanus booster DTaP stops at the 7th

Tetanus immune globulin is for a dirty or deep wound in someone who is not up to date — fewer than three documented doses, or an unknown history. A child who is up to date does not need it, however deep the puncture. TIG and the tetanus toxoid may be given at the same visit, but never mixed in one syringe . Separate syringes, and a different anatomical site .

A child aged 7 to 10 who never finished the DTaP series gets Tdap to catch up on pertussis — that is a catch-up decision, not a wound decision. For the wound itself, the 7-and-older answer is still Td .
An 8-year-old, up to date , comes to the ED with a deep puncture wound . What does the nurse anticipate giving?

Td — the adult tetanus booster. Age 8 is past the 7th birthday, so DTaP is out. Tdap is not the wound-prophylaxis product. And because the child is up to date, TIG is not indicated — which also rules out the “TIG mixed with DT” option twice over, since TIG and a toxoid are never drawn into the same syringe. Product-by-age and TIG rules checked against the CDC Pink Book tetanus chapter and the CDC/ACIP routine wound-management guidance.

The tetanus decision is only half of it. The other half is the wound , and a puncture is a worse wound than it looks: a small opening, a deep track, and bacteria carried in and then sealed under the skin. 💧 Let it bleed briefly — that flushes the track — then wash with soap and running water for several minutes. Do not scrub ; scrubbing adds tissue injury. 🧹 Do not dig for something embedded. A retained fragment is a reason to be seen, not a reason to probe at home. 🩹 Cover it, and check it daily . A puncture throu

Vastus lateralis for infants — the largest muscle they have Deltoid once walking well and the muscle is developed (usually 3+ years) Give the most painful injection last Different sites for different vaccines; document site, lot number and expiry Comfort: swaddle, breastfeed or give sucrose to infants; hold upright afterwards

Expected: soreness, redness, mild swelling, low-grade fever, fussiness for a day or two Acetaminophen or ibuprofen for comfort — not routinely before, as it may blunt the response Cool compress to the site; move the limb normally MMR and varicella reactions come late — a rash or fever 7–14 days afterwards is normal Report a fever over 40C, a seizure, persistent inconsolable crying over 3 hours, or any breathing difficulty.

Listen first, do not lecture. Ask what specifically worries them and answer that. Acknowledge the concern as reasonable rather than dismissing it Give concrete local information — what these diseases actually do Hib vaccine all but eliminated epiglottitis ; that is a vivid, true example Document the discussion and any refusal; keep the door open for next visit

Live = MMR, varicella, rotavirus, nasal flu — not for immunocompromised or pregnant Mild illness is not a reason to postpone MMR/varicella not before 12 months Vastus lateralis in infants MMR reaction appears 7–14 days later After IVIG, delay live vaccines about 11 months Sources. Written from CDC Vaccines & Immunizations , HealthyChildren.org (AAP) , MedlinePlus and OpenStax A&P 2e (CC BY 4.0).
What to do first, what never to induce, and why lead damages the nervous system silently.

Exposure Ingestion, inhalation or skin contact may occur. Toxic effect The substance, amount and timing determine risk. Specific response Support vital functions and obtain toxicology guidance. Immediate safety Stop exposure without endangering rescuers; keep product information available. Ingestion Do not induce vomiting or attempt chemical neutralization. Lead Often causes no early symptoms; testing and removal of the source are central. Toddlers explore by mouth, so poisoning peaks around age 2. 1 Assess the chi

Never induce vomiting. Syrup of ipecac is no longer recommended. Never induce vomiting with a caustic substance - lye, drain cleaner, oven cleaner. It burns the esophagus a second time on the way back up. Never induce vomiting with a petroleum product - petrol, paraffin, furniture polish. Aspiration causes chemical pneumonitis. Take the container. Identifying the substance and its concentration changes the treatment entirely, and a frightened parent’s description is often wrong.

entries.h: 🧪 Corrosives — bleach, drain cleaner, oven cleaner
entries.t: Nothing goes in and nothing comes back up. Every instinct here — make them sick, cancel it out, give charcoal — makes the burn worse. Never neutralize it. Putting a weak acid on an alkali (or the reverse) is an exothermic reaction — it releases heat, so you add a thermal burn on top of the chemical one. No activated charcoal. It does not bind corrosives, and it coats the mucosa so the damage cannot be seen on endoscopy. Never induce vomiting. The corrosive burns the esophagus a second time on the way back up. 👀 A c

Locked cupboards, high shelves — child-resistant is not child-proof Keep everything in its original container — never in a drinks bottle Do not call medicine “candy” to get a child to take it Handbags and visitors’ bags are a common source — tablets in a pocket Poison Control number saved in the phone and on the fridge

Lead damages the developing nervous system, and it does it silently. Most children with raised levels have no symptoms at all — which is why screening exists. The commonest source is deteriorating lead paint in housing built before 1978 - chips and, more importantly, the dust.

Old paint — chips, and dust from friction on windows and doors Contaminated soil near old buildings or busy roads Old plumbing — run the tap and use cold water for drinking and formula Imported pottery, cosmetics, some traditional remedies, some toys A parent’s work or hobby — brought home on clothing Pica — eating non-food items — raises the risk considerably. When there are symptoms Neurological Irritability, poor attention, developmental delay or regression , learning problems GI Abdominal pain, vomiting, consti

Find and remove the source — this is the definitive treatment; treating the child while they return to the same house achieves nothing Chelation for high levels — succimer, EDTA, dimercaprol. Ensure good hydration and monitor renal function Iron and calcium-rich diet — a well-nourished gut absorbs less lead. Deficiency increases absorption Frequent wet mopping and damp dusting ; wash hands and toys often Developmental follow-up — effects can appear later as school difficulties There is no known safe blood lead leve

Never induce vomiting — especially caustics and petroleum products Take the container to hospital Call Poison Control before giving anything Acetaminophen antidote is N-acetylcysteine Lead is usually asymptomatic — screening finds it Remove the source ; good iron and calcium reduce absorption Sources. Written from CDC , NIDCD , National Eye Institute , HealthyChildren.org (AAP) and MedlinePlus .

Learn the position and the complication for each and most of the questions answer themselves. Lumbar puncture Flat 4 to 12 h after · headache is the complication Thoracentesis Sitting, leaning forward · pneumothorax after Paracentesis Empty the bladder f

Assess the goal Comfort, respiratory support, procedure access or protection. Choose the position Account for diagnosis, precautions and mobility. Reassess tolerance Check symptoms, pressure areas, alignment and circulation. Respiratory care Upright positioning may ease breathing when appropriate. Pressure prevention Reposition and offload using an individualized schedule. Procedure-specific care Follow instructions for the procedure and patient condition. The same four steps every time Before: signed consent, alle

Lumbar puncture — CSF from the spinal canal Position: side-lying, knees to chest, chin tucked — a C shape. Or sitting, leaning over a table. Empty the bladder first. After: lie flat 4 to 12 hours and push fluids. The complication: post-dural-puncture headache — positional, worse sitting up, better lying flat. Treat with flat bed rest, fluids, caffeine, and a blood patch if it persists. Report: leaking clear fluid at the site, numbness or weakness in the legs, fever, neck stiffness. Contraindicated when intracranial

entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Med-Surg Course

Prevention first · alternatives before restraints · the order rules NG-402 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition Restraints are a last resort , and almost every exam question is really asking what did you try first? The correct answer is nearly always an alternative, a reassessment, or moving her closer to the desk. Always first Try every alternative before any restraint The order Provider order required · never PRN · time-limited After a fall Assess her first, then vital signs, then notify The knot Quick-relea

Find the contributors Review previous falls, mobility, cognition, vision, orthostatic symptoms, medications, toileting needs and equipment in the walking path. Make movement safer Keep the bed low and locked, call bell accessible and route clear. Provide appropriate footwear, walking aids and assistance. Agree on a toileting plan. Use the least restrictive care Reorientation, symptom relief and appropriate observation may help. Restraints can cause injury; they are not a routine fall-prevention measure. Respond aft

The restraint rules, in order Try alternatives first and document what you tried. A provider order is required — with the type, the reason and a time limit. In an emergency a nurse may apply one, but the order must be obtained within one hour and the provider must see her face to face. Never a PRN or standing order. Every restraint episode needs its own order. Time limits: adults 4 hours, ages 9 to 17 two hours, under 9 one hour. Renewed by a new order, not automatically. Use the least restrictive type that works.

If she falls — what you do, in this order Stay with her. Do not move her. Assess her first — level of consciousness, pain, obvious deformity, head injury, range of motion. Assessment comes before anything else. Vital signs and a neurological check. Call for help; only then move her, with enough people and a lift if needed. Notify the provider and the family. Monitor closely — neuro observations if the head was hit or she is anticoagulated. Complete an incident report . The incident report rules It is a quality and

Show answer Every less restrictive alternative, tried and documented. Can a restraint be ordered PRN? Show answer No. Never. Each episode needs its own order. SBAR · what goes in the chart · the abbreviations that are banned NG-403 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition If it is not documented, it did not happen — and if it is documented wrongly, it is evidence against you. Chart what you observed and what you did , in that order, and never anything you did not see yourself. SBAR Situation · Background · Assessment · Recommendation Never chart Opinion, blame, or that an incident report was filed An error One line through it, initial and date. Never erase or white out.

Assess and act Record relevant observations, measurements, care provided, communication and the patient’s response. Attribute information obtained from another person. Separate fact and report Use objective descriptions. Identify the patient’s own account and quote important words accurately. Avoid unsupported judgments or blame. Record at the right time Document promptly after care. Identify a delayed entry and the actual event time according to policy. Authenticate your own entry. Correct without concealing Use t

SBAR — the handoff format S — Situation. Who, where, and what is happening right now. One or two sentences. “This is Sarah on 4 East. Mrs Doyle in bed 12 is short of breath.” B — Background. The relevant history only. Admitting diagnosis, day post-operative, code status, allergies. A — Assessment. Your vital signs and findings, and what you think is going on. R — Recommendation. What you want. “I need you to see her now,” or “can I have an order for a chest x-ray?” The R is the part people leave out and it is the p

Charting that holds up Timely. As close to the event as possible. Specific. “300 mL of bright red drainage”, not “moderate amount”. Complete. Assessment, action, patient response, and who was notified with the time. Teaching is documented with what was taught, how it was taught, who was present, and how she demonstrated understanding. “Patient taught” alone proves nothing. Declined care is documented with her stated reason and who was notified. Confidentiality Access only the records of patients in your care. Curio

Late entry Label it “late entry” with both times What does SBAR stand for, and which part is most often missed? Show answer Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation. Contact · droplet · airborne · protective · and the ones that are not isolation NG-406 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition Three transmission-based categories, one protective category, and a handful of “precautions” that are not isolation at all. Getting the room and the mask right is most of the mark. Airborne Negative pressure room · N95 · MTV — Measles, TB, Varicella Droplet Private room · surgical mask within 1 meter Contact Gown and gloves · C. diff needs SOAP AND WATER Protective SHE is protected · posi

Source and route Identify how organisms can spread. Appropriate barrier Hand hygiene, equipment practices and PPE reduce transfer. Reliable technique Correct use matters as much as equipment selection. Standard precautions Apply to all patient care based on anticipated exposure. Transmission-based precautions Add contact, droplet or airborne measures when indicated. Aseptic practice Protect key sites and sterile fields from contamination. The four categories Contact — spread by touching her or her surroundings. Gow

Putting it on and taking it off On, in this order: gown → mask or respirator → goggles → gloves. The gloves go over the gown cuffs. Off, in this order: gloves → goggles → gown → mask. Then hand hygiene. Gloves come off first because they are the most contaminated. The mask comes off last , and outside the room for airborne precautions. Remove the mask by its ties or elastics , never the front. Peel the gown away from the neck and shoulders, turning it inside out, and roll it. Hand hygiene after everything , every t

The other “precautions” — which are not isolation Bleeding precautions (low platelets, anticoagulated): soft toothbrush, electric razor, no rectal temperatures or suppositories, no intramuscular injections if avoidable, pressure to sites, no NSAIDs or aspirin, watch for bruising and black stools. Aspiration precautions : upright at 90° for meals and for 30 to 60 minutes after, chin tuck, small bites, thickened fluids if prescribed, suction available, no straws for a dysphagic patient. Seizure precautions : padded r

Readiness · the three domains · teach-back · health literacy NG-407 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition Teaching is a nursing intervention with an assessment step, and the assessment step is the one that gets tested. Readiness to learn comes before content — someone in pain, frightened or in denial cannot learn anything. Assess first Readiness, then what she already knows, then teach Teach-back “Tell me how you would explain this to your daughter” Never “Do you understand?” — everyone says yes Literacy Write

Prepare Ask what matters to the patient and what they already know. Address pain, fatigue, hearing, vision, language and readiness to learn. Explain a small amount Use plain language and a few essential points. Demonstrate a practical skill and provide time to practice. Use a qualified interpreter when needed. Check understanding Ask the patient to explain the plan in their own words. For a skill, ask for a return demonstration. Avoid relying on “Do you understand?” Teach again if needed If something is unclear, ex

How to actually teach it Small chunks. Three key points per session, not twenty. Most important first and last — that is what is remembered. Plain language. “High blood pressure” not “hypertension”. “Heart attack” not “myocardial infarction”. Show, then let her do it. Nobody learns an injection by being told about one. Repeat and reinforce across several short sessions rather than one long one. Include the family or caregiver who will actually be doing it. Quiet room, glasses and hearing aid on, pain controlled, no

Teaching older adults Slower pace, more time , and short sessions. Processing takes longer; intelligence is unchanged. Teach in the morning when she is rested, not last thing before discharge. Large print, at least 14 point, high contrast , matte paper — glossy paper glares. Lower your pitch , do not raise your volume. High tones go first. Connect new information to what she already knows from a lifetime of experience. Reduce distractions; one topic at a time. Involve the caregiver, and give written material to tak

Assess first Readiness, then what she already knows, then teach Teach-back “Tell me how you would explain this to your daughter” Never “Do you understand?” — everyone says yes Literacy Write at 5th to 6th grade level, whatever her education What do you assess before teaching anything? Show answer Readiness — physical comfort, emotional state, what she already knows, and motivation. How do you evaluate a psychomotor skill? Show answer Return demonstration. Not by asking whether she understands. Why is "Do you unders

Before, during and after a procedure. Most of the exam points live in the before and the waking up — the checklist that has to be complete, and the airway that has to come back.

Every perioperative question is really asking “what is the nurse responsible for in this phase?” 1 · Preoperative Verify. Consent, identity, allergies, NPO, baseline vitals, teaching. This is the phase with the checklist, and the phase most questions come from. 2 · Intraoperative Protect. Positioning, sterile field, counts, normothermia. The client cannot advocate for themselves, so the nurse does. 3 · Postoperative Watch. Airway first, then bleeding, then pain. Complications announce themselves in the vital signs

Signed consent on the chart — and the provider obtains it. The nurse witnesses the signature and confirms she understands; the nurse does not explain the procedure. Allergies , and say the awkward ones out loud: iodine, contrast, shellfish, latex . Baseline vital signs , recorded. Without a baseline nothing afterwards means anything. How long she has actually been NPO — not whether she was told to be. Site marked, jewellery, dentures and prosthetics removed, bladder emptied. The identification band stays on. It is

Four things, and a client who can say them back has understood: Nothing to eat or drink after midnight Moderate sedation, not general anaesthesia , for most scopes — drowsy and comfortable, not unconscious Someone else drives her home. No driving for 24 hours after sedation After a bronchoscopy or an EGD , nothing by mouth until the gag reflex returns — the throat was numbed, and swallowing is not safe until it wears off

Airway first, every time. Then the numbers, then comfort. Vital signs every 5 to 15 minutes until stable NPO until the gag reflex returns Warm blankets — theatres are cold and anaesthesia blunts thermoregulation, so hypothermia is expected and shivering raises oxygen demand Position to protect the airway; suction within reach Pain treated on a scale, not on stoicism She does not eat, drink or walk the hallway in PACU. Clear liquids and ambulation belong to the unit, after she has met discharge criteria.

Five parameters, each scored 0, 1 or 2 — out of 10. It answers one question: is she recovered enough to leave PACU? Most units want 9 or better , or back to her pre-procedure baseline. 🥋 Activity Moves four extremities, two, or none — voluntarily or on command. 🫁 Respiration Breathes deeply and coughs freely, or is dyspneic and shallow, or apneic. 🧡 Circulation Blood pressure within 20% of pre-anaesthetic level, or 20–50% off, or further. 🧠 Consciousness Fully awake, rousable on calling, or not responding. 🟨 Oxygen

Preemptive analgesia means giving the dose before the thing that hurts , not after she reports pain. Physiotherapy at 10:00 and a PRN oral opioid available → give it at about 09:15 to 09:30 . An oral opioid needs 30 to 45 minutes to work, so a dose given when she starts hurting arrives after the session is already ruined. Waiting for her to report pain, shortening the session, or holding the opioid “so she can participate” all cost her the therapy. Pain is what stops her moving; treating it is what lets the knee be

entries.h: 🩸 After a bowel or bariatric operation
entries.t: An anastomosis is a surgical join between two tubular structures — two ends of bowel, a vessel to a vessel, a duct to a duct. Not an opening onto the abdominal wall — that is a stoma . Where there is a join, there can be a leak , and a leak spills bowel contents into the abdomen. 🚨 Unexplained tachycardia is the earliest sign of an anastomotic leak — often the only sign, and it shows up before the fever, before the rigid abdomen, before the pain gets bad. Day 2 after a sleeve gastrectomy, a heart rate of 128 with o

The provider obtains consent; the nurse witnesses it The ID band stays on Ask about iodine, contrast, shellfish and latex by name Check how long she has actually been NPO PACU: airway first , vitals q5–15 min , warm blankets , NPO until the gag reflex returns Aldrete = activity, respiration, circulation, consciousness, oxygen saturation — not bowel sounds. entries.h: 1 / 3 Congenital defects: pulmonary flow and mixing

entries.t: Aorta–pulmonary artery connection; left-to-right shunt. Open: prostaglandin E1 if duct-dependent. Close: ibuprofen/indomethacin in selected preterm infants; catheter/surgery.

Opening between atria → usually left-to-right shunt. Often asymptomatic; murmur/fixed split S2. Larger defects may need closure. Left-sided HF clues: tachypnea, crackles, feeding fatigue and pulmonary congestion.

Opening between ventricles → usually left-to-right shunt. Murmur; large shunt causes pulmonary overcirculation, tachypnea, poor feeding/growth. Small defects may close; HF treatment and repair when indicated.
Absent tricuspid opening restricts right-heart flow. Survival requires mixing and a route to lungs. Cyanosis; prostaglandin if duct-dependent. Staged surgical palliation.
Aorta from RV; pulmonary artery from LV → parallel circuits. Blood must mix through ASD/VSD/PDA. Severe neonatal cyanosis. Prostaglandin, possible atrial septostomy; arterial switch repair.

Four: VSD, pulmonary outflow obstruction, overriding aorta, RV hypertrophy. Cyanosis depends on obstruction. Hypercyanotic spell: calm child, knee-chest position, urgent help/O2 and ordered treatment. Repair; prostaglandin only when pulmonary flow is duct-dependent.

Narrow aorta → high arm BP, weak femoral pulses, lower leg BP. Compare upper/lower extremity pulses and pressures. Critical newborn: shock as duct closes. Prostaglandin if duct-dependent; catheter/surgical repair.
Obstruction from RV to pulmonary artery. RV workload rises; murmur, exertional symptoms. Severe disease can cause cyanosis. Balloon valvuloplasty or surgery; critical newborn may need prostaglandin.

Obstructed LV outflow; increased LV workload. Murmur; exertional syncope/chest pain are concerning. Critical newborn may develop low output/shock. Activity advice and catheter/surgical treatment by cardiology.

Diuretics: reduce congestion; check weight, electrolytes and urine. ACE inhibitors: reduce afterload; monitor BP, renal function and potassium. Digoxin: prescribed contractility support; apical pulse and toxicity monitoring. Prostaglandin E1: maintains ductal flow; monitor apnea and BP. Use individualized pediatric dose/hold parameters.

Small, frequent high-energy feeds; rest breaks. Daily weight; strict intake/output. Monitor work of breathing, perfusion and oxygenation. Cluster care; oxygen as prescribed. Follow fluid/sodium and medication plan; teach worsening signs.

Before: consent, fasting, baseline pulses and allergies. After: monitor access site, bleeding, distal pulses/color/temp. Keep affected limb positioned as ordered; check vitals and urine. Report bleeding or impaired limb perfusion immediately.

Systemic vasculitis; coronary artery aneurysm risk. Persistent fever with red eyes, red/cracked lips or strawberry tongue, rash, extremity changes and cervical node enlargement. Incomplete presentations also occur. Echocardiography and inflammatory labs support evaluation. IV immunoglobulin + aspirin under specialist direction. Monitor cardiac status, hydration and response. Follow cardiology/echo plan; discuss live-vaccine timing after IVIG.

Immune complication after group A streptococcal infection. Major Jones manifestations: carditis, migratory polyarthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules. Diagnosis uses criteria plus evidence of preceding infection. Eradicate strep; anti-inflammatory treatment and cardiac care. Long-term antibiotic prophylaxis may prevent recurrence. Teach completion of antibiotics and follow-up. Main concern: lasting valve damage.

Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is a life threatening complication of type 1 diabetes. Osmotic diuresis in DKA causes polyuria and without rapid fluid replacement can lead to severe dehydration . Acidosis and dehydration create electrolyte imbalances, placing the client at risk for deadly arrhythmias and cardiac arrest . When administering IV fluids to treat DKA, the sud
Neurologic: assess level of consciousness. Cardiac: continuous cardiac monitoring. Respiratory: assess acid-base status (the course option is ABGs). Endocrine: prescribed IV regular insulin infusion.

Cannot adequately break down phenylalanine. Lifelong controlled phenylalanine intake + medical formula. Avoid aspartame; monitor blood levels. NOT a zero-protein diet.

entries.h: Medications and too much / too little

Galactosemia: dietary treatment; specialist-directed supplements. Diabetes: excess insulin can cause hypoglycemia; monitor glucose.

Often follows Shiga-toxin diarrheal illness. Triad: hemolytic anemia, low platelets, acute kidney injury. Monitor urine output, BP, CBC, renal labs and fluid balance. Supportive hospital care; dialysis/transfusion if indicated. Prevent foodborne infection and dehydration.

Urine flows backward from bladder toward kidneys. Recurrent febrile UTI; risk of renal scarring. Ultrasound/voiding study as ordered. Prompt UTI treatment, regular voiding, constipation care. Selected patients: prophylactic antibiotics or repair.

Bedwetting beyond expected developmental control. Assess constipation, UTI, diabetes and stress. No blame or punishment; scheduled voiding. Bedwetting alarm; prescribed desmopressin in selected cases. Follow fluid instructions with desmopressin.
Urethral opening is on the underside of penis. Do not circumcise before urology evaluation. Surgical repair; protect catheter and incision. Monitor urine flow and pain after repair.

Infant: fever, poor feeding, vomiting. Older child: dysuria, frequency, urgency. Obtain appropriate urine specimen; culture. Give prescribed antibiotics, encourage fluids/regular voiding, teach hygiene.

Bladder is exposed through abdominal wall. Protect exposed tissue with ordered sterile nonadherent covering; keep clean/moist per protocol. Prevent contamination, monitor urine and skin. Surgical/urology care; support family.

Inflamed glomeruli; often after streptococcal infection. Cola-colored urine/hematuria, edema, oliguria and hypertension. Check urinalysis, renal function, complement and infection evidence. Strict intake/output, daily weight and BP. Sodium/fluid limits and antihypertensives/diuretics as ordered. Treat remaining infection; watch fluid overload and encephalopathy.

Glomerular protein loss → heavy proteinuria and low albumin. Generalized edema, weight gain; hyperlipidemia. Infection and thrombosis risks. Daily weight, edema/skin checks, urine protein and intake/output. Corticosteroids for steroid-sensitive disease; other treatment per cause. Sodium restriction; fluid/albumin/diuretics only as ordered.

AKI: sudden loss of filtration. CKD: persistent kidney damage/dysfunction. Monitor creatinine, potassium, acid-base balance, BP, weight and urine. Fluid overload and hyperkalemia can be urgent. Adjust drugs for renal function; avoid nephrotoxins. Dialysis when indicated; individualized nutrition/fluid plan.

mL/kg/hr = urine in mL ÷ weight in kg ÷ hours. Convert pounds: lb ÷ 2.2 = kg. Example: 220 mL in 6 hr; child weighs 50 lb. 220 ÷ (50 ÷ 2.2) ÷ 6 = 1.61 mL/kg/hr. Interpret against age, hydration and ordered targets; trend changes.

Lateral spinal curve with rotation. Uneven shoulders/hips; rib prominence on forward bend. Radiographs measure Cobb angle. Observation, brace or surgery depends on curve and growth. Brace adherence and skin checks; support body image.
Tight sternocleidomastoid → head tilt with rotation. Early physical therapy and gentle prescribed stretching. Encourage turning both ways; assess head shape.
Flattening from external pressure. Supervised awake tummy time; vary head position. Always place infant supine for sleep. Helmet in selected cases; assess for craniosynostosis.
Early fusion of skull suture(s). Abnormal head shape/growth. Craniofacial evaluation; surgery may be needed.
Foot turns inward/downward. Ponseti serial casts; often Achilles tenotomy, then brace. Check skin, toes and circulation; follow brace schedule.

Adolescent growth-plate slip; hip/groin or referred knee pain, limp. Limited internal rotation; leg may turn outward. Stop weight bearing; urgent orthopedic assessment. Surgical fixation prevents further slip.

Loss of blood supply to femoral head in childhood. Limp, hip/knee pain, restricted hip motion. Imaging; preserve motion and femoral-head containment. Activity/weight-bearing plan, therapy; selected surgery.

Shallow/unstable hip joint. Limited abduction, unequal leg length; infant screening. Ultrasound or radiographs by age. Pavlik harness/cast or surgery as ordered. Do not adjust harness straps; skin/neurovascular checks. Use hip-safe swaddling, allowing flexion/abduction.

Pain, swelling, deformity or reduced use. Immobilize; assess distal color, warmth, pulse, sensation and movement. Growth-plate injuries can affect future growth. Open fracture: cover and seek urgent treatment. Reassess pain and neurovascular status after reduction/casting.
Support wet plaster with palms; keep dry. Never insert objects or powders. Elevate for routine initial swelling as ordered. Report escalating pain, numbness, cool/pale digits or restricted movement.
Maintain prescribed alignment and pull. Weights hang freely; ropes stay in pulleys. Skin/pin care and neurovascular checks; do not remove weights without an order.
Compartment syndrome: severe unrelieved pain, pain with passive stretch, paresthesia. URGENT surgical assessment; pulse loss is late. Monitor skin injury, infection and immobility effects.

Progressive muscle weakness; Duchenne commonly affects boys. Gowers maneuver: uses hands to climb up legs when standing. Monitor respiratory and cardiac function. Preserve mobility; stretching, assistive devices, prescribed therapies. Support family, nutrition and genetic counseling.

Persistent inflammatory arthritis beginning in childhood. Pain, swelling, morning stiffness; some types have fever/rash. Balance rest with range-of-motion and low-impact activity. NSAIDs, disease-modifying drugs/biologics as prescribed. Regular eye exams for silent uveitis. Monitor growth, function and medicine effects.
