What: Sideways spinal curve with vertebral rotation. Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis often appears during a growth spurt. Recognize: Uneven shoulders, waist or hips; rib prominence on the Adams forward-bend test. Often painless. Diagnosis: Standing spinal X-rays measure the Cobb angle and guide follow-up. Treatment: Depends on curve size, progression and remaining growth. Smaller curves are observed; bracing limits progression while growing; severe curves may need spinal fusion. Typical thresholds: Observe below 25

What: Tight/short sternocleidomastoid (SCM) muscle. Signs: Head tilts toward the tight side; chin turns away. Limited neck motion; sometimes an SCM lump. Assess: Neck motion, head shape and feeding; screen for associated DDH. Usually a clinical diagnosis. Care: Early physical therapy, gentle taught stretches and varied awake positioning; supervised tummy time. Supine sleep. Follow-up: Check symmetry and progress. New painful or acute torticollis needs evaluation for other causes. [2]

What: Positional skull flattening from external pressure; sutures remain open. Signs: Flat occiput; ear/forehead may shift forward on that side. Assess torticollis. Diagnosis: Clinical exam; assess for craniosynostosis if atypical or worsening. Care: Vary awake positioning, supervised tummy time and PT if needed. Always supine for sleep; no positioning pillows. Treatment: Helmet for selected persistent severe cases after specialist review. [3]

What: Premature fusion of one or more skull sutures. Signs: Abnormal head shape; a firm suture ridge or altered head growth. Care: Early craniofacial/neurosurgical referral; imaging as directed. Surgery often occurs in infancy. Monitor head growth and neurologic status; raised intracranial pressure is a risk. [4]

What: Congenital rigid foot deformity: foot turns inward and down, with a high arch and inward heel. Diagnosed by examination. Treatment: Early Ponseti stretching and serial casts; often Achilles tenotomy, then boots-and-bar bracing for several years. Nursing: Check toes, circulation and skin; keep casts dry. Brace adherence prevents relapse. Report swelling, cool toes or persistent pain. [5,10,12]

What: Shallow acetabulum with an unstable, subluxed or dislocated femoral head. Risks include breech position, family history and female sex. Signs: Limited hip abduction, unequal leg length or later limp. Trained clinicians perform Barlow (provokes instability) and Ortolani (reduces a dislocated hip) maneuvers. Diagnosis: Hip ultrasound in young infants; radiographs become useful as the femoral head ossifies. Treatment: Pavlik harness in early infancy; reduction and hip-spica cast or surgery when indicated. Nursin

What: Femoral head slips at the growth plate, usually during adolescence. Risks include obesity and endocrine disorders. Signs: Limp, hip/groin/thigh or referred knee pain; outward-turned leg and reduced internal rotation. Diagnosis: Hip/pelvis X-rays. Inability to bear weight indicates an unstable slip. Priority: Stop weight bearing and obtain urgent orthopedic evaluation. Do not force hip movement. Treatment: Surgical fixation; follow ordered activity limits and assess pain/neurovascular status. Watch for avascul

What: Temporary loss of femoral-head blood supply causes avascular necrosis, followed by repair. Usually ages 4-10, more often boys. Signs: Limp with hip, thigh or knee pain; reduced abduction and internal rotation. Activity may worsen pain. Diagnosis: Hip X-rays; follow imaging over the healing period. Treatment: Maintain range of motion and contain the femoral head in the socket while it heals. Activity/weight-bearing limits, physical therapy, anti-inflammatory medication; selected casting, bracing or surgery. Nu

Types: Buckle = compression; greenstick = incomplete break with bending; complete = through the bone. Growth-plate injury may affect future growth. Signs: Pain, swelling, deformity and refusal to use the limb. Confirm with X-rays. First care: Immobilize, manage pain and check distal color, warmth, capillary refill, pulses, sensation and movement before and after treatment. Treatment: Splint/cast; reduction or fixation if displaced or unstable. Cover an open wound with a sterile dressing and obtain urgent care. Foll

Care: Support wet plaster with palms; keep cast dry and avoid pressure on edges/heels. Routine swelling: Elevate as ordered and encourage finger/toe movement. Follow prescribed weight-bearing limits. Never: Insert objects, powders or lotions; trim or alter the cast yourself. Assess/report: Increasing pain, numbness, pale/cool digits, reduced motion, odor, drainage, fever or a tight/damaged cast. Check neurovascular status regularly. [10,12]

Purpose: Maintain alignment, immobilize the limb and reduce muscle spasm. Skin traction uses straps; skeletal traction uses bone pins. Maintain: Prescribed line of pull and countertraction; ropes in pulleys and weights hanging freely. Do not change/remove weights without an order. Nursing: Skin/pin-site care per protocol, neurovascular checks, pressure relief, pain control and immobility prevention. [11,12]

Compartment syndrome: Escalating pain despite analgesia, pain with passive stretch, tingling and tense swelling. Pulses may remain present; pulse loss/paralysis are late. Action: Urgent surgical review. Keep limb at heart level; trained staff relieve constriction as directed. Fasciotomy may be required. Also monitor: Pressure injury, infection, stiffness and muscle wasting with immobilization. [10,12]

What: Genetic disorders causing progressive muscle weakness. Duchenne (DMD) is X-linked, mainly affects boys and involves absent/deficient dystrophin. Signs: Early-childhood proximal weakness, frequent falls, waddling/toe-walking, enlarged calves and Gowers maneuver (hands push up thighs to stand). Diagnosis: Elevated creatine kinase suggests muscle injury; genetic testing identifies the cause. Biopsy is sometimes needed. Care: Prescribed disease-specific therapy/corticosteroids, stretching, PT and assistive device

What: Immune-mediated inflammatory arthritis beginning before age 16, lasting at least 6 weeks after other causes are excluded. Signs: Swollen, warm joints; morning stiffness and limp. Systemic forms may cause fever and rash. Diagnosis: History/exam, inflammatory markers and selected imaging; no single confirmatory blood test. Treatment: Rheumatology care; NSAIDs for symptoms, DMARDs such as methotrexate and/or biologics to control inflammation; selected corticosteroids. Nursing: Balance rest with gentle motion and

entries.h: 1 / 2 Caring for a client with a neurologic disorder

entries.t: Baseline: compare with the child's usual behavior and the caregiver's report. LOC first: alertness, orientation/response and pediatric GCS (eye, verbal, motor). Check pupils (size, equality, reaction), limb movement/strength and sensation. Trend HR, BP, breathing pattern, temperature, oxygen saturation and pain. Infants: head circumference, fontanel, sutures, feeding, cry and tone. Urgent change: falling LOC, new weakness, unequal or nonreactive pupils, or seizures.

CT: rapid look for injury or bleeding. MRI: detailed brain and spine anatomy. Head ultrasound: infant ventricles through an open fontanel. EEG: seizure activity. LP/CSF: cells, glucose, protein, Gram stain and culture; obtain ordered blood cultures. LP safety: suspected dangerous raised ICP or mass effect needs medical review first. Do not delay antibiotics. Labs: glucose, electrolytes and CBC as indicated.

Drains ventricular CSF to the peritoneum. Assess neuro checks, infant head growth, the incision and the abdomen. After surgery: follow positioning/activity orders; no pressure on the incision. Report urgently: headache, vomiting, unusual sleepiness, bulging fontanel, fever, redness or abdominal pain. Teach follow-up and malfunction signs. Programmable valve: ask about checks after MRI.

Seizures: rescue midazolam/diazepam per plan; maintenance medicines as ordered. Raised ICP: ordered hypertonic saline (your M7 page also lists mannitol). Monitor sodium, fluids and neuro status. Infection: IV antibiotics; dexamethasone in selected cases. Spasticity: baclofen or botulinum toxin when prescribed. Verify weight-based doses, watch breathing/sedation, never stop antiseizure drugs abruptly.

Rising ICP: headache, vomiting, irritability, reduced alertness. Infants: bulging fontanel, high-pitched cry. Late sign — Cushing triad: hypertension with widening pulse pressure, bradycardia, irregular respirations. EMERGENCY. Head midline, HOB about 30° if ordered; avoid neck/hip flexion and straining. Serial neuro checks, fluid balance, ordered ICP/CPP targets. CPP = MAP − ICP.

During: stay, call for help, time it, clear hazards, protect the head; turn to the side when safe. Airway: watch breathing, oxygen and suction ready, check glucose when feasible. Never restrain or put anything in the mouth. Nothing by mouth until fully alert. Escalate at 5 minutes, repeated seizures without recovery, or breathing difficulty; give rescue medicine per plan. After: reassess airway/LOC, let the child rest, document, teach the seizure action plan.

entries.h: 2 / 2 Neuro disorders: hydrocephalus to cerebral palsy

entries.t: CSF builds up in the ventricles from blocked flow or poor absorption. Clues: fast head growth, bulging fontanel, separated sutures, “sunset” eyes; older child: headache, vomiting, drowsiness. Care: trend head size and neuro status; assess feeding, vomiting and skin. Treat: VP shunt or selected endoscopic surgery; return urgently for renewed symptoms or fever.

Bacterial infection inflames the meninges; risk of sepsis and raised ICP. Clues: fever, headache, stiff neck, photophobia. Infant: poor feeding, irritability, bulging fontanel. Nonblanching rash is urgent. Prompt IV antibiotics; cultures/LP when safe, without delaying treatment. Monitor neuro status, seizures, fluids. Meningococcal/Hib: droplet + standard precautions until 24 h of effective antibiotics. Vaccines, contact prophylaxis, hearing follow-up.

Trauma causes concussion, bleeding or swelling; hypoxia and hypotension worsen it. Clues: altered LOC, headache, vomiting, seizures, unequal pupils. ABCs and cervical-spine protection if injury is suspected; serial GCS, pupils, vital signs; CT when indicated. Escalate worsening drowsiness, repeated vomiting or new deficits. After concussion: gradual return to school and activity.

Neural tube defect: meninges and spinal cord/nerves in an open sac on the back. Clues: leg weakness or sensory loss, bladder/bowel dysfunction; hydrocephalus may follow. Before repair: prone or side-lying; sterile, saline-moistened nonadherent dressing; prevent drying and soiling; latex-free supplies. After: watch for infection, skin, head growth and movement; bladder/bowel program and catheterization plan.

Nonprogressive injury or abnormal development of the immature brain affects movement and posture. Clues: delayed motor skills, abnormal tone, spasticity/scissoring, poor coordination. Care: feeding/swallowing, communication, skin and mobility; prevent contractures; assess for seizures. Early PT/OT/speech therapy, braces, selected medicines or surgery; support independence and family goals.

entries.t: Management of Frostbite Immediate treatment: cover affected areas and rewarming Controlled but rapid rewarming with warm bath (104 to 108 °F) Administer tetanus toxoid Administer analgesics for pain during rewarming Do not massage or rub If feet are involved, do not allow client to walk Once re-warmed, elevate affected extremity Assess for compartment syndrome Swelling Increase in pain Needs immediate treatment! entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: The source lists 104–108°F. Wilderness Medical Society guidance recommends controlled water rewarming at 37–39°C (98.6–102.2°F). Use a thermometer; avoid burning numb tissue. Do not rub or massage. Protect the part and avoid walking on injured feet when possible. Do not thaw tissue if it will refreeze before rescue. Treat associated hypothermia, provide pain relief and obtain specialist assessment; injury depth can evolve after rewarming.

Give ordered analgesic/antiemetic; reassess pain, sedation, respiratory rate and nausea. Monitor glucose, electrolytes, renal function and withdrawal symptoms. entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Life-threatening bleeding/shock: hematemesis, blood-stained clothing, HR 142, BP 82/38, weak pulses, pallor and diaphoresis. Airway threat: reduced responsiveness and vomiting create aspiration risk. Assess airway and ventilation immediately. Anticoagulation: warfarin can worsen the hemorrhage. Activate urgent resuscitation, notify the team and prepare blood and bleeding-control treatment.
ACC: Management of anticoagulant-related bleeding Original slide 66

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Leading concern: acute GI hemorrhage causing hypovolemia and reduced tissue perfusion. Ulcer disease or another GI lesion requires diagnostic evaluation. Warfarin may amplify bleeding; it does not identify the source. Altered consciousness can result from shock or another concurrent problem. Tachycardia and tachypnea are compensatory responses. Obtain glucose and evaluate additional causes while resuscitation continues.
Original slide 67

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Warfarin reduces vitamin K-dependent clotting factors, increasing bleeding risk. Review INR, dose history, interacting drugs and recent illness. Ramipril lowers blood pressure and may worsen hypotension during volume depletion; seek an order to hold it during acute shock. The mechanical valve also creates thrombosis risk. Emergency reversal and the eventual anticoagulation restart need coordinated medical decisions.
ACC: Management of anticoagulant-related bleeding Original slide 68

entries.t: Continuous assessment: airway protection, suction readiness, oxygen/ventilation as needed, cardiac monitoring and repeated perfusion/neuro checks. Access and labs: large-bore IVs, CBC, coagulation studies, metabolic tests and type/crossmatch. Prepare transfusion and urgent endoscopy or other bleeding control. Keep NPO; quantify bleeding, monitor I&O and reactions to treatment. Administer ordered fluids, reversal agents and GI medications with frequent reassessment.

Continue rapid hemorrhage resuscitation and prepare blood; do not treat the maintenance-fluid rate as adequate resuscitation for persistent shock. entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Look for improving consciousness, BP/perfusion, pulse quality and urine output, with decreasing visible bleeding and stable oxygenation. Trend INR and hemoglobin/hematocrit; watch for fluid overload or transfusion reactions. INR 6.6 is markedly elevated; a typical non-anticoagulated INR is 0.8–1.1. B: She is frequently in the ED after missing dialysis when she is on a winning streak at the casino. entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Missed two dialysis sessions: anuria plus weakness, fatigue and palpitations raises concern for hyperkalemia and toxin accumulation. Fluid overload: coarse crackles/wheezing, RR 30 and severe hypertension suggest pulmonary congestion. Neurologic change: lethargy and disorientation may reflect uremia, hypoxia or another metabolic problem. Obtain ECG, glucose, oxygenation and urgent renal assessment.
UK Kidney Association: Acute hyperkalaemia guideline Original slide 73

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Potential lethal dysrhythmia from potassium accumulation; do not wait for arrest to escalate. Pulmonary edema from retained fluid and possible worsening cardiac function; assess work of breathing and oxygenation. Uremia/metabolic disturbance and limited vascular access. Protect the functioning dialysis access and coordinate urgent dialysis and safe alternative IV access.
UK Kidney Association: Acute hyperkalaemia guideline Original slide 74

entries.h: 94 / 129 Ms. Green: interpret the ECG image
Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: The prominent, tall peaked T waves are concerning for hyperkalemia in this clinical context. Confirm with serum potassium and compare serial ECGs; ECG appearance does not reliably predict the potassium concentration. Treat the combination of suspected hyperkalemia, symptoms and ECG changes as urgent. Other ECG abnormalities still require clinician interpretation.
UK Kidney Association: Acute hyperkalaemia guideline Original slide 75

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Prioritize Hypotheses What could be causing the irregularities you noted on Ms. Green’s ECG? Completed answer

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Missed dialysis plus ESRD prevents adequate potassium removal; potassium accumulates outside cells. Raised extracellular potassium alters cardiac conduction and repolarization, causing peaked T waves and potentially progressing to severe dysrhythmia. Acidosis, medications, tissue injury or a hemolyzed specimen may also affect potassium; assess them without delaying treatment when toxic ECG changes are present.
UK Kidney Association: Acute hyperkalaemia guideline Original slide 76

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Continuous cardiac monitoring, urgent 12-lead ECG and prompt labs. Assess airway, breathing, mentation, volume status and the dialysis-access thrill/bruit. Sit upright if tolerated, support oxygenation and obtain urgent nephrology/medical review. Avoid routine fluid boluses in this fluid-overloaded, anuric patient. Prepare prescribed hyperkalemia treatment and dialysis. Monitor response, glucose and repeat potassium; arrange practical support for attending future dialysis.
UK Kidney Association: Acute hyperkalaemia guideline Original slide 77

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Escalate immediately for hyperkalemia with ECG changes and pulmonary congestion; maintain ECG monitoring and safe IV access. Give ordered IV calcium to stabilize the cardiac membrane, then potassium-shifting treatment such as insulin with glucose. Calcium does not lower potassium. Arrange urgent dialysis for potassium/fluid removal. Reassess ECG, breathing and consciousness; monitor closely for hypoglycemia after insulin.
UK Kidney Association: Acute hyperkalaemia guideline Original slide 78

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes

entries.h: 102 / 129 Ms. Green: interpret the laboratory values
Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Potassium 6.1 mEq/L (3.5–5.0): high and urgent with ECG changes. Sodium 134 (135–145) and chloride 96 (98–106 mEq/L): mildly low. BUN 55 mg/dL (7–20) and creatinine 5.4 mg/dL (approximately 0.6–1.3): high, consistent with markedly impaired renal clearance in this ESRD case. CO2 26 mEq/L (22–29): within a typical serum bicarbonate range. Glucose 128 mg/dL: above fasting 70–99, but fasting status is unknown. Ranges vary by laboratory; use the reporting lab for interpretation.
Original slide 79

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Generate Solutions What nursing management is appropriate to lower serum potassium levels for this client? Completed answer

entries.h: 104 / 129 How to lower Ms. Green’s potassium
Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Shift potassium into cells: prescribed IV insulin with glucose; nebulized albuterol may be an adjunct. Monitor glucose before and repeatedly after treatment. Remove potassium: urgent hemodialysis is definitive for an anuric ESRD patient; prescribed binders may be adjuncts but must not delay emergency care. Stop potassium intake/supplements as ordered and review contributing medications. Recheck potassium and ECG for rebound. IV calcium protects the heart but does not remove potassium.
UK Kidney Association: Acute hyperkalaemia guideline Original slide 80

entries.t: Nonsurgical Management of Breast Cancer Hormonal therapy Most effective in cancer cells with estrogen receptors that can be inhibited Selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) — tamoxifen Used for those who are high risk for breast cancer or have advanced breast cancer Suppresses the growth of cancer cells Increases the risk of endometrial cancer (vaginal bleeding) Increases the risk of DVT/PE (leg swelling or SOB) Common side effect is hot flashes 36 Original slide 34

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Nonsurgical Management of Breast Cancer Chemotherapy Combination of antineoplastic drugs Usually given over 3 – 6 months Radiation therapy Targeted therapies Most effective for breast cancer with HER2/neu gene 37 Original slide 35

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Breast Cancer in Males <1% of men develop breast cancer Average onset age is 68 years Usually diagnosed later (40% late-stage disease) Poorer prognosis Can present with a hard, painless mass Gynecomastia can be present Risk factors Low testosterone BRCA1 & BRCA2 genetic mutation Klinefelter syndrome (decreased testosterone) 38 Original slide 36

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Ovarian Cancer Leading cause of death in female reproductive cancers Frequently metastatic at the time of diagnosis 70% are stage III or IV at time of diagnosis Risk factors Family history of ovarian, breast cancer, or colon cancer Most significant risk factor BRCA-1 or BRCA-2 gene mutations Early menarche and late menopause (more cycles) Nulliparity (more cycles) Obesity Original slide 37

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Ovarian Cancer Clinical manifestations are usually non-specific Abdominal/pelvic pain Abdominal bloating Abdominal mass Weight loss Vaginal bleeding Urinary urgency/frequency Tumor markers: CA-125 Useful in follow-up care, but not as a diagnostic tool Treatment includes surgery, chemotherapy, palliative care Original slide 38

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Endometrial (Uterine) Cancer Most common female reproductive cancer Most often diagnosed after menopause Risk factors Cumulative exposure to estrogen is the major risk factor Obesity (estrogen production by fat cells) Increases mortality and morbidity of disease Estrogen replacement therapy Nulliparity Use of tamoxifen Early menarche and/or late age at menopause Original slide 39

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Endometrial (Uterine) Cancer Clinical manifestations Irregular or post-menopausal bleeding Pelvic/back pain Diagnosed by endometrial biopsy Treatment: Hysterectomy, radiation therapy, chemotherapy Original slide 40

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS) Dysfunction of the hypothalamic-pituitary ovarian axis Complex disorder, not well understood Highly associated with insulin resistance Elevated levels of testosterone Common disorder affecting 10 to 47% of women in the U.S. Two of the three criteria must be met for diagnosis Hyperandrogenism (increased facial hair) Chronic anovulation (irregular cycles) Polycystic ovaries on ultrasound 43 Original slide 41

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: 44 Original slide 42

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: PCOS Treatment Weight loss Eat food with a low-glycemic index Medications Metformin Regulates periods & helps with weight loss Spironolactone Reduces hirsutism Oral contraceptives Infertility treatments Surgery to remove cysts 45 Original slide 43

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Infertility Treatments Pharmacologic therapy (clomiphene) Increases the risk of multiple births >25% Artificial insemination Places prepared sperm in the uterus In vitro fertilization (IVF) Collect client’s egg, fertilizing the egg in the lab then transferring to uterus Gamete intrafallopian transfers (GIFT) Mix the egg and sperm into the fallopian tube Surgical laparoscopy procedure Original slide 44

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Uterine Fibroids Common, benign smooth muscle tumors of the uterus Can be asymptomatic or cause abnormal, heavy menstrual bleeding and abdominal pain Complications Iron deficiency anemia Infertility Miscarriage Treatment Myomectomy Hysterectomy 47 Original slide 45

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Hysterectomy Surgical removal of the uterus to treat cancer, dysfunctional uterine bleeding, endometriosis, fibroids, persistent pain, prolapse, and previous injury to the uterus Total hysterectomy Subtotal hysterectomy Bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy Panhysterectomy Radical hysterectomy Completed answer

entries.h: 49 / 108 Hysterectomy: fill in the procedure meanings
Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Total: uterus and cervix. Subtotal/supracervical: uterine body removed, cervix remains. Bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (BSO): both fallopian tubes and ovaries; it is a separate removal that may accompany hysterectomy. Panhysterectomy: commonly used for uterus/cervix plus both tubes/ovaries; confirm the operative definition. Radical: uterus/cervix, surrounding supporting tissue and upper vagina, with node assessment as indicated; ovaries are not automatically removed.
ACOG: Hysterectomy Original slide 46

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Hysterectomy: Surgical Approaches Laparoscopic Vaginal Abdominal Total abdominal hysterectomy Robotic 50 Original slide 47

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Hysterectomy Perioperative Care Preoperative care Negative pregnancy test Administer preop antibiotics Place anti-embolism stockings Postoperative care Indwelling urinary catheter inserted intraoperatively Kept in place for 24 hr. Monitor vaginal bleeding Excessive bleeding 1 pad saturation in 4 hours Monitor for signs of infection, atelectasis, paralytic ileus, wound dehiscence, DVT, bleeding, and hypovolemia Original slide 48

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Hysterectomy: Client Education Well-balanced diet high in protein and vitamin C to promote wound healing If ovaries have been removed Menopausal manifestations HRT may be an option Vaginal atrophy can cause itching and dryness - instruct client to use artificial lubrication Activity restrictions including no sexual intercourse for 4 to 6 weeks Avoid tampons Report complications 52 Original slide 49

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Hysterectomy: Complications Hypovolemic shock Monitor VS, labs, vaginal bleeding Administer IVF and blood transfusions as needed Infection Monitor for fever (greater than 37.8°C/100°F), foul-smelling drainage, redness and swelling Psychological reactions Can occur months to years later Depression Refer to support groups 53 Original slide 50

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Menstrual Disorders Menorrhagia - excessive menstrual bleeding (amount and duration), possibly with clots, saturate more than one tampon or pad per hour Metrorrhagia - bleeding between menstrual periods, common in adolescents and those entering menopause Dysmenorrhea - painful menstruation Amenorrhea - absence of menses, can indicate pregnancy, thyroid disorder, or other disorder 54 Original slide 51

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Premenstrual Syndrome (PMS) PMS is thought to be a caused from an imbalance of estrogen and progesterone Premenstrual dystrophic disorder (PMDD) Severe form of PMS Unable to carry out daily activities Original slide 52

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Endometriosis Overgrowth of endometrial tissue that extends outside of the uterus into the fallopian tubes, ovaries, pelvis Results in bleeding, inflammation, and scarring Manifestations Pelvic pain Painful intercourse (dyspareunia) Menorrhagia Pain with defecation Depressed mood 56 Original slide 53

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Endometriosis Major cause of infertility Treatment Manage pain and limit the progression of implants Hormone therapy/BCP, steroids, GnRH agonists (see next slide) Pain is often unresponsive to NSAIDS Surgical options Severe cases Excision of endometrial implants and adhesions 57 Original slide 54

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Endometriosis Treatment Nafarelin Gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist that decreases ovarian function (suppressed release of estrogen) Results in medical-induced menopause Administration is 1 spray into one nostril in the morning; 1 spray into the opposite nostril in the evening May lead to rhinitis and nasal irritation Original slide 55

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Perimenopause Perimenopause is the time (approx. 4 years) before menopause Ovarian function declines as ova slowly diminish Clinical manifestations Irregular menstrual flow Vaginal and urethral atrophy Hot flashes Night sweats Fluctuations of vasoconstriction/vascular spasms  dizziness, numbness/tingling, headaches Insomnia Fatigue Depression 59 Original slide 56

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Perimenopause Client Education Pregnancy can still occur, maintain birth control Complications Osteoporosis Increase calcium and vitamin D intake Avoid caffeine and tobacco Coronary artery disease Avoid obesity, tobacco, alcohol Treat hyperlipidemia, HTN, and DM since heart disease increases at menopause 60 Original slide 57

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Menopause Permanent physiologic cessation of menses associated with declining ovarian function Complete when there is no menses for 12 months Natural or surgically induced Laboratory testing FSH/LH increased Pelvic exam and pap to r/o cancers Original slide 58

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Menopausal Hormone Therapy Benefits of estrogen therapy Suppresses hot flashes Prevents atrophy of vaginal tissue Consider estrogen vaginal creams Reduces the risk of osteoporosis/fractures Original slide 59

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Menopausal Hormone Therapy Contraindicated in women with history of breast cancer, DVT, impaired liver function, uterine cancer, and undiagnosed vaginal bleeding Risks of estrogen therapy CAD MI DVT Stroke Breast, ovarian, and endometrial cancer Original slide 60

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Alternatives to HT Herbal therapy Black cohosh, ginseng, red clover Research findings are inconsistent Phytoestrogens Dandelion greens, alfalfa sprouts, black beans, and soy Can decrease s/s of menopause Vitamin E and Vitamin B6 Decrease hot flashes in some clients 64 Original slide 61

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) Original slide 62

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Human Papilloma Virus (HPV) Most common sexually transmitted infection in the US Vaccine Starting at age 11 or 12 before they are sexually active and available for those 9-26 years of age Treatment of genital warts Topical agents or surgical removal of warts Associated with cervical dysplasia and cervical cancer Need regular Pap smears If cervical dysplasia is present, will need colposcopy, and further treatment Also increased risk of vulvar, vaginal, oropharyngeal, and penile cancers Original slide 63

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Genital Herpes (HSV) Recurrent, lifelong viral infection More than 87% of infected individuals are unaware Education: May be transmitted when the carrier is asymptomatic (viral shedding) Avoid sexual intercourse with active herpes Safe sexual practices using barrier contraception Outbreak triggers Causes painful itching and burning herpetic lesions Diagnosis may be based on H&P but can be confirmed with lab testing Original slide 64

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Trichomoniasis (Trich) Protozoal infection transmitted by asymptomatic carrier with infection of urogenital tract Only about 30% of cases are symptomatic Vulvovaginal itching and burning Frothy yellow-green or yellow-white vaginal discharge Treatment: metronidazole All sexual partners should receive treatment Original slide 65

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Syphilis Painless ulcer on genitals, rectum, or mouth Bacterial disease with 3 stages Primary stage is a painless sore (chancre) All stages can be treated with penicillin Secondary stage occurs with body rash including palms and soles Latent stage occurs with rash resolving Tertiary syphilis can occur years later, affecting the blood vessels, brain, eyes, heart, nerves, and joints Original slide 66

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Chlamydia Common bacterial STI Clear vaginal or penile discharge, dysuria Many women are unaware of infection - asymptomatic Can lead to pelvic inflammatory disease and infertility Can result in ectopic pregnancies Treated with antibiotics Standard STI precautions Use condoms Limit sexual partners Obtain screening test Original slide 67

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Gonorrhea Bacterial infection affecting the urethra, vaginal, rectum, or throat Copious penile discharge, painful urination, vaginal discharge, and pelvic pain Can result in infertility in men and women Standard STI precautions Condoms Limit sexual partners Testing for condition Original slide 68

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) Infection of the upper female reproductive tract Usually develops from a bacterial infection in the vagina or cervix Gonorrheal and chlamydial organisms are common causes Some are associated with more than one infection Can result in scarring, infertility, and abscess formation Increases the risk of ectopic pregnancy and chronic pelvic pain later Original slide 69

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) Manifestations range from asymptomatic to severe Fever Pain and tenderness in the lower abdomen Post coital bleeding Cervical motion tenderness Abnormal vaginal discharge Original slide 70

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease: Treatment Mix of broad-spectrum antibiotics Cephalosporin injection (ceftriaxone), followed by PO doxycycline and metronidazole Avoid sexual intercourse during treatment Treat sexual partners Acetaminophen and ice packs No tampon use during treatment No baths during treatment May shower May need surgery to remove adhesions or drain abscesses if severe 74 Original slide 71

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Male ReproductiveDisorders Original slide 72

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Male Reproductive System Includes conditions that affect reproduction, sexuality, and urine elimination Client may experience anxiety and embarrassment from condition Be sensitive to cultural and emotional issues related to sexuality and the genitals to accomplish effective assessment and communication Provide for privacy and education Conditions include BPH, erectile dysfunction and prostate cancer, epididymitis, testicular torsion, testicular cancer, orchitis Original slide 73

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Diagnostic Tests: Digital Rectal Exam (DRE) Performed in an office or clinic Client positioned to lean over the exam table, placed on one-side, or lithotomy position If prostate gland is abnormally large, hard, or irregular shape or lumps, evaluation by ultrasound and transrectal biopsies indicated Screening guidelines Age 40 for client who are at greatest risk Age 45 for client who are at high risk Age 50 for client who are average risk Original slide 74

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Diagnostic Tests: Prostate Specific Antigen (PSA) Protein produced by prostate that is found in the blood; sensitive but not specific to cancer Perform prior to DRE Increased PSA levels may indicate cancer, BPH, acute urinary retention, acute prostatitis; UTI can elevate PSA for up to 6 weeks PSA value >4 ng/mL requires further evaluation ACS recommends against routine screening for clients at average risk 78 Original slide 75

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Diagnostic Tests (cont.) EPCA-2 (serum test) Highly sensitive at detecting prostate cancer Transrectal ultrasound (TRUS) Indication: elevated PSA or abnormal DRE Position client on the left, side-lying position Used to guide biopsy May be prescribed an enema prior Contraindication: latex allergy Original slide 76

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Diagnostic Tests (cont.) Penile Doppler ultrasonography Used to determine the normal anatomy and blood flow of the penis Can detect many conditions of the penis including erectile dysfunction Culture and sensitivity of prostatic fluid Determines the organism causing prostatitis Determines the type of antibiotic to treat the infection Original slide 77

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) As an adult male ages, the prostate gland enlarges Affects half of men over age 60 and 90% of men over age 85 Risk factors: Increased age Smoking ETOH use Sedentary lifestyle Obesity Western diet (high-fat, high-protein, high-carbs; low-fiber) DM Heart disease Original slide 78

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: This slide’s content is in the original picture. Use Open full size to enlarge it. Original slide 79

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: BPH Clinical Manifestations Urinary symptoms Increased frequency Urgency Hesitancy Incontinence Incomplete emptying of the bladder Dribbling post-voiding Nocturia Diminished urinary stream Hematuria Original slide 80

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: BPH Medications Goal is to re-establish unobstructed urine flow from the bladder Dihydrotestosterone (DHT)-lowering medications (finasteride) Inhibits the enzyme 5-alpha-reductase, which converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT). This reduces DHT levels, decreases prostate size, and improves symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). Can take 6 months for any therapeutic effect Alpha-blocking agents (tamsulosin) Relaxes the bladder outlet and prostate gland = stronger flow 84 Original slide 81

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Transurethral Resection of the Prostate (TURP) Most common surgical procedure for BPH to relieve the urinary obstruction Resectoscope is inserted through the urethra and trims away excess prostatic tissue  enlarges the passageway of the urethra through the prostate gland Original slide 82

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Postoperative Nursing Actions Client will have a three-way catheter that allows for continuous bladder irrigation (CBI) to keep the catheter free of obstruction Adjust rate to keep the output pink or lighter (NEVER place on IV pump) If irrigation becomes bright-red, increase CBI flow rate For obstructions: turn off the CBI and hand irrigate with 50 mL syringe of irrigation solution Record I & O Catheter may be taped tightly to the leg to create traction to prevent bleeding Catheter has a large balloon - 30 to 45 mL

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: This slide’s content is in the original picture. Use Open full size to enlarge it. Original slide 84

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: TURP Irrigation 88 Original slide 85

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: TURP Client Education Avoid heavy lifting, strenuous exercise, straining, and sexual intercourse for 2-6 weeks Maintain hydration Avoid NSAIDS Avoid bladder stimulants like caffeine and alcohol If urine becomes bloody, stop activity, rest, and increase fluid intake 89 Original slide 86

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Prostate Cancer Second most common cancer in men Slow-growing cancer in elderly Can be an aggressive cancer in younger clients Potential to metastasize, especially to bones Risk factors Risk increases with age Familial predisposition African-American race High fat/red meat, low fiber diet Gene mutations Original slide 87

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Prostate Cancer Manifestations Early disease has few/no symptoms Urinary obstruction usually with advanced disease Blood in urine or semen Painful ejaculation Symptoms of metastasis (usually spreads to bones) Backache, hip pain, weight loss, weakness May be first indications of prostate cancer Regular screenings and early diagnosis Original slide 88

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Prostate Cancer: Surgical Management Prostatectomy Retropubic Laparoscopic Robotic-assisted Original slide 89

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Prostate Cancer Management Radiation therapy Brachytherapy or external beam Hormonal therapy Decreases circulating testosterone or interrupts conversion of testosterone to DHT causing prostate epithelium to atrophy Chemotherapy If cancer has spread to distant sites Cryosurgery Probes inserted under US guidance and freezes tissue Original slide 90

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Brachytherapy for Prostate Cancer Original slide 91

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Prostate Surgery: Potential Complications Hemorrhage and shock Highest priority for post-op clients Decreased cardiac output Infection DVT Catheter obstruction Are you getting out what you’re putting in? Sexual dysfunction 95 Completed answer

entries.h: 96 / 108 CBI: are you getting out what goes in?
Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Calculate actual urine: total drainage minus irrigant infused for the same interval. Example: 3,000 mL drainage − 2,400 mL irrigation = 600 mL urine. Less drainage than irrigation, suprapubic pain/distention or leakage can mean obstruction. Assess tubing and stop inflow if outflow is blocked; follow the ordered irrigation protocol and notify the team. Persistent bright-red bleeding, large clots or unstable vital signs need urgent escalation. Increasing irrigation alone does not treat uncontrolled hemorrhage.
Original slide 92

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Prostate Surgery: Nursing Management Maintain fluid balance Monitor urinary drainage and fluid amount used for irrigation, keep catheter patent Pain relief Bladder spasms cause feelings of pressure and fullness, urgency to void, and bleeding from the urethra around the catheter Medication and warm compresses or sitz baths can relieve spasm Administer analgesics and antispasmodics (B&O) as needed Encourage client to walk but to avoid sitting for prolonged periods Prevent constipation Irrigate catheter as prescribed

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Prostate Surgery: Client Education Explanation of anatomy & function, diagnostic tests and surgery, and the surgical experience Drainage devices Regaining of bladder continence Gradual process (dribbling may continue for up to one year depending on type of surgery) Perineal exercises Avoid straining, heavy lifting, long car trips, strenuous exercise Increased risk of bleeding Original slide 94

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Prostate Surgery: Client Education Diet Encourage fluids and avoid coffee, alcohol, spicy foods which may cause bladder discomfort Sexual issues Erectile dysfunction, decreased libido, fatigue Provide privacy and a confidential environment Always be mindful of issues that may be embarrassing or of cultural concern to the client Allow client to discuss concerns Assess and provide referrals as needed 99 Original slide 95

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Erectile Dysfunction (ED) Impotence Inability to achieve or maintain an erection More than 50% of men 40 to 70 years of age Psychogenic causes: (functional) Organic causes: (gradual reduction in function) 100 Completed answer

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Psychogenic: performance anxiety, stress, depression, relationship difficulties or other emotional distress; symptoms may vary by situation. Organic: vascular disease/diabetes, neuropathy or spinal injury, pelvic surgery, low testosterone, certain medicines, tobacco or heavy alcohol use. Mixed causes are common. Assess medical, medication and sexual history sensitively; do not assume a psychological cause without evaluating physical contributors.
NIDDK: Erectile dysfunction symptoms and causes Original slide 96

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Erectile Dysfunction: Management Pharmacologic therapy Prior to medication therapy, a cardiovascular work up is recommended Oral medications: sildenafil Adverse effects include headache, flushing, dyspepsia Take one hour before sexual intercourse Contraindicated with any nitroglycerin use for heart disease Penile implants - semirigid rod vs. Inflatable Negative pressure (vacuum) devices 102 Original slide 97

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Penile Implant or Penile Vacuum 103 Original slide 98

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Prostatitis Inflammation/infection of the prostate gland Often associated with UTI Clinical Manifestations Fever, chills Urethral discharge Perineal discomfort/pain Urinary urgency, frequency, hesitancy, burning Boggy, tender prostate Elevated PSA, elevated WBC Treated with oral antibiotics for 3-5 weeks Original slide 99

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Prostatitis: Management Antibiotic therapy Alpha-adrenergic blockers (tamsulosin) to promote bladder and prostate relaxation Comfort measures - analgesics, sitz baths Client teaching- antibiotic therapy, s/s of recurrent prostatitis Encourage fluids Avoid indwelling catheters - suprapubic may be needed for severe urinary retention Original slide 100

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Epididymitis Infection of epididymis that spread from urethra, bladder, or prostate Symptoms are tender and swollen area behind testicle Confirmed with urinalysis and urethral culture Treatment: oral antibiotic therapy May take a month to fully recover Original slide 101

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Testicular Cancer Most common cancer in men ages 15 to 35 Highly treatable and curable 95% cure rate (ATI, 2023) Risk factors Undescended testicles Positive family history Personal history of testicular cancer Caucasian American race HIV-positive Original slide 102

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Hemodynamic shock A condition in which tissue perfusion is inadequate to deliver oxygen and nutrients to support vital organs and cellular function and can lead to organ failure Any condition that compromises oxygen delivery to organs and tissues can lead to shock Low blood pressure occurs in all forms of shock! Affects all body systems, resulting in potential organ failure Rapidly-progressing and life-threatening process Certain physiologic responses are common to all types of shock: hypoperfusion of tissues, hype

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Types of shock (ATI, 2023) Hypovolemic: A decrease in intravascular volume of at least 15% to 30% Cardiogenic: failure of the heart to pump effectively due to a cardiac factor Obstructive: Impairment of the heart to pump effectively as a result of a noncardiac factor Distributive: Widespread vasodilation and increased capillary permeability, including neurogenic, septic, and anaphylactic shock Original slide 5

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: This slide’s content is in the original picture. Use Open full size to enlarge it. Original slide 6

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Stages of shock (ATI, 2023) All types of shock progress through the same stages of shock and produce similar effects on body systems Initial: no visible changes in client parameters; only changes on cellular level MAP decreases 5 to 10 mm Hg from baseline; mild vasoconstriction; HR increases Compensatory (non-progressive): Measures that increase CO to restore tissue perfusion and oxygenation Vasoconstriction increases; HR increases; MAP decreases 10 to 15 mm Hg from baseline; mild acidosis and hyperkalemia Progress

entries.h: 7 / 74 EVOLVING STAGES OF SHOCK OCCUR FROM INABILITY TO MAINTAIN BLOOD PRESSURE RESULTING IN ORGAN FAILURE
Read slide text and study notes

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Compensatory Stage of Shock Sympathetic NS causes vasoconstriction, increased HR, and increased contractility This attempts to maintain blood pressure and CO Body shunts blood away from skin, kidneys, and GI tract Results in cool, clammy skin, hypoactive BS, and decreased UO Perfusion of tissues has become inadequate Acidosis occurs because of anaerobic metabolism (lactic acid formation) Respiratory rate increases due to acids circulating in the bloodstream Confusion may occur from evolving acidosis Original slide

entries.h: 9 / 74 Compensatory Mechanisms in Shock1) Activation of Sympathetic NS2) Activation of RAAS3) Release of cortisol* *
Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Compensatory Mechanisms in Shock1) Activation of Sympathetic NS2) Activation of RAAS3) Release of cortisol* * It's all about mechanisms trying to maintain blood pressure to vital organs** Original slide 10

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Progressive Stage of Shock Mechanisms that regulate BP can no longer compensate, and BP and MAP decrease All organs suffer from hypoperfusion (including heart, lung, and brain) Vasoconstriction of arterioles continues, further compromising cellular perfusion to organs Mental status further deteriorates because of decreased cerebral perfusion and hypoxia Original slide 11

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Progressive Stage of Shock Lungs begin to fail: Hypoxemia develops, CO2 increases, alveoli collapse, pulmonary edema can occur Inadequate perfusion of the heart leads to dysrhythmias and ischemia GFR cannot be maintained, and acute renal failure may occur when MAP falls below 65 mmHg- metabolic acidosis develops Liver function, GI function, and hematologic function are all affected by low blood pressures DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation) may occur as a complication of shock Widespread clotting and bleedi

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Irreversible Stage of Shock Original slide 13

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: For All Types of Shock Early identification of shock state and timely treatment are critical Identify and treat the underlying cause of shock (Bleeding? Anaphylaxis? Sepsis?) The sequence of events/treatments for the different types of shock will vary depending on type of shock Therefore, the management and care of the client will vary based on the type of shock occurring Original slide 14

entries.h: 14 / 74 Nursing care for all types of shock
Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Nursing care for all types of shock Monitor the following: Oxygenation status- PRIORITY! VS Continuous ECG monitoring Hourly urine output LOC (level of consciousness depends on BP) Skin color, temp, moisture, cap refill, turgor Place the client on high-flow oxygen such as 15 L nonrebreather mask (if the client has COPD use 2 L NC) Be prepared to intubate Maintain patent IV access For hypotension, place the client flat with both legs elevated (modified Trendelenburg) Prepare for and perform hemodynamic monitoring CV

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Modified Trendelenburg (passive leg raising [plr]) How does this position help with shock or low blood pressure conditions? Completed answer

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Temporary preload test: raising the legs shifts venous blood toward the heart. A measurable rise in stroke volume or cardiac output suggests fluid responsiveness. Reassess promptly: use a real-time flow measurement when available. Blood pressure alone is less reliable; responsiveness does not automatically mean fluid is needed. Nursing role: follow the ordered technique and consider injuries or positioning restrictions. This is a reversible assessment, not definitive treatment for shock.
SCCM: Surviving Sepsis Campaign adult guidelines Original slide 16

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Intubation and mechanical ventilation Pre-intubation nursing actions Monitor ECG, SaO2, breath sounds, and skin color Preoxygenate with 100% oxygen Assist with ventilation with manual resuscitation bag and mask Suction as needed Sedation and paralysis will be usually required (Ex: propofol and succinylcholine) Postintubation nursing actions Assess bilateral breath sounds, symmetrical chest movement End-tidal CO2 monitoring and O2 saturation CXR to confirm placement of tube in trachea Secure ETT to avoid dislodgment

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Hypovolemic Shock (fluid/blood loss) Most common type Decreased intravascular volume Decreased CVP 15-30% reduction in volume 750 to 1500 mL of blood (in 70kg person) Excessive fluid loss from burns, diuresis, vomiting or diarrhea, or blood loss secondary to surgery, trauma, gynecologic/obstetric causes Remember the symptoms and signs! (BP, HR, RR, skin color, urine output?) Completed answer

entries.t: BP and heart rate: falling pressure or a narrowing pulse pressure with tachycardia; compensation can initially maintain BP. Upon presentation to the emergency department, his vital signs are temperature, 100.9°F; heart rate, 120 bpm; respiratory rate, 20 breaths/min; and blood pressure, 90/54 mm Hg. His abdomen is firm, with bruising around the umbilicus. He is alert and oriented but complains of dizziness when changing positions. The patient is admitted for management of suspected hypovolemic shock. Complete

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Suspect internal hemorrhage: blunt abdominal trauma, a firm abdomen and periumbilical bruising suggest abdominal injury and concealed blood loss. Perfusion is threatened: BP 90/54, pulse 120/min and positional dizziness are concerning even though he is oriented. Act: activate the trauma response; reassess airway, breathing, circulation and bleeding. Keep him supine as tolerated, monitor closely, establish large-bore IV access and prepare blood and urgent source control.

Manage perfusion and the cause of shock; monitor urine output and renal function. entries.t: Teaching point: exercise can briefly raise heart rate and respiratory rate enough to meet two old SIRS thresholds. Interpretation: these numbers are nonspecific. Exercise is not the same as pathologic systemic inflammation, and SIRS alone does not establish infection or sepsis. Sepsis assessment: evaluate suspected infection with organ dysfunction and the whole clinical picture; normal temperature does not rule out serious infection.

entries.t: THE SEQUENTIAL ORGAN FAILURE ASSESSMENT (SOFA) Identifies clients at higher risk for mortality from their suspected infection Measure of organ dysfunction If score decreases by 2 or more from baseline, this is suggestive of organ dysfunction This is a tool that is part of a hospital toolkit for sepsis surveillance Clinical side note

entries.h: 40 / 74 Side note: direction of the SOFA score
Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Correction: an acute INCREASE of 2 or more SOFA points from baseline supports organ dysfunction associated with suspected infection. The source says “decreases.” That direction is reversed: a lower score generally reflects less organ dysfunction. Sepsis does not require positive blood cultures or organisms circulating in the bloodstream; infection may begin at a localized site.

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Septic Shock Most common type of distributive shock Widespread infection (usually bacterial) that has entered the bloodstream Endotoxins and other mediators causing massive vasodilation and inflammation The deadliest type is gram-negative bacteria (UTI? Pneumonia? Cholecystitis?) 40% mortality rate One of the most common causes of death in ICUs Continues to rise, so important to notice SIRS criteria initially Original slide 33

entries.t: Septic Shock risk factors Immunosuppression (disease state or from chemotherapy) Age extremes Malnourishment Chronic illness Invasive procedures Lack of immunizations Emergent and/or multiple surgeries Serious illness that causes bacteria to enter the blood (pyelonephritis, pneumonia, etc.) ** Anything that allows bacteria to enter the bloodstream may result in sepsis** Original slide 34

entries.t: LR is a balanced crystalloid: its electrolyte composition and buffer reduce the chloride load compared with 0.9% saline. Large saline volumes can contribute to hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis. Balanced solutions are suggested for many adults with sepsis; the choice remains individualized. Reassess after fluid: watch perfusion, oxygenation, lung sounds and fluid balance. Heart/kidney disease or brain injury may change the plan; more fluid is not always better.

entries.t: Neurogenic Shock Caused by widespread vasodilation r/t loss of balance between parasympathetic and sympathetic stimulation Usually occurs from injury to the sympathetic nervous system BP drops due to this vasodilation and bradycardia d/t PNS response Risk Factors Head trauma SCI Epidural anesthesia Depressant action of medications Lack of glucose Original slide 38

Water seal: intermittent bubbling can occur as air exits a pneumothorax; continuous bubbling suggests an air leak requiring assessment. Tidaling: the water-seal level may move with breathing. entries.t: Multiple Organ Dysfunction Syndrome (MODS) Altered organ function that requires medical intervention to support continued organ function Occurs from the release of toxic metabolites and destructive enzymes in response to inadequate oxygenation Can develop from inadequate tissue perfusion and reperfusion of ischemic cells, causing further tissue injury High mortality rate 60% when more than 4 organs fail Prevention and aggressive treatment of shock is key to avoiding MODS Original slide 50

entries.h: 66 / 74 Mr. Smith: what increases his sepsis risk?
Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Likely source: urinary instrumentation/indwelling catheter and abnormal urine suggest a urinary infection. Culture results and assessment are needed to confirm the organism. Risk context: older age, institutional care and impaired continence increase exposure or vulnerability; incontinence alone does not prove infection. Do not be reassured by no fever: older adults may present with confusion, weakness, tachypnea or hypotension instead.

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Shock cues: BP 82/44, confusion and RR 28/min indicate threatened organ perfusion; SpO2 88% on room air shows hypoxemia. Inflammation/infection cues: WBC 15,000/µL is elevated (typical adult range 4,500–11,000/µL); CRP is reported high, but the slide supplies no number or laboratory range. Glucose 160 mg/dL: above a typical fasting range of 70–99 mg/dL, though fasting status is unknown. Follow ordered glucose checks; this value alone does not diagnose diabetes.

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Convert and find concentration: 16 mg = 16,000 mcg. 16,000 mcg ÷ 250 mL = 64 mcg/mL. Calculate: (2 mcg/min × 60 min/hour) ÷ 64 mcg/mL = 1.875 mL/hour, approximately 1.9 mL/hour if rounding to tenths. Safety: independently verify the concentration and smart-pump setting per policy. Titrate to the actual order with continuous hemodynamic monitoring; use the ordered line and assess the site.
Original slide 57

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Correct starting rate: 1.875 mL/hour (about 1.9 mL/hour), not the 3 mL/hour printed in the original image. Reverse check: 3 mL/hour × 64 mcg/mL ÷ 60 = 3.2 mcg/min. That is higher than the ordered 2 mcg/min. The original graphic is preserved so you can compare it with the corrected arithmetic. Confirm the order and concentration before administering any medication.
Original slide 58

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Question 4 Explain the importance of nutritional support for this patient and which type of nutritional support should be provided. Completed answer

entries.h: Read slide text and study notes
entries.t: Stress is catabolic: inflammation and stress hormones increase energy needs and break down muscle/protein. Nutrition supports healing and recovery. After stabilization: use enteral nutrition when the gut is usable and the patient can tolerate feeding; coordinate with the dietitian and critical-care team. Safety: uncontrolled shock or worsening perfusion may require withholding or adjusting feeds. Monitor tolerance, glucose, fluid balance and electrolytes.

Answer: bNasopharyngitis, commonly known as the common cold, is typically viral and self-limiting, meaning it will resolve on its own over time. Treatment focuses on relieving symptoms such as congestion, fever, and sore throat using supportive measures, such as hydration, rest, and fever-reducing medications. Antibiotics are not effective for viral infections, and cough suppressants should be used cautiously in young children
