entries.h: Heart Defects · Patho & Causes · NG-001 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Cardio · Congenital Heart Defects — Foundation · Pathophysiology Course 🫀 HEART DEFECTS SET NG-001 Patho & Causes NG-151 ASD·VSD·PDA·AVSD NG-118 Tetralogy of Fallot NG-183 Stenosis & Coarctation NG-201 Surgery & Chest Tubes

Pathophysiology & Causes — the foundation page for the whole set NG-001 CARDIO · PEDS ADHD-friendly visual edition A congenital heart defect is an abnormality in the heart that develops before birth , where one or more problems with the heart's structure change the way blood flows through the heart and out to the body . There are more than 150 described types , but they all end in the same sentence: less oxygen-rich blood OUT to the body → decreased cardiac output → murmurs, dysrhythmias, heart failure & hypoxia .

🏗️ Structure → flow The problem is plumbing , not muscle. A wrong hole, a wrong valve, or a wrong connection changes the direction and the amount of blood flow. 📉 Less OUT to the body Every defect ends in decreased cardiac OUTput = less oxygen-rich blood OUT. Remember: OUT put = OUT to the body. 🚨 The big four Abnormal rhythms · murmurs · heart failure · hypoxia . Those four are the exam answer for “complications.” 🧬 Genes + pregnancy Family hx & Down syndrome · in pregnancy: rubella , alcohol/drugs , maternal diab
STEP 0 · LEARN THIS ONCE You cannot see what is broken until you can see what is normal. Learn this one picture and all 150+ defects become variations on it.

entries.h: 🫀 Anterior cutaway — chambers, septa, valves & great vessels
entries.t: EXAM TIP Blue side and red side never mix in a normal heart — the septum is the wall that keeps them apart, and the valves are the one-way doors that keep blood moving forward.

entries.h: 🅥 V–V: V eins V acuum blood back to the heart
entries.t: In a normal heart, deoxygenated blood is vacuumed back to the heart through the VEINS — through the vena cava into the right side . It is then pushed into the lungs to get oxygenated. That oxygen-rich blood returns to the LEFT side and is pumped OUT to the body — this is cardiac OUT put.
STEP 1 · WHAT ACTUALLY BREAKS Three things can go wrong with the plumbing — a hole, a narrowing, or a wrong connection. Everything else is detail.

entries.h: 🔀 Shunt direction is the whole exam question
entries.t: A shunt is blood taking a shortcut through an abnormal opening. Blood always flows from HIGH pressure to LOW pressure. Normally the left side runs at much higher pressure than the right — so if you punch a hole, blood goes LEFT → RIGHT first.

entries.h: 🗂️ Four hemodynamic families — 150+ defects, four buckets
entries.t: Do not memorize 150 names. Memorize what the blood is doing , then drop each defect into a bucket.

entries.h: 📉 The final common pathway — decreased cardiac OUTput
entries.t: Whatever the defect, less blood is pumped OUT of the heart . Decreased cardiac output = less oxygen-rich blood OUT to the body. 🏗️ Structural defect ▼ 🔀 Abnormal blood flow direction / volume ▼ 📉 ↓ Cardiac OUTput ▼ 🫁 ↓ O₂ delivery to tissues = HYPOXIA 🧠 Every complication on this page is downstream of that one arrow. Fix the flow → fix the output.

Abnormal heart rhythms — stretched, overloaded chambers fire dysrhythmias Murmurs — turbulent blood crossing a hole or a tight valve makes noise Heart failure — the chamber that is volume- or pressure-overloaded eventually fails Hypoxia — low oxygen in the blood , the reason a cyanotic baby is blue 🧠 “RM-HH” — R hythms · M urmurs · H eart failure · H ypoxia. Read My Heart's History.

entries.h: 🔊 Why a murmur happens at all
entries.t: Answer first: a murmur is the sound of turbulence . Smooth flow is silent; blood squeezing through a hole or a tight valve is not.
STEP 2 · WHY IT HAPPENED Two columns only: what the baby was born with, and what happened during the pregnancy.

entries.h: 🗓️ When it happens — the heart is built early
entries.t: The heart forms in the first trimester , roughly weeks 3–8 of gestation. That is often before a person knows they are pregnant — which is exactly why prevention is a preconception teaching point.

Family history of congenital heart disease Down syndrome (trisomy 21) — the classic exam association; strongly linked with AVSD and VSD 👉 Any newborn with a known chromosomal syndrome gets a cardiac evaluation — do not assume the heart is fine. 🧠 Down = Down the middle. Trisomy 21 → the middle of the heart (the AV canal / septum) is the usual problem.

Infection — rubella 🦠 (maternal rubella in the first trimester) Alcohol / drug use 🍷💊 Diabetes 🩸 — poorly controlled maternal diabetes ❌ There is no “safe amount” of alcohol in pregnancy — this is a teaching point, not a judgment call. 🧠 “RAD” babies — R ubella · A lcohol & drugs · D iabetes. Three pregnancy exposures, one heart.

entries.h: ✅ Prevention & preconception teaching — what the nurse actually says
entries.t: 💉 Rubella immunity check & vaccinate BEFORE pregnancy 🩸 Glucose control tight control before & during 🚭 No alcohol no tobacco, no illicit drugs 💊 Review meds with the provider before conception 🥬 Folic acid preconception supplementation 🧬 Genetic counseling if family hx or a prior affected child EXAM TIP The rubella (MMR) vaccine is a live vaccine — it is not given during pregnancy. Screen and immunize before conception, or postpartum. 🧠 Live vaccine + pregnancy = ✋. If the question offers “give MMR now” to a pregn
STEP 3 · WHAT YOU SEE A baby cannot tell you they are short of breath — they tell you with feeding, weight, color and work of breathing.

entries.h: 👶 Head-to-toe: where a heart defect shows up on the body
⭐ Acyanotic vs cyanotic — tell them apart
entries.t: 💗 ACYANOTIC 💙 CYANOTIC Shunt LEFT → RIGHT Shunt RIGHT → LEFT or mixing ↑ pulmonary blood flow ↓ pulmonary blood flow / mixed Baby looks pink Baby looks blue — central cyanosis Ends in HF & pulmonary HTN Ends in hypoxia, polycythemia, clubbing ASD · VSD · PDA · AVSD · stenosis · coarctation Tetralogy of Fallot · TGA · truncus · TAPVR · tricuspid atresia 🧠 The 5 T's of cyanotic disease: T etralogy of Fallot · T ransposition · T runcus arteriosus · T otal anomalous pulmonary venous connection · T ricuspid atresia.

Echocardiogram ⭐ — the definitive non-invasive test; shows structure and flow direction Pulse oximetry screening — routine newborn screen for critical defects Chest X-ray — heart size & pulmonary vascular markings ECG — chamber hypertrophy, dysrhythmia Cardiac catheterization — invasive; measures pressures & O₂ saturations chamber by chamber, and can be therapeutic 🧠 Echo = the eyes. Cath = the pressure gauge . If the question asks “which test confirms the structural defect,” echo is your first instinct.

entries.h: 🚨 Cyanosis that does NOT improve with oxygen
entries.t: HIGH YIELD In a cyanotic (right-to-left) defect , blood is bypassing the lungs altogether — so giving more oxygen does not fix the saturation. That failure to respond is a red flag for a structural problem rather than a lung problem. ❌ Never assume a blue newborn who doesn't “pink up” on oxygen just needs a higher FiO₂ — escalate. 🧠 “O₂ can't fix a detour.” If the blood never meets the alveoli, the FiO₂ doesn't matter. 🩺
STEP 4 · WHAT YOU DO Foundation nursing care that applies to every defect in the set — the specifics live on the four linked pages.

entries.h: ✅ Priority ladder — the shared nursing plan
entries.t: 1 Oxygenation & work of breathing — assess color, respiratory rate/effort, SpO₂; position for comfort; cluster care to limit oxygen demand. ▼ 2 Cardiac output — apical pulse for a full minute, blood pressure, capillary refill, peripheral pulses, level of consciousness. ▼ 3 Feeding & growth — small, frequent feeds; rest periods; strict intake & output; daily weights on the same scale at the same time. ▼ 4 Infection prevention — keep immunizations current; teach families about fever and about dental/procedure prophyl

entries.h: 🍼 Feeding is the infant's stress test
entries.t: Small, frequent feeds — a long feed burns more calories than it delivers Limit each feed and allow rest periods Higher-calorie feeds may be prescribed to support growth Watch for sweating, tiring, tachypnea, color change during the feed 🧠 “Sweating at the bottle = running a race.” Diaphoresis with feeding is one of the earliest and most quotable signs of a peds cardiac problem.

Color change — new or worsening blueness around lips Breathing harder — faster, retractions, grunting, flaring Feeding worse or fewer wet diapers Sudden weight gain or new puffiness around the eyes Fever , or extreme sleepiness / difficulty waking 🧠 “Blue, breathing, bottle, balance (weight).” Four B's the parents can remember at 3 a.m.

entries.h: 📚 Go deeper — the rest of this set
entries.t: This page is the foundation . Each linked page takes one family of defects and works it all the way through: NG-151 — ASD · VSD · PDA · AVSD — the four left-to-right acyanotic shunts NG-118 — Tetralogy of Fallot — the classic cyanotic defect & tet spells NG-183 — Stenosis & Coarctation — the obstructive family NG-201 — Surgery & Chest Tubes — post-op care 🧠 Learn this page once and the other four stop being memorization — they become the same story with a different hole in it. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🏗️ Structure changes flow A defect is plumbing, not muscle. 📉 ↓ Cardiac OUTput = less O₂-rich blood OUT to the body. 🚨 Rhythms · Murmurs · HF · Hypoxia The four complications, every time. 🧬 RAD + Down Rubella · Alcohol/drugs · Diabetes · genetics.

Q1: What is a congenital heart defect, in one sentence? Show answer An abnormality in the heart that develops before birth, where a problem with the heart's structure changes how blood flows through the heart and out to the body. Q2: Which direction does a shunt flow first, and why? Show answer Left → right. Blood always moves from high pressure to low pressure, and the left side of the heart is the high-pressure side. That is why these defects are acyanotic (pink) at first. Q3: Name the four big complications of c

Normal-heart illustration: NHLBI, NIH . Flow and congenital-defect information: CDC: how the heart works , CDC: congenital heart defects , and American Heart Association . Embryonic timing: human embryonic heart atlas .

entries.h: ADPIE I · NG-002 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Fundamentals of Nursing

The Nursing Process I — Assessment · Diagnosis · Planning · Implementation · Evaluation NG-002 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition The nursing process is the systematic approach used to guide client care . It is the skeleton under every care plan, every clinical-judgment question and a huge share of NCLEX items. It is a circle, not a list — you never stop at Evaluation, you loop back and assess again. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🔤 A · D · P · I · E Assess → Diagnose → Plan → Implement → Evaluate. In that order. Every time. 1️⃣ ASSESS is always first Unless the client is in immediate danger, you gather data before you act . 🫁 Physical before psychological Maslow: airway beats anxiety . Ask “what kills fastest?” 🎯 SMART outcomes S pecific · M easurable · A ttainable · R ealistic · T imely 🔁
STEP 1 · THE FRAME Five steps, one loop. Learn the wheel first and every care-plan question stops being scary.

entries.h: 🔁 The nursing process is a wheel — it never ends at step 5
entries.t: EXAM TIP Evaluation feeds straight back into Assessment. If the outcome was not met, you do not invent a new intervention out of thin air — you re-assess , then re-diagnose, then re-plan.

Assess Gather and validate subjective and objective information. Plan and implement Prioritize needs, set goals and carry out appropriate care. Evaluate Compare response with goals and revise the plan. Diagnosis Identify nursing problems supported by assessment data. Prioritization Consider immediate threats, patient preferences and the clinical context. Documentation Record findings, actions, response and communication accurately. 🧠 “ A ll D ogs P lay I n E vening.” Say it while you trace the wheel with your finge

entries.h: 📖 Say the definition the way the source says it
entries.t: Nursing process = “the systematic approach used to guide client care.” It shapes clinical judgment about a client's physical & psychological status , and it also folds in the client's social factors, family, and community experiences . 🧠 Systematic = same steps, same order, every client. That is the whole point — it stops you from “just doing something.”

entries.h: ⭐ The five steps in one line each
entries.t: A Assessment gather info & review history D Diagnosis identify the problem P Planning goals, outcomes, action plan I Implementation do the interventions E Evaluation did it work? 🧠 Five steps = five fingers. Tap each finger as you say it; on the thumb (E) you fold the hand shut and open it again — back to A .

entries.h: 🚨 The #1 NCLEX trap: “what does the nurse do FIRST?”
entries.t: Almost always ASSESS — A comes before D-P-I-E for a reason. You cannot diagnose or intervene on data you do not have. The only exception: when the client is in immediate danger — an unwitnessed collapse, an active seizure, an obstructed airway, a disconnected ventilator. Then you act first (position, protect, call for help) and assess as you go. ❌ “Administer the PRN acetaminophen” — before you took a temperature? No. ❌ “Notify the provider” — before you have data to report? Usually no. ✅ “Auscultate lung sounds,”

entries.h: 🔤 ADPIE vs ADOPIE — why you may see six steps
entries.t: Some texts (and the ANA Standards of Practice ) split Planning in two and teach six steps: A ssessment D iagnosis O utcome identification ← the extra one P lanning I mplementation E valuation Same process. ADOPIE just pulls “write the measurable outcome” out as its own step. 🧠 ADPIE + O = ADOPIE. The O is the O utcome — the sentence you will grade yourself against later.

entries.h: 🧭 Where this page sits in the batch
entries.t: ADPIE is the spine. Two other pages are its arms and legs: 📎 NG-190 Head-to-Toe Assessment — how to actually do the A : the systematic head-to-toe sequence, inspection → palpation → percussion → auscultation. 📎 NG-180 Delegation & the 5 Rights — how the I gets shared: what you may hand to an LPN/UAP and what you may never delegate. 🧠 You may delegate TASKS, never the nursing PROCESS. Assessment, nursing diagnosis, planning, teaching and evaluation stay with the RN. 🩻

entries.h: A + D · GATHER, THEN NAME IT
entries.t: STEP 2 · THE DATA Assessment collects it. Diagnosis names the human response you are going to treat.

entries.h: 🗣️ vs 👁️ Subjective = what they SAY · Objective = what you OBSERVE
entries.t: Subjective data is what the client reports . Objective data is what can be observed or measured . 🧠 “Subjective = Spoken. Objective = Observed.” Both start with the same letter as their cue. If you had to put quotation marks around it, it is subjective .

Primary source = the client. Always. Their report outranks everyone else's. Secondary sources = family, caregivers, the chart, old records, the previous nurse, other disciplines, diagnostic results. Then validate (does the subjective match the objective?), cluster related findings, and document in the client's own words where possible. 🧠 The client is the PRIMARY source — even a confused client is still assessed; you just add corroboration.

Initial / comprehensive — on admission, full database. Focused / problem-focused — one system or one complaint, done constantly through the shift. Emergency — ABCs during a crisis; rapid, life-threat only. Time-lapsed / ongoing — compare to baseline later (clinic follow-up, next shift). 🧠 Every re-check is an assessment. Reassessing after an intervention is technically Evaluation — same skill, different step of the wheel.

entries.h: 🏷️ Diagnosis = identify the problem — the human response , not the disease
entries.t: Using the assessment data you collected, the goal is to address both actual and potential health problems for the client . 🩺 MEDICAL diagnosis 👩‍⚕️ NURSING diagnosis Made by the provider Made by the RN Names the disease — pneumonia, CHF, stroke Names the human response to it — impaired gas exchange, activity intolerance, impaired swallowing Stays the same until the disease resolves Changes as the client changes — you rewrite it constantly Treated with medicine & surgery Treated with nursing interventions the RN can

entries.h: 🧱 The three types of nursing diagnosis
entries.t: Actual / problem-focused — it is happening now, and you have signs & symptoms to prove it. Risk — not happening yet, but risk factors are present. “Risk for…” has no signs & symptoms — if it had them it would be actual. Health-promotion — the client is ready to improve something. “Readiness for enhanced…” Format (PES): Problem related to Etiology as evidenced by Signs & symptoms . e.g. Impaired gas exchange r/t alveolar-capillary membrane changes AEB SpO₂ 89% , crackles, restlessness. 🧠 PES = Problem · Etiology · S

entries.h: 🪜 Prioritizing the diagnosis: Maslow, then ABC
entries.t: CAUTION Physical needs always come before psychological needs , as outlined by Maslow's hierarchy. “We are always going to prioritize an airway issue before we treat an emotional one.” Ask the question the source gives you: “What is going to kill your client the fastest?” That is what goes first on the care plan. 🧠 “Breath before feelings.” A client who is anxious and hypoxic gets oxygen first — you cannot talk someone out of a saturation of 89% .

entries.h: ❓ Practice Q1 — the classic diagnosis question
entries.t: A client with pneumonia has an oxygen saturation of 89% . Which nursing diagnosis is most appropriate? ✅ Impaired gas exchange. Pneumonia is the medical diagnosis; the human response you can treat is the failure to move oxygen across the alveolar–capillary membrane, and the SpO₂ is your AEB evidence. 🧠 Low SpO₂ + lung problem = impaired gas exchange. Airway secretions you can't clear = ineffective airway clearance . Poor effort/rate/depth = ineffective breathing pattern . Three different diagnoses — match the evide

entries.h: ❓ Practice Q2 — a SATA diagnosis question
entries.t: A client with Crohn's disease feels overwhelmed and has had no outside support since a recent divorce. Which nursing diagnoses fit the plan of care? (Select all that apply.) ✅ Ineffective coping — “overwhelmed,” lost her support system. ✅ Imbalanced nutrition: less than body requirements — malabsorption is expected in Crohn's. ✅ Risk for deficient fluid volume — diarrhea is the hallmark. ⚠️ Hopelessness — only if the client has said something that supports it. Don't diagnose a feeling she never reported. 🧠 Every di

entries.h: P + I + E · PLAN, DO, CHECK
entries.t: STEP 3 · THE ACTION Write a goal you could grade. Carry it out. Then be honest about whether it worked.

entries.h: 🎯 Planning = goals, outcomes & an action plan — and it must be SMART
entries.t: Develop an action plan with specific goals and the desired outcome of the plan — then always discuss the plan with the client to check that their perceived needs are being met. ❌ Poorly written outcome “Client will walk without dizziness.” No number, no distance, no deadline. Walk how far? By when? You cannot chart “met” or “not met.” ✅ SMART outcome “Client will demonstrate improved activity tolerance as evidenced by walking 20 feet without dizziness by day 3 of hospitalization.” Specific behavior, measurable dist

entries.h: 🗣️ ATI-style question — checking the plan fits
entries.t: What is the MOST appropriate way to assess whether the plan of care correlates with the client's perceived needs? ✅ Discuss the plan of care with the client. Don't forget the client's opinion here — but make sure what they want is realistic . 🧠 “Perceived needs” = ask the person who is perceiving them. Not the chart, not the family, not the last shift.

entries.h: 🛠️ Implementation = carry it out (and reassess as you go)
entries.t: Independent — RN-initiated: repositioning, HOB elevation, teaching, skin care, encouraging fluids. Dependent — needs a provider order: medications, IV fluids, treatments, diets. Collaborative / interdependent — with PT, RT, dietitian, social work, pharmacy. ⭐ Reassess immediately before you act. The blood pressure from two hours ago is not permission to give the antihypertensive now. 📎 NG-180 Delegation & the 5 Rights — you may delegate a task to an LPN/UAP, but never assessment, never the nursing diagnosis, never

entries.h: 📊 Evaluation = did the OUTCOME happen? Three answers, three next moves
entries.t: Evaluation is not “was the intervention done.” It is compare the client's actual response to the outcome criteria you wrote . 🧠 “Not met → go back to A.” The most common wrong answer is “change the intervention.” The right first move is to re-assess — the intervention may have been fine and the diagnosis wrong.

entries.h: 🚨 Five ADPIE traps that cost points
entries.t: ❌ Writing a medical diagnosis on the nursing care plan. ❌ Writing an outcome that starts “The nurse will…” ❌ Adding “ as evidenced by ” signs to a risk diagnosis. ❌ Choosing an intervention when an assessment option is available. ❌ Delegating assessment, teaching, or evaluation to a UAP. 🧠 “R.I.S.K. has no evidence.” Risk = no signs yet. If you can see it, it isn't a risk any more — it's actual.

entries.h: ✅ Putting one client through the whole wheel
entries.t: A — 72-y-o post-op day 1, reports “I can't catch my breath,” SpO₂ 89% , RR 28 , crackles at the bases, splinting the incision. D — Impaired gas exchange r/t retained secretions and shallow splinted breathing AEB SpO₂ 89%, RR 28, crackles. P — Client will maintain SpO₂ ≥ 94% on room air and use the incentive spirometer 10× per hour while awake by end of shift. I — HOB up, splint pillow, coach incentive spirometry, pain control before deep breathing, ambulate, O₂ per order. E — SpO₂ now 95% , spirometer used 8× /hr →

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🔁 A D P I E Assess · Diagnose · Plan · Implement · Evaluate — and loop. 🗣️ vs 👁️ Subjective = Spoken . Objective = Observed . 🪜 Maslow then ABC Physical before psychological. “What kills fastest?” 🎯 “The CLIENT will…” SMART outcome, with a number and a deadline.

Q1: A client is anxious about surgery and has an SpO₂ of 88%. Which problem comes first? Show answer The oxygenation. Maslow — physiological needs before psychological. Airway/breathing beats anxiety every time. Q2: “Client reports 8/10 stabbing pain in the right lower quadrant.” Subjective or objective? Show answer Subjective — it is what the client says. A rigid abdomen you palpate and a temp of 101.4 °F are the objective data that go with it. Q3: Rewrite “Client will eat better” as a SMART outcome. Show answer S

entries.h: All Electrolytes Cheat Sheet · NG-003 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Renal + Fluid · Fluid & Electrolyte Basics II

The one-page master cheat sheet — Na⁺ · K⁺ · Cl⁻ · Ca²⁺ · Mg²⁺ · PO₄³⁻ NG-003 Renal + Fluid Master comparison sheet The MOST deadly conditions are typically the MOST tested conditions — the whole point of nursing school is to create safe nurses. This page puts all six electrolytes side by side : range, job, causes, signs, and the priority action. Two deep-dive pages back it up — NG-088 (potassium · sodium · chloride) and NG-134 (magnesium · calcium · phosphate). 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🧂 Na⁺ Swells the body with FLUID Blood pressure + blood volume. 135–145 💓 K⁺ Pumps the heart PRIORITY. 3.5–5.0 — either direction kills. 🦴 Ca²⁺ Mellows the muscles Bones · Bloodletting (clotting) · Beats. 9.0–10.5 🧘 Mg²⁺ is the OTHER mellow one 1.3–2.1 mEq/L. Low Mg = torsades .

entries.h: ⚠️ Read this before you memorize a single number
entries.t: Every range on this page is a typical adult reference range . Reference ranges differ between laboratories and between textbooks — always verify against the range printed on your own facility's lab report. Also: a serum level tells you what is in the blood , not what is in the cells. A “normal” potassium in DKA can still mean a large total-body deficit. 🔬
STEP 1 · WHY THEY MATTER Electrolytes are charged particles held in unequal piles on either side of every cell membrane. That inequality is the electricity.

entries.h: 🔬 Inside vs outside — the gradient is the whole story
entries.t: Sodium, chloride and calcium live mostly OUTSIDE the cell. Potassium, magnesium and phosphate live mostly INSIDE. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump spends energy all day keeping it that way.

Concentration changes Losses, intake, kidney function and shifts alter levels. Cellular effects Membrane excitability and water movement change. Clinical response Symptoms, ECG and laboratory trends guide urgency. Sodium Primarily reflects water balance; rapid changes can affect the brain. Potassium Important for cardiac and muscle electrical activity. Calcium, magnesium, phosphate Support neuromuscular, cardiac and metabolic functions. 🧠 “Salty banana” — salt outside, banana inside. Sodium (salt) is the main ECF c

entries.h: 🧠 The four function mnemonics from the source
entries.t: 🧂 Sodium Swells the body with FLUID — it drags water with it, so it drives blood pressure & blood volume . 💓 Potassium Pumps the heart — every dysrhythmia question starts here. 🦴 Calcium Mellows the muscles — and the three B's : B ones · B loodletting (clotting) · B eats (heart). 🧘 Magnesium is the other mellow mineral — a natural sedative for nerve & muscle. 🧠 S-P-M-M: S welling · P umping · M ellowing · M ellowing again. Sodium swells, potassium pumps, calcium and magnesium mellow.

Cl⁻ copies Na⁺. Chloride follows sodium almost everywhere — so low sodium usually means low chloride. The difference is acid–base: high Cl⁻ pushes toward metabolic acidosis , low Cl⁻ toward metabolic alkalosis . Ca²⁺ and PO₄³⁻ are INVERSE. One up, the other down. Na⁺ and K⁺ are pushed apart by aldosterone — A dds sodium, L oses potassium. Mg²⁺ guards K⁺. You often cannot correct a stubborn low potassium until you fix the magnesium. 🧠 “Fix the mag, then the K will lag no more.” Refractory hypokalemia = check the mag

entries.h: 🚨 One cause explains a huge share of abnormal values: RENAL FAILURE
entries.t: The kidney is the final regulator of every electrolyte on this page. When it fails, the pattern is predictable: ⬆ GOES UP in renal failure ⬇ GOES DOWN in renal failure Potassium — cannot excrete it → the lethal one Phosphate — cannot excrete it Magnesium — cannot excrete it Calcium — pushed down by the high phosphate, and the failing kidney cannot activate vitamin D Never give a potassium-containing IV or a potassium-sparing diuretic to a client in renal failure without a very deliberate order and a current level.
STEP 2 · ALL SIX SIDE BY SIDE Range · job · causes · signs · priority action. This is the page you photograph before the exam.

entries.h: 📏 Low ← Normal → High, with the signs written on the scale
entries.t: 🧠 Draw these six bars on your whiteboard from memory. If you can put the number in the middle and one sign on each side, you know the electrolyte well enough for the exam.

entries.h: 📊 THE CHEAT SHEET — every electrolyte, every column
entries.t: Electrolyte Typical adult range Job Causes of LOW Causes of HIGH 🧂 Sodium Na⁺ 135–145 mEq/L Swells the body with fluid · BP & blood volume · nerve conduction Excess water intake · SIADH · vomiting & diarrhea · diuretics & diuresis · sweating in extreme heat High-sodium diet · DKA · excess aldosterone · water loss (fever, rapid respirations, watery diarrhea) · no access to water / loss of thirst · diabetes insipidus 💓 Potassium K⁺ PRIORITY 3.5–5.0 mEq/L Pumps the heart · skeletal & smooth muscle · nerve impulse Diur

entries.h: 💓 The potassium strip — the single highest-yield picture on this page
entries.t: 🧠 “High and PEAKED, low and FLAT with a U.” Tall tented T = too much K. Flat T with a U wave tagging along = too little. The U wave is the “Uh-oh, potassium is low.”

entries.h: 🔨 Reflexes tell you which way the mellow minerals went
entries.t: 🧠 “Mellow gone = jumpy. Too mellow = floppy.” Low Ca or low Mg → tetany, twitching, hyperreflexia. High Ca or high Mg → sedation, hyporeflexia, depressed respirations.

entries.h: 🚨 Hyperkalemia — the signs, in body-system order
entries.t: Heart (high pumps): tall peaked T waves , then a widened QRS, flattened/absent P waves → V-fib & cardiac arrest . Hypotension & bradycardia. Neuromuscular: early increased DTR and paraesthesia (tingling) → then muscle weakness, paralysis . GI (high = hyperactive): hyperactive bowel sounds , cramping, diarrhea. 🧠 “High K = tight and tingly, then limp and lethal.” Muscles fire too easily first, then stop firing entirely.

Respiratory: SHALLOW respirations — the most deadly sign , because the diaphragm is a muscle. Neuromuscular: decreased DTR, weakness, leg cramps, a limb that feels “paralyzed.” GI (low = hypoactive): constipation, hypoactive bowel sounds, paralytic ileus . Heart: flat T waves , ST depression, prominent U wave , PVCs. 🧠 Check the RESPIRATIONS first in hypokalemia. Everyone reaches for the cardiac monitor; the exam wants the breathing.

entries.h: 🧂 Sodium — the brain is the target organ
entries.t: HYPERnatremia — “big & bloated, dry inside”: edema, flushed red skin, increased muscle tone, swollen dry sticky tongue , nausea & vomiting, extreme thirst , restlessness & agitation → seizures. HYPOnatremia — brain low & slow: headache from cerebral edema , mental status changes, seizures & coma ; fatigue and muscle cramps; nausea. Never correct a sodium abnormality rapidly. Too-fast correction of a low sodium risks osmotic demyelination; too-fast correction of a high sodium risks cerebral edema. Slow, ordered, mon

entries.h: 🦴 Calcium — the two named signs everyone gets asked
entries.t: Trousseau's sign — inflate a BP cuff on the arm and the hand draws into a carpal spasm. “Twerking arm when the BP cuff is on.” Chvostek's sign — tap/stroke the cheek over the facial nerve and the face twitches. “Cheeky smile when stroking the face.” Both mean LOW calcium (and they also show up in low magnesium and high phosphate , because those push calcium down). Low Ca also gives: tetany, diarrhea, a prolonged QT, laryngospasm, and the weak B's — weak B ones (fractures), weak B loodletting (bleeding), weak B eats

entries.h: 🧘 Magnesium & 🧬 phosphate — the two everyone forgets
entries.t: LOW Mg²⁺ (below 1.3 ): the mellow is gone → hyperreflexia , hyperactive bowel sounds, tremor, seizures, and the top-tested rhythm — torsades de pointes and V-fib. Cause: malnourishment , chronic alcohol use. HIGH Mg²⁺ (above 2.1 ): super-mellow → depressed respirations , hypoactive bowel sounds, hyporeflexia / absent DTR , heart block, hypotension & bradycardia. Cause: renal failure , Mg-containing antacids/laxatives. HIGH PO₄³⁻: think LOW calcium signs — Trousseau's, Chvostek's, tetany, itching. Cause: renal failu
STEP 3 · WHAT YOU DO One priority action per abnormality. Learn the first move; the rest is documentation.

entries.h: 🔄 Who controls what — kidney, aldosterone, PTH
entries.t: 🧠 Three regulators: the kidney (all of them), aldosterone (Na up, K down), PTH (Ca up, phosphate down). Name the regulator and you can predict the lab.

Problem Priority nursing action 🚨 HYPERkalemia Cardiac monitor first — this is a rhythm emergency. Hold all K⁺ sources (IV, supplements, salt substitutes, K-sparing diuretics). Expect the provider to order calcium gluconate to protect the heart , insulin with dextrose to shift K into the cell , and a binder or dialysis to remove it. Recheck the level. 🚨 HYPOkalemia Assess respirations and the rhythm. Replace K⁺ — never IV push, always diluted, always on a pump , never exceeding the ordered rate. Check urine output

Cardiac monitor / rhythm — K⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺. Respiratory rate & depth — low K⁺, high Mg²⁺, low PO₄³⁻. Deep tendon reflexes — Mg²⁺ and Ca²⁺, both directions. Neuro status & LOC — Na⁺ in either direction. Bowel sounds — hyperactive with high K⁺ / low Mg²⁺, hypoactive with low K⁺ / high Mg²⁺ / high Ca²⁺. Daily weight, strict I&O, urine output — every one of them. 🧠 Weigh them daily, same scale, same time, same clothes. 1 kg ≈ 1 L of fluid — the fastest fluid-status number you have.

Potassium 🍌 — bananas, oranges, potatoes, tomatoes, avocado, spinach, beans, salt substitutes. Sodium 🧂 — table salt, canned soup, processed & cured meats, cheese, fast food. Calcium 🥛 — dairy, fortified plant milks, sardines, leafy greens, tofu. Magnesium 🥬 — dark leafy greens, nuts & seeds, whole grains, legumes, dark chocolate. Phosphate 🥩 — meat, dairy, nuts, cola drinks, processed foods. 🧠 “Salt substitute” is a potassium trap. A client on an ACE inhibitor or a K-sparing diuretic who switches to salt substitut

SAY IT OUT LOUD 💓 K⁺ 3.5–5.0 Peaked T = high. Flat T + U = low. Never IV push. 🧂 Na⁺ 135–145 Low = brain swells & seizes. High = thirsty, dry, agitated. 🦴 Ca 9.0–10.5 · Mg 1.3–2.1 Low = twitchy (Trousseau/Chvostek/torsades). High = floppy. 🧬 PO₄ 3.0–4.5 · Cl⁻ 97–107 Phosphate is inverse to calcium. Chloride copies sodium.

entries.h: Anatomy of the Lungs · NG-004 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Respiratory · Assessing Lungs I · Fundamentals

The upside-down tree — and the one place gas exchange actually happens NG-004 RESPIRATORY ADHD-friendly visual edition The respiratory system looks like an upside-down tree : the trachea is the trunk, branching into the right & left bronchus , then smaller bronchi , then tiny bronchioles , ending at the alveolar sacs — this is where all the action happens. Right lung = 3 lobes . Left lung = 2 lobes . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🌳 Upside-down tree Trachea → bronchus → bronchi → bronchioles → alveolar sacs . 3️⃣ Right = 3 · Left = 2 The heart takes the space where the left lung's third lobe would be. 🫧 Alveolus = the action Gas exchange happens only there — CO₂ out, O₂ in, across the capillary bed. 🩺 Listen BETWEEN the ribs IN tercostal = the space IN between the ribs. Skin, not clothing. 🌳
STEP 1 · THE ROAD MAP Air takes exactly one road in and one road out. Learn the road and every respiratory topic gets easier.

entries.h: 🫁 The airway tree & the lobes — one picture, everything labeled
entries.t: EXAM TIP The RIGHT mainstem bronchus is shorter, wider and more vertical than the left — which is why aspirated food, fluid and a too-deep endotracheal tube all end up in the right lung.

Conducting airways Air travels through trachea, bronchi and bronchioles. Alveoli Thin walls permit exchange with surrounding capillaries. Pulmonary blood flow Blood carries oxygen away and brings carbon dioxide back. Ventilation Movement of air into and out of the lungs. Diffusion Movement of gases across the alveolar–capillary barrier. Perfusion Blood flow through pulmonary capillaries. 🧠 “Trunk → two big branches → little branches → twigs → grapes.” Trachea → bronchus → bronchi → bronchioles → alveolar sacs. And

entries.h: 🔢 Lobes: 3 on the right, 2 on the left
entries.t: Right lung — 3 lobes: upper, middle, lower. Divided by the horizontal and oblique fissures. Left lung — 2 lobes: upper, lower. One oblique fissure. The left upper lobe has a tongue-shaped tip called the lingula — the “missing middle lobe” in disguise. 🧠 “The heart stole the left lung's middle lobe.” The cardiac notch is the dent where the heart sits — 2 lobes on the left, forever.

Visceral pleura — hugs the lung itself Parietal pleura — lines the inside of the chest wall Pleural space — a thin film of fluid between them; it lets the two surfaces glide instead of grinding Air in that space = pneumothorax . Fluid in that space = pleural effusion . Inflamed, dry surfaces rubbing = a pleural friction rub . 🧠 “Visceral = viscera (organ). Parietal = the wall (like a parapet).”

entries.h: 🌬️ Follow one breath, start to finish
entries.t: 👃 Nose / mouth — warmed, humidified, filtered ▼ 🗣️ Pharynx → larynx (epiglottis closes over it when you swallow) ▼ 🌳 Trachea — the trunk, held open by C-shaped cartilage rings ▼ 🔀 Carina → right & left bronchus ▼ 🌿 Bronchi (smaller branches) → bronchioles (tiny branches) ▼ 🫧 ALVEOLAR SACS — where all the action happens Conducting zone vs respiratory zone: everything from the nose down to the terminal bronchioles is a pipe — it moves air but exchanges nothing (this is the anatomic dead space ). Only the alveoli exch
STEP 2 · THE ACTUAL POINT The alveolar sac is where gas exchange occurs — exchanging CO₂ for oxygen, in the little capillary beds wrapped around each alveolus.

entries.h: 🔬 Inside an alveolus — the respiratory membrane, cut open
entries.t: Blood in, blood out. Deoxygenated blood arrives from the pulmonary artery, drops off CO₂ , picks up O₂ , and leaves through the pulmonary vein. The whole trade happens across a membrane thinner than a sheet of tissue paper. 🧠 “Blood in, blood out — grapes trade with the vine.” The alveolus hands over O₂ and takes back CO₂. Anything that sits between them (fluid, pus, scar) blocks the trade.

entries.h: ➡️ Why gases move at all — diffusion
entries.t: Answer first: gases move from high concentration to low concentration . No pump required. Alveolar air is high in O₂ → O₂ moves into the blood Returning blood is high in CO₂ → CO₂ moves into the alveolus and gets exhaled Speed depends on surface area , membrane thickness , and the pressure gradient 🧠 “Gases roll downhill.” Every respiratory disease either flattens the hill (low FiO₂, low gradient), thickens the wall (edema, pneumonia, fibrosis) or shrinks the field (atelectasis, emphysema).

V = ventilation (air getting in). Q = perfusion (blood getting there). Gas exchange needs both, in the same place, at the same time. Shunt — blood arrives, air doesn't (pneumonia, atelectasis, pulmonary edema) Dead space — air arrives, blood doesn't (pulmonary embolism) 🧠 “Shunt = wasted blood. Dead space = wasted air.” Both end in hypoxemia, for opposite reasons. 🩺
STEP 3 · WHERE & HOW TO LISTEN Listen in between the ribs — the IN-tercostal space, the space IN between the ribs.

Anterior = front, on the chest. Posterior = back, and it mostly assesses the LOWER lobes — because most of the lung mass sits behind you. 🧠 “IN-tercostal = IN between.” Ribs block sound; the spaces don't. And always go side to side , never straight down one lung — you are comparing, not touring.

1 Position the client upright — high Fowler's. Sitting up lets the bases expand. 2 Use the diaphragm — the big flat part of the stethoscope — pressed firmly. 3 Place it in the intercostal spaces , the part in between the ribs. 4 Have the client breathe through the mouth, slowly and deeply . Listen to a full inspiration AND expiration at each spot. 5 Compare side to side , apex → base, front and back. ❌ Never listen through a gown or clothing — it manufactures fake crackles. 🧠 “Sit up · big side · between the ribs ·

Q: What are normal breath sounds? Vesicular breath sounds — soft & low-pitched breezy sounds heard over most of the peripheral lung fields . Sound Where it's NORMAL Vesicular — soft, low-pitched, breezy Most of the peripheral lung fields ⭐ Bronchovesicular — medium pitch, equal in and out Around the upper sternum and between the scapulae Bronchial / tracheal — loud, high-pitched, hollow Directly over the trachea TRAP Hearing a bronchial sound out in the periphery is abnormal — dense, consolidated tissue (like pneum

entries.h: 📊 Breath sounds at a glance — normal vs adventitious
entries.t: 🧠 “Crackles = wet · Wheeze = tight · Rhonchi = gunk · Stridor = STOP.” Stridor is the only one on this list that means get help right now . 🚨
STEP 4 · IT'S CRITICAL TO KNOW Three things happen to alveoli: they fill up, they collapse, or they get infected. All three block gas exchange.

entries.h: 🫧 One alveolus, four states — normal vs. the three things that go wrong
entries.t: It's critical to know: it is typical for clients in heart failure (with heavy fluid in the body) to have fluid in the lungs — pulmonary edema. The wet lungs block oxygen from getting in. Or, if these little alveoli collapse — like in atelectasis — then gas exchange can't happen, and infection settles in, resulting in pneumonia . 🧠 “Wet, flat, or infected — pick your poison, same result.” All three widen the distance between air and blood. That is the entire pathophysiology of hypoxemia in one sentence.

entries.h: 🚨 The cascade the source warns about
entries.t: 💓 Heart failure — heavy fluid in the body ▼ 💧 Fluid in the lungs = pulmonary edema ▼ 🎈 Alveoli collapse = atelectasis ▼ 🦠 Infection settles in = pneumonia 🧠 “Wet → flat → infected.” That's the order the source teaches it, and it's the order it happens in a real post-op or heart-failure client.

entries.h: ✅ Prevent the collapse — the nursing wins
entries.t: Incentive spirometry — the single best post-op tool; teach slow, deep inhalation and hold Turn, cough & deep breathe · early ambulation Reposition every 2 hours · sit upright — high Fowler's for anyone short of breath Adequate pain control — a client splinting from pain will not breathe deeply Hydration to keep secretions thin (unless fluid-restricted) 🧠 “Deep breaths pop the balloons back open.” Atelectasis is the one respiratory complication nurses genuinely prevent.

entries.h: 🚨 Red flags at the bedside — escalate, don't chart and wait
entries.t: 🔇 Absent sounds over a lung field 😮‍💨 Stridor upper airway obstruction 💙 Central cyanosis lips, tongue 🧠 New restlessness earliest hypoxia sign 🫁 Accessory muscles retractions · tripoding 🩸 Pink frothy sputum flash pulmonary edema 👉 Full detail on hypoxia and the oxygen devices is on NG-006 — Hypoxia & O₂ Devices . 🧠 Restlessness before cyanosis. The brain complains long before the lips turn blue. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🌳 Trachea → bronchus → bronchi → bronchioles → alveolar sacs Upside-down tree. 3️⃣ / 2️⃣ Lobes Right 3 , left 2 — the heart takes the space. 🫧 Alveolus = gas exchange CO₂ out, O₂ in, in the capillary beds. 🩺 Vesicular = normal Soft, low-pitched, breezy, peripheral fields.

Q1: Say the airway road in order. Show answer Trachea (windpipe, the trunk) → right & left bronchus → bronchi (smaller branches) → bronchioles (tiny branches) → alveolar sacs, where all the action happens. Q2: How many lobes in each lung, and why the difference? Show answer Right lung 3 lobes, left lung 2 lobes. The heart sits in the cardiac notch on the left, so there's no room for a third lobe. Q3: Where exactly does gas exchange happen? Show answer In the alveolar sac — specifically across the respiratory membra

entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Fundamentals of Nursing

Nutrition I — the six nutrients, the assessment, and the feeding interventions that keep clients safe NG-005 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition A nutritional assessment matters because the needs are different for every client . You have to account for their religious and cultural needs, their illnesses, and their allergies — and then think about how the food is actually presented to someone lying in a hospital bed. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

6️⃣ Six nutrients Carbs · Protein · Fat · Vitamins · Minerals · Water . Water counts. 🍞 Simple = spike Low fiber, high glycemic index . Complex = most fiber, slow & steady . 🪑 High Fowler's + 1 hr Sit up to eat; stay up 1 hour after. Aspiration prevention. 🥩 Protein heals Growth · maintenance · tissue repair — the big one for a healing client. 🍽️
STEP 1 · WHAT FOOD IS MADE OF Six nutrient classes. Three of them give you calories; three of them make the machinery work.

entries.h: 🍽️ Build the plate before you build the meal plan
entries.t: TEACHING Half the plate vegetables & fruit, a quarter lean protein, a quarter grains — and make at least half of those grains whole grains .

Assess requirements Age, illness, activity and healing affect needs. Match the plan Food texture, nutrients and route fit the person. Monitor outcomes Weight, intake, function and relevant labs guide changes. Diet types A prescribed diet targets a particular need; restrictions should have a clear purpose. Swallowing Texture and liquid changes require assessment and instructions. Collaboration Include preferences, access, culture and dietitian input. 🧠 “Half green, quarter grain, quarter gain.” Half the plate green

Carbohydrates — break down into glucose for fuel . Fats — provide energy & carry vitamins. No more than 35% of caloric intake. Protein — growth, maintenance & tissue repair . Big one for healing clients. Vitamins — necessary for metabolism . Minerals — needed for the body's chemical reactions . Water — critical for cell function ; replaces fluid lost to sweating, elimination & respiration. 🧠 “CPF — VMW.” The first three ( C arb, P rotein, F at) give calories. The last three ( V itamins, M inerals, W ater) give zero

entries.h: 🔢 Calories per gram — memorize these four
entries.t: 🍞 Carbohydrate — 4 kcal/g 🥩 Protein — 4 kcal/g 🥑 Fat — 9 kcal/g (more than double) 🍷 Alcohol — 7 kcal/g (calories with no nutrients) That is why fat is capped: it is the most calorie-dense thing on the plate. 🧠 “4-4-9, alcohol is 7.” Say it as a phone number. Fat is nine because it's the naughty one.

entries.h: 🍞 vs 🫘 Simple carbs SPIKE · complex carbs are SLOW & STEADY
entries.t: Simple carbs = less fiber → FAST sugar spikes → high glycemic index. Complex carbs = most fiber → slow, steady sugar levels → low glycemic index. 🍞 SIMPLE carbohydrate 🫘 COMPLEX carbohydrate Less fiber MOST fiber FAST sugar-level spikes Slow, steady sugar levels → High glycemic index → Low glycemic index (usually) White bread · white pasta · white bagels · candy · juice Beans · lentils · whole-grain bread · oats · potatoes Spike then crash → hunger and another spike Steadier energy, better satiety, better glycemic

entries.h: 💊 Vitamins — the two families behave differently
entries.t: Water-soluble (B complex, C) — not stored; excess is urinated out, so they are needed regularly . Deficiency shows up faster. Fat-soluble (A, D, E, K) — stored in fat & liver, so they build up → real toxicity risk from megadoses. Fat in the diet is what lets A, D, E & K be absorbed at all — a very low-fat diet can create a fat-soluble vitamin problem. 📎 NG-227 Vitamins & Electrolytes for the individual deficiencies. 📎 NG-084 Diet Types for clear liquid, full liquid, soft, mechanical soft, low-residue, renal and car

entries.h: 🔬 Where the nutrients actually get in — the villus cutaway
entries.t: Nearly all absorption happens in the small intestine , across a lining folded into millions of finger-like villi . Sugars & amino acids go into the blood capillaries; most fats go into the lymphatic lacteal. 🧠 “Sugar takes the highway, fat takes the back road.” Glucose and amino acids ride the capillary straight to the liver; fat detours through the lymph before it ever reaches the blood. 🔎

entries.h: ASSESS THE CLIENT, NOT THE FOOD
entries.t: STEP 2 · GATHER Every client's needs are different. Get the history before you get the tray.

entries.h: 📋 The nutritional assessment — what to actually ask
entries.t: Dietary history. What does the client like to eat at home ? Dislikes? What are they usually eating? Who cooks? How many meals a day? Illnesses that change dietary needs — diabetes, kidney disease, heart disease , liver disease, GI disorders, cancer. Medications that change dietary habits or cause loss of appetite — chemotherapy, opioids, digoxin, metformin, antibiotics, appetite-suppressing stimulants. Culture & religion — halal, kosher, Hindu vegetarian, Lent, Ramadan fasting, hot/cold food beliefs. Allergies & in

Weight trend — the single most useful number. Same scale, same time, same clothing. BMI — under 18.5 underweight · 18.5–24.9 normal · 25–29.9 overweight · 30+ obese. (Standard adult categories only — they do not apply to children, pregnancy, or athletes, and BMI is a screening number, not a diagnosis. Read it alongside the weight trend and the whole clinical picture.) Intake & output , and the percentage of the meal eaten . Labs — albumin and prealbumin reflect protein status (both drop with inflammation too, so re

entries.h: 🚨 Who is at highest nutritional risk
entries.t: Older adults — decreased appetite, taste changes, dentition, isolation, fixed income. Post-op & wound-healing clients — protein demand goes up , not down. NPO for repeated tests, or held for procedures again and again. Cancer / chemotherapy — nausea, mucositis, taste change. Dysphagia after a stroke — aspiration risk . Anyone with unintentional weight loss. Never let a client sit NPO shift after shift without escalating it — “still NPO” is not a nutrition plan. 🧠 Healing costs protein. A pressure injury or a surgic
STEP 3 · MAKE THE MEAL WORK Half of hospital nutrition is not the food — it is the position, the mouth, and the room.

entries.h: 🪑 Position is a nursing intervention — sit up, and stay up for 1 hour
entries.t: Sit up in a chair if possible. If the client cannot get out of bed, use high Fowler's position and keep that position for 1 hour after eating . 🧠 “Up to eat, up to stay.” High Fowler's to swallow, and one full hour upright afterwards. The hour is the part everyone forgets — and it is the part the exam asks about.

1 📄 Review the diet plan with the client ↓ 2 🤝 Build a meal plan that works for BOTH the restrictions and the client ↓ 3 🪥 Oral hygiene before AND after eating ↓ 4 🌤️ Make the environment conducive to eating ↓ 5 🪑 Sit up — chair, or high Fowler's + 1 hour 🧠 Oral care BEFORE the meal is the one people skip. A clean, moist mouth tastes food properly — that alone raises intake.

entries.h: 🌤️ “Environment conducive to eating” — what that means in practice
entries.t: Remove bedpans, emesis basins, soiled linen and dressing supplies before the tray arrives. Control odors; open the curtain, turn on the light. If a client on a diet is roomed with a client who has diarrhea, ask whether a room change is possible. Pain and nausea medicated before the meal, not after. Open packages, cut food, position the tray in reach — and give unhurried time. Encourage family to visit at mealtimes; eating is social. 🧠 Nobody eats next to a bedpan. If the room smells, the tray goes back full — and t

entries.h: 🚨 Aspiration precautions — the safety layer under every feeding
entries.t: Assess swallowing first in anyone post-stroke, with dysphagia, decreased LOC, or newly extubated. If in doubt, keep NPO and get the speech-language pathologist swallow evaluation. Upright 60–90° to eat; chin tucked toward the chest when swallowing. Small bites, slow pace, one bite at a time ; check the mouth is empty before the next bite. Thin liquids are the most dangerous — thickened liquids may be ordered. No straws for many dysphagia clients (they deliver a fast bolus) — follow the SLP's plan. Suction available

entries.h: 📈 Boosting intake without a new order
entries.t: Offer small, frequent meals rather than three large ones. Serve the highest-protein item first while energy is best. Honor preferences — the food they will actually eat beats the food that is technically ideal. Fortify: milk powder, cheese, peanut butter, oral supplements between (not with) meals. Chart % eaten , not “ate well.” Involve the dietitian early — a collaborative intervention, and the right escalation. 🧠 Supplements go BETWEEN meals. Given with the tray, they just replace the food instead of adding to it

SAY IT OUT LOUD 6️⃣ C·P·F·V·M·W Carbs, Protein, Fat, Vitamins, Minerals, Water. 🍞 White spikes Simple = low fiber = high GI. Complex = fiber = slow. 🪑 60–90° + 1 hr High Fowler's to eat, upright a full hour after. 🥩 Fat ≤ 35% and fat is 9 kcal/g — carbs & protein are 4 .

Q1: Name the six basic nutrients. Show answer Carbohydrates, fats, protein, vitamins, minerals and water. The first three carry calories; the last three do not. Q2: Which nutrient matters most for a client with a healing surgical wound? Show answer Protein — growth, maintenance and tissue repair. Requirements go UP during healing. (Vitamin C and zinc support it too.) Q3: A client must eat in bed. What position, and for how long afterwards? Show answer High Fowler's, and keep them in that position for 1 hour after e

Low oxygen — how to spot it, and what to put on the face NG-006 RESPIRATORY ADHD-friendly visual edition Hypox emia = low oxygen levels in the blood . Hypox ia = low oxygen supply in the body tissues . Hypoxemia dominoes into hypoxia — low oxygen in the blood means low oxygen delivery to the tissues. Then you pick the device that fixes it. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🩸 emia = blood · ia = tissue Hypox emia is the lab. Hypox ia is the patient. 🧠 Restlessness is FIRST Brain first: restless → agitated → confused . Cyanosis is LATE. 📈 Early vitals go UP ↑RR ↑HR ↑BP. Bradycardia & hypotension are LATE and BAD. 🎈 Deflated NRB bag? INCREASE the oxygen flow. Don't open the valves. Don't tighten the straps first. 🧨
STEP 1 · TWO WORDS, ONE DOMINO Get the two words straight first — half the exam questions are just testing the vocabulary.

entries.h: 🩸 The domino — blood first, tissue second

entries.t: Assess the problem Oxygen deficiency, ventilation failure or both. Choose support Device and settings match the clinical need. Reassess response Symptoms, work of breathing, saturation and gases guide care. Oxygen devices Delivered concentration varies with device, flow, fit and breathing pattern. Noninvasive ventilation Supports ventilation through a mask in appropriate patients. Invasive airway Needed when airway protection or effective ventilation cannot be maintained. 🧠 “-EMIA is in the blood (an- emia , hyperg

entries.h: 🧯 Why the oxygen is low — 4 reasons
entries.t: Not enough air in — hypoventilation, opioid oversedation, airway obstruction Membrane too thick — pulmonary edema, pneumonia, fibrosis Blood bypassing air — shunt from atelectasis or consolidation Air bypassing blood — dead space, as in a pulmonary embolism Also: low hemoglobin (anemia) means fewer carriers, and poor perfusion (shock) means the loaded blood never arrives. 🧠 “Can't get air in · can't cross over · wrong place · no truck.” Four failure points on the same delivery route.

entries.h: 🚩 Who is at risk right now on your unit
entries.t: 🛌 Post-op anesthesia + pain + flat 💊 Opioids sedation → ↓RR 🫁 COPD/asthma chronic disease 💓 Heart failure pulmonary edema 🦠 Pneumonia consolidation 🧓 Immobility atelectasis 🧠 The post-op client on opioids lying flat is the classic exam setup. Sit them up and assess before anything else. 🔎
STEP 2 · EARLY vs LATE The brain complains first. If you wait for blue lips you waited too long.

entries.h: 🧠 Head-to-toe — early signs (act) vs late signs (emergency)
entries.t: ATI QUESTION “Which of the following are early indications that the client is developing hypoxemia? Select all that apply.” ✅ Restlessness · Confusion · Hypertension · Tachypnea. ❌ Bradycardia — that is a LATE finding. 🧠 “Everything goes UP before it goes DOWN.” Rate up, pressure up, agitation up. When the numbers finally fall, the client is crashing.

Answer first: the earliest sign of hypoxia is a change in mental status — restlessness. The brain is the most oxygen-hungry organ in the body, so it complains first. ❌ Never medicate new restlessness or agitation as “anxiety” before you have checked oxygenation. 🧠 “A restless patient is a hypoxic patient until proven otherwise.” Sedating them is the classic wrong answer.

entries.h: 🚨 Paradoxical breathing — what it looks like
entries.t: Normally the abdomen rises on inspiration. In paradoxical breathing the chest and abdomen move in opposite directions — the abdomen sinks in as the chest rises. It signals diaphragmatic fatigue or flail chest and is a sign of impending respiratory failure . 🧠 “See-saw belly = call for help.” This is not a “watch and see” finding. 😷
STEP 3 · WHAT GOES ON THE FACE Low flow first, then the masks, then the precision device. Learn the picture and the numbers follow.

entries.h: 👃 Low-flow & simple: nasal cannula · simple face mask · Venturi
entries.t: 🧠 V · V — Venturi Mask = Very Accurate O₂. The color-coded barrel mixes a fixed amount of room air with the oxygen, so the FiO₂ stays exactly where you set it.

entries.h: 🎈 Reservoir devices & the special cases: partial rebreather · non-rebreather · face tent
entries.t: 🧠 “Partial has holes. Non-rebreather has flaps.” The flutter valves are the whole difference — they stop room air (and exhaled air) from diluting the oxygen, which is why the NRB gets the highest percentage.

entries.h: 🚨 Don't let the EXAMS trick you — the non-rebreather rules
entries.t: Answer first: if the reservoir bag is fully deflated on inspiration → INCREASE the oxygen flow rate. The bag must stay at least partly inflated so the client always has a full breath of oxygen waiting. ❌ Do NOT open the flutter valves ❌ Do NOT tighten the face mask straps first ✅ Turn the flow up first, then reassess the bag with each breath ✅ Used for medical emergencies and for carbon monoxide poisoning — CO binds hemoglobin far more tightly than O₂, so you flood the system with the highest FiO₂ available TRAP In

entries.h: 📏 FiO₂ comparison — line them all up
entries.t: 🌡️ Face tent is not on the scale because its delivered FiO₂ is variable and imprecise — it is chosen for humidity and comfort (facial trauma, burns), not for a specific percentage. 🧠 Order of climbing: cannula → simple mask → partial rebreather → non-rebreather. Venturi steps out of the ladder — it is for precision , not for maximum.

entries.h: 📋 All of it in one table
entries.t: Device Flow FiO₂ Use it when / watch for Nasal cannula 1–6 L/min ~24–44% Short-term low oxygenation after surgery . Long-term use dries the nasal mucous membranes → humidify. Client can eat & talk. Simple face mask 6–10 L/min 40–60% The step between cannula and the rebreathers. Never run it below the minimum flow — exhaled CO₂ gets rebreathed. Partial rebreather 6–11 L/min ~60–75% Looks very similar to the NRB. Key difference = the flutter valves (the partial rebreather's ports are open). Non-rebreather 10–15 L/min
STEP 4 · OXYGEN IS A DRUG It needs an order, it has a dose, it has side effects, and it can start a fire.

🚭 NO smoking post the sign, in the room & on the door 🕯️ No open flame candles, lighters, matches 🧴 No petroleum products use water-soluble lubricant 🔌 Check electricals no frayed cords, no static-prone blankets 🧯 Know the extinguisher and the shut-off valve 🛢️ Secure cylinders upright, chained, away from heat ❌ Oxygen does not burn — it makes everything else burn faster and hotter. That is why a single spark matters. 🧠 “Oxygen is the accelerant, not the flame.”

Oxygen requires an order — flow rate, device, and target saturation (unless it's an emergency, where you act and then obtain the order) Titrate to the prescribed target SpO₂ , then reassess Humidify for higher flows and long-term use — dry gas cracks the mucosa and causes nosebleeds Skin checks : behind the ears, over the cheekbones, the bridge of the nose, and the nares — pad the pressure points Oral & nasal care — masks dry everything out Reassess after every change: LOC, RR, work of breathing, SpO₂, color 🧠 “Ord

Clients with chronic CO₂ retention are usually given controlled, low-flow oxygen titrated to a lower target saturation prescribed by the provider, and the Venturi mask is preferred because the FiO₂ does not drift. ❌ Never withhold oxygen from a client who is acutely hypoxic. Treat the hypoxia, then titrate down and monitor for rising drowsiness or a falling respiratory rate. 🧠 “Low and precise, not none.” The wrong answer is refusing to oxygenate a blue patient.

entries.h: 🪜 Priority action when you find a hypoxic client
entries.t: 1 Stay with the client and position upright — high Fowler's, or tripod if that is what they are already doing. Gravity is free oxygen. ▼ 2 Assess airway & breathing — patency, rate, effort, breath sounds, SpO₂, color, level of consciousness. ▼ 3 Apply / increase oxygen per the order or protocol; step up to a higher-delivery device if the target is not met. ▼ 4 Call for help — rapid response or provider — and prepare for an ABG, chest X-ray and further treatment. ▼ 5 Treat the cause — suction secretions, reverse ove

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🩸 Hypoxemia = blood PaO₂ less than 80 mmHg (typical adult reference range — verify against your lab). Hypoxia = tissues. 🧠 Restless first Then agitated, then confused. Cyanosis is LATE. V = Very Accurate Venturi = the most precise device · unstable COPD. 🎈 Deflated bag → ↑ flow NRB 10–15 L/min · 60–100% · emergencies & CO poisoning.

Q1: Define hypoxemia and hypoxia, and state the link. Show answer Hypoxemia = low oxygen levels in the blood. Hypoxia = low oxygen supply in the body tissues. Hypoxemia dominoes into hypoxia, because low oxygen in the blood means low oxygen delivery to the tissues. Q2: Which findings are EARLY indications of hypoxemia? Show answer Restlessness, agitation/irritability, confusion, tachypnea (RR over 20), tachycardia (HR over 100), and hypertension (systolic over 140). Bradycardia, hypotension and cyanosis are LATE. Changes & Cautions — intervals, site assessment, and the four complications you must tell apart NG-007 Renal + Fluid ADHD-friendly visual edition IV insertion through peripheral veins is the fastest route to get medication into the body — which is exactly why it is the most dangerous one. This page is about keeping the line safe : when you change what, what a site should look like every time you walk past it, and how to tell infiltration from extravasation from phlebitis from infection . 📄 Simple Nursing original —

💊 IV infusions ARE medications The HCP must prescribe type · volume · rate . 🚨 NEVER push potassium K⁺ / KCl is always diluted, always on a pump . IV push = death. ⏱️ 24 / 72 / 1× Bags 24 h · tubing & site 72 h · blood tubing single use . 🧊 Cool & pale vs 🔥 red & hot Infiltration is cool, pale, swollen . Phlebitis is red, warm, streaky . 💉
STEP 1 · WHAT YOU ARE PUTTING IN Know what a good site looks like on the inside, and you will recognize a bad one from the doorway.

entries.h: 🔬 What is actually happening under that dressing
entries.t: The catheter tip sits inside the vein lumen and the fluid joins the bloodstream immediately. Every complication on this page is a version of “the tip is no longer where it should be,” or “the vein does not like what is going through it.”

Confirm access and order Solution, medication, compatibility and rate. Deliver safely Use the correct line, pump and aseptic technique. Monitor Inspect the site and assess systemic response. Infiltration Nonvesicant fluid enters tissue, causing swelling or coolness. Extravasation A damaging agent enters tissue; follow the drug-specific response immediately. Other complications Phlebitis, infection, occlusion and overload require different responses. 🧠 Picture the tip. Tip in the vein = fluid goes with the blood. Ti

Absorbs quickly — the fastest route there is. Keeps a constant therapeutic level with a continuous infusion. Less tissue damage than the other routes (SQ, IM, PR, PO) for irritating drugs. Usable when the client is NPO, vomiting, or unable to swallow. 🧠 Fast in = fast wrong. There is no taking it back once it is in the vein — which is why the checks happen before you connect.

Fluid volume overload Infection — local, or a bloodstream infection Infiltration & extravasation Phlebitis & thrombophlebitis Air embolism · catheter embolism · speed shock Allergic & anaphylactic reactions 🧠 “FIIPAS” — F luid overload · I nfection · I nfiltration · P hlebitis · A ir embolism · S peed shock.

entries.h: 🩻 Types of IV access — short term vs long term
entries.t: 🖐️ PERIPHERAL veins — SHORT term 🫀 CENTRAL lines — LONG term Forearm, hand, antecubital (AC); newborn scalp veins CVC (central venous catheter) · PICC (peripherally inserted central catheter) · tunnelled catheters · implanted ports Ordinary fluids & most IV medications Vesicants, chemotherapy, TPN, hypertonic solutions , long courses, and clients with no usable peripheral veins Tip stays in a small peripheral vein Tip sits in a large central vein where the drug is diluted immediately — placement confirmed by X-ray

A port is a small reservoir under the skin of the chest with a catheter into a central vein. Nothing shows on the skin when it is not in use. Find the septum by touch and use sterile technique to access it. Non-coring (Huber) needle only , usually 19–22 gauge. An ordinary needle cores the silicone septum and ruins the port. Change the needle every 7 days while the port stays accessed. Check for blood return before you give anything. No blood return means the line may not be in the vein, so stop and report it. Flush

entries.h: 📏 Which device — decided by how long the therapy runs
entries.t: Short vs long is the first cut. The second cut is the expected duration , and that is what an exam stem is telling you when it says “a five-day course” or “six weeks of IV antibiotics”. How long Device — and where the tip sits Up to about 5 days Peripheral IV A small peripheral vein. Ordinary fluids and most IV medications About 6–14 days Midline — a long peripheral catheter Still a peripheral vein, just further up the arm. Outlasts an IV — but not central , so no vesicants, no chemo, no TPN About 2 wk–3 mo PICC A

entries.h: 🗺️ Site selection — go here, never there
entries.t: ✅ Start distal and work proximal — if a distal site fails you can still move up the arm; if you start at the AC you have burned everything below it. Use the client's non-dominant arm when you can. 🧠 “No Fistula, No Flap, No Feeble arm.” Never the dialysis fistula/graft arm, never the mastectomy (lymph node) side, never a paralyzed limb. ⏱️
STEP 2 · THE ROUTINE Two habits keep clients safe: change things on schedule, and look at the site every single time you touch the line.

entries.h: ⏱️ When to change IVs — the intervals
entries.t: ⚠️ Practice varies and it has changed over time. Your source teaches 72 hours for tubing and site; national guidance allows peripheral catheters and continuous tubing to run to 96 hours , and many hospitals now replace peripheral IVs only when clinically indicated . Answer with your facility's policy — and say “72 hours” if the question comes from this study guide. Other intervals worth knowing (verify locally): lipid / TPN tubing every 24 hours , intermittent (“secondary”) tubing every 24 hours , and a transparent

entries.h: 👁️ Site assessment — what you do EVERY time
entries.t: Assess the site at least hourly for a continuous infusion (and per policy), before and after every IV medication , and any time the pump alarms or the client complains. 👀 LOOK redness, swelling, blanching, leaking, streaking ✋ FEEL warm? cool? taut? a cord along the vein? ↔️ COMPARE to the other arm — size, color, temperature 🗣️ ASK “any pain, burning or tightness?” 🩸 CHECK blood return & easy flushing 📉 WATCH the rate — slowing or alarming = investigate EXAM TIP A client who says the IV “feels tight” or “burns” is

1 Potassium (K⁺, KCl) — NEVER IV push. Instant death. Always diluted , always on an IV pump , never faster than the ordered rate. Check urine output before you give it, and watch the site — potassium burns. 2 NO adding medications to blood transfusion bags or TPN bags. Ever. Blood runs with 0.9% normal saline only . 3 Compatible medications only in the same tubing — check compatibility and check hospital policy . When in doubt, flush between, or run a separate line. Add two more that examiners love: never let air i

NO tourniquets — fragile veins and paper-thin skin. Use a blood pressure cuff instead , inflated just below the systolic pressure. Don't slap the extremity. Tap gently, or use warmth and gravity to fill the vein. Anchor the vein — older veins roll. Watch for fluid volume overload : smaller cardiac and renal reserve, so a rate that is fine for a 30-year-old can put an 85-year-old into pulmonary edema. Use the smallest gauge that will do the job, and secure with minimal tape/paper tape to protect skin. 🧠 “BP cuff, no

Universal / standard precautions (PPE) and hand hygiene before and after every contact. Firmly use the alcohol swab, applying pressure over the vein , and let it dry — friction and dry time are what kill the organisms. Scrub the hub before every access, per policy. Change the catheter if aseptic technique was broken at insertion (e.g. an emergency line) — do not wait for the interval. Remove the IV as soon as it is no longer needed. The most effective infection-prevention measure there is. Keep the dressing clean,
STEP 3 · TELL THEM APART Four complications, four different first actions. Getting the name right is how you get the action right.

entries.h: 🔍 The same site, three pathologies — drawn side by side
entries.t: 🧠 “COOL and pale = fluid OUT of the vein. HOT and red = the vein itself is angry.” Temperature is the fastest discriminator at the bedside — and it is free.

entries.h: 📊 The comparison table — infiltration vs extravasation vs phlebitis vs infection
entries.t: 💧 Infiltration 🔥 Extravasation 🌡️ Phlebitis 🦠 Infection What it is Non-vesicant fluid leaks into the tissue around the vein The same leak, but the drug is a VESICANT — it destroys tissue Inflammation of the vein wall — mechanical, chemical or bacterial Micro-organisms at the site or in the bloodstream Skin color Pale / blanched Dusky, then blistered & necrotic Red , often a streak along the vein Red, may have purulent drainage Temperature COOL Cool → then hot as tissue dies WARM Warm; client may be febrile Swelling

entries.h: 🚨 Fluid volume overload — the systemic complication
entries.t: Signs: crackles, dyspnea, cough with frothy sputum, JVD , bounding pulse, raised BP, rapid weight gain , edema, restlessness. Action: slow the infusion to KVO (keep vein open) rate, sit the client up , oxygen, notify the HCP, expect a diuretic order, monitor breath sounds, I&O and weight. Highest risk: older adults, infants, heart failure, renal failure. 🧠 Crackles + a new 2 kg overnight = you gave too much, too fast. Slow it, sit them up, call.

Air embolism — sudden dyspnea, chest pain, hypotension, tachycardia, anxiety, altered LOC. Action: clamp the line , place the client on the LEFT side in Trendelenburg , give oxygen, call for help, stay with them. Speed shock — a bolus given too fast: flushing, headache, chest tightness, irregular pulse, hypotension, loss of consciousness. Action: stop the infusion immediately, keep the line open with saline, call for help. 🧠 Air → LEFT side, head DOWN. Trapping the air in the right ventricle keeps it out of the pul

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🚨 Never push K⁺ Diluted · on a pump · never a bolus. ⏱️ 24 · 72 · 1× Bag 24 h · tubing & site 72 h · blood tubing single use. 🧊 Cool & pale = infiltration 🔥 Red, warm, streak & cord = phlebitis. 🔥 Extravasation: leave the catheter Aspirate, antidote, notify — then remove.

Q1: Three things the HCP must prescribe for an IV infusion? Show answer Type of solution, volume (amount), and rate. IV infusions are medications. Q2: The site is swollen, cool and pale with no blood return. Name it and give the first action. Show answer Infiltration. Stop the infusion, remove the catheter, elevate the limb, apply a warm or cool compress per the solution, and restart in the other extremity.
