entries.h: Irritable Bowel Syndrome · NG-299 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / GI · Pathophysiology Course

IBS — A Functional Gut Disorder NG-299 GI ADHD-friendly visual edition IBS is a functional disorder of the large intestine — cramping, bloating, pain, and altered bowel habits (diarrhea, constipation, or both) with no structural damage and no inflammation on scope or biopsy. Keep in mind: IBS is NOT IBD (Crohn's/ulcerative colitis) and it is NOT celiac disease — same symptoms, completely different pathology. 🌀 Functional, not structural The colon looks normal on scope — it's how it behaves , not how it looks. 🚩 Red
STEP 1 · WHY THE GUT MISBEHAVES Nothing is structurally wrong — the gut-brain signaling and motility are just miswired.

entries.h: 🌀 A functional disorder — the colon "acts up" without being damaged
entries.t: IBS involves visceral hypersensitivity (the gut feels normal stretch as pain) and altered motility (too fast → diarrhea, too slow → constipation), driven by dysregulated brain–gut axis signaling. There is no inflammation, no ulceration, no villous atrophy — a colonoscopy and biopsy in true IBS come back essentially normal.

Gut sensitivity and motility Signals and movement may be altered. Recurring symptoms Abdominal pain occurs with changes in bowel habits. Individualized management Patterns and triggers guide care. Assess Stool pattern, pain, food relationships, stress and medication use. Manage Nutrition, activity, symptom-directed therapy and gut–brain approaches may help. Alarm findings Bleeding, anemia, fever or unexplained weight loss need evaluation for other causes. 🧠 "Miswired, not damaged." IBS is a signaling problem, not a

😖 Stress / anxiety 🍽️ Certain foods (gas-producing, high-FODMAP) 🦠 Post-infectious (after a GI infection) 🩸 Hormonal changes 🧠 Triggers flare IBS — they don't cause tissue damage the way IBD's triggers do.
IBS-D — diarrhea-predominant IBS-C — constipation-predominant IBS-M — mixed (both) 🧠 Same disease, three different bowel habits — treatment (fiber vs. antidiarrheal) depends on which one. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT IT — AND SPOT WHAT IT ISN'T Symptoms overlap with IBD and celiac disease on paper — the exam wants you to know the tell.

😣 Crampy abdominal pain, relieved by defecation 🎈 Bloating, excess gas 🔄 Alternating diarrhea & constipation (or one predominant pattern) 💧 Mucus in the stool ⏱️ Chronic/recurrent — ≥3 months , symptom-based diagnosis (Rome IV criteria) 🧠 Pain that gets better after a bowel movement is a hallmark of IBS.

entries.h: 🚩 Red flags that mean it is NOT just IBS
entries.t: Blood in the stool Unintentional weight loss Fever Nighttime symptoms that wake the client from sleep Symptom onset after age 50 🧠 IBS is a diagnosis of exclusion — red flags mean rule out IBD, celiac disease, or colorectal cancer first.

🌀 IBS Functional No inflammation 🩹 IBD (Crohn's/UC) Structural inflammation 🌾 Celiac Autoimmune Villous atrophy 🧠 Look, don't just listen. Same complaints on history — but only IBD and celiac show up on scope/biopsy. IBS never does.

entries.h: 🧪 Common exam question — spot the correct diet picks
entries.t: Which meal choices demonstrate correct understanding of an IBS diet? Beans · Cornbread · Fruit salad · Steak · Tomato basil soup · Yogurt with granola ❌ Beans (legume — classic gas-producer) ❌ Cornbread (refined, low fiber, doesn't help symptom control) ✅ Fruit salad (low-gas fiber source) ✅ Steak (protein, not a gas producer) ✅ Tomato basil soup (well-tolerated, non-gas-forming) ❌ Yogurt with granola (dairy + high-fiber granola can both trigger gas/bloating) 🧠 Correct answers = 3, 4, 5. The pattern: skip legumes,
STEP 3 · MANAGE THE TRIGGERS There's no cure — management is diet, stress control, and symptom-targeted medication.

📓 Keep a symptom/diet/stress journal to identify personal triggers 🏃 Exercise 3× per week 💧 Increase fiber & fluid intake — gradually , to avoid worsening gas/bloating 🧘 Stress management techniques 🧠 Journal first. You can't limit a trigger you haven't identified yet.
🫘 Legumes beans 🥚 Eggs 🥛 Dairy yogurt, milk 🍎 Some fruits gas-producing ☕ Caffeine 🍷 Alcohol 🧠 "LEDA" — L egumes, E ggs, D airy, A lcohol/caffeine — the reduce-and-limit list.

Symptom pattern Drug class / example Why 💢 Cramping / spasm (any subtype) Antispasmodics — e.g., dicyclomine Relaxes smooth muscle, reduces cramping 💩 IBS-D Antidiarrheals — e.g., loperamide Slows transit, firms stool 🚽 IBS-C Fiber supplements (psyllium), osmotic laxatives Adds bulk/water to soften & regulate stool 🦠 Either Probiotics May help rebalance gut flora & reduce bloating 🧠 Treat the bowel pattern , not just the diagnosis — IBS-D and IBS-C get opposite medications. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🌀 Functional = no inflammation, no structural damage 🚩 Blood, fever, weight loss = NOT IBS — work it up 📓 Journal + fiber + exercise = core management 🚫 IBS ≠ IBD ≠ Celiac = three different pathologies, same complaints

Q1: What makes IBS "functional" rather than structural? Show answer No inflammation, ulceration, or villous atrophy is found on colonoscopy/biopsy — the problem is altered motility and visceral hypersensitivity, not tissue damage. Q2: Name 3 red-flag symptoms that mean it's probably NOT just IBS. Show answer Blood in stool, unintentional weight loss, fever, nighttime symptoms, or onset after age 50 — any of these should prompt work-up for IBD, celiac, or colorectal cancer. entries.h: Celiac Disease · NG-300 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / GI · Pathophysiology Course

Autoimmune Reaction to Gluten NG-300 GI ADHD-friendly visual edition An autoimmune reaction to gluten (the protein in wheat, rye & barley) causes the immune system to attack the lining of the small intestine , flattening the villi that absorb nutrients. Less absorptive surface = malabsorption of fats, nutrients, and fat-soluble vitamins. This is autoimmune , not functional (IBS) and not the same as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) — three different diseases that all show up with GI complaints. 🌾 Gluten = the trigge
STEP 1 · GLUTEN TRIGGERS AN IMMUNE ATTACK One protein sets off an autoimmune reaction that flattens the gut's absorptive surface.

entries.h: 🏔️ Normal villi vs. celiac villous atrophy
entries.t: MECHANISM Ingested gluten triggers an autoimmune response that damages the small intestine's mucosa. The finger-like villi that normally increase absorptive surface area flatten out (villous atrophy) — nutrients, especially fats, pass through unabsorbed.

Gluten exposure Triggers an immune response in susceptible people. Small-bowel damage Villi become less effective at absorption. Malabsorption Nutritional and extraintestinal effects may occur. Recognize Diarrhea, bloating, poor growth, anemia or other symptoms; some people have few symptoms. Diagnosis Testing is affected by gluten avoidance; follow the diagnostic plan. Long-term care A strict gluten-free diet and nutrition support after diagnosis. 🧠 "Flat villi, empty tank." No finger-like projections left = no ef

entries.h: 🌾 The gluten grains — what to avoid
entries.t: 🌾 Wheat — bread, pasta, spaghetti, breaded meats 🍞 Rye 🍺 Barley — including most beer 🧠 "WRB" — W heat, R ye, B arley. Hidden in dinner rolls, breaded meat, spaghetti, and beer.

🧬 Genetic link — HLA-DQ2 / DQ8 , tends to run in families 🦋 Often coexists with Type 1 diabetes and autoimmune thyroid disease 🧒 Can present in childhood or adulthood 🧠 One autoimmune disease raises suspicion for another — celiac travels with T1DM and thyroid disease. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT MALABSORPTION Everything downstream traces back to one thing: fat and nutrients aren't getting absorbed.

🌾 Gluten ingested ▼ 🛡️ Autoimmune attack on small intestine mucosa ▼ 🏔️ Villous atrophy — absorptive surface lost ▼ 💩 Steatorrhea, weight loss, vitamin/mineral deficiency 🧠 Every symptom below is just this cascade wearing a different hat.

💩 Steatorrhea — fatty, foul-smelling, floating stools (fat malabsorption) 🌀 Diarrhea, abdominal pain, bloating ⚖️ Weight loss, fatigue (iron-deficiency anemia) 🧒 In children: stunted growth , delayed puberty 🦴 Osteoporosis/osteopenia (Ca²⁺ & vitamin D malabsorption) 🔴 Dermatitis herpetiformis — itchy, blistering rash 🧠 "Steatorrhea = the fat you didn't absorb, floating in the toilet."

Fat malabsorption takes vitamins A, D, E, K down with it. A night vision D bone health E antioxidant K clotting 🧠 "ADEK" — the fat-soluble vitamins go wherever fat goes. No fat absorption, no A/D/E/K absorption.

🧪 Serology first — tissue transglutaminase IgA (tTG-IgA), endomysial antibody (EMA) 🔬 Confirm with small bowel biopsy — shows villous atrophy Do NOT start a gluten-free diet before testing — it causes a false-negative result 🧠 Test first, treat second. Going gluten-free early erases the very evidence the test is looking for. 🧒 In children: Celiac disease Picture, memory hook and nursing care → 🩺
STEP 3 · LIFELONG GLUTEN-FREE The only treatment is diet — there is no medication that lets a celiac client eat gluten safely.

🍗 Plain meats — fish, beef, chicken, turkey 🌾 Grains: rice, corn, potatoes, soy, quinoa 🥜 Nuts, beans, legumes 🍎 Fruits & vegetables 🧠 "RCPSQ" — Rice, Corn, Potatoes, Soy, Quinoa — the go-to safe starches.
🍞 Dinner rolls 🍗 Breaded meat 🍝 Spaghetti 🍺 Beer rye & barley 🧠 Read every label — sauces, soups, and processed foods can hide wheat as a thickener.

entries.h: 🌀 Tell them apart — the 3-way mix-up (same as IBS/IBD)
entries.t: 🌾 Celiac Autoimmune Villous atrophy 🌀 IBS Functional No inflammation 🩹 IBD (Crohn's/UC) Structural inflammation Celiac = immune system attacking gluten-exposed mucosa. IBS = motility/sensitivity problem, nothing structurally wrong. IBD = chronic structural inflammation/ulceration independent of gluten. 🧠 Gluten-free helps celiac only — it will not fix IBS or IBD, even though all three can cause diarrhea and abdominal pain.

Gluten-free is not just wheat-free — rye and barley are excluded too Oats are naturally gluten-free but are frequently cross-contaminated during processing — advise caution unless labeled "certified gluten-free" The diet is lifelong , not just during symptomatic flares Monitor for fat-soluble vitamin deficiency (A, D, E, K) and iron-deficiency anemia even after diagnosis 🧠 "Lifelong, not just flare-long." Stopping the diet once symptoms improve lets the villi flatten right back out. ⚡
SAY IT OUT LOUD 🌾 Gluten = wheat, rye, barley autoimmune trigger 🏔️ Villous atrophy = malabsorption, steatorrhea 🅰️🅳🅴🅺 fat-soluble vitamins lost 🥗 Lifelong gluten-free test before treating

Q1: What causes celiac disease's intestinal damage? Show answer An autoimmune reaction to gluten (wheat, rye, barley) that attacks the small intestine mucosa, causing villous atrophy — flattened villi and a smaller absorptive surface. Q2: Why does celiac disease cause fatty, foul-smelling stools? Show answer Steatorrhea — with fewer villi to absorb fat, undigested fat passes into the stool. Q3: Which vitamins are at risk, and why? Show answer Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K — they require fat absorption to be t

Open original PDF in Drive ↗ CAUSE → CLUES → CARE NG-300 · GI Absorption · ADHD-friendly visual edition
Nursing Field Notes / GI · Pathophysiology Course

When the Gut Goes Quiet NG-301 GI ADHD-friendly visual edition Inability to pass stool — fancy words for: infrequent bowel movements or difficult passage of stools that persists for several weeks or longer . Defined as fewer than 3 stools/week plus hard, lumpy stools and straining. 🚽 <3/week = the rule Fewer than 3 stools/week + hard/lumpy + straining. 🧂 Fiber NEEDS fluid Fiber without fluid makes constipation worse , not better. 🪜 3-step ladder Laxatives → Fluid & fiber → Change habits. 🚨 Ache ≠ surgical belly Rig
STEP 1 · WHY THE GUT SLOWS Slow transit = more time for the colon to pull water back out of the stool.

entries.h: 🐌 Mechanism: slow transit = a drier, harder stool
entries.t: EXAM TIP The colon's job is to reabsorb water from stool as it passes through. The slower the transit, the longer water has to be pulled out — so a sluggish colon makes a harder, drier stool that is painful and difficult to pass.

Stool remains longer More water may be absorbed. Stool becomes difficult to pass Hardness or outlet difficulty affects elimination. Cycle of discomfort Pain and withholding can worsen the problem. Assess Baseline pattern, medications, fluid, diet, activity and red flags. Care Individualize fiber, fluids, movement, toileting and prescribed therapy. Complications Impaction can produce overflow leakage; evaluate rather than assuming diarrhea. 🧠 "Slow gut, dry rock." The longer stool sits, the more water the colon stea

😖 Stress 🥦 Low fluid & fiber intake — not enough fruits, veggies, whole grains 🛌 Immobility — bedrest, post-op, low activity 💊 Medications — opioids , iron, anticholinergics, calcium-channel blockers, aluminum/calcium antacids 🦋 Hypothyroidism — slows everything, including the gut 🧪 Hypokalemia — low K⁺ slows smooth muscle motility 🤰 Pregnancy , aging, ignoring the urge to go 🧠 "SLIM-HH" — S tress · L ow fiber/fluid · I mmobility · M edications (opioids!) · H ypothyroid · H ypokalemia.

entries.h: 🧂 The trap: fiber WITHOUT fluid backfires
entries.t: Fiber inflates with fluid to scrub the GI tract and bulk the stool. Too much fiber without high fluid intake can actually cause constipation — a dry fiber mass is harder to move, not easier. The fix is never fiber alone — it's fiber + fluid , together, every time. 🧠 Fiber is a sponge, not a broom. A dry sponge just sits there — it needs water to expand and do its job. 🔎
STEP 2 · READ THE STOOL The Bristol scale turns "what does the stool look like" into a number you can chart.

Use this scale to describe & chart stool consistency objectively — type 1–2 signals constipation , type 3–4 is the goal (normal), type 5–7 signals diarrhea. 1 Hard lumps “nuts” 2 Lumpy log 3 Cracked log 4 Smooth log ideal 5 Soft blobs 6 Mushy 7 Watery diarrhea 🧠 1–2 = plugged, 3–4 = perfect, 5–7 = flooded. Chart the number, not just "constipated" or "loose."
🚽 Passing fewer than 3 stools/week 🪨 Lumpy or hard stools — Bristol type 1–2 😣 Straining to have a bowel movement 🎈 Abdominal bloating, distension 🙁 Sensation of incomplete evacuation

A hard mass of stool becomes stuck ( fecal impaction ). Liquid stool from higher up leaks around the blockage and looks like diarrhea — this is fecal incontinence (encopresis) , an easy trap to mistake for the opposite problem. 🧠 "Leaky around the rock." "Diarrhea" in a chronically constipated client = check for impaction before you chart it as loose stool.

entries.h: 🚨 Tell it apart from an acute surgical abdomen
entries.t: Simple constipation pain is diffuse, crampy , and eases after a bowel movement. A different pattern means STOP — this is not simple constipation. 💩 Simple constipation 🚨 Acute surgical abdomen Pain Diffuse, crampy, comes & goes Localized — e.g. RLQ, worsening, constant Palpation Soft abdomen Rigid / board-like + rebound tenderness Vitals Normal Fever, tachycardia, tachypnea Action Fiber, fluid, laxative per protocol Report to HCP immediately — see Appendicitis ( NG-302 ) 🧠 Never treat a rigid, feverish, rebound-ten
STEP 3 · REBUILD THE HABIT Three steps, always in this order — meds get the backlog moving, then fiber/fluid, then a rebuilt habit.

1 💊 Laxatives & stool softeners — get things moving now 2 🥦 Fluid & fiber — the long-term fix 3 🕐 Change habits — schedule regular toilet visits after meals (gastrocolic reflex), keep a bowel diary, use a reward system for effort 🧠 NCLEX TRAP: reward the effort — sitting on schedule, trying — NOT the bowel movement itself . Rewarding only successful BMs teaches shame, not habit.

Class Example / clue Bulk-forming 🌾 Psyllium (Metamucil) — needs fluid! Osmotic 💧 PEG (MiraLAX), lactulose, milk of magnesia Stimulant ⚡ Senna, bisacodyl — short-term only Stool softener 🧴 Docusate sodium — prevention, not rescue 🧠 Softeners prevent, stimulants rescue. Give docusate before straining starts; save senna/bisacodyl for when it already has.

💧 Fluids 1.5–2 L/day (unless restricted) 🥦 Fiber 25–30 g/day — increase gradually 🚶 Ambulation / regular exercise ⏱️ Respond to the urge — don't hold it 🌀 Abdominal massage, warm fluids in the AM 🧠 "Move it, wet it, feed it." Ambulation + fluid + fiber, every single day.

🚫 Chronic stimulant laxatives risk of dependence 🩸 Ignore blood in stool report — r/o cancer 🪵 Rigid, feverish belly = NOT simple constipation ⚖️ Unexplained weight loss refer for workup 🧠 New-onset constipation with weight loss or blood, especially in an older adult, is a red flag — not routine constipation teaching. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🚽 <3/week + hard stool + straining = constipation. 🧂 Fiber needs fluid or it makes things worse. 🪜 Laxative → fiber/fluid → habit always in that order. 🚨 Rigid + rebound + fever = surgical abdomen, not constipation.

Q1: How many stools/week defines constipation? Show answer Fewer than 3/week, plus hard/lumpy stools and straining. Q2: A client increases fiber but not fluid — what happens? Show answer Constipation can get worse — fiber needs fluid to expand and move through the GI tract. Q3: What's step 3 of the 3-step treatment ladder? Show answer Change habits — scheduled toileting after meals, bowel diary, and a reward system for effort (not for each BM). Q4: What does "diarrhea" in a chronically constipated client make you s

The Classic RLQ Surgical Abdomen NG-302 GI ADHD-friendly visual edition Inflammation of the appendix , located in the RLQ (Right Lower Quadrant) of the abdomen. Untreated, it can perforate → peritonitis — a medical emergency . 🎯 Pain migrates Starts at umbilicus → moves to RLQ / McBurney's point. 🙅 3 NEVERs NO heat · NO laxatives · NO enemas. 💉 NPO + IV fluids first Pain meds ONLY after the surgeon has seen the client. 🚨 Sudden pain relief = 🚩 Can mean the appendix just ruptured — not that it's "better." 🧨
STEP 1 · A BLOCKED TUBE One obstruction explains the entire cascade — from swelling to rupture.

entries.h: 🧭 Where it lives & the obstruction → perforation cascade

entries.t: Appendiceal inflammation The wall becomes swollen and irritated. Local pain develops Pain may migrate toward the right lower abdomen. Progression risk Perforation can spread infection into the peritoneum. Recognize Abdominal pain, anorexia, nausea and fever may occur; patterns vary by age and anatomy. Assessment Clinical examination, laboratory tests and imaging guide diagnosis. Care Prompt surgical or medical evaluation, prescribed analgesia and preparation for the treatment plan. 🧠 "Blocked pipe, backed-up pressu

Most often a fecalith (hardened stool) obstructs the appendiceal lumen. Can also be lymphoid tissue swelling, a foreign body, or a tumor. 🧠 Appendicitis = "the left-behind organ that gets clogged." No real digestive job — but it can still get plugged and become dangerous.

🚫 The appendix has no room to swell — a rigid tube 🩸 Swelling → cuts off its own blood supply → ischemia 💥 Ischemic tissue ruptures → gut contents spill into the sterile peritoneal cavity 🧠 A ruptured appendix is a race against the clock — this is why "watch and wait" is never the plan. 🔎
STEP 2 · READ THE PAIN PATTERN Where the pain starts, where it ends up, and what happens when you press and let go.

entries.h: 🎯 The classic pain migration — this IS the exam question
entries.t: COMMON EXAM QUESTION What's the typical pain presentation? Pain starts around the umbilicus, then moves to the right lower quadrant — described as "pain between the right hip area and belly button." 🔵 Vague, dull pain around the umbilicus (belly button) ▼ hours later 🔴 Sharp, localized pain at McBurney's point (RLQ) 🧠 Wrong-answer traps on this question: pain starting in the LUQ, radiating to the shoulder, or "diffuse all over" are distractors — the correct pattern is umbilicus → RLQ .

🌡️ Low-grade fever 📍 RLQ pain with rebound tenderness 🤢 Nausea, vomiting, anorexia 🪵 Rigid, "board-like" abdomen 💓 Tachycardia, tachypnea 🧠 "Rebound tenderness" = pain that spikes when you release the pressure, not when you press it — this is the hallmark peritoneal sign.
🧪 CBC — leukocytosis (↑ WBC) 📷 CT scan — confirms diagnosis 📡 Ultrasound — preferred in children & pregnancy ⚠️ Minimize repeated palpation — raises perforation risk

entries.h: 🚨 Complication: perforation = peritonitis — a medical emergency
entries.t: 🌡️ Fever — over 100.3°F 🤲 Rebound tenderness 🪵 "Rigid" or "board-like" abdomen 📈 Increasing pain, tenderness 😰 Restless 💓 Fast HR & RR (tachycardia / tachypnea) 🧠 Sudden, total pain relief after hours of steady RLQ pain is NOT a good sign — it can mean the appendix just ruptured and the pressure released. Report it immediately, don't chart it as "improved." 🧒 In children: Appendicitis Picture, memory hook and nursing care → 🩺
STEP 3 · PROTECT THE SURGICAL PICTURE Before surgery: don't mask it, don't move it, don't feed it. After surgery: get them up and breathing.

1 🚫 NPO — nothing by mouth, surgery is likely 2 💧 IV normal saline or LR (Lactated Ringer's) 3 💊 Pain meds: IV morphine/hydromorphone — ONLY after the surgeon has assessed the client 🧠 Why wait on pain meds? Masking the pain and exam findings too early can hide the very signs (rebound tenderness, location, rigidity) the surgeon needs to make the call.

🔥 NO heat pad or blanket 💊 NO laxatives 💦 NO enemas All three can increase pressure or blood flow to an inflamed appendix and trigger rupture. 🧠 Constipation care (fiber, fluid, laxatives — see NG-301 ) is the opposite of what an inflamed appendix needs.

Definitive treatment — surgical removal of the appendix, done urgently once diagnosis is confirmed to prevent rupture. 🧠 Appendectomy = PRIORITY once diagnosed — this is not a "schedule it for next week" surgery.

🚶 Early ambulation 🌬️ Deep breathe & cough + incentive spirometer 🛁 Shower ONLY no tub baths 🏋️ Avoid heavy lifting 👀 Report redness/swelling/drainage at incision site Prevent pneumonia: assist with early ambulation, deep breathing/coughing, incentive spirometer. Prevent infection: shower-only bathing, monitor incision. 🧠 "Walk, breathe, watch the wound." The three post-op jobs that prevent the two big complications — pneumonia and wound infection. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🎯 Umbilicus → RLQ the classic pain migration. 🙅 NO heat, laxatives, enemas all can trigger rupture. 💉 NPO + IV fluids first pain meds only after surgeon sees them. 🚨 Sudden relief = 🚩 rupture not improvement — report immediately.

Q2: Name the 3 never-do interventions before an appendicitis diagnosis is confirmed. Show answer No heat pad/blanket, no laxatives, no enemas — all can increase pressure or blood flow and trigger rupture. Q3: When can the client receive pain medication? Show answer Only after the surgeon has assessed the client — masking pain too early can hide key exam f

entries.h: Diverticulitis & Diverticulosis · NG-303 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / GI · Pathophysiology Course

Diverticulosis vs Diverticulitis — Pouches vs Pouches on Fire NG-303 GI ADHD-friendly visual edition Diverticulosis = little pouches ("stress bubbles") on the colon wall — usually silent. Diverticulitis = those pouches become inflamed & infected — pain, fever, and a possible medical emergency . 🫘 -OSIS = pouches, quiet -ITIS = pouches inflamed & infected. 📍 LLQ pain "Left-sided appendicitis" — sigmoid colon. 🍿 Flip the diet Flare = low fiber/NPO. Quiet = HIGH fiber. 🚫 NO barium enema/colonoscopy during an acute fla
STEP 1 · POUCHES FORM, THEN CATCH FIRE Low fiber → chronic constipation → high pressure → pouches. Then something plugs a pouch and it gets infected.

entries.h: 🫘 Two stages of the same disease

entries.t: Diverticulosis Diverticula are small pouches in the colon wall. Many people have no symptoms; bleeding or other complications may occur. Diverticulitis A diverticulum becomes inflamed. Pain, often in the lower left abdomen, fever and changes in bowel habits may occur. Complications Abscess, perforation, fistula or obstruction can develop. Severe or worsening pain, fever or instability needs urgent assessment. Care follows severity The care plan depends on whether disease is uncomplicated or complicated and on the p

🥦 Low fiber diet → chronic constipation 📈 Increased pressure within the bowel from straining 🌰 Popcorn, seeds, nuts — classically taught to lodge in a pouch and trigger inflammation 👴 Aging — colon wall weakens over time ⚖️ Obesity, low activity, smoking 🧠 Note: newer evidence questions whether seeds/nuts/popcorn truly trigger flares, but this pairing is still classically tested — know it for the exam.

entries.h: 📍 Where it hurts — and why it's called "left-sided appendicitis"
entries.t: Diverticula form most often in the sigmoid colon (descending colon), which sits in the Left Lower Quadrant (LLQ) — a mirror image of appendicitis' RLQ location. 🧠 RLQ = appendicitis. LLQ = diverticulitis. Same pain pattern, mirrored side. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT THE FLARE Fever + LLQ pain + rising WBC = an active flare, not the quiet pouches.

entries.h: ⚖️ Diverticulosis vs Diverticulitis — the exam table
entries.t: 🫘 Diverticulosis 🔥 Diverticulitis What Pouches present, no inflammation Pouches inflamed & infected Symptoms Usually asymptomatic , found incidentally Fever & chills , LLQ pain Labs Normal ↓ H/H · ↑ WBC Diet High fiber — keeps bowels clean NPO → clear liquids → low fiber during flare Danger Low — manage with diet Can perforate → peritonitis — emergency 🧠 Flip the diet with the diagnosis: quiescent = load up on fiber; flaring = starve the inflamed pouch (NPO/low residue).
🌡️ Fever & chills 📍 Pain LLQ (descending & sigmoid colon) 🤢 Nausea, change in bowel habits
Decrease H/H (Hemoglobin & Hematocrit) — from bleeding/inflammation. Increase WBC — infection is present. 🧠 ↓H/H + ↑WBC — bleeding down, fighting cells up. Chart both.

entries.h: 🚨 Complication: perforation → peritonitis — Report to HCP
entries.t: 🪵 Rigid, "board-like" abdomen 📈 Worsening abdominal pain, distension 🌡️ High fever, tachycardia NCLEX TIP Report to HCP immediately — this is a medical emergency. 🧠 Same peritonitis picture as appendicitis ( NG-302 ) — different organ, identical red flags. 🩺
STEP 3 · MATCH THE DIET TO THE PHASE The single most tested idea on this topic: the diet flips depending on whether the bowel is inflamed right now.

entries.h: 🍽️ Diet progression during an acute flare
entries.t: 🚫 NPO nothing by mouth 🥤 Clear liquids jello, broth, juices 🥣 Low fiber diet let the bowel rest 🥦 High fiber again once resolved HIGHLY TESTED Diverticulitis flare-up: NPO → clear liquid diet → low fiber → eventually back to high fiber. Diverticulosis (quiescent): high fiber diet = clean bowels & avoids constipation — the opposite instruction. 🧠 "Starve the flare, feed the quiet." Low fiber only exists to rest an inflamed bowel — it is never the long-term diet.
💉 IV normal saline 💊 Pain meds — morphine, hydromorphone 🚫 NPO — bowel rest 🌡️ Monitor for fever, rising pain, rigidity
💦 NO barium enema ↑ abdominal pressure 🔬 NO colonoscopy perforation risk Both procedures push pressure or air into an already-inflamed, possibly weakened bowel wall.

🥦 High fiber diet — cleans the bowel, prevents constipation 💧 Adequate fluids to go with that fiber 🚶 Regular exercise, avoid straining 🌰 Avoid: popcorn, seeds, nuts (classic teaching) 🧠 "POPCORN" — the classic 3: P opcorn · seeds/n O ts · avoid — P revent straining, C onstipation control, O bserve for flare, R egular exercise, N utrition = high fiber. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🫘 -OSIS = quiet pouches 🔥 -ITIS = inflamed & infected. 📍 LLQ pain = "left-sided appendicitis," sigmoid colon. 🍽️ Flip the diet Flare = NPO→low fiber. Quiet = high fiber. 🚫 No enema/colonoscopy during an acute flare.

Q1: What's the difference between diverticulosis and diverticulitis? Show answer Diverticulosis = pouches present, no inflammation, usually asymptomatic. Diverticulitis = those pouches are inflamed and infected — fever, LLQ pain, ↑WBC. Q2: What diet do you give during an acute diverticulitis flare? Show answer NPO → clear liquids → low fiber, progressing back to high fiber once the flare resolves. Q3: What diet is recommended for diverticulosis (no active flare)? Show answer High fiber diet — keeps bowels clean and

entries.h: GI Bleed · NG-304 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / GI · Pathophysiology Course

Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage — Upper vs. Lower NG-304 GI ADHD-friendly visual edition Bleeding anywhere inside the GI tract — the whole job is figuring out WHERE . Split the tube at the ligament of Treitz : bleed above it is an upper GI bleed , bleed below it is a lower GI bleed . Enough blood loss fast enough → hypovolemic (hemorrhagic) shock . 🩸 Coffee grounds & tar = UP Hematemesis / melena = upper GI bleed. 🍷 Bright red = DOWN Hematochezia = lower GI bleed. 🧪 Hgb < 7 = transfuse "Hemoglobin less than 7 = heaven"
STEP 1 · FIND THE TUBE, PICK A SIDE One landmark splits the whole GI tract into "upper" and "lower" — everything else follows from that split.

entries.h: 🗺️ The ligament of Treitz is the dividing line
entries.t: DEFINITION A GI bleed is bleeding anywhere inside the GI tract , classified as upper or lower — one of the biggest jobs is figuring out the exact location because it changes every intervention that follows (NGT? scope type? drug?).

Bleeding source May arise anywhere in the gastrointestinal tract. Visible or hidden loss Presentation depends on location and bleeding rate. Perfusion effects Significant blood loss can cause shock. Upper tract clues Hematemesis, coffee-ground emesis or melena may occur. Lower tract clues Red or maroon stool may occur; brisk upper bleeding can also appear red. Priorities Assess airway and circulation, trend vitals and labs, establish ordered access and escalate. 🧠 "Treitz splits the tube." Above the ligament of Tre

🔥 Gastritis 🚪 GERD / esophagitis 🕳️ Peptic ulcer disease — most common cause 🩸 Esophageal varices — from portal hypertension / cirrhosis, can rupture & exsanguinate fast 🤮 Mallory-Weiss tear — forceful vomiting/retching 🧠 "GGPV" — G astritis · G ERD · P eptic ulcer · V arices. The V is the scary one — varices bleed the fastest and hardest.

🩹 Hemorrhoids — most common lower cause 🎗️ Colorectal cancer 🕳️ Diverticulosis 🔥 Ulcerative colitis 🌸 Angiodysplasia (older adults) 🧠 "HeCDU" — He morrhoids · C ancer · D iverticulosis · U lcerative colitis.

entries.h: 🚨 RED FLAG — call the provider now (hemorrhagic shock)
entries.t: Any GI bleed can outrun the body's ability to compensate. These signs mean the client is decompensating — report immediately: 📉 Hypotension falling BP 💓 Tachycardia HR > 100 🥶 Cool, clammy diaphoretic 😶 Pale skin 😵 Dizzy, fatigue 🧪 Hgb < 7 transfusion trigger 🧠 "Cool, pale, fast, low" — cool clammy skin + pale + fast HR + low BP is the classic hemorrhagic shock picture. Don't wait for BP to crash — tachycardia is the FIRST compensatory clue. 🔎
STEP 2 · READ THE BLOOD What color, and which end — that's the whole exam question.

entries.h: 🔬 Upper vs. lower GI bleed — side by side
entries.t: Feature ⬆️ Upper GI bleed ⬇️ Lower GI bleed Vomit Hematemesis — vomiting blood; classic "coffee-ground emesis" (blood partially digested by acid) Not typical Stool Melena — black, tarry, foul-smelling stool (digested blood) Hematochezia — bright red blood per rectum (fresh, undigested) BUN:Cr ratio Often elevated — digested blood protein is absorbed and broken down to urea Usually normal Scope used EGD (esophagogastroduodenoscopy) Colonoscopy 🧠 "Coffee grounds and tar are OLD — bright red is FRESH." The higher up t

entries.h: 🖼️ Coffee-ground emesis vs. bright red stool

entries.t: 🩸 Blood volume drops ▼ 💓 Compensatory tachycardia ▼ 📉 Hypotension — decompensating ▼ 🥶 Cool, clammy, pale, dizzy, confused 🧠 Tachycardia shows up before BP drops — it's the body compensating. Don't wait for hypotension to call it a bleed.

Low CBC labs = low H/H (hemoglobin & hematocrit). critical low normal Adult reference (varies by lab): Hgb M 14–18 / F 12–16 g/dL . Hgb < 7 g/dL = transfusion trigger. 🧠 "Hemoglobin less than 7 = heaven" — rhymes on purpose. Below 7 , send blood.

entries.h: 🧫 Diagnostics — Guaiac Fecal Occult Blood Test (gFOBT)
entries.t: 1 🧤 Gather supplies, wash hands, don non-sterile gloves 2 📦 Open card, apply stool sample to both boxes on the slide 3 🧴 Open the back, apply 2 drops developing solution, wait 30–60 sec 4 📝 Document results — blue = positive for occult blood Definitive location & source is found by EGD (upper) or colonoscopy (lower) — the scope both diagnoses and treats. 🩺
STEP 3 · STOP THE BLEED, REPLACE THE VOLUME Stabilize first, scope second, feed last.

1 Lower the head of the bed — improves perfusion to vital organs 2 IV normal saline — 2 large-bore IVs, stabilizes blood pressure 3 Oxygen 4 Blood transfusion — when Hgb < 7 , type & crossmatch PRBCs 🧠 "LOB" — L ower HOB · O xygen & IV fluids · B lood if Hgb < 7 . Also: keep the client NPO in case of emergency endoscopy.

entries.h: ❌ NGT lavage — upper GI only, one huge exception
entries.t: Nasogastric lavage (NGT) can be used to assess/clear an upper GI bleed. NEVER insert an NGT if esophageal varices are known or suspected — the tube can rupture the fragile varix and cause catastrophic bleeding. 🧠 "Varices + tube = trouble." If the chart says cirrhosis or varices, the NGT answer on the exam is always "no."

entries.h: 💊 Drugs that stop a variceal bleed
entries.t: 💧 Octreotide — reduces splanchnic blood flow & portal pressure 💊 IV PPI (e.g., pantoprazole) — reduces acid, protects a healing ulcer 🩸 Blood products — PRBCs, FFP, platelets as ordered 🧠 Octreotide = "shrink the plumbing." It squeezes down splanchnic vessels so varices bleed less.

entries.h: 🔪 Surgery / procedures — find it & fix it
entries.t: 🔭 Endoscopy (EGD) — upper GI: cauterize, clip, or band a bleeding varix/ulcer 🔭 Colonoscopy — lower GI: locate & treat the source 🩹 Angiography / embolization if bleeding can't be localized or controlled by scope 🧠 "Scope up = upper, scope down = lower." EGD goes in the mouth; colonoscopy goes in the rectum.

Client stays NPO before the procedure, then advances slowly once bleeding is controlled and gag reflex has returned: 🍎 Apple juice clear liquid 🍲 Broth soup clear liquid 🍵 Unsweetened tea clear liquid Advance diet as tolerated — clear liquids → full liquids → soft → regular, watching for return of nausea, pain, or bleeding. ⚡
SAY IT OUT LOUD 🩸 Coffee grounds / melena = upper GI bleed 🍷 Hematochezia = lower GI bleed, bright red 🧪 Hgb < 7 = transfuse (heaven) ❌ Varices = never NGT lavage

Q1: Client has coffee-ground emesis and black tarry stools. Upper or lower GI bleed? Show answer Upper — hematemesis/coffee-ground emesis and melena are both upper GI bleed clues. Q2: What lab value triggers a blood transfusion? Show answer Hemoglobin less than 7 g/dL — "Hgb less than 7 = heaven." Q3: Client with known esophageal varices needs gastric lavage. What do you do? Show answer Do NOT insert an NGT — it can rupture the varix. Notify the provider instead. Q4: HR 128, BP 84/52, skin cool and clammy. What's h

entries.h: Small Bowel Obstruction · NG-305 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / GI · Pathophysiology Course

SBO — Mechanical vs. Non-Mechanical (Paralytic Ileus) NG-305 GI ADHD-friendly visual edition A blockage in the small intestine — food, fluid & gas back up behind the block. Two flavors: mechanical (a physical block — adhesions, hernia, tumor, volvulus) and non-mechanical ( paralytic ileus — the bowel just stops moving). Untreated → bowel perforation & peritonitis . 🌀 The classic triad Colicky pain + distension + vomiting. 🚨 Fever + tachycardia + rigid belly = bowel perforation, notify HCP. 🎧 Bowel sounds tell locat
STEP 1 · WHAT'S BLOCKING THE TUBE Split obstruction into two categories: something physically in the way, or the bowel simply stopped moving.
DEFINITION A small bowel obstruction is a blockage in the small intestine that stops the normal flow of contents.

Mechanical obstruction A physical blockage impedes contents. Causes include adhesions, hernias, tumors or twisting; fluid and gas may accumulate upstream. Ileus or pseudo-obstruction Movement is impaired without a fixed mechanical blockage. Assessment seeks the underlying illness, medication effect or other cause. Watch for compromise Persistent or worsening pain, peritoneal signs, fever or instability raise concern for ischemia, perforation or other serious complications. Initial care and reassessment Escalate for

🩹 Adhesions (scar tissue) — from prior surgery, most common cause 🕳️ Hernias 🌀 Volvulus — twisting of the bowel 📥 Intussusception — bowel telescopes into itself 🎗️ Tumor (cancer) 🧠 "AHVIT" — A dhesions · H ernias · V olvulus · I ntussusception · T umor. Adhesions from a past surgery are the #1 answer.

entries.h: ⚠️ Non-mechanical (paralytic ileus) — think "why isn't it moving?"
entries.t: 🔪 Recent abdominal surgery (bowel handling) 💊 Opioids & anticholinergics slow motility 🧂 Electrolyte imbalance — hypokalemia is classic 🦠 Peritonitis / sepsis 🧠 A quiet, non-tender, evenly distended belly after surgery = suspect ileus, not a mechanical block.

entries.h: 🚨 RED FLAG — call the provider now (bowel perforation)
entries.t: An unrelieved obstruction stretches the bowel wall until it perforates → contents spill into the peritoneum → peritonitis is a medical emergency . 🌡️ Fever sudden 💓 Tachycardia 💨 Tachypnea 🪵 Rigid, board-like abdomen 🎈 Worsening distension 🧠 COMMON EXAM QUESTION Client with an SBO suddenly develops tachycardia, tachypnea, and a high fever. Most likely problem? Bowel perforation — notify the HCP immediately. (Not PE, pneumonia, or atelectasis — those don't fit a sudden fever + rigid abdomen picture in this context.)
STEP 2 · THE CLASSIC TRIAD Colicky pain, a swelling belly, and vomiting that won't quit — plus bowel sounds that tell you exactly where the block is.

⚡ Colicky pain intermittent, cramping 🎈 Abdominal distension 🤮 Frequent nausea & vomiting 🧠 "Colic, Cramp, Can't-keep-it-down." Three C-sounding clues = triad of SBO: C olicky pain, belly bloats like a b C alloon (distension), and C an't stop vomiting.
🧠 Loud before, quiet after. The gut is straining to push past the block (hyperactive above); nothing gets through to the segment below (hypoactive/absent).

🌀 Obstruction — pain, distension, vomiting ▼ 🎈 Worsening distension, dehydration, electrolyte loss ▼ 🚨 Peritonitis — medical emergency 🧠 If it's not relieved, the bowel wall stretches until it tears. Every unmanaged SBO is a countdown to perforation.

"Client with a small bowel obstruction suddenly develops tachycardia and tachypnea with a high fever . What is most likely the problem?" 1. Pulmonary embolism — ❌ no chest/leg clue given 2. Bowel perforation, notify HCP — ✅ correct answer 3. Pneumonia — ❌ no respiratory clue given 4. Atelectasis — ❌ doesn't cause fever/tachycardia like this 🧠 New fever + tachycardia + tachypnea in the context of a known obstruction = perforation until proven otherwise. 🩺
STEP 3 · REST THE GUT, RELIEVE THE PRESSURE Stop feeding it, decompress it, and don't slow it down further with opioids.

1 NPO — nothing by mouth, rest the bowel 2 NGT insertion — nasogastric tube for decompression + IV fluids 3 Semi-Fowler's position 4 Pain control — non-opioid preferred 🧠 "NNSP" — N PO · N GT · S emi-Fowler's · P ain control (non-opioid). Rest it, drain it, sit it up, treat pain smartly.

Opioids further slow GI motility — the last thing a stalled bowel needs. 💊 Morphine 💊 Hydrocodone 💊 Hydromorphone 🧠 Opioids = "constipation in a syringe." They slow the very motility the bowel is already failing at.

Clients who fail to improve need a bowel resection to remove the diseased/dead segment, and may need a temporary ostomy until the bowel heals. 🧠 NGT + NPO buys time — surgery is the fallback if the obstruction won't resolve or perforation occurs.

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🌀 Triad Colicky pain + distension + vomiting 🚧 Mechanical = physical block (adhesions #1 cause) 😴 Paralytic ileus = bowel just stops moving ❌ No opioids NPO + NGT + semi-Fowler's + non-opioid pain control

Q1: What's the classic triad of small bowel obstruction? Show answer Colicky abdominal pain, abdominal distension, and frequent nausea/vomiting. Q2: Client's bowel sounds are hyperactive in the upper abdomen and absent lower down. What does that tell you? Show answer The obstruction is between the two — hyperactive sounds occur above the block, hypoactive/absent sounds occur below it. Q3: What's the most common cause of mechanical SBO? Show answer Adhesions (scar tissue) from prior abdominal surgery. Q4: Why avoid

entries.h: Colon & Esophageal Cancer · NG-306 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / GI · Pathophysiology Course

Risk Factors, Screening & Early Clues NG-306 GI ADHD-friendly visual edition Colorectal cancer = cancer of the colon (large intestine) & rectum, the "exit door" of the GI tract. Esophageal cancer = cancer of the "food tube" carrying food from mouth to stomach. Both share the same three modifiable risk factors — Obesity, Alcohol, Tobacco — and both are caught early with screening , not waiting for symptoms. 🔤 "OAT" risk factors Obesity · Alcohol · Tobacco — shared by both cancers. 🔥 GERD → Barrett's → cancer Chronic
STEP 1 · WHO'S AT RISK Two different organs, the same three lifestyle risks, plus organ-specific ones.

Colorectal pathway Some polyps can progress to cancer over time. Screening can identify cancer early and colonoscopy can remove many precancerous polyps. Colorectal symptoms Blood in stool, a persistent bowel-habit change, unexplained anemia or weight loss require assessment. Symptoms are not a screening test. Esophageal pathway Cancer can narrow the swallowing passage. Progressive difficulty swallowing or unexplained weight loss needs evaluation. Reflux and Barrett’s Barrett’s esophagus increases the risk of esoph

O — Obesity (BMI over 30 ) A — Alcohol T — Tobacco (cigarettes, cigars, chewing tobacco) 🧠 "Eat your OATs — or don't." Obesity, Alcohol, Tobacco raise the risk of BOTH colorectal and esophageal cancer — and they're the same three things you teach the client to change.

🕳️ Diverticulosis 🔥 Ulcerative colitis (long-term, chronic inflammation) 🧬 Family history of colorectal cancer 🧠 Long-standing colon inflammation (UC, Crohn's) + family history = earlier & more frequent screening than average risk. Most colorectal cancer follows this polyp → cancer sequence over years — which is exactly why screening catches it early.

🔥 Chronic GERD / acid reflux — the #1 organ-specific risk 📈 Untreated reflux → esophagitis → Barrett's esophagus → cancer 🧠 Barrett's = the "burnt" esophagus. It's a precancerous change (normal cells replaced by intestinal-type cells) — the reason GERD is treated seriously, not just as heartburn. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT IT EARLY Early cancer is often silent — these are the clues that finally show up, plus the exact exam scenario.

A — Abdominal pain B — Bleeding : blood in stools, low hemoglobin C — Change in bowel habits Unexplained weight loss is also a major red-flag clue for both cancers. 🧠 "ABC — and don't forget the C" (weight loss). Any client with new bowel habit changes + unexplained weight loss + falling H&H needs a colonoscopy, not reassurance.

🍽️ Dysphagia — progressive difficulty swallowing (solids → liquids) ⚖️ Unexplained weight loss 😖 Chest/retrosternal pain 🍽️ Odynophagia — painful swallowing 🧠 Esophageal cancer symptoms often start subtle and progress — "food gets stuck" is the classic early complaint.

Client with a family history of colorectal cancer , unexplained weight loss , change in bowel habits , and Hgb of 9 (down from 14 just 12 months earlier) — which diagnostic test is expected? Correct answer: Colonoscopy 🧠 A dropping H&H over months + bowel habit change + family history = colon cancer workup, and the test is always the scope.

entries.h: 🚨 Post-colonoscopy complication — perforation is an emergency
entries.t: 🌡️ Fever 💓 Tachycardia 💨 Tachypnea 🪵 Rigid, board-like abdomen = distension A perforated bowel spills contents into the peritoneum → peritonitis, a medical emergency. 🧠 Any procedure that goes through bowel wall (colonoscopy, EGD) carries the same perforation red flags — memorize this cluster once, apply it everywhere. 🩺
STEP 3 · CATCH IT EARLY, MODIFY THE RISK Screening intervals, bowel prep, and the same three lifestyle changes that lower risk for both cancers.

Risk category Screening plan Average risk Start age 45 , repeat every 10 years if normal Family history of colorectal cancer Start earlier & screen more often — provider individualizes timing Ulcerative colitis / Crohn's (long-standing) More frequent surveillance colonoscopy per GI provider 🧠 "45 and alive, every decade you thrive" — average-risk screening starts at 45 , repeats every 10 years if results are normal.

🥤 Clear liquid diet + laxative bowel prep — e.g., polyethylene glycol (brand: GoLYTELY ) 🌙 NPO after midnight 🧠 A clean colon = a scope that actually sees the polyp. Bowel prep compliance is the #1 reason a screening exam fails.

entries.h: 🔭 What the scope is used for
entries.t: Passed up through the rectum to inspect the colon for tumors, polyps , and to evaluate other GI conditions like ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease . 🧠 It's both a screening tool AND a treatment tool — polyps can be removed (polypectomy) during the same procedure.

O Obesity → lose weight — BMI goal < 30 A Alcohol → stop T Tobacco → smoking cessation High-fiber diet (e.g., cabbage, whole grains) also supports colon health and regular bowel elimination. 🧠 Same "OAT" letters from risk factors become the teaching plan — reduce the exact same three things that raised the risk. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🔤 OAT Obesity · Alcohol · Tobacco — shared risk, shared teaching 🔥 GERD → Barrett's → cancer The esophageal cancer pathway 🔭 Age 45 , every 10 years Average-risk colonoscopy screening 📉 ABC Abdominal pain · Bleeding · Change in bowel habits

Q1: What three lifestyle risk factors raise the risk of BOTH colorectal and esophageal cancer? Show answer Obesity, Alcohol, Tobacco — "OAT." Q2: What untreated condition can progress to esophageal cancer, and what's the precancerous step in between? Show answer Chronic untreated GERD → esophagitis → Barrett's esophagus (precancerous) → esophageal cancer. Q3: When does average-risk colorectal cancer screening start, and how often does it repeat? Show answer Age 45, repeated every 10 years if colonoscopy results are

entries.h: 🍽️ Pediatric GI — Pyloric Stenosis, Intussusception & Hirschsprung
entries.t: Three conditions defined by how the baby vomits and what the stool looks like.

The pyloric muscle thickens and blocks the stomach outlet. Metabolic alkalosis with hypokalemia and hypochloremia — from losing gastric acid Dehydration, weight loss, fewer wet diapers Treated surgically (pyloromyotomy); feeds resume within hours The acid-base picture is the exam point: vomiting stomach contents means losing hydrogen and chloride, so the blood turns alkalotic. 🧒 Pyloric stenosis Picture, memory hook and nursing care →

One segment of bowel telescopes into the next , cutting off its blood supply. Sudden severe intermittent pain — the child draws the knees to the chest and screams, then is calm between episodes Currant-jelly stool — blood and mucus Palpable sausage-shaped mass A normal brown stool before surgery may mean the bowel has reduced itself. Report it immediately - the operation may be canceled. Treated by air or contrast enema , which often reduces it; surgery if that fails or the bowel is necrotic. 🧒 Intussusception Pict

A segment of colon has no ganglion cells , so it cannot relax and propel stool. No meconium within 48 hours — the classic newborn clue Ribbon-like, foul stools; distension; poor feeding Diagnosed by rectal biopsy; treated surgically Watch for enterocolitis - explosive diarrhea, fever and a rapidly worsening child. It is the life-threatening complication. 🧒 Hirschsprung disease Picture, memory hook and nursing care →

entries.h: 🩺 Dehydration — the thread through all of them
entries.t: Weight change is the most accurate measure of fluid loss in a child. Children have proportionally more body water and lose it faster than adults. 🧒 Dehydration Picture, memory hook and nursing care → Sign Mild Moderate Severe Weight loss 3–5% 6–9% ≥10% Capillary refill <2 s 2–3 s >3 s Mucous membranes Slightly dry Dry Parched, no tears Urine Slightly reduced Reduced, dark Minimal or none Behavior Normal, thirsty Irritable Lethargic , sunken fontanelle In an infant, the earliest reliable signs are fewer wet diapers

Projectile vomiting + still hungry + olive mass = pyloric stenosis , with metabolic alkalosis Currant-jelly stool = intussusception ; a normal stool before surgery must be reported No meconium in 48 hours = Hirschsprung Daily weight is the best measure of dehydration ORS, not water or juice Sources. Written from CDC , HealthyChildren.org (AAP) , MedlinePlus and OpenStax A&P 2e (CC BY 4.0).

entries.h: 👶 Cleft Lip & Palate, PKU & Newborn Screening
entries.t: Feeding a baby who cannot make suction, and the two screened conditions where early treatment prevents permanent damage.

Cleft palate leaves an opening between mouth and nose, which makes suction difficult Cleft lip alone may still allow effective feeding; a cleft palate often needs a specialised feeding system and an individual plan Feed upright , pace and burp as taught, and monitor intake and growth After repair , follow the surgical team’s feeding and positioning instructions PKU is separate — phenylalanine can build up. Newborn screening allows early treatment with an individualised low-phenylalanine diet and medical nutrition P

Special wide-based or squeezable bottle with a long soft nipple Hold upright — near-sitting — to reduce nasal regurgitation and aspiration Burp frequently — they swallow a lot of air Aim to finish a feed in about 20–30 minutes ; longer burns more calories than it delivers Breastfeeding is often possible with an isolated cleft lip The first priority is always weight gain , because surgery requires adequate growth.

Nothing hard or pointed in the mouth - no straws, no spoons into the mouth, no pacifiers, no suctioning of the suture line. Elbow restraints to stop hands reaching the face — removed regularly for range of movement and cuddles Position: after lip repair, on the back or side , never prone on the suture line. After palate repair, prone or side-lying is often allowed to drain secretions — follow the surgeon Prevent crying — it stresses the suture line. Anticipate needs, cuddle, medicate for pain Clean the suture line

The heel-prick screen looks for conditions where early treatment prevents permanent damage and late treatment cannot undo it. Taken after the baby has had 24–48 hours of feeding — some tests need protein intake to be accurate.

The enzyme that breaks down phenylalanine is missing, so it builds up and damages the developing brain. Untreated → irreversible intellectual disability , seizures, a musty body odor, fair hair and skin Treated → normal development . The entire difference is diet Lifelong low-phenylalanine diet: restrict high-protein foods — meat, fish, eggs, dairy, nuts, beans — with a special formula providing the rest. Aspartame contains phenylalanine. Diet drinks and sugar-free products must be avoided - that is why they carry

Also screened, also silent at birth, also causes irreversible intellectual disability if missed. Late signs: prolonged jaundice, poor feeding, constipation, large tongue, hoarse cry, sluggishness, cool mottled skin. Lifelong levothyroxine started early prevents all of it. Crush the tablet and give in a small amount of formula or water — never in a full bottle, because an unfinished feed means an unknown dose . 🧒 Congenital hypothyroidism Picture, memory hook and nursing care →

Sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis, galactosemia, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, and various metabolic disorders — the exact list varies by state or country. A positive screen is not a diagnosis — it triggers confirmatory testing. Say that clearly to parents, who are usually frightened by the call.

Cleft lip repaired ~2–3 months; palate ~9–18 months Nothing pointed in the mouth after repair; elbow restraints Prevent crying — it stresses the suture line PKU = low-phenylalanine diet for life ; no aspartame Screen needs 24–48 hours of feeding first Congenital hypothyroidism: start levothyroxine early , never in a full bottle Sources. Written from CDC Diabetes , NIDDK , HealthyChildren.org (AAP) and MedlinePlus .

Rigid abdomen · rebound tenderness · a surgical emergency NG-397 Gastrointestinal ADHD-friendly visual edition The peritoneum is inflamed, almost always because something perforated and spilled into it. The abdomen becomes board-like and silent , and she will not let you press on it. This is a surgical problem, not a medical one. The classic finding Rigid, board-like abdomen with rebound tenderness The position Knees drawn up, absolutely still — moving hurts Bowel sounds Absent. The gut has stopped. Never No heat,

Possible causes Perforation or leakage from an abdominal organ can contaminate the peritoneum. Infection can also occur with peritoneal dialysis or in other settings. Concerning findings Abdominal pain or tenderness, fever, vomiting, distension and reduced bowel function may occur. Assess vital signs, perfusion, mental status and urine output. Why deterioration occurs Inflammation and fluid shifts can reduce circulating volume. Infection may progress to sepsis or shock; worsening pain or instability needs urgent re

How she presents Severe, constant abdominal pain , worse with any movement — even the bed being bumped. Rigid, board-like abdomen. Involuntary guarding — she cannot relax it. Rebound tenderness — it hurts more when you release than when you press. Absent bowel sounds , distension, nausea and vomiting. She lies still with her knees drawn up . Anyone rolling around is probably colicky, not peritonitic. Fever, tachycardia, shallow rapid breathing — deep breaths hurt. Later: hypotension, oliguria, altered mental status

What you do Nothing by mouth. Immediately. NG tube to suction — decompresses the gut and stops more spilling. Large-bore IV, aggressive fluids. She has lost liters into her abdomen. Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics after cultures. Semi-Fowler’s — it localizes the contamination to the lower abdomen and eases breathing. Analgesia, oxygen, urinary catheter to track output. Prepare for surgery. The source has to be closed. What you monitor Urine output — the first thing to fall when she is volume depleted. Under 30 mL/hr

The classic finding Rigid, board-like abdomen with rebound tenderness The position Knees drawn up, absolutely still — moving hurts Bowel sounds Absent. The gut has stopped. Never No heat, no enema, no laxative, nothing by mouth What does a board-like abdomen with rebound tenderness mean? Show answer Peritonitis. Surgical emergency — NPO, NG to suction, fluids, antibiotics, call. Appendicitis pain suddenly stops. Is that good? Show answer No. It usually means it has ruptured. Expect a rigid abdomen next. The prep · during · the complication you watch for NG-398 Gastrointestinal ADHD-friendly visual edition Most of the exam questions about colonoscopy are about the preparation and the hours afterwards , not the procedure itself. The one complication that matters is perforation . Screening starts Age 45, then every 10 years if normal Clear liquids Nothing red or purple — it looks like blood The complication Perforation — pain, rigidity, fever, bleeding After Left side, expect cramping and flatus. That is normal.

Before preparation Review the prescribed diet, bowel-prep schedule and medication instructions. Ask the team about anticoagulants, diabetes medicines and other individual risks. Complete the preparation Take the entire preparation as directed. Follow the exact clear-liquid and fasting times provided by the endoscopy team; schedules differ. After sedation Monitor recovery and follow discharge instructions. Arrange the required escort. Mild bloating or cramping can occur as gas passes. Report warning signs Severe or

Preparation — where the questions are Clear liquid diet for 1 to 3 days beforehand. Nothing red, purple or blue — the dye looks like blood on the screen. Broth, apple juice, plain tea, clear sports drinks are fine. Bowel prep (polyethylene glycol) the evening before. She must finish it. Chilling it and using a straw helps. NPO after midnight , or as the unit directs. Hold anticoagulants and antiplatelets as prescribed — polyps may be removed. Diabetes: the insulin and oral agents need adjusting for a day of clear l

After the procedure Vital signs per protocol until she is fully awake. Nothing by mouth until the gag reflex returns if the throat was sprayed — that applies to an EGD; for colonoscopy alone it is sedation recovery that governs. Encourage ambulation and passing flatus — it relieves the cramping. Resume the usual diet once alert, starting light. Sedation teaching: no driving, no legal documents, no alcohol for 24 hours . Tell her results and biopsy timing before she leaves. What she reports to you at home Severe or

Screening starts Age 45, then every 10 years if normal Clear liquids Nothing red or purple — it looks like blood The complication Perforation — pain, rigidity, fever, bleeding After Left side, expect cramping and flatus. That is normal. At what age does average-risk colorectal screening start, and how often? Show answer Age 45, then every 10 years if it is normal. Which clear liquids are not allowed? Show answer Anything red, purple or blue — the color is mistaken for blood. She is cramping and passing a lot of gas

Colostomy vs ileostomy vs urostomy · the stoma colors · diet and appliance NG-401 Gastrointestinal ADHD-friendly visual edition The further along the bowel the stoma is, the thicker the output and the lower the fluid loss . That single sentence answers most ostomy questions. The other half is the stoma color . Healthy stoma Pink to beefy red, moist, slightly swollen at first Report now Pale, dusky, purple or black — the blood supply is failing Ileostomy Liquid output, high fluid and electrolyte loss Colostomy The f

Ileostomy — the ileum brought to the abdominal surface; output is generally more liquid Colostomy — part of the colon brought to the surface; a more distal stoma’s output is often thicker A healthy stoma is moist and pink to red Daily checks — protect the surrounding skin, check the pouch seal, follow the individual hydration plan A dusky or black stoma, or cramping with markedly reduced output, needs urgent clinical advice. Plate sources: NIDDK ostomy surgery · NIDDK overview · NIDDK complications Three ostomies,

Assessing it Color: pink to beefy red is healthy. Pale, dusky, purple, black — report. Moisture: moist and shiny is healthy. Dry and dull is not. Height: should protrude slightly. A retracted stoma leaks under the wafer; a prolapsed one telescopes out and needs review. Surrounding skin: intact, no redness or erosion. Excoriation means the appliance is leaking or the opening is cut too large. Output: amount, consistency and color, matched to the type. What to report Any color other than pink or red No output for 4 t

Appliance technique Empty the pouch when it is one-third to one-half full. A heavy pouch pulls the wafer off. Change the wafer every 3 to 7 days , or immediately if it leaks. Change it in the morning before eating , when output is lowest. Measure the stoma and cut the opening 1/8 inch (2 to 3 mm) larger . Too big exposes skin to effluent; too small strangles the stoma. Clean with warm water only . No soap with oils, no alcohol, no adhesive removers that leave residue — they stop the wafer sticking. Dry the skin com

Healthy stoma Pink to beefy red, moist, slightly swollen at first Report now Pale, dusky, purple or black — the blood supply is failing Ileostomy Liquid output, high fluid and electrolyte loss Colostomy The further along, the more formed the stool What color is a healthy stoma? Show answer Pink to beefy red, moist and shiny. Purple or black stoma — what do you do? Show answer Report immediately. The blood supply is compromised. How much larger than the stoma do you cut the wafer opening? Show answer About 1/8 inch,
