entries.t: 1 Assess safety — suicidal ideation, plan, means, and command hallucinations (voices telling the client to harm self/others) 2 Provide a safe, low-stimulation environment — decrease noise, light, and crowding, which can worsen psychosis 3 Build trust — consistent staff, honesty, predictable routine (therapeutic milieu — detailed on NG-128 ) 4 Monitor continuously through every phase, not just during an acute admission 🧠 "S-S-S" — S chizophrenia has a S cattered pattern of thinking and S uicide risk is high. Say it

entries.h: 🗺️ Where the rest of this topic lives — the 4-page series
entries.t: NG-049 — You are here Signs & Symptoms: definitions, positive/negative/cognitive, disorganized speech. NG-128 — Communication Therapeutic techniques for psychosis: don't argue with delusions, don't pretend to hear voices, reality orientation, the milieu. NG-165 — Pharmacology (schizophrenia-specific) Treatment approach, adherence barriers, anosognosia, long-acting injectables. NG-235 — Antipsychotics (drug reference) Typical vs. atypical, mechanism, EPS, NMS, agranulocytosis. 🧠 Think of this page as the dictionary

SAY IT OUT LOUD ➕ Positive Hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech/behavior ➖ Negative Flat affect, anhedonia, avolition, alogia, asocial (5 A's) 🧩 Cognitive Memory, attention, executive function, insight 🚨 Suicide risk HIGH Assess every time — top priority in this whole disease

Q1: A client says "I don't hear any voices, but the ceiling cameras are watching me." Which symptom category and type? Show answer Positive symptom — a persecutory (paranoid) delusion. Q2: A client with schizophrenia sits alone, has a blank expressionless face, and rarely initiates conversation. Symptom category? Show answer Negative symptoms — flat affect + asociality (part of the 5 A's). Q3: Nurse asks "How was your sleep?" and the client answers "Absolutely splendid" to every question asked afterward. What is th

entries.h: Death & Dying · NG-065 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Psychiatric Care Course

Defense Mechanisms & the Grieving Process NG-065 Mental Health ADHD-friendly visual edition Loss activates two things at once: unconscious defense mechanisms that protect the ego from the blow, and a grief process that moves (unevenly) toward acceptance. Know the mechanisms so you can name the behavior — know the stages so you know it's normal , not pathology. Pairs with NG-222 (Loss types, complicated grief & end-of-life decisions). 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🔤 DABDA D enial → A nger → B argaining → D epression → A cceptance (Kübler-Ross, not always in order). 🎯 Aim of the emotion matters Sideways at a safer person = displacement . Pinned onto someone else = projection . Copied from someone powerful = identification . 🧸 Kids can't verbalize grief Use play , art, honesty — not euphemisms. 🤱 NCLEX classic Stillborn loss: "You may hold your baby as long as you want." 🛡️
STEP 1 · WHY THEY ACT THAT WAY Before someone can grieve, the ego often protects itself first — these are unconscious, not manipulative.

entries.h: 🧠 What a defense mechanism actually is
entries.t: An unconscious mental strategy the ego uses to reduce anxiety when a person faces stress, conflict, or loss they can't process head-on yet. They are normal and adaptive in moderation — the problem is only when one gets used rigidly, alone, or in place of coping.

Loss or anticipated loss Emotional and practical needs change. Individual response Feelings and coping vary over time. Supportive care Presence, comfort and choice guide the response. Grief There is no required linear sequence of stages. Communication Listen without forcing reassurance or a timeline for recovery. End-of-life priorities Relieve symptoms, clarify goals and support the person and family. 🧠 Where does the feeling END UP? Displacement = lands on a safer person . Projection = lands on someone else, disgu

entries.h: 📋 The full defense-mechanism table — definition + NCLEX-style example
entries.t: Mechanism Definition Example from practice questions Displacement Shifting anger/impulses from an outside situation onto a safer, less threatening person Man loses his job, goes home and yells at his wife Repression Unconsciously blocking painful memories from awareness (not a conscious choice) 20-year-old sexually molested at age 10 can no longer remember the incident Rationalization Justifying illogical or irrational ideas/feelings with a logical-sounding excuse Client with alcoholism: "I need a drink or two to r

entries.h: ⚠️ Denial is BOTH a defense mechanism AND grief stage 1
entries.t: When a client says, after being told their feet will need amputation, "I'm sure if I start taking my medication my feet will heal," that is denial — difficulty accepting a new body image. It shows up under CAUSE here as a mechanism and again under CLUES as stage 1 of Kübler-Ross. 🧠 Same word, two jobs: denial as a defense mechanism happens anytime, not just with death. Denial as a grief stage is specific to the loss timeline below. 🌗
STEP 2 · WHERE ARE THEY ON THE TIMELINE Two models the NCLEX pulls from — Kübler-Ross's 5 stages and Bowlby's 4 phases. Neither is a strict staircase.

🧠 “DABDA” — say it like a heartbeat: D enial- A nger- B argaining- D epression- A cceptance. Any client can jump backward — a calm client at "acceptance" can flare back into anger on the anniversary of the loss. That's still normal grief, not regression to treat.

entries.h: 🌊 Bowlby's 4 Stages of Grief — the attachment-theory version
entries.t: 🧠 Bowlby ≠ Kübler-Ross — Bowlby describes the bond breaking (attachment theory); Kübler-Ross describes the emotions felt . If a question says "numbness," "yearning/searching," or "reorganization," it's testing Bowlby, not DABDA.

entries.h: 🎯 Tell the stage from the quote
entries.t: Client says Stage "I'm sure if I start taking my medication, my feet will heal" (after being told amputation is needed) Denial Appears angry & demanding after a below-the-knee amputation Anger "I feel like I can barely get out of bed in the morning" Depression 🧠 A grieving client is not "being difficult" on purpose — anger and demanding behavior are expected grief work, not a behavior problem to punish.

entries.h: ✅ ATI SATA — feelings that show healthy grief insight
entries.t: "I might experience feelings of resentment" "I might have some guilt over how my partner died" "I might have angry feelings that I should express" All correct — naming and expecting a range of emotions (including anger, resentment, guilt) shows insight, not pathology. 🧠 The trap: students want to mark anger/resentment/guilt as "bad" answers. In acute grief, expecting to feel and express them is the healthy answer. 🤍
STEP 3 · MEET THEM WHERE THEY ARE Adults need presence and honesty; children need developmentally-matched honesty plus a way to express what they can't say out loud.

entries.h: 🧒 Kids understand death differently by age — match your words to the stage
entries.t: 🧠 Why the nurse says "young children have difficulty verbalizing emotions" when a parent asks about play therapy: at preschool/school age, play IS their language — coloring, dolls, and games surface feelings a 6-year-old cannot say out loud.

🎨 Play therapy — young children can't verbalize emotions ✅ Honestly answer questions — age-appropriate wording, no euphemisms like "went to sleep" 🤲 Therapeutic touch — hold and cuddle to reinforce closeness 🖍️ Encourage expressing feelings through coloring/art 🎈 Promote activities the child enjoys — normal routine is grounding 🧠 "HAPPI" — H onest answers · A ctivities they enjoy · P lay therapy · P hysical closeness (hold/cuddle) · I llustrate feelings (coloring).

🗣️ Therapeutic communication — open-ended, non-judgmental 🪑 Sit with the client — presence over words 🤝 Support groups 📷 Focus on good memories 🧠 You don't have to fix the grief — sitting with the client is itself the intervention.

A nurse is caring for a client who just delivered a stillborn fetus at 36 weeks. Best statement: "You may hold your baby as long as you want." 🧠 Never rush or remove the baby. Bonding time supports the grieving process even after loss — this is one of the most frequently tested single lines in this topic.

entries.h: 👵 What effective adult coping looks like — HESI SATA pattern
entries.t: An older client whose spouse died 6 months ago. Behaviors that indicate effective coping: 📷 Looking at old snapshots of the family 🧑‍🤝‍🧑 Participating in a senior citizens' program 🪦 Visiting the spouse's grave occasionally (e.g., once a month) These show engagement with life alongside remembrance — social participation plus healthy reminiscing, not avoidance and not fixation. 🧠 Watch the frequency/intensity word. Occasional remembrance = healthy. A shrine-like need to preserve everything untouched, refusal to re-e

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🪜 DABDA Denial → Anger → Bargaining → Depression → Acceptance 🌊 Bowlby Numbness → Yearning/searching → Disorganization → Reorganization 🛡️ Displacement vs projection vs identification Redirect vs. blame-shift vs. copy 🤱 Stillbirth Let them hold the baby as long as they want

Q1: A client with alcoholism says, "I need a drink or two to relax after a busy day — I have an incredibly high-stress job." Which defense mechanism? Show answer Rationalization — justifying the behavior with a logical-sounding excuse. Q2: A man loses his job, goes home, and yells at his wife. Which defense mechanism? Show answer Displacement — anger shifted from the real (unsafe) target to a safer one. Q3: A client on the psych unit seeks out a particular nurse and imitates her mannerisms. Which defense mechanism?

entries.h: Dissociative Identity Disorder · NG-070 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Psychiatric Care Course

DID — formerly called "Multiple Personality Disorder" NG-070 Mental Health ADHD-friendly visual edition 2 or more distinct identity states rotate control of the client's behavior. Each identity state can have its own name, voice, memories, and mannerisms . It almost always starts with severe, repeated trauma in childhood — dissociation is the mind's way of protecting itself from what it cannot yet process. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🎭 2+ identities Distinct identity states take turns controlling behavior — each with its own memories. 🧠 Trauma = the cause Usually severe, repeated childhood abuse or profound neglect. ⏳ Amnesia = the clue "Lost time" — gaps in memory the client cannot explain. 🎯 Goal = integration Merge the identities into one whole person by processing the trauma. 🧨
STEP 1 · WHY IT SPLITS One protective reflex explains the whole disorder — the mind walls off what it cannot survive feeling all at once.

EXAM TIP Severe, repeated trauma — usually starting in early childhood (physical or sexual abuse, profound neglect) overwhelms a child's ability to cope. Instead of processing the trauma as one continuous self, the mind compartmentalizes it — walling pieces of memory and identity off into separate identity states ("alters") so the core self doesn't have to feel it all.

Traumatic exposure Can disrupt a person’s sense of safety. Stress symptoms Intrusion, avoidance, arousal or dissociation may occur. Recovery support Safety, choice and trauma-informed care guide engagement. Acute stress and PTSD Time course and diagnostic criteria differ; symptoms deserve assessment. Dissociation Disconnection in memory, identity or awareness can occur; medical and substance causes also need consideration. Nursing approach Explain actions, obtain consent, use grounding and avoid forcing disclosure.

👶 Onset in early childhood — trauma repeated over years, not a single event 🚫 No protective adult present to help the child feel safe or process what happened 🔁 Chronic, severe abuse or neglect — physical, sexual, or emotional 🧠 "Split young, stays hidden long." DID almost always begins before age 6–9 , but is often not diagnosed until adulthood.

Stress and anxiety that remind the client of the original trauma — a sound, a smell, a tone of voice, a place — can trigger control to switch to a different identity state. 🧠 Trigger → switch → time lost. The alter that emerges is usually the one built to handle that specific kind of threat. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT IT The client isn't lying about the gap — the gap is real, and they usually don't know the other identities exist.

The client has recurrent gaps in memory for everyday events, personal information, or traumatic events — beyond ordinary forgetting . They are typically not aware the alternate identities exist and become confused and distressed by the gaps. 🧠 "Lost time, not lies." A client insisting they "don't remember" doing something is a clinical clue — not defiance.

entries.h: 🚨 HESI — select all that apply: a dissociative episode
entries.t: ✔️ Dissociation is a method for coping with severe stress ✔️ Dissociative symptoms are not under the client's conscious control ✔️ The existence of 2 or more subpersonalities , each with its own patterns of thinking 🧠 "Can't help it, can't fake it." All three describe DID — none of them describe the client choosing to act this way.

🗣️ Identity confusion — uncertainty about who they are 😶 Depersonalization — feeling detached from own body/actions 🌫️ Derealization — surroundings feel unreal or dreamlike 📉 High comorbidity: PTSD , depression, anxiety, self-harm 🧠 DID nearly always travels with PTSD — same root cause, trauma.

Disorder Identity change? Key feature Dissociative Identity Disorder ✔️ Yes — 2+ distinct identity states take turns controlling behavior Amnesia between identity states; trauma-based Dissociative Amnesia ❌ No new identity Inability to recall important personal information, usually trauma/stress-related; no alternate identities Depersonalization / Derealization Disorder ❌ No new identity Persistent feeling of being detached from self (depersonalization) or that the world isn't real (derealization); reality testing
STEP 3 · SAFETY & INTEGRATION Build trust with every identity, ground the client in the present, and never force the trauma memory before they're ready.

entries.h: 🎯 Goal: integration, not "getting rid of" the alters
entries.t: Long-term psychotherapy works in phases: 1) safety & stabilization → 2) gently processing the trauma memories → 3) integration of the identities into one cohesive sense of self. 1 🛡️ Stabilize & build trust — with each identity, not just the one that talks the most 2 🗝️ Process the trauma — slowly, only when the client is ready, with a therapist 3 🧩 Integrate — identities merge into one whole personality HESI Successful treatment = the patient has integrated past events . 🧠 "Stabilize, then story, then whole." Skip

entries.h: 🚨 NEVER ask the client to recall memories
entries.t: Forcing recall of traumatic memories before the client is ready — or before a trauma-trained therapist is guiding it — can retraumatize and destabilize the client. 🧠 "Don't dig, just ground." If they aren't ready to remember, your job is safety and grounding — not excavation.

👂 Monitor & listen for any expression of self-harm — from any identity state 🤝 Develop a trusting relationship with each identity , not only the "host" 😌 Stay calm, consistent, and non-judgmental — the client cannot control the switching 🧠 Every identity state deserves the same respect and safety monitoring — dismissing an alter as "not real" breaks trust with the whole client.

Teach concrete grounding techniques to pull the client back into the present moment and reduce dissociation. 🧠 "Cold, count, breathe, write." Sensory grounding pulls attention into the here-and-now body, which interrupts the dissociative drift.

😐 Use a calm, matter-of-fact tone if a switch happens — don't react with shock or fear 🗓️ Keep a predictable, structured environment — reduces anxiety that can trigger switching 🧑‍⚕️ Coordinate care across the team so every staff member responds consistently to every identity 📓 A journal during hospitalization helps the client and team track triggers, feelings, and switches over time 🧠 Consistency is the medicine. A predictable environment and a calm, unified care team lower the anxiety that drives dissociation. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🎭 2+ identities Take turns controlling behavior, each with own memories 🧠 Childhood trauma = the root cause, dissociation = protection ⏳ Lost time = amnesia clue, client isn't lying 🎯 Integration = the treatment goal — never force the memory

Q1: What is the root cause of DID? Show answer Severe, repeated trauma, usually beginning in early childhood (abuse or profound neglect) — the mind dissociates to protect itself. Q2: What is the hallmark clue on assessment? Show answer Amnesia / "lost time" — memory gaps the client cannot explain and is often unaware of. Q3: What indicates successful treatment? Show answer The client has integrated past events — the identities merge into one cohesive personality. Q4: What should the nurse NEVER do? Show answer Neve
Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Anxiety-Spectrum Disorders

Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder NG-075 MENTAL HEALTH ADHD-friendly visual edition OCD runs on a two-part loop: an obsession (an intrusive, unwanted thought) fires off anxiety, and a compulsion (a ritual behavior) relieves that anxiety — temporarily . That temporary relief is exactly what keeps the loop spinning. The client usually knows the thought or ritual is irrational and it distresses them — that's ego-dystonic , the feature that separates true OCD from OCPD. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🔁 Obsession → Compulsion Obsession = the intrusive thought. Compulsion = the ritual that relieves the anxiety it causes — for a little while. 🚫 Never yank the ritual Interrupting a compulsion abruptly spikes anxiety fast. Allow it first, then gradually shorten it. 💊 SSRIs, higher dose, slower onset Sertraline, fluoxetine, paroxetine, fluvoxamine — OCD doses run higher than depression doses; response can take up to 8–12 weeks. 🪞 OCD ≠ OCPD OCD = unwanted, distressing (ego-dystonic). OCPD = feels correct to the clien
STEP 1 · THE LOOP One loop explains the whole disorder — an unwanted thought creates anxiety, a ritual relieves it, and the relief is what keeps the loop spinning.

entries.h: 🔁 The OCD loop — draw this before anything else

entries.t: Trigger or intrusive thought Distress rises. Compulsion or avoidance Short-term relief can reinforce the cycle. Targeted therapy Structured treatment helps change the cycle. OCD Obsessions are intrusive thoughts; compulsions are repetitive responses, not simply a preference for order. Specific phobia Marked fear and avoidance center on a particular situation or object. Care Use a collaborative plan; exposure-based therapies require consent and appropriate guidance. 🧠 “Trigger, Think, Terror, Try (the ritual), Tempo

Obsessions = recurrent, intrusive, unwanted thoughts, images, or urges that cause marked anxiety (contamination fears, doubt/checking, need for symmetry, taboo/aggressive intrusive thoughts). Compulsions = repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed to reduce the anxiety the obsession causes (handwashing, checking locks, counting, ordering/arranging, silent praying or counting). 🧠 Obsession = in the head. Compulsion = in the hands (or the mind's ritual). One creates the itch, the other is the scratch.

Thought to involve serotonin dysregulation plus an overactive circuit linking the orbitofrontal cortex → anterior cingulate → basal ganglia → thalamus — a “worry circuit” that gets stuck signaling something is wrong even after the ritual is done.

entries.h: 🪞 OCD vs OCPD — the mix-up the exam wants you to make
entries.t: Feature OCD OCPD (personality disorder) Insight Ego-dystonic — client knows it's irrational, hates it Ego-syntonic — feels correct, "this is just how I am" Distress High — thoughts/rituals are unwanted and exhausting Low — the person is comfortable, others are bothered instead Presentation True rituals: washing, checking, counting, ordering Perfectionism, rigid rules, need for control, preoccupied with orderliness Treatment SSRIs + Exposure & Response Prevention (ERP) — good response Psychotherapy focused on insigh
STEP 2 · SPOT IT Watch the ritual categories — and know exactly what happens physically if a ritual gets blocked.

🧼 Washing hands, showering 🔒 Checking locks, stove, iron 🔢 Counting steps, objects, words 📐 Ordering symmetry, arranging 📦 Hoarding can't discard items 🙏 Mental rituals silent praying, counting 🧠 Every category answers the same job description: quiet the anxiety the obsession just triggered.

entries.h: 🚨 If the ritual gets blocked — same physiology as a panic attack
entries.t: 🧠 This is why you never yank the ritual. A sudden stop can trigger a full sympathetic surge — remember panic attacks can occur inside OCD too.

Never suddenly deny a ritual, especially early in treatment Never make judgmental comments about the ritual ✅ Give a time reminder before interrupting ("5 minutes left") ✅ Gradually decrease ritual time session by session ✅ Give positive feedback for non-ritual coping and group participation 🧠 “Warn, then Wean.” Warn before the time is up, wean the minutes down slowly.

entries.h: ⭐ Top-missed NCLEX pattern: what counts as improvement?
entries.t: The answer is almost never "the ritual works better." Look for alternative coping replacing the ritual — "I used to wash my hands 10 times before opening a door, but for 2 weeks now I can open doors without washing." 🧠 If the option describes the client still doing the ritual — even calmly — it is not improvement. Improvement = less ritual, more coping skill. 🩺
STEP 3 · SHRINK THE RITUAL Support first, then shrink the ritual on a schedule — never yank it away.

1 Allow time to complete the ritual — especially early in the admission; do not interrupt abruptly 2 Identify triggers that increase the client's anxiety 3 Set limits gradually — decrease ritual time little by little ("5 minutes today, 4 minutes next time") 4 Teach alternative coping — deep breathing, relaxation, exercise/short walk 5 Reinforce non-ritual behavior — positive feedback during group activities and coping attempts 🧠 “Warn, Wean, Win.” Warn before time's up → wean the minutes down → win with praise for

Gold-standard psychotherapy for OCD. The client is exposed to the trigger (e.g., "unclean" object) and coached to resist the compulsive response, so the brain learns the anxiety falls on its own without the ritual. Thought-stopping technique: the client is taught to interrupt an intrusive thought on command (e.g., mentally shouting "stop") and redirect attention. 🧠 ERP = "Expose, then Endure." No ritual allowed during the exposure — that's the whole treatment.

Drug Note Sertraline SSRI, FDA-approved for OCD Fluoxetine SSRI, FDA-approved for OCD Paroxetine SSRI, FDA-approved for OCD Fluvoxamine SSRI, FDA-approved specifically for OCD Clomipramine TCA — second-line for treatment-resistant OCD 🧠 Compare to depression dosing: OCD typically needs a higher SSRI dose and a longer trial — response can take 8–12 weeks, longer than the usual 4–6 weeks for depression.

entries.h: 🚨 Never do this with an OCD client
entries.t: Never criticize, mock, or express frustration about the ritual Never suddenly deny or forcibly stop a ritual, especially in the first days of admission Never rush the client through the ritual — rushing raises anxiety, it doesn't shorten the behavior ✅ Do reinforce every non-ritual coping attempt, no matter how small 🧠 Priority nursing action in the first days after admission = allow the ritual and build trust. Limit-setting comes later, once the trigger list and coping plan exist. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🔁 Obsession → Compulsion thought → anxiety → ritual → temporary relief → repeat 🚫 Never yank the ritual allow it, then gradually shrink the time 💊 SSRIs higher dose, slower onset than depression — ERP is gold-standard therapy 🪞 Ego-dystonic = OCD. Ego-syntonic = OCPD

Q1: A client with OCD is reorganizing books for the third time. What's the best nursing action? Show answer Gradually limit the time spent on the activity — don't stop it abruptly. The ritual decreases the client's anxiety to a tolerable level. Q2: What is the priority nursing action in the first days after admitting a client with OCD? Show answer Allow time to complete rituals while you build trust and identify triggers — don't confront or deny the ritual suddenly. Q3: Which statement best shows improved coping in

entries.h: Personality Disorders · NG-076 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Psychiatric Care Course

10 patterns, 3 clusters — one of them (Borderline) is tested the hardest NG-076 Mental Health ADHD-friendly visual edition A personality disorder is an enduring, inflexible pattern of thinking, feeling, and relating that starts by adolescence/early adulthood , is stable over time, and causes real distress or impairment. There are 10 disorders sorted into 3 clusters (A, B, C) — and Borderline Personality Disorder from Cluster B is the single most heavily tested one, because of splitting and the fact that DBT is its

🧩 3 clusters A = Mad (odd), B = Bad (dramatic), C = Sad (anxious) 🎭 Borderline = splitting Staff are "the best nurse ever" one day, "the worst" the next. 🚨 #1 safety priority Assess borderline clients for self-harm / suicidal behavior first. 🧠 DBT = first-line Dialectical Behavior Therapy is the go-to treatment for Borderline PD. 🧩
STEP 1 · SORT THEM Every personality disorder question gets easier once you know which of the 3 clusters it lives in.

entries.h: 🗺️ The map — Cluster A · B · C

entries.t: Establish trust Respectful communication supports engagement. Set shared boundaries Clear expectations make care predictable. Support coping Reinforce effective skills and collaborative goals. Listen Use open questions, reflection and clarification when appropriate. Respond Describe observable behavior without judgment or labels. Coordinate Consistent team communication reduces mixed messages and conflict. 🧠 "Mad, Bad, Sad." Cluster A looks Mad (odd/paranoid), Cluster B acts Bad (dramatic/erratic), Cluster C feels

Paranoid: pervasive distrust & suspicion of others Schizoid: detached, prefers to be alone, restricted emotion Schizotypal: odd beliefs, magical thinking, "special powers" 🧠 They look like they're bracing for schizophrenia but aren't psychotic — reality testing stays mostly intact.

Antisocial: disregard for others' rights, lack of remorse Borderline: unstable relationships/mood, splitting, fear of abandonment Histrionic: excessive emotionality, attention-seeking, flirtatious Narcissistic: grandiosity, need for admiration, lack of empathy 🧠 This cluster is the NCLEX heavyweight — nearly every personality disorder question comes from here, especially Borderline.

Avoidant: feels inadequate, hypersensitive to rejection, avoids social contact Dependent: excessive need to be taken care of, fears separation, clingy Obsessive-Compulsive PD (OCPD): preoccupied with order, control, and perfectionism 🧠 "Avoidant fears people, Dependent fears losing people, OCPD fears losing control." 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT THE PATTERN Exam questions usually give you a quote or a behavior — match it to the disorder.

Disorder Hallmark Exam clue / quote Paranoid Distrust, suspicion of others' motives Sees clients laughing and assumes "I bet they are making fun of me." Improving = starts discussing feelings of anxiety with the nurse instead of accusing. Schizoid Withdrawn, prefers to be alone, flat affect Detached loner; little interest in relationships Schizotypal Odd beliefs / magical thinking "I believe we can all read each other's thoughts at times" + describes having "special powers"

Disorder Hallmark Exam clue / quote Antisocial Impulsive, manipulates for personal gain, lacks empathy & remorse Shoves another client out of the way → nurse should calmly confront the behavior and remind of consequences . Improvement statement: "I get into trouble because I don't think before I act." Borderline ⭐ Unstable relationships, splitting, impulsivity, chronic emptiness, fear of abandonment "Last night the nurse let me go outside to smoke. I can't believe you aren't letting me — I used to think you were th

Disorder Hallmark Exam clue / quote Avoidant Fear of rejection/criticism, avoids social situations despite wanting connection Feels inadequate; hypersensitive to negative evaluation Dependent Extreme dependency, fear of separation, submissive/clingy Makes numerous minor requests, lingers near the nurses' station = fear of abandonment + attention-seeking . Improvement: "My sister couldn't drive me, so I took the bus." Nurse should give positive feedback when the client is assertive . OCPD Preoccupied with rules, ord

entries.h: 🚨 Borderline — the pattern that's tested the most: splitting
entries.t: Splitting = black-and-white thinking — people (often staff) are seen as all good or all bad , with no in-between. It flips fast, often after a limit is set. This same "all-good / all-bad" pattern fuels manipulation (pitting one staff member against another) and clinging to one favorite staff member . 🧠 "No halos, no horns." The fix is a consistent team — every staff member is neither idealized nor demonized because everyone enforces the same limits the same way.

Of all the personality disorders, Borderline carries the highest risk for self-harm and suicide — often superficial cutting tied to overwhelming emotion or fear of abandonment. 🧠 Priority action: assess immediately for any self-harm behavior, including superficial cuts. 🩺
STEP 3 · MANAGE THE PATTERN Consistency is the nursing intervention for almost every personality disorder — and DBT is the specific first-line treatment for Borderline.

entries.h: 🧠 DBT — Dialectical Behavior Therapy — first-line for Borderline PD
entries.t: DBT (developed by Marsha Linehan) is the evidence-based, first-line treatment for Borderline Personality Disorder . It teaches 4 skill modules to replace splitting/self-harm with regulated coping. 🧠 "Mind the Distress, Regulate the People." Mindfulness + Distress tolerance + Emotion regulation + Interpersonal effectiveness = the 4 DBT pillars. DBT balances acceptance and change — that's the "dialectical" part.

entries.h: 👥 "One team, one message" — the #1 nursing intervention
entries.t: Because splitting and manipulation thrive on inconsistency, the whole care team must set and enforce identical limits . 🧠 "No favorite, no fight." Rotate staff assignments so the client cannot cling to one "favorite" nurse — that clinging is itself a red flag for splitting.

Assess immediately for self-harm / suicidal behavior — including superficial cuts Never let the client cling to one favorite staff member Rotate staff assignments across the team 🧠 Assess first, structure second. Safety before behavior plans.

Calmly confront the behavior and remind the client of consequences Institute consequences for manipulative behavior — follow through every time Don't get pulled into arguing, bargaining, or rescuing 🧠 Calm + consistent beats confrontational. Consequences work only when they're predictable.

Use a matter-of-fact, non-reactive tone — don't feed grandiosity or flattery-seeking Redirect dramatic/attention-seeking behavior calmly, without excess reassurance Set boundaries around excessive demands for admiration or attention 🧠 Reacting with irritation or with excess praise both reinforce the pattern — neutral wins.

entries.h: 🗣️ Paranoid, Avoidant & Dependent — build trust & independence
entries.t: Paranoid: give honest, neutral, reality-based responses — "They are laughing at a joke another client told. They are not laughing at you." Dependent: give positive feedback when the client is assertive with staff or other clients Avoidant: gradual exposure & consistent, non-judgmental encouragement to socialize 🧠 "Truth, praise, patience." Reality-orient the paranoid client, praise assertiveness in the dependent client, and be patient with the avoidant client's pace. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧩 Mad, Bad, Sad Cluster A odd · B dramatic · C anxious 🎭 Splitting All-good / all-bad thinking = Borderline's signature 🧠 DBT Mindfulness · Distress tolerance · Emotion regulation · Interpersonal effectiveness 👥 One team, one message Consistency defuses manipulation & splitting

Q1: A client says, "Last night you let me smoke outside — I used to think you were the best nurse here, now I can't believe you're doing this to me." What is this? Show answer Splitting — classic Borderline Personality Disorder pattern of all-good/all-bad thinking. Q2: What is the first-line treatment for Borderline Personality Disorder? Show answer DBT — Dialectical Behavior Therapy (mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness). Q3: A client with paranoid personality disorder s
Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Anxiety-Spectrum Disorders

Specific Phobia · Agoraphobia · Social Anxiety NG-077 MENTAL HEALTH ADHD-friendly visual edition A phobia is an excessive, irrational fear of a specific object or situation, out of proportion to the actual danger, that drives avoidance . The client usually has insight — they know the fear "doesn't make sense" — but can't switch it off. First-line treatment is systematic desensitization : exposure, in small steps, paired with relaxation. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

😨 Fear + Avoidance Excessive, irrational fear of one object/situation that drives the client to avoid it. 🚪 Agoraphobia ≠ one object Fear of being trapped or unable to get help/escape — open spaces, crowds, public transit, being outside alone. 🪜 Systematic desensitization First-line: gradual, ranked exposure to the feared stimulus, paired with relaxation. 🗣️ Validate, don't argue logic "Your fear doesn't make sense to you, but it's very real to you." 😨
STEP 1 · THE FEAR MAP One definition drives the whole topic — an out-of-proportion fear that the amygdala refuses to downgrade.

entries.h: 😨 Three fear disorders, easy to blur together
entries.t: Disorder What's feared Example Specific phobia One object or situation Spiders, heights, needles, flying Social anxiety disorder Being watched, judged, or embarrassed in front of others Public speaking, eating in front of coworkers Agoraphobia Being trapped — unable to escape or get help if panic strikes Open spaces, crowds, riding trains/buses, being outside alone 🧠 Agoraphobia is not "fear of open spaces" alone — it's fear of not being able to escape . It's the disorder most often paired with panic attacks.

entries.h: 🧬 Mechanism: a conditioned alarm that won't reset
entries.t: A learned/conditioned fear response (classical conditioning) — sometimes after one bad experience, sometimes with no clear trigger — paired with an amygdala that overreacts to the stimulus and a prefrontal cortex that struggles to override it with logic. 🧠 “The alarm is real, the danger isn't.” The amygdala fires exactly like it would for a real threat — that's why reassurance alone doesn't fix it.
🕷️ Arachnophobia spiders 🐾 Zoophobia animals 🚪 Claustrophobia closed-in spaces 🏙️ Agoraphobia trapped / no escape

entries.h: 🎯 Specific phobia vs. Agoraphobia — same fear machinery, different target

entries.t: Trigger or intrusive thought Distress rises. Compulsion or avoidance Short-term relief can reinforce the cycle. Targeted therapy Structured treatment helps change the cycle. OCD Obsessions are intrusive thoughts; compulsions are repetitive responses, not simply a preference for order. Specific phobia Marked fear and avoidance center on a particular situation or object. Care Use a collaborative plan; exposure-based therapies require consent and appropriate guidance. 🧠 Both are fear-driven avoidance — but agoraphobia
STEP 2 · SPOT IT Anticipatory dread before exposure, a full sympathetic surge during it, and one exact phrase to say back.

entries.h: 🚨 Exposure to the phobic stimulus = sympathetic surge
entries.t: 🧠 Same autonomic surge seen in panic attacks, PTSD flashbacks, and blocked OCD rituals — the anxiety-spectrum disorders all share one alarm system.

entries.h: 🗣️ Therapeutic communication — say this exact type of line
entries.t: Client: "I am so terrified of heights that the thought of going up my stairs makes me feel like I am going to hyperventilate. I know it sounds ridiculous." Best nurse response: "You feel like your fear does not make sense, but it is very real to you." 🧠 Assess first, reflect the feeling — don't argue the logic. Never say "that's silly" or try to talk the client out of the fear with facts.

Increased comfort while exposed to the phobia Verbalizing feelings & insight about the anxiety (self-observation) Self-distraction — focusing on something other than the phobia 🧠 Improvement = staying in the situation longer, not avoiding it faster. "I planned to skip the party" is avoidance, not coping.

entries.h: ⭐ Phobias can be a piece of a bigger picture
entries.t: Phobic symptoms can be a manifestation of PTSD — a trauma survivor may develop a specific, situational fear tied to reminders of the event. Screen broadly; don't assume every phobia stands alone. 🩺
STEP 3 · EXPOSE GRADUALLY Build a ladder of fear, climb it slowly, and pair every rung with relaxation.

The client and therapist build a fear hierarchy — least feared to most feared — then move up one rung at a time , pairing each exposure with a relaxation technique, until anxiety at that step is tolerable before advancing. 🧠 “Desensitize = de-SIZE the fear, one small step at a time.” The opposite approach — flooding (rapid, full-intensity exposure) — is more distressing and is not the typical first-line choice.

Benzodiazepines — short-term / situational use for acute exposure anxiety, not a long-term fix SSRIs — first-line long-term medication for social anxiety disorder Beta-blockers (e.g., propranolol) — sometimes used off-label before a specific feared performance event to blunt physical symptoms (tremor, racing heart) 🧠 Medication supports exposure therapy — it does not replace it. Desensitization is the durable fix.

entries.h: 🚨 Never do this with a phobic client
entries.t: Never argue the client out of the fear with logic or facts Never force full, unprepared exposure without a hierarchy Never dismiss the fear as silly or exaggerated ✅ Do validate: the fear doesn't have to make sense to be real to them

Daily stress-reduction practice (breathing exercises, scheduled relaxation, regular exercise) builds resilience between exposure sessions and lowers the baseline anxiety the client brings into each new hierarchy step. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 😨 Fear + Avoidance excessive, irrational, drives avoidance 🚪 Agoraphobia fear of being trapped / no escape — pairs with panic disorder 🪜 Systematic desensitization gradual hierarchy + relaxation = first-line 🗣️ Validate the feeling don't argue the logic

Q1: A client says "I am terrified of being outside alone." Which phobia? Show answer Agoraphobia — fear of being in places/situations where escape or help might not be available, including being outside alone, crowds, or public transit. Q2: What is the best nursing response to "I know my fear of heights sounds ridiculous"? Show answer "You feel like your fear does not make sense, but it is very real to you." Validate the feeling, don't argue the logic. Q3: Which intervention is a client who avoids flying most likel

entries.h: PTSD & Acute Stress Disorder · NG-078 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Anxiety-Spectrum Disorders

& Acute Stress Disorder (ASD) NG-078 MENTAL HEALTH ADHD-friendly visual edition Both ASD and PTSD are anxiety-spectrum responses that can develop after exposure to a traumatic event. One clock separates them: symptoms in the first month = ASD; symptoms past one month = PTSD. Four symptom clusters describe the whole clinical picture, and the nurse's first job — every time — is a safety check before anything else. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🕐 One-month line ASD = first month after trauma. PTSD = symptoms persisting beyond 1 month. 🧩 4 symptom clusters Intrusion · Avoidance · Negative mood/cognition · Hyperarousal. 🚨 Priority #1, always Assess for self-harm / suicidal ideation before anything else. 💊 Trauma-focused CBT / EMDR First-line therapy; SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) FDA-approved. Avoid long-term benzodiazepines. 🌩️
STEP 1 · THE TIMELINE Same trauma-response biology — the only thing that changes the diagnosis is the calendar.

entries.h: 🕐 ASD → PTSD: one timeline, one cutoff

entries.t: Traumatic exposure Can disrupt a person’s sense of safety. Stress symptoms Intrusion, avoidance, arousal or dissociation may occur. Recovery support Safety, choice and trauma-informed care guide engagement. Acute stress and PTSD Time course and diagnostic criteria differ; symptoms deserve assessment. Dissociation Disconnection in memory, identity or awareness can occur; medical and substance causes also need consideration. Nursing approach Explain actions, obtain consent, use grounding and avoid forcing disclosure.

Directly experiencing a threat to life, serious injury, or sexual violence Witnessing the event happen to someone else Learning it happened to a close family member or friend Repeated professional exposure to trauma details (e.g., first responders) 🧠 Keep assessment clinical and non-graphic — you do not need event detail to identify the diagnosis or plan safe care.
Prior trauma history Lack of social support after the event Co-occurring substance use Severity/duration of the traumatic exposure 🔎
STEP 2 · FOUR CLUSTERS Four symptom clusters cover the whole clinical picture — plus the physiology behind a flashback.

entries.h: 🧩 The 4 symptom clusters — memorize this grid
entries.t: 🧠 “I AM H” — I ntrusion · A voidance · M ood/cognition (negative) · H yperarousal. All four must be present for the PTSD diagnosis, not just one.

entries.h: 🚨 A trauma reminder can trigger a full sympathetic surge
entries.t: 🧠 A war veteran hearing a car backfire and feeling like they're back in combat is hyperarousal + intrusion firing together — reassure them of present safety first.

Client: "The war was years ago, but I still remember my friends who were killed. I don't know why I lived and they died." Nurse's priority response: "Are you having any thoughts of harming yourself?" 🧠 Survivor's guilt is a red flag for self-harm risk. Always screen for safety before exploring the feeling further.

Self-harm: thoughts or plans Substance use (drugs & alcohol) — common coping attempt Relationships with family & friends — isolation is a warning sign For sexual assault survivors: assess for guilt/shame; reinforce they could not have anticipated it and did not deserve it 🩺
STEP 3 · PACE & PROCESS Let the client set the pace, normalize the reaction, and lean on trauma-focused therapy before medication.

1 Safety screen first — self-harm/suicidal ideation, every encounter 2 Encourage the client to talk at their own pace — never force detail before they're ready 3 Explain that difficult symptoms after trauma are normal — normalize, don't pathologize the reaction 4 Assess substance use and relationships — common coping/withdrawal patterns 5 Connect to trauma-focused therapy — CBT, EMDR, or group therapy as tolerated 🧠 “Pace, Place, Process.” Let them set the pace, keep them safe in place, then help them process — in

Trauma-focused CBT — helps the client reframe distorted trauma-related beliefs (guilt, danger, self-blame) and gradually process memories. EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing) — the client recalls the trauma in brief segments while following bilateral stimulation (e.g., guided eye movements); thought to help the brain reprocess the memory so it feels less distressing. Prolonged exposure therapy — structured, repeated recounting of the memory in a safe setting to reduce its emotional charge over time

Drug class Note SSRIs — sertraline, paroxetine FDA-approved, first-line pharmacologic option TCAs — amitriptyline, imipramine Older alternative, more side effects Prazosin Off-label, targets trauma-related nightmares specifically 🧠 Avoid long-term benzodiazepines in PTSD — dependence risk, and evidence doesn't support them as an effective core treatment; they don't treat the underlying avoidance/re-experiencing symptoms.

entries.h: 🚨 Never do this with a trauma client
entries.t: Never push the client to describe trauma details before they're ready Never minimize the reaction ("it was years ago, just move on") Never assume every trauma survivor's symptoms look the same ✅ Do reinforce: the feelings are a normal response to an abnormal event ✅ For assault survivors: reinforce they could not have anticipated it and did not deserve it ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🕐 1 month ASD before it, PTSD after it 🧩 4 clusters Intrusion · Avoidance · Mood/cognition · Hyperarousal 🚨 Safety first always screen for self-harm before anything else 💊 Trauma-focused CBT / EMDR + SSRIs; avoid long-term benzos

Q1: What separates Acute Stress Disorder from PTSD? Show answer Duration. ASD occurs within the first month after trauma; if symptoms persist beyond one month, it's PTSD. Q2: Name the 4 PTSD symptom clusters. Show answer Intrusion/re-experiencing, avoidance, negative alterations in mood/cognition, and hyperarousal/reactivity. Q3: A veteran expresses survivor's guilt about friends killed in combat. What's the nurse's priority response? Show answer Ask directly: "Are you having any thoughts of harming yourself?" Safe

entries.h: Sleep & Circadian Rhythm · NG-089 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Fundamentals: Rest & Sleep I

The Body Clock, Sleep Architecture & Circadian Disorders NG-089 Mental Health ADHD-friendly visual edition One master clock, the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), uses light hitting the retina to time everything — melatonin release, body temperature, cortisol, and when you feel sleepy. Chronic sleep loss raises risk for HTN, obesity, depression, diabetes & stroke . This is the biology page — see Sleep Hygiene ( NG-135 ) for the practical nursing-teaching companion. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🧠 SCN = master clock Hypothalamus nucleus, entrained by light through the eyes. 🌑 Melatonin ↑ in dark Pineal gland releases it as light fades — signals "time to sleep." 🔁 REM every ~90 min Cycles repeat all night; REM periods get longer toward morning. ✈️ 3 circadian disorders Shift work · Jet lag · Delayed sleep phase — the clock and the schedule disagree. 🧨
STEP 1 · THE BODY CLOCK Light in, melatonin out — one feedback loop drives the entire 24-hour rhythm.

PATHWAY Light hits photoreceptors in the retina → signal travels the retinohypothalamic tract → reaches the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) in the hypothalamus, the brain's master circadian clock → SCN tells the pineal gland to hold back or release melatonin .

Circadian rhythm Light and timing help set the daily body clock. Sleep pressure The need for sleep builds during wakefulness. Restorative opportunity A consistent, suitable environment supports sleep. Schedule Use regular sleep and wake times and daytime activity. Environment Reduce noise and light; review evening caffeine and other stimulants. Assess disorders Snoring with breathing pauses, severe daytime sleepiness or persistent insomnia needs evaluation. 🧠 "No light, all right (to sleep)." Any bright light late
Core body temperature dips to its lowest point in the early morning hours, then climbs through the day and peaks in the evening — the two rhythms run in sync to time sleep onset and wake.

Even a few days of poor sleep raises risk for: ❤️ Hypertension ⚖️ Obesity 😔 Depression & decreased cognitive function 🩸 Diabetes 🧠 Stroke 🧠 "HODDS." HTN · Obesity · Depression · Diabetes · Stroke — the five-condition list chronic sleep debt drags up. 🔎
STEP 2 · ARCHITECTURE & DISORDERS A normal night cycles through stages every 90 minutes — a misaligned clock or a broken cycle both look different from the outside.

entries.h: 🔁 Stages of sleep — repeats about every 90 minutes
entries.t: Stage What's happening Stage 1 Wakefulness → sleep, non-REM. Lasts a few minutes; loss of awareness but easily aroused. Stage 2 Light sleep, non-REM. 10-20 minutes; vitals & metabolism start to decrease. Stage 3 Deep / slow-wave / delta sleep, non-REM. Vitals decrease further; difficult to awaken; physical/cognitive restoration . REM Rapid eye movement; vivid dreaming; begins ~ 90 min after falling asleep and recurs every ~ 90 min; psychological rest . 🧠 "1-2-3-REM, then repeat." Deeper each stage, then REM breaks

entries.h: ✈️ Circadian rhythm disorders — the clock and the schedule disagree

entries.t: Rotating or night-shift work forces sleep against the SCN's light-set schedule → insomnia during intended sleep + excessive sleepiness on shift, with real accident/error risk.

Crossing time zones faster than the SCN can re-entrain (roughly 1 day per time zone) → fatigue, GI upset, trouble sleeping/waking on the new local clock. Eastward travel is typically harder to adjust to than westward.

The internal clock runs later than the desired schedule — can't fall asleep until very late (e.g., 2-6am ), then struggles to wake for school/work. Common in adolescents/young adults. 🧠 Management lever = light & melatonin timing. Bright light exposure at the right time of day (and avoiding it at the wrong time), plus timed melatonin, helps re-entrain the SCN in all three — the specific timing differs by disorder and is individualized by a sleep specialist.
Difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, awakening too early, or not feeling rested on waking. Chronic insomnia: occurs 3 + nights/week for more than 3 months.

Obstructive (OSA): soft tissue in the mouth/throat relaxes and blocks the airway Central: the CNS fails to signal the body to breathe — no airway blockage, the drive to breathe itself pauses Both show cycles of breathing stops/starts, with pauses lasting more than 10 seconds .

😴 Sudden "sleep attacks" — falls asleep without warning 💪 Cataplexy — sudden muscle weakness triggered by strong emotion 👁️ Hypnagogic hallucinations — vivid hallucinations at sleep onset 🧠 Linked to a lack of REM regulation — REM-like features intrude into wakefulness 🧠 Huge safety risk — driving, walking, standing. The highest-priority assessment question is about safety during high-risk activities: "Do you have difficulty staying awake while driving?" 🩺
STEP 3 · ASSESS & SUPPORT Ask about safety first, then hand off to the practical teaching page for what to actually change.

Disorder Priority nursing question / focus Narcolepsy Safety during driving/high-risk activity — "Do you have difficulty staying awake when you are driving?" Insomnia Sleep pattern history, safety, and contributing factors (stress, environment, meds, substances) before jumping to a sleep aid Sleep apnea Witnessed breathing pauses, snoring, daytime sleepiness — screen for OSA vs. central pattern Circadian disorders Work schedule, travel history, and usual bed/wake times — mismatch between the clock and the required
Disturbed sleep pattern related to anxiety or alteration in client routine — common framing when the SCN's schedule is disrupted by stress, travel, or shift changes.

entries.h: 🔗 Where the "what to do about it" lives
entries.t: This page explains why the clock runs the way it does and what disrupts it. The actionable teaching — light exposure timing, caffeine/alcohol cutoffs, bedroom environment, hospital-unit strategies — is the companion page. 🔗 See NG-135 — Sleep Hygiene for the practical nurse-teaching checklist built directly on this page's biology. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧠 SCN Master clock in the hypothalamus, set by light through the eyes 🌑 Melatonin Pineal gland releases it in the dark → sleepy 🔁 90-min cycle Stage 1 → 2 → 3 (delta) → REM, repeating all night ✈️ 3 disorders Shift work · Jet lag · Delayed sleep phase — clock vs. schedule mismatch

Q1: What structure is the body's master circadian clock, and what sets it? Show answer The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) in the hypothalamus — set primarily by light entering the eyes via the retinohypothalamic tract. Q2: What gland releases melatonin, and when? Show answer The pineal gland — release increases as light fades in the evening and is suppressed by light exposure. Q3: How often does the sleep-stage cycle repeat, and which stage brings vivid dreaming? Show answer About every 90 minutes; REM sleep brings

entries.h: ADD & ADHD · NG-093 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Psychiatric Care Course

Attention Deficit (Hyperactivity) Disorder NG-093 Mental Health ADHD-friendly visual edition Low dopamine & norepinephrine in the brain's reward/focus circuits means the brain can't rank what deserves attention — so it either drifts (inattentive), revs (hyperactive-impulsive), or both (combined type). Treatment lives on a separate page — see ADHD Meds ( NG-234 ) . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🧪 2 low chemicals Dopamine & norepinephrine — the "reward vs. risk" & impulse-control messengers. 🎭 3 presentations Inattentive · Hyperactive-Impulsive · Combined — same disorder, different face. 🚨 #1 nursing diagnosis Risk for injury — impulsivity outruns judgment. 🗣️ Teach in 4 steps Eye contact → simple language → repeat back → praise. 🧨
STEP 1 · THE BRAIN CHEMISTRY One circuit explains the whole picture — the brain's "is this worth my attention" filter runs low on fuel.

entries.h: 🧠 The prefrontal circuit runs low on dopamine & norepinephrine
entries.t: EXAM TIP Low dopamine & norepinephrine in the prefrontal cortex — the neurotransmitters that help the brain weigh reward vs. risk and control impulsivity & mood . Clients with ADHD are therefore more likely to also carry anxiety and substance use risk — the brain chases whatever raises dopamine fastest.

Neurodevelopmental pattern Attention and/or activity regulation is affected. Functional difficulty Symptoms impair life across relevant settings. Individualized support Behavioral, educational and medication strategies can help. Assess Sleep, learning, anxiety and other contributors or coexisting conditions. Medication Monitor target symptoms, sleep, appetite, growth when relevant, pulse and pressure. Teaching Use routines, short instructions, positive feedback and appropriate accommodations. 🧠 "Low fuel, low filte

🧬 Genetic / family history — highly heritable 🤕 History of head trauma — TBI (traumatic brain injury) 🚬 Prenatal exposure — nicotine, alcohol, or substance use in pregnancy 👶 Low birth weight / prematurity 🧠 "Hit head, hooked on risk." A documented head injury is the classic ATI risk-factor trap — kids with a serious TBI are more likely to develop ADHD later.

entries.h: 🔤 Say the terms — ADD vs. ADHD
entries.t: ADD = Attention Deficit Disorder — inattentive symptoms without the motor hyperactivity ADHD = Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder — the umbrella term used in current diagnostic criteria (DSM-5-TR), covering all three presentations below "ADD" is older/lay terminology — on exams, ADHD is the umbrella and the presentation (inattentive / hyperactive-impulsive / combined) is the specifier. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT THE PRESENTATION Three faces of the same low-dopamine circuit — know which symptoms build which type.

entries.h: 🎭 Three DSM presentations — same disorder, different symptom mix

entries.t: Reduced ability to focus, easily distracted, poor follow-through, disorganized, loses items, forgetful in daily activities.
Restless "always on the go," excessive talking, blurts answers, interrupts, difficulty waiting turn.

Meets criteria for both — the most commonly diagnosed presentation, especially in school-age children. 🧠 DSM checklist = "6-6-12-2." 6 or more symptoms · lasting more than 6 months · onset before age 12 · present in 2 + settings (home and school). One setting only ≠ ADHD — it might just be that classroom.

🏃 Hyperactivity — "restless," can't stay seated 🧠 Inattention — "reduced ability to focus" 🗣️ Impulsiveness — "excessive talking," blurts, interrupts 😔 Low self-esteem & impaired social skills — from repeated correction/rejection 🧠 "HII-L" — H yperactive · I nattentive · I mpulsive · L ow self-esteem. Say it like "hee-ill" — the disorder hurts before it heals.

entries.h: 🚨 Priority nursing diagnosis: Risk for injury
entries.t: Impulsivity + hyperactivity outrun judgment — a child may run into traffic, climb, or act before thinking. On a HESI/ATI question, "risk for injury" is the nursing diagnosis to pick when ADHD is the stem. 🧠 Aggressive/agitated child? Distract & redirect — e.g., ask them to blow up a balloon. Gives the excess energy somewhere safe to go instead of escalating. 🩺
STEP 3 · STRUCTURE, SAFETY, COMMUNICATION Non-drug care is structure and predictability; medication management lives on its own page — see NG-234 .

1 👁️ Get eye contact BEFORE speaking — confirms attention is captured first 2 💬 Use simple, short language — one instruction at a time 3 🔁 Have the child repeat back what was said — confirms it was received 4 🌟 Offer praise upon task completion — reinforces the behavior you want repeated 🧠 "Eye-Say-Say-Yay." Eye contact → Say it simply → child Says it back → Yay (praise). Kaplan's favorite right answer is a hug/praise after the task is completed — not before, and not as a bribe up front.

entries.h: 📋 Structure & scheduling — the #1 classroom/home teaching point
entries.t: 📅 Provide a written or typed daily schedule — predictability lowers anxiety and impulsive behavior ⏱️ Allow regular breaks 👁️ Combine verbal instructions with visual cues 📏 Establish consistent rules — same expectations every day 📉 Do not overload with homework — decrease amount assigned 🧠 On an ATI-style stem — "9-year-old on bedrest with ADD, which action should the nurse prioritize?" — the answer is give a written/typed daily schedule , not medication or restraint.

Stimulants (methylphenidate, amphetamine salts) and non-stimulants (atomoxetine, guanfacine/clonidine ER) treat the same low-dopamine/norepinephrine circuit covered above. Full mechanism, monitoring, and teaching are on the ADHD Meds page ( NG-234 ) — this page is diagnosis & non-drug care only, so the two pages together are the complete topic. 🔗 See NG-234 — ADHD Meds for: stimulant mechanism, growth/cardiac monitoring, controlled-substance status, drug holidays, and non-stimulant options. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧪 Low dopamine + norepinephrine = poor reward/risk filter + poor impulse control 🎭 3 types Inattentive · Hyperactive-Impulsive · Combined 📅 Best intervention Written/typed daily schedule — structure & consistency 🚨 Priority Dx Risk for injury — impulsivity outruns judgment

Q1: What two neurotransmitters are low in ADHD, and what do they normally do? Show answer Dopamine & norepinephrine — they help the brain weigh reward vs. risk and control impulsivity/mood. Q2: A child has a serious head injury history. What's the connection to ADHD? Show answer TBI (traumatic brain injury) is a documented risk factor — increases the likelihood of developing ADHD later. Q3: What's the priority nursing diagnosis for a hospitalized child with ADHD? Show answer Risk for injury — impulsivity and hypera

entries.h: Alcohol Abuse · NG-096 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Communication & Therapy Foundations

CNS depression, the withdrawal clock, and the two emergencies that follow it NG-096 MENTAL HEALTH ADHD-friendly visual edition Alcohol is a CNS depressant — chronic use quiets the brain, and the brain compensates by revving up its own excitability. Stop the alcohol suddenly, and that compensation is unopposed — vitals spike, seizures can happen, and delirium tremens (DTs) can kill. Two other life-or-death traps live on this page: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome and the thiamine-before-glucose rule. 📄 Simple Nursing ori

😴 Intoxication = low & slow CNS depressant — vitals drop, coordination & balance suffer. 📈 Withdrawal = high & fast Vitals spike as the brain rebounds — seizures & DTs are the danger. 🧠 Thiamine BEFORE glucose Prevents Wernicke-Korsakoff — a rule that can be tested on its own. 🚫 Recovery goal = total abstinence No alcohol, ever — identify triggers, not moderation. 🍺
STEP 1 · WHAT ALCOHOL DOES One mechanism explains both intoxication and withdrawal — alcohol depresses the CNS, and the brain fights back by upregulating itself.

entries.h: 😴 Alcohol = CNS depressant — vitals go low & slow
entries.t: EXAM TIP Alcohol is a toxin that causes central nervous system depression — vital signs run low and slow, and coordination & balance suffer (ataxia, slurred speech).

Exposure A substance alters CNS or other organ function. Adaptation Tolerance or physical dependence may develop. Reduced exposure Withdrawal can follow abrupt reduction or cessation. Intoxication Assess airway, breathing, circulation, temperature, glucose and injury as indicated. Withdrawal Alcohol and sedative withdrawal can be life-threatening and require monitored treatment. Recovery care Use respectful language, symptom treatment and evidence-based ongoing support. 🧠 "Low and slow means alcohol's in tow." Any

Escape from problems Cover up depression & anxiety 🧠 Alcohol use disorder is often a symptom of an underlying mood problem — that's why counseling's primary goal is identifying triggers, not just stopping the drink.

Alcohol metabolism in the liver disrupts normal glucose production. Monitor blood glucose levels at night — hypoglycemia can happen hours after the last drink, especially in malnourished or diabetic clients. 🧠 Alcohol intoxication can look like a diabetic emergency — always check a glucose on an intoxicated or withdrawing client; don't assume it's "just the alcohol." 🔎
STEP 2 · THE CLOCK THAT CAN KILL Withdrawal severity rises on a predictable timeline — DTs are the single most dangerous point on it.

entries.h: ⏱️ Alcohol withdrawal timeline — know every stage
entries.t: 🧠 "24 shakes, 48 seizes, 72 crazes." ~24 hr = anxious & shaky · ~48 hr = seizure risk · 48–72 hr = DTs, the peak danger window.

entries.h: 🌡️ DTs vital sign pattern — read the numbers
entries.t: 🧠 If a chart shows fever + tachycardia + hypertension + tachypnea in a client with a recent drinking history, think withdrawal — not just "anxiety."

Hyperreflexia — hand tremors Diaphoresis (sweating) Hallucinations Tachycardia — HR over 100 bpm Hypertension Fever Confusion & restlessness 🧠 "SHAKE-HHF" — S weating · H and tremors/hyperreflexia · A gitation/confusion · K razy visions (hallucinations) · E levated HR · H ypertension · F ever. DTs is a medical emergency.

The CIWA-Ar (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol, revised) is a structured bedside scoring tool — tremor, sweating, anxiety, agitation, hallucinations, orientation, headache, nausea are each scored, and the total drives symptom-triggered treatment decisions. Higher score = more severe withdrawal = closer monitoring. 🧠 Score drives care, not the calendar. CIWA-Ar lets the team treat the client's actual symptom burden instead of a fixed timer. For the specific medication class and taper approach used
STEP 3 · PROTECT THE BRAIN Seizure precautions come first; then protect against a second, quieter emergency — Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

Any client in alcohol withdrawal (or sudden benzodiazepine/barbiturate withdrawal — cross-tolerant, same mechanism) needs seizure precautions in place immediately : padded rails, bed in low position, suction & oxygen at bedside, quiet low-stimulation environment. 🧠 Sudden withdrawal from alcohol, benzodiazepines, or barbiturates can all cause seizures — they share the same GABA mechanism, so nursing precautions look the same across all three.

entries.h: 🧠 Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome — the "why thiamine first" rule
entries.t: Chronic alcohol use causes poor nutrition and impairs thiamine (vitamin B1) absorption. Thiamine is required as a cofactor to metabolize glucose. If glucose is given before thiamine is replaced, the sudden glucose load consumes the little thiamine the client has left — precipitating or worsening Wernicke's encephalopathy. 🧠 "Thiamine before the sweet stuff." Any malnourished or chronic-alcohol-use client who needs IV glucose (D50, dextrose fluids) should get thiamine first — this is a classic standalone NCLEX point

After detox, the primary goal of recovery is total abstinence — meaning NO alcohol, forever. Moderation is not the treatment goal for alcohol use disorder. 🧠 Abstinence, not moderation — a very common wrong-answer trap is "cut back to a couple drinks a week."

The primary goal of counseling is to help the client identify factors that trigger alcohol use — not to lecture about consequences or "cover up" the underlying depression/anxiety that drives the drinking. 🧠 "Triggers, not tricks." Effective intervention = develop motivation & self-help skills, and pinpoint the trigger, every time.

📎 The specific drug class used to prevent seizures/DTs (benzodiazepines, dosed by CIWA-Ar symptom score) and the general safety comparison with opioid withdrawal are covered in detail on the Pharmacology batch's Withdrawal Meds ( NG-277 ) page — refer there for drug names, taper approach, and monitoring parameters rather than duplicating them here. Use Therapeutic Communication ( NG-271 ) techniques when counseling: open-ended questions to explore triggers, reflecting instead of lecturing, and never giving false re

SAY IT OUT LOUD 😴 Intoxication = low & slow Withdrawal = high & fast — opposite directions. ⏱️ 24-48-72 Anxious → seizures → DTs, the killer window. 🧠 Thiamine before glucose Prevents Wernicke-Korsakoff — high-yield standalone fact. 🚫 Total abstinence Recovery goal is zero alcohol, not moderation.

Q1: A client reports drinking a pint of vodka daily and is 48–72 hours post-last-drink. What is the priority concern? Show answer Delirium tremens — the most dangerous window (48–72 hours), with confusion, hallucinations, tachycardia, hypertension, and fever. Q2: Why must thiamine be given before IV glucose in a chronic alcohol use client? Show answer Glucose metabolism requires thiamine as a cofactor — giving glucose first in a thiamine-deficient client can precipitate or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy. Q3: What i

entries.h: Atypical Antidepressants · NG-101 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Psychiatric Care

Trazodone · Bupropion (Wellbutrin) · Mirtazapine — the ones that don't fit the SSRI/SNRI/MAOI mold NG-101 MENTAL HEALTH ADHD-friendly visual edition "Atypical" just means none of these three work through the standard SSRI/SNRI/MAOI mechanism — each has its own quirky target, and each earns its spot on the exam through one signature side effect : trazodone's priapism, bupropion's seizure risk, mirtazapine's weight gain. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

😴 Trazodone = sleep Sedating → used off-label as a sleep aid; take at night. ⚡ Bupropion = seizures Lowers seizure threshold — avoid in seizure or eating disorder history. 🍽️ Mirtazapine = appetite Sedation + weight gain — good pick for poor sleep/appetite. 🚨 Priapism Erection lasting hours on trazodone = go to the ER now. 💊
STEP 1 · MECHANISM Three drugs, three different targets — none of them are classic serotonin reuptake blockers.

entries.h: 🧠 Three different mechanisms, one drug class label

entries.t: Neurotransmitter effects Drug classes affect signaling in different ways. Clinical response Mood and anxiety benefits usually develop over time. Ongoing review Benefit, adverse effects and safety guide adjustment. SSRIs and SNRIs Monitor activation, serotonin toxicity, bleeding interactions and discontinuation symptoms. TCAs and MAOIs Have additional cardiac, anticholinergic or food/drug interaction concerns. Teaching Do not stop or combine drugs without review; report worsening suicidality or possible mania. 🧠 “SA

Indication: depression; very commonly used off-label as a sleep aid at lower doses because of its sedating effect. Mnemonic: TraZZZadone / TRANCE-adone — sleepy and sedated. 🧠 If the question describes a depressed client with severe insomnia getting a low-dose bedtime medication that isn't a benzodiazepine — think trazodone .

Indication: depression and as an aid to stop smoking (marketed as Zyban for that indication, same drug). Comes in SR (sustained-release) and XL (extended-release) formulations. 🧠 “Bupropion helps you quit and stay energized.” It's the antidepressant of choice when a client also wants to stop smoking or is worried about sexual side effects/weight gain.

Indication: depression, especially useful when the client also has significant insomnia and poor appetite/weight loss — the side effects become the therapeutic benefit. 🧠 “Mirtaz-appetite.” Picture a fork and a pillow — this drug makes people eat and sleep, which is exactly what an underweight, sleepless depressed client needs. ⚠️
STEP 2 · SIDE EFFECTS Each drug has one signature danger sign the exam loves to test.

entries.h: 🚨 Trazodone — priapism is a medical emergency
entries.t: 😴 Sedation, drowsiness 📉 Orthostatic hypotension — dizziness with position changes 🚨 Priapism — rare but serious: an erection that persists for hours unrelated to sexual activity Priapism is a urologic emergency — untreated, it risks permanent tissue damage. Teach the client to go to the emergency department immediately if this occurs. 🧠 Rare ≠ ignorable. Priapism is the one trazodone side effect tested over and over precisely because students forget to mention it's an emergency.

Avoid bupropion in clients with: 🌀 A seizure disorder or history of seizures 🍽️ A current or past eating disorder (anorexia or bulimia nervosa) — electrolyte shifts from purging further lower the seizure threshold 🧠 “Bu-PRO-pion, PRO the seizures? No — PRO-tect against giving it in seizure/eating-disorder history.” Seizure risk is the #1 safety flag for this drug.

😴➡️😳 Insomnia (opposite of trazodone/mirtazapine) 🤕 Headache ⚖️ Weight loss — unlike most antidepressants 💚 No significant sexual side effects — a real advantage over SSRIs (see NG-205 ) 🧠 If the question says a client switched antidepressants because of sexual dysfunction, bupropion is a classic answer choice.

😴 Significant sedation — dose at bedtime ⚖️ Weight gain and increased appetite (the flip side of bupropion) 😵 Dizziness, dry mouth Low sexual side-effect profile, similar advantage to bupropion, but the mechanism and target population differ. 🧠 Bupropion and mirtazapine are opposites on sleep and weight — insomnia/weight loss vs. sedation/weight gain — pick based on what the client needs more of.

entries.h: 🧍 Side-effect body map — three drugs, three signature effects
entries.t: 🧠 One glance, one drug: droopy face + warning = trazodone , alert face + down arrow = bupropion , droopy face + up arrow = mirtazapine . 🗣️
STEP 3 · PATIENT EDUCATION Formulation rules, timing, and what to do if a warning sign shows up.

entries.h: 🚫 Bupropion SR/XL — never crush, chew, or cut
entries.t: 🚫 Never crush 🚫 Never chew 🚫 Never cut 🚫 Never double up on a missed dose Crushing/chewing an XL (extended-release) or SR (sustained-release) tablet dumps the full dose at once — this spikes blood levels and raises seizure risk sharply. 🧠 Extended-release + seizure-risk drug = never crush, ever. The whole point of the SR/XL coating is to prevent exactly the kind of dose spike that could trigger a seizure.

💊 Take at night — sedation is expected and useful for sleep Avoid alcohol and other sedatives (benzodiazepines, antihistamines) — additive CNS depression 🧍 Teach slow position changes to reduce orthostatic hypotension/fall risk 🚨 Go to the ED for any erection lasting more than a few hours

Can be started while the client is still smoking, with a target quit date set during treatment Take earlier in the day — insomnia is common if dosed at night Report new or worsening seizures, tremor, or agitation immediately

Take at bedtime — sedation is the point, not a problem to fight Expect increased appetite and possible weight gain — monitor weight over time Avoid driving/operating machinery until the sedating effect is known 🧠 Mirtazapine and trazodone both sedate, but only mirtazapine reliably drives appetite up — that's the differentiator.

entries.h: 🌳 Decision path — from patient picture to drug
🎯 Pick the right drug for the patient
entries.t: Patient picture Best-fit drug Why Depressed + severe insomnia, no other complaints Trazodone Sedating; low-dose off-label sleep aid Depressed + wants to quit smoking, worried about sexual side effects Bupropion Dual indication; no sexual side effects; energizing Depressed + poor appetite, underweight, can't sleep Mirtazapine Sedating + appetite-stimulating Seizure disorder or active eating disorder Avoid bupropion Lowers seizure threshold 🔗 For SSRI, SNRI, and MAOI mechanisms, interactions (serotonin syndrome, tyra

SAY IT OUT LOUD 😴 Trazodone sedating, sleep aid, watch for priapism ⚡ Bupropion seizure risk — avoid in seizure/eating disorder hx, never crush SR/XL 🍽️ Mirtazapine sedation + weight gain, good for poor sleep & appetite 💚 No sexual side effects bupropion (and mostly mirtazapine) — unlike SSRIs

Q1: A client on trazodone reports an erection lasting several hours with no sexual activity. What should the nurse instruct? Show answer Go to the emergency department immediately — priapism is a urologic emergency. Q2: Which client would be a poor candidate for bupropion? Show answer A client with a seizure disorder or an active/past eating disorder (anorexia or bulimia) — bupropion lowers the seizure threshold. Q3: A client is prescribed bupropion XL.
