entries.h: Bulimia Nervosa · NG-106 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Psychiatric Care Course

A serious, treatable eating disorder — the electrolytes are the emergency NG-106 Mental Health ADHD-friendly visual edition Bulimia nervosa is defined by recurrent episodes of binge eating followed by compensatory behaviors to prevent weight gain — self-induced vomiting, laxative or diuretic misuse, fasting, or excessive exercise. Clients often maintain a normal or near-normal body weight , which can hide the diagnosis. The #1 nursing priority is fluid & electrolyte monitoring — especially hypokalemia , because it

🔄 Binge → compensate Two-part cycle: binge eating, then behavior to prevent weight gain. 🚨 Watch potassium Hypokalemia (K⁺ < 3.5 ) → cardiac dysrhythmia risk. ⚖️ Often normal weight Unlike anorexia, weight can look unremarkable — don't rule it out by appearance. 🍽️ Supervise meals 1-on-1 during meals + 1–2 hr after, to prevent compensatory behavior. 🧨
STEP 1 · THE CYCLE One repeating cycle explains the whole disorder — and it's driven by a distorted body image, not appetite.

EXAM TIP Bulimia nervosa involves 2 linked phases : 1) recurrent episodes of binge eating — consuming a large amount of food with a sense of loss of control — 2) followed by compensatory behavior to prevent weight gain, such as self-induced vomiting, misuse of laxatives/diuretics, fasting, or excessive exercise. Underneath it all sits a distorted body image and an obsessive drive to control weight.

Restrictive or compensatory behavior Food intake and elimination patterns become unsafe. Physiologic effects Malnutrition, dehydration and electrolyte changes may develop. Multidisciplinary treatment Medical stabilization and psychological care are both needed. Anorexia nervosa Restriction and weight-related fears can cause severe nutritional compromise. Bulimia nervosa Binge episodes with compensatory behaviors may occur at many body weights. Safety Monitor circulation, electrolytes, rhythm and refeeding risk when

Distorted body image — perception doesn't match reality Obsessive desire to control or lose weight Often coexists with anxiety, depression, or low self-esteem 🧠 The behaviors are about control , not hunger — treat the underlying emotional driver, not just the eating pattern.

entries.h: ⚖️ Bulimia vs. Anorexia — don't confuse them
entries.t: Bulimia Nervosa Anorexia Nervosa Body weight Usually normal or near-normal Significantly low for age/height Pattern Binge eating + compensatory behavior Severe, sustained food restriction Insight Often feels shame/guilt, more likely to recognize the behavior is a problem Frequently denies the severity of low weight 🧠 "Bulimia hides in a normal-looking body." Don't rule out bulimia just because weight looks unremarkable — this is the exact trap the exam sets. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT IT The body keeps the score — dental, glandular, and electrolyte clues, plus the environmental evidence.
🧠 "Teeth, cheeks, knuckles, skin." These four findings appear even when the scale gives no clue at all.

Repeated vomiting and laxative/diuretic misuse drain potassium, chloride, and hydrogen ions , producing hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis . 🧠 "K+ below normal = call it a cardiac problem." Hypokalemia is the single most dangerous complication of bulimia — it can trigger a fatal dysrhythmia.

Hidden or discarded food wrappers Laxative or diuretic boxes found discarded Frequent bathroom trips right after meals Weight fluctuations without an obvious dietary explanation 🧠 The evidence is usually environmental, not verbal — clients rarely disclose these behaviors on their own.

Bulimia is a medical and psychiatric condition, not a choice or a moral failing. Approach assessment and conversation with the same clinical neutrality used for any other disease — avoid commenting on weight, food choices, or appearance, and focus questions on feelings, stress, and control . 🧠 Sample short-term goal (ATI): "Verbalizing the desire to increase control over stressful situations" — reframes the goal around coping, not weight. 🩺
STEP 3 · STABILIZE & TREAT Electrolytes first, structure second, therapy for the long haul — and watch for refeeding syndrome if nutrition rehab begins.

🧪 Hypokalemia (K⁺ < 3.5 mEq/L ) → cardiac dysrhythmia risk — obtain baseline ECG, trend labs 🧪 Watch chloride and acid-base status — vomiting causes metabolic alkalosis 💧 Assess for dehydration from vomiting, laxative, or diuretic misuse 🧠 "Electrolytes before everything." A bulimic client can look medically stable and still be in cardiac danger from their potassium level alone.

entries.h: ⚠️ Refeeding syndrome — risk during nutritional rehabilitation
entries.t: If treatment includes structured nutritional rehabilitation after a period of chaotic or restricted intake, the reintroduction of food can trigger refeeding syndrome : an insulin surge drives potassium, phosphate, and magnesium into cells, causing a dangerous drop in serum levels. See NG-298 (TPN & Enteral Feeding) for the full refeeding syndrome electrolyte workup — same mechanism applies here whenever malnourished clients begin structured nutrition rehabilitation. 🧠 "Feeding too fast can crash the labs." Start nu

1 👀 1-on-1 supervision during meals 2 ⏱️ Supervise 1–2 hours after each meal to prevent compensatory behavior 3 📓 Food diary during hospitalization to track intake and patterns 4 🍽️ Regular, structured meals — helps break the binge/compensate cycle 🧠 "Watch the meal, then watch the hour after." The compensatory behavior almost always happens right after eating.

Drug Role Fluoxetine (SSRI) FDA-approved pharmacologic option for bulimia nervosa Bupropion (Wellbutrin) Avoided — associated with increased seizure risk in bulimia nervosa 🧠 "Fluoxetine yes, Bupropion no." If bupropion shows up as an answer choice for bulimia, it's the trap, not the treatment.

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is the first-line, evidence-based psychotherapy for bulimia nervosa Explore stress, control, and coping — the eating pattern is a symptom, not the root problem Approach with a calm, non-judgmental, therapeutic tone — shame worsens the cycle Coordinate with dietitian, therapist, and medical team for a whole-person plan 🧠 "Treat the person, not the plate." Sustainable recovery comes from addressing the emotional drivers alongside the physical stabilization. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🔄 Binge → compensate The defining two-part cycle 🚨 Hypokalemia Most dangerous complication — cardiac dysrhythmia risk 🦷 Teeth, cheeks, knuckles Dental erosion, parotid swelling, Russell's sign 🍽️ Supervise meals 1-on-1 during + 1–2 hr after, plus food diary

Q1: What electrolyte imbalance is the priority to monitor in bulimia nervosa, and why? Show answer Hypokalemia (K⁺ below 3.5 mEq/L) — it can cause life-threatening cardiac dysrhythmias. Q2: A client with bulimia nervosa has a normal body weight. Does that rule out the diagnosis? Show answer No — clients with bulimia often maintain a normal or near-normal body weight, unlike anorexia nervosa. Don't rule it out based on appearance. entries.h: Depression: Nursing Care · NG-112 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Psychiatric Care

Suicide risk assessment · therapeutic communication · milieu safety NG-112 MENTAL HEALTH ADHD-friendly visual edition Once you know a client is depressed, the nursing job shifts to one priority : is this client safe? That means asking about suicide directly , recognizing the paradox where a sudden lift in mood can mean rising danger, and building a safe, structured, low-demand environment while therapy and medication take weeks to work. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🚨 Ask directly “Do you have thoughts of hurting yourself? Do you have a plan?” — never dance around it. ⚠️ Calmer + more energy after being severely depressed = INCREASED risk, not improvement. 👁️ 1:1 continuous observation is the priority intervention for active suicidal ideation with a plan. 🗣️ Sit. Listen. Simple, direct language + your presence — therapeutic communication is an intervention. 🧨
STEP 1 · WHAT KIND, AND WHY Depression isn't one thing — the type changes the teaching. The mechanism is the same low-neurotransmitter picture underneath all of them.

entries.h: 🗓️ Four faces of depression — same low mood, different timeline

entries.t: Persistent mood change Low mood or loss of interest may occur. Whole-person effects Sleep, appetite, energy, cognition and function can change. Care and recovery Assessment, therapy and medication may help. Assess Duration, impairment, medical contributors, substance use and history of mania. Safety Ask directly about suicidal thoughts, intent, plan and access to means. Support Offer concrete assistance, realistic goals and follow-up; track response over time. 🧠 “The Big 4” — M DD hits hard & leaves, D ysthymia sta

Depression is linked to low levels of serotonin, norepinephrine & dopamine in the brain — everything runs low and slow : mood, energy, sleep, appetite, concentration. 🔗 Full neurotransmitter diagram & the 9-symptom "SIG E CAPS" breakdown live on NG-031 Depression: Signs & Symptoms — this page assumes that baseline and focuses on what the nurse does about it . 🧠 Low & slow = the whole disease in three words.

👪 Family history of depression or suicide 🔁 Prior suicide attempt — the single strongest predictor 🍺 Substance use disorder 🏥 Chronic or terminal illness, chronic pain 😔 Recent loss — job, relationship, bereavement 🧍 Social isolation, lack of support system 🧠 A prior attempt is the single biggest red flag in the whole chart — always screen history before you screen today's mood. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT THE RISK Symptoms tell you the client is depressed. Risk clues tell you whether they are about to act on it — a completely different question.

S leep changes I nterest lost (anhedonia) G uilt / worthlessness E nergy loss (anergia) C oncentration poor A ppetite/weight change P sychomotor slowing or agitation S uicidal ideation + depressed mood most of the day, most days. Diagnostic threshold and full detail on NG-031 .

entries.h: 🚨 A PRIORITY: suicide risk — the warning signs that override everything else
entries.t: 🎁 Giving away cherished/valued possessions 💬 Statements: “I can't go on,” “I do not want to live,” “I won't be a problem much longer,” “This will all be over soon” 📈📉 A sudden, abrupt change in energy — in either direction 🗒️ Making final arrangements, settling affairs, saying goodbye 🧠 “Gifts + goodbyes = red flags.” A depressed client who suddenly starts giving things away or sounds like they're wrapping things up is telling you something — take it literally, not figuratively.

entries.h: ⚠️ The classic NCLEX trap — calmer or more energetic can mean MORE danger, not less
entries.t: Early in treatment, physical energy and psychomotor drive can return before the depressed, hopeless mood lifts. The client now has both the intent (still hopeless) and the energy (newly restored) to act on a plan — this is one of the highest-yield NCLEX points in psych. A client who suddenly seems calm, smiling, and "cured" after being severely depressed needs closer observation, not less. 🧠 “Energy comes back before hope does.” Never chart a sudden mood lift as reassuring without reassessing suicidal ideation firs

entries.h: 🗣️ Ask it directly — the exact assessment questions
entries.t: “Have you had any thoughts of hurting yourself?” “Do you have a plan to end your life?” “Do you have access to the means to carry out that plan?” “Do you want to die?” Asking directly does not plant the idea and does not increase risk — it is the single most important, evidence-based nursing action. Vague or indirect questions get vague, unreliable answers. 🧠 “Plan + means + intent” = the three things every suicide risk assessment must uncover. The more specific and immediate the plan and access, the higher the ris
STEP 3 · KEEP THEM SAFE Least restrictive environment that is still safe — then presence, structure, and time while treatment works.

1 Continuous 1:1 observation — active plan, means, and intent = highest risk, arm's-length supervision at all times 2 Room close to the nurses' station , not an isolated private room 3 Remove harmful objects from the room and environment per unit protocol (means restriction) 4 Supervise during meals and personal care 5 Reassess every shift — thoughts can escalate or de-escalate quickly 🧠 Risk level sets the observation level. The more specific the plan and the more available the means, the further right on this sta

✅ Use simple, direct language — depressed clients have low concentration/energy for complex conversation ✅ Sit with the client , even in silence — your presence is an intervention ✅ “I'd like to hear about how you are feeling now” — open, non-judgmental ✅ Reflect and validate feelings without minimizing them Never use empty reassurance — “everything will be fine,” “you have so much to live for” — it shuts the conversation down and feels dismissive. 🧠 Presence > advice. The best therapeutic response is almost always

Offer a structured program of activities the client can choose to join Invite and encourage group participation — do not command it Assist with ADLs — offer to help the client get dressed, sit with them, walk with them Look for improvement clues : talking about future plans, goals, family, holidays — a genuine sign of progress vs. the false calm of a fixed plan 🧠 A client who says “I talked with my family about ways we can celebrate the holidays together” is showing real improvement — future-oriented language is re

Depression commonly causes appetite and weight change (usually loss) — poor intake is a real medical risk, not just a symptom to note. Small, frequent, high-calorie / high-protein meals and snacks Stay with the client during meals Weekly weighing — the most reliable way to evaluate whether nutrition interventions are working 🧠 Trend the weight, not the tray. A client can pick at food and still be losing ground — the weekly weight is the objective outcome measure.
🧠 Exact time frames vary by client and reference — the concept, not the calendar, is what's tested: stabilize → protect against relapse → protect long-term . ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🎁 Giving things away + goodbye statements = act on it, don't dismiss it ⚠️ Sudden calm/energy = reassess risk, not reassurance 👁️ Highest risk = continuous 1:1 observation 🗣️ Ask directly “Do you have a plan?” never increases risk

Q1: A client with major depression and suicidal ideation is suddenly calmer and more energetic. What should the nurse consider? Show answer This can mean INCREASED suicide risk — the client may now have the energy to act on a plan. Increase the level of observation/precautions and reassess immediately, don't assume improvement. Q2: A client says he has no reason to continue living. What should the nurse ask first? Show answer Ask directly and specifically: "Do you have any plans to end your life right now?" — asses

entries.h: Panic Attack · NG-126 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Anxiety-Spectrum Disorders

Discrete Episode of Intense Fear + Autonomic Surge NG-126 MENTAL HEALTH ADHD-friendly visual edition A panic attack is a sudden surge of intense fear or discomfort that peaks within about 10 minutes , dominated by physical symptoms so convincing the client often believes they're dying. It can occur on its own (panic disorder) or inside OCD, phobias, or PTSD. Classic ER teaching point: rule out a cardiac event first — panic attacks can mimic an MI closely enough that you don't get to assume. 📄 Simple Nursing origina

⏱️ Peaks within ~10 min Sudden onset, physical symptoms dominate, resolves — cardiac symptoms don't follow this pattern. 🧍 #1 priority: REMAIN Stay with the client. Don't leave them alone during an attack. ❤️ Rule out MI first ECG + troponin before calling chest pain "just anxiety." 🖐️ Grounding: 5-4-3-2-1 5 things you see, 4 hear, 3 touch, 2 smell, 1 taste + slow paced breathing. ⚡
STEP 1 · THE SURGE One nervous-system event explains the entire attack — a sympathetic surge with no "off" switch for several terrifying minutes.

entries.h: ⚡ The full sympathetic ("fight or flight") surge

entries.t: Threat response Autonomic arousal increases. Symptoms intensify Palpitations, dyspnea, fear or dizziness may occur. Support restores control A calm setting and focused assistance can help. During panic Stay present, speak briefly and calmly, and reduce stimulation. Assess alternatives New chest pain, hypoxia or other medical warning signs require medical assessment. Long-term care Therapy, coping skills and prescribed medication address recurring symptoms. 🧠 Same surge as OCD/phobia/PTSD, maximum volume. This diagr

Panic attack = the discrete episode itself — can occur inside OCD, a phobia, PTSD, or generalized anxiety, or entirely out of the blue. Panic disorder = recurrent, unexpected panic attacks plus persistent worry about having another one — often leading to avoidance behavior (agoraphobia). 🧠 One attack ≠ a disorder. It's the pattern + fear of the next one that upgrades it to panic disorder.

Can be spontaneous/unexpected (no identifiable cause) or situational — inside a phobia exposure, an OCD ritual interruption, or a PTSD trauma reminder. All share the same underlying nervous-system surge. 🔎
STEP 2 · RULE OUT THE HEART The symptoms overlap with a heart attack closely enough that the ER workup comes before the psych label.

entries.h: ❤️ Panic attack vs. myocardial infarction — the classic mimic
entries.t: 🧠 “Rule the heart out before you rule the mind in.” A client having surgery with chest pain, choking, and hot flashes still gets worked up for cardiac causes first — the diagnosis of panic disorder comes after that workup is clear.
Fear of death — "impending doom" Feelings of detachment / derealization Chest pain & heart palpitations Trembling & numbness Hyperventilation Sweating & hot flashes Nausea & choking sensation

A client becomes increasingly anxious, sweats profusely, breathes rapidly, and states "I feel like I'm having a panic attack." Best actions (select all that apply pattern): stay by the client's side, escort to a quiet place, use a comforting tone. 🧠 If an option involves leaving the client to get something (even a good idea, like medication) before staying with them first, it's usually a distractor — presence comes first. 🩺
STEP 3 · STAY & GROUND Presence and grounding stop the acute attack; SSRIs and CBT prevent the next one.

1 REMAIN with the client — the #1 priority, do not leave them alone 2 Move to a quiet, low-stimulation room 3 Speak calmly , using simple, short, clear sentences 4 Coach slow, paced breathing — counted inhale/exhale to break hyperventilation 5 Once it resolves , assess triggers and connect to a longer-term coping plan 🧠 “Stay, Space, Speak, Slow (breathing).” All four before you ever reach for a medication.
🧠 Pair with slow, paced breathing (in for 4 counts, hold 4 , out 4 ) to break the hyperventilation cycle.

Drug class Role Benzodiazepines Short-term / PRN for an acute attack — rapid onset SSRIs / SNRIs First-line long-term prevention for panic disorder Beta-blockers ("-lol", e.g. atenolol) Blunt physical symptoms (racing heart, tremor) 🧠 Benzos calm the attack ; SSRIs prevent the next one. CBT is the durable, non-drug foundation either way.

entries.h: 🚨 Never do this during a panic attack
entries.t: Never leave the client alone during the episode Never assume "it's just anxiety" without ruling out a cardiac cause when symptoms are new or ambiguous Never crowd the client's space or raise your voice ✅ Do stay, keep it quiet, keep your voice calm, and coach the breathing ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD ⏱️ Peaks <10 min sudden onset, self-resolving 🧍 REMAIN with client #1 priority, never leave them alone ❤️ Rule out MI first ECG + troponin before "it's anxiety" 🖐️ 5-4-3-2-1 grounding + slow paced breathing

Q1: A client having surgery reports chest pain, choking, and hot flashes. What should the nurse do first? Show answer Rule out a cardiac cause (ECG, troponin) before attributing the symptoms to panic — panic attacks are a diagnosis of exclusion in this setting. Q2: What is the nurse's #1 priority action during an active panic attack? Show answer Remain with the client — stay by their side, don't leave them alone. Therapeutic Communication — Part 2 of a 4-page Schizophrenia series NG-128 Mental Health Series 2 of 4 · communication techniques This page assumes you already know the vocabulary from NG-049 (hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech). Here we cover how to talk to a client experiencing psychosis — what to say, what never to say, reality orientation vs. validation, and the therapeutic milieu. Drug therapy is on NG-165 & NG-235 . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🚫 Never argue You cannot logic someone out of a delusion — arguing only breaks trust. 🙅 Never pretend Don't claim to see/hear what isn't there — it's dishonest & damages trust. ❤️ Validate the feeling The emotion behind the delusion/hallucination is always real — respond to that. 🌍 State reality once, gently Then move on — don't debate it. 🧭
STEP 1 · THE RULES BEHIND EVERY RESPONSE Every "correct" NCLEX answer for psychosis traces back to these four rules.

1 Never argue with or challenge a delusion. A fixed false belief cannot be reasoned away — trying only proves to the client that you're "against" them too. 2 Never pretend to see or hear a hallucination. Lying breaks trust the moment the client realizes it — and they usually do. 3 Do not directly reinforce the false belief either — you also don't say "yes, I believe the FBI is watching you." 4 Respond to the feeling under the content. Fear, isolation, and distress are real even when their cause is not. 🧠 "Honest +

entries.h: ⚖️ Reality orientation vs. validation therapy — know the debate

entries.t: Altered perception or thought Hallucinations, delusions or disorganization may occur. Functional effects Motivation, expression, cognition and daily activity can change. Support and treatment Medication, therapy and practical support work together. Communicate Use calm, concrete language and acknowledge distress without affirming a delusion. Assess safety Ask about command hallucinations and the person’s intent or ability to resist them. Support function Reduce overload, maintain predictable routines and collaborat

"What are the voices saying?" "What do you see?" "Describe what you are seeing right now." "How does it feel to think you are being watched?" "What activities did you enjoy in the past?" (assesses anhedonia/avolition from NG-049 ) 🧠 Open-ended assessment questions gather data without confirming or denying the content — the safest way to explore a hallucination or delusion. 💬
STEP 2 · SCRIPTED RESPONSES Real NCLEX/HESI/Kaplan-style stems — memorize the shape of the correct answer, not just the words.

Client: "There are strange people in the corner of my room laughing at me and saying horrible things." ✅ therapeutic "I don't hear any voices, but I know this is frightening for you." ❌ avoid "There's no one there, you're imagining it." (dismissive, argues the point) ❌ avoid "Oh yes, I can see them too." (dishonest, reinforces the hallucination) 🧠 Formula: "I don't [see/hear] X, but I [know/understand] it feels real/frightening to you." Same sentence shape works for every hallucination question.

Client: "Do you see those cameras in the ceiling? I'm being watched all the time." ✅ therapeutic "Those are sprinklers, not cameras. It might be frightening to think that others want to hurt you." (brief factual correction once, then pivot to feeling) ❌ avoid Long explanations/arguing about why the belief is false — repeated debate reinforces the delusion's importance instead of reducing it. Client refusing food: "The voices say the food is poisoned." ✅ therapeutic "I understand the voices are very real to you, but

"You see yourself as the savior" — accusatory, shuts down trust Arguing facts repeatedly — cannot out-logic a fixed delusion Ignoring the client and walking away — client with schizophrenia leaving the room when a nurse asks about their day is not the nurse's cue to just "let them go quietly" — approach again later, offer a shorter/simpler interaction, don't abandon the therapeutic relationship Whispering or laughing near the client — easily misread as part of a persecutory delusion 🧠 "I see you as my client" is a

entries.h: ✅ Building blocks of every good response
entries.t: State the facts calmly, once — "I see you are frightened, let's go to your room and talk about this." Acknowledge the client's feelings explicitly, every time. Focus on reality and reinforce it verbally, without arguing. Keep sentences short and concrete — disorganized speech + concrete thinking ( NG-049 ) means idioms and long explanations may not land. 🧠 "FACTS-FEELINGS-REALITY" — every correct answer stacks these three in some order. 🏥
STEP 3 · THE ENVIRONMENT AS TREATMENT Communication isn't just words — the unit environment itself is a therapeutic tool.
🧠 Decrease environmental stimuli — dim lighting, fewer people, less noise — reduces the raw sensory input that psychosis has to sort through, which can lower agitation and hallucination intensity.

entries.h: 🧊 Catatonic presentation — a special communication case
entries.t: Catatonia with catalepsy can include immobility, bizarre posturing, muscle rigidity, mutism, severe negativism, and staring. 🧠 Priority: ensure physical safety (fall/injury prevention, nutrition/hydration, skin integrity) while continuing to speak to the client normally — hearing may be intact even without a visible response.

entries.h: ✅ Nutrition & fluid monitoring belongs in the plan too
entries.t: Disorganized behavior, paranoia about food, or catatonia can all reduce oral intake. Fluid and nutritional intake is a standard plan-of-care item — not just a "medical" concern, it's a communication + safety issue (offering sealed food, eating with the client, structured mealtimes). 🧠 Don't let "communication" tunnel-vision you away from basic physiologic needs on a care-plan question. 🩺
STEP 4 · WHAT OUTRANKS COMMUNICATION Good communication supports safety — it never replaces a safety assessment.

If voices are instructing the client to harm self or others, this is a priority safety issue , not just a communication moment — assess plan/means/intent and escalate per unit protocol immediately. 🧠 Carrying NG-049 forward: suicide risk is HIGH in schizophrenia at every phase — command hallucinations raise that risk further and change your very next action.

NG-128 — You are here Communication: say/don't say scripts, reality orientation vs. validation, milieu. NG-165 — Pharmacology (schizophrenia-specific) Treatment approach, adherence barriers, anosognosia, long-acting injectables. NG-235 — Antipsychotics (drug reference) Typical vs. atypical, mechanism, EPS, NMS, agranulocytosis. 🧠 If a question is testing what to say , you're on the right page. If i

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🚫 Never argue Delusions can't be reasoned away 🙅 Never pretend Don't claim to see/hear what isn't there ❤️ Validate feelings "I don't hear voices, but I know this is scary for you" 🏥 Milieu matters Safety, structure, low stimulation, consistent staff

Q1: A client says "I understand that the voices are very real to you, but I do not hear them" — is this therapeutic? Show answer Yes — it is honest (the nurse denies hearing the voices) while validating the client's experience as real to them. Q2: What should the nurse NEVER do when a client reports a hallucination? Show answer Never pretend to see or hear it (dishonest) and never argue that it isn't real (ineffective, damages trust). Q3: What is the difference between reality orientation and validation therapy? Sh

entries.h: Sleep Hygiene · NG-135 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Fundamentals: Rest & Sleep II

The Teaching Checklist — What To Actually Tell The Patient NG-135 Mental Health ADHD-friendly visual edition The practical companion to the biology. Every habit below exists to protect the light-melatonin-SCN loop taught on Sleep Circadian Rhythm ( NG-089 ) — this page is the actionable half: what to do at home, and what to do at the bedside in the hospital. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

☀️ Bright & active by day Sun in the morning sets the clock; save the dim, quiet room for night. ☕ Cut caffeine/nicotine 4-6h before bed Alcohol is NOT a sleep aid — skip the routine nightcap. 🛏️ Bed = sleep only No TV, phone, work, or reading in bed — read elsewhere if you can't sleep. 🚨 Hospital safety Never silence essential monitor/equipment alarms to "help" a patient sleep. 🌙
STEP 1 · THE 60-SECOND RECAP Every recommendation on this page is protecting the same light-melatonin loop — full mechanism on NG-089 .

entries.h: 🔁 Light & timing set the clock — habits either help or fight it
entries.t: The SCN uses light exposure to time melatonin release and body temperature. Bright light + activity by day, dim light + quiet by night is the whole strategy — every bullet below is one specific way to deliver that pattern consistently.

Circadian rhythm Light and timing help set the daily body clock. Sleep pressure The need for sleep builds during wakefulness. Restorative opportunity A consistent, suitable environment supports sleep. Schedule Use regular sleep and wake times and daytime activity. Environment Reduce noise and light; review evening caffeine and other stimulants. Assess disorders Snoring with breathing pauses, severe daytime sleepiness or persistent insomnia needs evaluation. 🔗 See NG-089 — Sleep Circadian Rhythm for the full SCN/mel
STEP 2 · WHAT TO TEACH A short, consistent list beats a long one nobody remembers — group it by when it happens in the day.

entries.h: ✅ Routine sleep schedule — the foundation habit
entries.t: 1 🛏️ Go to bed & wake up at the same time every day — including weekends 2 ☀️ Open blinds/curtains in the morning — bright light resets the clock 3 🏃 Be sunny, bright & active during the day — schedule activities/interventions in daylight hours 4 🌡️ Quiet, cool, dark room at night — lower the temperature, dim the lights 🧠 "Bright by day, dim by night." Consistency in timing matters as much as any single behavior — an irregular schedule fights the SCN even if every other habit is perfect.

entries.h: ❌ Avoid in the hours before bed
entries.t: 🍷 NO nightcap alcohol ≠ sleep aid ☕ NO caffeine coffee, tea, soda, chocolate 🚬 NO nicotine cigarettes, chew 🏋️ Strenuous exercise avoid late afternoon 🌶️ Spicy food before bed 🍔 Large meal/snack right before bed 🍞 Going to bed hungry either extreme disrupts sleep 📱 Non-sleep activities in bed TV, phone, work, reading Caffeine & nicotine — avoid 4-6 hours before bed ; alcohol is never a routine sleep aid despite the common "glass of wine at night." 🧠 "Bed is for sleep only." If reading helps you wind down, do it in
⏱️ Limit naps to 20 minutes, up to 2 times per day 🚫 No naps in the late afternoon/evening — eats into nighttime sleep drive 🏥
STEP 3 · NURSING PROCESS The same habits, translated into a unit — plus one safety rule that overrides all of them.

entries.h: 🚨 Hospital safety rules — the two you cannot compromise
entries.t: 🔔 NEVER turn off/disable essential equipment alarms at night to let a patient sleep — cardiac monitor, ventilator, and other patient-safety alarms stay on; that is a safety risk, not a comfort measure 💊 NEVER increase a client's sedation dose at night just to promote sleep — sedation is not the same as restorative sleep and adds respiratory/fall risk 🧠 Comfort measures are never a substitute for safety. If a stem offers "silence the alarms" or "increase the sedative" as ways to help a hospitalized client sleep, bot

entries.h: ✅ What actually helps in the hospital
entries.t: ☀️ Open blinds/curtains in the morning for sunlight 📅 Schedule interventions & activities during the day when possible 🌙 Dim the lights at night 🤫 Cluster care — group tasks to limit waking the client overnight 📋 Determine the client's usual bedtime and plan the routine around it 😷 CPAP for known sleep apnea, if ordered 🌿 OTC options — melatonin or chamomile for rest, when appropriate 💊 Prescription sleep medication — a last resort, not the first intervention

A Assess sleep pattern history, disorders, and life changes affecting sleep (e.g., anxiety, routine disruption) D Disturbed sleep pattern r/t anxiety or alteration in client routine P Client will sleep 8 hours nightly, lights out at 10:00 pm , in a quiet cool dark room away from the nurses' station at 68°F I Implement the daily-habit & hospital-safety interventions above E Evaluate — did the client sleep 8 hours, lights out at 10 pm as planned? 🧠 "ADPIE ends where it starts." The evaluation question is always a dir

Every intervention above is protecting the light → SCN → melatonin pathway. If a question asks why morning light or a dark bedroom matters, the mechanism — not just the checklist — is what's being tested. 🔗 See NG-089 — Sleep Circadian Rhythm for the SCN/melatonin mechanism, sleep-stage architecture, and circadian disorders (shift work, jet lag, delayed sleep phase) this checklist is built on. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD ☀️ Bright/active by day Dim/quiet/cool by night — same schedule daily ☕ 4-6 hour cutoff Caffeine & nicotine before bed; alcohol is never a sleep aid 🛏️ Bed = sleep only No screens/work/reading in bed — 20-min naps max, 2x/day 🚨 Hospital rule Never silence safety alarms or increase sedation just to promote sleep

Q1: What two things should a client avoid 4-6 hours before bed? Show answer Caffeine and nicotine — and alcohol should not be used routinely as a sleep aid at all. Q2: What is the single most important morning habit for circadian health? Show answer Opening the blinds/curtains for bright light exposure at a consistent wake time — it resets the SCN each day. Q3: What are the two hospital "never" actions for helping a client sleep? Show answer Never turn off/disable essential equipment alarms, and never increase seda

entries.h: Abuse & Neglect · NG-139 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Psychiatric Care Course

Recognition · Mandatory Reporting · Safety Planning NG-139 Mental Health ADHD-friendly visual edition Nurses are mandated reporters . This page covers recognition of physical, emotional, sexual, financial abuse and neglect across child, elder, and intimate-partner contexts, plus the objective documentation and safety-planning steps that follow — clinical and factual, not graphic . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🧩 5 forms Physical · emotional · sexual · financial · neglect. 🚪 IPV priority action Separate the partner — interview & examine privately . 📣 Mandated reporter Nurses must report suspected abuse — not optional. 📈 Highest danger Risk of harm rises when the victim moves toward independence/leaving. 🧩
STEP 1 · NAME THE TYPE Abuse is not only physical — and it happens across every age group in different patterns.

Possible indicators Injuries, history, behavior or unmet needs raise concern. Private assessment Use a safe, respectful approach and document objectively. Protection and reporting Follow the applicable legal and clinical pathway. Immediate safety Treat urgent injuries and assess current danger. Interview Use nonleading questions; do not promise secrecy that cannot be maintained. Documentation Record exact statements and observed findings according to policy. 🧠 "PESFN" — say it like "pieces-fin": P hysical · E motio

A form of abuse that happens when the caregiver fails to provide for the needs of the elderly client — either emotionally, physically, or socially . 🧠 Neglect is a failure to act , not a direct act — that's what separates it from active physical/emotional abuse in documentation.

entries.h: 💔 Intimate partner violence (IPV) — key word definition
entries.t: Intimate partner violence is domestic violence or abusive behavior inflicted by one partner against the other — physically, emotionally, verbally, sexually, or financially. Abusive partner traits: extreme jealousy & possessiveness Abuse gets more intense during pregnancy 🧠 Pregnancy is a documented high-risk window for IPV escalation — screen every pregnant client privately, every visit. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT THE PATTERN Signs cluster differently by population — know the elder-neglect picture and the IPV screening questions cold.

entries.h: 👵 Elder neglect — what the nurse observes
entries.t: 🧠 Assessment case: a 79-year-old weighs 93 lbs, wears old dirty clothes, and is admitted with pneumonia. The comment that suggests significant abuse risk : "Our family is poor, so my daughter gets my monthly retirement and Social Security checks." → financial exploitation as part of neglect .

entries.h: 🩹 Caregiver Role Strain (CRS) — a risk factor to assess, not blame
entries.t: Assess stressors & unmet needs of the caregiver Ask about the nature & requirements of providing daily care 🧠 Neglect isn't always malicious — an overwhelmed, unsupported caregiver is a known risk factor . Assessing CRS is prevention, not accusation.

PRIORITY Have the partner leave the room to speak with and examine the client in private . "Is anyone hurting you?" "When you and your spouse disagree, what happens?" "Has your spouse ever threatened you verbally or with violence?" 🧠 Bruises in various stages of healing on assessment = ask these three direct, private questions — never in front of the suspected abuser.

entries.h: ⚠️ Why victims stay — and when danger peaks
entries.t: Financial dependence Fear of harm (to self, children, pets) Child custody concerns Religious or cultural beliefs Abuse is expected to worsen when the victim moves toward independence from the abuser — leaving is statistically the most dangerous point in an abusive relationship. 🧠 Never judge "why don't they just leave." The nurse's job is safety planning for whenever the client is ready — not pressuring them to leave on the nurse's timeline. 🛡️
STEP 3 · REPORT, DOCUMENT, PLAN SAFETY Reporting is mandatory; documentation and safety planning are the nurse's core interventions.

entries.h: 📣 Mandatory reporting — a nurse's legal duty
entries.t: 1 🚨 Ensure immediate safety — treat injuries, separate client from suspected abuser for the interview 2 📞 Report per state law & facility policy — nurses are mandated reporters for suspected child abuse/neglect and elder abuse in every U.S. state; reporting is not optional and does not require the client's/family's consent 3 📝 Document objectively — direct quotes, measured/described findings, no personal conclusions 4 🧷 Preserve evidence if applicable per facility protocol 5 🏠 Safety-plan & connect to resources bef

Assure the victim they are not alone Preserve physical evidence , if applicable Convey concern & respect — nonjudgmental attitude Affirm the client did not deserve or cause the abuse Help identify triggers and destructive patterns; learn alternative responses (psychotherapy/talk therapy) Develop a safety plan — local shelter contact information 🧠 Priority action before discharge home: provide contact information for the local shelter.

Use the client's own words in direct quotes Describe findings objectively (size, location, color) — avoid concluding "abuse" in the chart; describe, don't diagnose intent Use a body map/diagram where available Note who was present during the exam and interview Avoid leading questions; ask open-ended questions in private 🧠 Objective ≠ vague. "3 cm bruise, left forearm, purple-yellow" is objective. "Client was clearly beaten" is not — that's a conclusion, not a finding.

A client experiencing IPV states: "I should try to identify issues that increased my partner's stress level." This statement needs correction — it reflects internalized responsibility for the abuser's behavior. Effective teaching redirects the client toward recognizing that the abuse is not their responsibility to prevent or manage , and toward safety planning instead. 🧠 A common NCLEX trap: a statement that sounds like insight ("I'll manage their stress") can actually indicate the client still blames themselves —

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧩 5 forms Physical · emotional · sexual · financial · neglect 🚪 IPV Interview privately, away from the partner 📣 Mandated reporter Suspicion is enough — report per policy/law 🏠 Before discharge Give local shelter contact info

Q1: A 79-year-old weighs 93 lbs, wears dirty clothes, and says a family member controls her retirement checks. What's the concern? Show answer Elder neglect with financial exploitation — a caregiver failing to meet physical/financial needs. Q2: A client has bruises in various stages of healing. What must the nurse ask? Show answer "Is anyone hurting you?" / "What happens when you and your spouse disagree?" / "Has your spouse ever threatened you verbally or with violence?" — asked in private. Q3: When is IPV danger

entries.h: Depression: Procedures (ECT/TMS) · NG-149 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Psychiatric Care

ECT · TMS · Vagus Nerve Stimulation — non-drug options for treatment-resistant depression NG-149 MENTAL HEALTH ADHD-friendly visual edition When medication and therapy alone haven't worked, or a client needs a fast, safe response (severe suicidality, catatonia, psychotic depression, pregnancy), the next step is a brain-stimulation procedure . ECT is the most tested — think of it as a controlled, monitored "reset" that induces a brief, therapeutic seizure. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

⚡ ECT = brief seizure Electrical stimulus induces a controlled, generalized seizure under anesthesia. 🍽️ NPO first No food/fluids 6–8 hr before + signed informed consent. 🧠 Memory loss Short-term confusion & memory loss after ECT is expected — and temporary. 🚫 No anticonvulsants They raise the seizure threshold and blunt the treatment — hold before ECT. 🧲

SIDE BY SIDE Two procedures for the same client. Almost every exam item turns on one of the four rows highlighted in red. ⚡ ECT Asleep. A seizure is induced on purpose under anesthesia. Memory loss expected. 🧲 TMS Awake. Magnetic pulses, no seizure intended — but a seizure is its rare serious adverse effect. 🚨 The trap “TMS causes no seizure” describes the mechanism . Asked for an adverse effect , the answer is seizure .

Feature ⚡ ECT 🧲 TMS What it does Electrical stimulus induces a brief generalized seizure Repeated magnetic pulses to a mood-regulation area (left prefrontal cortex) Anesthesia Yes — general anesthesia + muscle relaxant None. Client is awake and alert Seizure Induced — that is the treatment Not induced, but a rare, serious adverse effect Adverse effects Confusion + short-term memory loss (expected, temporary) · headache · muscle aches · nausea Scalp discomfort at the site · headache · lightheadedness · facial twitch

Both statements are true at once, and exams are built on the gap between them: ECT — a seizure is deliberately induced . It is the therapy. Roughly 30–60 seconds, under anesthesia with a muscle relaxant so the body stays still. TMS — no seizure is intended . Magnetic pulses only, client awake. But a seizure is TMS's rare and most serious adverse effect — which is why metal in the head and a seizure history matter so much. 🧠 Read the stem twice. “How does it work?” → TMS induces no seizure. “What adverse effect do y

entries.h: 🧲 Why metal is the TMS dealbreaker
entries.t: TMS is a magnet . A strong, rapidly changing magnetic field will heat or move ferromagnetic metal, so anything metal in or near the head rules it out: Aneurysm clips and coils Cochlear implants Deep-brain stimulators and other implanted electrodes Bullet fragments or shrapnel Dental fillings and braces are generally fine — they sit far enough from the coil. 🧠 Magnet = metal question. If an implant appears in a TMS stem, it is almost always the answer.

entries.h: ✅ What you teach, side by side
entries.t: Before ECT: nothing to eat or drink for 6–8 hours, you will be asleep, you will be confused for a while afterward and that is expected, and you may not drive for the whole course. Before TMS: you stay awake, it takes 20–40 minutes, you will hear loud clicking so you will wear earplugs, your scalp may feel sore where the coil sits, and you can drive yourself home . 🧠 The single teaching difference clients ask about first: ECT costs you the day. TMS costs you the hour.

ECT seizes on purpose. TMS pulses — and seizes by accident. ECT = A nesthesia · S eizure · M emory loss TMS = A wake · M agnet · M etal is the contraindication 🧠 If the stem mentions NPO, consent, or a crash cart it is ECT. If it mentions an office visit, earplugs, or driving home it is TMS. 📋
STEP 1 · PREP & SCREEN Same prep as any procedure under brief general anesthesia — plus a few psych-specific holds.

entries.h: 🚨 Screen the whole history — report to the HCP
entries.t: ECT briefly raises intracranial pressure and stresses the cardiovascular system during the seizure, so the biggest contraindication-style concerns are: 🧠 Cerebral neoplasm / space-occupying brain lesion — raised ICP risk ❤️ Recent myocardial infarction — cardiac stress risk 👁️ Recent stroke, retinal issues, or other high anesthesia risk — verify per facility screening 🧠 Same red flags as any general anesthesia case — a fresh MI or a brain lesion means the heart or the skull can't safely tolerate the stress of a sei

✅ Signed informed consent ✅ NPO 6–8 hours before the procedure ✅ Have the client void immediately before ✅ Remove dentures and contact lenses ✅ Baseline vital signs 🧠 Read this list and you're really reading a pre-op checklist — ECT is done under brief general anesthesia, so treat it like surgery prep.

Do not give anticonvulsant medications — e.g. valproic acid , carbamazepine — before ECT. These drugs work by raising the seizure threshold , which fights the entire point of the treatment: ECT needs a seizure to be therapeutic. 🧠 Anticonvulsant = anti-seizure = anti-ECT. If the goal is to trigger a seizure, don't give the drug whose job is to prevent one.

A client with depression often has poor nutritional intake going into the procedure — assess and correct this beforehand where possible: offer high-calorie fluids/snacks earlier in the day, and let the client help select menu items when eating is allowed. 🧠 Depression's appetite loss doesn't pause for procedure day — keep nutrition on the plan right up to the NPO window. ⚡
STEP 2 · THE PROCEDURE A brief, monitored, medically induced seizure — not the uncontrolled event people picture.

Specialist assessment Indication, medical factors and consent guide selection. Treatment session ECT or other neuromodulation uses a specific protocol. Recovery and follow-up Monitor benefit, adverse effects and ongoing needs. ECT A controlled seizure is induced under anesthesia with monitoring. Before treatment Follow fasting, medication, consent and anesthesia instructions. After treatment Assess airway, vital signs, orientation and memory-related concerns. ECT induces electrical activity across the scalp to trig

entries.h: 🧰 Equipment that must be at bedside
entries.t: ❤️ Cardiac monitor 🛒 Crash cart 🫁 Oxygen 🧹 Suction 🧠 “C-C-O-S” — Cardiac monitor · Crash cart · Oxygen · Suction. If it's on a code cart, it needs to be in the ECT room.

ECT is performed by a team including anesthesia provider + psychiatrist , typically in a monitored procedural setting (often same-day/outpatient once stable). The nurse's role during the procedure is continuous monitoring and immediate post-ictal recovery care. 🧠 Same team structure as any brief anesthesia procedure — anesthesia manages sedation, psychiatry manages the treatment itself.
STEP 3 · RECOVER & TEACH Expect brief confusion and short-term memory loss — reassure, reorient, and protect until it clears.

entries.h: 🧠 Expected side effect: temporary confusion & short-term memory loss
entries.t: The most important nursing action when a client wakes up confused with memory gaps is to remind the client that the memory loss is temporary — reorient to person/place/time, stay calm and simple, and reassess after the full course. 🧠 Expected ≠ ignored. Confusion/memory loss is a known, temporary effect — but the nurse still reorients every time and documents severity.

entries.h: 🚗 Teaching: no driving during the course
entries.t: No driving for the duration of the ECT treatment course — confusion/memory effects make it unsafe Arrange transportation to and from every session Avoid major decisions or signing important documents until memory clears 🧠 If confusion is expected after the treatment, driving is off the table for the whole course — not just treatment day.

Recovery-room style monitoring: vitals, airway, LOC until fully awake Reorient frequently — person, place, time Reassess mood & suicidal ideation once alert — ECT does not remove the need for ongoing safety checks Offer food/fluids once fully awake and gag reflex intact 🧠 Waking up from ECT is a lot like waking up from any anesthesia — airway, orientation, and safety come first, memory reassurance comes right after.

entries.h: 🧲 Non-drug alternatives: TMS & Vagus Nerve Stimulation
entries.t: Feature ⚡ ECT 🧲 TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) Anesthesia Yes — general anesthesia + muscle relaxant No anesthesia needed Mechanism Electrical stimulus induces a generalized seizure Repeated magnetic pulses stimulate a targeted mood-regulation area of the brain — no seizure induced (though a seizure is its rare adverse effect — see ECT vs TMS ) Memory effects Temporary short-term memory loss/confusion is expected Minimal to no memory effects Setting Monitored procedural/OR-style setting Outpatient office v

SAY IT OUT LOUD 📋 Before Consent + NPO 6–8h + hold anticonvulsants + remove dentures/contacts 🧰 Equipment Cardiac monitor · crash cart · oxygen · suction, every time 🧠 After Confusion & short-term memory loss — remind: it's temporary 🚗 Teach No driving for the whole treatment course

Q1: A client with severe depression and poor nutritional intake is scheduled for ECT. Which orders would the nurse expect (select all that apply)? Show answer NPO 6–8 hours before the procedure, signed informed consent, remove dentures/contacts, screen for recent MI or cerebral neoplasm and report to the HCP, hold anticonvulsant medications (e.g. valproic acid, carbamazepine). Q2: A client has temporary confusion and memory loss after ECT. What is the most important nursing action? Show answer Remind the client tha

Pharmacology — Treatment Approach & Adherence — Part 3 of a 4-page series NG-165 Mental Health Series 3 of 4 · schizophrenia-specific drug approach 📍 SCOPE OF THIS PAGE: schizophrenia treatment strategy — why adherence fails, insight/anosognosia, and long-acting injectables. For the full antipsychotic drug reference (typical vs. atypical, mechanism, EPS, NMS, agranulocytosis) go to NG-235 . Medication only works if it's taken. This page is about why clients with schizophrenia stop taking antipsychotics and what the

🧠 Anosognosia Not "denial" — a neurological inability to recognize one's own illness. The #1 adherence barrier. 🚨 NMS = medical emergency Rigidity + hyperpyrexia + altered mental status + autonomic instability → hold drug, notify HCP now. 💉 LAIs solve the "forgot the pill" problem Long-acting injectables remove the daily-decision barrier to adherence. 🧪 Clozapine = weekly labs ANC/CBC monitoring is mandatory — priority to protect against agranulocytosis. 🎯
STEP 1 · THE STRATEGY Medication controls symptoms — it does not cure schizophrenia. The plan is lifelong management, not a short course.

entries.h: 🎯 The 3-part non-drug foundation every regimen sits on

entries.t: Receptor effects Dopamine and other signaling pathways are affected. Symptom benefit Psychotic symptoms may improve. System-wide effects Movement, metabolic and autonomic effects require monitoring. Movement effects Dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism and tardive dyskinesia need recognition. Metabolic effects Track weight, glucose and lipids according to the medication plan. Emergency signs Fever, rigidity, altered mental status and autonomic instability may indicate neuroleptic malignant syndrome. 1 🏠 Safe, structur

entries.h: 💊 What antipsychotics are FOR in schizophrenia
entries.t: Primarily reduce positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, disorganized thinking) by blocking excess dopamine in the mesolimbic pathway (mechanism detail on NG-049 & NG-235 ). Negative and cognitive symptoms respond far less — they need psychosocial rehab, social skills training, and sustained therapeutic engagement alongside medication. 🧠 A client whose hallucinations stopped but who is still flat, avolitional, and isolated is not "treatment failure" — it means the drug did its job on the pathway it can reach.

entries.h: 🚫 Delusions & hallucinations — the caution rules again
entries.t: Never label the voices as "not real" or argue with the delusion Always present reality gently, without debate 🧠 Full scripted responses and the reasoning behind them live on NG-128 — this page only flags that the rule applies during medication teaching conversations too. 🚧
STEP 2 · WHY CLIENTS STOP TAKING MEDS Nonadherence is the single biggest driver of relapse back into the active phase ( NG-049 ) — and it's rarely about "not caring."

Because the same disease process that causes positive/negative/cognitive symptoms ( NG-049 ) can also impair the brain's ability to recognize it has an illness, many clients genuinely believe nothing is wrong — this drives medication refusal more than any other single factor. 🧠 An-osos-GNOSIA = "no knowledge" (a- without, gnosis- knowledge). Approach with patience and repetition, not confrontation — arguing with impaired insight works about as well as arguing with a delusion.

Distressing side effects — EPS, sedation, weight gain (full list on NG-235 ) make clients stop on their own Cognitive symptoms — trouble remembering to take a daily pill Cost & access — some agents and required lab monitoring are expensive Stigma — fear of being seen taking psychiatric medication Substance use — co-occurring use disorders interfere with routines 🧠 A good adherence assessment asks about all five , not just "did you take your pills."

entries.h: 📉 The relapse cascade — why adherence is the priority intervention
entries.t: 💊 Medication stopped ▼ 🧠 Dopamine dysregulation returns unchecked ▼ 🔁 Relapse into the ACTIVE phase ( NG-049 ) 🧠 Every barrier above is really a fork in this cascade — the earlier you intervene, the more relapses you prevent. 💉
STEP 3 · SOLVING THE DAILY-PILL PROBLEM When a client understands the plan but the barrier is remembering or wanting to take a pill every day, the fix is architectural, not motivational.

entries.h: 💉 What a long-acting injectable (LAI) antipsychotic actually solves
entries.t: 🧠 LAIs don't fix anosognosia — the client still has to agree to come in for the injection. What they fix is forgetting and daily ambivalence . They are one tool among several, not a cure for lack of insight.

entries.h: ✅ Who is a good LAI candidate
entries.t: Client tolerates the oral form of that same drug well (a trial oral dose usually precedes the first injection) History of relapse specifically tied to missed oral doses Prefers less frequent dosing / values not having a daily pill routine 🧠 Injectables still carry the same warnings and adverse effect profile as the oral version of that drug — check NG-235 for the specific agent's side-effect and EPS profile.

Keep every scheduled injection appointment — missing the window lets drug levels fall Report injection-site reactions (pain, induration, redness) Continue attending follow-up and monitoring appointments — an LAI does not remove the need for ongoing psychiatric care 🧠 "Set it and forget it" ≠ "never follow up." The injection schedule is set, but monitoring is not optional. 🩺
STEP 4 · THE TWO EMERGENCIES YOU MUST CATCH Full mechanism and drug-by-drug detail for both of these lives on NG-235 — this is the "don't miss it" summary.

Key signs: fever/hyperpyrexia , muscle rigidity , altered mental status , and autonomic instability (diaphoresis, unstable BP, tachycardia). Priority action: 1. Hold the antipsychotic 2. Assess the client 3. Notify the HCP immediately. 🧠 Full pathophysiology and the complete drug list live on NG-235 — remember it here as "the emergency that can happen on any antipsychotic, at any point in treatment."

Clozapine requires mandatory, regular monitoring of the complete blood count (CBC) and absolute neutrophil count (ANC) due to agranulocytosis risk. 🧠 Priority to monitor = ANC/CBC. Report sore throat, fever, or flu-like symptoms immediately — full mechanism and reporting thresholds are on NG-235 .

entries.h: 🗺️ Where the rest of this topic lives — the 4-page series
entries.t: NG-049 — Signs & Symptoms Definitions used here: positive/negative/cognitive symptoms, phases of illness. NG-128 — Communication Full say/don't say scripts for delusions & hallucinations, the milieu. NG-165 — You are here Pharmacology: treatment approach, adherence barriers, anosognosia, LAIs. NG-235 — Antipsychotics (drug reference) Typical vs. atypical, mechanism, EPS, NMS detail, agranulocytosis, QT prolongation. 🧠 If the question is "why won't the client take their meds" or "what's an LAI," you're on the right

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧠 Anosognosia ≠ denial Neurological, not a choice — the #1 barrier to adherence 🚨 NMS Fever + rigidity + altered mental status + autonomic instability → hold, assess, notify HCP 💉 LAIs Remove the daily-pill decision, not a cure for lack of insight 🧪 Clozapine Mandatory ANC/CBC monitoring — agranulocytosis risk

Q1: A client insists nothing is wrong with them despite an active schizophrenia diagnosis. Is this denial or anosognosia — and does it matter? Show answer Likely anosognosia — a neurological inability to recognize the illness, not a conscious choice. It matters because arguing or confronting doesn't work; patience and repeated gentle reality-based conversation does. Q2: What problem does a long-acting injectable antipsychotic solve — and what does it NOT solve? Show answer It removes the daily pill-taking decision/

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy — first-line talk therapy NG-221 MENTAL HEALTH ADHD-friendly visual edition CBT is talk therapy that reframes thinking to change how a client feels and behaves. It's first-line treatment for anxiety, phobias, PTSD, OCD, depression, and eating disorders — this page's cognitive triangle and distortion list is the toolkit those disease-specific pages point back to. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🔺 Thoughts → Feelings → Behaviors Change the thought, and the feeling & behavior downstream change too. 🌀 Distortions = broken thinking patterns Catastrophizing, all-or-nothing, overgeneralization — name the distortion to fix it. 🪜 Systematic desensitization Gradual, ranked exposure to the feared thing — the phobia answer. ⭐ First-line for many disorders Phobias, PTSD, OCD, depression, eating disorders all start here. 🧠
STEP 1 · THE MECHANISM One triangle explains why CBT works — thoughts drive feelings, feelings drive behavior, and behavior reinforces the original thought.

entries.h: 🔺 Thoughts ↔ Feelings ↔ Behaviors — a closed loop
entries.t: EXAM TIP CBT works by interrupting the loop at the thought — because thoughts are the easiest of the three to catch and challenge in the moment.

Situation An event is interpreted through thoughts and context. Emotional and physical response Feelings, bodily reactions and behavior follow. Coping choice Skills and support can change the next response. CBT Examines links between thoughts, emotions and behavior and practices alternative responses. Crisis care Prioritize immediate safety, reduce overwhelm and identify practical supports. Follow-up Make a concrete plan and review what helped. 🧠 "Catch it, check it, change it." CBT teaches clients to catch the aut

A common type of psychotherapy (talk therapy) that helps clients reframe thought processes to slowly cope with stress & anxiety. PTSD & OCD Eating disorders — anorexia & bulimia Depressive disorders Phobias & panic disorder 🧠 CBT = the default first answer. When an NCLEX question asks "what non-drug therapy," CBT is very often the correct first-line choice.

This mechanism is assumed knowledge on the Phobias , PTSD & Acute Stress Disorder , and Depression pages in this batch — they will say "treat with CBT" without re-explaining it. 🧠 Know this triangle cold — it's the shared foundation under several other disease pages. 🌀
STEP 2 · NAME THE BROKEN THOUGHT These are the specific "thought errors" CBT targets — spotting the pattern is half the treatment.

Distortion Example Catastrophizing ⚡ "If I fail this quiz, I'll fail nursing school and never get a job." All-or-nothing / black-and-white thinking ⚪⚫ "If I'm not perfect at this, I'm a total failure." Overgeneralization 🔁 "I got one bad grade — I'm always going to be bad at this." Mind reading 🔮 "My coworker didn't say hi — she must hate me." Emotional reasoning 💭 "I feel anxious about the flight, so it must actually be dangerous." Personalization 🎯 "My patient's blood sugar dropped — that's totaly my fault." Labe

Examining negative automatic thoughts and consciously restating them in a more balanced, positive way. Nurse teaches reframing to counteract depression. Effective teaching indicator: client says "I have many friends who love me and care for me." 🧠 Reframe = same facts, new lens. The event doesn't change — the interpretation does.

Gradual, ranked exposure to a feared object or situation, paired with relaxation, until anxiety fades. Client: "I only travel by train — I'm terrified of flying." → Best intervention: systematic desensitization . 🧠 Desensitization = a fear ladder , climbed one safe rung at a time, never jumping to the top. 🛠️
STEP 3 · WHAT SESSIONS LOOK LIKE Five building blocks, used together across a course of treatment.

1 Learn about the disorder — psychoeducation on symptoms & triggers 2 Exposure — systematic desensitization to feared situations/events (behavioral strategy) 3 Self-observation & monitoring — track thoughts, moods, triggers 4 Relaxation techniques — deep breathing, guided imagery, biofeedback 5 New coping skills & cognitive restructuring — reframe distorted thoughts 🧠 "LEARN, EXPOSE, OBSERVE, RELAX, REFRAME." Say it as a checklist for any CBT-based question — most answer choices map onto one of these five.

A mind-body intervention: the client concentrates on mental images to reduce stress and anxiety and improve concentration. Advantages: relaxation, inner peace, improved concentration. Focuses on descriptive mental pictures. 🧠 Guided imagery = a mental vacation the client controls.

Like guided imagery, but with machines/monitors that give real-time feedback (heart rate, muscle tension) to help the client learn to control the stress response — teaching the body to respond differently to stress. 🧠 Biofeedback = guided imagery + a screen. The device turns an invisible stress response into something the client can actually watch and change.

entries.h: 👥 Milieu & group therapy — supporting structures around CBT
entries.t: Therapeutic milieu: a safe, structured social & physical environment — the goal of every psych/behavioral health unit. Group therapy goal: reduce isolation in a structured, controlled environment; primary focus is personal feelings that affect behavior. Silent member → encourage interaction, or divide into pairs. Aggressive/interrupting member → "You seem very upset" — let the group handle it first. For personality disorders specifically, milieu's primary goal is managing the effect of the behavior on the entire gr

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🔺 Thought → Feeling → Behavior Interrupt the thought to change the loop. 🌀 Name the distortion Catastrophizing, all-or-nothing, mind reading, personalization, labeling. 🪜 Fear = desensitize gradually Systematic desensitization, ranked exposure. 🛠️ 5 strategies Learn, expose, observe, relax, reframe.

Q1: What are the three points of the cognitive triangle? Show answer Thoughts, feelings, and behaviors — each influences the other two, forming a loop. Q2: A client says "I made one mistake at work, so I'm a complete failure." Which cognitive distortion is this? Show answer All-or-nothing (black-and-white) thinking, with elements of labeling. Q3: A client is terrified of flying and only travels by train. Best CBT-based intervention? Show answer Systematic desensitization — gradual, ranked exposure paired with relax

entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Psychiatric Care Course

Types of Loss · Complicated Grief · End-of-Life Decisions NG-222 Mental Health ADHD-friendly visual edition Not every loss looks the same, and not every grief resolves normally. This page maps what kind of loss a client is facing, when grief has become unhealthy , and the spectrum of end-of-life decisions nurses must understand and document objectively — factually, without personal judgment. For the full DABDA / Bowlby grief-stage content and defense mechanisms, see NG-065 (Death & Dying) — not repeated here. 📄 Sim

📦 4 sources of loss Aspect of self · external object · environment · loved one. 🔎 Actual vs perceived vs anticipatory Verifiable by others · felt only by the client · grieved before it happens. 🌀 Complicated grief = >6 months + inability to perform daily activities. ⚖️ Passive ≠ active Withdrawing/withholding care (DNR) is legally & ethically distinct from active euthanasia. 📦
STEP 1 · NAME WHAT WAS LOST "Loss" isn't only death — sorting the source and the verifiability of a loss shapes how the nurse responds.

Loss or anticipated loss Emotional and practical needs change. Individual response Feelings and coping vary over time. Supportive care Presence, comfort and choice guide the response. Grief There is no required linear sequence of stages. Communication Listen without forcing reassurance or a timeline for recovery. End-of-life priorities Relieve symptoms, clarify goals and support the person and family. 🧠 "SEEL" — S elf-aspect · E xternal object · E nvironment · L oved one. Ask "what category did this client just los

entries.h: 🔎 Actual, Perceived & Anticipatory loss — is it verifiable, and has it happened yet?
entries.t: Type Definition Example Actual loss Can be recognized / verified by others Death, divorce Perceived loss Experienced by the person but cannot be verified by others Loss of freedom when becoming a stay-at-home parent; loss of a valued personal item; loss of financial independence Anticipatory loss Grief experienced before the loss has actually occurred A family member is actively dying but has not yet passed 🧠 Perceived loss is real grief even though no one else can see it. A classic NCLEX trap is to under-validate

entries.h: ⏳ Bonus pair: Situational vs. Maturational loss
entries.t: Situational loss — unexpected, caused by an external event (e.g., a new cancer diagnosis in a family member) Maturational loss — expected with normal life transitions (e.g., graduating high school and leaving friends behind) 🧠 Situational = sudden/unplanned. Maturational = scheduled by life stage. Both are still legitimate grief, even though maturational loss is "supposed to happen."

Kübler-Ross's 5 stages (DABDA), Bowlby's 4 stages, defense mechanisms (displacement, projection, identification, sublimation, etc.), and adult/pediatric grief-support interventions are covered in full depth on the paired page. → Open NG-065: Death & Dying (grief stages + defense mechanisms) 🌀
STEP 2 · WHEN GRIEF STOPS BEING HEALTHY Normal grief softens with time. Watch for grief that gets stuck, gets buried, or gets dangerous.

entries.h: 📉 Normal grief tapers — unhealthy grief subtypes don't
entries.t: 🧠 Complicated grief needs a duration AND a functional criterion: lasts more than 6 months and leaves the person unable to perform daily activities. Sadness alone at 7 months is not automatically "complicated."

Subtype What it looks like Unresolved Extended in length & severity — same stages, but grieved far longer than expected Inhibited Normal stages of grieving are suppressed rather than experienced Exaggerated Uses dangerous activities (e.g., substance use, self-harm) to lessen the pain of grieving Complicated Lasts >6 months and causes inability to perform daily activities 🧠 "UIEC" — U nresolved lasts too long · I nhibited is bottled up · E xaggerated turns dangerous · C omplicated disables daily life.

Fails to grieve at all Refuses to participate in normal cultural/memorial activities Recurrently symptomatic on the anniversary of the loss or on holidays Persistent guilt Continued searching for the lost person Small, unrelated events trigger grief symptoms Unable to discuss the loss without crying/becoming tearful, even long after Relationships with friends and family deteriorate 🧠 Not one sign alone — it's the pattern plus duration that flags complicated grief for referral (e.g., grief counseling, psychiatric ev

STEP 3 · KNOW THE VOCABULARY, STAY OBJECTIVE This is ethics/policy content — legality varies by state and country. The nurse's job is to know the definitions, follow facility policy, and document objectively without personal judgment.

entries.h: ⚖️ The end-of-life decision spectrum — from direct action to non-intervention
entries.t: 🧠 Direction matters, not just outcome. Active euthanasia and assisted death cause death directly; passive euthanasia and DNR allow death by not intervening or by stopping extraordinary measures. Legality of the first two varies widely by jurisdiction — always defer to current law and facility policy, not personal opinion.

Active euthanasia — actions that bring about the client's death directly, with or without the client's consent Physician-assisted death (assisted suicide) — giving the client the means to end their life if they request it; the client, not the clinician, performs the final act Passive euthanasia — withholding life-sustaining therapy or withdrawing extraordinary means of life support (e.g., removing a feeding tube or ventilator, allowing the client to die without intervention) DNR / no-code status — an order specifyi

entries.h: 🩺 The nurse's role — stay factual, stay neutral
entries.t: Know your facility's policy and your state's law before discussing any of these terms with a client/family Clarify code status and advance directives on admission; confirm the client (or their designated surrogate) actively participated in the decision Provide factual information within your scope; refer ethics/legal/spiritual-care questions to the appropriate resource Document objectively — what was said and done, not personal opinion Support the client's and family's decision without imposing personal values (non

Grief-stage recognition (DABDA, Bowlby), defense mechanisms, and adult/pediatric grief-support interventions are covered in depth on the paired page — use it alongside this one rather than duplicating that content here. → Open NG-065: Death & Dying ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 📦 4 sources of loss Self · object · environment · loved one 🔎 Actual / perceived / anticipatory Verifiable · felt-only · before it happens 🌀 Complicated grief >6 months + can't function daily ⚖️ DNR ≠ do not treat Comfort/symptom care continues; only resuscitation is withheld

Show answer Anticipatory loss — grief experienced before the loss has actually occurred. Q2: A client says becoming a stay-at-home parent cost them their independence, but no one else seems to notice or validate it. What type of loss is this? Phases of Crisis · De-escalation · Restraints & Seclusion NG-228 Mental Health ADHD-friendly visual edition A crisis moves through predictable phases — recognizing which phase a client is in tells you whether to talk, redirect, or physically intervene. The core rule: always use the least restrictive intervention that keeps everyone safe , and escalate toward restraints/seclusion only when verbal and environmental measures fail. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🌡️ 4 phases Trigger → Escalation → Crisis → Post-crisis disorganization/depression. 🎯 First move Eliminate the trigger using nursing measures before anything else. 🪜 Least restrictive first Verbal de-escalation → meds → seclusion → restraints, in that order. 📝 Restraints clock HCP assess within 1 hr · document q 15 min · renew q 4 hr (adult). 🌡️
STEP 1 · WHERE ARE THEY IN THE CRISIS A crisis is not a single event — it's a rising and falling curve, and each phase calls for a different response.

Situation An event is interpreted through thoughts and context. Emotional and physical response Feelings, bodily reactions and behavior follow. Coping choice Skills and support can change the next response. CBT Examines links between thoughts, emotions and behavior and practices alternative responses. Crisis care Prioritize immediate safety, reduce overwhelm and identify practical supports. Follow-up Make a concrete plan and review what helped. 🧠 "TECP" — T rigger · E scalation · C risis · P ost-crisis. A client sa

A client becomes agitated and threatens to punch another client. Priority action: Eliminate the trigger using nursing measures and interventions 🧠 Stopping the trigger stops the climb up the curve — act at phase 1–2, before the crisis peak, whenever possible.

entries.h: 🔎 Determine the true source of anger
entries.t: A client is yelling and screaming at staff. Action to take: Determine the true source of the client's anger 🧠 The visible target (a staff member, a roommate) is often not the real trigger — assess before assuming. 🗣️
STEP 2 · CALM COMMUNICATION & SAFE APPROACH Words and environment first — most crises never need to reach restraints.

1 💬 Explain all activities of care clearly & calmly 2 🎯 Eliminate the trigger 3 🔇 Low-stimulation environment — NOT near the nurses' station 4 🔎 Determine the source of the anger 5 🤲 Acknowledge the client's emotions 🧠 Sample scripting: "I'm Lily and I'm here to help" (identify yourself, calm tone) → "I see you are upset" (acknowledge the emotion, don't argue with it).

entries.h: 🪑 First action when a client throws a chair
entries.t: A client becomes angry and throws a chair in the dayroom. First intervention: Acknowledge the client's emotions 🧠 Validate before you redirect — arguing or issuing commands first tends to escalate further.

A client with a history of poor impulse control bursts into a verbal tirade in the dayroom. Priority action: Remove other clients from the day room 🧠 Milieu safety first — protect bystanders before continuing to work with the escalated client.

entries.h: 🛡️ Personal safety when approaching an angry client
entries.t: 🧠 4 safety rules: have other staff as backup · stand far enough away to avoid injury · identify yourself & remain calm · give simple directions in a calming voice. Never let yourself be positioned between the client and the exit. 🔒
STEP 3 · LEAST RESTRICTIVE → MOST RESTRICTIVE Medication and seclusion come before restraints — and restraints carry strict legal timelines once used.

🗣️ Verbal de-escalation & environmental changes ▼ 💊 PRN medication (anxiolytic/antipsychotic) ▼ 🚪 Seclusion (alone in a safe room) ▼ ⛓️ Physical restraints — last resort 🧠 Always try the least restrictive option that keeps the client and others safe before moving to the next step. Restraints/seclusion require a provider's order — they are never a first response or a punishment.

Class Example drug (brand) Anxiolytic — benzodiazepine "-pam" / "-lam" Lorazepam (Ativan) Typical antipsychotic Haloperidol (Haldol) Atypical antipsychotic Ziprasidone (Geodon) For a client displaying violent behavior, the provider may prescribe lorazepam, haloperidol, and/or ziprasidone — select-all-that-apply pattern. 🧠 "-pam/-lam" = benzo family (lorazepam, diazepam) — fast-acting anxiolytic for acute agitation, distinct from the antipsychotics used for the same scenario.

1 📄 Get a provider's order for restraints — renewed every 4 hours for adults 2 🩺 Client must be assessed by the HCP within 1 hour of the order 3 📝 Document every 15 minutes 4 🤲 Monitor & meet physical needs continuously 🧠 Within the first hour after restraints + seclusion are applied , the nurse must: meet the client's physical needs, obtain a prescription for the restraints, and objectively document the client's behavior.

When intervening with a violent client, the nurse should: identify themselves to the client and remain calm. When a client threatens to harm a staff member, the appropriate intervention is: address the patient with simple directions and a calming voice. 🧠 Never argue, raise your voice to match theirs, or make sudden movements — calm, simple, predictable communication is itself a de-escalation tool. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🌡️ 4 phases Trigger → Escalation → Crisis → Post-crisis 🎯 First move Eliminate the trigger 🪜 Least restrictive first Verbal → meds → seclusion → restraints ⏱️ Restraints HCP assess in 1 hr · document q15min · renew q4h adult

Q1: A client says, "I feel like I can barely get out of bed in the morning" the day after an outburst. Which crisis phase? Show answer Post-crisis disorganization & depression (phase 4). Q2: A client threatens to punch another client. What is the nurse's priority action? Show answer Eliminate the trigger using nursing measures and interventions. Q3: How often must a restrained adult client be reassessed by the HCP, and how often must the nurse document? Show answer HCP assessment within 1 hour of the order, renewed
