entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Psychopharmacology Course

Stimulants & Non-Stimulants for ADHD NG-234 Mental Health ADHD-friendly visual edition Two families, one goal — boost dopamine & norepinephrine signaling in the prefrontal circuit described on the ADD & ADHD page ( NG-093 ) . Stimulants work fast and are first-line; non-stimulants are the option when stimulants aren't tolerated, are contraindicated, or carry abuse risk. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

💊 First-line = stimulants Methylphenidate & amphetamine salts — Schedule II controlled substances. ❤️ Screen the heart FIRST Cardiac history, family history of sudden death, baseline VS before starting. 📏 Track growth Height & weight trends every visit — appetite suppression can slow growth. 🌙 No evening dosing Give doses early in the day — late dosing → insomnia. 💊
STEP 1 · MECHANISM Both drug families raise dopamine & norepinephrine in the synapse — they just get there differently.

entries.h: ⚡ Stimulants — flood the synapse with dopamine & norepinephrine
entries.t: MOA Methylphenidate and amphetamine salts block reuptake and increase release of dopamine & norepinephrine at the synapse — the opposite problem from the low-dopamine circuit on the ADHD page, corrected chemically.

Neurodevelopmental pattern Attention and/or activity regulation is affected. Functional difficulty Symptoms impair life across relevant settings. Individualized support Behavioral, educational and medication strategies can help. Assess Sleep, learning, anxiety and other contributors or coexisting conditions. Medication Monitor target symptoms, sleep, appetite, growth when relevant, pulse and pressure. Teaching Use routines, short instructions, positive feedback and appropriate accommodations. Drug Brand Class Methy

entries.h: 🧭 Non-stimulants — a different route to the same circuit
entries.t: Atomoxetine (Strattera) — selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (blocks NE reuptake specifically, not dopamine directly) Guanfacine ER (Intuniv) & Clonidine ER (Kapvay) — central alpha-2 agonists that improve prefrontal signaling and calm hyperactivity/impulsivity 🧠 Non-stimulants take longer to reach full effect (days–weeks) but carry no abuse potential and are not controlled substances — the trade-off for a slower onset.

History of substance use disorder in the child/family Cardiac contraindication to stimulants Significant anxiety — stimulants can worsen anxiety; alpha-2 agonists can help both Prefer to avoid controlled-substance prescribing/storage issues ⚠️
STEP 2 · PRIORITY MONITORING Screen the heart before the first dose, then track growth and vitals at every visit after.

entries.h: 🚨 Cardiac screening — BEFORE starting a stimulant
entries.t: 🧠 "Heart first, pill second." The exam trap is jumping straight to prescribing — the priority assessment is always the cardiac screen before therapy starts.
Appetite suppression from stimulants can slow growth velocity. Monitor and report height/weight trends with the HCP at each visit — a crossing percentile line is the flag, not a single low number.

entries.h: ⚠️ Expected side effects to teach families
entries.t: 🍽️ Loss of appetite & weight loss 😴 Loss of sleep / insomnia 🌀 Restlessness 💓 Increased HR & BP 🧠 "WAR" — W eight/appetite loss · A ppetite down · R estlessness + racing heart. Stimulant side effects mirror the drug's own name.

Methylphenidate and amphetamine salts are Schedule II controlled substances — high abuse/diversion potential, no automatic refills, prescriptions typically limited to a set supply and cannot be called in. Drug holiday: a planned, HCP-directed medication-free period (e.g., weekends, school breaks, summer) sometimes used to let appetite/growth catch up and to reassess whether continued therapy is still needed. Practice varies by provider and patient — always an HCP decision, never a parent-initiated stop. 🧠 Never abr
STEP 3 · PATIENT & FAMILY EDUCATION Timing prevents the worst side effect, and knowing the non-stimulant alternatives prevents an exam trap.
🧠 A late dose = a wired brain at bedtime. Schedule the last daily dose early enough that stimulant effects wear off well before bedtime.

entries.h: ✅ What to teach at every visit
entries.t: 📈 Track appetite & weight — report a declining growth curve 💤 Report new or worsening insomnia ❤️ Report chest pain, palpitations, or fainting immediately 📚 Watch for improvement in school performance — expected therapeutic response 🔒 Store securely — Schedule II, diversion risk in the household

entries.h: 🧭 Stimulant vs. non-stimulant — tell them apart
entries.t: Feature Stimulants Non-Stimulants Examples Methylphenidate, amphetamine salts, dextroamphetamine Atomoxetine, guanfacine ER, clonidine ER Onset Fast — hours Slow — days to weeks for full effect Controlled substance Yes — Schedule II No Key risks Appetite/growth suppression, insomnia, ↑HR/BP Sedation, hypotension; alpha-2 agonists → rebound HTN if stopped abruptly 🧠 "Stim = Schedule II, Non-stim = no schedule." If a stem mentions abuse potential, refill restrictions, or diversion risk, the drug is a stimulant. If it

entries.h: 🔗 Clonidine & guanfacine — same drug class, more than one job
entries.t: Clonidine and guanfacine are central alpha-2 agonists . In ADHD, extended-release forms calm the hyperactive-impulsive circuit. But clonidine specifically shows up on other pages of this course too — same mechanism, different indication each time : 🔗 See the Cardiovascular batch ( NG-110 ) for clonidine's use in hypertension management, and the Pharmacology batch ( NG-243 ) for its broader alpha-2 agonist profile — including use in opioid/alcohol withdrawal symptom control. Same drug, three different course units.

SAY IT OUT LOUD 💊 First-line Stimulants — methylphenidate & amphetamine salts, Schedule II ❤️ Screen first Cardiac history + baseline VS before the first dose 📏 Track Height/weight trend every visit — growth suppression risk 🧭 Alternative Atomoxetine, guanfacine/clonidine ER — non-stimulant, no abuse risk

Q1: What must be assessed before starting a stimulant for ADHD? Show answer Cardiac history — personal and family history of sudden cardiac death/arrhythmia, plus baseline BP, HR, and ECG if indicated. Q2: What two growth parameters need ongoing monitoring on a stimulant? Show answer Height and weight trends — report to the HCP if percentiles start declining. Q3: When should the last daily dose be given, and why? Show answer Early in the day, not in the evening — late dosing causes insomnia. Q4: Name a non-stimulan

Typical vs. Atypical Drug Reference — Part 4 of a 4-page Schizophrenia series NG-235 Mental Health / Pharmacology Series 4 of 4 · the drug reference 📍 SCOPE OF THIS PAGE: the broad antipsychotic drug reference — first-generation (typical) vs. second-generation (atypical), mechanism, and every major side effect including EPS, NMS, and agranulocytosis. For schizophrenia-specific adherence issues and LAIs, see NG-165 . Antipsychotics are used far beyond schizophrenia — bipolar mania, Tourette's, agitation, and more. T

🔷 Typical = 1st gen Strong D2 blockade → more EPS. Haloperidol is the prototype. 🔶 Atypical = 2nd gen D2 + serotonin blockade → less EPS, more metabolic effects. Clozapine, risperidone. 🚨 NMS = fever + rigidity Life-threatening on ANY antipsychotic. Hold drug, notify HCP. 🧪 Clozapine = agranulocytosis Weekly ANC/CBC. Report sore throat/fever immediately. 💊
STEP 1 · MECHANISM & THE TWO GENERATIONS Every antipsychotic blocks dopamine — the generations differ in how selectively, which sets up their whole side-effect profile.

Receptor effects Dopamine and other signaling pathways are affected. Symptom benefit Psychotic symptoms may improve. System-wide effects Movement, metabolic and autonomic effects require monitoring. Movement effects Dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism and tardive dyskinesia need recognition. Metabolic effects Track weight, glucose and lipids according to the medication plan. Emergency signs Fever, rigidity, altered mental status and autonomic instability may indicate neuroleptic malignant syndrome. 🧠 Every antipsycho

Blocks D2 receptors broadly across dopamine pathways, including the ones that control movement (nigrostriatal pathway) — this is exactly why EPS is common and prominent with this class. Prototype: Haloperidol (Haldol) Indications: schizophrenia; Tourette's syndrome (to control motor tics/movements); severe agitation. 🧠 "Typical = Tics." Strong D2 blockade in the movement pathway is a package deal with typicals — expect EPS.

Also blocks serotonin (5-HT2A) receptors in addition to D2 — this extra serotonin blockade is thought to indirectly restore some dopamine release in the movement pathway, lowering EPS risk compared to typicals. Prototypes: Clozapine, Risperidone Indications: schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder, especially clients not responding to other antipsychotics (clozapine specifically reserved for treatment-resistant cases). 🧠 "Atypical = Ate-ypical calories." Trade less EPS for more metabolic side effects — weight ga
STEP 2 · MOVEMENT SIDE EFFECTS EPS = movement disorders from D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway. Four distinct presentations — know them by name and by timeline.
STEP 3 · WHAT YOU CANNOT MISS Two reactions turn a routine antipsychotic order into an emergency — recognize them fast.

entries.h: 🚨 Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) — can occur with ANY antipsychotic
entries.t: Life-threatening reaction characterized by: 🌡️ High fever & diaphoresis (hyperpyrexia) 🧠 Change in mental status 💪 Muscle rigidity 🫨 Tremors Priority actions: 1 HOLD the antipsychotic 2 Assess the patient (vitals, mental status, labs) 3 Notify the HCP immediately 🧠 NCLEX trap: "I should not be concerned about fever and muscle stiffness" is a statement that needs further teaching — fever + rigidity on an antipsychotic is never a "wait and see."

Priority to monitor: CBC and absolute neutrophil count (ANC) — required regularly (e.g., weekly during initial treatment per protocol) for as long as clozapine is prescribed. Report to provider immediately: Sore throat Fever Flu-like symptoms These are early infection signs from a dangerously low neutrophil count — high risk for serious, potentially fatal infection. 🧠 "CloZAPine ZAPs WBCs." No lab work, no clozapine refill — this is one of the strictest monitoring requirements in psychiatric pharmacology. 📋
STEP 4 · NAME, SIDE EFFECTS, TEACHING Four commonly tested antipsychotics, side by side.

Drug Generation Normal side effects Killer / must-report side effects Notes Haloperidol (Haldol) 1st gen (typical) Sedation, anticholinergic effects, EPS (all 4 types) NMS Schizophrenia; Tourette's for motor tics Clozapine 2nd gen (atypical) Weight gain, drooling, sedation — no need to report these Agranulocytosis (report sore throat/fever/flu-like sx); NMS Reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia; requires ANC/CBC monitoring Risperidone 2nd gen (atypical) Weight gain, sedation, orthostatic hypotension NMS; u
🧠 Get a baseline ECG before starting, and avoid stacking with other QT-prolonging drugs.

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🔷 Typical vs 🔶 Atypical Typical = more EPS. Atypical = more metabolic side effects. ⚠️ 4 EPS types Dystonia (fast), akathisia, pseudoparkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia (slow, may be permanent) 🚨 NMS Fever + rigidity + altered mental status + tremor → HOLD, assess, notify HCP 🧪 Clozapine Agranulocytosis — ANC/CBC monitoring, report sore throat/fever

Q1: What's the core mechanistic difference between typical and atypical antipsychotics? Show answer Typicals block D2 receptors broadly and strongly (more EPS); atypicals add serotonin (5-HT2A) blockade, which lowers EPS risk but raises metabolic side effect risk. Q2: A client on a new antipsychotic is pacing constantly and reports feeling like they "can't sit still." What is this, and what should the nurse NOT assume it is? Show answer Akathisia (an EPS) — the nurse should not simply assume it's anxiety or worseni

Benzodiazepines & Buspirone — Two Opposite Strategies for Anxiety NG-236 MENTAL HEALTH ADHD-friendly visual edition This page is the pharmacology companion to every anxiety-spectrum page in this batch. Two very different drugs both treat anxiety: benzodiazepines work in minutes by boosting GABA, but carry real dependence risk and are meant for short-term use only . Buspirone works on serotonin instead, takes weeks to kick in, and carries essentially no abuse potential — the trade-off is right there in the numbers.

🧪 Benzos = ↑GABA Fast, effective, habit-forming — short-term use only. 🐢 Buspirone = delayed Non-habit-forming, but takes 2–4 weeks — not for an acute attack. 🆘 Antidotes Benzo → flumazenil. Opioid → naloxone (Narcan). Buspirone needs neither. 🚫 Never stop a benzo cold Abrupt discontinuation risks rebound anxiety and withdrawal seizures. 💊
STEP 1 · HOW IT WORKS Two receptor systems, two speeds — GABA calms fast, serotonin calms slow.

entries.h: 🧬 GABA vs. serotonin — the whole page in one diagram

entries.t: Threat response Autonomic arousal increases. Symptoms intensify Palpitations, dyspnea, fear or dizziness may occur. Support restores control A calm setting and focused assistance can help. During panic Stay present, speak briefly and calmly, and reduce stimulation. Assess alternatives New chest pain, hypoxia or other medical warning signs require medical assessment. Long-term care Therapy, coping skills and prescribed medication address recurring symptoms. 🧠 “Benzos open a door, buspirone retrains the doorman.” One

Alpra zolam , Mida zolam — " -lam " Tema zepam , Clona zepam , Dia zepam — " -pam " MOA: increases GABA (the brain's major inhibitory neurotransmitter) effect at the GABA-A receptor → widens the chloride channel → CNS-wide slowing. Indications: anxiety, seizures, muscle spasm, alcohol/sedative withdrawal, procedural sedation. 🧠 “Low and slow vitals” — expect BP, HR, and RR to trend down with a working dose. Too far down = toxicity.

MOA: partial agonist at serotonin 5-HT1A receptors (with some dopamine activity) — a completely different pathway from benzos or barbiturates. Key point: non-habit-forming, no abuse potential — and it does not potentiate CNS depression from alcohol the way benzos do. Patient teaching: "drive the BUSpirone" — okay to drive/operate machinery, unlike a benzo. 🧠 NOT used for acute attacks — onset is 2–4 weeks, so it has no role in stopping a panic attack in progress.

Phenobarbital — increases GABA effect similarly to benzos, but by prolonging how long the chloride channel stays open rather than how wide. Lasts longer in the body ("takes longer to kick in, takes longer to get out"), which means a higher risk of toxicity — hypotension, respiratory depression. Largely replaced by benzodiazepines for anxiety because of this narrower safety margin, though still used for seizure control. 🧠 “PHENO-barbital, stuck behind bars a long time” — sedation lasts long, and so does the risk. ⚠️
STEP 2 · SAFETY Onset speed and dependence risk are mirror images of each other — chart it out side by side.
🧠 If the question says "acute panic attack, right now" — the answer is a benzodiazepine , never buspirone.

Feature Benzodiazepines Buspirone Mechanism ↑ GABA at GABA-A receptor Partial agonist at serotonin 5-HT1A Onset Minutes 2–4 weeks Use in acute attack Yes — first choice No — too slow Dependence / abuse potential High — short-term use only None Sedation Significant Minimal Alcohol interaction Dangerous — additive CNS/respiratory depression No significant potentiation Driving / machinery Avoid OK — "drive the BUSpirone" Antidote Flumazenil None needed

entries.h: ⚠️ Benzo dependence & withdrawal — the trade-off for speed
entries.t: Physical dependence can develop with regular use, even at therapeutic doses. Never stop a benzodiazepine abruptly — withdrawal can include rebound anxiety, tremor, autonomic instability, and seizures . Always taper. 🧠 Don't confuse the two uses of benzos: here they're the drug being taken for anxiety (short-term only, dependence is the risk). Separately, benzodiazepines are also the drugs used to manage other withdrawal syndromes (like alcohol withdrawal, on a taper protocol) — a supervised, monitored, very differe

Benzos: sedation, respiratory depression, hypotension, fall risk (especially older adults) Additive risk: combining with alcohol or opioids compounds CNS/respiratory depression Barbiturates: same risks, amplified by the longer half-life ✅
STEP 3 · PATIENT EDUCATION Antidotes, interactions, and the exact points that show up on the exam.

Toxicity Antidote Benzodiazepine overdose Flumazenil Opioid overdose Naloxone (brand: Narcan) Buspirone No specific antidote needed — minimal CNS-depressant overdose risk 🧠 “Flu-mazenil flushes the benzo. Nal-oxone knocks out the opioid.” Keep the two straight — a classic mix-and-match NCLEX question.

Take at bedtime if prescribed that way; don't skip doses Stop drinking alcohol — dangerous additive sedation Do not operate dangerous machinery or drive Avoid muscle relaxants and other CNS depressants Avoid valerian root, ginkgo, and ginseng — can add to sedation or affect anxiety/bleeding risk Report any history of reaction to another benzodiazepine (e.g., midazolam) — cross-sensitivity within the class Never stop abruptly — taper under supervision

OK to drive — "drive the BUSpirone" Explain the delayed onset ( 2–4 weeks) up front, or clients stop taking it thinking it "isn't working" Not for an acute panic attack — it will not help in the moment No physical dependence, no withdrawal taper required 🧠 If a question describes a client wanting relief "right now," buspirone is the wrong answer every time.

Never combine a benzodiazepine + opioid + alcohol — the classic respiratory-depression triad Never discontinue a benzodiazepine abruptly after regular use — seizure risk Never expect buspirone to abort an active panic attack 🚨 Phenobarbital toxicity picture: hypotension + increasing sedation — report immediately ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧪 Benzos = ↑GABA fast, effective, short-term only 🐢 Buspirone = 2–4 wks non-habit-forming, no abuse potential 🆘 Flumazenil / Naloxone benzo antidote / opioid antidote 🚫 Never stop benzo cold taper — withdrawal seizures possible

Q1: Why can't buspirone be used to stop an acute panic attack? Show answer Its onset is delayed 2–4 weeks — it works on serotonin 5-HT1A receptors through gradual adaptation, not the immediate GABA boost a benzodiazepine provides. Q2: What's the antidote for a benzodiazepine overdose? For an opioid overdose? Show answer Flumazenil for benzodiazepines; naloxone (Narcan) for opioids. Q3: Why should a client never stop a benzodiazepine abruptly? Show answer Physical dependence can develop even at therapeutic doses; ab

The classic mood stabilizer — narrow therapeutic index, big teaching load NG-250 MENTAL HEALTH ADHD-friendly visual edition Lithium is the oldest, most classic mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder — and it has one of the narrowest therapeutic windows of any drug you'll give. The dose that treats mania and the dose that poisons the client are close together, so almost everything taught about lithium is really teaching about staying in that window . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🔋 Lithium = bipolar Long-term mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder (also schizoaffective disorder). 🧂 Salt matters Low sodium or dehydration → lithium climbs toward toxic levels. 🚫 Hold NSAIDs Ibuprofen/naproxen reduce renal blood flow → lithium rises. 🧪 Check labs Baseline & routine renal + thyroid function, plus lithium level. 🧨
STEP 1 · WHY WE GIVE IT A long-term mood stabilizer — not a fast fix, and not forgiving of a narrow miss.

Mood episodes Mania/hypomania and depression have different features. Stabilization Medication and structured care reduce episode risk. Long-term monitoring Adherence, sleep and adverse effects need follow-up. Mania Reduced need for sleep, increased activity and impaired judgment may threaten safety. Lithium Kidney function, thyroid function, hydration and interacting drugs affect safety. Possible toxicity Vomiting, worsening tremor, ataxia or confusion needs urgent review. 🧠 Never memorize just one number. Ranges

Bipolar disorder — primarily to control/prevent manic episodes and stabilize mood over the long term Schizoaffective disorder Given for long-term (maintenance) treatment — it is not a fast-acting rescue medication for acute agitation. 🧠 Lithium Battery — “B” for Bipolar. A battery is a long-lasting power source, and lithium is a long-term mood stabilizer — both about the long haul, not a quick charge.

The exact mechanism isn't fully settled, but lithium is thought to stabilize neuronal cell membranes and alter sodium transport/second-messenger signaling in neurons, dampening the mania cycle over time. Because lithium is handled by the kidneys largely like sodium, everything about its safety profile traces back to fluid and sodium balance — that connection is the highest-yield idea on this whole page. 🧠 Lithium rides the same train as sodium. Whatever changes sodium and fluid balance changes the lithium level too
STEP 2 · TOXICITY SIGNS Early toxicity is mild and easy to miss — late toxicity is a medical emergency.

entries.h: 📈 Early → late toxicity — a progression, not a single moment
entries.t: 🧠 “GI + tremor + ringing ears = catch it early.” Any client on lithium with new nausea, a fine tremor, or tinnitus needs a level checked before symptoms progress to confusion and seizures.

entries.h: 🫘 Kidney signs the source flags directly
entries.t: 🧪 Rising creatinine above the client's baseline — a general marker of reduced kidney function; know your lab's normal range and trend the client's own baseline 🚽 Low urine output — roughly <30 mL/hr is a widely-used nursing threshold for concerning oliguria and should be reported 🧠 Kidneys clear lithium — hurt kidneys mean lithium has nowhere to go but up. That's why renal signs and lithium toxicity travel together.

Ringing in the ears is a distinctive, easy-to-remember early sign that shows up disproportionately often on exams for lithium specifically — flag it whenever it appears alongside a mood-stabilizer client. 🧠 If a psych-unit client on a mood stabilizer suddenly complains their ears are ringing, think lithium level before anything else. 🩺
STEP 3 · MONITOR & TEACH Almost every teaching point here exists to protect the narrow therapeutic window.

entries.h: 🧂 The single highest-yield teaching point — sodium & fluid intake
entries.t: Do NOT restrict sodium or water intake while on lithium — a low-sodium diet raises the lithium level toward toxic Maintain consistent, adequate daily sodium and fluid intake — don't swing between diets Replace fluids aggressively during vomiting, diarrhea, heavy sweating, or fever ("stomach flu" is a real high-risk toxicity trigger) — report excessive urination too, since both dehydration and unusual polyuria disturb the balance Serum sodium <135 mEq/L (hyponatremia) raises toxicity risk and needs prompt attention

Avoid NSAIDs — ibuprofen, naproxen — in clients on lithium. NSAIDs decrease renal blood flow , which reduces lithium clearance and pushes levels up toward toxic. A client who says "I take ibuprofen for headaches" while on lithium needs further teaching. 🧠 Less blood to the kidney = less lithium leaving the body. Same underlying logic as the sodium teaching — anything that stresses the kidney raises the level.

🫘 Renal function — baseline and periodic (BUN/creatinine) — lithium is renally cleared 🦋 Thyroid function (TSH) — baseline and periodic — lithium can cause hypothyroidism/goiter over time 🩸 Lithium level — routine trough levels, drawn per protocol (commonly ~12 hours after the last dose) to guide dosing ❤️ Baseline ECG may be considered in some clients, per facility protocol 🧠 “Kidney, thyroid, level” — the routine lithium labs. All three get checked before starting and then on an ongoing schedule for the life of t

entries.h: ✅ Continue vs. hold — reading a level correctly
entries.t: If the lithium level comes back within the client's therapeutic range and the client has no toxicity symptoms , the correct answer is usually to continue the current dose — a therapeutic level is a normal, expected finding, not a reason to hold or adjust the medication. ✅ Level in range, no symptoms → continue current dose ⚠️ Level high or symptomatic → hold the dose, notify the HCP, reassess hydration/sodium/renal status 🧠 A common test trap is treating a normal, in-range level as if it were a problem. Read the le

Lithium carries known reproductive/teratogenic risk , particularly with first-trimester exposure — this is generally taught as a reason for close specialist involvement and risk-benefit discussion, not a page to memorize an exact defect statistic from. Any client of childbearing age on lithium should be counseled about pregnancy planning and contraception. 🧠 Pair this with the reproductive-risk contrast already flagged for anticonvulsant mood stabilizers: different mechanisms, but the same nursing habit — always sc

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🔋 Long-term bipolar drug narrow therapeutic window — that's the whole story 🧂 Don't restrict salt/water low sodium/dehydration → toxic lithium levels 🚫 No NSAIDs ↓ renal blood flow → ↑ lithium level 🧪 Renal + thyroid + level baseline, then routine, for the life of therapy

Q1: A client on lithium develops a stomach virus with vomiting and diarrhea. What's the nursing priority? Show answer Aggressively replace fluids/sodium and monitor closely for toxicity — vomiting/diarrhea causes dehydration and sodium loss, which raise the lithium level toward toxic. Hold the dose and notify the HCP if toxicity signs appear. Q2: A client on lithium reports taking ibuprofen regularly for headaches. What's the concern? entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Communication & Therapy Foundations

Real symptoms, no medical cause — and the imposter that isn't a mental illness at all NG-270 MENTAL HEALTH ADHD-friendly visual edition These disorders are constantly confused with each other and with a condition that isn't even a psychiatric diagnosis. The physical symptoms are real — the client is not faking, and there is NO medical cause on testing. The one exception on this whole page is malingering , which IS intentional and IS for a clear external reward. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🩻 SSD = unexplained symptoms Real pain, real distress, no medical cause found on testing. 😨 Illness anxiety = fear, not symptoms Convinced they're sick despite few/no actual symptoms. 🎭 Factitious = fakes it, no reward Intentional, but for the sick role itself — not money or time off. 🎯 Malingering = NOT a mental illness Intentional faking for a clear external gain (money, avoiding work/jail). 🩹
STEP 1 · DEFINITIONS Same theme across all four: the mind is producing (or fixating on) physical illness — the difference is what drives it and whether it's conscious.

EXAM TIP Unexplained physical symptoms — abdominal pain, weakness, chest pain, shortness of breath — with NO medical cause. All diagnostic tests come back negative. Symptoms are real; the client is not making them up or faking it.

Distressing bodily symptoms The person experiences real suffering. Thoughts and behaviors Health anxiety can amplify disability or care seeking. Coordinated care A consistent plan supports function and reassessment. Validate Acknowledge symptoms without dismissing them as imaginary. Assess Evaluate new or changing findings appropriately rather than assuming a psychiatric cause. Support function Set collaborative activity goals and use planned follow-up. Clients obsessively focus time & energy on the symptoms, often

Preoccupation with having or getting a serious illness, despite few or no actual physical symptoms and reassuring test results. The fear itself is the disorder — not the symptom. 🧠 SSD = symptom-focused. Illness anxiety = fear-focused — one has the body complaint front and center, the other is mostly worry about a disease that isn't there.

Neurological-type symptoms (paralysis, blindness, seizures, numbness) that have no medical explanation — the classic teaching example is a symptom appearing after a major psychological stressor. 🧠 Conversion = stress "converted" into a neuro symptom — not fabricated, and often triggered by an identifiable stressful event.

Intentionally produces or fakes symptoms/injuries — but the motivation is internal: to assume the "sick role" and receive care/attention, not for money, time off, or any other outside reward. 🧠 Factitious = fakes it on purpose, for the attention of being sick itself — the "gain" is psychological, not material. 🔎
STEP 2 · THE MASTER COMPARISON Two axes decide everything here: is the symptom production conscious, and is there an external reward?

entries.h: 🧭 Conscious vs. unconscious, internal vs. external gain
entries.t: 🧠 "Fake it for feelings vs. fake it for a favor." Factitious disorder fakes illness for the emotional payoff of being cared for. Malingering fakes illness for a concrete outside reward — and that distinction is exactly why malingering isn't classified as a mental illness.

Disorder Core feature Intentional? Gain Somatic Symptom Disorder Real, unexplained physical symptoms; obsessive focus on them No None Illness Anxiety Disorder Preoccupied with fear of having/getting a serious illness No None Conversion Disorder Neuro symptom (paralysis, blindness) tied to a stressor No None Factitious Disorder Deliberately fakes/produces symptoms or injury Yes Internal — the "sick role" Malingering (not a mental illness) Deliberately fakes symptoms for a specific known reason Yes External — money,
STEP 3 · WHAT NOT TO DO MATTERS MOST The nursing approach across SSD, illness anxiety, and conversion disorder is almost entirely about what to avoid.

entries.h: 🚫 Don't let the exam trick you — the 3 big NEVERs
entries.t: 💊 NEVER reinforce negative test results → asking for more pain meds 🗣️ NEVER debunk don't say "your symptoms aren't real" 🔬 NEVER over-test don't advocate for more diagnostics or a new diet plan — it's psychological 🧠 "Don't feed it, don't fight it, don't chase it." Don't feed the sick role, don't fight the client's reality, don't chase more tests that won't find anything.

Gently limit the time spent discussing physical symptoms in conversation — redirect toward coping and function instead of the symptom itself. 🧠 Redirect, don't dismiss. Acknowledge the symptom once, then pivot to coping strategies.
Deep-breathing Meditation Exercise 🧠 Since the physical symptoms are stress-driven, stress-reduction is the actual treatment lever — not more imaging.

Help the client connect symptom flares to specific life stressors — building the mind-body insight is the long-term goal, alongside CBT-based reframing (see NG-221 ). 🧠 Insight is the win condition. The goal isn't "no more symptoms" overnight — it's the client starting to see the stress connection.

📎 Use Therapeutic Communication ( NG-271 ) techniques here: state facts without debating the client's reality, use open-ended questions to explore stressors, and never give false reassurance ("it's all in your head" is never acceptable). CBT ( NG-221 ) cognitive restructuring is a common adjunct treatment for the anxiety driving these disorders. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🩻 SSD = real symptom, no cause Not faked, stress-driven. 🎭 Factitious = fakes for sick role Intentional, internal/psychological gain. 🎯 Malingering ≠ mental illness Intentional, external gain (money, avoiding work). 🚫 Never debunk or over-test Limit focus on symptoms; teach coping instead.

Q1: A client has chronic unexplained abdominal pain with all negative workups and is not faking it. What disorder fits? Show answer Somatic Symptom Disorder — real symptoms, no medical cause, not intentional. Q2: How is factitious disorder different from malingering? Show answer Both are intentional faking, but factitious disorder is for internal/psychological gain (the sick role); malingering is for a clear external gain (money, avoiding work or legal trouble) and is NOT classified as a mental illness. entries.h: Therapeutic Communication · NG-271 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Communication & Therapy Foundations · MASTER REFERENCE

The techniques that carry every mental health page in this batch NG-271 MENTAL HEALTH ADHD-friendly visual edition This is the reference page. Every other Mental Health topic — schizophrenia communication, crisis management, grief & loss, panic attacks — assumes you already know these techniques. Learn them here , once, cold. Therapeutic = client-centered, open, exploring. Non-therapeutic = nurse-centered, closing, judging. One word test: does it hand the floor back to the client, or take it away? 📄 Simple Nursing

❓ Open beats closed "How," "what," "tell me about" > any yes/no question. 🚫 Never ask "Why?" It sounds accusatory & puts the client on the defensive. 🪞 Reflect, don't advise Hand feelings back to the client instead of giving your opinion. 🤝 Silence & presence Sitting with someone in silence is still therapeutic communication. 🗣️
STEP 1 · WHAT TO SAY Every therapeutic technique does one of three jobs: opens the door, hands back the feeling, or confirms you heard right.
EXAM TIP Therapeutic communication is client-centered — the nurse's opinions, advice, and personal stories stay out of it. The nurse's only jobs are to open , reflect , and clarify .

Establish trust Respectful communication supports engagement. Set shared boundaries Clear expectations make care predictable. Support coping Reinforce effective skills and collaborative goals. Listen Use open questions, reflection and clarification when appropriate. Respond Describe observable behavior without judgment or labels. Coordinate Consistent team communication reduces mixed messages and conflict. 🧠 "Ask, don't answer." If the nurse's sentence gives information the client didn't ask for (advice, an opinion

Require an in-depth response — not a yes/no answer. "How do you cope with anxiety?" "What event in your life has been the most stressful?" "Tell me more about what led to your hospitalization." "What are you feeling right now?" 🧠 "What/How, not Do/Did." Closed questions start with a verb ("Did you..."); open questions start with what, how, tell me .

entries.h: 🪞 Reflecting — return focus to the client
entries.t: Bounce the client's own feeling or question back to them, so they keep exploring it instead of the nurse answering for them. Client: "Do you think I should leave him?" → Nurse: "What do you think you should do?" 🧠 Reflecting = a mirror. The client's own feeling comes right back at them.

Repeat the patient's own words (or close to it) to confirm understanding — not just parroting. "Am I correct in restating that you are feeling less anxious today?" "In looking back at what you said, you stated you are feeling better." 🧠 Restating = echo with a purpose. It checks accuracy before the conversation moves on.

Broad opening: a wide-open invitation with no agenda — "Tell me what's on your mind today." Offering self: the nurse's presence, without demanding a response — "I'll stay with you for a while." 🧠 "You seem to be in pain; I'll stay with you for a while" is both offering self and stating an observation in one line — a classic exam answer.

Sitting with a client without filling every gap gives them room to think, cry, or organize their thoughts. Silence is therapeutic, not awkward. 🧠 Never leave the room to "give them privacy" to grieve — that's abandonment, not silence. Stay, and be quiet.

entries.h: 📌 Stating facts / voicing doubt — reality check
entries.t: Presents objective reality without arguing, used to gently challenge misconceptions or delusions without direct confrontation. "I don't hear any voices, but I know this is frightening for you." 🧠 State facts, don't debate. The nurse reports their own reality — never says "that's not real" or argues the delusion away.

entries.h: 🧩 The combo answer — often the "most correct" NCLEX choice
entries.t: The highest-scoring answer often states an observation AND asks an open-ended follow-up in the same sentence. "This experience has been overwhelming for you. What are you feeling right now?" "The sudden death of your husband is hard to accept. Tell me about how you are feeling?" "You seem very distressed over learning you have asthma." "You're feeling angry that your family continues to hope for you to be cured?" 🧠 "Name it, then ask it." Name the feeling you observe → invite them to say more. When two answer choic
STEP 2 · WHAT NOT TO SAY These blocks show up as wrong-answer distractors on almost every psych question — know them as well as the right answers.

entries.h: ⚖️ Side by side — the master comparison

entries.t: Open-ended question "What are you feeling right now?" Reflecting "What do you think you should do?" Restating "You stated you're feeling better today." Silence / offering self Sitting quietly with the client, present & available. Stating facts "I don't hear voices, but I know this feels real to you." Broad opening "Tell me what's on your mind."

Closed / yes-no question "Are you feeling better?" Giving advice / opinion "I think you should leave him." False reassurance "Everything is going to be alright." Leaving the room "I'll give you privacy to grieve." Asking "Why?" "Why do you feel angry when...?" Personal experience "I lost my grandfather too, so I understand." 🧠 "THERAPEUTIC hands the mic to the client. NON-THERAPEUTIC grabs it back." Every non-therapeutic block on the left column below does the same thing: it centers the nurse , not the client.

entries.h: 🚫 Never: give advice or personal opinions
entries.t: "I'm sure you'll do the correct thing" or "I think you should..." — the nurse's job is to help the client find their own answer, not hand over one. 🧠 Advice = the nurse's problem to solve, not the client's — it removes the client's autonomy.

"It will be ok" / "Don't worry" — minimizes the client's real fear and shuts the conversation down instead of opening it. 🧠 "Ok" is a closed door. False reassurance sounds kind but ends the exploration.

"Why do you feel angry?" / "Why did you leave your child alone?" — "why" sounds accusatory and makes the client defensive, even when the nurse means well. 🧠 Swap "Why" for "What" or "How" — "What led you to feel angry when...?" gets the same information without the blame tone.

Stepping out "to give privacy" during a crying or grieving moment is abandonment, not kindness. Stay and offer silent presence instead. 🧠 Presence > privacy. On the top-missed NCLEX grief question, "leave the room" is almost always the wrong choice.

Changing the subject, dismissing, or rushing past an emotional statement tells the client their feelings don't matter. 🧠 Name it, don't skip it. If the client says something heavy, the nurse's next line should acknowledge it — not move on.

Arguing with a delusion ("that's not real") or defending yourself/the facility puts the nurse on the opposite side of the client instead of alongside them. 🧠 State your own reality — don't attack theirs. Compare: "I don't hear any voices" (ok) vs. "You're wrong, there are no voices" (not ok). 🩺
STEP 3 · REAL SCENARIOS These techniques come back on every other Mental Health page in this batch — schizophrenia, crisis management, grief & loss. Practice choosing the therapeutic line here first.

Scenario: An elderly client is losing their spouse to pancreatic cancer. Which response is most therapeutic? Response Verdict "I know this is a difficult time for you. Tell me how you have been coping with this loss." ✅ Best — states observation + open question "What are your feelings & thoughts about attending a support group?" ✅ Therapeutic — open, explores "It takes time to deal with a lost spouse, but it will be ok." ❌ False reassurance "I recently lost my grandfather to cancer, so I understand." ❌ Personal exp

Silent member: encourage interaction, or pair them off in smaller groups. Aggressive/interrupting member: "You seem very upset" — allow the group to handle it before the nurse intervenes directly. 🧠 Group therapy goal = reduce isolation in a structured, controlled environment — not to "fix" any one member.

A safe, structured social & physical environment — the goal of every behavioral health unit. Clients are oriented to their environment, rights, and responsibilities and encouraged to interact within the community. 🧠 Milieu = the unit itself is the treatment. Structure + community + safety, all day, not just during scheduled therapy.

entries.t: 📎 Use these exact techniques when reading: Schizophrenia — Communication , Crisis Management , Death, Dying, Grief & Loss , and Abuse & Neglect . This page is the master reference — those pages will assume you already know open-ended questions, reflecting, restating, silence, and the non-therapeutic blocks above. When another page says "use therapeutic communication," it means: ask open-ended , reflect their words , stay present in silence , and never advise, falsely reassure, ask "why," or leave the room. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD ❓ Open, not closed "What/How/Tell me" — never a yes/no question. 🚫 Never "Why?" Sounds accusatory — swap for "what." 🪞 Reflect & restate Hand the feeling back; confirm you heard right. 🤝 Stay, don't leave Silence + presence beats "I'll give you privacy."

Q1: A client says "I can't believe my wife died yesterday. I keep expecting to see her." Best response? Show answer "It must be hard to accept that she has passed away" — states the observation, invites more without arguing or reassuring falsely. Q2: Why is asking "Why did you...?" avoided in therapeutic communication? Show answer It sounds accusatory and puts the client on the defensive — swap "why" for "what" or "how." Ask directly · a plan is the risk · safety comes before everything NG-399 Mental Health ADHD-friendly visual edition Asking someone directly whether they are thinking of killing themselves does not plant the idea . It is the single most important assessment question in psychiatric nursing, and it has to be asked in plain words. Ask it directly “Are you thinking of killing yourself?” What raises risk most A specific plan, the means, and a time The dangerous lift Sudden calm after depression — she has decided Priorit

Ask clearly Ask about current suicidal thoughts, a plan, access to means, past attempts and protective supports. Listen without judgment; do not promise secrecy. Protect now Current suicidal thoughts require urgent assessment. Keep the patient accompanied and reduce access to dangerous items under the clinical safety protocol. Escalate and hand over Notify the responsible team and obtain the indicated mental-health evaluation. Communicate observation requirements clearly during every handover. Plan collaboratively

What she might say or do “Everyone would be better off without me.” “I won’t be a problem much longer.” Giving away possessions, making a will, saying goodbye Sudden withdrawal, or sudden calm Increased alcohol or drug use Hoarding medication, buying a weapon Reckless behavior, a sense that nothing matters Take every statement literally. Do not reinterpret it as attention-seeking. How to respond in the moment Stay with her. Do not leave to go and find someone. Use her words back. “You said you would not be a proble

What you actually do Ensure immediate safety. One-to-one observation for high risk — that means constant, arm’s-length, including in the bathroom . Remove the means. Belts, shoelaces, cords, razors, glass, plastic bags, medication. Search belongings per policy. Notify the provider and document the exact words she used. Build a safety plan with her, not for her. Restrict access at home: lock or remove firearms and medication, involve family. Treat the underlying illness and the substance use. Environment and observa

Ask it directly “Are you thinking of killing yourself?” What raises risk most A specific plan, the means, and a time The dangerous lift Sudden calm after depression — she has decided Priority Safety first. Never leave a high-risk patient alone. Does asking about suicide put the idea in someone’s head? Show answer No. Asking directly is the correct action and it does not increase risk. Which single factor best predicts a future attempt? Show answer A previous attempt. A severely depressed patient suddenly seems peac
These newly drawn concept diagrams consolidate the retired illustration sets. The accompanying study notes and original handout links remain on this page. NIMH adult inpatient safety assessment
The last nursing care a person receives, and the first hour of the family's grief. Almost every exam question here turns on one fork: is this a medical examiner case?

Has the death been pronounced and documented — and is this body cleared for you to touch? Three things can hold the lines in: a medical examiner case , an organ or tissue donation referral, or a death that has not yet been formally pronounced. An expected death alone does not grant clearance. ✅ Cleared — ordinary postmortem care Cleared means all three: death pronounced and documented , not an ME or coroner case, and donation addressed — the OPO notified and finished with the body. Then remove the tubes, lines and

For a cleared death — the fork above answered, the ME ruled out, donation addressed. Time matters for only one reason: rigor mortis begins in about 2 to 4 hours , and after that the face cannot be arranged. 1 Confirm the death has been pronounced and documented. Nothing else starts until it has. 2 Gloves, and standard precautions throughout. They do not stop applying because the client has died. 3 Remove tubes, lines and drains — only once cleared : death documented, not an ME case, and donation addressed. Not mere

They stay as long as they need. There is no correct amount of time, and the body is not waiting on anyone. Dim the lights, give them privacy , offer a chair and a glass of water. Touching and holding are encouraged , not discouraged — including holding an infant who has died. Offer the chaplain, cultural or religious rites, and ask rather than assume which apply. Say the person's name. “Please step out so we can prepare the body” is the wrong answer on any exam and in any room.

The nurse notifies the organ procurement organization. The OPO does the asking. That is the whole answer, and it holds even when the family objects to a signed donor card. Federal rules require every death to be referred to the OPO, and require the approach to be made by trained requestors — not by the bedside nurse, and not in an argument. What the nurse does not do: Tell the family the donor card is legally binding and proceed Pressure them by naming the people waiting Document the refusal and stop there — the re

Kübler-Ross — five stages, and nobody moves through them in order. Denial — “the scan must belong to someone else” Anger — at the staff, the family, the world, herself Bargaining — “if I can just make it to my daughter's wedding in June” — a deal offered in exchange for time. This is the one most often tested. Depression — the sadness of what is actually being lost Acceptance — not happiness; quiet Disenfranchised grief is grief the world will not let someone have. The loss is real, but it is not socially recognise

Three reasons every tube, line and drain stays in: an ME case , a pending donation , or a death not yet pronounced — and in an ME case, do not bathe the body either "The death was expected" is not clearance on its own Do not discard tubing or dressings in an ME case — evidence Dentures in and mouth closed early — rigor mortis starts in 2 to 4 hours Head of the bed slightly raised , never flat, to stop the face discolouring ID tags on the body and on the shroud Standard precautions still apply after death Valuables

entries.h: 5 Step EKG Interpretation · NG-011 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Cardiac · Rhythm · Med-Surg & Critical Care 📈 RHYTHM SET NG-011 · The 5-step METHOD NG-090 · The 9 rhythms NG-019 · Antidysrhythmics

One order. Every strip. Every time. — rate ▸ rhythm ▸ P ▸ PR ▸ QRS NG-011 CARDIAC · RHYTHM ADHD-friendly visual edition Students try to read strips by recognizing pictures , and then panic when the picture is slightly off. This page teaches the other way: a five-question procedure you run in the same order on every strip, so the rhythm names itself at the end. This page is the method. Its sister page NG-090 — the 9 ECG strips is the rhythm album; come here to learn how to measure , go there to learn what each rhyth

📏 0.04 & 0.20 Small box = 0.04 s . Large box = 0.20 s . Every measurement is box-counting. 🔢 ×10 or 300-150-100 6-second strip ×10 works on any rhythm. The 300 sequence only on regular ones. 🖐️ 5 questions Rate → Regular? → P waves? → PR 0.12–0.20? → QRS <0.12? Then name it. 🚨 Patient first Any rhythm change → check a pulse and check the patient . Leads lie. Patients don't. 📐

entries.h: THE PAPER, THE WAVES, THE ORDER
entries.t: STEP 0 · SET-UP Before you can measure anything, you have to know what one box is worth and what each bump is.

entries.h: 🧭 The loop — run it in this order, always
🧪 What every wave, segment and interval means
entries.t: MARK WHAT IT IS NORMAL (adult) P wave Atria depolarizing <0.12 s wide, <2.5 mm tall, upright in II PR interval Start of P → start of QRS: atria + the AV delay 0.12–0.20 s (3–5 small boxes) QRS complex Ventricles depolarizing <0.12 s (under 3 small boxes) ST segment Ventricles fully depolarized, plateau flat on the baseline T wave Ventricles repolarizing (recharging) upright, rounded, same direction as QRS QT interval Total ventricular depolarize + recharge ≈0.36–0.44 s; rate-dependent Side note (newer guidance): Us

entries.h: 🚨 STEP 0 — look at the patient, not the monitor
entries.t: Before you interpret anything, answer three things: Is there a pulse? A perfect-looking rhythm with no pulse is PEA — a cardiac arrest . Is the patient symptomatic? Chest pain, syncope, hypotension, altered mental status, shortness of breath. Symptoms drive urgency far more than the rhythm name. Is it real, or is it artifact? Shivering, brushing teeth, a loose lead or a disconnected electrode all mimic dangerous rhythms. Never treat a monitor tracing without laying hands on the patient. 🧠 “Feel before you fix.” Pul

entries.h: ✅ Artifact vs a real rhythm — how to tell fast
entries.t: Artifact usually has real QRS complexes marching through it — look for the underlying beats inside the noise. Artifact often stops when you touch the leads or ask the patient to hold still. The patient looks fine : talking, pink, good color, normal blood pressure. Real V-tach or V-fib has no pulse or a very sick patient to go with it. Side note (newer guidance): Ventricular tachycardia may occur with a pulse and can initially be tolerated. Ventricular fibrillation produces no effective pulse. Assess the patient and

entries.h: 📍 Why lead II is the monitoring lead
entries.t: Lead II runs from the right arm to the left leg — almost exactly along the normal direction of atrial depolarization. That makes the P wave biggest and clearly upright in lead II. Since three of your five steps depend on seeing the P wave, this is the lead you monitor in. If the P waves are hard to see, change the lead before you decide they are absent . 🧠 “Two to see the P.” Lead II is where P waves live.

entries.h: ⭐ The three questions this method answers
entries.t: ⏱️ How fast? Step 1 — the rate. 📍 Where did the beat start? Steps 3 and 5 — P waves say atria/SA, QRS width says above or below the ventricles. Side note (newer guidance): Where did the beat start? Steps 3 and 5 — P waves say atria/SA, QRS width describes ventricular activation; it does not establish the origin by itself. 🚦 Did it get through? Steps 2 and 4 — regularity and PR interval tell you whether every signal made it to the ventricle. GO DEEPER Once you have those three answers, the rhythm name is almost auto
HOW FAST? Normal 60–100 /min. Two counting methods; you must know which one is legal on which strip.

entries.h: ⭐ Which method, when — the rule that gets tested
entries.t: METHOD USE IT WHEN NEVER USE IT WHEN 6-second × 10 Any strip. Regular or irregular. — (always allowed) 300-150-100 Rhythm is regular and you want a fast answer Rhythm is irregular — the answer changes with every pair you pick 1500 ÷ small boxes Regular, and you need a precise number Irregular rhythms If the rhythm is irregular, the 6-second method is the only correct one. Side note (newer guidance): For an irregular rhythm, count beats over a known time interval and calculate an average rate. A 6-second count multi

entries.h: 🧮 Method C — the 1500 rule (the precise one)
entries.t: 1500 ÷ number of SMALL boxes between two R waves = rate Why 1500? There are 1500 small boxes in one minute ( 25 mm/s × 60 s = 1500 mm ). 20 small boxes → 1500 ÷ 20 = 75 15 small boxes → 1500 ÷ 15 = 100 25 small boxes → 1500 ÷ 25 = 60 🧠 1500 small · 300 large · 30 large in a 6-second strip. Three numbers, one ruler.

entries.h: 📈 Count the ATRIAL rate too when they disagree
entries.t: The rate you report is normally the ventricular rate — count QRS complexes, because that is what produces a pulse and a blood pressure. But if there are more P waves than QRS complexes, count both : count P waves for the atrial rate and QRS complexes for the ventricular rate. Atrial ~300 , ventricular ~150 → 2:1 atrial flutter. Atrial ~80 , ventricular ~35 → think complete heart block. 🧠 QRS makes the pulse. P waves that never reach a ventricle move no blood. Side note (newer guidance): QRS complexes count ventricu

entries.h: 🚨 Rate red flags at the bedside
entries.t: Below 60 with symptoms — dizziness, hypotension, chest pain, confusion. Symptomatic bradycardia needs action; asymptomatic athletes do not. Above 150 — filling time drops so far that cardiac output falls even though the heart is racing. Sudden change in rate is more alarming than a rate that has been stable for hours. Any rate with no pulse = arrest. Start CPR. 🧠 “Too slow to perfuse, too fast to fill.” Both ends of the scale drop cardiac output.

Under 60 “…bradycardia” 60–100 “normal…” / “sinus…” Over 100 “…tachycardia” The rate supplies half the rhythm's name. Step 3 and Step 5 supply the other half (where the beat came from). 🧠 Name = SPEED + ORIGIN. “Sinus” + “bradycardia”. “Atrial” + “fibrillation”. “Ventricular” + “tachycardia”. 2️⃣
EVEN GAPS? Measure R to R. Regular means every gap is the same — not “roughly the same”.

entries.h: ✅ How to actually march it out
entries.t: 1 Lay a plain paper edge along the top of the strip. 2 Pencil a tick on two neighboring R waves. 3 Slide the paper so the second tick sits on the third R wave. 4 Does the first tick land on the second R? Keep sliding along the whole strip. 5 Ticks keep hitting R waves = regular. Ticks drift = irregular. Calipers do the same job faster; the paper trick works when you have no calipers, which is most of the time on a med-surg floor. 🧠 Two ticks and march. Same technique for P-P as for R-R.

PATTERN WHAT YOU SEE CLASSIC CAUSE Regular All R-R gaps identical Sinus rhythms, SVT, V-tach, flutter with fixed conduction Regularly irregular An irregularity that repeats in a pattern Wenckebach; a bigeminal pattern of extra beats Irregularly irregular No pattern at all, ever Atrial fibrillation — the classic answer Regular with an interruption Regular, then one odd beat or one pause A single premature beat (PAC/PVC) or a dropped beat 🧠 “Irregularly irregular” is nearly always A-fib on an exam. Say the phrase, pi

Two rulers, two answers: P-P regular but R-R irregular → the atria are steady; some signals are not getting through. Think AV block . Both regular and equal → normal conduction, one signal one beat. P-P not measurable at all → there are no organized P waves. Think A-fib or flutter . 🧠 Atria have their own ruler. When R-R is a mess, always go back and check P-P.

An irregular rhythm is not just a naming problem: Pulse deficit — some beats are too weak to reach the wrist. Apical and radial pulses differ. Count apical for a full minute. Loss of atrial kick — in A-fib the atria quiver instead of contracting, costing roughly a fifth to a third of cardiac output. Clot risk — blood pooling in a quivering atrium forms clots, which is why A-fib is an anticoagulation conversation. 🧠 Quiver → pool → clot → stroke. That chain is the whole reason A-fib is scary.

Write it the way the chart wants it: “R-R regular” , “R-R irregularly irregular” , or “regular with one premature beat” . Avoid “kind of regular”. If the gaps are not equal, it is irregular , and that changes which rate method you are allowed to use in Step 1. 🧠 Step 2 feeds back into Step 1. If you find irregular, go back and re-count with the 6-second method. 3️⃣
WHO STARTED IT? Three questions: is a P there, do they all look alike, and does each one own a QRS?

entries.h: ✅ The three P questions, in order
entries.t: 1 PRESENT? Is there a P wave at all? No P → the SA node is not driving. 2 UNIFORM? Do all the Ps look the same? Different shapes = beats starting in different places. 3 1 : 1? One P before every QRS, one QRS after every P? Extra Ps = something is being blocked. 🧠 “P·U·1” — Present, Uniform, One-to-one. Three ticks and Step 3 is done.

entries.h: 🧪 What a normal P wave looks like
entries.t: Upright in lead II (the impulse is traveling toward the positive electrode). Rounded and smooth — not notched, peaked or biphasic. Under 0.12 s wide (under 3 small boxes) and under 2.5 mm tall. All identical to each other across the strip. One per QRS , at the same distance in front of each QRS. A P wave that satisfies all five means the beat is sinus in origin — this is what earns the word “sinus” in a rhythm name. Side note (newer guidance): These features support a sinus origin. Interpret P-wave appearance and i

entries.h: ⚠️ Inverted, buried or missing P waves
entries.t: If the beat starts in the AV junction instead of the SA node, the atria depolarize backwards . That gives you one of three pictures: Inverted P before the QRS — the atria fired just before the ventricles. No visible P — the P is hidden inside the QRS because both fired together. Inverted P after the QRS — the atria fired late. All three = a junctional beat or rhythm. The QRS stays narrow , because the signal still uses the normal ventricular highway below the AV node. Side note (newer guidance): These findings can

entries.h: 🚨 “No P waves” — what it narrows down to
entries.t: BASELINE INSTEAD OF P RHYTHM R-R Fine wavy, chaotic quiver Atrial fibrillation Irregularly irregular Repeating sawtooth F waves Atrial flutter Often regular Flat, P hidden in QRS Junctional rhythm Regular Nothing at all, wide bizarre QRS Ventricular rhythm / V-tach Usually regular P waves present but too fast to see clearly SVT (P buried in the T wave) Very regular, very fast SEE THE STRIPS Each of these is drawn full size on NG-090 · The 9 ECG strips .

entries.h: ❌ The trap: calling a P wave absent when it is only hidden
entries.t: Before you write “no P waves”, do two things: Change the lead. P waves can be tiny in one lead and obvious in another. Lead II is your friend. Look inside the T wave. At fast rates the P wave sits on top of the previous T, giving it a strange notch or extra peak. That notch is the P wave. Never diagnose A-fib on a single noisy lead without checking regularity as well. 🧠 “Camel-hump T” = a P wave hiding. Fast and regular with a lumpy T is SVT, not A-fib. 4️⃣
DID IT GET THROUGH? Start of P to start of QRS. Normal 0.12–0.20 s — three to five small boxes.

entries.h: 📐 Measuring it — and what the number means
🪜 The block ladder — what a bad PR looks like

entries.t: 1 Count the small boxes from the start of P to the start of QRS. 3–5 is normal. 2 Is it the SAME on every beat? Constant vs lengthening is the whole difference between type I and type II. 3 Is every P followed by a QRS? A P with nothing after it is a dropped beat. 🧠 Length · consistency · completeness. Three checks, one interval.

entries.h: 📊 Sorting the AV blocks side by side
entries.t: BLOCK PR DROPPED QRS? WORRY LEVEL 1st degree >0.20 s, constant No Usually benign; watch and document 2nd degree type I (Wenckebach / Mobitz I) Progressively longer Yes, cyclically Often stable; watch, treat if symptomatic 2nd degree type II (Mobitz II) Constant Yes, suddenly Unstable — can progress to complete block 3rd degree (complete) No relationship at all P and QRS independent Emergency — needs pacing Type I lengthens then drops. Type II drops without warning. 🧠 “Type I is polite — it warns you. Type II just l

entries.h: 🚨 The blocks that need a pacemaker conversation
entries.t: Mobitz II and complete (3rd degree) heart block are the two that classically progress and classically need pacing — transcutaneous pacing at the bedside, then a transvenous or permanent pacemaker. Have the transcutaneous pacer pads and the crash cart available; keep the patient on continuous monitoring and on bed rest until a decision is made. Atropine is the standard first drug for symptomatic bradycardia by protocol, but it works at the AV node and is often ineffective in high-grade/infranodal block — do not let

entries.h: ⚠️ A short PR is a finding too
entries.t: A PR under 0.12 s means the signal reached the ventricle faster than the AV node should allow — it took a shortcut, or the beat did not start in the SA node. Junctional beats — starts below the atria, so there is less distance to travel. Pre-excitation (an accessory pathway) — the signal bypasses the AV delay entirely. 🧠 Short PR = the signal cheated. Long PR = the signal queued. 5️⃣

FROM ABOVE OR BELOW? Under 0.12 s (under 3 small boxes) is narrow. Narrow and wide are two different worlds. ↔️ Narrow vs wide — and why the width tells you the origin Side note (newer guidance): ↔️ Narrow vs wide — how the ventricles activate A narrow QRS usually indicates rapid activation through the ventricular conduction system. A wide QRS indicates prolonged ventricular activation; ventricular rhythms, conduction delay, pacing and other causes can produce it. QRS width describes how the ventricles activate. It

entries.h: ⭐ The single most useful line on the page
entries.t: NARROW <0.12 s Beat started above the ventricles — sinus, atrial or junctional. “Supraventricular.” WIDE ≥0.12 s Beat started in the ventricle, or a bundle branch is blocked, or a pacemaker is firing. Combine it with rate and you have a working diagnosis before you name anything: wide + fast + regular is treated as ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise. 🧠 “Wide and fast — assume the worst.” Treat wide-complex tachycardia as V-tach.

entries.h: 📊 Four reasons a QRS is wide
entries.t: CAUSE CLUE ON THE STRIP Ventricular origin (PVC, V-tach, idioventricular) No related P wave; T wave points the opposite way to the QRS Bundle branch block Normal P with a normal PR, but the QRS is wide — often notched, “rabbit ears” Paced beat A sharp vertical pacer spike right before the wide QRS Severe hyperkalemia / some drug toxicity Progressive widening, peaked T waves, flattening P waves LINK Potassium ranges and the hyperkalemia picture live on NG-088 · Potassium, sodium & chloride (potassium 3.5–5.0 mEq/L )

Measure from the start of the QRS to the end of the T wave . Typical adult ≈0.36–0.44 s , but it shortens as the rate rises, so it is always read against the rate. Quick bedside sanity check: at a normal rate, the QT should be less than half the R-R interval . Long QT → risk of torsades de pointes . Causes include low potassium, low magnesium, low calcium and QT-prolonging drugs. Check the QT whenever a patient is on a rhythm drug, an antipsychotic or certain antibiotics. 🧠 “Low K, low Mag, long QT, torsades.” Magn

entries.h: 🚨 The two strips that end the assessment early
entries.t: Wide, fast, no pulse → pulseless V-tach. Shock. Start CPR. Chaotic with no identifiable complexes → V-fib. Shock. Start CPR. Flat line → asystole. Do NOT shock. CPR and epinephrine, and check leads in more than one lead first. Never work through five interpretation steps on a pulseless patient — start compressions. 🧠 Shock the V's — V-tach (pulseless) and V-fib. Asystole and PEA are never shocked.

Your five answers assemble into a sentence: [rate word] + [origin word] + [regularity/qualifier] Rate 45, regular, upright Ps 1:1, PR 0.16, QRS 0.08 → sinus bradycardia . Rate 130, irregularly irregular, no Ps, QRS 0.08 → atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response . Rate 180, regular, no Ps, QRS 0.16 → ventricular tachycardia . 🧠 Measure first, name last. The name is the output, never the starting point. 🧪

entries.h: WORKED STRIPS — RUN ALL FIVE STEPS
entries.t: PRACTICE Cover the answer boxes, work the strip yourself, then check. Do this three times and the order sticks.

entries.h: 🟩 PRACTICE STRIP 1 — run the five steps before you read the boxes
🟦 PRACTICE STRIP 2 — the rate changed, nothing else did
🟧 PRACTICE STRIP 3 — two boxes fail at once
🟪 PRACTICE STRIP 4 — everything looks fine until Step 4
🟥 PRACTICE STRIP 5 — stop at Step 0 and check a pulse
🎓 Quick-fire self test — cover the answers
entries.t: Q. A strip is irregularly irregular. Which rate method are you allowed to use? ▸ Only the 6-second strip × 10 . Box-counting methods need equal R-R intervals. Side note (newer guidance): ▸ Use a timed beat count to estimate the average rate, such as 6 seconds × 10 or 10 seconds × 6. Single-interval box counting is intended for regular rhythms. Q. How many small boxes is a normal PR interval? ▸ 3 to 5 small boxes = 0.12–0.20 s . Q. The PR gets longer, longer, longest, then a QRS is missing. Name it. ▸ Second-degree
