What the Body Does to the Drug NG-262 Pharmacology ADHD-friendly visual edition Pharmacokinetics = the journey a drug takes through the body : in, around, changed, and out. Four steps — Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion (ADME) — explain why a pill takes longer to work than a shot, why liver failure changes your dosing, and why some drugs need blood levels drawn. Every other pharmacology page on this site leans on these concepts. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🚶 ADME Absorption → Distribution → Metabolism → Excretion. 🔄 First-pass effect Oral drugs get metabolized by the liver before reaching the body. ⏳ Half-life Time for the body to eliminate 50% of the drug. 🎯 Therapeutic index Narrow window drugs need blood levels — peak & trough. 🚶
STEP 1 · IN, AROUND, OUT Every drug you'll ever give follows the same 4-stop route through the body.

entries.h: 🚶 ADME — the drug's route through the body

entries.t: Absorption Drug enters the circulation. Distribution and metabolism Drug reaches tissues and is transformed. Elimination Drug or metabolites leave the body. Exposure Route, formulation, food and interactions can change concentrations. Clearance Kidney or liver dysfunction can prolong effects. Timing Half-life, onset, peak and duration describe different properties. 🧠 "A Dizzy Man Excretes" — A bsorption, D istribution, M etabolism, E xcretion. Say it in order every time you think about a drug's journey.

entries.h: ① Absorption — getting into the blood
entries.t: Moves the drug from the site of administration into body fluids via active transport, passive transport, or pinocytosis. IV/IM = fastest absorption; IV = 100% bioavailability , no absorption step at all Oral = slowest — depends on GI motility, pH, food, and solubility Affected by: route, solubility, condition of body tissues 🧠 "Straight to vein, straight to work." IV skips absorption entirely — that's why it's the fastest route in an emergency.

entries.h: ② Distribution — only free drug works
entries.t: The systemic circulation carries the drug to body tissues. Depends on protein binding, blood flow, and solubility . Drug binds albumin or stays free — only free circulating drug is active Low albumin (liver disease, malnutrition, elderly) → more free drug → higher effect/toxicity risk Fat-soluble drugs cross the blood-brain barrier more easily 🧠 "Bound and gagged does nothing." A drug stuck to albumin is inactive until it's released.

entries.h: ③ Metabolism — the liver changes it
entries.t: Also called biotransformation — the body changes the drug to be more or less active, and more excretable. Mostly the liver (cytochrome P450 enzymes); also kidneys, lungs, plasma, intestinal mucosa Liver disease → drugs metabolize slower → higher risk of toxic accumulation 🧠 "Liver = the drug's chemistry lab." It rebuilds the molecule before the kidneys can flush it.

After the liver renders it inactive, it's excreted mainly by the kidneys via urine . Other routes: bile/feces, lungs (volatile drugs), sweat, breast milk Renal failure = drug accumulation risk — dose adjustments needed 🧠 "Bad kidneys, bad exit — the drug gets stuck inside." Always check renal function before dosing in older or renally-impaired clients. 🔄
STEP 2 · WHY ROUTE CHANGES THE DOSE Same drug, same dose, different route — the amount that actually reaches circulation can be wildly different.

entries.h: 🔄 First-pass effect — oral drugs get "taxed" by the liver first
entries.t: First-pass effect : the concentration of an oral drug is greatly reduced before it ever reaches systemic circulation , because it's absorbed through the intestine, travels via the portal vein , and passes through the liver first. Sublingual, rectal, and IV routes bypass some or all of this. 🧠 "Oral pays a liver toll before it can spend itself in the body." That's why oral doses of some drugs are much higher than IV doses of the exact same drug.

The drug must dissolve before it can be absorbed. Liquids and IV meds are already dissolved → absorb fastest. CAUTION A tablet/capsule must pass through the GI tract to dissolve. Enteric-coated / time-released capsules are built to dissolve only in the alkaline environment of the small intestine. 🧠 Never crush an enteric-coated or extended-release tablet — it destroys the coating meant to protect the stomach or delay release.

This phase is ADME itself — how the drug is transported and distributed through absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion. 🧠 Pharmaceutic → Pharmacokinetic → Pharmacodynamic. Dissolve it, move it, then let it act.

entries.h: 🎯 Pharmacodynamic phase — what the drug does
entries.t: Deals with the drug's action and effect on the body — two mechanisms: alteration in cellular function or alteration in cellular environment . Primary effect = the desired therapeutic effect Secondary effect = any other effect — e.g. sildenafil was developed for hypertension, its secondary effect treats erectile dysfunction 🧠 A secondary effect isn't a mistake — sometimes it becomes the drug's most famous use. ⏳
STEP 3 · TIMING THE DOSE This is the math behind why dosing schedules exist — and why some drugs need blood levels drawn.

entries.h: ⏳ Half-life decay curve — 50% gone every interval
entries.t: Half-life (t½) = the time it takes for the body to eliminate 50% of the drug. A short half-life needs frequent dosing; a long half-life needs infrequent dosing — but takes longer to reach a stable ("steady state") level. 🧠 "Half, half, half again." Each half-life cuts what's left in half — it never technically hits zero, but after ~4–5 half-lives it's clinically gone.

Onset of action = time to reach a therapeutic effect after administration Peak concentration = when the absorption rate equals the elimination rate (the highest point) Duration = how long the drug keeps producing a therapeutic effect 🧠 "Onset starts it, peak is the top, duration is how long it lasts."

entries.h: 🎯 Therapeutic index — narrow vs. wide window
entries.t: 🧠 Narrow window = tight rope, no net. Too little = no effect; too much = toxicity — with barely any room in between.

The therapeutic index is the range between the minimum effective concentration and the minimum toxic concentration . Narrow-index drugs (digoxin, warfarin, lithium, phenytoin, theophylline, aminoglycosides) require routine blood levels and careful dose titration — this connects directly to peak/trough monitoring and toxic ranges & antidotes. 🧠 "Wide window, wing it a little; narrow window, watch it like a hawk." ⚠️
STEP 4 · WHEN THE MATH GOES WRONG Different words for different kinds of "this didn't go as planned" — the vocabulary examiners love to mix up.

entries.h: 🚨 Adverse, allergic, anaphylactic, angioedema — severity ladder
entries.t: Term What it means Adverse drug reaction Undesirable effect — mild, severe, or life-threatening; can occur at first dose or after repeated doses Allergic reaction Immune-mediated hypersensitivity — the body treats the drug as a foreign invader; can be immediate or delayed Anaphylactic shock 🚨 Extremely serious, usually immediate — requires emergency treatment to support BP & breathing; can be fatal Angioedema Fluid collects in subcutaneous tissue — most commonly eyes, lips, mouth, throat → airway risk 🧠 "Adverse is

Toxic reaction — levels build up because the body can't excrete the drug Cumulative effect — seen in liver/kidney disease; one dose isn't cleared before the next is given Idiosyncrasy — an unusual, unpredictable reaction, often genetic Drug tolerance — decreased response over time, requiring a higher dose (e.g., opioids) 🧠 "Toxic builds up, tolerance wears off." Opposite problems, both from repeated dosing.

entries.h: 🔗 Drug interactions — additive vs. synergistic vs. antagonistic
entries.t: Type Effect Additive Combined effect equals the sum of each drug given alone Synergistic Combined effect is greater than expected — e.g. hypnotics + alcohol → increased CNS depression Antagonistic One drug blocks another — e.g. naloxone reverses opioids 🧠 Synergy stacks the danger, antagonism cancels it out.

Food interaction — some foods increase or decrease drug metabolism (e.g. grapefruit juice + many CYP3A4 drugs) Teratogen — any substance causing abnormal fetal development Pharmacogenomics — genetic makeup alters how a person responds to a drug 🧠 EXAM TIP influence on metabolism also includes age, weight, disease state, and route — not just genetics or food.

entries.h: 🧭 Sympathomimetic vs. sympatholytic vs. parasympathomimetic vs. parasympatholytic
entries.t: Term Effect Sympathomimetic Mimics the sympathetic nervous system ("fight or flight") Sympatholytic Blocks/inhibits sympathetic nervous system transmission Parasympathomimetic (cholinergic) Stimulates the parasympathetic nervous system via acetylcholine (ACh) Parasympatholytic (anticholinergic) Reduces parasympathetic nervous system activity 🧠 "Mimetic mimics, lytic blocks." Pair that with sympathetic (fight/flight) vs. parasympathetic (rest/digest) and you can predict the effect of almost any autonomic drug. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🚶 ADME Absorption → Distribution → Metabolism → Excretion 🔄 First-pass Oral drugs lose potency through the liver first ⏳ Half-life Time to eliminate 50% — sets dosing frequency 🎯 Narrow index Digoxin/warfarin/lithium need blood levels

Q1: What do the letters ADME stand for? Show answer Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion — the four pharmacokinetic phases a drug moves through. Q2: What is the first-pass effect, and which routes avoid it? Show answer Oral drugs travel via the portal vein through the liver before reaching systemic circulation, reducing the amount that's active. IV bypasses it completely; sublingual and rectal routes bypass some of it. Q3: Define half-life. Show answer The time it takes for the body to eliminate 50% of t

entries.h: Withdrawal Meds · NG-277 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Pharmacology · Substance Withdrawal Management

Alcohol vs. opioid withdrawal — different drugs, different priorities, one nurse watching vitals NG-277 PHARM ADHD-friendly visual edition Withdrawal management is not one protocol — it's two very different physiologic pictures. Alcohol withdrawal can kill via seizures and delirium tremens , so benzodiazepines are the safety net. Opioid withdrawal is miserable but rarely lethal on its own, so care focuses on symptom control and medication-assisted treatment (MAT) . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🍺 Alcohol = benzos are safety Prevent seizures/DTs — dosed by CIWA-Ar symptom score. 💉 Opioid = MAT + clonidine Methadone/buprenorphine treat cravings; clonidine controls autonomic symptoms. 🍷 Disulfiram = arts & crafts caution Any alcohol source (even rubbing alcohol, mouthwash) can trigger a severe reaction. 🫀 Methadone = watch QT ECG for prolonged QT, monitor O2 sat and sedation level. 🍺
STEP 1 · THE ONE THAT CAN KILL Untreated alcohol withdrawal can progress to seizures and delirium tremens — benzodiazepines are the life-saving drug class here.

EXAM TIP Benzodiazepines (e.g., chlordiazepoxide, diazepam, lorazepam) are first-line for alcohol withdrawal because they cross-tolerate with alcohol at the GABA receptor — they prevent the two most dangerous complications: withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens (DTs) .

Exposure A substance alters CNS or other organ function. Adaptation Tolerance or physical dependence may develop. Reduced exposure Withdrawal can follow abrupt reduction or cessation. Intoxication Assess airway, breathing, circulation, temperature, glucose and injury as indicated. Withdrawal Alcohol and sedative withdrawal can be life-threatening and require monitored treatment. Recovery care Use respectful language, symptom treatment and evidence-based ongoing support. 🧠 "No benzo, no brake." Benzodiazepines are t

Many units dose benzodiazepines using the CIWA-Ar (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol, revised) — a structured symptom score (tremor, sweating, anxiety, hallucinations, orientation, etc.). A higher score → more medication ; exact cutoffs vary by facility protocol. 🧠 "Score drives the dose." CIWA-Ar lets the nurse titrate benzodiazepines to the client's actual symptom burden instead of a fixed schedule.

Disulfiram deters drinking by causing a severe reaction (flushing, nausea/vomiting, palpitations, hypotension) if alcohol is consumed. Teach patients to avoid all alcohol sources — not just drinks. 🧠 "ARTS & CRAFTS caution." Rubbing alcohol, mouthwash, cooking wine, and alcohol-based hobby/craft products (glues, paints, hand sanitizer) can all trigger a reaction — teach clients to check labels broadly, not just beverages. 💉
STEP 2 · SYMPTOM CONTROL + MAT Rarely life-threatening on its own, but three very different tools are used together: full agonist, partial agonist, and non-opioid symptom control.
🧠 Full details on clonidine's withdrawal role are on NG-243 · Clonidine — this page places it alongside methadone/buprenorphine so you can see the whole picture at once.

🌡️ Long half-life — can accumulate; effects may lag behind dosing 🤢 Early signs of toxicity: nausea/vomiting, lethargy, frequent emesis 📉 Monitor: prolonged QT interval on ECG 😴 Client "falls asleep easily" — a red flag for over-sedation/toxicity, not just fatigue 🧠 "Sleepy and sick = stop and check." A methadone client who is unusually drowsy and vomiting needs an urgent reassessment, not just reassurance.
🧠 <90% on a methadone client is not "borderline" — treat it as an early sign of opioid over-sedation until proven otherwise.

As a partial agonist , buprenorphine has a ceiling effect on respiratory depression — a safety advantage over full agonists like methadone at typical doses. It's frequently combined with naloxone (an opioid antagonist) to deter misuse, since naloxone has little effect orally/sublingually but blocks euphoria if the product is misused by injection. 🧠 "Partial credit, full safety net." Buprenorphine won't fully activate the receptor the way methadone does, which is exactly why its overdose ceiling is safer. 🩺
STEP 3 · CROSS-CUTTING PRIORITIES Different drugs, same nursing job underneath: watch vitals, watch sedation level, and never assume "just withdrawal" explains a symptom.

1 🩺 Vital signs frequently — HR, BP, RR, temp, SpO₂ 2 😴 Sedation/LOC checks — especially with methadone or clonidine on board 3 📉 ECG for QT if on methadone 4 🧮 Symptom scoring (e.g., CIWA-Ar) to guide alcohol withdrawal dosing 5 🗣️ Full medication reconciliation — disulfiram + hidden alcohol sources, other CNS depressants 🧠 The tools differ by substance, but the underlying nursing job is the same: catch deterioration early, before it becomes a code.

entries.h: 🆚 Alcohol vs. opioid withdrawal — tell them apart
entries.t: Feature Alcohol Opioid Can it kill untreated? Yes — seizures, DTs Rarely, on its own Primary safety drug Benzodiazepines None required to prevent death; MAT for cravings Scoring tool CIWA-Ar Facility-specific opioid withdrawal scales exist, less universally standardized Long-term relapse prevention Disulfiram (deterrent), naltrexone (varies by protocol) Methadone / buprenorphine (MAT) 🧠 "Alcohol can kill you leaving it; opioids rarely do." That single fact is why the safety-drug priority is so different between the

⚡ New seizure alcohol withdrawal emergency 🌀 Confusion/hallucinations possible DTs — escalate 😴 Excess sedation methadone/clonidine toxicity 💓 Prolonged QT methadone — ECG changes 🧠 See NG-243 · Clonidine for that drug's specific withdrawal role and safety profile in more depth. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🍺 Benzos = alcohol safety net prevent seizures & DTs, dosed by CIWA-Ar 💉 MAT = methadone/buprenorphine full vs. partial opioid agonist for cravings 🩹 Clonidine = symptom control not MAT — see NG-243 🚫 Disulfiram = any alcohol source even rubbing alcohol/hobby products can react

Q1: Why are benzodiazepines the priority drug class in alcohol withdrawal? Show answer They cross-tolerate with alcohol at the GABA receptor and prevent the two most dangerous complications — withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens (DTs). Q2: What's the key difference between methadone and buprenorphine? Show answer Methadone is a full opioid agonist; buprenorphine is a partial agonist with a ceiling effect on respiratory depression, giving it a wider safety margin. Both are used for MAT in opioid use disorder. Q3
Bright painless bleeding or a rigid painful uterus — the classic pair, with the caveat that neither picture is guaranteed. Plus the one exam you must not perform.

entries.h: ⚖️ The comparison that answers the question

entries.t: 🩸 Previa Painless bright red bleeding, often first noticed on waking Uterus soft and non-tender Fetal position often abnormal — the placenta blocks engagement Bleeding may stop and recur 🚨 Abruption Sudden constant pain , often described as tearing Rigid, board-like uterus that does not relax Bleeding may be concealed behind the placenta — so the visible loss underestimates the real loss Signs of shock out of proportion to what you can see — hypotension and tachycardia may be the only clue to a concealed bleed The

In abruption, blood can be trapped behind the placenta. A rising fundal height, worsening pain and shock with little visible bleeding is a concealed abruption. Trust the vital signs, not the pad count.

1 Assess maternal vitals and fetal heart rate 2 Left side-lying position 3 Oxygen; two large-bore IVs 4 Type and crossmatch; CBC, coagulation studies 5 Continuous monitoring; prepare for C-section Nothing by mouth — surgery may be imminent Weigh pads to quantify blood loss (1 g ≈ 1 mL) Strict input and output; indwelling catheter RhoGAM if the mother is Rh negative — any bleeding event can sensitize her Steroids to mature fetal lungs if preterm delivery is likely

DIC is a real risk in abruption — the damaged placenta releases thromboplastin, which consumes clotting factors. Watch for bleeding from IV sites, gums and the nose , petechiae, and oozing that will not stop. Labs: low platelets, low fibrinogen, prolonged PT/aPTT, raised D-dimer.

No digital cervical exam until previa is excluded — ultrasound first Painless bright = previa. Painful rigid = abruption. Concealed abruption: shock out of proportion to visible bleeding Hypertension and cocaine are the classic abruption risks Two large-bore IVs, left side, oxygen — for both Sources. A whole-body vascular disease, not a blood pressure number. The three symptoms that mean a seizure is coming, and how magnesium is monitored.

The whole spectrum on one plate — the current definition (new hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria or qualifying organ dysfunction), severe-range numbers, magnesium and its toxicity checks, HELLP, and the reminder that both can develop after the birth .

Vessels constrict and leak. Every organ gets less blood, and fluid moves out of the circulation into tissue. That single mechanism explains everything: the hypertension, the protein in urine, the facial edema, the headache, the liver pain and the seizures. Gestational hypertension Preeclampsia Severe features Blood pressure New ≥140/90 after 20 weeks New ≥140/90 after 20 weeks ≥160 systolic or ≥110 diastolic Proteinuria None Usually present — but not required if new organ dysfunction (below) is present May or may n

These three mean a seizure may be imminent. Report immediately. 1 Severe headache not relieved by acetaminophen 2 Visual changes — blurring, spots, flashing lights 3 Epigastric / RUQ pain — the liver capsule stretching Epigastric pain in preeclampsia is not indigestion. It is a late, ominous sign and the patient may seize within hours.
The same warning symptoms as pictures, next to what makes it eclampsia : a new seizure . A bad headache on its own is not eclampsia.
Timing: usually after 20 weeks of pregnancy. Both can also occur after birth .

High blood pressure with proteinuria or other organ involvement. It may cause no noticeable symptoms ; it can show up first on the blood pressure, urine or labs. Warning symptoms Severe, persistent headache Blurred vision, spots or flashing lights Upper-right abdominal or epigastric pain New nausea or vomiting later in pregnancy Sudden swelling of the face or hands Shortness of breath or reduced urine output Clinical findings: high blood pressure; possible protein in the urine, low platelets, or kidney/liver abnorm

Defining feature: new seizures associated with preeclampsia, without another identified cause. Often body stiffening and rhythmic jerking Loss of consciousness Confusion or marked sleepiness afterward May occur without warning symptoms or a recognized preeclampsia diagnosis A medical emergency.
Systolic ≥160 OR diastolic ≥110 mmHg needs urgent assessment.

Proteinuria is not required when other organ dysfunction is present. Swelling alone is not diagnostic. Not every case of preeclampsia progresses to eclampsia. A seizure still needs assessment for other causes.

Hydralazine → lowers severe blood pressure. Magnesium sulfate → prevents or treats eclamptic seizures. It is not the blood pressure medicine. Memory cue: Eclampsia adds seizures. Sources checked 12 October 2026: ACOG Practice Bulletin 222 · MedlinePlus: Preeclampsia · MedlinePlus: Eclampsia · NICE NG133 . A classroom learning aid, not an official ACOG or NICE graphic.

Five questions on the plate above. Pick your answer, then tap Show the answer . They are also in the NUR 234 Module 9 quiz and the Mega Quiz. 1 of 5. A client at 34 weeks with preeclampsia reports "the worst headache of my life." BP is 162/104. She is awake, talking and has not had a seizure. How does the nurse classify her condition? A. Eclampsia, because a severe headache with severe-range BP is eclampsia B. Preeclampsia with a severe feature: a warning symptom and a severe-range systolic pressure C. Eclampsia, b

Answer: B Eclampsia means a new seizure. A severe headache is a warning symptom, and a systolic of 160 or more is severe range, so this is preeclampsia with severe features: report it now and keep seizure precautions in place. It is not eclampsia until she seizes, and the diastolic does not need to reach 110 when the systolic is already 160 or more. 2 of 5. Which blood pressure in a client with preeclampsia is in the severe range? A. 158/108 B. 155/105 C. 150/112 D. 145/100

Answer: C Severe range is systolic 160 or more OR diastolic 110 or more . Either number alone is enough, so 150/112 qualifies on the diastolic. 158/108 and the others miss both cut-offs, though they still need close follow-up. 3 of 5. On postpartum day 3, a client who had normal blood pressures throughout pregnancy reports a severe headache and seeing spots. BP is 164/100. What does the nurse do? A. Give acetaminophen and recheck in 4 hours; preeclampsia ends once the placenta is delivered B. Reassure her that head

Answer: D Preeclampsia and eclampsia can both start after birth , even with no hypertension during pregnancy. A severe headache, visual changes and a severe-range systolic are warning signs, so the provider is notified now. Delivering the placenta does not rule it out. 4 of 5. A client receiving IV magnesium sulfate for preeclampsia with severe features has a BP of 168/112. She asks, "Isn't the magnesium supposed to bring my blood pressure down?" What is the nurse's best response? A. "Yes. Your pressure will come d

Answer: B Magnesium sulfate prevents or treats eclamptic seizures; it is not the blood pressure medicine. Severe-range pressure is treated with an antihypertensive such as hydralazine. Turning up the magnesium to chase a blood pressure risks toxicity: lost reflexes, then slowed breathing. 5 of 5. Which statements about preeclampsia and eclampsia are true? (Select all that apply.) A. Swelling of the face and hands alone confirms preeclampsia B. Proteinuria is not required when other organ dysfunction is present C. E

Answer: B, D, E Preeclampsia is new hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria or other organ involvement, so proteinuria is not required. Eclampsia can arrive without warning or a prior diagnosis, and both can begin postpartum. Swelling alone is common in pregnancy and is not diagnostic, and most preeclampsia never progresses to seizures.

Stay with her ; call for help Turn on her side ; protect from injury; do not restrain Nothing in the mouth Oxygen by mask once the seizure ends; suction as needed Note the time and duration ; assess fetal heart rate after Prepare for delivery once she is stable

H aemolysis · E levated L iver enzymes · L ow P latelets. A severe variant — and dangerous because it can occur with only mildly raised blood pressure . Presents with malaise, nausea and RUQ pain . Do not rule out severe disease because the blood pressure looks acceptable. Check the platelets and liver enzymes.

Magnesium prevents seizures. It is not an antihypertensive. That distinction is worth marks on its own — severe-range blood pressure is treated separately, with labetalol, hydralazine or immediate-release nifedipine . Therapeutic range 4–7 mEq/L Serum magnesium — what is lost, in order mEq/L 4–7 therapeutic >8 reflexes lost >12 respiratory arrest

entries.t: Check Hold and report if Deep tendon reflexes Absent or diminished — usually the earliest toxicity sign Respiratory rate <12/min Oxygen saturation and lung sounds Falling SpO 2 ; crackles or shortness of breath — pulmonary edema Urine output <30 mL/hr — magnesium is cleared renally, so it accumulates Level of consciousness Lethargy, slurred speech, confusion Serum magnesium , when ordered Above the therapeutic range How often each is checked is set by your protocol — it is the same panel every time. Antidote: calci

Quiet, dim room ; minimal stimulation — light and noise can trigger a seizure Seizure precautions : padded rails, suction and oxygen at the bedside Left lateral position to maximize placental perfusion Daily weights; strict input and output; the magnesium panel above as often as protocol requires Continuous fetal monitoring

Magnesium prevents seizures , it does not lower blood pressure Reflexes are usually the first thing lost in toxicity — but monitor reflexes, respirations, urine output, LOC, SpO 2 , lung sounds and levels together Proteinuria is not required for preeclampsia when new organ dysfunction is present Severe-range BP ( ≥160/110 ) is treated with labetalol, hydralazine or nifedipine — not magnesium Calcium gluconate is the antidote Facial and hand edema is abnormal; dependent ankle edema is normal HELLP can occur with nea

The leading cause of maternal death worldwide. Call for help early, feel the fundus, and work out which of the four Ts is causing it.

entries.h: 🧬 What counts, and why it happens

entries.t: Bleeding recognized Quantify loss and assess circulation. Cause assessment Tone, trauma, tissue and thrombin organize the differential. Coordinated treatment Treat the cause while restoring perfusion. Tone A poorly contracted uterus is a common cause; assess fundus and bladder. Other causes Genital tract injury, retained tissue and coagulation problems need different treatment. Escalation Activate the hemorrhage pathway; monitor response and give prescribed therapies promptly. Blood loss over 500 mL after a vaginal

Cause Recognize it by Fix Tone — atony (most common) Boggy, soft uterus Massage and uterotonics Trauma — laceration, hematoma FIRM uterus but still bleeding — a bright red steady trickle; or severe perineal or rectal pain and swelling (hematoma) Find and repair; a hematoma may need evacuating Tissue — retained placenta Placenta not intact on inspection; bleeding persists despite treatment Manual removal, D&C Thrombin — clotting disorder Oozing everywhere, no clots forming Blood products If the uterus is FIRM and sh

Overdistended uterus — twins, big baby, polyhydramnios Prolonged or very rapid labor ; oxytocin augmentation Grand multiparity — the muscle is tired Retained placental fragments; previous PPH Chorioamnionitis; magnesium sulfate (it relaxes smooth muscle)

entries.h: 🩺 What to do — urgently, and all at once
entries.t: This is not a ladder. Help is called at the start, and these happen together: Call for help and notify the provider early — in parallel, not after everything else Assess the fundus. Boggy: massage it, with the other hand supporting the lower uterine segment. Firm: do not keep massaging — look for another cause Empty the bladder — void or catheter; if the uterus is deviated to the right, this comes before massage IV access and fluids ; oxygen 10 L/min by nonrebreather mask; uterotonics per order Quantify the blood l

A uterus displaced to the RIGHT and sitting above the umbilicus means a full bladder. A distended bladder physically prevents the uterus from contracting down. Boggy + deviated right = empty the bladder Boggy and deviated to the right : empty the bladder first (void or catheterize), then reassess and massage if it is still boggy. Boggy in the midline : massage first . Either way, call for help early. Drug Note Oxytocin First line; IV infusion or IM Methylergonovine Contraindicated in hypertension — it raises blood

Should be firm, midline, at or just below the umbilicus right after birth Descends about 1 cm per day If it is boggy, massage it — support the lower uterine segment with one hand while massaging with the other — otherwise you risk inverting the uterus Lochia Days Color Abnormal if Rubra 1–3 Dark red Saturating a pad in under an hour ; clots larger than a golf ball Serosa 4–10 Pinkish-brown Returns to bright red Alba 11–21+ Creamy white Foul odor = infection

Tachycardia comes first. Blood pressure falls late. A young healthy postpartum woman can compensate for a large loss and then crash suddenly. Rising pulse, then falling BP Cool clammy skin, pallor Restlessness and anxiety — cerebral hypoxia Urine output below 30 mL/hr Do not be reassured by a normal blood pressure in a bleeding postpartum patient. Watch the pulse.

Call for help early — at the same time as everything else Boggy fundus → massage , lower segment supported. Massage is for a boggy uterus, not every bleed Firm uterus + still bleeding = not atony — check for trauma, retained tissue and a clotting problem Deviated right + boggy = full bladder Methylergonovine + hypertension = no . Carboprost + asthma = no Tachycardia is the early sign; hypotension is late Sources. Written from NICHD , CDC Reproductive Health , MedlinePlus and OpenStax A&P 2e (CC BY 4.0).
The cord slips ahead of the baby and gets compressed. You lift the presenting part off it with your hand and you do not let go.

Almost always at rupture of membranes — the gush of fluid can carry the cord down. Higher risk when the presenting part is not engaged: Breech or transverse lie Polyhydramnios — a large gush Preterm or small baby ; multiple gestation High presenting part; artificial rupture of membranes The very first action after any rupture of membranes is to check the fetal heart rate. Not the pad, not the color - the heart rate.

Sudden prolonged fetal bradycardia or deep variable decelerations The cord may be visible at the introitus, or felt on examination Often immediately after membranes rupture Variable decelerations mean cord compression — VEAL CHOP. A prolapse is the extreme form.

entries.h: 🩺 What to do — act, do not investigate
entries.t: 1 Call for help — press the emergency bell 2 Gloved hand lifts the presenting part OFF the cord — and stays there 3 Knee-chest or Trendelenburg position 4 Oxygen 8–10 L by face mask; stop oxytocin 5 Prepare for immediate cesarean

Never push the cord back in - handling it causes vasospasm and makes it worse Never leave the patient to go and call - use the bell, keep your hand in place Never remove your hand until the surgical team takes over, even in the lift If the cord is outside the body, cover it with a sterile saline-soaked gauze to prevent drying and vasospasm — but do not attempt to replace it.

Knee-chest and Trendelenburg use gravity to shift the baby’s weight away from the pelvic inlet, taking pressure off the cord. Both are uncomfortable and undignified, and both save the baby. Explain briefly and keep going.

Relieve the pressure with your hand — that is the first nursing action, before oxygen or position Never replace the cord Check FHR immediately after rupture of membranes , every time Knee-chest or Trendelenburg, oxygen, stop oxytocin, straight to theater Sources. Written from NICHD , CDC Reproductive Health , MedlinePlus and OpenStax A&P 2e (CC BY 4.0).

entries.h: Fetal Heart Rate Tracing Categories — Visual Study Guide
entries.t: Category I, II and III on page 1; variability, the three dips and the nursing response on page 2. Tap a page to open it full size. 🖨️ Download both pages as PDF

All must fit: baseline 110 to 160 bpm, moderate variability (6 to 25 bpm), no late or variable decelerations. Early decelerations and accelerations may be present or absent. Continue routine intrapartum care.

Anything that is not I or III: tachycardia over 160, minimal or marked variability, recurrent lates or variables with variability remaining, a prolonged deceleration. Evaluate the cause, correct what can be corrected, reassess. Category II alone does not mean acidemia or require a cesarean.

Absent variability plus one of: recurrent late decelerations, recurrent variable decelerations, or bradycardia under 110. Or a true sinusoidal pattern: smooth regular waves, 3 to 5 cycles a minute for 20 minutes or more. Act now: team evaluation and corrective measures; if it does not resolve, prepare for expedited birth. Absent variability alone is not III; minimal is not the same as absent.

Absent: undetectable. Minimal: 5 bpm or less. Moderate: 6 to 25 bpm. Marked: more than 25 bpm. Early: gradual, mirrors the contraction — head compression. Late: gradual, lowest point after the contraction peak — uteroplacental insufficiency. Variable: abrupt, onset to lowest point under 30 seconds — cord compression.

Check and call: confirm the fetal signal against the maternal pulse, check vitals, alert the team. Reposition: turn her to her side; avoid lying flat. Reassess. Pause stimulation: reduce or stop oxytocin for concerning changes or tachysystole, per protocol. Treat the cause: ordered IV fluid for hypotension, treat fever, amnioinfusion may be ordered for recurrent variables. Oxygen: your ATI book includes oxygen by mask for late decelerations; the 2025 ACOG guideline on this page limits it to maternal hypoxia. Escala

Baseline and variability Establish the ongoing pattern. Accelerations and decelerations Describe timing, shape, depth and duration. Context and response Consider contractions, medications and maternal condition. Early decelerations Often mirror contractions and relate to head compression. Variable decelerations Abrupt falls commonly relate to cord compression. Late decelerations Begin and recover later in relation to contractions and need contextual assessment. The lowest heart rate lines up with the contraction pe

The dip follows the contraction peak The lowest heart rate comes after the contraction peak. Recovery occurs after the contraction ends. WHY IT HAPPENS Reduced oxygen transfer through the placenta. NURSING RESPONSE Turn her onto her left side. Stop the oxytocin if it is running. Increase IV fluids. Give oxygen if indicated by maternal hypoxia, or per agency policy or provider prescription. Notify the provider. (ATI’s list; correct hypotension, check blood pressure and contractions.) Late = placental insufficiency R

An abrupt drop with changing timing The drop is abrupt: onset to lowest point takes less than 30 seconds. The relationship to contractions may vary. WHY IT HAPPENS Usually umbilical cord compression. NURSING RESPONSE Reposition the mother. Assess new decelerations after membrane rupture for possible cord prolapse. Escalate persistent or recurrent concerning patterns. Variable = cord compression Reveal pattern 3 04

WHY IT HAPPENS Often a normal response to fetal movement. NURSING RESPONSE A reassuring feature. Continue routine assessment of the whole tracing and the clinical situation. entries.h: 🧠 How to tell early from late in one look
entries.t: Early decelerations line up with the contraction. The lowest point of the dip sits directly under the peak. Late decelerations lag. The dip begins after the contraction starts, its lowest point comes after the contraction’s peak, and it has not recovered by the time the contraction is over. Early decelerations usually mirror contractions and reflect head compression. Late decelerations recover after contractions and can indicate reduced placental oxygen transfer. Interpret the whole tracing and the clinical situati

entries.h: 🚨 Late decelerations — assess, then resuscitate in utero

entries.t: A late deceleration is never read on its own. Check, every time: Baseline rate — normal, tachycardic or bradycardic? Variability — moderate is reassuring; minimal or absent is not Accelerations present or absent; decelerations — which type, and are they recurrent (with half or more of contractions)? Contractions — more than 5 in 10 minutes (averaged over 30) is tachysystole The trend — better or worse than the last review — and the category below Category What it looks like Response I — normal Baseline 110–160, mod

entries.h: 🩺 Intrauterine resuscitation — matched to the cause
entries.t: Turn her to a side-lying position first (your ATI decelerations section lists it as the first action), then add the measures that fit what is causing the pattern; often several happen at once. Reposition — lateral, left or right, whichever improves the tracing IV fluid bolus per order or protocol Stop or reduce oxytocin , especially with tachysystole Treat maternal hypotension — common after an epidural Cervical exam — rule out cord prolapse or rapid descent Notify the provider early, alongside the rest — not as th

The uterus rests on the inferior vena cava when the mother is supine. That reduces venous return, which drops cardiac output, which drops placental blood flow. Turning her onto her side lifts the uterus off the vessel. Venous return recovers, so placental perfusion recovers. Left side is the classic answer , but either side relieves the vena cava — and for cord compression, the right position is whichever one frees the cord.
For repetitive variable decelerations, sterile fluid is infused into the uterus to cushion the cord. It treats compression, not placental insufficiency.

Normal fetal heart rate is 110–160 bpm , assessed over 10 minutes between contractions. Tachycardia >160 — maternal fever, infection, dehydration, drugs Bradycardia <110 — cord compression, maternal hypotension, rapid descent

entries.h: ✅ Variability — the most important single feature
entries.t: Moderate variability means the fetal nervous system is well oxygenated. The line should look slightly bumpy, fluctuating 6–25 bpm . Variability Means Moderate (6–25) Reassuring — the single best sign of fetal wellbeing Absent Concerning — hypoxia, acidosis, or sedation Minimal May be sleep cycle, drugs, or early hypoxia Marked Investigate A flat line with no variability is more worrying than an occasional deceleration. Variability is the thing to protect.

External Internal How Belts on the abdomen — ultrasound + toco Scalp electrode + intrauterine pressure catheter Needs Nothing Ruptured membranes , dilated cervix, engaged head Gives Rate and contraction timing Accurate rate AND contraction strength Risk None; can lose signal with movement Infection Only internal monitoring measures how strong a contraction is — external toco shows frequency and duration only.

Late = placental = the bad one. Variable = cord = reposition Early decelerations need no action No fixed ladder — read the whole tracing, then reposition, fluids, stop or reduce oxytocin, treat hypotension, check for prolapse, and notify Oxygen only for maternal hypoxia or per protocol — not routine Category III = absent variability with recurrent decels or bradycardia, or sinusoidal — prepare for expedited delivery Moderate variability is the best reassurance there is Internal monitoring requires ruptured membrane

Four stages, what happens in each, and the nursing priority that changes at every transition. 🧘 Also on this topic: Labor — the 5 Ps, true vs false, and the four stages (NG-375) — how a contraction is measured and where the baby is (station). This page is the stage-by-stage nursing priorities.
🖼️ Open readable diagram & course labels
First Onset → 10 cm . The longest Second 10 cm → birth of baby Third Birth → placenta out . 5–30 min Fourth First 1–4 hours after

Phase Dilation She is You Latent 0–5 cm Talkative, excited, sociable Encourage walking, eating lightly, resting Active 6–7 cm Serious, inward, focused Breathing support, position changes, epidural often here Transition 8–10 cm Irritable, nauseated, shaking, "I can't do this" Firm calm reassurance; it is nearly over "I can't do this any more" is the classic transition line - and the correct response is to tell her this is the shortest phase and the baby is nearly here.

Full dilation to birth; urge to push, often involuntary Crowning — the head stays visible between contractions Encourage open-glottis pushing with contractions; rest between Monitor fetal heart rate every 5–15 minutes depending on risk Maternal vital signs every 5–30 minutes — not hourly; this is the stage where hypotension and exhaustion show up fastest

entries.h: 🚶 Keep her moving in second stage
entries.t: Encourage her to change position often. There is no one correct pushing position, and staying in one for the whole stage is what stalls descent. Each position does something different: Squatting or supported standing — opens the pelvic outlet the most; uses gravity Hands and knees — takes the pressure off the back, helps a baby rotate out of occiput-posterior Side-lying — slows a fast descent, protects the perineum, good with an epidural Semi-Fowler’s or upright in bed — the default, easy to monitor from Never leav

Open-glottis (do this) Valsalva / breath-holding (avoid) She pushes while breathing out — grunting, groaning, air moving Deep breath held 10 seconds while bearing down, three times per contraction Pushes when she feels the urge, for as long as it lasts Coached to a count, whether or not she feels anything Intrathoracic pressure stays near normal, so venous return holds Intrathoracic pressure rises, venous return falls, cardiac output falls Fetal oxygenation is maintained Placental perfusion drops — late deceleratio

Signs of separation: a gush of blood, the cord lengthens, the uterus becomes globular and rises. Never pull on the cord. Traction can invert the uterus, which is a catastrophic emergency. After delivery, inspect the placenta for completeness — retained fragments cause hemorrhage and infection.

The most dangerous hours. Assess every 15 minutes for the first hour: Fundus — firm, midline, at or below the umbilicus Lochia — amount, clots Bladder — a full bladder prevents contraction Vital signs — watch the pulse, it rises before the BP falls Perineum — swelling, hematoma

The very first action is to check the fetal heart rate - rupture is when cord prolapse happens. Then note TACO : T ime · A mount · C olour · O dour. Clear = normal Green = meconium — possible fetal distress; prepare for suction at birth Foul = infection Port-wine = abruption
P assenger · P assageway · P owers · P osition · P syche When labor stalls, the question is always which P has failed .

Position changes — upright and mobile shortens labor Counter-pressure on the sacrum for back labor Warm shower or bath; breathing techniques; a focal point Empty the bladder every 2 hours — a full bladder slows descent and hurts Epidural: fluid bolus first , then BP every 5 minutes; hypotension is the main risk

Cervical change defines true labor Irritable and saying she cannot cope = transition , nearly there FHR immediately after rupture of membranes Never pull the cord in the third stage Fourth stage: assess every 15 minutes ; check the bladder Second stage: encourage frequent position changes — that is the answer far more often than any single position Open-glottis pushing, never a 10-second breath-hold Fully dilated and pushing = no trips to the bathroom Sources. Written from NICHD , CDC Reproductive Health , MedlineP
Scored at 1 and 5 minutes — but it never decides the resuscitation. Plus the normal findings that frighten parents.

Birth transition The newborn establishes breathing and circulatory adaptation. Clinical assessment Breathing, heart rate and tone guide immediate support. Apgar documentation Summarizes condition and response at specified times. Five components Appearance, pulse, grimace, activity and respiration are scored separately. Resuscitation Begin indicated support based on assessment; do not wait for an Apgar score. Ongoing care Monitor temperature, breathing, feeding and perfusion. entries.h: 🧡 What decides resuscitation — NRP, in the first seconds
entries.t: At birth, ask three questions: Term? Good tone? Breathing or crying? All three yes — she stays skin-to-skin with her mother for routine care. Any answer no Warm, dry and stimulate; position the airway, and clear secretions only if needed Apneic, gasping or HR <100 Start positive-pressure ventilation (PPV) Then Keep reassessing the heart rate — NRP sets each next step Effective ventilation is the most important action in newborn resuscitation. The Apgar score is recorded alongside it, never waited for.

A newborn cannot shiver. Cold stress drives up oxygen and glucose consumption, so a cold baby quickly becomes a hypoglycemic, acidotic baby. Drying the baby immediately is one of the very first steps at birth — warm, dry, stimulate. For a baby who is not breathing, ventilation comes straight after and matters most. Heat loss How Prevent Evaporation Wet skin Dry immediately , remove wet linen Conduction Cold surface Pre-warm the scale, warm blankets Convection Draughts Away from vents, doors, fans Radiation Nearby c

Milia — tiny white spots on the nose. Do not squeeze; resolve alone Mongolian spots — blue-gray patches over the sacrum. Document them so they are not mistaken for bruising Erythema toxicum — blotchy red rash with pale centers; harmless Acrocyanosis — blue hands and feet for 24–48 h Pseudomenstruation and swollen breasts — maternal hormones Vernix, lanugo, molding of the head Weight loss up to 10% in the first days, regained by 2 weeks

Caput succedaneum Edema in superficial scalp tissue. It can cross sutures and is often apparent at birth. Usually resolves over a short period with observation. Cephalohematoma Blood beneath the periosteum over a skull bone. It does not cross that bone’s sutures. Monitor for jaundice and other complications. Subgaleal hemorrhage Blood collects beneath the galea and can spread across sutures. Diffuse or enlarging boggy swelling may accompany pallor, tachycardia or poor perfusion. Urgent response Suspected subgaleal

Caput succedaneum Cephalhematoma Crosses sutures? YES NO Present At birth Appears hours later Resolves Days Weeks Jaundice risk Low Higher — blood breaks down Caput Crosses. Cephalhematoma is Contained.

Within the first 24 hours = pathological. Usually hemolytic — Rh or ABO incompatibility. Always reported. After 24 hours, day 2–3 = usually physiological. Immature liver plus rapid breakdown of fetal red cells. Feeding is treatment - it moves bilirubin out through the stool. Phototherapy if levels rise: protect the eyes, monitor temperature and fluid balance.

Warm and dry first — part of the initial steps, before weighing; if she is not breathing, ventilation follows at once Acrocyanosis is normal ; central cyanosis is not Jaundice under 24 hours is always pathological Caput crosses sutures; cephalhematoma does not APGAR never delays resuscitation — 0–3 is a low score, not the trigger ; tone, breathing and heart rate decide Normal newborn: HR 110–160 , RR 30–60 , glucose above 40–45

Blood in a newborn’s stool is reported promptly. It is often maternal blood swallowed at the birth or from a cracked nipple — but only the provider’s workup can say so. Assess colour, amount and consistency, how she looks and feeds, and her belly, then report. Meconium — thick, tarry, dark green-black. First one within 24 hours . Transitional — greenish-brown and looser, around days 3 to 4 Milk stools — seedy, mustard-yellow if breastfed; paler and firmer if formula-fed Blood in the stool gets reported the day you

Early pregnancy bleeding sorted by where the pregnancy is. Shoulder pain means rupture; very high hCG means a mole.
🖼️ Open readable diagram & course labels

Unruptured — may be treated with methotrexate . Teach: avoid folic acid supplements and alcohol, and no intercourse until hCG is undetectable Ruptured — two large-bore IVs, type and crossmatch, oxygen, straight to theater RhoGAM if Rh negative Acknowledge the loss — this is a pregnancy loss as well as an emergency

Abnormal placental tissue grows instead of a fetus — grape-like vesicles filling the uterus. Sign Detail hCG Extremely high — far above expected for dates Uterus Larger than dates Bleeding Dark brown “prune juice”, may pass grape-like vesicles Fetal heart Absent ; no fetus on ultrasound Other Severe nausea and vomiting ; preeclampsia before 24 weeks Preeclampsia before 24 weeks is not normal preeclampsia — it points to a molar pregnancy. That detail is asked directly.

A baseline pelvic exam and an ultrasound scan of the abdomen , straight after evacuation — that is ATI’s wording for the baseline. Serum hCG weekly for 3 weeks, then monthly for 6 months, up to a year , to detect gestational trophoblastic disease Reliable contraception as part of follow-up care Rho(D) immune globulin after the procedure if she is Rh-negative A hysterectomy may be considered if she does not want future fertility, or if the risk of GTN is high ATI lists the baseline as a pelvic exam and abdominal ult

Shoulder pain = ruptured ectopic Very high hCG + uterus large for dates + no fetal heart = mole No pregnancy for one year after a mole. The schedule is weekly for 3 weeks, then monthly — an option saying only “monthly” has dropped the weekly phase. Preeclampsia before 24 weeks suggests a mole RhoGAM after any early pregnancy loss if Rh negative
Before 37 weeks. What stops it, what matures the lungs, and the two drugs with very different jobs.

Symptoms before term Contractions, pressure, backache or fluid loss may occur. Clinical evaluation Assess cervical change, membranes, infection and fetal status. Gestation-specific care Treatment depends on gestational age and the cause. Assessment Timing, fetal monitoring and appropriate examinations guide diagnosis. Treatments Corticosteroids, tocolysis, magnesium or antibiotics have specific indications. Teaching Explain symptoms that require reassessment and the individualized follow-up plan. Regular contractio

Teach every pregnant woman to report: Regular contractions — more than 4–6 an hour before 37 weeks Low, dull backache that comes and goes Pelvic pressure — “the baby feels like it is pushing down” Change in vaginal discharge — more, watery, or bloody Menstrual-like cramping; abdominal tightening Any gush or trickle of fluid Women often dismiss backache and pressure as normal pregnancy discomfort. Teaching them the difference is what gets them in early enough for steroids to work.

entries.h: 🩺 The two drugs, and why they differ
entries.t: One buys time. The other uses it. Tocolytics Corticosteroids Purpose Delay birth for about 48 hours Mature the fetal lungs Examples Nifedipine, indomethacin, terbutaline Betamethasone , dexamethasone Why 48 hours? That is how long the steroids need to work. The tocolytic exists to create the window

entries.h: 💉 Magnesium sulfate here does something different
entries.t: In preterm labor before about 32 weeks, magnesium is given for fetal neuroprotection — it reduces the risk of cerebral palsy. Same drug, same monitoring ( reflexes first , respirations, urine output, calcium gluconate at the bedside) — but a different purpose from its use in preeclampsia, where it prevents seizures.

Tocolysis is contraindicated when continuing the pregnancy is more dangerous than delivering: Chorioamnionitis or any intrauterine infection Severe preeclampsia or eclampsia Fetal distress or fetal death Significant hemorrhage, abruption Cervix already advanced If there is infection, delivery is the treatment. Stopping labor would keep the baby in an infected uterus.

Left lateral position; bed rest as ordered Hydration — dehydration itself can trigger contractions Continuous fetal and contraction monitoring Look for the cause : urinalysis, vaginal swabs, temperature Emotional support — fear for the baby is the dominant experience Involve neonatal team early; tour the NICU if there is time

Tocolytics buy 48 hours so steroids can work — that is the whole logic Betamethasone matures the lungs , it does not stop labor Magnesium here is neuroprotection , not seizure prevention Infection = deliver , do not tocolyse Treat UTIs promptly — a preventable cause Sources. Written from NICHD , CDC Reproductive Health , MedlinePlus and OpenStax A&P 2e (CC BY 4.0).
You cannot measure a breastfeed, so you judge it by output. Wet diapers, latch, and why mastitis is not a reason to stop.

entries.h: ⭐ Judge it by output, not intake

entries.t: Feeding cues Early hunger cues support timely feeding. Effective transfer Latch, suck–swallow coordination or appropriate bottle technique. Adequacy assessment Growth, urine/stool patterns and clinical condition matter. Breastfeeding Comfortable positioning, effective latch and support improve transfer. Bottle feeding Use paced, responsive feeding and the prescribed preparation method. Safety Never prop a bottle or microwave feeds; follow safe storage instructions. Nobody can measure how much a breastfed baby took.

A good latch takes the nipple AND a good mouthful of areola , with the lips flanged outward, chin touching the breast and nose free. Nipple pain almost always means a shallow latch. The fix is to re-latch, not to stop feeding. Never pull the baby off the breast. Break the suction first with a clean finger in the corner of the mouth, or the nipple tears. Problem What helps Engorgement Feed more often. Warm compress or shower before to let down; cold pack after for swelling Sore, cracked nipples Fix the latch; expres

Refrigerated: about 4 days Freezer: about 6 months (deep freeze longer) Store in sealed containers or milk bags , in small portions Thaw in the fridge or under warm running water Swirl to mix — separation is normal Never microwave breast milk or formula. It creates hot spots that burn, and microwaving destroys immune components in breast milk.

entries.h: 🥛 What breast milk is low in
entries.t: Vitamin D — supplementation is recommended for breastfed infants. Iron stores run down around 6 months — which is why iron-fortified cereal is the usual first solid. Breast milk provides immunoglobulins the baby cannot make yet, which formula cannot replicate.

entries.h: 🚨 Absolute feeding rules for the first year
entries.t: No honey before 12 months - infant botulism No cow's milk before 12 months No solids before about 4–6 months ; start with iron-fortified cereal One new food every 4–7 days so reactions can be identified Never prop the bottle — choking and ear infections Discard formula left more than 1 hour after a feed begins

6–8 wet diapers is the answer to “how do I know she is getting enough?” Keep feeding through mastitis Warm before, cold after for engorgement Break suction before removing the baby No honey, no cow’s milk, no microwaving Breastfeeding is not reliable contraception Sources. Written from NICHD , CDC Reproductive Health , MedlinePlus and OpenStax A&P 2e (CC BY 4.0).
The infections that cross the placenta and harm the fetus. What to avoid, what to screen, what to treat.

Maternal exposure or infection Routes and symptoms vary by organism. Fetal or newborn exposure Transmission may occur before, during or after birth. Targeted prevention and care Testing, vaccination or treatment depends on the infection. TORCH grouping A memory aid for several congenital infections, not one disease. Assessment Exposure history, gestational timing and test results guide counseling. Prevention Food safety, hand hygiene, indicated screening and vaccination planning reduce selected risks.
