entries.h: 👀 Each one, and the teaching that matters
entries.t: Infection Effect on the baby Prevention / teaching Toxoplasmosis Hydrocephalus, intracranial calcification, chorioretinitis Do not change cat litter. Wear gloves gardening. Cook meat thoroughly. Wash produce Rubella Deafness , cataracts, cardiac defects, intellectual disability Vaccinate BEFORE pregnancy; live vaccine, so not during CMV Commonest congenital infection; hearing loss, microcephaly Hand hygiene, especially around diapers and toddlers Herpes (HSV) Neonatal herpes — severe, often fatal C-section if activ

Rubella and varicella vaccines are LIVE - never give during pregnancy. Give postpartum, before discharge, and advise avoiding pregnancy for 4 weeks. Active genital herpes lesions at the onset of labor means cesarean delivery. Vaginal birth would infect the baby. Pregnant women do not change cat litter. Someone else does it, or gloves and thorough handwashing.

Rubella immunity at the first visit — if not immune, vaccinate postpartum Hepatitis B, HIV, syphilis serology Group B strep swab at 35–37 weeks Urine culture — asymptomatic bacteriuria is treated in pregnancy

A positive swab means IV antibiotics during labor — usually penicillin, ideally at least 4 hours before delivery so levels reach the baby. GBS is normal flora in the mother and harmless to her. The risk is entirely to the newborn.

Newborns show infection non-specifically — often without fever: Temperature instability — low as often as high Poor feeding , lethargy, irritability Respiratory distress, grunting, apnea Hypoglycemia, jaundice appearing early A newborn who is simply "not feeding well and floppy" may be septic. Absence of fever means nothing at this age.

No cat litter — toxoplasmosis Rubella vaccine postpartum , never during pregnancy Active herpes lesions = cesarean GBS swab at 35–37 weeks , IV antibiotics in labor Earlier infection = worse damage Sources. Written from NICHD , CDC Reproductive Health , MedlinePlus and OpenStax A&P 2e (CC BY 4.0).
Counting pregnancies, dating the birth, and the three levels of certainty that decide whether a sign is presumptive, probable or positive.

G: gravida Total pregnancies, including the current one. T, P and A Pregnancies ending at term, preterm or before the threshold used. L: living Number of living children. One pregnancy Twins count as one pregnancy in gravida and the outcome category. More than one child Twins may add two to the living-child count. Thresholds Use the gestational definitions specified by the course and clinical system. G — Gravida : total pregnancies, including the current one T — Term births, 37 weeks and beyond P — Preterm births,

A woman is pregnant now. She has had: a term daughter, twin boys born at 34 weeks (both alive), and one miscarriage at 10 weeks. G T P A L 4 1 1 1 3 G = 4 (current + daughter + twins + miscarriage). P = 1 because the twin pregnancy was one preterm birth. L = 3 because three children are alive. Twenty-four more like this, with the counting shown for every pregnancy: 🧮 GTPAL Case Lab

Level Source Examples Presumptive What she feels — subjective Amenorrhea, nausea, fatigue, breast tenderness, quickening Probable What the examiner finds Positive pregnancy test , Goodell’s, Chadwick’s, Hegar’s signs, Braxton Hicks, ballottement Positive Comes from the fetus itself Fetal heart tones , ultrasound visualization, examiner palpates fetal movement A positive pregnancy test is only PROBABLE, not positive. hCG can be raised by a hydatidiform mole and some tumors. Only direct evidence of the fetus — heartb

LMP − 3 months + 7 days + 1 year Example: LMP 10 May 2025 → minus 3 months = 10 February → plus 7 days = 17 February 2026 . It assumes a regular 28-day cycle, so it is an estimate. Ultrasound dating in the first trimester is more accurate.

12 weeks — at the symphysis pubis 20 weeks — at the umbilicus 20–36 weeks — height in cm roughly equals weeks of gestation More than 2 cm off suggests growth restriction, macrosomia, multiples, or a fluid problem.

entries.h: 📆 Visit schedule and what is checked
entries.t: Weeks Frequency Up to 28 Every 4 weeks 28–36 Every 2 weeks 36 to birth Weekly Every visit: weight, blood pressure, urine for protein and glucose, fundal height, fetal heart rate , and from later pregnancy, fetal movement.

entries.h: 🚨 Danger signs to teach at every visit
entries.t: Vaginal bleeding ; gush or leaking of fluid Severe headache, visual changes, epigastric pain — preeclampsia Swelling of the face and hands (ankle swelling alone is normal) Decreased or absent fetal movement Persistent vomiting; fever; burning on urination Regular contractions before 37 weeks

Twins = one G, one birth, two L Positive pregnancy test is only probable Only fetal heart tones, ultrasound or palpated movement are positive Fundal height ≈ weeks between 20 and 36 Face and hand edema is abnormal ; ankle edema is not Sources. Written from NICHD , CDC Reproductive Health , MedlinePlus and OpenStax A&P 2e (CC BY 4.0).
The placenta makes the mother insulin resistant on purpose. Why the baby is big and then goes hypoglycemic within an hour of birth.

Placental hormones Increase insulin resistance during pregnancy. Maternal hyperglycemia Glucose crosses the placenta. Fetal response Increased fetal insulin affects growth and post-birth adaptation. During pregnancy Monitor glucose and follow nutrition, activity and medication plans. At birth The newborn may be at risk for hypoglycemia after placental glucose delivery stops. After pregnancy Postpartum testing and long-term risk follow-up remain important. The placenta produces hormones — chiefly human placental lac
1-hour glucose challenge at 24–28 weeks — no fasting needed. An elevated result leads to… 3-hour glucose tolerance test — fasting, then timed draws. Two or more abnormal values confirm the diagnosis

1 Diet — controlled carbohydrate, small frequent meals 2 Exercise — walking after meals 3 Monitoring — fasting and post-meal glucose 4 Insulin if targets are not met Insulin is the drug of choice — it does not cross the placenta. Insulin needs rise through pregnancy as placental hormones increase, then drop sharply after delivery once the placenta is gone. Insulin requirements fall dramatically immediately after the placenta is delivered. A woman on insulin needs close glucose monitoring postpartum or she will go h

Maternal glucose crosses the placenta. Maternal insulin does not. So the fetus receives excess glucose and its own pancreas ramps up insulin production. Insulin is a growth hormone, which is why the baby grows large. At birth the glucose supply stops abruptly, but the baby's high insulin level does not - so it drops hypoglycemic within the first hour. In utero Excess glucose crosses Fetal response Pancreas makes extra insulin Growth Macrosomia — large baby At birth Glucose supply cut off First hour Hypoglycemia

Check blood glucose within the first hour and regularly after Feed early — breast or formula Watch for jitteriness, poor feeding, lethargy, weak cry, temperature instability Also at risk of hypocalcemia, polycythemia and hyperbilirubinemia Examine for birth injury — clavicle, brachial plexus — after a large delivery

Shoulder dystocia and operative delivery, from macrosomia Preeclampsia , polyhydramnios Recurrence in later pregnancies Roughly half develop type 2 diabetes within 10 years — so screening at 6–12 weeks postpartum, and regularly for life, is essential teaching

Screen at 24–28 weeks Insulin, not oral agents — it does not cross the placenta Insulin needs rise in pregnancy, crash after delivery Big baby, low sugar — check glucose in the first hour She needs lifelong diabetes screening afterwards Sources. Written from NICHD , CDC Reproductive Health , MedlinePlus and OpenStax A&P 2e (CC BY 4.0).
BUBBLE-HE, what each letter is actually looking for, and the three postpartum mood disorders that are not the same thing.

Immediate recovery Circulation, uterine tone and bleeding take priority. Early adaptation Pain, voiding, feeding and mobility need support. Ongoing surveillance Infection, thrombosis and mental-health concerns can emerge. Fundus and lochia Assess tone, position, amount and character; heavy or increasing bleeding is concerning. Comfort and function Review perineum/incision, bladder, bowel, breasts and mobility. Teaching Explain urgent warning signs, follow-up and available support. Letter Assess Normal B reasts Soft

Immediately after birth it should be firm, midline, at or just below the umbilicus . Boggy, midline → massage → empty bladder → reassess Deviated to the right and high → full bladder → empty it first , then reassess Not descending → think retained fragments or infection Always support the lower uterine segment with one hand while massaging with the other, or you risk inverting the uterus.

Complication Recognize by Key point Hemorrhage Boggy uterus, saturating a pad in <1 h Massage first ; pulse rises before BP falls Endometritis Fever after 24 h , foul lochia, uterine tenderness Antibiotics; a fever in the first 24 h is often dehydration UTI Frequency, burning, suprapubic pain Catheterization in labor raises risk Mastitis Red wedge on one breast, flu-like, fever Keep breastfeeding + antibiotics DVT / PE Unilateral calf pain and swelling; sudden dyspnea and chest pain Pregnancy is a hypercoagulable s

Baby blues Postpartum depression Postpartum psychosis Onset Days 3–5 Weeks to months Usually first 2 weeks Duration Up to 2 weeks Months if untreated Emergency Picture Tearful, mood swings, still functioning Hopeless, guilty, cannot function, may not bond Hallucinations, delusions , thoughts of harming self or baby Treatment Support, reassurance, rest Therapy, medication, screening Psychiatric emergency , hospitalization Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency. The infant must not be left alone with her, an

Fever after 24 hours = infection. In the first 24 h, suspect dehydration Severe perineal pain + firm uterus = hematoma Do not use Homans sign Blues resolve by 2 weeks ; beyond that, screen for depression Psychosis = emergency, never leave her alone with the baby Sources. Written from NICHD , CDC Reproductive Health , MedlinePlus and OpenStax A&P 2e (CC BY 4.0).
Two arteries and one vein, three shunts around the lungs, and the eight-week window when everything can go wrong.

Placenta and umbilical vein Oxygenated blood returns from the placenta. Fetal shunts Ductus venosus, foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus direct flow. Umbilical arteries Carry blood back toward the placenta. Ductus venosus Routes part of umbilical venous flow past the liver into systemic venous circulation. Foramen ovale Permits right-atrial to left-atrial flow. Ductus arteriosus Connects pulmonary artery and descending aorta, bypassing much pulmonary flow.

Gestational dating Usually counted from the last menstrual period. Embryonic development Organ formation occurs during early development. Ongoing growth Structures mature and function changes throughout pregnancy. Timing Gestational age is approximately two weeks greater than age from fertilization in a typical cycle. Exposure context Effects of an exposure depend on timing, dose and other factors. Assessment History, ultrasound and clinical findings guide dating and evaluation. Week 1–2 Fertilization, implantation
Heart begins beating — around week 3–4 Detectable on ultrasound — about 6 weeks Quickening (mother feels movement) — 16–20 weeks Viability — around 24 weeks Surfactant adequate — 34–36 weeks

entries.h: ⭐ The cord rule that is backwards
entries.t: AVA — 2 Arteries, 1 Vein The umbilical VEIN carries OXYGENATED blood TO the baby. The two arteries carry deoxygenated blood away to the placenta. It is the opposite of adult circulation, which is exactly why it is asked. A two-vessel cord - one artery missing - is abnormal and prompts investigation for kidney and other anomalies. Count the vessels at birth. Structure Job Note Placenta Exchange + endocrine organ Makes hCG, estrogen, progesterone, hPL Wharton’s jelly Cushions the cord vessels Prevents compression Amn

The lungs are full of fluid and do no work in utero , so blood is routed around them by three shunts. Shunt Bypasses Route Ductus venosus The liver Umbilical vein → inferior vena cava Foramen ovale The lungs Right atrium → left atrium Ductus arteriosus The lungs Pulmonary artery → aorta

entries.h: 👶 What happens at the first breath
entries.t: The lungs inflate, pulmonary resistance falls, and pressure in the left side of the heart rises. That pressure change closes the foramen ovale. Rising oxygen levels close the ductus arteriosus. A patent ductus arteriosus is one of these shunts failing to close — common in preterm infants, and treated with indomethacin or surgery.

Oligohydramnios (too little) — suggests kidney problems or a leak. The fetus makes the fluid by urinating Polyhydramnios (too much) — suggests the fetus cannot swallow : esophageal atresia, neural tube defects; also maternal diabetes Too little = kidneys. Too much = swallowing.

Two arteries, one vein — and the vein carries the oxygen Weeks 3–8 is the teratogen window Folic acid before conception Three shunts exist because the lungs do not work yet Oligo = kidneys; poly = swallowing Sources. Written from NICHD , CDC Reproductive Health , MedlinePlus and OpenStax A&P 2e (CC BY 4.0).
Most contraception questions are really contraindication questions. Learn who cannot have estrogen and the rest follows.

Estrogen increases clotting. Every contraindication below is either a clot risk or a hormone-sensitive cancer. Smoker over 35 - the classic exam stem History of DVT, PE or a clotting disorder Migraine with aura — stroke risk Uncontrolled hypertension Known or suspected pregnancy Breast cancer; active liver disease Under 6 weeks postpartum, or breastfeeding early on
A bdominal pain · C hest pain · H eadache (severe) · E ye problems · S evere leg pain Every one of those is a possible clot. This mnemonic is worth more marks than the method list.

entries.h: 📊 The methods, by how well they work
entries.t: Method Typical use Key teaching Implant / IUD >99% Most effective; nothing to remember. Copper IUD also works as emergency contraception Sterilization >99% Consider permanent; counsel accordingly Injection (Depo) ~96% Every 12 weeks ; bone density loss — calcium, vitamin D, weight-bearing exercise Combined pill / patch / ring ~93% Same time daily; estrogen rules above Condom ~87% The ONLY method that prevents STIs Diaphragm ~83% Refit after childbirth or big weight change; leave in 6 h after Withdrawal / fertility
An IUD or implant is more effective than sterilization on paper — but only condoms protect against infection . A woman with an IUD and a new partner still needs condoms. That is dual protection .

One pill missed — take it as soon as remembered, even if two in one day. No backup needed Two or more missed — take the most recent, continue the pack, and use backup for 7 days Vomiting or diarrhea counts as a missed dose Antibiotics and anticonvulsants can reduce effectiveness — use backup

A 28-day cycle in two halves, with ovulation in the middle. Follicular (days 1–14) Luteal (days 15–28) Hormone FSH , then estrogen LH , then progesterone Ovary Follicle matures Corpus luteum forms Uterus Lining rebuilds Lining becomes secretory, ready to implant Ovulation is triggered by the LH surge , about day 14. Menstruation begins about 14 days AFTER ovulation - that half is fixed, and cycle length varies in the first half.

Cervical mucus becomes clear, stretchy and slippery — like raw egg white (spinnbarkeit) Basal body temperature dips, then rises about 0.5°F and stays up Mittelschmerz — one-sided mid-cycle pain The temperature rise confirms ovulation after it has happened, so it is poor for avoiding pregnancy but useful for achieving it.

Smoker over 35 = no estrogen ACHES = report immediately Only condoms prevent STIs Depo = bone density, so calcium and weight-bearing exercise Luteal phase is fixed at 14 days ; the follicular phase varies Breastfeeding is not reliable contraception 📌
FROM YOUR SAVED SET

Start every conversation with one question: “Would you like to become pregnant in the next year?” Counselling is person-centered and noncoercive . The client chooses the method — or chooses no method. You make the choice informed, you do not steer it. Family What it is The hook Fertility awareness Track fertile days; avoid or use a barrier in the window Needs consistent monitoring and predictable cycles Barrier Condom, diaphragm, cap, sponge, spermicide Used at each act Hormonal Pill, patch, ring, injection, implan

entries.h: 🌿 Natural methods — and the one that is not contraception
🤝 LAM — all three or it does not count
entries.t: No return of menses Fully or nearly fully breastfeeding , day and night Less than 6 months postpartum Reassess immediately when any one criterion changes. Miss one and the method has stopped working.
Requires correct timing every single time , is less effective with typical use than most alternatives, and gives no STI protection.
This is not contraception. Sperm reach the cervix within seconds. Douching does not prevent pregnancy and must never replace emergency contraception.

Sign How it is measured What trips students up Calendar Standard Days Method is built for cycles 26–32 days Irregular cycles make it unreliable Basal body temp Before rising , same time daily, with a thermometer The rise happens after ovulation; illness and poor sleep skew it Cervical mucus Slippery, clear, stretchy — like raw egg white This is the classic exam answer for “how do I know I am fertile” LH testing Urine kit detects the pre-ovulatory LH surge Predicts ovulation; does not confirm it happened Fertility a

New condom for every act — never reuse either type Water- or silicone-based lubricant only. Oil weakens latex The internal condom goes in before any penile contact — pre-ejaculate carries sperm and STIs. It can be placed up to 8 hours ahead

Diaphragm — leave in 6 hours after intercourse, out within 24 hours Patch — weekly × 3, then a patch-free week Ring — monthly: 3 weeks in, 1 week out Depo — every 12 weeks IM Implant — 3 years , inner upper arm

Black-box warning for bone mineral density loss → calcium, vitamin D, weight-bearing exercise. Return of fertility can take 9–10 months . Progestin-only methods all share one headline side effect: irregular bleeding , heaviest early on.

entries.h: 🔩 IUDs — strings, timing, and who cannot have one
entries.t: Copper Levonorgestrel Duration up to 10 years 3–8 years by product Hormone none progestin Bleeding heavier or longer at first irregular early, then often lighter Also most effective emergency contraception not used with current breast cancer

Check monthly, after each period . Missing, longer, or shorter strings can mean expulsion or perforation — call the provider and use backup. Placed more than 7 days after bleeding began? Backup for 7 days .

Known pregnancy Current purulent cervicitis Current chlamydial or gonococcal infection Seek care for severe pelvic pain, fever, foul discharge, very heavy bleeding, changed strings, or a positive pregnancy test. Two myths exams love: IUDs are not restricted to people who have given birth, and fertility returns almost immediately after removal.
Blocks the vas deferens Does not reduce testosterone, erection, or desire Not immediately effective — backup until semen analysis confirms it

Occludes or removes the fallopian tubes Effective immediately Pregnancy is rare — if it happens, evaluate for ectopic Tubal ligation is a roadblock, not a shutdown. Ovulation, hormones, and periods all continue — the egg is simply reabsorbed. Sperm can no longer reach the ovum because the tubes are blocked.

Option Window Key points Copper IUD within 5 days Most effective. Works immediately and keeps working as ongoing contraception Ulipristal 30 mg within 5 days Better than LNG late in the window. Wait 5 days before starting hormonal contraception, then backup 7 days Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg ASAP, within 5 days Better the sooner it is taken. Start or resume hormonal contraception immediately , then backup 7 days EC does not end an established pregnancy and gives no STI protection. No bleeding within 3 weeks → pregnancy t
Preterm complications are all about organs that had not finished. RDS, NEC, and the signs of respiratory distress.

entries.h: 🧬 Why preterm babies get into trouble
entries.t: 🖼️ Open readable diagram & course labels

1 Tachypnea — over 60/min 2 Nasal flaring , grunting 3 Retractions — sternal, intercostal, subcostal 4 Central cyanosis , see-saw breathing 5 Apnea , bradycardia Grunting is the newborn trying to hold the alveoli open against collapse. It is never normal and always reported.

Antenatal steroids given to the mother — the single intervention that transformed RDS survival Surfactant replacement down the endotracheal tube after birth CPAP or ventilation ; oxygen carefully titrated Thermoregulation — incubator or radiant warmer; cold stress worsens everything Minimal handling; cluster care Acrocyanosis is normal. Central cyanosis of the lips, tongue and trunk is not.

entries.h: 💎 NEC and the diabetic mother's baby

entries.t: Ischemic bowel that becomes necrotic and can perforate. Risk rises with prematurity, formula feeding and hypoxic events. Distended, shiny, tender abdomen Feeding intolerance , increasing gastric residuals, bilious vomiting Blood in the stool Lethargy, temperature instability, apnea In suspected NEC, stop all feeds immediately and report. Feeding an ischemic gut makes it worse. Expect NPO, an orogastric tube for decompression, antibiotics and IV nutrition. Breast milk is protective — a real teaching point for mother

entries.h: 🥬 The infant of a diabetic mother
entries.t: Large baby, low sugar. Maternal glucose crossed; the baby’s pancreas overproduced insulin. At birth the glucose stops but the insulin does not. Check glucose within the first hour , then regularly Feed early Watch for hypocalcemia, polycythemia, hyperbilirubinemia Examine for birth injury — clavicle, brachial plexus

Withdrawal in a baby exposed to opioids in utero: high-pitched cry, jitteriness, poor feeding, sneezing, sweating, loose stools, difficulty settling . Swaddle ; dim lights , reduce noise and handling Small frequent feeds; high-calorie formula Scored regularly; medication if severe Support the mother without judgment — it improves outcomes for both

Bilirubin is fat-soluble and the newborn liver cannot conjugate it fast enough. Phototherapy changes its shape so it can leave in stool and urine without the liver. That is why feeding is half the treatment — nothing leaves if nothing moves through the gut. Timing decides everything: jaundice before 24 hours is pathologic (hemolysis — Rh or ABO incompatibility, infection). After 24 hours , usually day 2–3, is physiologic.

entries.h: 💡 Caring for a baby under the lights
entries.t: Do Why Change the position every 2–3 hours Only the skin facing the light is being treated. Rotating exposes all of it, and it prevents pressure areas on a baby who is lying still Naked except for a diaper , eyes covered Maximum skin exposed; the mask protects the retina Take the mask off every 4 hours Check for corneal irritation, drainage and pressure — and let the parents see the baby’s face Feed 8–12 times a day , breast milk or formula Stool is the exit route. More feeds, more stools, faster clearance Temperat

Expected — keep going Report A fine maculopapular rash Bilirubin still climbing after 4–6 hours Bronze discoloration of the skin Signs of dehydration — sunken fontanelle, few wet diapers Loose, greenish, frequent stools Temperature instability A sleepy baby who needs waking to feed Lethargy, hypotonia, arching, a high-pitched cry A fine rash is not a reason to stop the lights. That is a wrong answer written to look cautious. The one thing on the right-hand list you must never sit on is the last row — that is acute

Reposition every 2–3 hours under phototherapy No lotion, no oil on skin under the lights No water or glucose water — feed more milk instead A fine rash and bronzing are expected , not a reason to stop Jaundice under 24 hours old is always pathologic Grunting is never normal NEC → stop feeds, report Surfactant is inadequate before 34–36 weeks ; steroids to the mother accelerate it Big baby, low sugar — glucose in the first hour NAS care is swaddle, dim, quiet — reduce stimulation Sources. Written from NICHD , CDC Re
When to stop the oxytocin, what tachysystole does to the placenta, and the care that follows a cesarean.

entries.h: 💉 Oxytocin — and when to stop it

entries.t: Oxytocin effect Stimulates uterine contractions. Excess contraction activity Too little relaxation may reduce placental reperfusion. Assessment and response Evaluate maternal condition and fetal heart rate promptly. Recognize More than five contractions in ten minutes, averaged over thirty minutes, meets the standard tachysystole definition. When infusing oxytocin Reduce or stop the infusion and follow the fetal-response protocol when indicated. Reassess Position, pressure, fluid status and the tracing guide furthe

Contractions more often than every 2 minutes Contractions lasting longer than 90 seconds Resting tone does not return between contractions Any late decelerations or non-reassuring pattern Suspected uterine rupture Then: left side, oxygen 8–10 L, increase the maintenance IV, notify the provider. Oxytocin is a high-alert medication. It always runs as a secondary infusion on a pump, so it can be stopped instantly without losing IV access.

An unfavorable cervix is ripened first — prostaglandin gel or a mechanical balloon — because inducing an unripe cervix usually fails and ends in cesarean. The Bishop score rates dilation, effacement, station, consistency and position. A higher score means induction is more likely to succeed.

Deliberate rupture of membranes to speed labor. Check fetal heart rate immediately before and after Note TACO : time, amount, color, odor The head must be engaged first — otherwise the cord can prolapse Temperature every 2 hours afterwards — infection risk rises once the barrier is gone
Failure to progress — the commonest reason Fetal distress Malpresentation — breech, transverse Placenta previa ; cord prolapse; active herpes lesions Previous classical cesarean

Consent; IV access; bloods including type and crossmatch Indwelling catheter — keeps the bladder out of the surgical field Antacid to reduce aspiration risk Wedge under the right hip to tilt the uterus off the vena cava Antibiotic prophylaxis

entries.h: ✅ After — it is abdominal surgery AND postpartum
entries.t: You are assessing two things at once: Postpartum Post-surgical Fundus — firm, midline (palpate gently) Incision — REEDA Lochia — still occurs after cesarean Pain control , often PCA Breasts, bonding, feeding support Early ambulation — prevents DVT and ileus Bladder function after catheter removal Incentive spirometry , turn, deep breathe Lochia still happens after a cesarean — the placental site still has to heal. Students often forget to assess it.

Boggy uterus or heavy lochia Incision redness, separation, drainage, or a fever after 24 h Calf pain, sudden dyspnea or chest pain — DVT or PE Absent bowel sounds with distension — ileus Urine output under 30 mL/hr

Contractions closer than 2 min or longer than 90 s → stop oxytocin Oxytocin always runs as a secondary line on a pump FHR before and after amniotomy ; head must be engaged Assess lochia and fundus after a cesarean too Early ambulation is the key post-cesarean intervention Sources. Written from NICHD , CDC Reproductive Health , MedlinePlus and OpenStax A&P 2e (CC BY 4.0).
What is normal, what is not, and the fixes that actually work — plus where morning sickness stops being morning sickness.
🖼️ Open readable diagram & course labels

Complaint Why What actually helps Morning sickness hCG, first trimester Dry crackers before rising ; small frequent meals; avoid an empty stomach Heartburn Relaxed sphincter + pressure Small meals, stay upright after eating, avoid spicy and fatty food Constipation Slowed motility + iron Fiber, fluids, walking. No stimulant laxatives Leg cramps Circulation, calcium Dorsiflex the foot — do not point the toes Backache Shifted center of gravity Pelvic tilt exercises, low heels, side-lying with a pillow between the knee

entries.h: 🏃 Exercises that prepare the body for birth
entries.t: These are taught in prenatal class and they come up on exams, because each one has a specific target and students mix them up. None of them is about fitness or losing weight. Exercise What it does How it is taught Squatting Stretches and strengthens the perineal muscles and the pelvic floor, and widens the pelvic outlet for the second stage About 15 minutes a day. Feet flat and apart, hold onto a chair or a partner for balance, sink down with the back straight Kegel exercises Strengthens the pelvic floor — less lea

entries.h: 🚨 The wrong answers this question is built from
entries.t: “Squatting tones your abdomen and helps you lose weight faster after delivery.” — wrong twice over. It targets the perineum , not the abdomen, and weight loss is never the goal of a prenatal exercise. “It will reduce lower back pain during labor.” — that is the pelvic tilt , not squatting. “Three times a week improves your overall fitness.” — too vague, wrong frequency, and again the wrong purpose. Squatting = perineal muscles, about 15 minutes daily. Hold that pairing and the whole item falls out.

Tell her to stop and call: vaginal bleeding, leaking fluid, contractions, dizziness, chest pain, calf pain or swelling, headache, or decreased fetal movement. No lying flat on the back after the first trimester — vena cava again No contact sports, no scuba diving, nothing with a fall risk Do not get overheated — no hot tubs, no saunas Drink water; relaxin loosens the joints, so do not stretch to the very end of the range

This is not morning sickness. It is persistent vomiting causing: Weight loss over 5% of pre-pregnancy weight Dehydration — dry mucous membranes, poor turgor, concentrated urine Ketonuria — the body is burning fat for fuel Electrolyte imbalance — often hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis from losing gastric acid It needs IV fluids and often admission - not dietary advice.

1 NPO initially to rest the gut 2 IV fluids with electrolyte replacement 3 Antiemetics; vitamin B6, thiamine 4 Advance slowly — clear fluids, then bland small meals Daily weights and strict input and output — the objective measures of progress Quiet environment; remove strong smells, including food trays and perfume Sit upright for 45 minutes after eating Monitor for thiamine deficiency with prolonged vomiting It is associated with molar pregnancy and multiple gestation — both produce very high hCG. An ultrasound i

Face and hand edema is abnormal ; ankle edema is not Dorsiflex for leg cramps Left side for supine hypotension Do not restrict fluids for urinary frequency Hyperemesis = weight loss, ketones, IV fluids , not crackers Sources. Written from NICHD , CDC Reproductive Health , MedlinePlus and OpenStax A&P 2e (CC BY 4.0).
Leukemia, Wilms tumor, neuroblastoma, retinoblastoma — and the abdomen you must never palpate.

Abnormal cell growth Cancer can arise in marrow, organs or other tissues. Functional disruption Normal blood production or organ function is affected. Treatment and support Specialized care addresses disease and complications. Leukemia Marrow involvement can cause anemia, infection risk and bleeding. Solid tumors Persistent mass, bone pain or neurologic findings require evaluation. Nursing priorities Monitor infection, bleeding, pain, nutrition and treatment toxicity. The marrow fills with immature white cells, so

When chemotherapy kills large numbers of cells, they release purines that become uric acid , which can crystallize in the kidneys. Allopurinol plus generous hydration prevents that — part of preventing tumor lysis syndrome (high potassium, high phosphate, high uric acid, low calcium ).

Tumor Signature Key point Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) Firm, smooth abdominal mass , usually one side, often found on diaper change or bathing DO NOT PALPATE THE ABDOMEN Neuroblastoma Irregular abdominal mass crossing the midline ; often already metastatic at diagnosis Also do not palpate; usually under 5 years Retinoblastoma White pupillary reflex (leukocoria) instead of red reflex; squint Often noticed first in a photograph Osteosarcoma Pain and swelling near the knee in an adolescent; worse at night Long bone me

Hand hygiene above everything else Private room; screen visitors and staff for infection No fresh flowers, plants or standing water No raw fruit or vegetables; no undercooked food Daily soft-brush oral care ; check for mucositis No live vaccines for the child or household contacts

Effect Care Mucositis Soft brush or sponge, saline rinses, bland cool foods. No alcohol-based mouthwash, no lemon-glycerine swabs Nausea Antiemetics before chemotherapy, not after it starts Alopecia Prepare the child; hats, caps; hair grows back Fatigue Cluster care; short activity with rest

entries.h: 👅 Mucositis — the one they ask about
entries.t: Why it happens: chemo kills any rapidly dividing cell , and oral mucosa turns over every 7–14 days . The same lining runs the whole gut, so ulcers can appear from lip to anus . When: about 5–10 days after chemo starts; it heals as the ANC recovers . What you see: redness → white patches → open ulcers, with pain, drooling, bad breath, and a child who will not eat or drink. ✅ Do ❌ Never Soft toothbrush or foam swab; normal saline (or saline + baking soda) rinses q2–4h and after meals Alcohol mouthwash — burns and dri

entries.h: 🧠 Talking to the child by age
entries.t: Toddler / preschool — say plainly it is not a punishment ; keep the parent present School age — explain what the treatment does; give them jobs and choices; they worry about school and friends Adolescent — body image and fitting in matter enormously; confidentiality; involve them in decisions Encourage school attendance and normal activity whenever counts allow — normality is protective.

Never palpate a Wilms tumor abdomen White pupil = retinoblastoma Fever + ANC < 500 = emergency No rectal anything; no aspirin Allopurinol + fluids prevent uric acid stones Neuroblastoma crosses the midline ; Wilms usually does not Sources. Written from CDC Vaccines & Immunizations , HealthyChildren.org (AAP) , MedlinePlus and OpenStax A&P 2e (CC BY 4.0).

entries.h: 🧘 Labor — the 5 Ps, true vs false, and the four stages
entries.t: One picture for how a contraction is measured, one for where the baby is, and the four stages in the order you will be asked about them. 🏁 Also on this topic: The Stages of Labor (NG-324) — what happens in each stage and the nursing priority that changes at every transition. This page is the 5 Ps, true vs false labor, contractions and station.

Cervical change is what makes labor real. Not how much it hurts, not how often the contractions come — dilation and effacement . Everything else on this page is a way of describing or supporting that change.

entries.h: 🧮 The 5 Ps — what labor needs to go well

entries.t: The fetus — its size, lie , presentation , attitude and position . A well-flexed vertex presentation passes most easily.
The bony pelvis and soft tissues . A gynecoid pelvis is the most favorable shape.
The contractions (involuntary, primary power) plus maternal pushing in the second stage (voluntary, secondary power).
The mother’s position. Upright and side-lying use gravity and open the pelvis; flat on the back does neither.

Fear and exhaustion raise catecholamines, which slow labor . Support, information and rest are clinical interventions, not niceties. 🧠 Passenger, Passageway, Powers, Position, Psyche. If labor stalls, walk the five and ask which one is failing.
The 5 Ps above, drawn. Start with the one-page plate, then each idea on its own.
Three numbers get charted, and they are measured from different points . This is the picture worth memorizing.

Duration: start to end of one contraction. Frequency: onset of one contraction to onset of the next. Intensity means strength; an external tracing does not reliably quantify it. Sources checked October 3, 2026: www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov — reference 1 Frequency and duration use different start and end points.

Frequency Beginning of one contraction to beginning of the next. Duration Beginning to end of the same contraction. Rest interval End of one contraction to beginning of the next. Intensity External monitoring does not directly measure contraction strength; palpation and internal monitoring provide different information. Resting tone The uterus should relax between contractions; assessment method matters. Fetal response Interpret contractions together with the fetal heart-rate pattern. Number Measured from Units Fre

A contraction lasting longer than 90 seconds , contractions closer than 2 minutes , or a uterus that does not relax between them is tachysystole. Blood reaches the placenta only during the rest period — no rest, no oxygen. Do first: stop the oxytocin, turn her to her side, give oxygen and a fluid bolus, and call the provider.

TRUE labor FALSE labor (Braxton Hicks) Contractions Regular, and they get closer, longer and stronger Irregular; they do not build Felt where Back , radiating around to the abdomen Abdomen and groin only Walking Makes them stronger Often makes them stop Cervix Dilates and effaces No change Show Bloody show is common Usually none The cervix is the tiebreaker. Everything above it can be argued; cervical change cannot.

entries.h: 🏠 What to do for false labor
entries.t: Rest, hydrate, change position, reassess. Dehydration alone can set off irritable contractions, so a glass of water and a walk are real interventions. Teach her when to come in: contractions 5 minutes apart, lasting 1 minute, for 1 hour — and immediately for ruptured membranes, bleeding, or reduced fetal movement.

entries.h: 📏 Station — where the baby actually is
entries.t: Station is the presenting part measured against the ischial spines . Minus is above them, plus is below, and 0 means engaged — that is how the exams key it. Strictly the two are defined separately: station is where the presenting part sits against the spines, and engagement is the widest diameter having passed the pelvic inlet, which usually lands at about station 0.

Station describes the presenting bony part relative to the maternal ischial spines. Negative station is above the spines; zero is at the spines; positive is below. Station describes descent. It is not the cervical dilation measurement. Sources checked October 3, 2026: www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov — reference 1 These measurements describe different aspects of progress and should not be substituted for one another.

Dilation Cervical opening increases toward complete dilation. Effacement The cervix becomes shorter and thinner. Station The presenting part is described relative to the ischial spines. Dilation Recorded in centimeters. Effacement Commonly recorded as a percentage. Station Zero is at the ischial spines; negative is above and positive is below.

entries.h: First stage — onset of true labor to full dilation
entries.t: The long one. It ends at 10 cm , not at the urge to push. Phase Dilation Contractions What she is like Latent 0–5 cm Mild, every 5–10 min Talkative, excited, can walk Active 6–10 cm Moderate to strong, every 2–5 min Inward, focused, wants help Transition 8–10 cm Strong, every 2–3 min Irritable, nauseated, shaky, “I can’t do this” Transition is the shortest phase and the one she remembers. Saying “this is transition, it means you are nearly there” is genuinely useful nursing.

entries.h: Second stage — full dilation to the birth of the baby
entries.t: Pushing. Contractions every 2–3 min , lasting 60–90 s . Watch: the fetal heart rate with pushing, the perineum, and her energy. Support: upright or side-lying positions, and let her push with the urge rather than to a count.

entries.h: Third stage — birth of the baby to delivery of the placenta
entries.t: Usually 5–30 minutes . Three signs the placenta has separated: A sudden gush of blood The cord lengthens at the introitus The uterus becomes firm and globular and rises Never pull on the cord to hurry it. That is how you get a uterine inversion.

entries.h: Fourth stage — the first 1 to 4 hours after the placenta
entries.t: Recovery, and the highest-risk window for hemorrhage . Assess every 15 minutes for the first hour: fundus (firm, midline, at or below the umbilicus), lochia, blood pressure and pulse, and the bladder. 🧠 A boggy fundus is the first sign of hemorrhage. Massage it first; if it stays boggy, or it is firm and she is still bleeding, escalate.

Never leave a woman alone once she is in active labor or after the membranes rupture. Never check the cervix if she is bleeding and previa has not been ruled out. Never pull on the umbilical cord to deliver the placenta. Never leave the fundus unmassaged when it is boggy. Never put her flat on her back — it compresses the vena cava. Wedge or turn her. POWERS → PASSAGE → BIRTH NG-375 · Maternal & Newborn unit · ADHD-friendly visual edition
PROM and AROM, what oxytocin can do to a uterus, and the difference between forceps and a vacuum — including which newborn injury goes with which.

The moment the membranes rupture — however they rupture — the first thing you assess is the fetal heart rate. Not the fluid, not the clock. Fetal heart rate first. The cord can wash down with the fluid. A sudden deep variable or prolonged deceleration right after rupture is cord prolapse until proven otherwise.

entries.h: 💧 PROM, PPROM, SROM, AROM — four words, two questions
entries.t: Every one of these terms answers only two questions: did labor start yet , and how many weeks is she . Term What it means Why it matters SROM Spontaneous rupture — it broke on its own Normal in labor AROM Artificial rupture — the provider does it (amniotomy) Needs an engaged presenting part first PROM Rupture before labor starts , at term Infection clock starts PPROM Rupture before labor and before 37 weeks Prematurity and infection 🧠 The extra P in PPROM is Preterm . Same event, worse week.

entries.h: 📋 What you chart about the fluid
entries.t: Time, Amount, Color, Odor. Clear with white flecks — normal Green or brown — meconium; have the resuscitation team ready Cloudy or foul-smelling — infection Port-wine — think abruption Then take her temperature every 2 hours and limit vaginal exams. Fever, maternal or fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness and foul fluid together are chorioamnionitis .

entries.h: 🔄 What to do the second the membranes go

entries.t: Document the time and circumstances, then assess fetal status promptly. Record fluid amount, color and odor, plus maternal condition and temperature. Escalate abnormal fetal findings or suspected cord prolapse immediately. Monitoring and examinations follow the individualized plan. Sources checked October 3, 2026: www.nice.org.uk — reference 1 www.nice.org.uk — reference 2 Avoid unnecessary vaginal examinations and follow the maternity team’s plan for monitoring and birth.

Characterize the fluid loss Record the reported time, amount, color and odor. Ask about contractions, bleeding, fetal movements and how the patient feels. Assess the mother Check temperature and other vital signs. Evaluate for infection, pain and other concerns; confirm rupture according to the clinical protocol. Assess the baby Evaluate fetal heart rate and movement. An abnormal heart-rate pattern or suspected cord prolapse requires immediate escalation. Plan ongoing care Management depends on gestational age, lab

entries.h: 💉 Oxytocin — a high-alert drug on a pump
entries.t: Oxytocin makes the uterus contract. That is the whole benefit and the whole danger, because the placenta is perfused between contractions. Always a secondary line piggybacked into a mainline, at the port closest to the patient , so it can be stopped instantly. Always on a pump . Titrate to a contraction pattern, not to a number on the bag. Aim for contractions no closer than every 2 minutes , no longer than 90 seconds , with a soft uterus in between. 🧠 You are titrating to the uterus, not to the order. The order is

Recognize it: more than five contractions in ten minutes, or contractions that will not let the uterus relax. Order Action Why 1 Stop the oxytocin Removes the cause 2 Turn her to her side Off the vena cava 3 Open the mainline — fluid bolus Fills the circulation 4 Oxygen by non-rebreather Raises what is available 5 Notify; expect terbutaline Relaxes the uterus Water intoxication is the other oxytocin risk on a long induction — watch for headache, confusion and a falling sodium.

Both need the same five things first: fully dilated cervix, ruptured membranes, an engaged head, an empty bladder, and adequate anesthesia. Forceps Vacuum Applied to Sides of the head Top of the head Newborn injury Facial bruising, facial nerve palsy Cephalohematoma, scalp lacerations, subgaleal bleed Mother’s risk Higher — lacerations Lower Time limit Provider judgment Yes — and pop-offs are counted 🧠 ForCeps → Face. VaCuum → Cap. Forceps mark the face, the vacuum marks the scalp. After either: check the newborn’s
Consent, labs, IV, indwelling catheter, antibiotic within the hour before incision Wedge under the right hip on the table — never flat and supine Non-particulate antacid to reduce aspiration risk

entries.h: After — she is a surgical patient and a postpartum patient
entries.t: Postpartum half Surgical half Fundus firm and midline Incision: clean, dry, approximated Lochia amount and clots Pain control so she can move Bladder emptying after the catheter comes out Early ambulation, leg exercises — VTE risk Bonding and feeding support Breath sounds, incentive spirometry A cesarean does not protect against hemorrhage. Assess the fundus the same way — gently, supporting the incision.

Never assess anything before the fetal heart rate after the membranes rupture. Never replace a prolapsed cord, and never let go of the presenting part once you are holding it up. Never run oxytocin as a primary line or without a pump. Never keep oxytocin going through tachysystole while you wait for a call back. Never lay a pregnant woman flat on her back — wedge or turn her. RUPTURE → ASSESS → ACT NG-376 · Maternal & Newborn unit · ADHD-friendly visual edition

These newly drawn concept diagrams consolidate the retired illustration sets. The accompanying study notes and original handout links remain on this page. NICE: Intrapartum care ; NHS: Ruptured membranes at term
Preterm labor, shoulder dystocia, precipitous birth, cord prolapse, uterine rupture and inversion, amniotic fluid embolism, DIC and meconium — each one with the action that comes first.
In every emergency on this page the first action is a position change or stopping something — not a drug. Reposition, relieve, stop the oxytocin, call. The medication comes after.

entries.h: 🕵 Sudden pain or bleeding in labor — which one is it?
entries.t: What she has Think The tell Sudden tearing pain, contractions stop , presenting part rises Uterine rupture Fetal bradycardia is often the first sign, before the pain Sudden pain, board-like rigid uterus, dark bleeding Abruption Pain is constant, uterus does not relax Painless bright red bleeding Placenta previa No vaginal exam After the placenta: massive bleeding, fundus not palpable Uterine inversion Shock out of proportion to visible blood Oozing from IV sites and gums, petechiae DIC She bleeds from places nobody

Definition: regular contractions with cervical change between 20 and 36 6/7 weeks. Contractions alone are not preterm labor. What raises the risk What she may notice Infection — urinary tract, vaginal, chorioamnionitis Contractions every 10 minutes or closer A previous preterm birth Low, dull backache that comes and goes Twins or more; too much fluid Pelvic pressure — “the baby feels low” Short cervix Cramping, with or without diarrhea Smoking, substance use, abdominal trauma Change in discharge , or any bleeding 🧠

entries.h: 💉 What the treatment is actually for
entries.t: Given What it is really doing Betamethasone Fetal lung maturity — the single most valuable thing bought by delay Magnesium sulfate before 32 weeks Fetal neuroprotection — reduces cerebral palsy Nifedipine, indomethacin, terbutaline Tocolysis — buying 48 hours for the steroids to work Penicillin / ampicillin Group B strep prophylaxis Tocolytics do not save the pregnancy. They buy time for the steroids and for transfer to a hospital with a NICU.

The exams key it as reflexes → respirations → cardiac : lost deep tendon reflexes, then a respiratory rate under 12, then heart changes. That is the usual order, not a guaranteed one — monitor all of them together, with urine output.

Monitor reflexes, respiration, urine output, clinical condition and ordered laboratory values together. Reduced urine output can increase magnesium accumulation. Toxicity does not follow a mandatory sequence. If toxicity is suspected, stop the infusion, get urgent help and support breathing/circulation. Calcium gluconate is administered according to orders or emergency protocol. Sources checked October 3, 2026: dailymed.nlm.nih.gov — reference 1 Magnesium sulfate is not primarily an antihypertensive; blood-pressure

Prescribed indication Often seizure prevention or treatment in severe hypertensive disease. Neuromuscular effects Excess exposure can suppress reflexes and breathing. Renal clearance Kidney function influences accumulation. Monitor Respiratory status, reflexes, urine output, consciousness and ordered levels. Possible toxicity Diminished reflexes, respiratory depression and marked sedation need urgent assessment. Response Stop the infusion when indicated, escalate and follow the calcium-gluconate rescue protocol.
The turtle sign: the head delivers and then retracts back against the perineum, and restitution does not happen.

An impacted shoulder may lodge behind the pubic bone after the head delivers. McRoberts: the team assists with marked hip flexion, bringing the thighs toward the abdomen. Suprapubic pressure is applied just above the pubic bone to help release the shoulder. Fundal pressure must not be used. Call for help and follow the trained team’s emergency protocol. Sources checked October 3, 2026: www.rcog.org.uk — reference 1 www.rcog.org.uk — reference 2 A memorized maneuver must be matched to the correct emergency.

Recognize the pattern Cord prolapse, shoulder dystocia and other emergencies differ. Activate the team Time and coordinated roles are critical. Use the specific maneuver Follow the emergency pathway for the identified problem. Cord prolapse Relieve cord compression under protocol while arranging urgent delivery. Shoulder dystocia Use trained maneuvers and team assistance; avoid fundal pressure. Assessment Monitor maternal and fetal status and document timing and actions. Afterwards, look for: in the baby, a fractur

entries.h: ⚡ Precipitous birth — under 3 hours start to finish
entries.t: Stay with her. Do not leave to find someone; use the call bell. Never hold the head back. Support the perineum and let it deliver slowly between contractions. Afterwards expect lacerations and hemorrhage — the uterus has had no time to work up to it.

Cord COMPRESSION Cord PROLAPSE On the monitor Variable decelerations Deep variables or a prolonged deceleration You can feel it? No Yes — or you can see it First action Reposition her — side, then other side, then knee–chest Lift the presenting part off the cord and keep it there Then Oxygen, fluids, consider amnioinfusion Knee–chest or Trendelenburg, oxygen, straight to cesarean Do not push a prolapsed cord back in, and do not take your hand out. You travel to the operating room with it in place.

Who: a previous uterine scar, especially a classical incision; oxytocin overstimulation; grand multiparity; trauma. Fetal heart rate change is usually the first sign — a prolonged deceleration or bradycardia. Sudden tearing pain; contractions may stop . The presenting part rises — station goes backwards. Signs of shock; fetal parts may become easy to feel through the abdomen. Pain that suddenly stops during strong labor is not relief. It is rupture until proven otherwise. Action: stop the oxytocin, oxygen, fluids,

Who: traction on the cord, fundal pressure, a fundal placenta, a long labor. The fundus cannot be found , or there is a mass at the introitus. Sudden severe pain and heavy bleeding . Shock out of proportion to the blood you can see. Action: call for help, stop uterotonics so the uterus can be replaced, large-bore IV and fluids, and expect the provider to replace it manually. Uterotonics go back on only after it is back in. Both of these are made more likely by the same two mistakes: pulling on the cord, and pressin

Recognize the pattern Cord prolapse, shoulder dystocia and other emergencies differ. Activate the team Time and coordinated roles are critical. Use the specific maneuver Follow the emergency pathway for the identified problem. Cord prolapse Relieve cord compression under protocol while arranging urgent delivery. Shoulder dystocia Use trained maneuvers and team assistance; avoid fundal pressure. Assessment Monitor maternal and fetal status and document timing and actions. Amniotic fluid and fetal cells enter the mat

Turtle sign → McRoberts + suprapubic. Never fundal pressure Pain stops = uterine rupture Never pull the cord — inversion Sudden dyspnea + collapse + DIC = amniotic fluid embolism Maternal diabetes is the classic dystocia risk factor

It is always secondary. Look for the trigger: abruption, fetal death in utero, amniotic fluid embolism, sepsis, severe preeclampsia or HELLP. What you see What the labs do Oozing from IV sites, gums, the incision Platelets down Petechiae, bruising Fibrinogen down Bleeding that will not clot PT and aPTT up Hematuria D-dimer up Treatment is the trigger plus replacement — blood products, oxygen, fluids. You cannot fix the clotting while the cause is still running.

Green or brown fluid means the fetus has passed stool in utero. The worry is that it is inhaled . Have the resuscitation team at the birth . A vigorous baby — good tone, crying, heart rate over 100 — goes skin to skin and is watched. A non-vigorous baby gets resuscitation; airway suctioning is done if the airway is obstructed, not routinely. Watch for respiratory distress, a barrel chest and greenish staining of cord and nails. REPOSITION → RELIEVE → CALL NG-378 · Maternal & Newborn unit · ADHD-friendly visual edit
What normal lochia does over two weeks, the four causes of hemorrhage, and the complication where the fundus is firm and she is still bleeding to death.

A boggy fundus means massage it. A firm fundus with heavy bleeding means something else is wrong — a tear, a retained fragment, or a hematoma. Firm and still bleeding is not reassuring; it is a different diagnosis.

Rubra: red/bloody during the first 3–4 days. Serosa: pink or brown, generally through about day 10. Alba: yellow-white, beginning around day 10 and becoming lighter over subsequent weeks. Timing varies. Heavy or increasing bleeding, large clots, foul odor, fever or dizziness warrant assessment. Soaking a pad within an hour requires prompt reporting. Sources checked October 3, 2026: www.merckmanuals.com — reference 1 www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov — reference 2 Color alone does not establish normal recovery; quantity, symptom

Rubra Early lochia is predominantly bloody. Serosa Becomes more pink or brown as composition changes. Alba Later discharge is lighter and whitish or yellowish. Trend Timing varies; assess amount and the overall recovery pattern. Concern Heavy bleeding, large clots, dizziness or a return to increasing bleeding needs assessment. Infection clues Foul odor, fever or uterine tenderness requires review. Amount on the pad in 1 hour Called A stain under about 2.5 cm (1 inch) Scant Under about 10 cm (4 inches) Light Under a

T Cause What you find Tone Uterine atony — the most common by far Boggy fundus, often displaced by a full bladder Trauma Laceration, hematoma, uterine inversion or rupture Firm fundus, still bleeding Tissue Retained placental fragments Bleeding that continues or restarts days later Thrombin A clotting problem — DIC, low platelets Oozing from IV sites and gums too 🧠 Boggy → Tone. Firm and bleeding → Trauma. That one distinction sorts most questions.

entries.h: ✅ What you do — call for help, then work in parallel
entries.t: Do Action At once Call for help — at the same time as everything else, not after it Feel the fundus Boggy and midline → massage it , one hand supporting the lower uterus. Boggy and deviated to the right → empty the bladder first , then massage if still boggy. Firm but still bleeding → stop massaging and look for trauma, retained tissue or a clotting problem Bladder Empty it — void or catheter. A full bladder pushes the uterus up and to the side and stops it clamping Lines and drugs Large-bore IV and fluids; oxygen

entries.h: 💉 The uterotonics — and who cannot have them
entries.t: Drug Do not give if Oxytocin First line; watch for water intoxication on long infusions Methylergonovine Hypertension or preeclampsia — it raises blood pressure Carboprost Asthma — it causes bronchospasm Misoprostol Few restrictions; expect fever and shivering 🧠 Methyl → hypertension. Carboprost → asthma. Check the blood pressure and the lungs before you hand either over.

entries.h: 🧵 Hematoma — the bleed you cannot see
entries.t: The pattern is the diagnosis: severe perineal or rectal pain that pain relief is not touching, a firm fundus, very little visible bleeding, and a pulse and blood pressure that say she has lost a lot of blood. Unrelieved pressure or “I need to have my bowels open” not long after birth A bulging, tense, purple-blue area at the perineum or vulva Difficulty passing urine Rising pulse and falling blood pressure with a firm fundus Do: report immediately, ice for the first 12 hours, catheterize if she cannot void, and kee

Fever after the first 24 hours is the opening move — a temperature of 38°C or more on two occasions after day one. Uterine tenderness ; a uterus that is not shrinking as it should Foul-smelling lochia Chills, tachycardia, malaise More likely after: a long time with ruptured membranes, many vaginal exams, cesarean birth, or retained tissue. Nursing: IV antibiotics, fluids, and sit her upright — Fowler position encourages drainage rather than pooling. Not to be confused with endometri osis — lining-like tissue growin

Pregnancy and the postpartum period are hypercoagulable on purpose , which is what stops her bleeding to death — and what puts her at risk. DVT Pulmonary embolism One leg painful, swollen, warm Sudden breathlessness Calf tenderness Sharp chest pain, worse on breathing in Redness, a hard cord under the skin Fast pulse, anxiety, a feeling of doom Prevention is nursing work: get her up and walking early, keep her hydrated, use the compression devices, and never leave legs dangling over the bed edge. Scoring the first minutes, and the two bits of newborn care parents ask the most questions about.

The Apgar score describes how the baby is doing. It does not decide what you do about it. Resuscitation starts on assessment, not on a score. Nobody waits until one minute to dry, warm and stimulate a baby who is not breathing.

Five things, 0 to 2 each, at 1 minute and 5 minutes — and again at 10 minutes if the five-minute score is under 7. Sign 0 1 2 Heart rate Absent Under 100 Over 100 Respiratory effort Absent Slow, weak, irregular Good cry Muscle tone Limp Some flexion Active movement Reflex irritability No response Grimace Cry, cough or sneeze Color Blue or pale all over Body pink, hands and feet blue Pink all over

Appearance, pulse, grimace/reflex response, activity/tone and respiration each score 0–2, for a total of 0–10. Assess at 1 and 5 minutes. If the 5-minute score is below 7, repeat at 5-minute intervals through 20 minutes according to guidance. For term/late-preterm infants, a 5-minute score of 7–10 is reassuring, 4–6 moderately abnormal and 0–3 low. The score does not determine whether to initiate resuscitation or predict an individual child’s outcome. Sources checked October 3, 2026: www.acog.org — reference 1 Apga

Birth transition The newborn establishes breathing and circulatory adaptation. Clinical assessment Breathing, heart rate and tone guide immediate support. Apgar documentation Summarizes condition and response at specified times. Five components Appearance, pulse, grimace, activity and respiration are scored separately. Resuscitation Begin indicated support based on assessment; do not wait for an Apgar score. Ongoing care Monitor temperature, breathing, feeding and perfusion. 🧠 Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity,

Clean and dry, and left alone. It usually separates somewhere between 7 and 14 days. Fold the diaper down below the cord so urine does not sit against it Sponge baths only until it has come off — no tub Let it dry in the air; do not cover it with the vest If it gets soiled, clean with water and let it dry The cord should have two arteries and one vein. A single artery is noted and reported — it can go with other anomalies. Report to the provider: redness spreading onto the abdomen, a foul smell, pus, bleeding more

Gomco and Mogen: both clamps come off. Petroleum jelly prevents sticking. Plastibell: the ring stays until it separates. Leave it alone and follow the clinician’s ointment instructions. Read the methods, diaper care and urgent warning signs

Informed consent , and it is the parents’ decision Check for hypospadias — if the opening is not at the tip, the procedure is postponed, because that foreskin may be needed for the repair Vitamin K given and the baby has voided Pain relief is not optional — a nerve block or topical anesthetic, plus sucrose and swaddling

entries.t: Clamp method (Gomco, Mogen) Plastibell Apply petroleum jelly on gauze with each diaper change No petroleum jelly — it makes the ring slip Keeps the raw area from sticking to the diaper The plastic ring falls off by itself in about 5–10 days Both: clean with warm water at each change, fasten the diaper loosely, and place the baby on the back for every sleep.

Active bleeding — apply gentle pressure with sterile gauze. Seek urgent assessment if bleeding persists or exceeds a few drops No urine within 6 to 8 hours after the procedure Increasing swelling, a foul smell, or the ring not falling off after two weeks A yellowish film over the site around day two is normal healing granulation. What each structure does, the two cycles running underneath, and where a pregnancy starts — the whole of Reproductive System I and II on one page.
Ovulation happens about 14 days before the next period — not 14 days after the last one. The second half of the cycle is the fixed part. In a 35-day cycle, ovulation is around day 21, not day 17.
Front view · simplified cutaway. Follow the leader lines to the named structures.
Two labeled views: external structures on the left; clitoral and vestibular structures on the right.

Five structures, outside in. Exams ask them as a list, so learn them as a list. Mons pubis — the fatty pad over the pubic bone Labia majora and labia minora — the outer and inner folds Clitoris Vestibule — the space the folds enclose; the urethral and vaginal openings sit in it Perineum — the tissue between the vaginal opening and the anus 🧠 The perineum is the one that carries into every other maternity topic — it is what tears or is cut in an episiotomy, and what you assess after a birth.
Top: side view, with the front of the body on the left. Bottom: front view of the reproductive organs.

A hollow pear sitting between the bladder in front and the rectum behind. Top to bottom: Part Where Why it matters Fundus The dome at the top What you palpate and massage after birth Corpus The body — the bulk of it Where the pregnancy grows Uterine isthmus The narrow waist above the cervix Becomes the lower uterine segment — the low transverse C-section site Cervix The neck, opening into the vagina Dilates and effaces in labor Where the cervix dips down into the vagina it forms arch-shaped pockets around itself —

entries.h: 🥪 The fallopian tube has three segments
entries.t: Muscular corridors running from the top of the uterus out toward each ovary. Outer end first: Infundibulum — the funnel-shaped end whose finger-like fimbriae sweep the egg in Ampulla — the wide middle. Fertilization normally happens here Isthmus — the narrow part that joins the uterus 🧠 The ampulla is both where fertilization happens and the commonest site of an ectopic pregnancy — one fact, asked two ways.
Top: external views. Bottom: a side view that locates the glands, ducts and testis.

External: the penis , which serves both reproduction and urinary elimination, and the scrotum , the sac that houses the testes. The scrotum has two jobs: protect the testes from trauma and regulate their temperature — sperm need to sit cooler than core body temperature. Internal: the testes , which make male sex hormone and sperm; the ductal system , beginning with the vas deferens ; and the accessory glands .

entries.h: 💧 The accessory glands, and what their fluid is for
entries.t: The seminal vesicles are a pair that empty an alkaline, fructose-rich fluid into the ejaculatory ducts. The prostate is a muscular gland wrapped around the first part of the urethra as it leaves the bladder, and adds alkaline fluid too. That fluid does three things — a favorite exam list: Motility — it helps sperm move Nourishment — fructose is the fuel they run on Protection — being alkaline, it shields sperm from the acidic vagina 🧠 Move, feed, protect. And the two facts explain each other: the vagina is acidic o

Day 1 is the first day of menstrual bleeding. Follicular development and estrogen support rebuilding the uterine lining. An LH surge helps trigger ovulation. The corpus luteum produces progesterone during the luteal phase. Without pregnancy, hormone levels fall before menstruation. A 28-day cycle is illustrative; ovulation is not always on day 14. Sources checked October 3, 2026: www.nichd.nih.gov — reference 1 Ovarian events and endometrial changes are linked but describe different tissues.

Follicular phase Follicles develop; rising estrogen supports endometrial growth. Ovulation An LH surge triggers release of an oocyte. Luteal phase The corpus luteum produces progesterone and estrogen. Without pregnancy Hormone levels fall as the corpus luteum regresses, and menstruation follows. Endometrium Proliferative and secretory changes prepare the uterine lining. Timing Cycle length and ovulation timing vary; day 14 is not universal. Hormone From What it does FSH Pituitary Grows the follicle LH Pituitary The
“The menstrual cycle” is really two cycles happening together — one in the ovary, one in the lining of the uterus. The ovary answers to the pituitary; the lining answers to the ovary.

entries.h: 🧸 Ovarian cycle — driven by the pituitary
entries.t: Two phases, each named for the hormone that runs it : Phase Days In charge Follicular 1–14 FSH — follicle-stimulating hormone Luteal 15–28 LH — luteinizing hormone 🧠 F before L — alphabetically and on the calendar. FSH grows the follicle; LH surges, releases the egg, and leaves the corpus luteum behind.

entries.h: 🩸 Uterine cycle — driven by the ovary
entries.t: What the endometrium does in response to estrogen and progesterone. Four phases, and the order is usually the answer: Menstrual — the lining sheds Proliferative — estrogen rebuilds it Secretory — progesterone makes it rich and ready to implant Ischemic — no pregnancy, so hormones fall, the blood supply fails, and it is about to shed again 🧠 Ovarian has 2 phases, uterine has 4. If the question names FSH or LH it wants the ovarian cycle; if it names the lining it wants the uterine one.

Cell What it is Somatic cells Every ordinary body cell — what the organs and tissues are made of Gametes The sex cells , found only in the reproductive glands — egg and sperm The nucleus holds 23 pairs of chromosomes — 46 in all. 22 pairs are autosomes — they carry ordinary inherited traits: eye color, hair color, even ear-wax consistency 1 pair is the sex chromosomes Each parent contributes one member of every pair — 23 chromosomes each, which is why the two together make 46. 🧠 Your lecture’s hook: 46 chromosomes

The tier is decided by who noticed it and how sure it makes you — not by how convincing it sounds. Tier Kind of data Example Presumptive Subjective — what she reports “My breasts hurt” Probable Objective — what you can observe Cervical changes Positive Diagnostic — the fetus itself Fetal heartbeat, ultrasound 🧠 She says it, you see it, the baby proves it. Only the third tier is positive — everything she feels, and even a positive home test, sits below it.

Stage Gestation Pre-embryonic 3–4 weeks Embryonic 5–10 weeks Fetal 11–40 weeks These are the weeks on your NUR 234 handout, so these are the ones to answer with. Some textbooks count from conception rather than from the last menstrual period and print roughly two weeks earlier for each stage. For a question from your course, use the numbers above. 🧠 The embryonic stage is short, and it is when the organs form — which is exactly why it is the window where teratogens do the most damage. Getting the latch right, knowing the baby is actually getting milk, and preparing formula safely.

Feeding cues Early hunger cues support timely feeding. Effective transfer Latch, suck–swallow coordination or appropriate bottle technique. Adequacy assessment Growth, urine/stool patterns and clinical condition matter. Breastfeeding Comfortable positioning, effective latch and support improve transfer. Bottle feeding Use paced, responsive feeding and the prescribed preparation method. Safety Never prop a bottle or microwave feeds; follow safe storage instructions. Nipple pain and a clicking sound are not things to

Step What it looks like 1 · Skin to skin In the first hour if both are stable — it steadies temperature, glucose and breathing, and most babies find the breast themselves 2 · Watch for cues Stirring, turning the head, hand to mouth. Crying is a late cue — a crying baby latches badly 3 · Position Baby’s whole body facing her, ear–shoulder–hip in a line, nose level with the nipple 4 · Wait for a wide mouth Brush the lip, wait for a wide gape , then bring the baby to the breast — not the breast to the baby 5 · Check t

Mouth wide open , chin pressed into the breast, nose clear Lips flanged outward , like a fish — not tucked in More areola visible above the top lip than below the bottom one Slow, deep sucking with audible swallowing ; cheeks rounded, not dimpled No pain after the first few seconds, and no clicking To take the baby off: slide a clean finger into the corner of the mouth to break the suction first. Pulling off is what damages nipples.

You count what comes out, because you cannot measure what went in. By day 4 onwards Expect Wet diapers 6 or more a day Stools 3–4 a day, yellow and seedy Swallowing Heard during feeds Weight Up to 10% lost at first, back to birth weight by about 10–14 days

Stage When What it is Colostrum First few days Thick, yellow, small in volume and that is correct — full of antibodies Transitional About days 3–5 Volume rises — “the milk coming in” Mature From about day 10 Thin and bluish at the start of a feed, creamier at the end Engorgement: both breasts, hard, hot, painful, around days 3–5. Warmth before a feed to get it flowing, cold after for swelling, and feed often. Do not skip feeds — that makes it worse.

One breast , a red wedge-shaped painful area, fever and feeling like flu. Keep feeding or expressing from that breast. Stopping is what turns mastitis into an abscess. The milk is safe for the baby. Plus: antibiotics as prescribed and finished, rest, fluids, and check the latch, because a poor latch is usually why it happened.

Do Why Use iron-fortified formula Iron stores from birth run down at around 4–6 months Mix exactly as the tin says Never dilute it — extra water causes seizures from low sodium, and under-feeding Warm in a jug of warm water Never a microwave — it heats unevenly and scalds the mouth Hold the baby, semi-upright Never prop a bottle — choking, and ear infections Keep the teat full of milk Less swallowed air Throw away what is left Saliva has got into it; it is not safe to keep No honey before 1 year — infant botulism.

Standard powdered infant formula is one level scoop to every 2 fl oz of water . The scoop in the tin is measured for that tin — do not swap scoops between brands, and do not pack the powder down. Wash hands. Put the water in first , then add the powder. One level scoop per 2 oz — so 4 oz takes two scoops, 6 oz takes three. Cap and shake or swirl until no lumps are left. Test the temperature on your wrist. It should feel barely warm, not hot. Adding extra water to make a tin last is dangerous, not thrifty. Dilute fo

Bottle How long Then Made up, straight into the fridge 24 hours Throw it out Made up, left at room temperature 2 hours Throw it out Started — the baby has fed from it 1 hour from the start of the feed Throw it out Opened tin of powder About 1 month Check the label Twenty-four hours, not four days. Expressed breast milk keeps about 4 days in the fridge; prepared formula does not, because it has no living cells and no antibodies to hold bacteria back. That contrast is exactly what a test question is built on.

entries.h: 🧺 Cleaning bottles — what is actually required
entries.t: Before the very first use: sterilize — boil for 5 minutes, or use a steam or chemical sterilizer. After every feed: take everything apart, rinse, then wash in hot soapy water with a bottle brush, or run it through the dishwasher. Air-dry on a clean rack. Sterilize again every day only for a baby under 2 months, born preterm, or immunocompromised — that is the group where the extra step earns its keep. Boiling bottles for 20 minutes after every single use is not the instruction , and it is a common wrong answer. It

Where Roughly how long Room temperature About 4 hours Fridge About 4 days Freezer Months, depending on the freezer Thaw in the fridge or in warm water. Never in a microwave, and never refrozen. Label with the date, use the oldest first, and swirl rather than shake. LATCH → COUNT WHAT COMES OUT → PREPARE SAFELY NG-386 · Maternal & Newborn unit · ADHD-friendly visual edition

entries.h: 💉 Drugs in pregnancy, labor & the newborn
entries.t: What is avoided and why, what gets given in labor, the three things every newborn is offered, and how Rh immune globulin is timed.

The first trimester is when the organs are built , so that is when a drug does structural harm. Later exposure tends to affect growth and function rather than formation — which is why the timing of an exposure is always part of the question.

entries.h: 🚫 Avoided in pregnancy — and what each one does
entries.t: Drug What it does to the fetus ACE inhibitors & ARBs “-pril”, “-sartan” Kidney damage, too little amniotic fluid, skull defects Warfarin Crosses the placenta — bleeding and bone defects. Heparin does not cross and is used instead Isotretinoin Severe malformations — two forms of contraception are required alongside it Tetracyclines Stain the developing teeth and affect bone growth NSAIDs , especially late Close the ductus arteriosus early; reduce amniotic fluid Valproate, carbamazepine Neural tube defects — folic ac

Acetaminophen / acetaminophen for pain and fever Penicillins and cephalosporins for infection Insulin — it does not cross the placenta Labetalol, methyldopa, nifedipine for blood pressure Levothyroxine — the dose usually needs to go up Folic acid and iron , and the inactivated influenza and Tdap vaccines

entries.h: 🩸 Rh immune globulin — the timing is the question
entries.t: It is given to an Rh-negative mother to stop her making antibodies against Rh-positive fetal blood. It protects the next pregnancy, not this one.

Eligibility depends on maternal RhD type, sensitization status and clinical situation. Routine prophylaxis is generally around 28 weeks and within 72 hours after an RhD-positive birth when indicated. Other potential sensitizing events require assessment. Early-pregnancy loss recommendations depend on gestation and current guidance. Rh immune globulin prevents sensitization; it does not treat established immune anti-D. Sources checked October 3, 2026: www.acog.org — reference 1 Rh immune globulin is prevention for a

Identify risk An Rh-negative pregnant patient may become sensitized after exposure to Rh-positive fetal red cells. Maternal antibodies can affect a current or future Rh-positive fetus. Check the antibody screen Rh immune globulin helps prevent formation of anti-D antibodies in an unsensitized patient. It does not reverse established sensitization. Give when indicated Routine pregnancy prophylaxis and additional doses after birth or a sensitizing event depend on the care protocol, gestational age and testing. Verify

Drug For Watch Oxytocin Induce or augment Tachysystole — stop it first, then reposition Magnesium sulfate Seizure prevention in preeclampsia; neuroprotection before 32 weeks Reflexes go first on the exam sequence, then respiratory rate and urine output — in practice watch them together. Antidote calcium gluconate Betamethasone Fetal lung maturity Maternal glucose rises Terbutaline Relax the uterus, short term Maternal tachycardia Penicillin / ampicillin Group B strep prophylaxis Started early enough to work Epidura

Given Why Vitamin K , intramuscular Newborns cannot make clotting factors yet — prevents bleeding disease Erythromycin eye ointment Prevents eye infection acquired during birth Hepatitis B vaccine First dose of the series Give the injection in the vastus lateralis , and give sucrose or a feed for comfort.

Rh immune globulin if she is Rh-negative and the baby is Rh-positive Rubella vaccine if she is not immune — it is live, so it is given after birth, and she avoids pregnancy for a month Tdap if she has not had it, to protect the baby from whooping cough Uterotonics if she is bleeding — and remember which two are barred: methylergonovine in hypertension, carboprost in asthma

Most medicines are compatible with breastfeeding , and stopping unnecessarily does more harm than the drug would. Where there is a choice, take the dose right after a feed so the level is falling by the next one A few genuinely need the feeding plan reviewed — chemotherapy, some radioactive agents, amiodarone Check each drug rather than assuming , in either direction WHEN IN PREGNANCY → DOES IT CROSS → WHAT TO WATCH NG-387 · Maternal & Newborn unit · ADHD-friendly visual edition

Exposure Sexual contact can transmit bacterial or viral infections. Infection pattern Symptoms may be absent or involve skin, mucosa or other tissues. Testing and treatment The organism determines management. Gonorrhea A bacterial infection requiring the recommended antibiotic regimen and partner management. HSV A viral infection with possible recurrent ulcers; antivirals manage episodes or suppress recurrence.
