Otherwise discharge, dysuria, postcoital bleeding Bacteria Doxycycline (azithromycin in pregnancy) Gonorrhea Often silent too; otherwise thick discharge and dysuria Bacteria IM ceftriaxone — resistance is a real problem Trichomoniasis Frothy yellow-green discharge , itching, “strawberry cervix” Parasite Metronidazole — client and partner Syphilis Painless chancre , then a rash that includes the palms and soles Bacteria Benz

entries.h: 🦠 Herpes: the numbers that get asked
entries.t: HSV type 1 HSV type 2 Usually Cold sores around the mouth Genital herpes Course An episode clears on its own in about 10–14 days Recurs for life First outbreak About 14 days after exposure Cure? No. Acyclovir shortens and suppresses episodes — it never clears the virus “With medication I will be able to cure my herpes” always signals a client who needs more teaching. Either type can appear in either place through oral sex.

entries.h: 🚨 The two discharges students mix up
entries.t: Trichomoniasis Bacterial vaginosis Discharge Frothy, yellow-green Thin, grey-white Smell Can be foul Fishy , worse after sex Itch Yes, and it is sore Usually not Sexually transmitted? Yes — treat the partner No — an overgrowth, partner not treated Treatment Metronidazole, both people Metronidazole, her only Same drug, different rule about the partner. That is what the question is usually testing.

Six cover most exam questions, but these turn up too — and two of them are the reason “treated but still symptomatic” happens. Infection What to know Mycoplasma genitalium Bacterial. A common cause of urethritis and cervicitis that persists after the usual treatment , because resistance is widespread. Suspect it when symptoms continue after doxycycline HIV Viral, treatable, not curable. Test everyone 13–64 at least once. PrEP before exposure; PEP must start within 72 hours after one Hepatitis B Viral, vaccine-preve

NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhea — urine or a swab, from every site of exposure : genital, rectal and pharyngeal. A negative urine test does not clear a throat infection. Syphilis: screen with RPR or VDRL, confirm with a treponemal test. One test alone is not a diagnosis. Herpes: PCR or culture from the lesion, taken while it is still fluid-filled. Trichomonas: wet mount or NAAT. Diagnose one, test for the rest — including HIV and hepatitis B and C. Having one STI raises the risk of every other. Possible HIV exposu

Chlamydia and gonorrhea annually in all sexually active women under 25 , and older women with risk factors Everyone 13–64 tested for HIV at least once ; more often with ongoing risk Syphilis, HIV and hepatitis B at the first prenatal visit , repeated in the third trimester if at risk HPV vaccine at 11–12 , available from age 9 and caught up to 26 — it works by being given before exposure, which is why it is offered years before anyone expects it to be needed Annual Pap alongside it — the vaccine does not replace sc

entries.h: 🤰 In pregnancy — where the stakes change

entries.t: It can cross at any stage and cause stillbirth, prematurity, or congenital syphilis in a baby who looks well at birth and is damaged months later. So it is screened for repeatedly, not once. Screen for syphilis When Everyone At the first prenatal visit Everyone Again in the third trimester Higher risk Again at delivery

entries.h: 🚨 Penicillin is the only treatment that works in pregnancy
entries.t: Doxycycline is teratogenic and the alternatives do not reliably cross the placenta to treat the fetus. Penicillin is the only option , so a reported allergy does not change the drug — it changes the route in. Assess what kind of reaction it was. A rash decades ago is not anaphylaxis, and most reported penicillin allergy is not true allergy. If it is genuine, the answer is penicillin desensitization — tiny escalating doses under supervision — then treat. Teach her why. The reason to accept the drug is what happens t

entries.h: Herpes at the time of birth
entries.t: Active genital lesions at term mean a cesarean birth. Neonatal herpes is devastating, and a baby passing through an actively shedding birth canal is how it happens. Report active lesions in pregnancy to the provider — it is a priority , not a “mention it at the next visit” Do not touch the lesions; wash hands afterwards every time Keep them clean and dry; avoid scented soaps No sex while lesions are present — and condoms do not make it safe , because the virus sheds from skin a condom does not cover

entries.h: 🚨 What happens if nobody catches it

entries.t: Untreated chlamydia or gonorrhea climbs from the cervix into the uterus and tubes. The finding that names it: cervical motion tenderness — moving the cervix on exam hurts. With lower abdominal pain, fever and discharge, that is PID. Scarred tubes do not unscar. PID leaves infertility, chronic pelvic pain, and a permanently raised risk of ectopic pregnancy — which is why a silent chlamydia infection at 19 matters at 30.

Untreated syphilis goes quiet for years, then returns as neurosyphilis and cardiovascular syphilis. Latent does not mean gone. In pregnancy — congenital syphilis, neonatal conjunctivitis and pneumonia from chlamydia, and neonatal herpes, which is why active lesions at term mean a cesarean birth. HPV causes cervical cancer, and anal, oropharyngeal and penile cancers too. Any STI raises HIV transmission — broken mucosa is a doorway.

Ask directly, routinely and without flinching. Partners, practices, protection — asked the same way you ask about anything else. Your comfort is what decides whether she tells you the truth, and a client who senses judgment gives you a useless history. Ask about every site of exposure , because that is where you swab.

Finish the whole course , even once the symptoms stop The partner is treated too — otherwise they hand it back and forth No sex for 7 days after starting treatment — and not until the partner has been treated too, not until one of them feels better All sex — oral and anal included. “We avoided vaginal sex but oral was fine” is a classic wrong answer Come back for a test of cure where one is indicated, and retest in 3 months — reinfection is common Condoms every time — but say plainly that they reduce and do not rem

Painless ulcer = syphilis → penicillin. Painful blisters = herpes. Cervical motion tenderness = PID Chlamydia is usually silent — screen under 25 annually Antivirals control herpes; nothing cures it The HPV vaccine is given before exposure — at 11–12 Trichomonas: treat the partner. Bacterial vaginosis: do not Swab every site of exposure , not just the genital one Rash on the palms and soles → think secondary syphilis Penicillin allergy in pregnancy → desensitize , do not substitute No sex for 7 days after starting

Tissue like the lining of the uterus, growing where it does not belong — bleeding every cycle with nowhere to drain. It is the commonest reason a young woman is told her crippling periods are normal.

Tissue similar to the uterine lining grows outside the uterus — on the ovaries, the ligaments behind the uterus, the tubes, the bowel or the bladder. It still answers to estrogen, so it builds up and bleeds with every cycle . But there is no way out. Blood that cannot leave becomes inflammation, and inflammation becomes scar tissue and adhesions. That is the whole disease: pain, organs stuck to each other, and trouble getting pregnant. It is not an infection. Nothing about it is treated with antibiotics.

Anatomy, symptoms, assessment and treatment on one plate — and the two distinctions that get missed: endometriosis grows outside the uterus while adenomyosis grows within the uterine muscle , and pain severity does not track the extent of disease .

Endometri​ osis and endometr​ itis are a letter apart and share nothing but the word root. Mixing them up is the commonest mistake on this topic — and they turn up in the same courses, so the test knows it. Endometri osis Endometr itis What it is Lining- like tissue growing outside the uterus Infection of the uterine lining Who gets it Anyone who menstruates — often from the first period on Most often postpartum , especially after a cesarean birth Timing Chronic , cycling with her periods for years Acute — fever af

Staged at laparoscopy , on a point score built from how many implants there are, how deep they go, where they sit, and how much scarring ties things together. Four stages come out of it. I Minimal A few small, shallow implants . Little or no scar tissue. II Mild More implants, and deeper ones. Minor adhesions starting to form. III Moderate Many deep implants, endometriomas — blood-filled ovarian cysts, the “chocolate cysts” — and significant adhesions . IV Severe Widespread deep implants, large endometriomas, and d

Ovaries — the classic site, and where endometriomas form Behind the uterus : the cul-de-sac and the uterosacral ligaments , which is why a pelvic exam can feel tender nodules there Fallopian tubes — scarring here is a route to infertility and to ectopic pregnancy Bowel and bladder — giving cyclic bowel or urinary symptoms that flare with her period Rarely further afield, including old surgical scars

The classic triad. Three kinds of pain, and all three track the cycle. Dysmenorrhea Painful periods that are secondary — they started later in life, not at menarche — and get worse over the years. Pain often begins 1–2 days before the flow. Dyspareunia Deep pain with intercourse, from implants on the ligaments behind the uterus. Dyschezia Painful bowel movements, worst during the period. And alongside them: Chronic pelvic pain between periods Heavy or irregular bleeding Infertility — often the reason she is finally

There is no blood test. The work-up is: History — the cyclic pattern of the pain is the strongest clue Pelvic exam — tender nodules on the uterosacral ligaments, a fixed, retroverted uterus Ultrasound or MRI — can show an endometrioma, but a normal scan does not rule it out Laparoscopy with direct visualization ± biopsy — the definitive diagnosis and the moment it is staged Years pass before most women are diagnosed. The pain is cyclic, the exam is often normal, and “bad periods” gets normalized. Believing her is a

Nothing cures it. Everything below either quiets the inflammation or takes the estrogen away, because the disease is estrogen-dependent . It settles at menopause — usually. Step What it is What she needs to know 1. NSAIDs Ibuprofen, naproxen Start before the pain does — a day ahead of the flow, on a schedule. Take with food. 2. Combined hormonal contraception Pills, patch, ring — often taken continuously to skip periods Fewer periods means less bleeding into the implants. Not for a smoker over 35. 3. Progestins Nor

Expected — teach her it is coming: Shoulder and neck pain from the CO 2 used to inflate the abdomen. It is referred pain, it is normal, and walking plus a heating pad and lying on the left side move it along. It clears in a day or two. Some bloating, and a small amount of vaginal spotting Discharge teaching: no heavy lifting and nothing in the vagina for about 2 weeks — no tampons, no douching, no intercourse. Warm compresses for comfort. Shower, do not soak. 🚨 Call the provider for: fever, heavy vaginal bleeding,

Pain A scheduled plan around the cycle beats chasing the pain Heat to the lower abdomen or back Regular exercise; rest positions that ease pelvic pressure Track symptoms against the calendar — it makes the pattern visible to her and to the provider The rest of her Fertility counselling early , before decisions are urgent Screen for depression at every visit Name the disbelief she has met, and validate the pain Support groups and reliable information

Tissue like the lining, growing outside the uterus — not an infection The triad: dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, dyschezia Secondary dysmenorrhea that worsens over years is the pattern Laparoscopy is the definitive diagnosis — and where it is staged Stage does not predict pain Endometrioma = chocolate cyst on the ovary It is estrogen-dependent ; every hormonal treatment works by taking estrogen away GnRH agonist → medical menopause → watch the bone Danazol → androgenic effects; the voice change is permanent Post-laparos

entries.h: Anemia vs acute GN vs CKD · ABSN Study Hub
entries.t: Skip to study content Anemia · Acute glomerulonephritis · Chronic kidney disease
Compare headache, skin color, urine color and blood pressure. Start with the picture or jump to one finding below.
All three: headache and pallor may occur. Both kidney disorders: blood pressure may be elevated. Acute GN: tea- or cola-colored urine. CKD: urine may still look light yellow.
Light yellow is an expected urine color. Its appearance alone does not rule out chronic kidney disease.
Anemia May occur. Acute GN May occur. CKD May occur. Headache is a shared finding, so it does not distinguish these conditions by itself.
Anemia Pallor. Acute GN Pallor. CKD Pallor. Pallor means paler than usual for the person. Compare with their usual skin appearance.

Anemia — Not emphasized. Acute GN Tea- or cola-colored (blood in the urine). CKD May remain light yellow. Acute GN leaks blood, so the urine looks tea- or cola-colored — your NUR 235 Module 13 page (“Nephrotic leaks protein. Nephritic leaks blood.”). Light yellow is an expected urine color, and normal-looking urine does not rule out chronic kidney disease.
Anemia — Not emphasized. Acute GN May be elevated. CKD May be elevated. Elevated blood pressure is emphasized with both kidney disorders in this comparison.

— means not emphasized in this study comparison. It does not mean the finding is impossible. The graphic focuses on the associations in your supplied study material; it is not a complete symptom list. Findings alone do not establish a diagnosis.

Ask what helps. Offer choices. Reassess. Start with the picture, then use the short cards to review.

The client can change their plan and request medication later.

Warm water may ease pain and tension. The highlighted answer in your active-labor question is D: assist the client into a warm shower. Check that water use is appropriate and help with safe entry and exit. ↔
Try upright, side-lying or supported positions. Offer a comfortable position change or a supported birth ball when appropriate. Keep necessary monitoring possible. 🤲
Ask before touch; try sacral counterpressure. Offer lower-back massage or firm pressure over the sacrum if wanted. Stop or change the touch when it is uncomfortable. 🌬
Slow breathing, a focal point or guided imagery. Coach a calm breathing rhythm and relaxed shoulders. Imagining a familiar, peaceful place can support coping. ♨
Protect the skin; check comfort and temperature. Use a protective layer and check the skin. A cool, damp cloth can be soothing when the client feels warm. 🎵
Offer reassurance, quiet or preferred music. Stay present and ask what feels helpful. Music is a preference-based comfort option, not the best answer to the supplied exam item.

A shower for comfort is different from a decision about giving birth in water.

The picture to remember: the maternal thighs are brought back onto the abdomen. McRoberts is a positioning maneuver .
Pregnancy complications, labor and birth: readable notes, original course pictures and practice questions. High-yield review Complete study guide Shoulder dystocia pictures
McRoberts = maternal position. Suprapubic = pressure just above the pubic bone. Fundal = pressure on the top of the uterus — do not use.

entries.h: Read the picture in five chunks

entries.t: Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency. The head has delivered but the shoulders do not follow normally. Call for help and follow the unit response. ↶
Back flat; hips deeply flexed. The thighs move back onto the abdomen, with an assistant supporting each leg. McRoberts changes maternal pelvic alignment to help release the shoulder. ✓
Suprapubic pressure is a separate maneuver. It is often paired with McRoberts and is applied just above the pubic bone by the trained team. ⛔

No fundal pressure. No forceful head pulling. Fundal pressure means pressing on the top of the uterus. It can worsen shoulder impaction. Avoid forceful, lateral or downward traction on the baby’s head. 🗒

Assist positioning, note times and reassure. Use clear communication and document the event and maneuvers as directed. If the initial maneuvers do not work, the team promptly proceeds through its shoulder-dystocia protocol.

McRoberts and suprapubic pressure are commonly used first external maneuvers. They do not resolve every shoulder dystocia. Trained-team protocol and prompt escalation remain essential. This graphic supports recognition for nursing study; hands-on technique is learned in supervised obstetric training.

Opioid exposure near birth can affect newborn breathing. Your question’s answer is B: assess the newborn for respiratory depression.
B — assess the newborn for respiratory depression. Reflex checks, maternal bradycardia and newborn withdrawal are not the best response to this specific item.

entries.h: 01 Why the newborn is the focus
entries.t: Meperidine is an opioid that crosses the placenta. Near birth, exposure may cause excess sedation and weak or slow breathing. The question states the dose was given 1 hour before entering the second stage —not necessarily 1 hour before delivery. 🫁
Watch breathing rate and effort. Also assess heart rate, oxygenation, tone and responsiveness as part of newborn assessment. Poor breathing requires prompt evaluation and support. 📣

Tell the birth team the drug and administration time. Be ready for neonatal support. If breathing is ineffective, summon the neonatal team and support ventilation according to neonatal resuscitation protocol. 🩺
Check respirations and sedation. Maternal opioid effects also matter. Continue the prescribed maternal and fetal monitoring. ↔

A recent labor dose points to an immediate breathing concern. Possible withdrawal is associated with prolonged prenatal opioid exposure. It is a different concern from the acute respiratory depression emphasized in this question.

The screenshot’s statement that Narcan is ineffective should not become a general rule. The current meperidine label describes opioid-antagonist reversal of opioid-induced neonatal respiratory depression. That does not make naloxone the first response to a newborn who is not breathing effectively. AHA/AAP neonatal guidance prioritizes effective ventilation. entries.h: Pharmacological pain relief in labor · NUR 234
entries.t: Skip to study content Labor comfort · Compare the options
Match each method to what it does and what the nurse watches. Analgesia reduces pain; anesthesia blocks sensation.

Epidural/spinal: maternal blood pressure and fetal response. Systemic opioid near birth: maternal and newborn breathing. Nitrous: self-held mask; avoid the opioid/sedative combination. Pudendal/local: perineal pain, not contraction pain.

A catheter provides ongoing regional pain relief. Often combines local anesthetic and opioid. Watch maternal blood pressure and fetal heart rate, bladder function, and leg strength. Follow prescribed monitoring and assist mobility until function is assessed. ⚡

Spinal relief is rapid and time-limited. CSE means combined spinal–epidural: the spinal component starts relief, while an epidural catheter allows continued medication. Monitor blood pressure, breathing and block level; report a headache that changes with posture. 💊

IV or IM medicine reduces pain throughout the body. These medicines can cross the placenta. Watch maternal sedation and respirations, and prepare to assess newborn breathing. Medication, dose, route and proximity to birth affect planning. 😷

The client holds the inhalation mask. Nitrous oxide mixed with oxygen helps coping, with rapid onset and offset. Watch for dizziness, nausea and sedation. Do not co-administer with systemic opioids or sedative/hypnotic medicines. 🎯
Targets the perineal area for birth or repair. A pudendal block targets the nerve supply; local infiltration numbs a small tissue area. These approaches do not relieve uterine contraction pain.

Discuss preferences, allergies, contraindications, clinical status and available monitoring. The client can change their mind. This is a comparison aid—not a dosing guide, a complete contraindication list or a replacement for unit policy.

entries.h: Pregnancy hormones: who does what? · NUR 234
entries.t: Skip to study content Pregnancy physiology · Seven key signals
Remember one job first, then add the detail. Prolactin makes milk; oxytocin moves milk.

Prolactin → production. Oxytocin → ejection. After placental delivery, estrogen and progesterone fall. This enables the transition to copious milk production; the two milk hormones have different jobs.

Human chorionic gonadotropin supports the corpus luteum early. This helps sustain progesterone while the placenta develops its hormone-producing role. Pregnancy tests detect hCG. In your nursing sign categories, a positive hCG test is a probable sign, not a definitive fetal finding. 🛡
Maintains the uterine lining and supports uterine relaxation. The corpus luteum provides early progesterone; the placenta later becomes the major source. 🌱
Supports uterine growth and breast duct development. Placental estrogen production becomes important during pregnancy. 🔋

Human placental lactogen helps increase maternal insulin resistance. This supports fuel availability for the fetus. hPL is a placental hormone and also supports mammary development; it is one contributor to pregnancy’s metabolic changes. ↔
Helps relax pelvic ligaments and soften the cervix. Sources include the corpus luteum and placenta. The diagram highlights supporting tissues; it does not depict the bones separating widely. 🥛
Stimulates milk production in the breast. Produced by the anterior pituitary. Levels rise during pregnancy; the drop in placental hormones after birth permits copious milk production. 💧

Stimulates uterine contractions and milk ejection (let-down). Made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary. It helps move milk through ducts; it is not the hormone that makes the milk.

hCG signals · Progesterone maintains · Estrogen grows · hPL shifts fuel · Relaxin loosens · Prolactin produces · Oxytocin contracts and ejects. These are memory cues for major functions, not the only effects of each hormone.

Bone Breaks, Neurovascular Checks & Emergency Stabilization NG-056 Musculoskeletal ADHD-friendly visual edition A fracture is any break in the continuity of a bone — from a hairline crack to a shattered shaft. The nurse's job isn't the x-ray, it's everything around the bone : is the skin open, is the limb still getting blood flow and nerve signal, and is there a life threat (pelvic bleed, spinal shock, skull fracture) hiding behind the obvious injury? This page builds the 6 P's — the neurovascular assessment used o

🦴 Open vs closed Skin broken = open/compound = infection risk + check tetanus status. 🖐️ The 6 P's Pain · Pallor · Pulselessness · Paresthesia · Paralysis · Poikilothermia — neurovascular compromise. 🩸 Pelvic fracture Hypotension + tachycardia + hematuria = internal bleeding → report NOW. 🚨 Splint before you move Immobilize the joint above & below the break first — always. 🦴
STEP 1 · NAME THE BREAK Every fracture question starts by naming what kind of break it is — the name usually tells you the risk.

entries.h: 🩻 Six fracture patterns you must recognize on sight

entries.t: Bone disruption Injury affects bone and nearby tissue. Stabilization Reduction and immobilization support alignment. Healing and monitoring Protect the site while checking function and perfusion. Neurovascular checks Assess pain, sensation, movement, color, temperature and circulation. Cast care Keep it dry as directed; avoid inserting objects or altering the cast. Escalate Increasing pain, tightness, numbness or new weakness may indicate a complication. 🧠 “COGS-C” — C losed · O pen · G reenstick · S piral · obliqu

entries.h: 🚪 Closed vs Open — the one question that changes care
entries.t: Closed Open “compound” Skin intact — bone does not break the skin surface Skin surface broken — bone visible or was exposed Lower infection risk High infection risk — ask about last tetanus vaccine Cover, splint, x-ray Sterile dressing, never push the bone back in , IV antibiotics often started 🧠 HESI trap: open leg fracture → the nurse should ask “when was your last tetanus shot?” — broken skin + soil/debris exposure = tetanus risk.

entries.h: ⚠️ Risk factors — what sets a fracture up
entries.t: 🛏️ Prolonged bed rest — disuse osteoporosis, muscle atrophy & loss of tone 🦴 Osteoporosis — weak, porous bone (see the Osteoporosis page in this library) 💊 Steroids “-sone” — prednisone, dexamethasone, hydrocortisone, fludrocortisone — long-term use thins bone 💥 Trauma — falls, MVC, sports 🧠 Kaplan SATA: long-term bed rest effect the nurse should worry about most → loss of muscle tone and disuse atrophy (select-all-that-apply style question). 🖐️
STEP 2 · THE 6 P's This is the neurovascular check you will run on every injured or casted limb — memorize it here, it repeats on every page in this series.

entries.h: 🖐️ THE 6 P's — neurovascular assessment of an injured limb
entries.t: 🧠 “Early vs late.” Paresthesia (tingling) shows up first — that's your window to intervene. Pulselessness and paralysis are late signs — by the time you see those, tissue damage may already be underway. Never wait for all 6 P's — one abnormal P = notify the HCP .

entries.h: 🩸 Pelvic fracture — the priority finding you must catch
entries.t: 💥 Pelvic fracture — large vessels run right through the pelvis ▼ 🩸 Internal bleeding into the pelvic cavity (can be liters, hidden) ▼ 🚨 Hypotension + Tachycardia + Hematuria — report to HCP immediately Also watch for: crepitus (grating sensation/sound of bone ends rubbing) and muscle spasm around the fracture site. 🧠 Saunders trap: "Which is the most serious finding for a pelvic fracture?" → hypotension, tachycardia, and hematuria — signs of hemorrhagic shock and bladder/urethral injury, not just local pain.

entries.h: 🦵 Hip fracture — the classic exam picture
entries.t: 📏 Shortening of the affected leg 🔄 Affected leg often externally rotated 😖 Muscle spasm around the hip 🟣 Ecchymosis (bruising) over thigh/hip ⚡ Groin & hip pain that worsens with weight bearing 🧠 Hip fracture = “short & turned out.” A leg that looks shorter and rotated outward, in an older adult who fell, is a hip fracture until proven otherwise.

entries.h: 🧠 Skull, spine & mandible — trauma above the neck
entries.t: Basilar skull fracture: clear fluid from nose/ear ( CSF rhinorrhea/otorrhea ) — never suction or pack the nose , test for a "halo" ring on gauze. Spinal fracture at T6 or higher → neurogenic shock: hypotension + bradycardia + skin that stays pink & dry (loss of sympathetic tone, not hypovolemia). Mandibular fracture: bleeding/drooling from the mouth → suction the mouth , protect the airway first. 🧠 “Bradycardia + hypotension + warm dry skin” = neurogenic shock, NOT hypovolemic shock (which is tachycardic, cool, cla
STEP 3 · STABILIZE FIRST Immobilize before you move anything — then reassess the 6 P's before and after every intervention.

1 ABCs first — treat life threats (airway, breathing, hemorrhage) before the limb itself 2 Assess the 6 P's distal to the injury before touching it 3 Splint the joint above AND below the fracture before any movement 4 Reassess the 6 P's immediately after splinting — a tight splint can cause the exact injury it prevents 5 Elevate & ice the limb to reduce swelling 🧠 “Check, splint, check again.” Neurovascular status is assessed before AND after every splint, cast, or traction device is applied — that repeated check i

entries.h: ⏳ Fracture healing timeline — what's happening under the cast
entries.t: 🧠 “Clot → Soft → Hard → Remodel.” A soft callus (week 1–2) will bend or re-break under stress — that's exactly why a fresh cast means no weight-bearing yet , even though the limb is immobilized. Full remodeling can take up to two years.

entries.h: 🚨 Open fracture — do this, never that
entries.t: ✅ Cover exposed bone with a sterile dressing ✅ Immobilize/splint as-is ✅ Confirm tetanus vaccination status ❌ Never push exposed bone back under the skin ❌ Never irrigate or clean the wound aggressively in the field 🧠 Cover it, don't cover it up. The bone stays where it is — the HCP reduces it in a controlled, sterile setting.

entries.h: 🧊 Pain, swelling & the compartment syndrome watch
entries.t: Fracture pain classically includes bruising, swelling, muscle spasm, and crepitus (grating). Elevate the limb, apply ice, and treat pain proactively. Pain that keeps climbing despite analgesia — especially with passive stretch — is not "just a bad fracture." It is the first sign of compartment syndrome , covered in full on the Cast Care page in this series. 🧠 If pain doesn't match the picture — always think compartment syndrome , not "needs more pain meds."

Fracture care doesn't stop at the ED. This series follows the same patient forward: 🛏️ NG-058 Buck's Traction & postoperative musculoskeletal care 🫁 NG-061 Fat embolism & osteomyelitis — the two big fracture complications 🦿 NG-063 Cast care — teaching the 6 P's back to the patient at home 🧠 The 6 P's you learned above are the exact same checklist used for traction pin sites, casted limbs, and post-op neurovascular checks — one skill, reused everywhere in orthopedics. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🦴 Open = tetanus check closed = skin intact, open = skin broken + infection risk 🖐️ 6 P's Pain · Pallor · Pulselessness · Paresthesia · Paralysis · Poikilothermia 🩸 Pelvic fx priority hypotension + tachycardia + hematuria = internal bleed 🚨 Splint first joint above & below, reassess 6 P's before/after

Open/compound: bone breaks through the skin — high infection risk, check tetanus status, never push the bone back in. Q2: Name all 6 P's of neurovascular assessment. Show answer Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Paresthesia, Paralysis, Poikilothermia (temperature). Paresthesia is early; pulselessness and paralysis are late/ominous. entries.t: 🦴 Fracture & Trauma Care series: 1 · Fracture 2 · Buck's Traction & Post-Op 3 · Fat Embolism & Osteomyelitis 4 · Cast Care Nursing Field Notes / Musculoskeletal · Fracture & Trauma Care Series · Page 2 of 4

& Postoperative Musculoskeletal Surgery Care NG-058 Musculoskeletal ADHD-friendly visual edition Buck's traction is a temporary skin traction device used before hip/femur surgery to realign the bone and stop muscle spasms. This page covers setting it up safely, then follows the same patient through hip/femur surgery — ORIF or external fixation — and the postoperative priorities: bleeding, infection, positioning, and mobility. Uses the 6 P's from the Fracture page for every neurovascular check. 📄 Simple Nursing orig

⚖️ Weights hang FREE Never let traction weights rest on the bed or floor. 🛏️ Stay flat Supine, HOB not elevated over 25° while in Buck's traction. 🦵 Abduction pillow Post-hip-surgery: legs apart, never crossed, never flexed past 90°. 🩸 Bleeding > Infection Post-op priority order: hemorrhage first, then infection. 🛏️
STEP 1 · SET UP TRACTION Buck's traction buys time before surgery — it pulls, it doesn't fix. Setup errors lose the whole point of the device.

entries.h: ⚙️ Buck's traction anatomy — what's actually pulling on what

entries.t: Applied force Traction helps align or stabilize the affected area. Countertraction Body position provides the opposing force. Continuous checks Alignment and equipment determine the effect. Equipment Keep ropes aligned and prescribed weights hanging freely. Patient care Monitor skin, pressure areas, circulation, sensation and comfort. Postoperative phase Follow movement and weight-bearing restrictions and prevent immobility complications. 🧠 Kaplan trap: "Most important nursing action to maintain effective traction?

🦴 Short-term , used before surgery 🎯 Realigns hip & femur fractures 😖 Stops muscle spasms that would otherwise pull bone fragments out of place 🩹 It is skin traction — a boot/foam sleeve on the skin, no pins into bone 🧠 Skin vs skeletal traction: Buck's = skin traction (boot/foam, lighter pull). Skeletal traction uses pins placed directly into the bone for heavier, longer-term pulling — those pin sites need sterile pin care (see the card to the right).

🛏️ Client stays supine, flat ❌ Do NOT elevate the HOB over ~25° (commonly taught as 20–30°; follow facility/provider orders) — raising it pulls the line of traction off-axis ↔️ Keep the limb in neutral alignment — don't let it rotate 🚫 Ropes must not rest against the footboard or bed frame 🧠 “Flat line, straight pull.” Traction only works if the rope runs in a straight line from limb to weight — raise the head, bend the line, lose the pull. ⚙️
STEP 2 · MONITOR THE LIMB Same 6 P's you learned on the Fracture page — now applied to a limb under continuous pulling force.
🧠 Same skill, new device. Whether it's a splint, a cast, or traction — the neurovascular check never changes. If any P is abnormal, loosen nothing on your own — notify the HCP.

Skin traction pulls on skin, not bone — so skin breakdown under the boot/foam is the priority thing to monitor. 👀 Assess boot/foam contact points for redness, blistering, or breakdown 🧴 Reposition the client (not the limb out of alignment) to offload pressure 🦶 Check weights are hanging free and off the floor at every round 🧠 Saunders: priority monitoring for a client in skin traction = signs of skin breakdown at the traction interface.

entries.h: 💉 If it becomes skeletal traction: pin site care
entries.t: Skeletal traction and external fixation use pins through the bone. Typical care includes pin care with sterile technique — frequency varies by facility protocol (a commonly taught example is 3×/day ). Thick, yellow drainage from a pin site is the finding that worries the nurse most — it signals infection, not normal serous ooze. 🧠 Clear/serous ooze = expected. Thick yellow = infected. Compare color every shift. 🩹
STEP 3 · POST-OP PRIORITIES The traction comes off for surgery — ORIF or external fixation — then the priorities shift to bleeding, infection, positioning, and getting the patient moving.

entries.h: 🔧 Two ways to fix the fracture surgically
entries.t: ORIF External fixation O pen R eduction I nternal F ixation — plates/screws/rods placed inside via surgical incision Pins placed through skin into bone, connected to an external frame outside the body 🧠 ORIF = fixed on the inside. External fixation = frame on the outside. Both stabilize the same fracture, different approach.

entries.h: 🚨 Post-op priority order: bleeding, then infection
entries.t: 1️⃣ Bleeding — hypotension & tachycardia, monitor pulses distal to the surgical site ▼ 2️⃣ Infection — elevated WBC, wound pain/color/amount/odor of drainage 🧠 HESI: the priority post-op assessment for a hip fracture repair includes wound assessment with special attention to pain, and to color/amount/odor of exudate — plus positioning and education.

entries.h: 🦵 Total hip arthroplasty precautions — protect the new joint
entries.t: ✅ Abducted legs — pillow between the legs while turning/lying ✅ Toes pointing upward , neutral rotation ❌ No crossing legs ❌ No leaning forward (no tying shoes) ❌ No sitting in low chairs or bending the hip past 90° 🧠 “HESI: interventions after hip fracture repair” → positioning + education. Kaplan/Saunders: after internal fixation, position the leg abducted with toes pointing upward — a pillow between the legs while repositioning.
🧠 Kaplan: which lab value should the nurse report post-op THA? A hemoglobin below 7 or a markedly elevated WBC (e.g., 17,000 ) — both are call-the-provider numbers.

1 Pain control — around-the-clock scheduling, reassess after every intervention 2 Early mobilization — dangle, then ambulate with an assistive device (e.g., walker) as ordered; turn q2h if not yet ambulating 3 DVT prevention — sequential compression devices, anticoagulation per order, ankle pumps, early ambulation 4 Neurovascular checks — the 6 P's, every scheduled round 🧠 DVT prevention here matters twice: it protects the patient and reduces the risk of the fat embolism/PE picture covered on the next page in this

SAY IT OUT LOUD ⚖️ Weights free-hanging never on the bed or floor — the #1 traction rule 🛏️ Flat, HOB ≤25° keeps the traction line straight 🦵 Abducted, toes up pillow between legs, never crossed, never >90° 🩸 Bleed first, then infection hypotension/tachycardia before elevated WBC

Q2: Why must the HOB stay under 25° in Buck's traction? Show answer Raising the head pulls the traction line off a straight axis, reducing its effectiveness — the client stays supine and flat. Q3: How should the leg be positioned after total hip arthroplasty? Show answer Abducted, with toes pointing upward — a pillow between the le

entries.h: Fat Embolism & Osteomyelitis · NG-061 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🦴 Fracture & Trauma Care series: 1 · Fracture 2 · Buck's Traction & Post-Op 3 · Fat Embolism & Osteomyelitis 4 · Cast Care Nursing Field Notes / Musculoskeletal · Fracture & Trauma Care Series · Page 3 of 4

& Osteomyelitis — Two Fracture Complications That Aren't the 6 P's NG-061 Musculoskeletal ADHD-friendly visual edition Both of these hide behind a "routine" fracture. Fat embolism syndrome (FES) is a systemic emergency — marrow fat escapes into the bloodstream and lodges in the lungs, brain, or heart. Osteomyelitis is a bone infection that follows an open fracture, surgery, or puncture. Neither one is caught by the 6 P's from the Fracture page — those check the limb's blood flow; FES and osteomyelitis are whole-bod

🫁 The classic triad Respiratory distress + mental status change + petechial rash = FES until proven otherwise. ⏱️ 24–72 hours FES classically shows up 1–3 days after a long-bone or pelvic fracture. 🌡️ 103°F + yellow drainage High fever + purulent drainage at a puncture/surgical site = think osteomyelitis. 🏠 PICC + weeks of antibiotics Osteomyelitis treatment goes home with the patient — IV antibiotics for weeks to months. 🫁
STEP 1 · THE CLOT THAT ISN'T A CLOT Marrow fat, not a blood clot, blocks the vessel — but the destinations are just as deadly: lung, brain, heart.

entries.h: 🩻 Pathophysiology — bone marrow escapes into the bloodstream
entries.t: Fat embolism syndrome is a major complication of crushing fractures & long-bone injuries — femur, pelvis, and hip fractures carry the highest risk. The injured bone releases fat globules from the marrow directly into torn venous sinusoids. Those globules travel through the bloodstream and — just like a blood clot — can lodge somewhere far from the fracture, causing a deadly blockage in the lung (respiratory failure), brain (stroke-like picture), or heart (MI-like picture).

Long-bone or tissue injury Can release fat into the circulation. Infection reaches bone Can occur through blood, injury or surgery. Different complications Respiratory-neurologic change differs from focal bone infection. Fat embolism syndrome Hypoxemia, neurologic change and sometimes petechiae after injury need urgent evaluation. Osteomyelitis Bone pain, inflammatory signs or drainage may occur; fever can be absent. Care Support oxygenation when needed and follow imaging, cultures and antimicrobial or surgical pla

entries.h: 🚨 The classic triad — memorize this exact set of three
entries.t: 🧠 "Confused, can't breathe, covered in dots." All three don't have to appear at once — mental status change is often the earliest clue , before the rash ever shows up. Petechiae are the most specific finding but frequently arrive last.

🦴 Long-bone fractures — femur is the classic culprit 🩹 Pelvic fractures 💥 Multiple fractures / crush injuries 🔩 Orthopedic surgery, especially IM rod/nail placement 🧠 Closed fractures can carry higher FES risk than open ones — the marrow pressure has nowhere to release except into the bloodstream.

📉 Low pulse ox — hypoxia often precedes the rash 🩸 Thrombocytopenia — platelets consumed with fat globules 🌡️ Fever & tachycardia 💓 Tachypnea, chest pain, crackles KAPLAN An older adult client is diagnosed with a fractured femur. Which observation is an early sign of fat embolism? Answer: altered mental status — it can precede the dyspnea and the rash. 🦴
STEP 2 · BONE INFECTION Bacteria gets INTO the bone through a break in the barrier — then the immune response and the infection both damage the bone.

entries.h: 🚪 Pathophysiology — four doors bacteria use to reach bone
entries.t: Osteomyelitis is a bone infection , most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus , that enters the bloodstream — and then the bone — through one of these routes: 🧠 "If it breaches the skin near a bone, it can breach the bone." Open fracture, surgery, puncture, or needle — all four are just different doors to the same infection.

🔥 High fever — often high-grade (a commonly used exam example is ~103°F / 39.4°C ) 😣 Localized bone pain , constant, worse with movement 🟠 Swelling, warmth, erythema over the site 💛 Pus or yellow drainage from a wound or puncture site 🧠 Fever + yellow drainage days after a procedure = infection, not just "normal healing." Report it — don't wait it out.

KAPLAN Several days after a bone marrow aspiration, the nurse notes a client's temp of 103°F (39.5°C) and yellow drainage from the aspiration site. Most accurate interpretation? Answer: the client has developed osteomyelitis. 🩺
STEP 3 · TREAT & MONITOR FES is stabilized and supported; osteomyelitis is fought with weeks of antibiotics and, if needed, surgery.

1 IV antibiotics for weeks to months — targeted to the organism found on culture 2 Discharge home with a PICC line — a home-health nurse continues the long IV antibiotic course 3 Surgical debridement — drains abscesses and removes necrotic/dead bone tissue 4 Amputation — only if the infection doesn't respond to therapy 🧠 "PICC line goes home too." Osteomyelitis is one of the classic reasons a patient is discharged still on IV antibiotics — teach PICC site care, flushing, and signs of line infection before they leav

🩹 Minimize movement of the fracture — immobilize/splint early, this is the #1 prevention step 🫁 Oxygen — may progress to mechanical ventilation if severe 💧 IV fluids to maintain hemodynamic stability 🛏️ Bed rest, continuous pulse ox & LOC monitoring 🧠 Prevention beats treatment here. There's no antidote for fat emboli once released — the nursing priority is keeping the fracture still so fewer globules ever enter the bloodstream.

entries.h: 🚨 FES — recognize fast, and know what "getting better" looks like
entries.t: The classic triad (respiratory distress + mental status change + petechial rash) after a long-bone or pelvic fracture is a medical emergency — notify the HCP immediately . SAUNDERS What is the most favorable indication of resolution of the fat embolism? Answer: clear mentation. Improving mental status — not the rash fading — is the reassuring sign that oxygenation and cerebral perfusion are recovering.

entries.h: 🖐️ Not the same checklist as the 6 P's
entries.t: The 6 P's from the Fracture page (pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia) assess local blood flow and nerve function in the injured limb itself. FES and osteomyelitis are different problems — FES is a systemic embolic event hitting lungs/brain/heart; osteomyelitis is a localized bone infection with systemic fever. Keep running the 6 P's on the limb and watching for these two complications — they aren't mutually exclusive. 🧠 One patient, three checklists: 6 P's for the limb, the triad fo

entries.h: ⚔️ Tell them apart — side by side
entries.t: Fat Embolism Syndrome Osteomyelitis Onset: 24–72 hrs after fracture Onset: days after fracture, surgery, or puncture Marrow fat blocks vessels (lung/brain/heart) Bacteria infects bone tissue Triad: respiratory distress, mental status change, petechiae High fever, localized pain, yellow drainage PRIORITY: O2, immobilize, notify HCP now PRIORITY: IV antibiotics, wound/PICC care, notify HCP ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🫁 FES triad respiratory distress + mental status change + petechiae ⏱️ 24–72 hrs after a long-bone or pelvic fracture 🌡️ 103°F + yellow drainage = think osteomyelitis 🏠 PICC line home weeks-to-months of IV antibiotics

Q1: What are the three findings in the classic fat embolism triad? Show answer Respiratory distress, altered mental status, and a petechial rash (chest/neck/axilla/conjunctiva). Mental status change is often the earliest. Q2: What is the single best way to prevent fat embolism syndrome after a fracture? Show answer Minimize movement of the fracture — immobilize/splint it early so less marrow fat is released into the bloodstream. Q3: How does bacteria typically reach bone to cause osteomyelitis? entries.t: 🦴 Fracture & Trauma Care series: 1 · Fracture 2 · Buck's Traction & Post-Op 3 · Fat Embolism & Osteomyelitis 4 · Cast Care Nursing Field Notes / Musculoskeletal · Fracture & Trauma Care Series · Page 4 of 4

Living With a Cast — Watching For Compartment Syndrome NG-063 Musculoskeletal ADHD-friendly visual edition A cast protects a healing bone — but a cast can also become the injury if swelling inside it cuts off blood flow. This page teaches the patient (and you) how to live with a cast day to day, and how to run the same neurovascular check as the 6 P's from the Fracture page ( NG-056 ) every single time — because the earliest sign of compartment syndrome is pain that elevation and pain medicine don't touch . 📄 Simpl

🚨 Pain that won't quit Unrelieved by elevation/analgesia + worse with passive stretch = compartment syndrome red flag. 🖐️ PMSC every check Pulses · Movement · Sensation · Color/temp — the cast version of the 6 P's. 💧 Clean, dry, elevated Bag it for showers, elevate above the heart for the first 48 hours. ❌ Nothing goes inside the cast No objects for itching — cool hair dryer only. 🚨
STEP 1 · WHAT CAN GO WRONG A cast can hide swelling from view — which is exactly why the assessment matters more than what you can see.

entries.h: 🚨 Compartment syndrome — the emergency this whole page is built around
entries.t: Compartment syndrome is an extremely painful condition that happens when pressure within the muscle compartments builds to dangerous levels — cutting off blood flow and oxygen and, left untreated, resulting in permanent tissue death.

Bone disruption Injury affects bone and nearby tissue. Stabilization Reduction and immobilization support alignment. Healing and monitoring Protect the site while checking function and perfusion. Neurovascular checks Assess pain, sensation, movement, color, temperature and circulation. Cast care Keep it dry as directed; avoid inserting objects or altering the cast. Escalate Increasing pain, tightness, numbness or new weakness may indicate a complication. 🧠 "A cast doesn't stretch — but swelling doesn't stop." Once

😖 Unrelieved with opioids — even morphine doesn't touch it 📈 Not resolving with medication or elevation 🖐️ Extreme pain with passive movement — pain when someone else stretches the fingers/toes SAUNDERS Client reports severe, deep, unrelenting pain and pain as the nurse assesses finger movement. What condition? Answer: compartment syndrome — pain out of proportion to injury, worse with passive stretch.

⚡ Tingling, burning, numbness 🖐️ Trouble moving or extending fingers/toes — described as "great difficulty" KAPLAN A nurse is assessing a client with a short leg cast for compartment syndrome. Which finding matches? Answer: pain that increases with passive movement.

Watch for a "hot spot" on the cast — a localized area that feels hot , plus a foul odor coming from the cast. Both point to infection underneath, not just normal healing warmth. KAPLAN Three hours after arriving on the orthopedic unit, a client reports a hot feeling under the cast. First action? Answer: assess circulation in the casted extremity and change the client's position. 🧠 "Hot + foul smell = infection; cold + pale = compartment syndrome." Two different temperature clues point to two different emergencies —
STEP 2 · PMSC NEURO CHECK This is the 6 P's from NG-056 , re-packaged as the bedside "PMSC" check you run on every casted limb.

🧠 PMSC is the cast-specific shorthand for the 6 P's (see NG-056 for the full definitions of pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia). Any abnormal finding — even just one — gets reported.

💓 Pulses present , not pulseless 🖐️ Can move/grip fingers or wiggle toes ⚡ No tingling or numbness ⏱️ Capillary refill under 3 seconds 🎨 Skin color normal, not pale 🌡️ Extremity warm, not cold or cool 🧠 "NOT" is the operative word for every line above — the nurse is ruling OUT compromise, every single check.

entries.h: 🚨 When any of these appear — notify HCP immediately
entries.t: ❌ Pulselessness ❌ Numbness, tingling ❌ Cold, pale foot/hand ❌ Swelling that keeps increasing ❌ Pain unrelieved by elevation or analgesia SAUNDERS A plaster cast is placed on the lower extremity. Which instructions should be given to the client? Answer: notify the HCP immediately for numbness, swelling, or if the foot becomes cold and pale; assess capillary refill, temperature, color, and amount of pain. 🩹
STEP 3 · LIVING WITH THE CAST Keep it dry, keep it up, keep it empty of objects — and report pain that won't back down.

1 Clean & dry — NEVER wet. Cover the cast with a plastic bag for bathing/showers. 2 Elevate above the heart for the first 48 hours to limit swelling; continue elevating and icing as needed after. 3 Itch under the cast? Use a hair dryer on a cool setting — never insert an object. 4 Take it easy — no bearing weight on a plaster cast, no resting it on hard surfaces or letting fingers indent it while it's still setting. 🧠 "Bag it, prop it, blow it (cool), never poke it." Four rules, one cast — bathing, elevation, itchi

entries.h: ❌ Never do this to a cast
entries.t: 🪥 NO objects inserted coat hangers, pencils 💧 NO getting it wet plaster especially 🏋️ NO weight-bearing on a plaster cast 🪵 NO hard surfaces while setting 👉 NO finger indentations while damp 🧠 An itch feels urgent — an infected scratch wound under a cast is worse. Cool hair dryer only.
🧠 Handle a fresh plaster cast with open palms, not fingertips — fingertip pressure while it's still setting leaves indentations that can press on skin once hard.

entries.h: ⚔️ Normal cast pain vs compartment syndrome — tell them apart
entries.t: Expected post-fracture/cast pain 🚨 Compartment syndrome Improves with elevation, ice, and scheduled analgesia Not relieved by elevation or analgesia — even opioids Worse with active movement of the limb Worse with passive stretch — someone else moving the fingers/toes Gradually improves over days Pain that keeps climbing Sensation, pulses, color all normal Tingling/numbness, cold or pale skin may accompany it 🧠 The single red-flag phrase to remember: pain unrelieved by elevation and analgesia is not "a bad day" — i

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🚨 Pain unrelieved by elevation/analgesia = compartment syndrome red flag 🖐️ PMSC Pulses · Movement · Sensation · Color/temp — the cast's 6 P's check 💧 Keep it dry bag it for bathing; never insert objects for itching ⬆️ Elevate 48 hrs above the heart to control swelling

Q1: What is the earliest, most reliable red flag for compartment syndrome? Show answer Pain that is unrelieved by elevation and analgesia, especially pain with passive stretch of the fingers/toes. Q2: What does PMSC stand for, and why is it done on a casted limb? Show answer Pulses, Movement, Sensation, Color/temperature — the bedside version of the 6 P's used to catch neurovascular compromise early. Q3: How should a patient shower with a plaster cast? Show answer Cover the cast completely with a plastic bag — plas

Fitting, Gait Patterns, Stairs & Walker Safety NG-064 Musculoskeletal ADHD-friendly visual edition The device is only as safe as the technique. Crutches and canes both restore mobility while protecting a healing limb — but wrong fit or wrong gait turns an assistive device into an injury risk . This page goes deep on the mechanics: how to fit each device, the 4 crutch gait patterns, and exactly how weight moves on stairs. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🖐️ Weight on HANDS Never the armpits — axillary pressure = nerve damage. 🦯 Cane on the STRONG side Cane + weak leg move together, then the strong leg. 🪜 Up with the good, down with the bad The unaffected leg always leads going up; the crutches/cane + affected leg lead going down. 📏 2 finger-widths below axilla Crutch tip 6 in. out, 6 in. forward from the foot; elbow flexed ~ 15–30° . 🩼
STEP 1 · MEASURE IT RIGHT This builds on NG-167 (Ambulation) — that page covers the general body-mechanics/gait-belt overview. This page goes deep specifically on crutches, canes and walkers.

entries.h: 📏 Correct crutch fit — the numbers that get tested

entries.t: Assess ability Strength, balance, cognition and weight-bearing status. Fit the device Height and technique should match the person. Practice the sequence Move safely through walking, turns and transfers. Cane Often used on the stronger side; follow individualized instruction. Crutches Support weight through the hands, not the axillae. Walker Keep the frame stable and avoid stepping too far ahead of support. Weight bears on the hands/palms through the handgrips — the axillary pad is a balance point only, never a wei

entries.h: 🚨 The classic NCLEX trap: axillary nerve damage
entries.t: Crutch top pressing into the axilla compresses the brachial plexus . Presents as numbness/tingling in the hand , weak grip, and can progress to permanent nerve palsy ("crutch palsy") with prolonged pressure. Never let the client "hang" on the crutches between steps. 🧠 Armpit ≠ anchor. Any test question describing tingling hands or a client leaning heavily under the arms on crutches is pointing straight at brachial plexus compression.

Standard (single-tip) cane — mild balance/weakness on one side. Quad cane (4-point base) — more stability, e.g. hemiparesis. Held in the hand on the client's strong/unaffected side. Cane tip stays ~ 4–6 in. to the side of the foot; elbow flexed ~ 15–30° when the tip touches the floor. 🧠 "The cane babysits the bad leg from across the room." It's held opposite the weak leg so it can support that side's step.

Abbrev. Meaning NWB N on- W eight- B earing — no weight at all on the affected limb. TDWB / TTWB T oe- T ouch/ D own W eight- B earing — toes may touch the floor for balance only, no true weight. PWB P artial W eight- B earing — a set fraction of body weight allowed (e.g. 30–50%), per provider order. WBAT W eight- B earing A s T olerated — client self-limits based on pain. FWB F ull W eight- B earing — no restriction. 🧠 The weight-bearing order determines which gait pattern is used — that's why Section 2 pairs each
STEP 2 · MATCH THE GAIT TO THE ORDER Four crutch gaits exist because clients have four different weight-bearing statuses — pick the gait, don't guess it.

Gait Weight-bearing status 4-point Partial/full weight-bearing bilaterally; slowest, most stable — most closely resembles normal walking . 3-point One leg NWB or PWB, the other leg fully weight-bearing — the most common post-injury gait. 2-point Partial weight-bearing bilaterally; faster version of 4-point. Swing-to / swing-through Bilateral lower-extremity weakness or paralysis (e.g. paraplegia); swing-through is faster and covers more ground. 🧠 "3-point = 3 points of contact bearing weight." Two crutch tips + the

1 Advance both crutches forward together with the affected (bad) leg . 2 Shift weight onto the hands/crutches. 3 Swing the unaffected (good) leg through, past the crutches. 🧠 Bad leg travels with the crutches, good leg travels alone. That's the whole pattern.

entries.h: ⭐ Fitting & gait check — before the client walks away
entries.t: Client demonstrates weight on hands , not axillae. Elbows flex 15–30° at the handgrip. Gait matches the ordered weight-bearing status. Never use someone else's crutches — fit is individualized. 🧠 Re-teach on the spot if the client leans into the pads even once — bad habits under fatigue are how nerve injuries happen at home. 🪜
STEP 3 · UP GOOD, DOWN BAD One rule drives both crutches and canes on stairs — lead with the strong side going up, lead with the support going down.

entries.h: 🪜 Stairs with crutches — the tested sequence
entries.t: Up with the good leg, down with the bad leg — the crutches always travel with the affected leg. 🧠 "Good goes up to heaven, bad goes down to the basement." Whichever direction, the crutches stay glued to the affected leg's step.

entries.h: 🚨 Top-missed NCLEX pattern: cane on stairs
entries.t: Going up : lead with the strong leg, cane follows, weak leg last. Going down : cane descends first, weak leg next, strong leg last. 🧠 Same "good up / bad-side-support down" logic as crutches — the device (cane or crutches) always moves with the weaker side.
1 Cane + weak leg advance together . 2 Strong leg steps through, past the cane. 🧠 "The cane babysits the bad leg." They move on the same beat.

NG-167 covers the general assistive-device overview, gait belts, and body mechanics/fall-risk assessment that apply to every mobility aid. This page (NG-064) is the deep dive specifically on crutch and cane fitting and gait mechanics — read both together. ➡️ See NG-167 — Ambulation for gait-belt technique, walker use, and the broader fall-prevention checklist before any first ambulation. 🚶

STEP 4 · THE MOST-USED AID, THE LEAST-TAUGHT ONE A walker gives more support than a cane and needs less skill than crutches, which is why it is the aid most of your clients will actually go home with. The questions are about fit, sequence and the two things that cause falls .

All four legs of a standard walker are on the floor before any step is taken. Never "walk" a standard walker by shuffling two legs forward at a time — that is the single commonest error, and it is what tips a client over sideways. The walker stays about one step length ahead . Pushed out too far, the client leans forward to reach it, the center of gravity goes outside the base of support, and the walker becomes the thing that causes the fall. 🧠 "Walker, weak, well." Same logic as crutches and canes — the aid and th

Client stands inside the walker, arms relaxed at the sides. Handgrips sit level with the greater trochanter — the hip bone — or the crease of the wrist. Elbows flex about 15 to 30 degrees when gripping. Same angle as crutches. Too high and the shoulders shrug and tire; too low and the client stoops, which is both unsafe and exhausting.

Type Who it suits Standard (no wheels) Most stable. Must be lifted every step, so it needs upper-body strength. Used for non-weight-bearing and partial weight-bearing. Two-wheeled (front wheels) For a client who cannot lift a standard walker. Rear legs have glides or tennis balls so it slides, not catches. Four-wheeled (rollator, seat, brakes) For endurance problems rather than weight-bearing limits. Not for someone who needs to lean on it for weight — it rolls away.

entries.h: 🚨 The two things that cause walker falls
entries.t: The error What to teach instead Pulling up on the walker to stand. It is not anchored — it tips toward the client. Push up from the chair armrests , get steady, then reach for the walker one hand at a time. Backing into a chair blind and sitting down while still holding the walker. Back up until the legs touch the seat , reach back for one armrest, then the other, then lower. Lock a rollator's brakes first. 🚨 A walker is never used on stairs. If the question puts a walker on a staircase, the answer is about a diffe

Remove throw rugs and trailing cords — the classic exam answer. Rubber tips intact on every leg; replace them when worn smooth. Non-skid shoes that fit. No backless slippers. Clear a turning path; turn in a wide arc with small steps , never a pivot. Lighting on the routes to the bathroom and kitchen.

entries.h: 🆚 Cane vs walker vs crutches — one line each
entries.t: Aid The deciding fact Cane Mild one-sided weakness. Held on the strong side, advances with the weak leg . Walker Greater instability or bilateral weakness. Advance it, then weak, then strong. Crutches Weight kept off one limb entirely. Weight rides on the hands , never the axillae. 🧠 "Strong holds the cane, weak leans on the walker." ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🖐️ Hands, not armpits Weight on the handgrips — axillary pressure risks nerve palsy. 🩹 3-point gait Both crutches + bad leg together, then good leg. 🦯 Cane = strong side Cane + weak leg together, then strong leg. 🪜 Up good, down bad Unaffected leg leads up; device + affected leg lead down.

Q1: Where should crutch weight be borne, and what happens if it isn't? Show answer On the hands/palms through the handgrips. Resting weight on the axillary pads compresses the brachial plexus — numbness, tingling, weak grip, potentially permanent "crutch palsy." Q2: A client is non-weight-bearing on the left leg. Which crutch gait, and what's the sequence? Show answer 3-point gait — both crutches and the affected (left) leg advance together, then the unaffected (right) leg swings through past the crutches. Q3: A cl

entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Musculoskeletal · Pharmacology Course

Why They Can't Be Taken Together — Timing, Forms & Vitamin D NG-108 Musculoskeletal ADHD-friendly visual edition Calcium supplements and alendronate (a bisphosphonate) are both prescribed for osteoporosis — but they cannot be taken at the same time . Calcium physically blocks alendronate absorption in the gut. This page is entirely about the administration teaching that keeps both drugs working. For the full alendronate mechanism, empty-stomach protocol, and rare adverse effects (osteonecrosis of the jaw, atypical

⏰ Never together Calcium blocks alendronate absorption — separate them by several hours. 🍽️ Carbonate needs food Calcium carbonate needs stomach acid — take with meals. Calcium citrate absorbs with or without food. ☀️ No vitamin D, no absorption Vitamin D is required for the gut to absorb calcium at all. 🚫 >500mg not absorbed Split the daily calcium dose — under 500mg per dose, several times a day. ⏱️
STEP 1 · WHY THEY FIGHT Same goal — stronger bones — but taken at the same time, one cancels the other out.

entries.h: 🚫 Calcium physically blocks alendronate from being absorbed

entries.t: Bone remodeling Old bone is removed and new bone is formed. Net bone loss Strength and microarchitecture decline. Fragility fracture risk Low-energy trauma can cause fracture. Risk reduction Weight-bearing activity, fall prevention and adequate calcium/vitamin D when appropriate. Bisphosphonates Reduce resorption; oral administration has specific fasting and upright-position instructions. Monitoring Fracture history, bone density, renal function and medication risks guide the plan. Alendronate absorption is already

entries.h: 📋 The alendronate side of the schedule (recap)
entries.t: Full protocol lives on NG-238 Bisphosphonates — the short version needed here: Take first thing in the morning , on a completely empty stomach , with a full glass of plain water Stay upright — sitting or standing — for 30–60 minutes after Wait that same 30–60 minutes before eating, drinking anything else, or taking any other medication — including calcium

entries.h: ⚠️ Not just calcium — other blockers too
entries.t: 🧂 Iron supplements 🥛 Magnesium 🧴 Aluminum- or magnesium-containing antacids 💊 Multivitamins that contain minerals Any of these taken too close to alendronate can blunt its absorption the same way calcium does. 🧪
STEP 2 · NOT ALL CALCIUM IS THE SAME Two common calcium salts absorb differently — the difference decides whether the client needs to take it with food.

Feature Calcium carbonate Calcium citrate Elemental calcium per tablet ~40% — more calcium per pill ~21% — less per pill Needs stomach acid to absorb? Yes — take with food No — absorbs with or without food Best for Most healthy adults Older adults, PPI/H2-blocker users, low-stomach-acid clients Cost Cheaper, widely available (also an antacid) More expensive Common side effect Constipation, gas — more likely Somewhat gentler on the GI tract 🧠 "CARBonate needs CARBs (food)." Calcium carbonate needs stomach acid to di

entries.h: 🚫 Divided doses — >500mg at once is wasted
entries.t: Teach the client to split the total daily calcium requirement into doses under 500mg elemental calcium each, spread across the day — not one large dose.

Constipation is a common, expected side effect of calcium supplementation — not a reason to stop the drug. Increase fluids Increase ambulation/activity Add fiber as tolerated 🧠 "High CAL = Hard bowel. Low CAL = Loose bowel." Since calcium makes bones hard, think of it making bowels hard too — that's the trade-off, and it's expected, not dangerous.

entries.h: 🧪 No routine labs needed for alendronate itself
entries.t: Alendronate does not require frequent blood tests or routine lab monitoring on its own. Providers may still periodically check baseline calcium, vitamin D, and renal function as part of overall osteoporosis management — but this is not the same as required routine bloodwork for the bisphosphonate. 📅
STEP 3 · PUTTING IT ON A CLOCK Vitamin D is the piece that makes the calcium usable at all — then it's just a matter of timing everything around alendronate.

entries.h: ☀️ Vitamin D: the key that unlocks calcium absorption
entries.t: Without adequate vitamin D , the intestine cannot absorb dietary or supplemental calcium efficiently — vitamin D is converted to its active form ( calcitriol ) which works with parathyroid hormone to move calcium from the gut into the bloodstream and ultimately into bone. Sources: sunlight exposure, fortified foods (milk, cereal), fatty fish, and supplements Many calcium supplements are combined with vitamin D in the same tablet for this reason Low vitamin D = calcium supplementation underperforms no matter the dos

entries.h: 📅 A sample day — keeping alendronate & calcium apart
entries.t: This is one example schedule , not a fixed rule — the non-negotiable is keeping calcium/other minerals separated from alendronate by several hours , with alendronate always taken on an empty stomach first thing in the morning. 🧠 "Bone pill at dawn, calcium at noon and night." Alendronate opens the day alone; calcium shows up later, split, with food if it's the carbonate form. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD ⏰ Separate by hours calcium blocks alendronate absorption 🍽️ Carbonate + food citrate absorbs without food ☀️ Vitamin D required no D = poor calcium absorption 🚫 >500mg wasted split doses under 500mg each

Q1: Why can't a client take their calcium supplement at the same time as alendronate? Show answer Calcium (like iron, magnesium, and aluminum antacids) binds to alendronate in the gut and blocks its already-poor absorption. They must be separated by several hours. Q2: A client on a PPI for years is prescribed a calcium supplement. Which form absorbs best for her, and why? Show answer Calcium citrate — it doesn't require stomach acid to be absorbed, unlike calcium carbonate, which needs an acidic environment and sho
