The skull cannot expand. Why a change in consciousness comes first, why Cushing’s triad comes last, and the positioning that actually lowers pressure.

Fixed space Brain tissue, blood and CSF share the adult skull. Compensation Some blood or CSF displacement initially limits pressure. Rising pressure Further expansion can reduce cerebral perfusion. Early concern A declining level of consciousness or new neurologic change needs prompt assessment. Position and care Keep the head and neck aligned; use ordered positioning, oxygenation and sedation strategies. Late danger Abnormal posturing or the Cushing response signals severe deterioration. Do not wait for these fin

entries.h: 👀 Recognizing it — in the right order
🚨 Cushing’s triad — three changes, all late
entries.t: Sign Direction Blood pressure Systolic rises , diastolic stays → widening pulse pressure Heart rate Falls — bradycardia Respirations Irregular — Cheyne–Stokes Cushing's triad is never the answer to "earliest sign". It is the body's last-ditch attempt to force blood into a compressed brain.

entries.h: 👶 In an infant it looks different
entries.t: The fontanelles and open sutures let the skull expand, so the early picture is a bulging fontanelle, a high-pitched cry, separated sutures, poor feeding and irritability — not headache and vomiting.
Eye opening 1–4 · Verbal 1–5 · Motor 1–6. Maximum 15, minimum 3. 13–15 mild 9–12 moderate ≤8 severe — intubate GCS of 8 or less means the airway is not protected. "Less than 8, intubate"

Do Why Head of bed 30° Promotes venous drainage by gravity Head midline, neutral A turned or flexed neck kinks the jugular veins Avoid hip flexion Raises intra-abdominal and intrathoracic pressure No Trendelenburg Head-down position raises ICP directly

entries.h: 🚨 Things that spike ICP — cluster care to avoid them
entries.t: Suctioning — limit to 10 seconds , hyperoxygenate first Coughing, sneezing, straining — give stool softeners, avoid the Valsalva maneuver Hip flexion, neck flexion Clustering painful care together — space activities out and allow rest between Noise and bright light — keep the room quiet and dim Drug What it does Watch Mannitol (osmotic diuretic) Pulls fluid out of brain tissue Rising urine output means it is working ; watch osmolality and electrolytes Hypertonic saline (3%) Same osmotic effect Sodium levels Dexamet

CO 2 is a potent cerebral vasodilator. Letting it rise dilates cerebral vessels, adds blood volume and raises ICP. So oxygenation and ventilation are neuroprotective. Brief controlled hyperventilation may be used as a rescue — but prolonged hyperventilation causes ischemia by over-constricting the vessels.

Brain tissue is forced through an opening it does not belong in. Signs of impending herniation: Unilateral fixed dilated pupil — “blown pupil”, usually on the same side as the lesion Rapid drop in GCS Posturing , then flaccidity Cushing’s triad A newly blown pupil is a neurosurgical emergency. Report immediately - do not wait for the next scheduled assessment. Decorticate posturing Arms flexed in toward the core . Damage above the brainstem. CORE = flexion toward the core Decerebrate posturing Arms extended and rig
Pressure on the pituitary can stop ADH release — liters of dilute urine, rising sodium, falling blood pressure . Common after frontal craniotomy. Watch hourly urine output and sodium.

Earliest sign = change in LOC. Not pupils, not the triad Cushing’s triad is late — and the pulse pressure widens HOB 30°, head midline — never flat, never Trendelenburg Suction ≤10 seconds , hyperoxygenate first GCS ≤8 → intubate Rising urine output on mannitol is expected , not a complication
The points the practice quiz in NUR 258 Module 7 tests that are not spelled out above. The questions themselves are in the NUR 258 Mega Quiz.

Three things in the skull: brain, blood and CSF (Monro-Kellie). The body compensates by shifting CSF to the spinal canal, making less CSF and constricting cerebral vessels ; vasodilation and protein leaking into tissue (edema) push ICP up. PaCO2: CO2 dilates cerebral vessels — a PaCO2 above 45 raises ICP. Ventilate to 30–35 . Your course numbers: normal ICP 10–15 mmHg , report above 20 ; CPP goal above 50, ideally 60–70 . (Other sources quote ICP 5–15 and CPP 60–100.) MAP = (systolic + 2 × diastolic) ÷ 3; CPP = MAP

Earliest: change in level of consciousness — restlessness, confusion, irritability. Late: pupil changes, one-sided weakness, decorticate posturing ( flexion , arms to the core) then decerebrate ( extension , worse), Cheyne-Stokes or irregular breathing. Cushing’s triad: rising systolic with widening pulse pressure , bradycardia , slow irregular respirations — herniation is close. Doll’s eyes: eyes moving opposite to the head turn is normal; eyes fixed midline, moving with the head = brainstem damage . Unconscious (

Avoid: coughing, sneezing, straining (Valsalva), vomiting, hip flexion , neck flexion — give stool softeners and antiemetics early. HOB 30°, head midline. Fever raises ICP: antipyretic as prescribed, remove blankets, cool the room or bath — prevent shivering . Mannitol: an osmotic diuretic that blocks water and sodium reabsorption so they leave in the urine. Watch for fluid overload first (crackles, pulmonary edema) , then dehydration and electrolyte loss; not for anuria; thirst and dry mouth are expected. Sources.

Recognize a sudden rise in blood pressure after spinal cord injury, act promptly, and find the trigger. Compare the three conditions Nursing priorities BP rises suddenly Compare with the person’s usual baseline. Check bladder first A full bladder or blocked catheter is a common trigger. Sit upright + get help Monitor BP and follow the emergency plan. 01
Usually associated with spinal cord injury at or above T6; presentations vary.
A rise of more than 20 mmHg in adult systolic BP above the person’s usual baseline may signal autonomic dysreflexia. People with high spinal injuries often have lower baseline pressure.

Possible findings include a pounding headache, flushing or sweating above the injury, blurred vision, nasal congestion and goosebumps. Some episodes have few symptoms. Your textbook pattern: severe hypertension with bradycardia ; the pulse can vary, so a normal rate does not rule it out. 📘 Course study notes A blocked bladder can kill a patient with a spinal cord injury. The one emergency where sitting the patient UP is the treatment.

entries.h: 👀 The split picture — above vs below
entries.t: The signs divide at the level of injury, and that split is the giveaway. ABOVE the injury BELOW the injury Vessels Dilated Clamped shut Skin Flushed, sweating profusely Pale, cold, goosebumps Symptom Pounding headache , blurred vision, nasal congestion Nothing felt — no sensation

BP ↑↑↑ HR ↓ Severe hypertension with bradycardia. A systolic of 200+ is common, and a “normal” 120/80 may already be dangerously high — many people with high spinal injuries run a baseline systolic in the 90s . Always compare to the patient's OWN baseline. A 40 mmHg rise above their normal is a crisis, whatever the absolute number. The classic first complaint is a sudden pounding headache. Combined with sweating above the injury and goosebumps below, that is autonomic dysreflexia until proven otherwise. 02
Sit upright, call for help, monitor BP and investigate the trigger.

Autonomic dysreflexia: respond to rising BP A hypertensive emergency after spinal cord injury. AUTONOMIC DYSREFLEXIA: sudden BP rise, usually with injury at or above T6. A full bladder or blocked catheter is a common trigger. 1 Sit upright; get help Lower legs if safe, loosen tight items and check blood pressure. 2 Look for the trigger Check bladder drainage first; assess other triggers using the clinical protocol. 3 Recheck frequently Monitor BP every 2–5 minutes and escalate persistent or severe hypertension. 4 T

This is one of the few emergencies where the first action is to sit the patient UP, not lay them down. Raising the head uses gravity to drop the blood pressure immediately. 1 · FIRST Sit the patient upright ; lower the legs 2 Loosen everything tight — clothing, binders, stockings 3 Find the trigger — check the bladder first 4 Check for bowel impaction — use anesthetic jelly 5 BP every 2–5 min ; antihypertensive if it stays high

entries.h: 💧 Finding the trigger — most to least common
entries.t: Distended bladder — the cause in the large majority. Kinked catheter, blocked tubing, full drainage bag Impacted bowel or a needed bowel movement Skin — pressure injury, tight clothing, a wrinkle in the sheet, ingrown toenail, burn Other — menstrual cramps, labor, infection, a fracture below the level Never lay the patient flat, and never leave them to go and find help - use the call bell. When relieving impaction, use lidocaine jelly first and wait . Digital stimulation without it can make the crisis dramatically

Bladder program — catheterize on schedule, never let it overfill Bowel program — regular, consistent timing Skin checks and pressure relief every couple of hours Teach the patient and family the signs — they will often recognize it before staff do A medical alert card is standard, because many clinicians have never seen it

Sit them UP — the opposite of most hypotension/shock answers Check the bladder first — it is nearly always the cause Injury T6 or above Hypertension WITH bradycardia — an unusual pairing worth memorizing Flushed and sweating above , pale and goosebumps below

Recognize a sudden rise in blood pressure and respond urgently. Sit upright and call for help. Loosen constriction and check the bladder first. Read the steps and sources Open full-size image Original Study Hub nursing illustration. 03
Begin with bladder drainage, then assess bowel, skin and other causes.
Check for distension, kinked tubing, drainage problems or a blocked catheter. Follow the catheter-care protocol; avoid forceful manipulation.
Constipation or fecal impaction may trigger an episode. Assessment and intervention need the clinical protocol because stimulation can worsen the response.
Loosen constricting clothing or equipment. Check for pressure injury, burns, ingrown nails or another source of irritation.
Infection, fractures, procedures, sexual activity or labor may contribute. Look for a stimulus even if the person cannot feel it. 04
The injury interrupts the brain’s control of a strong sympathetic reflex.

Susceptible spinal injury Usually injury at or above T6. Stimulus below injury Bladder distention, bowel problems or skin pressure can trigger a response. Severe hypertension Uncontrolled sympathetic activity raises blood pressure. Recognize Sudden headache, flushing or sweating above the lesion and a significant blood-pressure rise; pulse may vary. Immediate response Sit upright, loosen constrictive items, call for help and measure blood pressure frequently. Remove the trigger Check bladder drainage first and asse

Below the injury, the body screams. Above it, nobody can hear. A painful stimulus below the level of injury triggers massive sympathetic vasoconstriction. The brain detects the resulting hypertension and tries to switch it off — but the signal cannot travel back down past the injury . So the constriction continues unopposed while everything above the injury dilates. 1 · Trigger Full bladder, impacted bowel, or skin irritation below the injury 2 Sympathetic surge → vasoconstriction below 3 Blood pressure spikes , da

Spinal cord injury at T6 or above . It usually begins after spinal shock resolves and can recur for life. This is a true medical emergency. Untreated it causes stroke, seizure, retinal hemorrhage or death. 05
Blood pressure and reflexes point to different problems.

Neurogenic vs spinal shock vs dysreflexia Compare blood pressure, reflexes and the immediate care focus. NEUROGENIC SHOCK BP FALLS WHAT CHANGES Loss of sympathetic control. Pulse is often slow; warm skin may occur. CARE FOCUS Support circulation and the injured spine; use prescribed fluids and vasoactive treatment. SPINAL SHOCK REFLEXES FALL WHAT CHANGES Acute loss or reduction of reflexes and muscle tone below a spinal injury. CARE FOCUS Support the spinal injury and repeat neurologic examinations. BP does not def
A personal plan helps the patient and caregivers act quickly.
Maintain the prescribed bladder and bowel routines, inspect skin and equipment, and address infections or new irritation.
Keep a record of usual BP, recognize personal warning signs and carry an emergency plan. Ensure caregivers know when to seek urgent help.

entries.h: Quick check: the patient has a headache and a BP rise, but the pulse is normal. Can it still be dysreflexia?
entries.t: Yes. Heart rate does not rule it out. Compare BP with baseline, assess promptly and follow the response plan.

A painless curtain across the vision. Why it is an emergency despite not hurting, and the one condition that gets face-down positioning.

Detachment separates the retina from its normal position Sudden new floaters, flashes, or a curtain or shadow need immediate eye care — even without pain The symptoms do not have to come in a fixed order After gas-bubble surgery : follow the surgeon’s exact positioning instructions, do not fly while gas remains, and tell every treating clinician about the bubble Sudden floaters, flashes or a curtain across your vision is an emergency, painless or not. Plate sources: NEI retinal detachment · NEI surgery The retina p

1 Floaters — sudden shower of spots or specks 2 Flashes of light, especially peripherally 3 Curtain or shadow moving across the field 4 Painless loss of vision in that area It is completely painless. There are no pain fibers in the retina - so patients delay coming in, and that delay is what costs them sight. The exam phrase is almost always “a curtain coming down” or “a veil across my vision” . Distinguish it quickly: Painless + sudden Painful + sudden Retinal detachment — curtain, floaters, flashes Closed-angle g
Detachment does not heal on its own. It is repaired by laser (photocoagulation), freezing (cryopexy), a scleral buckle , or vitrectomy with a gas bubble .

When a gas bubble is placed, the patient positions FACE DOWN — often for most of the day, for several days. The bubble floats upward and must press the retina back against the choroid. Bubble floats up → face down puts the bubble against the retina This is the one eye condition that gets prone or face-down positioning. Every other eye surgery avoids it.

Position exactly as prescribed — adherence determines the outcome No air travel while a gas bubble is present — altitude expands the gas and spikes eye pressure Avoid anything that raises intraocular pressure: bending at the waist, straining, heavy lifting, vigorous coughing, rubbing the eye Stool softeners; antiemetics for nausea Eye shield, especially at night

Sudden severe eye pain — raised pressure or hemorrhage Sudden decrease in vision Increasing redness, discharge, fever A new curtain — re-detachment Pain after eye surgery is never "expected discomfort". Report it.

Painless — the absence of pain does not make it less urgent Face down after a gas bubble; no flying Floaters and flashes are the warning , before the curtain Bending at the waist is forbidden — teach squatting instead Sources. Written from MedlinePlus , NINDS and OpenStax A&P 2e (CC BY 4.0).
Central vision goes, peripheral vision stays — the exact opposite of glaucoma. Dry vs wet, and what actually slows it.

Stimulus reaches the organ Vision, hearing and sensation begin peripherally. Signal transmission Cranial or peripheral nerves carry information. Central interpretation Brain networks identify and respond to the input. Vision Acuity, fields, pupils and eye movements test different functions. Hearing Screening and Weber/Rinne tests provide clues; audiometry establishes thresholds. Sensation Compare sides, modalities and distribution while accounting for cognition and communication. The macula is the small central pat

DRY (atrophic) WET (exudative) Share of cases ~85–90% ~10–15% Mechanism Macular cells thin and atrophy; drusen deposits New leaky vessels grow under the retina Onset Gradual, over years Sudden , over days to weeks Hallmark Slow central blurring Straight lines look wavy (metamorphopsia) Treatment Supplements, monitoring Anti-VEGF injections into the eye Wavy or bent straight lines - door frames, tiles, text - is the sign of WET macular degeneration and needs urgent referral. It is treatable if caught early.

A simple grid of straight lines with a central dot. The patient covers one eye, stares at the dot, and reports any wavy, missing or distorted squares. Used daily at home — it is how conversion from dry to wet gets caught in time.

Smoking — the single biggest modifiable risk; roughly doubles it UV exposure — sunglasses and a hat Hypertension and cardiovascular disease Diet — dark leafy greens, fish; the AREDS-type supplement formulations Unmodifiable: age over 60, family history, light-colored eyes .

Magnifiers , large print, high-contrast materials Bright, direct task lighting Teach eccentric viewing — looking slightly to the side of an object to use healthy retina Home safety: they retain peripheral vision, so mobility is usually fine, but reading medication labels is not Screen for depression — loss of reading and driving is a major life change

Central loss, peripheral kept — opposite of glaucoma Wavy lines = wet = urgent Amsler grid is used daily at home , not just in clinic Smoking cessation is the top teaching point Sources. Written from MedlinePlus , National Eye Institute , NINDS and OpenStax A&P 2e (CC BY 4.0).
Inflammation of the brain tissue itself — not just its lining. Why altered mental status dominates, and how it differs from meningitis.

Trigger Infection or an immune process may be responsible. Brain inflammation Function of affected brain networks is disturbed. Neurologic change Confusion, seizures or reduced consciousness may follow. Recognize Fever or headache with altered behavior, cognition, seizures or focal findings requires urgent assessment. Investigate Imaging, CSF testing and EEG may help identify the cause and complications. Support and treat Protect breathing, monitor neurologic status and give cause-specific treatment promptly. Menin

Fever + headache — the infectious base Altered mental status — confusion, disorientation, personality or behavior change Seizures Focal neurological signs — weakness, aphasia, cranial nerve palsies Photophobia, nausea and vomiting May progress to decreasing level of consciousness and coma

Test Shows CSF PCR Confirms the virus — HSV, enterovirus, arbovirus Lumbar puncture Raised lymphocytes, mildly raised protein, normal glucose (unlike bacterial meningitis) MRI Temporal lobe changes in HSV EEG Seizure activity; temporal focus CT before LP If focal signs or reduced consciousness — rule out raised ICP

Neuro observations frequently — LOC is the sensitive marker Seizure precautions from admission: padded rails, suction and oxygen at the bedside Quiet, dim room ; cluster care and allow rest Head of bed 30° , head midline — ICP rises with brain edema Fluid balance — watch for SIADH , which is common Antipyretics; fever raises cerebral metabolic demand

Airway and safety first. A confused, seizing patient with a falling GCS needs airway protection — GCS ≤ 8 means intubation. Never leave a confused, agitated encephalitis patient unattended with the rails down.

Mosquito-borne causes (West Nile, La Crosse, EEE) → repellent, covered skin, avoid dusk exposure, remove standing water . Vaccine-preventable causes: measles, mumps, varicella, rabies, Japanese encephalitis .

Altered mental status dominates , not neck stiffness Suspected HSV → start aciclovir immediately CSF glucose is normal in viral, low in bacterial Seizure precautions are set up on admission, not after the first seizure Sources. Written from MedlinePlus , National Eye Institute , NINDS and OpenStax A&P 2e (CC BY 4.0).

Where the nervous system divides, why it matters clinically, and how one fact predicts whether damage will heal.

Sensory input Peripheral nerves carry information toward the CNS. Integration Brain and spinal cord process information. Motor output Peripheral pathways carry signals to muscles and organs. Central nervous system Brain and spinal cord: processing, coordination and many reflex pathways. Peripheral nervous system Nerves outside the CNS include sensory, somatic motor and autonomic pathways. Localize the problem Distribution, reflexes, strength and sensation help identify which pathways may be affected. Central = brai

The PNS divides again by what it controls: Somatic Voluntary — skeletal muscle, conscious control Autonomic Involuntary — organs, glands, smooth muscle SYMPATHETIC — “fight or flight” PARASYMPATHETIC — “rest and digest” Heart rate Up Down Pupils Dilate Constrict Airways Dilate Constrict Digestion Slows, mouth dry Speeds up , salivation Bladder Retains Empties Transmitter Norepinephrine Acetylcholine

entries.h: ✅ Why this predicts drug side effects
entries.t: Anticholinergics block the parasympathetic system , so you get the sympathetic picture: "Can't see, can't pee, can't spit, can't poop" — blurred vision, urinary retention, dry mouth, constipation. Plus tachycardia and flushing. Beta blockers block the sympathetic system → slow heart rate, lower blood pressure, and bronchoconstriction — which is why non-selective ones are avoided in asthma.

entries.h: 🩺 Why the split matters at the bedside
🚨 The clinical consequences of “CNS does not regenerate”
entries.t: Spinal cord injury: the primary damage is usually permanent — the secondary injury (edema, hemorrhage) is what treatment can stop. “Treatment is needed to prevent partial injury from developing into more extensive, permanent damage.” Side note (newer wording): Spinal cord injury care prevents secondary injury and complications while supporting recovery, rehabilitation and independence. Stroke damage is permanent — rehabilitation retrains other areas rather than repairing dead tissue Prevention outranks treatment ev

It protects the brain from toxins — and also keeps most drugs out . That is why CNS infections need antibiotics that cross the barrier , at high doses, and why inflammation (as in meningitis) actually helps drugs get in.

MS = CNS demyelination. GBS = PNS demyelination. Anticholinergic effects = the four “can’ts” Peripheral nerve injury may recover; primary cord damage usually does not Sympathetic dilates pupils and airways; parasympathetic constricts both Sources. Written from MedlinePlus , NINDS , CDC and OpenStax A&P 2e (CC BY 4.0).

What to check, in what order, and which single finding matters more than all the others.

Mental status and speech Assess alertness, orientation, attention and speech. Describe the actual responses. Consider hearing, language, sedation and other factors that affect testing. Pupils and cranial functions Assess pupil size, equality and light response. Examine eye movement, facial symmetry, hearing and other cranial functions as indicated. Motor and sensory function Compare right and left movement, strength and sensation. Assess coordination, reflexes and gait when appropriate and safe. Document focal find

1 LOC — alert? oriented to person, place, time? 2 Pupils — PERRLA, size, symmetry, reaction 3 Motor — strength, symmetry, drift 4 Sensory — touch, pain, position 5 Vitals — the Cushing pattern Component What you are looking for Concerning LOC Alert → lethargic → obtunded → stuporous → comatose Any downward move Orientation Person, place, time, situation Lost in that order — time goes first Pupils Equal, round, reactive; 2–6 mm New unilateral dilation — emergency Motor Equal grip, no pronator drift, moves all four N

Decorticate Decerebrate Arms Flexed in toward the core Extended, rigid , palms out Damage Above the brainstem Brainstem Prognosis Bad Worse deCORticate = toward the CORE Moving from decorticate to decerebrate means the patient is deteriorating. Report it immediately.

LOC changes first — always Orientation is lost time → place → person GCS minimum is 3 , not 0 A new blown pupil is an emergency Decerebrate is worse than decorticate Sources. Written from MedlinePlus , NIAMS , National Cancer Institute and OpenStax A&P 2e (CC BY 4.0).

A walled-off pocket of infection inside the skull. An infection and a space-occupying lesion at the same time.

Infection reaches brain Spread may be local or through the bloodstream. Localized collection Inflammation and pus form a focal lesion. Edema and pressure Surrounding swelling can impair nearby brain function. Recognize Headache, fever, seizures, focal deficits or altered consciousness; not all findings are present. Assessment Urgent imaging and specialist evaluation help define location and treatment. Treatment Antimicrobials and sometimes drainage; monitor for seizures and raised intracranial pressure. Two problem

The triad: 1 Headache — usually the first and worst symptom 2 Fever — though it may be low grade or absent 3 Focal deficit — depends where the abscess sits Plus rising ICP: nausea and projectile vomiting, change in LOC, seizures, papilledema . Fever is unreliable here - up to half of patients do not have one. A worsening headache with a new neurological deficit is enough to investigate.

MRI with contrast — the test of choice; shows a ring-enhancing lesion CT with contrast if MRI unavailable Blood cultures before antibiotics Aspiration for culture guides definitive antibiotic choice Lumbar puncture is contraindicated when a mass and raised ICP are suspected - removing CSF from below can cause herniation.

High-dose IV antibiotics that cross the blood–brain barrier, often for 6–8 weeks Surgical aspiration or excision for larger abscesses Anticonvulsants — seizures are common and spike ICP Dexamethasone if edema is significant

Neuro observations — LOC is the earliest marker of deterioration ICP precautions — HOB 30°, head midline, no neck or hip flexion, avoid Valsalva Seizure precautions from admission Antibiotics strictly on schedule — levels must stay above the killing concentration Monitor for long-line complications over a many-week course Temperature control — fever raises cerebral metabolic demand

It is both an infection and a mass — expect ICP precautions, not just antibiotics No lumbar puncture with a suspected mass Cultures before antibiotics Treating ear, sinus and dental infections properly is the prevention Sources. Written from MedlinePlus , National Cancer Institute , NINDS and OpenStax A&P 2e (CC BY 4.0).

Two neural problems of infancy. One is about pressure and a shunt; the other is about protecting a sac and avoiding latex.

Hydrocephalus — excess cerebrospinal fluid and enlarged ventricles . In infants assess head growth, the fontanelle, feeding and alertness A shunt may divert cerebrospinal fluid Open spina bifida such as myelomeningocele exposes vulnerable spinal tissue Avoid pressure on the lesion , and prevent drying and contamination, under the specialist care plan Plate sources: NINDS spina bifida · NINDS hydrocephalus 🧒 Hydrocephalus Picture, memory hook and nursing care → CSF accumulates because it cannot drain or be absorbed.

A ventriculoperitoneal shunt drains CSF from the ventricles into the abdomen. Signs of malfunction or infection are the signs of raised ICP returning: Irritability, lethargy, poor feeding, vomiting Bulging fontanelle ; increasing head circumference Fever — suspect shunt infection Redness or swelling along the shunt tract After shunt insertion, position the infant FLAT or as prescribed on the UNOPERATED side. Raising the head too fast drains CSF too quickly and can collapse the ventricles. Teach parents that the shu

Type What it is Occulta Hidden defect; sometimes a dimple, tuft of hair or birthmark over the spine. Often no symptoms Meningocele Sac containing meninges and CSF; usually no nerve tissue , so function is often preserved Myelomeningocele Sac contains spinal cord and nerves . Motor and sensory loss below the level; bladder and bowel involvement

Position PRONE - never on the back. Pressure on the sac can rupture it. Keep the sac covered with a STERILE, MOIST, non-adherent dressing. It must not dry out. Latex-free environment — these children have a very high rate of latex allergy from repeated exposure. Flag it from birth Measure head circumference — hydrocephalus develops in most cases Meticulous perineal care; keep urine and stool away from the sac Assess movement and sensation in the legs; note the level

Clean intermittent catheterization for neurogenic bladder — taught to family, later to the child Bowel program Skin care — they cannot feel pressure injuries developing Mobility aids; orthopedic follow-up Intelligence is often normal — never assume otherwise

Folic acid 400 mcg daily for all women of childbearing age , and 4 mg if there has been a previous affected pregnancy. The neural tube closes by about week 4 - often before pregnancy is known. That is why it must be taken BEFORE conception.

Prone position, sterile moist dressing, latex-free Sunset eyes and a high-pitched cry = hydrocephalus in an infant Shunt malfunction looks like rising ICP returning Folic acid before conception Head circumference at every visit Sources. Written from CDC , HealthyChildren.org (AAP) , MedlinePlus and OpenStax A&P 2e (CC BY 4.0).
Why toddlers get ear infections and adults do not, plus the vision problems that must be caught before the brain stops using an eye.

Otitis media is inflammation and fluid behind the eardrum Children’s eustachian tubes are smaller and more level than adults’, so drainage is less efficient Ear pain, irritability, fever or reduced hearing may occur Fluid can remain after the infection itself improves An ear examination distinguishes infection from fluid alone — ear tugging by itself is not diagnostic Plate sources: NIDCD ear infections in children 🧒 Otitis media Picture, memory hook and nursing care → A young child’s eustachian tube is short, wide

Many resolve without antibiotics — watchful waiting is common; if antibiotics are given, finish the course Analgesia is the main comfort measure Feed upright, never prop a bottle — lying flat lets milk track into the tube Avoid tobacco smoke ; breastfeeding is protective Recurrent infections → tympanostomy tubes With tubes in place: keep water out per the surgeon’s advice; report tubes falling out early, or persistent drainage. The complication that matters: repeated or persistent middle-ear fluid causes conductive

The visual system is still wiring itself in early childhood. If one eye sends a blurred or mismatched image, the brain suppresses it — and after a certain age that suppression becomes permanent. That is why squints and refractive errors are treated urgently in small children and not in adults. Condition What it is Note Amblyopia “Lazy eye” — the brain suppresses one eye Must be treated early ; patching or drops to the strong eye forces the weak one to work Strabismus Eyes not aligned — one turns in or out Common ca

A WHITE pupillary reflex instead of red - retinoblastoma until proven otherwise. Often first seen in a photograph. A squint persisting beyond about 4 months of age needs referral — intermittent crossing is normal in the newborn period but not after that

entries.h: ✅ Patching — where the nursing effort goes
entries.t: The child will resist , because you are covering their good eye and making them function with the weak one. Adherence is the whole treatment. Explain to the parent why it must be the strong eye Use stickers, charts, a set routine; patch during a favorite activity Warn that vision will be poor while patched — supervise stairs and play Emphasize the window closes — late treatment does not work as well

Bacterial — thick purulent discharge, lids stuck together on waking. Antibiotic drops. Viral — watery discharge, often with a cold. Self-limiting. Allergic — itchy, both eyes, seasonal. Highly contagious: separate towels and washcloths, hand hygiene, no sharing , and usually off nursery or school until treated.

Pulling at the ear + poor feeding + irritable = otitis media in an infant Sudden pain relief + drainage = perforation Never prop a bottle ; feed upright Patch the STRONG eye in amblyopia White pupil = retinoblastoma , urgent Recurrent ear infections risk speech delay Sources. Written from CDC , NIDCD , National Eye Institute , HealthyChildren.org (AAP) and MedlinePlus .
Two systems, one nursing goal: preserve function. Most of these questions are decided by a single phrase in the stem — so learn the signature findings first.

Words in the stem Diagnosis Urgency Curtain across the vision · flashes · new floaters Retinal detachment Emergency Halos around lights · cloudy · faded color · glare Cataract Elective surgery Peripheral loss → tunnel vision · painless · gradual Open-angle glaucoma Lifelong treatment Central loss · straight lines look wavy Macular degeneration Wet AMD is urgent Severe eye pain · halos · nausea · fixed mid-dilated pupil Acute angle-closure glaucoma Emergency One word each: Curtain = detachment · Halos = cataract · T

Verify medication, which eye , dose, schedule Tilt the head back, look up , pull down the lower lid One drop into the conjunctival sac — never onto the cornea Do not touch the eye, lashes, or skin with the tip Wait 5 minutes between different drops · drops before ointment

Close the eye gently, then press the inner canthus for 30–60 seconds . That stops the drop draining down the tear duct into the bloodstream. With a beta blocker like timolol , skipping it can cause bradycardia, hypotension and bronchospasm — dangerous in asthma, COPD or heart block. Pressing the lower lid instead of the inner corner is the classic wrong answer.

Tonometry — intraocular pressure Amsler grid — central vision, distortion or missing areas Perimetry — maps the peripheral field Ophthalmoscopy, slit lamp, ultrasound, angiography — structure Dilating drops blur vision and increase light sensitivity for hours — arrange a driver and sunglasses.

Open-angle (chronic) Angle-closure (acute) Onset Slow, insidious Sudden Pain None Severe eye pain and headache Vision Peripheral loss → tunnel vision Blurred with halos, rapid decline Pupil Normal Fixed, mid-dilated Other Usually bilateral, often symptom-free Red eye, nausea and vomiting Urgency Lifelong pressure control Ocular emergency Open = silent. Closed = screaming. That is why glaucoma questions look contradictory — “painless peripheral loss” and “severe pain” are both correct, for different types. The stem

Recognize: severe eye pain or headache · red eye, blurred vision, halos · nausea and vomiting · fixed mid-dilated pupil · rapid vision decline. Act: notify the provider immediately · give ordered pressure-lowering therapy · treat pain and nausea · do not delay definitive ophthalmic care. Delay means permanent vision loss.

Damage is irreversible ; treatment only protects what is left. Glaucoma can also occur at normal pressure. Medication — drops that reduce production or increase outflow Laser — trabeculoplasty (open-angle) · iridotomy (angle closure) Surgery — trabeculectomy or drainage device The nursing priority is lifelong follow-up even when she feels completely well.

A cataract is a cloudy lens — not a retinal disorder. Painless and gradual. Progressive blur or haze Glare and halos , especially at night Colors look faded or yellowed Frequent prescription changes · monocular diplopia Risk: age, diabetes, smoking, steroids, UV exposure, trauma, prior eye surgery.

Outpatient; the cloudy lens is removed through a small incision and an intraocular lens is inserted. Shield for sleep, sunglasses as directed Do not rub or press the eye No bending, heavy lifting, or straining until cleared Keep water and soap out Report vision loss, severe pain, marked redness, flashes, or new floaters — those suggest a detachment.

Type Signs Care Allergic Itching , watery — not contagious Avoid triggers, cold compresses, antihistamine drops Viral Watery, URI symptoms — highly contagious Supportive care and strict precautions. Antibiotics do not treat viruses. Bacterial Purulent discharge, matted lids Complete the antibiotics; discard contaminated make-up All types: wash hands before and after eye care · do not share towels, make-up, drops or pillowcases · stop contact lenses until cleared and replace lenses and cases. Red flags: pain, photop

Type Where Examples Conductive Outer or middle ear — transmission blocked Cerumen, otitis media, otosclerosis Sensorineural Cochlea or CN VIII — hair cell or nerve damage Ageing, noise, ototoxicity Mixed Both together

Weber — fork at midline , ask where the sound is heard. Rinne — compare bone conduction at the mastoid with air conduction at the canal. Expected: air > bone. Conductive loss lateralizes to the BAD ear. Sensorineural lateralizes to the GOOD ear.
Gradual, usually bilateral age-related loss. High-frequency speech sounds go first — which is exactly why shouting does not help.

Reduce background noise first Face her at eye level , mouth visible, light on your face Lower your pitch ; normal-to-slightly-louder volume — do not shout Rephrase rather than repeat the same words Confirm with teach-back; make sure alarms are accessible

Pain when the tragus or pinna is moved — the giveaway Canal edema, erythema, itching , discharge Drops at room temperature ; affected ear up ; let them sit several minutes Keep the ear dry. Ear wick only if ordered

Causes reversible conductive loss: fullness, hearing change, tinnitus, cough. No cotton swabs. No ear candles. Avoid irrigation with suspected perforation, tubes, or prior ear surgery — refer instead.

Ear pain, tugging, fever, fullness , bulging red tympanic membrane , reduced hearing. Normal otoscopic exam: pearly grey, translucent, intact, visible malleus and cone of light. Fluid or bubbles behind the membrane is the abnormal finding — soft cerumen and a visible malleus are normal.

Do not irrigate or instil drops unless the provider confirms they are safe for a non-intact membrane Keep water out; no swimming No nose blowing ; avoid pressure changes until healed Report fever, worsening pain, purulent drainage, severe vertigo, facial weakness

Tympanoplasty reconstructs the membrane; mastoidectomy removes infected mastoid air cells or cholesteatoma. Restrict rapid movements and avoid bending from the waist for several weeks No heavy lifting or straining Do not blow the nose. Sneeze and cough with the mouth open Keep the ear completely dry ; hair washing waits about a week, ear protected The provider removes the dressing — not the client Expect hearing to be worse before it is better — edema and packing. Monitor temperature, drainage, facial movement and

Vertigo — episodes lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours Fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss Tinnitus Aural pressure or fullness Low salt (often 1,500–2,000 mg/day), no caffeine, move slowly. Avoid alcohol and nicotine too. “Increase sodium” and “increase caffeine” are always wrong answers.

Stay with her and reduce movement Safe position, head supported Dim the lights , reduce noise and visual stimulation Emesis supplies; ordered antiemetics or vestibular suppressants Assist with all ambulation; fall precautions

A minoglycosides — gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin A spirin and high-dose salicylates, some NSAIDs L oop diuretics — furosemide, especially rapid or high-dose IV C hemotherapy — cisplatin, carboplatin V ancomycin New tinnitus is the early warning sign. It triggers a prompt medication review — not abrupt self-discontinuation . Document a baseline hearing and balance assessment, review renal function and dose, and ask about tinnitus, fullness and dizziness each shift.

Deprivation vs overload · hearing aids · vision loss · aphasia NG-404 Neuro ADHD-friendly visual edition Too little input and too much input produce the same picture — confusion, irritability, disorientation. What tells them apart is the environment she is in , and that is what the questions test. Deprivation Too little input · isolation, boredom, drowsiness, hallucinations Overload Too much input · ICU, alarms, no sleep, racing thoughts Expressive aphasia Knows what she wants, cannot say it — frustrating Receptive

Too little useful input Isolation, impaired sight or hearing and an unfamiliar environment can make orientation difficult. Offer conversation, familiar objects and meaningful activity. Too much stimulation Repeated noise, interruptions and bright light can impair rest and concentration. Reduce avoidable stimulation and protect sleep. Restore access Make glasses and hearing aids available and working. Use clear communication, suitable lighting and an accessible clock or calendar. Assess a change New inattention, alt

Fixing the environment For deprivation: increase meaningful input. Open the curtains, a clock and a calendar in view, radio or television she chooses, familiar objects from home, regular conversation, visitors, get her out of the room. For overload: reduce and cluster. Turn down alarms and lights, close the door, cluster care so she gets uninterrupted sleep , one person speaking at a time, simple short instructions, quiet periods. Both benefit from orientation — say your name, the day and where she is, every time y
What each one looks like, how it is done, and what the result means. The pictures are the point — if you can picture the maneuver you can usually reason out the answer.

Whisper: test each ear separately while preventing lip-reading. Weber: a midline 512-Hz tuning fork screens for lateralization. Conductive loss tends toward the affected ear; sensorineural loss toward the better ear. Rinne: compare mastoid bone conduction with air conduction beside the canal. AC greater than BC is expected and can also occur in sensorineural loss. Otoscopy: straighten an adult canal up/back; under age 3 down/back. See Hearing assessment — panel 2 Weber: a midline 512-Hz tuning fork screens for lateralization. Conductive loss tends toward the affected ear; sensorineural loss toward the better ear. How: Strike a 512 Hz fork on the heel of your hand and stand the base on the middle of her forehead, or the top of her head. Ask where she hears it, not whether. Normal: Heard equally in both ears. No lateralization. Abnormal: Lateralizes to the bad ear = conductive loss on that side (wax, fluid, a perforation) — the block keeps roo

See Hearing assessment — panel 3 Rinne: compare mastoid bone conduction with air conduction beside the canal. AC greater than BC is expected and can also occur in sensorineural loss. How: Strike the fork, put the base on the mastoid and ask her to say when it stops. Immediately move the prongs 1–2 cm from the ear canal and ask whether she can still hear it. Normal: Still hears it in the air after the bone sound has gone — air conduction beats bone conduction, roughly 2 to 1. This is a positive Rinne, and positive i

See Hearing assessment — panel 4 Otoscopy: straighten an adult canal up/back; under age 3 down/back. Brace the examining hand and avoid forceful or deep insertion. Bedside screens do not replace formal audiology. How: Adult or child over 3: pull the pinna up and back . Child under 3: down and back . Brace your hand against her head so a sudden movement moves the scope with her, and insert 1–1.5 cm angled down and forward. Normal: Pearly gray, translucent, slightly concave, with the malleus visible and a cone of lig

Distance acuity: test one eye at a time with usual distance correction, at the chart’s calibrated distance. The pictured chart is only illustrative. Near acuity: use the near card’s specified distance and usual reading correction. Confrontation: compare patient and examiner fields. Cover opposite eyes so the open eyes face each other. Central interpretation Brain networks identify and respond to the input. Vision Acuity, fields, pupils and eye movements test different functions. Hearing Screening and Weber/Rinne tests provide clues; audiometry establishes thresholds. Sensation Compare sides, modalities and distribution while accounting for cognition and communication. How: Stand her 20 feet from the cha

See Vision assessment — panel 2 Near acuity: use the near card’s specified distance and usual reading correction. How: Hold a Rosenbaum or Jaeger card 14 inches away, one eye at a time, reading glasses on. Normal: 14/14, or reads the smallest line comfortably. Abnormal: Has to push the card further away to focus — presbyopia, which starts around 40 and is not a disease. Why it matters here. Distance vision can be perfect while near vision is useless. Check both, or a medication label she cannot read gets recorded a

See Vision assessment — panel 3 Confrontation: compare patient and examiner fields. Cover opposite eyes so the open eyes face each other. How: Sit about 2 ft away at her eye level. She covers her left eye, you cover your right. Both stare at each other’s nose. Bring a wiggling finger in from each of the four corners, midway between the two of you, and ask her to say the moment she sees it. Then swap eyes. Normal: She sees the finger at the same moment you do — you are the control, which is why your own fields have

See Vision assessment — panel 4 Extraocular movements: assess six cardinal gaze directions with the head still; cranial nerves III, IV and VI. How: Hold your finger about 12 inches away. Ask her to hold her head still and follow it with her eyes only, while you trace a wide H . Watch both eyes together, and pause at each corner. Normal: Smooth, conjugate movement in all six directions. A couple of beats of nystagmus at the extreme edge is normal. Abnormal: One eye lagging or not reaching a corner = a palsy of CN II

See Vision assessment — panel 5 Pupil light response: the illuminated pupil constricts directly; the opposite pupil constricts consensually. New acute vision loss or neurologic findings need prompt evaluation. How: Dim the room and ask her to look at something far away. Bring the penlight in from the side , never straight at her. Watch the lit pupil (direct) and the other one (consensual). Then hold a finger far away and move it toward her nose for accommodation. Normal: P upils E qual, R ound, R eactive to L ight

Light touch: use a light stimulus with the patient’s eyes closed; compare sides. Sharp/dull: use appropriate disposable testing equipment; do not puncture skin. Vibration: place the base of a vibrating 128-Hz tuning fork on a bony prominence. Position sense: hold the sides of a distal digit and move it slightly up or down. Romberg: guard against falls; compare stability with eyes open versus closed. Increased instability with eyes closed may reflect impaired proprioception or vestibular function. Protective sensati

Mental status and speech Assess alertness, orientation, attention and speech. Describe the actual responses. Consider hearing, language, sedation and other factors that affect testing. Pupils and cranial functions Assess pupil size, equality and light response. Examine eye movement, facial symmetry, hearing and other cranial functions as indicated. Motor and sensory function Compare right and left movement, strength and sensation. Assess coordination, reflexes and gait when appropriate and safe. Document focal find

See Peripheral sensation — panel 2 Sharp/dull: use appropriate disposable testing equipment; do not puncture skin. How: Snap a tongue blade in half — one end is now sharp, the other blunt. Eyes closed, alternate them at random and ask “sharp or dull?” each time. Normal: Identifies both correctly and consistently. Abnormal: Cannot tell them apart, or feels neither — loss of pain and temperature sensation. Why it matters here. One patient, then throw it away. Never use a needle that can break the skin, and never on s

See Peripheral sensation — panel 3 Vibration: place the base of a vibrating 128-Hz tuning fork on a bony prominence. How: Strike a 128 Hz fork and press the base on a bony point — the joint of the great toe, the medial malleolus, a knuckle. Ask her to say when the buzzing stops. Then damp it with your fingers while it is still on her skin, to check she is not guessing. Normal: Feels the buzz, and says it has stopped at about the moment it actually does. Abnormal: Cannot feel it, or loses it well before you do. Vibr

See Peripheral sensation — panel 4 Position sense: hold the sides of a distal digit and move it slightly up or down. How: Hold the great toe by its sides , not its top and bottom — pressure on the nail bed tells her the answer without any position sense at all. Move it clearly up or down, eyes closed, and ask which way. Normal: Correct every time, at the toe and at a finger. Abnormal: Gets it wrong, or needs a big movement to tell. Position sense travels in the posterior columns, the same tract as vibration, so the

See Peripheral sensation — panel 5 Romberg: guard against falls; compare stability with eyes open versus closed. Increased instability with eyes closed may reflect impaired proprioception or vestibular function. How: Feet together, arms at her sides. Eyes open for 20 seconds, then eyes closed for 20 seconds. Stand close with your arms ready — a positive Romberg means she falls. Normal: Slight sway with the eyes shut, and she stays up. Abnormal: Positive: she sways badly or falls only once the eyes close . She was u

See Peripheral sensation — panel 6 Protective sensation: use a 10-g monofilament at recommended sites with the recommended technique, avoiding ulcers/calluses. How: Eyes closed. Hold the filament perpendicular to the skin and press until it buckles into a C — that bend is what makes it exactly 10 grams. Hold about a second, then lift. Test the sites in no fixed order, and throw in a couple of moments where you touch nothing. Normal: Feels the filament at every site tested. Abnormal: Any site not felt = protective s

Stereognosis: identify a familiar object by touch with eyes closed; test each hand. Graphesthesia: identify a number traced on the palm. Bilateral stimulation: compare separate versus simultaneous touch. Extinction is missing one side only during simultaneous stimulation. Smell: test one nostril at a time with a familiar nonirritating odor, such as coffee. Avoid ammonia. Interpret findings with primary sensation, attention, language and cognition; one abnormal finding does not independently establish a lesion locat

See Sensory recognition and smell — panel 2 Graphesthesia: identify a number traced on the palm. How: Eyes closed. With the blunt end of a pen, draw a number 3–6 cm tall on her palm, the right way up from her point of view , and ask her what you wrote. Normal: Identifies the number. Abnormal: Agraphesthesia — again, parietal, and again only meaningful if plain touch is intact. Why it matters here. Draw it facing her, not facing you. A 6 drawn upside down is a 9, and you will chart a deficit she does not have.

Central interpretation Brain networks identify and respond to the input. Vision Acuity, fields, pupils and eye movements test different functions. Hearing Screening and Weber/Rinne tests provide clues; audiometry establishes thresholds. Sensation Compare sides, modalities and distribution while accounting for cognition and communication. How: Use a caliper, or the two ends

See Sensory recognition and smell — panel 3 Bilateral stimulation: compare separate versus simultaneous touch. Extinction is missing one side only during simultaneous stimulation. How: Eyes closed. Touch both sides at the same instant — both forearms, both cheeks — and ask how many places you touched and where. Check each side alone first, so you know plain touch is intact. Normal: Reports both touches, on both sides. Abnormal: Extinction: she feels only one side, even though that same side is felt normally when to

See Sensory recognition and smell — panel 4 Smell: test one nostril at a time with a familiar nonirritating odor, such as coffee. Avoid ammonia. How: Eyes closed. Press one nostril shut and hold a familiar, non-irritating smell under the other — coffee, vanilla, soap, orange. Repeat on the other side with a different smell. Normal: Detects and usually names it on both sides. Abnormal: Anosmia. Common after a head injury (the olfactory fibers shear as they pass through the skull base), with nasal disease, with age,

How: Eyes closed, tongue out. Place a small amount of a test substance on the front two thirds (CN VII, facial), then on the back third (CN IX, glossopharyngeal). Rinse with water between each one. Normal: Identifies sweet, salty, sour and bitter. Abnormal: Loss on the front two thirds points at the facial nerve — Bell’s palsy affects taste as well as movement. Taste is also blunted by chemotherapy, radiation, dry mouth and many medications. Why it matters here. The old tongue map is wrong . Every taste can be dete

Vision loss Announce yourself when you enter and say when you leave — otherwise she is talking to an empty room. Explain what you are about to do before touching her. Keep everything in the same place and tell her if you move something. Sighted-guide technique: she takes your arm just above the elbow and walks half a step behind. You do not take hers. Describe the meal tray as a clock face — potatoes at three, meat at six. At home: remove rugs and clutter, tape down cords, good lighting, contrasting colors on step

Deprivation Too little input · isolation, boredom, drowsiness, hallucinations Overload Too much input · ICU, alarms, no sleep, racing thoughts Expressive aphasia Knows what she wants, cannot say it — frustrating Receptive aphasia Speaks fluently but does not understand you Weber lateralizes to her left ear. What does that tell you? Show answer Either a conductive loss on the left, or a sensorineural loss on the right. Sound runs toward a blocked ear and away from a dead one — Rinne tells you which. Recognise it, tell the two kinds apart, predict what it took away, and keep her safe afterwards. Four questions, and every stroke item on an exam is one of them.

Nothing happens until the brain is imaged. Blocked and bleeding look identical from the doorway and are treated in opposite directions — so the treatment question is never answerable from symptoms alone. And the thing that decides what she gets offered is when she was last seen normal . Not when she was found. Last known well is the single most useful sentence you can put in a report, and it is the one families most often cannot answer.

B Balance Sudden loss of balance or coordination E Eyes Sudden vision change in one or both eyes F Face Uneven smile, one side droops A Arms Weakness, or one arm drifts down when both are raised S Speech Slurred, or the words come out wrong T Time Call 911 now — and note the last known well time Symptoms that resolve still get the full work-up. A TIA leaves no damage and is a warning shot; the risk of a completed stroke is highest in the days right after. Do not let her drive herself, and do not give food, drink or

🧯 Ischemic — a clot blocks an artery The commonest kind. Blood flow stops, and the tissue downstream starts to die. Eligible people may be offered clot-dissolving medicine or thrombectomy — eligibility depends on imaging, timing and clinical criteria, which is exactly why the last known well time matters so much. 🩸 Hemorrhagic — a vessel ruptures Blood escapes into or around the brain, and the pressure itself becomes the injury. Care is aimed at controlling the bleeding and the blood pressure , and reversing antico

entries.h: 🧠 3 · Side of brain, side of body
entries.t: The motor pathways cross. So the damage is on one side of the brain and the weakness is on the other side of the body. That crossing is what most of these questions are actually testing. ⬅️ Left brain Often right-sided weakness or sensory loss Language difficulty (aphasia) may occur — trouble finding words, understanding, reading or writing She may be slow, cautious and aware of the deficit, which is its own kind of distress ➡️ Right brain Often left-sided weakness or sensory loss Neglect — she may ignore the left

Swallow screen before anything by mouth — food, fluids and medicines. This is the first thing, every time, and it comes before the breakfast tray. Support the weak limbs. Never pull on the affected arm — the shoulder subluxes easily once the muscles cannot hold it. Use the prescribed transfer method. One idea at a time when you speak , then stop and wait. Silence is her processing, not her failing. Approach from her unaffected side at first if she has neglect, then work on teaching her to scan toward the neglected

BE-FAST : balance, eyes, face, arms, speech, time — and last known well , not when she was found Check the glucose. Hypoglycaemia mimics a stroke exactly Urgent brain imaging before treatment — blocked and bleeding are opposite No thrombolytics for a hemorrhagic stroke , and no aspirin before imaging Left brain → right body + aphasia. Right brain → left body + neglect Aphasia = language. Dysarthria = the speech muscles , words intact Swallow screen before food, fluids or medicines. Every time, first Never pull the
The points the practice quiz in NUR 258 Module 7 tests that are not spelled out above. The questions themselves are in the NUR 258 Mega Quiz.

Embolic: a clot forms elsewhere — classically in the heart in atrial fibrillation — and travels to the brain. Thrombotic: a clot forms on a narrowed, atherosclerotic artery in the neck or brain. Hemorrhagic: uncontrolled hypertension , aneurysm, anticoagulants, older fragile vessels. TIA: symptoms last minutes to hours and resolve fully — but it is a warning and always needs urgent medical work-up . Modifiable risks: smoking, obesity, inactivity, hypertension, diabetes, high cholesterol, atrial fibrillation, heavy

entries.h: 🧠 What each part of the brain does
entries.t: Frontal: personality, judgment, voluntary movement, Broca’s area (speaking). Parietal: sensation and spatial awareness. Temporal: hearing, memory and learning, emotion , Wernicke’s area (understanding). Occipital: vision . Cerebellum: balance and coordination . Brainstem: breathing, heart rate, swallowing, consciousness. Left brain: right-sided weakness, aphasia, agraphia, alexia, impaired math, right visual field loss, slow and cautious, aware of deficits so often depressed or frustrated . Right brain: left-sided

Receptive aphasia (Wernicke): cannot understand. Expressive aphasia (Broca): understands but cannot get the words out — ask yes/no questions, use a communication board, give time, do not finish their sentences. Dysarthria = slurred speech from weak muscles. Apraxia = cannot perform a purposeful movement despite strength. Agnosia = cannot recognize objects. Agraphia = cannot write. Alexia = cannot read. Hemianopia: half the visual field is lost — teach the client to turn the head and scan ; place items in the seen f

Recognize a sudden rise in blood pressure and respond urgently. Sit upright and call for help. Loosen constriction and check the bladder first.

Usually associated with spinal cord injury at T6 or above. Compare blood pressure with the person’s usual baseline. A sudden rise may occur with pounding headache, flushing or sweating. Pulse can be slow or fast, and symptoms may be limited.
Sit the patient upright and obtain help. Loosen constrictive clothing or devices. Check blood pressure and pulse frequently, commonly every 2–5 minutes under the response protocol.

Start with bladder drainage and check catheter tubing for kinks or obstruction. Follow the ordered catheter protocol. Then assess bowel and skin causes. Bowel examination or manipulation can worsen AD and requires the appropriate protocol.
Follow the emergency plan and administer the ordered rapid-onset antihypertensive when indicated. Continue urgent escalation if blood pressure remains elevated.
Blood pressure moves toward baseline, symptoms improve and the trigger is corrected. Continue monitoring for recurrence or hypotension after treatment.
The regular clinical infographic above gives the response steps. The original alarm-tower picture below remains available for recall.
A patient with a T4 injury develops a pounding headache and sudden hypertension. What comes first?
Sit upright, call for help, loosen constriction and monitor blood pressure. Investigate bladder causes first while following the emergency response plan.

Computed tomography angiography (CTA) uses IV contrast to map blood vessels and identify vascular problems. Report breathing difficulty, throat swelling, hives or pain and swelling at the IV site immediately.

CT angiography combines CT scanning with contrast through a peripheral IV to evaluate blood vessels. In stroke, distinguish the vessel study from the initial noncontrast head CT used to assess for bleeding.
Review prior contrast reactions, kidney risk, medicines and pregnancy possibility. Check IV access. Follow radiology instructions for preparation and any medication changes.

The patient keeps still and follows breathing instructions. Brief warmth or a metallic taste may occur. Breathing difficulty, throat swelling, hives or IV-site pain and swelling need immediate assessment.
Reassess symptoms and the IV site. Follow the ordered hydration and medication plan. CTA does not automatically require the groin-puncture precautions used after arterial catheter angiography.

Vessel road map — CTA shows vascular narrowing, blockage, aneurysm or injury. Kidney checkpoint — Review kidney risk and ordered laboratory testing. Reaction shield — Ask about previous reactions to contrast material. The small memory scene uses symbols. It is an original mnemonic, not an official Picmonic product.
After an IV CTA, should you automatically apply femoral arterial-puncture aftercare?
No. Identify the procedure actually performed. CTA generally uses a peripheral IV. Catheter angiography can involve arterial access and has different aftercare.

Degenerative disc disease (also spelled disk disease) may cause back pain. Use pillows and supported alignment to reduce strain. New bladder or bowel changes, saddle numbness or worsening leg weakness needs urgent assessment.
Support the head and neck. Slightly bend the knees and place a pillow between them, adjusting for comfort.
A pillow under the knees may reduce strain. Keep the head and neck supported.
Avoid twisting during turns. Use the transfer technique taught by the nurse or physical therapist. Change position and walk as tolerated.
Use the surgeon and physical therapist instructions for positioning, lifting and activity. A general comfort position does not replace a specific postoperative plan.

Pillow bridge — Support the spine without twisting. Pillow between knees — Side-lying support helps keep the hips and spine aligned. Pillow under knees — Supine support can reduce lower-back strain. The small memory scene uses symbols. It is an original mnemonic, not an official Picmonic product.
Which support can help a side-lying patient keep the pelvis and spine aligned?
A pillow between the knees, with the head and neck supported. Adjust to the patient and prescribed restrictions.

Protect alignment. Assess skin, pin sites and neurologic function. Report new weakness, numbness, breathing trouble or a loose device promptly.
Compare breathing, swallowing, limb strength and sensation with baseline.
Check pin sites for redness, drainage, swelling or pain. Check skin beneath the vest and keep the liner dry. Use the prescribed cleaning method.
Do not adjust pins or hardware yourself. The clinical team controls fit and tightening. Never pull on the metal rods to move the patient.
Effective care maintains alignment, intact skin, clean pin sites and stable neurologic function. New clicking, loose pins, fever or increasing pain needs review.

Locked helmet — Maintain the prescribed cervical alignment. Inspection mirror — Inspect pin sites and the skin beneath the vest. Stop hand — Never lift, pull or reposition by the rods. The small memory scene uses symbols. It is an original mnemonic, not an official Picmonic product. Use the device team’s instructions for clothing and skin access. The vest liner generally rests against the skin, and clothing goes over the brace. Keep the prescribed emergency-release tool available according to local policy.
A patient reports new clicking in a halo device. Should you tighten the pins?
No. Maintain alignment and contact the treating team promptly. Do not adjust the pins or use the rods as handles.

A lumbar puncture, also called a spinal tap, collects cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Check safety, support positioning and reassess afterward. Review contraindications before LP. Do not delay urgent antibiotics for an unsafe or delayed LP when bacterial meningitis is suspected.

Verify informed consent and baseline neurologic findings. Review anticoagulants, bleeding risk and puncture-site infection. Findings suggesting a mass lesion or dangerous raised ICP need clinician review before proceeding.
Support the ordered side-lying or seated position, preserve breathing and help the patient remain still. Maintain sterile technique. Label and send CSF specimens promptly according to policy.
Monitor neurologic status, vital signs and the puncture site. Follow the ordered activity and fluid plan. Report severe or persistent positional headache, fever, drainage or new weakness.
Compare the neurologic examination with baseline and reassess headache, puncture-site drainage and signs of infection.

Checklist gate — Verify consent, neurologic assessment and bleeding risk. Still statue — Help the patient maintain the ordered position and keep still. Sample vials — CSF is collected using sterile technique. Alarm bell — Reassess and report concerning symptoms. The small memory scene uses symbols. It is an original mnemonic, not an official Picmonic product.

entries.h: Course wording and current evidence on aftercare
entries.t: The existing course notes teach lying flat and hydration after LP. Use the assigned ATI/course wording for your exam and the ordered clinical plan for care. Current-evidence side note: Routine prolonged bed rest has not been shown to prevent post-dural-puncture headache. Lying down may relieve an established positional headache. This does not replace individual post-procedure orders.
This is the original meningitis handout, which provides context for CSF testing. It is not an LP-specific handout.
A patient awaiting LP develops new focal weakness and declining consciousness. Proceed with routine positioning?
No. Stop preparation, escalate the new neurologic findings and obtain urgent clinical review before LP.
