entries.h: Page 1 · why it happens + effects on the baby
entries.t: Pregnancy-related insulin resistance outgrows the body’s insulin supply, so glucose rises. Often no symptoms; thirst or frequent urination can occur. Routine screening at 24–28 weeks ; earlier testing may find diabetes that was there before pregnancy. Follow the glucose: maternal glucose up → crosses the placenta → baby’s insulin up → growth increases → after birth the supply stops but the baby’s insulin stays high → newborn glucose falls . Effects on the baby: large baby (LGA / macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, birth

Goals (ADA 2026): fasting under 95 mg/dL, plus either 1 hour after a meal under 140 or 2 hours after under 120 mg/dL, as ordered. Individualized to avoid hypoglycemia. Food + timing: individualized meal plan; spread carbohydrates across meals and snacks with fiber and protein; don’t skip meals. Move + monitor: pregnancy-safe activity such as walking if approved; check glucose and keep a log. Medicine if needed: insulin is preferred. Metformin crosses the placenta; use is individualized. Nursing focus: teach meter a

CDC: Gestational Diabetes (2024) ADA: How Gestational Diabetes Can Impact Your Baby ACOG: Gestational Diabetes FAQ ADA Standards of Care 2026, Section 15 Stanford Medicine: Newborn Hypoglycemia NIDDK: Managing & Treating Gestational Diabetes NIDDK: Pregnancy if You Have Diabetes Made by Codex, 21 Oct. Illustrations are educational. Follow course guidance and local protocols.

entries.h: 🩺 BP disorders in pregnancy Chronic HTN, gestational HTN, preeclampsia, eclampsia + HELLP
entries.t: 🖨️ PDF 💉 Jump to magnesium sulfate

Hypertension: 140 systolic or more OR 90 diastolic or more, usually confirmed on 2 readings at least 4 hours apart. Severe range: 160 systolic or more OR 110 diastolic or more. Repeat promptly and notify; if it persists, treat urgently. Chronic HTN: before pregnancy or before 20 weeks. Preeclampsia can develop on top of it. Gestational HTN: new at 20 weeks or later, no proteinuria or organ dysfunction. Keep reassessing. Preeclampsia: new HTN after 20 weeks plus proteinuria OR qualifying organ dysfunction. Eclampsia

Brain / eyes: persistent headache, vision changes. Liver / blood: RUQ or epigastric pain, low platelets, high enzymes. Lungs / kidneys: pulmonary edema, renal dysfunction. Assess + escalate: correct cuff and position; symptoms; urine protein; platelets, creatinine, liver enzymes; fetal status. Treat + prepare: antihypertensives control severe BP; magnesium prevents and treats seizures; prepare for the ordered birth plan. Baby: poor placental flow can cause growth restriction or early birth. Preeclampsia can first a

entries.h: 💉 Magnesium sulfate safety What it does, what to watch, toxicity and the antidote
entries.t: 🖨️ PDF

Breathing: rate and depth, oxygen saturation, work of breathing. Watch for depression. Reflexes + LOC: deep tendon reflexes, alertness, weakness. New absent reflexes are concerning. Urine + fluids: strict intake and output, renal function. Magnesium is cleared by the kidneys, so low output raises toxicity risk. Also: BP and pulse, the pump and line, ordered magnesium levels, fetal status. It runs on an infusion pump at the ordered rate.

Concerning: slow or shallow breathing or falling oxygen; absent reflexes; marked drowsiness or weakness; low urine output. Act: stop the magnesium infusion; call the obstetric or emergency team; support airway and breathing; obtain ordered levels and reassess. Antidote: calcium gluconate — keep it at the bedside; give IV as ordered. Don’t wait for a lab result when breathing is getting worse. Expected, not toxicity: warmth and flushing. Lost reflexes and slowed breathing are never reassuring. Exam separation: magne

entries.h: ⏳ Cervical insufficiency vs preterm labor Same result, different cause: opening without contractions vs contractions plus change
entries.t: 🖨️ PDF

Cervical insufficiency: the cervix opens in the second trimester without regular labor contractions, often with little pain. Clues: a prior painless second-trimester loss, pelvic pressure, new discharge. Preterm labor: contractions plus cervical change before 37 weeks. Tightening may be painless; pressure, low backache, discharge change or leaking fluid can occur.

Transvaginal ultrasound measures cervical length. A short cervix is not automatically cervical insufficiency. Progesterone: selected singleton pregnancies with a short cervix may benefit from vaginal progesterone. It is not a stitch. Cerclage: a stitch for selected cases based on history, ultrasound and/or exam. Not every short cervix needs one. SMFM pearl: singleton, no prior spontaneous preterm birth: 25 mm or less is short; if 20 mm or less before 24 weeks with no symptoms, vaginal progesterone is recommended. A
ACOG: Cervical Cerclage ACOG: Preterm Labor and Birth SMFM Consult Series 70: Short Cervix (2024) RCOG: Cervical Stitch

entries.h: 🤢 Hyperemesis gravidarum Restore fluids, electrolytes and nutrition; thiamine before dextrose
entries.t: 🖨️ PDF

More than occasional nausea: severe nausea and vomiting prevent normal eating or drinking and disrupt daily life. Dehydration, weight loss and electrolyte changes may follow. Get assessed if she can’t keep fluids or medicines down, has little urine, faints or loses weight. Confusion or severe weakness = urgent care. Fluids: vitals, intake and output, daily weight, ability to drink. Electrolytes: ordered labs and renal function; replace deficits as ordered. Other causes: fever, abdominal pain, urinary symptoms or ne

Rehydrate: IV isotonic fluids when oral intake is not enough; potassium by labs and orders. Control nausea: B6 with or without doxylamine is a common first option; other antiemetics may be needed. Restore nutrition: small tolerated foods and fluids; avoid odor triggers; dietitian support; tube feeding for selected severe cases. Thiamine before dextrose -containing fluids or parenteral nutrition. Mother + baby: assess clot risk during dehydration and immobility; support mental health. Persistent severe HG may affect

This chapter reviews pregnancy complications beyond bleeding: cervical insufficiency, hyperemesis gravidarum, iron-deficiency anemia, gestational diabetes, and gestational hypertensive disorders—covering risk factors, key labs, medications, and nursing priorities needed to protect mother and fetus.

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2024 . For pregestational diabetes, achieving an A1C below 6.5% before conception is the American Diabetes Association's recommended target. No clearly safe A1C threshold exists; congenital anomaly risk rises progressively as preconception glycemic control worsens. At an A1C around 10% , congenital anomaly rates run about 10% ; near an A1C of 13% , rates climb to about 20% . Preconception glycemic surveillance is considered the most effective way to prevent diabetic

In-utero DES exposure (banned after 1971) raises cervical insufficiency risk A history of cervical trauma or an early pregnancy loss raises insufficiency risk Multifetal gestation and gestational trophoblastic disease raise hyperemesis risk A history of migraines or family hyperemesis raises risk of recurrence Type 1 diabetes and hyperthyroidism raise hyperemesis risk A short gap between pregnancies or heavy pre-pregnancy menses raises anemia risk Obesity and maternal age over 25 years raise GDM risk A prior macros

Cervical insufficiency: pelvic pressure or urge to push, often with painless dilation Cervical insufficiency: ultrasound shows a cervix under 25 mm , funneling, or effacement Evidence update, not ATI: SMFM 2024 says a short cervix on ultrasound is not by itself cervical insufficiency; history and exam matter. Cervix vs preterm labor guide → Cerclage is typically placed around 13 to 14 weeks and removed at 36 to 37 weeks Hyperemesis: prolonged vomiting with dehydration, weight loss, and electrolyte imbalance Hyperem

Hyperemesis: urine ketones/acetones is the key initial test; specific gravity is elevated Evidence update, not ATI: RCOG 2024 says ketones don’t measure dehydration or severity — assess intake, weight, vitals and labs too. For ATI questions, ATI’s line stands. Hyperemesis guide → Hyperemesis: sodium, potassium, and calcium drop; metabolic acidosis or alkalosis can occur Hyperemesis: CBC shows an elevated Hct from hemoconcentration Anemia is diagnosed with Hgb under 11 g/dL Unit corrected: hemoglobin is g/dL, not mg

GDM: nonstress test checks fetal well-being; biophysical profile if the NST is nonreactive GDM: amniocentesis can check amniotic fluid phosphatidylglycerol for fetal lung maturity Preeclampsia: urine dipstick and a 24-hr collection assess proteinuria Preeclampsia fetal status can be tracked with an NST, contraction stress test, BPP, or repeat ultrasounds Doppler flow studies and daily kick counts also monitor fetal status in preeclampsia

Cervical insufficiency: watch for contractions, ROM, or infection signs after cerclage placement Hyperemesis: track intake/output, skin turgor, vital signs, and daily weight Iron-deficiency anemia: recommended intake is 27 mg/day ; prenatal vitamins have about 30 mg If iron-deficient, dosing increases to 60 to 120 mg/day elemental iron GDM: monitor maternal blood glucose and fetal status closely Preeclampsia: use a properly sized cuff and avoid talking during BP checks Preeclampsia: encourage side-lying positioning

Hyperemesis: IV fluids for hydration are the first priority Hyperemesis: pyridoxine (B6) alone or with doxylamine is first-line and ACOG-recommended Hyperemesis: antiemetics are used cautiously; corticosteroids are reserved for refractory cases GDM is managed first with diet and exercise; insulin is added if glucose stays high Glyburide is a limited oral option for GDM; most oral agents are contraindicated Evidence update, not ATI: ADA 2026 prefers insulin when medicine is needed and does not recommend metformin or

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2024 . Maternal echocardiography helps evaluate structural and functional cardiac status in pregnant patients with known or suspected heart disease. A 12-lead ECG and maternal BNP level are used alongside CBC and CMP to assess cardiac disease severity in pregnancy. StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf) · Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy · open the source →

Hyperemesis: avoid known triggers like specific odors Hyperemesis: start with bland foods (dry toast, crackers, rice) and advance as tolerated Severe hyperemesis may require enteral tube feeding or TPN Take iron supplements on an empty stomach with orange juice to boost absorption Pair an iron-rich diet with vitamin C foods; add fiber and fluids for constipation GDM: perform daily kick counts and self-monitor blood glucose GDM: follow a carb-restricted diabetic diet with dietitian guidance and regular exercise

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2024 . Pregnancy with cardiac disease requires coordinated care among high-risk obstetricians, cardiologists, and perinatologists. Pharmacists play a distinct role in managing cardiac medications during pregnancy since many drugs can harm the fetus. Nurses are highlighted for their role in early recognition of worsening cardiac disease states in pregnant patients. StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf) · Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy · open the source →

entries.t: Folic acid prevents neural tube defects, not anemia — and it has to be on board before conception to do it, which is why it is recommended from three months preconception.

Folate supports cell division and red-cell formation. Adequate folic acid before conception and in early pregnancy lowers neural-tube-defect risk; continue the recommended prenatal intake during pregnancy.

Baseline and variability Establish the ongoing pattern. Accelerations and decelerations Describe timing, shape, depth and duration. Context and response Consider contractions, medications and maternal condition. Early decelerations Often mirror contractions and relate to head compression. Variable decelerations Abrupt falls commonly relate to cord compression. Late decelerations Begin and recover later in relation to contractions and need contextual assessment.

Labor is measured by the cervix, not by the contractions. A woman contracting hard with no cervical change is not in true labor. TRUE labor FALSE labor Cervix Dilates and effaces — the deciding factor No change Contractions Regular, closer, stronger, longer Irregular, do not intensify Pain site Back , radiating to the front Front / abdomen only With walking Gets stronger Often eases off
1st Onset → 10 cm . The longest stage 2nd 10 cm → birth of baby . Pushing 3rd Birth → placenta delivered . 5–30 min 4th First 1–4 hours after. Hemorrhage watch

entries.h: 🚨 The moment that changes everything: ruptured membranes
entries.t: The very first action after the water breaks is to check the fetal heart rate. Rupture is when cord prolapse happens. FHR first - not the pad, not the time, not the color. Then note TACO : T ime · A mount · C olour · O dour. Fluid should be clear. Green = meconium. Foul = infection. NUR 234 / EXAM 2 / FETAL MONITORING

Compare the heart-rate change with the contraction below it. The timing gives you the clue. Fetal heart rate Uterine activity Quiz yourself Start with the timing, then connect the pattern to its cause. 01

The dip mirrors the contraction The lowest heart rate lines up with the contraction peak. The dip begins and ends with the contraction. WHY IT HAPPENS Head compression stimulates a vagal response. NURSING RESPONSE Usually benign when the rest of the tracing is reassuring. Continue assessment. Check cervical dilation and fetal descent when indicated. Early = head compression Reveal pattern 1 02

The dip follows the contraction peak The lowest heart rate comes after the contraction peak. Recovery occurs after the contraction ends. WHY IT HAPPENS Reduced oxygen transfer through the placenta. NURSING RESPONSE Turn her onto her left side. Stop the oxytocin if it is running. Increase IV fluids. Give oxygen if indicated by maternal hypoxia, or per agency policy or provider prescription. Notify the provider. (ATI’s list; correct hypotension, check blood pressure and contractions.) Late = placental insufficiency R

An abrupt drop with changing timing The drop is abrupt: onset to lowest point takes less than 30 seconds. The relationship to contractions may vary. WHY IT HAPPENS Usually umbilical cord compression. NURSING RESPONSE Reposition the mother. Assess new decelerations after membrane rupture for possible cord prolapse. Escalate persistent or recurrent concerning patterns. Variable = cord compression Reveal pattern 3 04

A rise above the baseline At 32 weeks or later: rise of at least 15 bpm for at least 15 seconds, but less than 2 minutes. Before 32 weeks: at least 10 bpm for at least 10 seconds. WHY IT HAPPENS Often a normal response to fetal movement. NURSING RESPONSE A reassuring feature. Continue routine assessment of the whole tracing and the clinical situation. Acceleration = reassuring feature Reveal pattern 4 Read the whole tracing. These simplified examples teach timing. Also assess baseline, variability, recurrence, cont

entries.h: 🔴 Cord prolapse — act, do not investigate
entries.t: 1 Call for help; press the emergency bell 2 Gloved hand lifts the presenting part off the cord 3 Knee-chest or Trendelenburg position 4 Oxygen, stop oxytocin, prepare for immediate C-section Never push the cord back in, and never leave the patient to go and call.

Oxytocin effect Stimulates uterine contractions. Excess contraction activity Too little relaxation may reduce placental reperfusion. Assessment and response Evaluate maternal condition and fetal heart rate promptly. Recognize More than five contractions in ten minutes, averaged over thirty minutes, meets the standard tachysystole definition. When infusing oxytocin Reduce or stop the infusion and follow the fetal-response protocol when indicated. Reassess Position, pressure, fluid status and the tracing guide furthe

Four stages : 1) dilation 0–10 cm · 2) full dilation to birth · 3) birth to placental delivery · 4) the first 1–4 hours of recovery. Phases of stage 1 as she teaches them : latent up to ~ 5 cm , active ~ 6–7 cm , transition 8–10 cm . Her worked case: 6 cm / 100% effaced / 0 station = active phase of the first stage . 9 cm with strong frequent contractions = transition. Do not push until fully dilated — cervical trauma. Support her. Avoid analgesia this late: rapid progression and neonatal effects. Crowning appears

LOA = left occiput anterior = optimal. OP / LOP causes severe back pain with contractions, prolonged labor and slower descent → hands-and-knees or lateral positioning plus counterpressure . Not supine, not oxytocin, not straight to cesarean. Precipitous labor = birth in under 3 hours. Ruptured membranes with an unengaged fetal head = cord prolapse risk → assess FHR and reposition immediately . Pain plus anxiety in active labor: patterned breathing and position changes first . entries.t: First action after ANY rupture of membranes is to check the fetal heart rate — you are ruling out cord prolapse. Color, odor and amount come second. Nitrazine turns blue at pH 6.5–7.5; ferning confirms. Once membranes rupture, temperature goes from q4h to q2h. Rupture longer than 18–24 h is an infection risk and a GBS prophylaxis trigger. True vs false labor : true contractions intensify with walking, start in the back and wrap forward, and change the cervix. False labor stays abdominal and quits with rest, hydrati

entries.t: Red-flag pattern : duration over 90 sec , more than 5 contractions per 10 min , or under 30 sec of relaxation. All three cut placental perfusion. Placental separation signs : a sudden gush of dark blood, the cord visibly lengthening, the fundus becoming firm and globular. Delayed cord clamping 30–60 sec is standard. Fourth stage schedule : BP and pulse q15 min for 2 h; fundus and lochia q15 min the first hour then q30 min the second; temperature q4h. Laceration degrees : 1st skin · 2nd into muscle · 3rd through the

entries.t: Induction sequencing : oxytocin no sooner than 4 h after misoprostol, 6–12 h after dinoprostone. Remove any vaginal insert first. Run oxytocin as a secondary line on a pump, into the port closest to the client . Amniotomy requires an engaged presenting part — the risk being prevented is cord prolapse. TOLAC favors a prior LOW TRANSVERSE incision , one or two prior cesareans, 18–19 months between births, and immediate surgical backup.

Pillitteri, Maternal and Child Health Nursing — ch. 15 (labor and birth). The four Ps: passage, passenger, powers, and psyche . The fourth is the one students drop, and the book is explicit that psychological readiness shapes the course of labor. Why labor starts is not fully known. The best explanation is an interplay of fetal and uterine factors amounting to progesterone withdrawal . "We do not fully know" is the accurate answer. Presentation is the part that meets the cervix first; position is how that part rela

She teaches active phase as both 4–7 cm and 6–7 cm in the same rationale — traditional vs current ACOG. Expect 6 cm as the modern cut-off and read the stem carefully. Transition is where students pick "encourage pushing." Not until fully dilated.

Passenger — fetal lie, presentation, position, attitude and size. Passageway — the bony pelvis and the soft tissue. Powers — contractions (involuntary) and pushing (voluntary). Psyche — fear and tension raise catecholamines and genuinely slow labor.

First — onset to full dilation. Latent 0–5 cm, active 6–10 cm. Second — full dilation to birth. The pushing stage. Third — birth to delivery of the placenta, usually within 30 minutes. Fourth — the first 1–4 hours after; the highest-risk window for hemorrhage.

Contraction frequency (start to start), duration , and intensity . Cervical change is what defines labor — contractions without change are not labor. Fetal heart rate between and during contractions. Signs of placental separation: a gush of blood, a lengthening cord, a firm globular uterus.

Position changes and upright postures shorten labor; left lateral improves placental flow. After rupture of membranes, check the fetal heart rate immediately — cord prolapse is the fear. After birth: fundal massage , and a boggy uterus is the first sign of hemorrhage. Assess the bladder — a full bladder displaces the uterus and prevents it contracting down.

entries.t: ATI Active Learning Template — System Disorder Processes of Labor and Birth Filled from ATI chapter 11 , row by row from that chapter’s own sections — 12 of 12 rows have content. 10 rows came from outside your ATI chapter — 3 cite a source, 7 are built from this page’s own notes. This chapter explains the four stages of labor, premonitory signs preceding labor, and the five factors influencing labor and birth: fetal passenger, passageway, powers (contractions), maternal position, and psychological response.

From this module — built from the notes above on this page, not a section of the ATI chapter. Childbirth education lowers fear, and fear is what drives much of the pain. Teach when to come in : contractions 5 minutes apart for 1 hour in a first labor, ruptured membranes, bleeding, or reduced fetal movement. Encourage upright positions and walking in early labor — they shorten it. Discuss the birth plan in advance, including what happens if it has to change.

Risks for a difficult labor — the 5 Ps : passenger, passageway, powers, position, psyche. Malpresentation (breech, transverse, occiput posterior) and macrosomia . Contracted or android pelvis; previous shoulder dystocia. Grand multiparity, over-distended uterus, previous cesarean scar. Maternal exhaustion, dehydration, and unmanaged fear all weaken the powers.

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2024 . True labor produces regular contractions plus objective cervical change, while false labor (Braxton Hicks) causes no cervical dilation or effacement. In active labor, contractions typically occur every 2 to 5 minutes and require the woman's focused attention. During the active phase, cervical dilation progresses from about 6 cm to full dilation at roughly 1 to 2 cm per hour. The second stage, from full dilation to delivery, averages about 0.6 hours (roughly 3

CBC on admission — baseline hemoglobin before any blood loss. Blood type and screen , in case transfusion is needed. Red cell donor and recipient chart GBS status from the 36 0/7–37 6/7 culture — positive means intrapartum antibiotics. Urinalysis for protein and glucose. Nitrazine or fern test to confirm ruptured membranes — amniotic fluid turns nitrazine paper blue.

Vaginal examination for dilation, effacement, station, presentation and position. Leopold maneuvers before the exam — they establish lie and presentation and locate the back for auscultation. Continuous or intermittent electronic fetal monitoring . Ultrasound to confirm presentation when it is uncertain. No vaginal exam if there is bright red painless bleeding — placenta praevia must be excluded first.

Leopold maneuvers, tocotransducer, and EFM assess fetal position and track contractions/FHR externally Obtain group B strep culture if none on file from 36 0/7-37 6/7 weeks ; give IV prophylactic antibiotic if positive Check maternal temperature every 2 hr once membranes are ruptured Grade contraction intensity by palpation: mild (like nose tip), moderate (chin), strong (forehead) Contractions longer than 90 sec , or more than 5 in 10 min , with under 30 sec rest between, risk fetal hypoxia Vaginal exam checks dila

Oxytocin for augmentation — titrated, always on a pump, with continuous monitoring. Penicillin G for GBS-positive clients, ideally ≥4 hours before birth. Analgesia and anesthesia per the pain chapter. Antiemetics as needed. Never leave oxytocin running through a period of tachysystole or a non-reassuring tracing — stop it, reposition, oxygen, call.

Amniotomy — check fetal position and station first, and the fetal heart rate immediately after , because of cord prolapse risk. Membrane sweeping and cervical ripening agents to start labor. Amnioinfusion for variable decelerations from cord compression. Position changes, birthing ball, hydrotherapy. Episiotomy is no longer routine and is used only for specific indications.

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2024 . Teach patients that true labor contractions come at regular intervals and intensify, unlike irregular Braxton Hicks contractions. Advise patients that contractions occurring every 2 to 5 minutes generally signal it is time to go to the hospital. Explain that Braxton Hicks contractions may be uncomfortable but do not cause the cervix to dilate or efface.

Obstetric provider or midwife ; anesthesia for regional analgesia. Neonatal team at the birth for any anticipated complication. Doula or support person — continuous labor support measurably shortens labor and reduces intervention. Interpreter where needed; consent in labor must be genuine.

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2024 . A third stage lasting longer than 30 minutes for placental delivery increases the risk of postpartum hemorrhage. Most third stages conclude within 10 to 20 minutes after delivery; placental retention beyond 30 minutes is considered abnormal and needs intervention. entries.h: 📋 Nursing Care During Stages of Labor 6 parts
entries.t: 🖼️ Infographics False Labor & Interventions ATI Active Learning Template — System Disorder Nursing Care During Stages of Labor Filled from ATI chapter 14 , row by row from that chapter’s own sections — 12 of 12 rows have content.

Outlines nurse responsibilities across the four stages of labor: admission and ongoing maternal/fetal assessment, supporting comfort and effective pushing, and monitoring recovery and bonding after delivery of the placenta.

Encourage upright and mobile positions in the first stage. Offer clear fluids and ice per policy; dehydration slows labor. Encourage voiding every 2 hours — a full bladder impedes descent and causes uterine atony afterwards. Support non-pharmacological comfort first: breathing, counter-pressure, position, water, massage.

Precipitous labor — under 3 hours — risks laceration, hemorrhage and an unattended birth. Prolonged labor risks infection, exhaustion and atony. Prolonged rupture of membranes over 18–24 hours raises infection risk. Frequent vaginal examinations raise infection risk — do them for a reason, not a routine. Full bladder, epidural, and supine position all slow descent.

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2024 . Maternal vital signs and fetal heart rate should be obtained and assessed for abnormalities on arrival to labor and delivery. Ongoing labor assessment periodically reviews vital signs, urine output, pain level, and oral intake as labor progresses.

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2024 . A complete blood count and blood type and screen are commonly obtained on admission to labor and delivery. Additional sexually transmitted infection testing is often added on admission for patients considered high risk.

Vaginal examination timed to a decision, not the clock. Continuous EFM or intermittent auscultation depending on risk. Fetal scalp stimulation to assess for acceleration when the tracing is unclear. Assess the amniotic fluid at rupture: color, odor, amount and time . Meconium-stained or foul-smelling fluid is reported immediately.

Teach relaxation strategies for labor: paced breathing, effleurage, and focal-point imagery. Support comfort with position changes, ambulation, warm/cold packs, or hydrotherapy if not contraindicated. Encourage frequent voiding throughout labor to prevent bladder distention. Help position the client and coach bearing down once the cervix is fully dilated. Promote rest between contractions during active pushing. Prepare for a possible episiotomy and have a neonatal-resuscitation-trained nurse ready at birth. Preheat

Oxytocin for augmentation; oxytocin again after delivery of the placenta to contract the uterus. Analgesia and epidural per the pain chapter — preload with IV fluid and monitor for hypotension . GBS prophylaxis if indicated. Rho(D) immune globulin postpartum for an Rh-negative mother with an Rh-positive newborn. Ophthalmic erythromycin and vitamin K for the newborn.

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from AWHONN Position Statement . For low-risk patients in the active phase of labor, AWHONN recommends auscultating the fetal heart rate every 15 to 30 minutes . During the passive second stage, before active pushing, fetal heart rate should be auscultated about every 15 minutes . Once a low-risk patient begins active pushing, auscultation frequency increases to every 5 to 15 minutes . These intervals are minimums; more frequent assessment is needed whenever maternal or fetal status

Explain each stage as it happens — understanding what is happening reduces the pain of it. Do not push until fully dilated , however strong the urge, or the cervix swells. Open-glottis pushing with the contraction; rest between. Explain that the urge to push may be blunted by an epidural, so coaching matters more. Prepare her for what the first hour after birth involves: skin-to-skin, the placenta, fundal checks that hurt.

Provider or midwife, anesthesia, and the neonatal resuscitation team . Charge nurse early — obstetric emergencies need people in the room fast. Blood bank for type and crossmatch when hemorrhage risk is high. Lactation support within the first hour if she is breastfeeding.

Cord prolapse — call for help, relieve pressure off the cord with a gloved hand, knee-chest or Trendelenburg, oxygen, prepare for immediate cesarean. Never push the cord back in. Uterine tachysystole — more than 5 contractions in 10 minutes. Stop oxytocin, reposition left, IV fluid, oxygen. Shoulder dystocia — McRoberts position and suprapubic pressure first. Never apply fundal pressure. Amniotic fluid embolism — sudden dyspnea, hypotension and DIC. Rare and catastrophic. Postpartum hemorrhage — the boggy uterus is

Surveys procedures used to assist labor and birth: version to turn a breech fetus, cervical-readiness scoring, ripening agents, oxytocin induction/augmentation, artificial rupture of membranes, fluid infusion for cord compression, vacuum or forceps delivery, perineal incision, cesarean surgery, and trial of labor after a prior cesarean.

Explain why an intervention is being offered and what happens without it — consent in labor is easily assumed rather than obtained. A Bishop score guides whether induction is likely to succeed; a favorable cervix scores higher. Elective induction before 39 weeks is not recommended without a medical indication. Discuss the possibility of cesarean in advance, so it is not the first time she hears it.

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2024 . Common indications for labor induction include oligohydramnios, fetal growth restriction, hypertensive disorders, and post-term pregnancy. Absolute contraindications to induction include vasa previa, placenta previa, transverse fetal lie, and umbilical cord prolapse. A prior classical cesarean incision is a contraindication to labor induction due to uterine rupture risk. Operative vaginal delivery (vacuum or forceps) is considered for maternal exhaustion, a n

After amniotomy: fluid clear , and the fetal heart rate unchanged . After a ripening agent: gradual cervical change without tachysystole. On oxytocin, an adequate pattern is contractions about 2–3 minutes apart lasting 60–90 seconds , with the uterus relaxing fully in between . After a vacuum or forceps birth: expect a caput or bruising on the newborn. A uterus that does not relax between contractions is not an expected finding — the fetus is only perfused during the rest.

Type and screen or crossmatch before cesarean. CBC before an operative birth. Coagulation studies where hemorrhage or abruption is suspected. Cord blood gases after an operative birth for a non-reassuring tracing.

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2024 . A Bishop score of 8 or higher predicts a favorable cervix and a likely successful vaginal delivery after induction. A Bishop score of 3 or lower predicts a low chance of successful induction, favoring cervical ripening first. StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf) · Induction of Labor · open the source →

Monitor FHR continuously during external cephalic version and for 1 hr afterward for bradycardia or variable decels. Give Rh-negative clients Rho(D) immune globulin after version unless birth is expected within 72 hr . Bishop score of 8 or higher at term means the cervix is favorable for induction. Bishop scoring rates 5 cervical/station factors, each scored 0 to 3 points. Misoprostol (prostaglandin E1) and dinoprostone (prostaglandin E2) are used to ripen the cervix. After a vaginal ripening insert, keep client si

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2024 . IV oxytocin for induction is titrated to produce contractions about 2 to 3 minutes apart to achieve cervical dilation. Misoprostol for cervical ripening is typically dosed between 25 and 50 micrograms. Uterine tachysystole, more than five contractions inside a 10-minute window, is a recognized risk of pharmacologic induction. StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf) · Induction of Labor · open the source →

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2024 . Vacuum extraction requires a fully dilated cervix, ruptured membranes, an engaged fetal head, and a known fetal head position. Emptying the bladder and obtaining informed consent are also prerequisites before attempting operative vaginal delivery. A cervical ripening Foley balloon is inflated with 30 to 80 mL of saline and generally removed once the cervix dilates 3 to 4 cm . Vacuum cup traction is applied only during contractions and maternal pushing, limite

Explain what she will feel with each procedure — pressure, not usually pain, with a vacuum. After cesarean: splinting the incision to cough, early ambulation, incision care, and what to report. Report to the provider: fever, foul discharge, a wound that opens or drains, calf pain, heavy bleeding. Explain that a vacuum or forceps birth does not mean the next birth will need one .

Anesthesia for regional or general; surgical team for cesarean. Neonatal team present for every operative birth. Blood bank on standby where hemorrhage risk is raised. Physiotherapy for recovery after cesarean where mobility is slow.

Stop oxytocin for tachysystole: more than 5 contractions per 10 min , duration over 90 seconds , or resting tone over 15 mmHg . Target oxytocin contraction pattern: every 2 to 3 min , lasting 40-70 seconds , with FHR staying 110-160/min . For tachysystole with nonreassuring FHR, give terbutaline 0.25 mg subcutaneously. Elective induction should wait until at least 39 weeks gestation to limit infection, preterm birth, and cesarean risk. Amniotomy raises risk of cord prolapse and infection; labor usually starts withi

Pain in labor is subjective and shaped by physical, emotional and cultural factors — tailor interventions to each client. Nonpharmacologic techniques : effleurage, counter-pressure, hydrotherapy, guided imagery, position changes (hands-and-knees, squatting). Essential for clients seeking natural childbirth. Encourage movement and positioning to help fetal descent and comfort. Support systems — doulas and birth partners — enhance comfort and a positive birth experience. Pharmacologic options : opioid analgesics (Sta

Analgesics Do not eliminate pain completely; they reduce the sensation for a limited time. Most used: butorphanol (Stadol), nalbuphine (Nubain), morphine sulfate, fentanyl (Sublimaze). Narcotic analgesics are potent, but all of them cause maternal respiratory depression and fetal CNS and respiratory depression — so they should not be given within 1 hour of delivery . Anesthesia — reduces ALL sensation, not just pain, for a set length of time Epidural (regional): an anesthetic such as bupivacaine plus an analgesic (

Choose pain relief by labor stage and her preferences . Know the indications and contraindications for epidural and spinal anesthesia, including pre-procedure hydration to prevent hypotension. Watch for a spinal headache after an epidural and know the follow-up care. Know nonpharmacologic measures for specific fetal positions — counter-pressure for occiput posterior . After an analgesic: monitor for side effects such as respiratory depression , and know when it is safe to medicate her in relation to the delivery. A

Read the deceleration by its shape and its timing against the contraction. That is the whole skill. VEAL CHOP tells you what each one means. V E A L C H O P Means Do V ariable decel C ord compression Cord squeezed Reposition the mother E arly decel H ead compression Normal — mirrors contraction Nothing. Document A ccelerations O xygenation OK Reassuring Nothing. Good sign L ate decel P lacental insufficiency Worst one — poor perfusion Full intervention NUR 234 / EXAM 2 / FETAL MONITORING

Compare the heart-rate change with the contraction below it. The timing gives you the clue. Fetal heart rate Uterine activity Quiz yourself Start with the timing, then connect the pattern to its cause. 01

The dip mirrors the contraction The lowest heart rate lines up with the contraction peak. The dip begins and ends with the contraction. WHY IT HAPPENS Head compression stimulates a vagal response. NURSING RESPONSE Usually benign when the rest of the tracing is reassuring. Continue assessment. Check cervical dilation and fetal descent when indicated. Early = head compression Reveal pattern 1 02

The dip follows the contraction peak The lowest heart rate comes after the contraction peak. Recovery occurs after the contraction ends. WHY IT HAPPENS Reduced oxygen transfer through the placenta. NURSING RESPONSE Turn her onto her left side. Stop the oxytocin if it is running. Increase IV fluids. Give oxygen if indicated by maternal hypoxia, or per agency policy or provider prescription. Notify the provider. (ATI’s list; correct hypotension, check blood pressure and contractions.) Late = placental insufficiency R

An abrupt drop with changing timing The drop is abrupt: onset to lowest point takes less than 30 seconds. The relationship to contractions may vary. WHY IT HAPPENS Usually umbilical cord compression. NURSING RESPONSE Reposition the mother. Assess new decelerations after membrane rupture for possible cord prolapse. Escalate persistent or recurrent concerning patterns. Variable = cord compression Reveal pattern 3 04

A rise above the baseline At 32 weeks or later: rise of at least 15 bpm for at least 15 seconds, but less than 2 minutes. Before 32 weeks: at least 10 bpm for at least 10 seconds. WHY IT HAPPENS Often a normal response to fetal movement. NURSING RESPONSE A reassuring feature. Continue routine assessment of the whole tracing and the clinical situation. Acceleration = reassuring feature Reveal pattern 4 Read the whole tracing. These simplified examples teach timing. Also assess baseline, variability, recurrence, cont

VEAL CHOP is a memory aid, not a complete interpretation system. Early decelerations alone do not require resuscitation or an automatic vaginal exam. Accelerations are reassuring but do not replace assessment of the full tracing. 🧠 Explore and quiz yourself on fetal heart patterns 🖼️ Open readable diagram &

entries.h: 🚨 Late decelerations — read the tracing, then resuscitate in utero
entries.t: Read the whole tracing first: baseline, variability, accels and decels, contractions, the trend and the NICHD category. Then match the response to the cause — there is no fixed order , and several happen at once. Reposition — side-lying, left or right, whichever improves the tracing Stop or reduce oxytocin if it is running IV fluid bolus ; treat maternal hypotension Cervical exam — rule out cord prolapse or rapid descent Notify the provider early — in parallel, not last. Category III → prepare for expedited deliver

Before: IV fluid bolus to prevent the drop in blood pressure, and empty the bladder. After: blood pressure every 5 minutes at first. The commonest complication is maternal hypotension , which causes fetal bradycardia. If BP drops: left side, IV fluids, oxygen, notify. Ephedrine if ordered. Assess bladder regularly - she cannot feel it full, and a distended bladder stalls labor.

entries.h: 💉 Epidural — what the nurse does · more
entries.t: Reassuring FHR : baseline 110–160 bpm with moderate variability of 6–25 bpm . VEAL CHOP : V ariable → C ord compression · E arly → H ead compression · A ccelerations → O K · L ate → P lacental insufficiency. Early decelerations = head compression. Benign and normal in labor — verify with a cervical exam . No oxygen, no repositioning, no cesarean. Late decelerations = uteroplacental insufficiency. Read the whole tracing, then resuscitate in utero, matched to the cause — no fixed order: reposition (lateral, either si

entries.h: 💉 Epidural — what the nurse does · more · more
entries.t: Epidural sequence : IV fluid bolus first to prevent hypotension → frequent maternal BP and FHR → keep her off her back → she stays in bed. Post-epidural priority is maternal BP and fetal heart rate — maternal hypotension causes fetal bradycardia. BP 88/50 at 30 minutes = act now : reposition, IV fluids, notify. Mild itching and pelvic pressure are expected. No ambulation immediately after an epidural — motor block, fall risk. Epidural complications: hypotension, fetal bradycardia, urinary retention, post-dural punc
Covered by ch. 13 & 12 .

entries.h: 📕 From your ATI review book · more
entries.t: Tachycardia and bradycardia require 10 minutes or more at the abnormal rate — not a passing dip. Variability tiers : absent · minimal ≤5 · moderate 6–25 , the goal · marked >25 . Category I needs ALL of : baseline 110–160, moderate variability, no late or variable decelerations. Category III is a sinusoidal pattern, or absent variability plus recurrent lates, recurrent variables, or bradycardia. Everything else is Category II. Late deceleration response — matched to the cause, not a fixed order: side-lying · stop t

entries.h: 📕 From your ATI review book · more · more
entries.t: Amnioinfusion treats VARIABLE decelerations from cord compression and oligohydramnios. Membranes must already be ruptured. Weigh pads to confirm return and prevent overdistention. Uterine tachysystole = more than 5 contractions in 10 min → terbutaline 0.25 mg subcut. Internal monitoring is the only way to measure true contraction intensity — needs ruptured membranes, 2–3 cm , and a descended presenting part. Epidural: IV fluid bolus FIRST. If hypotension develops — reposition laterally, increase fluids, oxygen, and

entries.h: 📕 From your ATI review book · more · more · more
entries.t: Spinal block → higher rate of postdural puncture headache ; definitive treatment is an autologous blood patch . Pudendal block goes in 10–20 min before birth for perineal anesthesia, with no systemic maternal or fetal effect. Hyperventilation from patterned breathing → tingling fingers, lightheaded. Breathe into cupped hands or a paper bag — not oxygen . Effleurage is abdominal and will not touch OP back pain — that needs sacral counterpressure and hands-and-knees. Before general anesthesia: NPO confirmed, oral ant

Pillitteri, Maternal and Child Health Nursing — ch. 15–16 (labor, and comfort during labor). Fetal heart tones are heard best over the fetal back , which is why Leopold's maneuvers come before placing the monitor.

Absent variability is the finding that should scare you , even with a normal baseline. Moderate variability is reassuring. Early vs late decel is the single highest-yield discrimination in this course. Early → do nothing but confirm. Late → act.
Built from this page's own content — the same four questions every time, so the shape is familiar before the topic is.

Baseline 110–160 bpm between contractions. Variability — the normal jitter. Moderate (6–25 bpm) is the single best sign of good oxygenation. Accelerations — reassuring, and they mean the same thing as moderate variability. Decelerations — classified by their timing against the contraction, not their depth.

V ariable → C ord compression. Abrupt, any time. E arly → H ead compression. Mirrors the contraction. Benign. A ccelerations → O kay. L ate → P lacental insufficiency. Begins after the contraction starts and recovers after it ends. The dangerous one.

Early is in step with the contraction; late lags behind it. Shape tells you the cause. Lates are shallow and unimpressive, which is exactly why they get missed. Absent variability is worrying even on a flat, peaceful-looking strip. Flat is not calm. Category I is reassuring, Category III requires immediate action.

entries.h: 🩺 Intrauterine resuscitation, matched to the cause
entries.t: Reposition to either side — fast and free. Stop the oxytocin if it is running. IV fluid bolus to raise placental perfusion. Oxygen only for maternal hypoxia or per protocol — not routine. Notify the provider early, alongside the rest. There is no fixed order.

This chapter reviews the sources and phases of labor pain, the gate-control theory behind nonpharmacological comfort measures, and pharmacological options from analgesics to regional and general anesthesia, plus nursing safety priorities for each.

From this module — built from the notes above on this page, not a section of the ATI chapter. Childbirth education and a known support person reduce reported pain and the need for analgesia. Offer non-pharmacological methods first and continuously , not only until the epidural. Hydrotherapy, position change, counter-pressure, massage, breathing and heat all have evidence behind them. Ask what she wants before labor and again in labor — and honor a change of mind without comment.

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2024 . Absolute contraindications to epidural anesthesia include patient refusal, infection at the injection site, and increased intracranial pressure. Uncorrected coagulopathy or therapeutic anticoagulation are relative contraindications to epidural placement. Hemodynamic instability and inability to hold the required positioning are additional relative contraindications. StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf) · Epidural Anesthesia · open the source →

First stage pain is visceral — dull, diffuse, felt over the lower abdomen and back. Second stage pain is somatic — sharp, well localized to the perineum. After an epidural, expect warmth and heaviness in the legs and loss of the urge to void. Hypotension after an epidural is expected enough to plan for, but never accepted — fluid, left-lateral position, and notify anesthesia. Expect maternal pruritus and occasional nausea with epidural opioids.

Platelet count before a regional block — thrombocytopenia is a contraindication. Coagulation studies where clotting is in question. No routine labs for non-pharmacological methods. Blood glucose if she has been fasting for a long labor.

Pain assessment is the procedure — a numeric scale, plus what she looks like between contractions. Continuous fetal monitoring after regional analgesia , because of the hypotension risk. Blood pressure every 5 minutes for the first 15–20 minutes after an epidural is dosed. Assess bladder fullness regularly — she will not feel it.

Epidural/spinal opioids (e.g., fentanyl, sufentanil) give analgesia while preserving sensation and the ability to bear down Epidural block : bupivacaine plus an opioid at the L4-L5 level blocks pain from umbilicus to thighs but may spare pressure sensation Give an IV fluid bolus before/with epidural placement to offset hypotension; position the client side-lying Watch epidural clients for hypotension, fetal bradycardia, and respiratory depression; keep O2 and suction ready Treat epidural hypotension with lateral po

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2024 . Labor epidurals typically combine a local anesthetic, such as bupivacaine or ropivacaine, with an opioid like fentanyl or sufentanil. A 3 mL test dose of 1.5% lidocaine with 1:200,000 epinephrine is commonly given before the full epidural dose. StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf) · Epidural Anesthesia · open the source →

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2024 . Standard American Society of Anesthesiologists monitoring equipment is applied before epidural placement begins. The patient is positioned in spinal flexion, either sitting or side-lying, to open the spaces between vertebrae for needle placement. Intravenous fluids are typically given before epidural placement to help prevent hypotensive episodes. StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf) · Epidural Anesthesia · open the source →

Opioids and sedatives cause drowsiness - client should request help with ambulation Sedatives are avoided when birth is imminent but can ease anxiety and promote sleep in early/latent labor Do not give sedatives if birth is expected within 12-24 hr due to neonatal respiratory depression risk Nitrous oxide is self-administered, intermittent, and reduces (not eliminates) pain; onset and clearance are rapid with no tissue buildup Metoclopramide controls nausea/vomiting as an opioid adjunct but does not relieve pain; c

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2024 . Epidural catheter placement requires a qualified clinician, typically an anesthesiologist or a nurse anesthetist. Safe epidural use relies on an interprofessional team of anesthesia clinicians, specialty-trained nurses, and pharmacists working together. StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf) · Epidural Anesthesia · open the source →

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2024 . Hypotension is a common complication of epidural anesthesia, one reason IV fluids are given beforehand. Postdural puncture headache can occur if the dura is unintentionally punctured during placement. Accidental intrathecal injection can cause total spinal anesthesia, a rare but serious complication. Epidural hematoma, abscess, and nerve injury are rare but serious complications requiring prompt recognition. StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf) · Epidural Anesthesia ·

ATI Active Learning Template — System Disorder Fetal Assessment During Labor Filled from ATI chapter 13 , row by row from that chapter’s own sections — 12 of 12 rows have content.

Covers assessing fetal well-being during labor using Leopold maneuvers to palpate lie, presentation, and descent, plus fetal heart rate and uterine contraction monitoring methods and how to interpret the tracings.

Explain what the monitor is showing — an unexplained tracing is frightening and the fear is avoidable. Intermittent auscultation is appropriate in low-risk labor and allows more movement. Encourage position changes; left lateral maximizes placental perfusion. Maintain hydration and avoid the supine position.

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2024 . Roughly 85% of US births now involve continuous electronic monitoring rather than intermittent listening alone. Maternal factors favoring continuous monitoring include chronic hypertension, diabetes, and obesity. Fetal and obstetric factors favoring continuous monitoring include growth restriction, decreased fetal movement, multiple gestation, and postterm pregnancy. StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf) · Fetal Heart Rate Tracing: Assessment and Clinical Interpretatio

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2024 . A normal fetal heart rate baseline falls between 110 and 160 beats per minute. Moderate variability, an amplitude range of 6 to 25 bpm , is considered reassuring; minimal variability is 5 bpm or less. An acceleration at or after 32 weeks peaks at least 15 bpm above baseline and lasts at least 15 seconds . Variable decelerations drop abruptly, with onset to lowest point in less than 30 seconds , a decrease of at least 15 bpm lasting at least 15 seconds .

No routine labs — assessment is the tracing itself. Cord blood gases after birth when the tracing was concerning, to document acid-base status. Maternal CBC and type and screen if operative birth becomes likely. Lactate or glucose if maternal exhaustion or ketosis is suspected.

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2024 . A Category I tracing is the reassuring pattern: a baseline within normal limits, moderate variability, and an absence of late or variable dips. Category II tracings are indeterminate, meaning they meet criteria for neither Category I nor Category III. Category III tracings are abnormal, showing absent variability with recurrent late or variable decelerations, bradycardia, or a sinusoidal pattern.

Leopold maneuvers : four external palpations to find fetal lie, presentation, descent, and back position. Cephalic presentation: fetal heart tones heard below umbilicus; breech: heard above umbilicus. Auscultation frequency: latent phase < 4cm hourly, 4-5cm q 15-30 min ; active phase q 15-30 min ; second stage q 5-15 min . Normal FHR baseline 110-160/min ; tachycardia and bradycardia are each defined as lasting 10 min or longer. Variability: absent is nonreassuring; minimal ≤ 5/min ; moderate 6-25/min (expected); m

The first response to a non-reassuring tracing is usually to stop the oxytocin , not to give something. IV fluid bolus to improve placental perfusion. Oxygen only for maternal hypoxia or per protocol — not routine. Terbutaline to relax the uterus in tachysystole. Ephedrine or phenylephrine, given by anesthesia, for hypotension after a block.

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2024 . For a nonreassuring tracing, first reposition the mother laterally, to either side, to improve uteroplacental blood flow. Supplemental oxygen to the mother was long a standard intervention for a nonreassuring pattern; ACOG’s 2025 guidance now reserves it for maternal hypoxia or unit protocol. Discontinuing oxytocin or cervical ripening agents reduces uterine activity that may be compromising fetal oxygenation. Amnioinfusion can relieve variable decelerations

Teach that accelerations are reassuring and that early decelerations are normal head compression . VEAL CHOP: Variable–Cord, Early–Head, Acceleration–OK, Late–Placenta. Explain why she is being repositioned, rather than repositioning her silently. Explain that the monitor tracks the baby’s response to labor, not a score of how she is doing.

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2024 . Nurses provide continuous monitoring, early recognition of abnormal patterns, and prompt communication of concerns to the team. Pharmacists contribute by helping optimize oxytocin adjustments and tocolytic medication use. Neonatal specialists prepare for possible resuscitation when a concerning fetal heart rate pattern persists.

Risk of misreading FHR tracings, leading to delayed recognition of fetal compromise. Internal monitoring carries risk of maternal or fetal infection. Scalp electrode or IUPC placement can cause fetal trauma if inserted or migrated improperly. Supine positioning during internal monitor placement can cause maternal hypotension.

Your slides (Pillitteri ch. 15, p. 17) use these cut-offs; ATI gives latent 0–5 cm and active 6–10 cm. The phase is set by the cervix , not by how painful she says it i

Bleeding in early pregnancy is sorted by where the pregnancy is and whether the cervix is open. Those two facts separate almost all of them. entries.t: A complete mole generally lacks fetal tissue; a partial mole may include fetal tissue. Both need specialist follow-up for persistent gestational trophoblastic disease. The risk is higher after a complete mole; persistent disease is not synonymous with choriocarcinoma.

Any vaginal bleeding in pregnancy is serious until proven otherwise , and the visible amount can badly understate the real loss because bleeding may be concealed internally. Miscarriage is loss before 20 weeks , most often from a chromosomal abnormality — worth saying to a parent who assumes she caused it. Covers infertility evaluation and care for people unable to conceive after 6 to 12 months , including causes, diagnostic workup, assisted reproductive technologies, genetic counseling, and psychosocial support for fertility-related grief and treatment decisions.

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from NICHD . Losing just 5% of body weight can meaningfully raise the odds of ovulation in women who have PCOS. Avoiding tobacco, heavy alcohol use, and illegal drugs protects fertility in both female and male partners. Limiting exposure to known reproductive toxins, such as certain pesticides and industrial chemicals, is advised to protect fertility. Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development · What lifestyle and environmental factors may be inv

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from NICHD . Both obesity and being underweight impair ovulation and reduce the chance of conception in women. In men, obesity is linked to lower sperm count, and high blood pressure can alter sperm shape. Radiation therapy and chemotherapy can cause infertility in either partner, depending on dose and treatment site. NICHD · What lifestyle and environmental factors may be involved with infertility in females and males? · open the source →

From this module — built from the notes above on this page, not a section of the ATI chapter. Infertility is a diagnosis of time : no conception after 12 months of unprotected sex, or 6 months if she is over 35. Expected on examination: often entirely normal findings in both partners — which is itself distressing and needs naming. Irregular or absent periods point toward an ovulation problem; PCOS commonly adds acne, hirsutism and weight gain. Painful periods and pain with intercourse suggest endometriosis . Expect

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from NICHD . A progesterone blood level drawn around day 23 of the cycle helps confirm that ovulation occurred. FSH and AMH blood tests estimate how many eggs remain in a woman's ovarian reserve. Semen analysis requires the male partner to avoid ejaculation for about 48 hours before the sample. NICHD · How is infertility diagnosed? · open the source →

Pelvic exam checks for uterine or vaginal structural anomalies. Hormone panel : prolactin, FSH, LH, estradiol, progesterone, and thyroid levels assess the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis. Postcoital test evaluates coital technique and how sperm interact with cervical mucus. Ultrasound (transvaginal or abdominal) visualizes the reproductive organs. Hysterosalpingography : dye study confirms tubal patency; screen for iodine or shellfish allergy beforehand.

Recognize infertility as a major life stressor; encourage clients to voice their feelings. Explain the roles of the genetic counselor, reproductive specialist, geneticist, and pharmacist. Monitor for adverse effects of fertility medications. Warn that ART significantly raises the odds of a high-risk multiple gestation pregnancy. Share info on ART options and alternatives such as adoption. Refer clients to grief and infertility support groups. Recommend genetic counseling when there's a family history of inherited d

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from NICHD . Clomiphene citrate triggers ovulation in about 80% of users, with roughly half going on to conceive. Clomiphene carries about a 10% chance of twins, with higher-order multiples occurring in under 1% of cases. Injectable gonadotropins stimulate egg growth directly but carry a multiple-birth rate near 30% , higher than clomiphene. Letrozole lowers estrogen production to trigger ovulation and may work better than clomiphene for PCOS-related infertility. NICHD · Fertility T

Clomiphene citrate and letrozole stimulate ovarian follicle production. Metformin supports ovulation; exogenous progesterone primes the endometrium for implantation. IUI : prepared sperm is placed directly into the uterus at ovulation. IVF-ET : eggs are retrieved, fertilized in the lab, and the embryo is transferred to the uterus. Gamete intrafallopian transfer : retrieved oocytes and motile sperm are injected together into the fallopian tube via laparoscopy. Donor oocyte : donor eggs are fertilized via IVF after t

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from NICHD . Instruct male partners to abstain from ejaculation for about 48 hours before providing a semen sample. Explain that more than one semen sample may be needed because sperm production varies over time. Gonadotropin injections typically run 7 to 12 days and require ultrasound monitoring of egg growth. NICHD · How is infertility diagnosed?; Fertility Treatments for Females · open the source →

Reproductive endocrinologist leads the workup and any assisted reproduction. Genetic counselor for recurrent loss, known carrier status, or maternal age over 35. Mental health — infertility care has a high dropout rate, and distress is the usual reason. Pharmacist for injection teaching and the ovulation-induction schedule. Financial counselor — treatment cost drives more decisions than clinicians tend to realize.

Ectopic pregnancy : ovum implants outside the uterus, often from endometrial tissue or adhesions in the tube. As an ectopic pregnancy grows, tube rupture can cause severe bleeding requiring surgical removal. Unruptured ectopic pregnancy is treated with surgical removal or methotrexate to dissolve it. Losing the tube from ectopic pregnancy raises risk of recurrence and future infertility. ART raises the incidence of multiple gestation, adding risk for the client and each fetus.

This chapter explains why any vaginal bleeding in pregnancy needs urgent evaluation. It covers early causes—miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, and molar pregnancy—and later causes—placenta previa, abruption, and vasa previa—along with their distinguishing signs, testing, and nursing priorities.

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2024 . Encouraging smoking cessation and cocaine avoidance is advised because both are modifiable risk factors for placental abruption. Getting a pregnant patient's blood pressure under control is linked to fewer cases of abruption overall. StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf) · Placental Abruption · open the source →

Laboratory and blood bank personnel are essential team members for rapid type-and-cross and transfusion support during hemorrhage. Preeclampsia is a whole-body vascular disease, not just a blood pressure number. Vessels constrict and leak, so every organ gets less blood and fluid moves into tissue. Chronic hypertension begins before pregnancy or before 20 weeks. Gestational hypertension develops after 20 weeks without preeclampsia findings. Preeclampsia adds proteinuria or qualifying organ dysfunction; severe features can occur without proteinuria. Severe-range pressure or organ symptoms require prompt escalation.

entries.h: 🚨 The three symptoms that mean a seizure is coming
entries.t: Severe headache unrelieved by acetaminophen Visual changes — blurring, spots, flashing lights Right upper quadrant / epigastric pain — liver capsule stretch Epigastric pain in preeclampsia is not indigestion. It is a late and ominous sign of impending eclampsia.

entries.h: ⭐ Magnesium sulfate — what it is actually for
entries.t: Magnesium prevents seizures. It is not an antihypertensive. That distinction is worth marks on its own. Therapeutic range 4–7 mEq/L Serum magnesium — and what is lost first mEq/L 4–7 therapeutic >8 reflexes lost >12 respiratory arrest

entries.h: 🔴 Monitoring magnesium — in the order they disappear
entries.t: Check Toxicity sign Deep tendon reflexes Absent or depressed reflexes: an important toxicity warning Respiratory rate <12/min — hold the infusion Urine output <30 mL/hr — magnesium is renally cleared Level of consciousness Lethargy, slurred speech Antidote: calcium gluconate — keep it at the bedside. Assess reflexes, respiratory status, urine output and mental status together. Suspected magnesium toxicity requires immediate action; do not wait for a fixed sequence of findings.

H aemolysis · E levated L iver enzymes · L ow P latelets. A severe variant of preeclampsia — and it can occur with only mildly raised blood pressure, which is what makes it dangerous.

Preeclampsia is new hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria OR qualifying organ dysfunction. Proteinuria is not required when qualifying severe features are present; edema alone is not diagnostic.

entries.t: Flushing, sweating, warmth, weakness and drowsiness are EXPECTED , not toxicity. Reduced FHR variability is an expected drug effect too. Pregnancy-compatible antihypertensives may include labetalol, nifedipine or hydralazine according to the indication and order. ACE inhibitors/ARBs are generally avoided. Magnesium may be prescribed alongside antihypertensive treatment with appropriate monitoring; it is not itself the blood-pressure treatment.

ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated. Use labetalol, hydralazine, nifedipine, methyldopa — and never combine magnesium with nifedipine . Magnesium doubles as a tocolytic and as fetal neuroprotection before 32 weeks . Low-dose aspirin from late first trimester for prior early-onset preeclampsia or chronic hypertension.

entries.h: 📝 Prof. Buhler’s Week 9 summary — sudden pregnancy complications
entries.t: Her own wrap-up for the week, posted in Canvas. Critical conditions that need prompt recognition and intervention to protect both maternal and fetal health.

Assess bleeding across trimesters and recognize the signs of hypovolemic shock . Bleeding during pregnancy is not normal and potentially serious; it needs to be investigated. Causes are grouped by the trimester they most commonly occur in — but any of them can happen at any time. First trimester Spontaneous abortion (miscarriage) — types: threatened, inevitable, incomplete, complete, missed and septic. Know each presentation and its nursing care. Ectopic pregnancy — symptoms, risk factors and emergency management,

Rare but life-threatening. Know the signs, the lab findings and the nursing priorities. Bleeding uses up the clotting factors, so the blood can no longer clot. Obstetric complications linked to DIC: sepsis , peripartum hemorrhage , placental abruption , and severe hypertensive disorders — preeclampsia with severe features and HELLP syndrome .

Labor between 20 weeks and 36 weeks 6 days of gestation. Risk factors: infection, dehydration, previous preterm labor, smoking, no prenatal care, preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM), partner violence, and accident or injury to the pregnant client. Nursing care: treat the underlying cause (infection, dehydration…), activity restriction, and medications: Tocolytics stop uterine contractions; the most common one used is terbutaline . Betamethasone — a steroid given IM to the mother — matures the baby’s lung

See table 21.6 in your textbook for how each one differs. Chronic hypertension · gestational hypertension · preeclampsia without severe features · preeclampsia with severe features · eclampsia. Know the pathophysiology, warning signs and treatment, including magnesium sulfate and antihypertensives . HELLP syndrome is a complication of preeclampsia in which liver function is affected: H emolysis, E levated L iver enzymes (ALT and AST), L ow P latelets (below 100,000 — thrombocytopenia). Treatment depends on how far
Oligohydramnios vs polyhydramnios — think fetal renal problems (too little) vs fetal GI problems (too much).

Can happen when an Rh-negative mother’s blood meets Rh-positive blood from the embryo or fetus. The mother makes antibodies against the fetal Rh-positive antigens on the fetal red cells. RhoGAM (Rh immune globulin) is an antibody given to the mother by injection: at 28 weeks of gestation; within 72 hours of birth if the baby is Rh positive; any time the blood may mix — invasive procedures, abortion, ectopic pregnancy, amniocentesis, miscarriage/D&C. Because the antibody is already present, her body does not make it

Monozygotic (identical) : one egg and one sperm that split into two identical embryos. Higher risk of complications such as twin-to-twin transfusion , because the placenta is shared. Dizygotic (fraternal) : two eggs and two sperm; the same or different sexes; each embryo has its own placenta.
Early recognition and intervention can save lives. Communication, assessment and patient education are vital. Nurses must be ready to respond to rapidly changing conditions.

This chapter reviews pregnancy complications beyond bleeding: cervical insufficiency, hyperemesis gravidarum, iron-deficiency anemia, gestational diabetes, and gestational hypertensive disorders—covering risk factors, key labs, medications, and nursing priorities needed to protect mother and fetus.

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2024 . For pregestational diabetes, achieving an A1C below 6.5% before conception is the American Diabetes Association's recommended target. No clearly safe A1C threshold exists; congenital anomaly risk rises progressively as preconception glycemic control worsens. At an A1C around 10% , congenital anomaly rates run about 10% ; near an A1C of 13% , rates climb to about 20% . Preconception glycemic surveillance is considered the most effective way to prevent diabetic

In-utero DES exposure (banned after 1971) raises cervical insufficiency risk A history of cervical trauma or an early pregnancy loss raises insufficiency risk Multifetal gestation and gestational trophoblastic disease raise hyperemesis risk A history of migraines or family hyperemesis raises risk of recurrence Type 1 diabetes and hyperthyroidism raise hyperemesis risk A short gap between pregnancies or heavy pre-pregnancy menses raises anemia risk Obesity and maternal age over 25 years raise GDM risk A prior macros

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2024 . Maternal echocardiography helps evaluate structural and functional cardiac status in pregnant patients with known or suspected heart disease. A 12-lead ECG and maternal BNP level are used alongside CBC and CMP to assess cardiac disease severity in pregnancy. StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf) · Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy · open the source →

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2024 . Pregnancy with cardiac disease requires coordinated care among high-risk obstetricians, cardiologists, and perinatologists. Pharmacists play a distinct role in managing cardiac medications during pregnancy since many drugs can harm the fetus. Nurses are highlighted for their role in early recognition of worsening cardiac disease states in pregnant patients. StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf) · Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy · open the source →

Preterm labor — contractions with cervical change between 20 and 36 6/7 weeks — together with membrane rupture before labor starts (PROM) and the preterm form (PPROM). Focus: spotting who is at risk, what to monitor, and what protects mother and fetus.

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2024 . Vaginal progesterone is recommended for patients with a shortened cervix under 25 mm , even without a prior preterm birth. Standard progesterone dosing is a single daily 90 mg 8% intravaginal gel, or a 200 mg micronized vaginal capsule. Combining cerclage with vaginal progesterone appears more effective at preventing preterm birth than either intervention alone. Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2024 . For a history-indicated cerclage, clinicians usually place the stitch around 12 to 14 weeks gestation, before problems arise. Exam-indicated cerclage is considered before 28 weeks when the cervix is dilated 1 to 4 cm without labor. The McDonald technique, a purse-string suture around the cervix, is generally preferred for its simpler placement and removal. The stitch is usually taken out around 36 to 37 weeks gestation once the pregnancy nears term. StatPearl

Change positions slowly, supine to upright; sit until dizziness resolves (nifedipine) Keep well hydrated to offset nifedipine-related hypotension Magnesium sulfate is a CNS-depressant tocolytic; may add fetal neuroprotection if given before 32 weeks gestation Perform daily fetal kick counts; report contractions to the nurse Stay on bed rest with bathroom privileges only

entries.t: Toxicity appears in this order : loss of patellar reflexes → urine output <30 mL/hr → respirations <12/min → decreased LOC → dysrhythmias. Stop the infusion FIRST , then calcium gluconate, then respiratory support.

During magnesium therapy monitor breathing, reflexes, urine output, mental status and ordered levels together. Reduced renal clearance increases toxicity risk. If toxicity is suspected, stop the infusion, call for help and support breathing; administer calcium gluconate as ordered.
Preeclampsia is defined by two findings: hypertension and proteinuria. Edema is common but is not part of the definition.

Preeclampsia is new hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria OR qualifying organ dysfunction. Proteinuria is not required when qualifying severe features are present; edema alone is not diagnostic.

entries.t: Slides 3–5 · Answer slide 14 Objective or subjective? Measured findings, such as blood pressure, urine protein and fetal heart rate, are objective. Breathlessness, fatigue and reduced fetal movement reported by the patient are subjective. What is the covered word? Orthopnea means breathlessness when lying flat. It usually points toward pulmonary congestion on the left side of the heart. Dependent edema and distended neck veins suggest systemic venous congestion. CDC · Urgent maternal warning signs · Existing Chapte

Slides 6–8 · Answer slide 15 How does care change around birth? Balance activity and rest, review medicines and nutrition, and assess for infection. During labor, avoid prolonged supine positioning. After birth, reassess breathing and fluid balance as blood returns to the circulation. What suggests an upper urinary infection? Fever with flank pain or costovertebral-angle tenderness suggests pyelonephritis. Ask about urinary symptoms; assess vital signs and urine output and obtain ordered urine studies. Escalate pro

entries.h: Screening and diagnosis of gestational diabetes
entries.t: Slides 9–12 · Answer slide 16 What changes during pregnancy? Placental hormones increase insulin resistance. If insulin production cannot compensate, maternal glucose rises. Maternal glucose crosses the placenta; excess fetal insulin may promote excessive growth. Does the 1-hour screen diagnose GDM? No. In the course’s two-step protocol, a 50-g screen of 140 mg/dL or higher leads to a fasting 100-g test. Diagnostic cutoffs are 95 fasting, 180 at 1 hour, 155 at 2 hours and 140 at 3 hours (mg/dL). At least two values

Slide 13 · Answer slide 17 What is the daily plan? Individualize meals and activity, teach glucose monitoring, and use prescribed medication when needed. Monitor fetal growth and well-being as ordered; report reduced fetal movement promptly. What changes after delivery? Insulin needs fall quickly after delivery. Reassess doses with the team. Arrange postpartum glucose testing at 4–12 weeks and ongoing screening for type 2 diabetes. ACOG · Gestational diabetes · Existing Chapter 20 study key

entries.t: Slide 4 · Answer slide 19 Why can implantation occur in the tube? Damage or impaired movement in a fallopian tube can delay the fertilized egg. Risk factors include previous ectopic pregnancy, tubal surgery and prior pelvic infection. An ectopic pregnancy can also occur without known risk factors. Which finding changes the priority? New severe pain, shoulder pain, faintness or signs of shock can indicate rupture. Obtain urgent obstetric help; instability requires emergency management rather than expectant care. ACO

Slides 13–14 · Answer slide 20 Which medications treat which problem? Magnesium sulfate prevents or treats eclamptic seizures. Severe hypertension requires prompt prescribed antihypertensive therapy, such as labetalol, hydralazine or immediate-release oral nifedipine. What does the nurse monitor? Assess respiratory rate, reflexes, level of consciousness and urine output during magnesium therapy. Suspected toxicity: stop the infusion, get help and prepare prescribed calcium gluconate. Delivery treats the underlying

Slides 16–17 · Answer slide 21 Fraternal versus identical? Fraternal twins come from two eggs fertilized separately; identical twins arise from one fertilized egg that divides. How do renal and GI disorders change fluid? Fetal urine contributes to amniotic fluid. Absent kidneys or obstructed urinary outflow can reduce it (oligohydramnios). Impaired fetal swallowing, as with esophageal atresia, can increase it (polyhydramnios). Neither finding establishes a single cause. SMFM · Polyhydramnios · ISUOG · Oligohydramni

Slide 6 · first stage · Answer slide 22 Can an unripe cervix slow induction? Yes. An unfavorable cervix may need ripening and more time. Slow early dilation alone does not establish active-phase arrest. Does an early epidural cause labor arrest? Timing alone does not establish the cause. Assess cervical change, contraction adequacy and fetal position. ACOG notes that neuraxial analgesia may be offered at any stage of labor. ACOG · First and second stage labor management

Slide 6 · second stage · Answer slide 23 What does OP mean? Occiput posterior: the back of the fetal head faces the mother’s back. Persistent OP can delay rotation and descent, prolong pushing and cause back pain. What is CPD? Cephalopelvic disproportion is a mismatch between the fetal presenting part and the maternal pelvis. Persistent lack of descent despite adequate contractions and pushing prompts assessment for position, fit and the safest route of birth. ACOG · First and second stage labor management

Slides 13–15 · Answer slide 24 Cord prolapse: what relieves compression? Call for help and use a gloved hand to elevate the presenting part off the cord while the team prepares urgent birth. Position to relieve pressure; follow the course emergency protocol for oxygen. Avoid handling the cord. Head delivered, shoulders do not follow: what next? Recognize shoulder dystocia. Call for help and assist with McRoberts positioning and directed suprapubic pressure. Do not apply fundal pressure. RCOG · Umbilical cord prolap

entries.t: Slides 2–5 · Answer slide 8 What comes first after amniotomy? Assess fetal heart rate immediately and compare it with the baseline. Sudden bradycardia or recurrent variable decelerations can indicate cord compression or prolapse. Assess the fluid’s color, amount and odor. What do the internal monitors measure? A fetal scalp electrode records fetal heart rate. An intrauterine pressure catheter measures contraction strength and resting tone. An acceleration after scalp stimulation is reassuring; its absence alone doe

Slides 6–7 · Answer slide 9 Classical versus low transverse? Classical describes a vertical incision in the upper uterus. A low transverse incision crosses the lower uterine segment and carries a lower risk of rupture in a later labor. The skin scar does not tell you which uterine incision was used. What are the maternal and newborn risks? Maternal: hemorrhage, infection, thromboembolism, and injury to nearby organs.
