Structural connection An opening links chambers or great vessels. Pressure gradient The gradient influences shunt direction and volume. Circulatory effect Pulmonary flow, chamber workload or oxygenation changes. ASD and VSD Openings in atrial or ventricular septa can create left-to-right flow after birth. PDA Persistent connection between aorta and pulmonary artery changes flow after birth. AV septal defect Septal and atrioventricular valve anatomy are affected.

Sort congenital heart defects by whether blood shunts the wrong way, and which way. Left-to-right = too much lung blood = heart failure. Right-to-left = blue baby. Group Blood goes Result Examples Acyanotic Left → right Pulmonary overload, heart failure , poor feeding, sweating ASD, VSD, PDA , coarctation Cyanotic Right → left Deoxygenated blood to the body — cyanosis Tetralogy of Fallot , transposition

P ulmonary stenosis R ight ventricular hypertrophy O verriding aorta V SD PROV. The classic sign is the “tet spell” — sudden deep cyanosis during crying or feeding. For a tet spell, put the infant in KNEE-CHEST position immediately. It raises systemic resistance and pushes blood back through the lungs. 🧒 Picture + mnemonic: Tetralogy of Fallot →

entries.h: ⭐ Heart failure in an infant looks like feeding trouble
entries.t: Sweating with feeds and tiring after a few minutes Poor weight gain — often the earliest sign Tachypnea, tachycardia at rest Hepatomegaly — the pediatric equivalent of peripheral edema Nursing care: small frequent feeds , higher-calorie formula, cluster care to allow rest. 🧒 Picture + mnemonic: Pediatric heart failure →

Count the apical pulse for a full minute before every dose. Hold and report if <90–110 in an infant or <70 in a child . Early toxicity in a child is usually vomiting and bradycardia , not visual changes. Never repeat a dose that was vomited, and never mix digoxin into a bottle of formula - if the feed is not finished, the dose is unknown.

Fever ≥5 days plus red eyes, strawberry tongue, cracked lips, rash, swollen red hands and feet with later peeling. It causes coronary artery aneurysms , so treatment is IVIG plus aspirin — the one situation where a child is given aspirin. 🧒 Picture + mnemonic: Kawasaki disease →

entries.h: PICC lines: parent teaching & nursing care
entries.t: PICC = peripherally inserted central catheter. A long, flexible IV catheter enters a peripheral vein, usually in the arm, and its tip ends in a large central vein near the heart. The answer in your question: “The PICC line will last several weeks with proper care.” For this endocarditis question, remember the course teaching of 2–6 weeks of IV antibiotics . The prescribed duration depends on the organism and treatment plan. 1 · Peripheral entry Usually enters through an arm vein. 2 · Central tip Reaches a large vei

Reliable access for prolonged IV antibiotics, some other IV medications and parenteral nutrition. Some PICCs also allow blood sampling when the device and policy permit. It reduces repeated needle sticks. A short peripheral IV or a midline does not have a central tip.

An operating room is not routinely required. Trained staff may place a PICC at the bedside or in interventional radiology. Local anesthetic is used; a child may also need sedation or anesthesia. Confirm and document the approved tip position before first use, using the facility’s imaging or tip-confirmation method.

Clean hands before care. Disinfect the access connector and allow it to dry before using it; follow the taught technique. Keep the dressing sealed, clean and dry. A wet, loose or dirty dressing needs prompt attention from someone trained to change it. Protect the site during bathing; do not submerge it. Avoid swimming and activities that tug on the line. An arm board is not a routine requirement for every PICC . Follow the child’s activity and securement plan; avoid contact sports or rough play that could damage it

entries.h: Use only the prescribed care plan
entries.t: Only trained caregivers should access or flush the line. Follow the ordered solution, volume, schedule and device instructions. Never force a flush. Resistance, pain or leaking means stop and contact the care team. Do not assume every child needs the same flush volume or heparin. A syringe’s capacity is not the prescribed flush volume. Inspect the site and visible catheter regularly. Never push a displaced catheter back in.

Contact the care team promptly: fever or chills; redness, warmth, pain, swelling or drainage; a swollen arm; leakage, a crack, trouble flushing, or a change in visible catheter length. Emergency: sudden trouble breathing, chest pain, collapse or severe bleeding needs emergency help. Stop an infusion if a line problem is suspected and follow the emergency plan provided by the care team.

“Rotate every 3 days”: not for PICCs. CDC guidance also recommends replacing a child’s short peripheral IV only when clinically indicated; a 3-day rotation is not a universal pediatric rule. “Never in the operating room”: too absolute. The teaching point is that an OR is not routinely required; the setting and sedation depend on the child. “Movement is unrestricted”: too broad. Normal gentle use may be allowed, but protect the catheter and follow activity restrictions. These clarifications do not change the keyed a

Exam connection: In the question about an alert, well-perfused 4-month-old with SVT, expect a vagal maneuver first . Clinical note: Assess stability and the rhythm first. This pathway is for regular, narrow-complex supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) with a pulse . What it does: Vagal stimulation increases parasympathetic activity and slows conduction through the atrioventricular (AV) node . It may interrupt the electrical loop causing SVT. It does not stop every type of fast rhythm.

A brief cold facial stimulus can trigger a vagal response. A clinician may use an ice-cold cloth or a sealed bag of ice-water slurry, following the age-specific protocol. Protect the airway and skin. Do not block breathing or press on the eyes. Cold application and timing vary by protocol; neonatal techniques require trained staff.

Coach the child to take a breath and blow against resistance , such as an empty, needle-free 10 mL syringe, for about 10–15 seconds , as directed. A modified Valsalva adds staff-assisted repositioning to lying flat with the legs raised after the strain. Use the local protocol and assess whether the child can cooperate.

entries.h: Nursing sequence: assess → monitor → attempt → reassess
entries.t: Assess: Check airway, breathing, pulse, mental status, perfusion and blood pressure. Distinguish SVT from sinus tachycardia caused by fever, pain or dehydration; treat the underlying cause of sinus tachycardia. Monitor: Apply continuous cardiac monitoring before the maneuver; obtain a rhythm strip / 12-lead ECG when available. Explain the maneuver to the child and parent. Reassess: Check rhythm and perfusion after the attempt. If stable SVT persists, prepare adenosine per order / PALS protocol . Record the response

New altered consciousness, signs of shock or hypotension mean cardiopulmonary compromise. Activate emergency support and prepare for synchronized cardioversion . For narrow-complex SVT, the PALS algorithm also permits adenosine when IV/IO access is already available. Do not delay urgent treatment for repeated vagal attempts. No eyeball pressure or carotid sinus massage in children. Parent teaching: For a child with diagnosed SVT, use only the technique and action plan taught by the cardiology team. A fainting, hard

Fetal shunts : foramen ovale closes with the first breaths, ductus arteriosus within 2–3 days , ductus venosus shortly after birth. Failure to close produces congenital defects. Left-to-right shunts (ASD, VSD, PDA) are acyanotic — the child stays pink. Right-to-left shunts (tetralogy, tricuspid atresia, transposition) are cyanotic — blue. Ductal dependence is determined by the specific anatomy and severity. Selected cyanotic lesions and some critical obstructive systemic lesions require a patent ductus and speciali

Earlier study notes, retained for comparison with the guidance above. These notes may reflect a book edition or lecture convention; check the assigned source for exam wording. All cyanotic lesions are ductal-dependent. Prostaglandin E1 keeps the duct OPEN pre-op and needs a reliable IV; watch for apnea and hypotension. Indomethacin does the opposite and CLOSES a PDA — the only defect medication can fix. Tetralogy of Fallot : pulmonary stenosis, RV hypertrophy, VSD, overriding aorta. For a tet spell, knee-to-chest r

Coarctation : four-point BP shows high pressure and bounding pulses in the arms with weak pulses and hypotension in the legs. Digoxin : apical pulse for a full minute before the dose, give on an empty stomach, never repeat a dose after vomiting . Toxicity = nausea, vomiting, bradycardia. Heart failure in infants : tachycardia at rest, sweating with feeds , poor weight gain, hepatomegaly as the earliest sign. Infants lose weight; older children gain fluid weight. Cluster care, feed upright, higher-calorie smaller fe

An elevated ASO or other streptococcal antibody result supports preceding group A streptococcal infection; it does not by itself diagnose acute rheumatic fever. Use the Jones criteria, examination and echocardiographic assessment.

Earlier study notes, retained for comparison with the guidance above. These notes may reflect a book edition or lecture convention; check the assigned source for exam wording. Rheumatic fever follows untreated group A strep; ASO titer confirms it; carditis is the most serious criterion . SVT : vagal maneuvers first, then adenosine. Clinical note: assess stability first; urgent treatment takes priority for a compromised child. See the pediatric vagal-maneuver guide and infographic.

Covered by ch. 20 (cardiovascular disorders) . Timing of repairs is examinable. Transposition of the great arteries is switched within the first 2 weeks ; truncus arteriosus within the first month ; tetralogy of Fallot is fully repaired within the first year . Hypoplastic left heart takes three staged operations : shunt, then Glenn, then modified Fontan. Infective endocarditis is treated with IV antibiotics for 2 to 6 weeks , usually through a PICC — a family who says "seven days" has misunderstood. A PICC can rema

Kawasaki disease: low-dose aspirin continues for about 6 months after the procedure or acute phase. This is the one childhood condition where aspirin is deliberately given. High altitude worsens hypoxia in a child with a cyanotic defect and is avoided where possible.

Pillitteri, Maternal and Child Health Nursing — ch. 41 (cardiovascular). Endocarditis prophylaxis is for the high-risk group only: prosthetic valves, previous endocarditis, unrepaired cyanotic defects. Treatment is IV antibiotics for 2 to 6 weeks .

Prostaglandin E1 (opens) vs prostaglandin inhibitor (closes) is the highest-yield reversal in the whole course. Aspirin may be prescribed for Kawasaki disease and certain other pediatric indications under specialist supervision. Teach the prescribed dose, bleeding precautions and illness/vaccine instructions; do not give aspirin routinely for a child’s viral illness.

Aspirin is the exception in Kawasaki — the one place you do give it to a child. More oxygen is not the answer for cyanotic defects. Some are kept at sats of 75–85% until surgery.

Pediatric heart disease is either congenital or acquired. A congenital defect is an anatomic abnormality present from birth that usually produces heart failure and hypoxemia. Heart failure means output cannot meet the body's metabolic and physical demands. Defects group by flow pattern: increased pulmonary flow (VSD, ASD, PDA), decreased pulmonary flow (tricuspid atresia, tetralogy of Fallot), obstructed flow (aortic stenosis, pulmonary stenosis, coarctation of the aorta), and mixed flow (truncus arteriosus, transp

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from AHA, n.d. . Children with certain congenital heart defects may need antibiotic prophylaxis before dental work involving the gum tissue. A cardiologist determines whether a specific heart condition warrants prophylaxis, since not every defect requires it. Families of at-risk children are advised to carry an AHA wallet card listing the recommended antibiotic and dose. American Heart Association · Infective Endocarditis · open the source →

Maternal factors: infection, alcohol or substance use during pregnancy, diabetes mellitus Genetic factors: family history of congenital heart disease, trisomy 21, other congenital anomalies or chromosomal abnormalities Pulmonary artery hypertension can have a familial link Infective endocarditis: congenital or acquired heart disease, indwelling catheters Cardiomyopathy: genetics, infection, deficiency states, metabolic conditions, collagen disease, drug toxicity, dysrhythmias Cardiogenic shock after cardiac surgery

Increased pulmonary blood flow defects shunt blood left to right from higher to lower pressure, raising pulmonary volume and producing heart failure signs VSD: opening in the ventricular septum, loud harsh murmur at the left sternal border, heart failure; many close on their own early in life ASD: opening in the atrial septum, systolic murmur with fixed split S2, often asymptomatic PDA: fetal connection between pulmonary artery and aorta stays open — machinery-hum systolic murmur, wide pulse pressure, bounding puls

CBC, urinalysis, ABGs with pH, hemoglobin, hematocrit, electrolytes Blood cultures — positive cultures diagnose infective endocarditis Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein elevated with inflammation Throat culture for group A strep; screening is recommended for all school-age children with sore throat Antistreptolysin O titer elevated or rising is the most reliable test for rheumatic fever

Chest radiograph for cardiomegaly ECG for conduction disturbances and to evaluate heart and valve function, and to identify dysrhythmias Echocardiography, transthoracic or transesophageal, shows vegetations and pericardial effusion, and evaluates heart size and ventricular and valve function; repeat 4-6 weeks after treatment for rheumatic fever Cardiac catheterization is the gold standard Modified Jones criteria diagnose rheumatic fever — two major criteria, or one major plus two minor, after a documented strep inf

Digoxin improves myocardial contractility Diuretics such as furosemide, and afterload reducers such as ACE inhibitors, for heart failure Beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, ACE inhibitors, and anticoagulants for cardiovascular management High-dose IV anti-infectives for 2-6 weeks for infective endocarditis Rheumatic fever prophylaxis: oral penicillin V twice daily or monthly IM penicillin G; with penicillin allergy use an oral cephalosporin, clindamycin, or a macrolide; duration ranges from 5 years to lifelong

VSD: watch for spontaneous closure, diuretics, catheter-based closure, or patch repair which carries heart block risk ASD: patch closure with cardiopulmonary bypass, low-dose aspirin for 6 months after the procedure PDA: indomethacin, ibuprofen, or acetaminophen to close the duct; coil occlusion during catheterization; furosemide; neutral thermal environment; treat anemia; thoracoscopic ligation Pulmonary stenosis: balloon angioplasty or valvuloplasty during catheterization, or pulmonary valvotomy in children Aorti

entries.h: 🧠 The three questions that sort them
entries.t: Is it expected for this condition, at this point? Vomiting after a pyloromyotomy is expected. Bilious vomiting never is. Is it a trend going the wrong way? One dry nappy is nothing. None in eight hours is a direction. Does it fit a complication I already know to fear? Fever in neutropenia, rupture in appendicitis, obstruction after bowel surgery. Answer first, then justify. Pick the finding, then say which complication it points at. If you cannot name the complication, it is probably not the answer.

A 5-week-old is back on the unit after surgical repair of pyloric stenosis and has just taken a first small feed. Which finding needs follow-up? EXPECTED — A small amount of emesis after the first feed Common in the first day or two after pyloromyotomy. Feeds are advanced slowly for exactly this reason. REPORT — Green, bile-stained vomit with a distended abdomen Bile means the obstruction is below the duodenal papilla. That is not a pyloromyotomy recovery — it points at obstruction, and it is never expected at any
Non-bilious projectile vomiting at 3–6 weeks is what brought the baby in. Bilious vomiting afterwards is a different problem entirely. The colour is the cue.

An 8-month-old has had diarrhoea for two days and is on oral rehydration solution. Which finding needs follow-up? EXPECTED — Loose stools are still happening ORS replaces losses; it does not stop the diarrhoea. Continuing stools alone are not deterioration. EXPECTED — Fussy, but consolable by a parent Irritable-but-consolable sits in the mild-to-moderate band. Lethargy is the word that changes the picture. REPORT — No wet nappy for eight hours Oliguria means the kidneys are holding on to water. Expected output in a

Daily weight is the most accurate measure of fluid loss in a child — but on the shift in front of you, urine output and level of consciousness are what move first. Plain water, juice and sports drinks all make it worse.

A 10-year-old has right lower quadrant pain and is nil by mouth awaiting an appendicectomy. Which finding needs follow-up? EXPECTED — Guarding over McBurney’s point Localised tenderness with rebound is the presentation, not a complication. REPORT — The pain suddenly stops and the child says they feel better Sudden relief is not improvement — it is rupture. The distended appendix has perforated and released the pressure. Peritonitis follows. EXPECTED — Low-grade fever Expected with inflammation. A climbing fever wit
This is the one the exam loves, because relief sounds like good news. Never apply heat and never give an enema — both raise the risk of rupture.

A 6-year-old having chemotherapy has mouth ulcers and is reluctant to eat. Which finding needs follow-up? EXPECTED — Red, sore oral mucosa with small ulcers That is the mucositis itself — a known effect of treatment on fast-dividing cells. REPORT — Temperature of 38.3°C (101°F) Fever in a child who may be neutropenic is an emergency , not a symptom to monitor. Broken mucosa is an open door for bacteria straight into the blood. EXPECTED — Choosing soft, bland foods and cool fluids Sensible self-management. Avoid any
Mucositis is expected. Fever on top of it is not. The mouth is the entry point, and in neutropenia there may be no pus, no redness and no other localising sign — the fever is the whole warning.

Parents describe their 4-year-old screaming and thrashing at night. Which finding needs follow-up? EXPECTED — Episodes start about 90 minutes after falling asleep Sleep terrors come out of deep non-REM sleep in the first third of the night. Nightmares are REM and come later. EXPECTED — No memory of it the next morning Little or no recall is typical. Remembering the dream points to a nightmare instead. EXPECTED — Eyes open, inconsolable, sweating during the episode Looks awake, is not fully awake. Stay calm, keep th

Nightmare = awake + recall + reassure. Sleep terror = partial arousal + little recall + protect. Escalate if episodes injure, happen very often, wreck daytime function, or come with snoring and breathing pauses.

You take handover on four children. Which one do you see first? LATER — Post-appendicectomy day 1, wants more analgesia Real and worth doing — but pain relief on a stable post-op child is not the first stop. LATER — Gastroenteritis, tolerating ORS, two wet nappies this shift Improving. Output is happening. FIRST — Leukaemia, mucositis, temperature 38.4°C Possible neutropenic sepsis. Cultures and antibiotics are time-critical — this child cannot wait behind the others. LATER — Sleep terrors, parents want to talk abo

When several options all sound reasonable, ask which one has a complication that gets worse while you deal with the others . Infection in an immunosuppressed child is almost always that one. Causes and risk factors Tonsillar inflammation may be viral or bacterial; recurrent significant infections or obstructive tonsillar enlargement may prompt surgical evaluation. What changes in the body Inflamed lymphoid tissue causes painful swallowing and sometimes upper-airway obstruction; surgery leaves a vascular wound with bleeding risk. Diagnostic evaluation Assess airway, hydration and infection findings, test for group A strep when indicated, and evaluate obstructive symptoms before a planned tonsillectomy.

Causes and risk factors Viral infection, commonly parainfluenza, most often causes croup in toddlers and preschool-aged children. entries.h: The child with a cardiac disorder
entries.t: Given anatomy and perfusion findings, explain the circulation problem, select a nursing plan for oxygenation/perfusion and growth, identify deterioration and evaluate the response and family readiness for home care.

Causes and risk factors Catheterization is a diagnostic or interventional procedure for selected structural/hemodynamic problems; bleeding, thrombosis, dysrhythmia and contrast reactions are procedure risks. What changes in the body A vascular catheter reaches the heart to measure pressures/oxygen content or perform an intervention such as device closure or balloon dilation. Diagnostic evaluation Before the procedure verify consent, baseline rhythm/vitals and distal perfusion, prior contrast reactions and ordered l

Causes and risk factors Congenital structural abnormalities arise during fetal development; genetic syndromes, family history and some maternal conditions contribute, although many causes are unknown. What changes in the body Classify the actual anatomy as increased pulmonary flow, obstructed flow, decreased pulmonary flow or parallel/mixing circulation; the defect name alone does not determine severity.

Causes and risk factors Persistence of the fetal ductus is more common in premature infants. What changes in the body After birth, aortic blood usually passes through the ductus into the pulmonary artery, increasing pulmonary flow and left-heart workload.

Causes and risk factors Incomplete formation of atrial septal tissue creates an ASD; location and associated defects vary. What changes in the body Blood usually shunts from left atrium to right atrium, increasing pulmonary blood flow and right-heart volume.

Causes and risk factors Incomplete ventricular septal formation produces a defect that may be isolated or part of a more complex lesion. What changes in the body As pulmonary resistance falls, left-to-right flow can increase pulmonary circulation and return volume to the left heart.

Causes and risk factors Congenital aortic narrowing may become evident as ductal tissue constricts or as the child grows. What changes in the body An obstructive lesion raises pressure before the narrowing and reduces flow beyond it; it is not a left-to-right shunt.

Causes and risk factors Congenital outflow narrowing may be valvar, subvalvar or supravalvar; a bicuspid valve is a common valvar cause. What changes in the body Left-ventricular outflow obstruction increases ventricular pressure/work and can reduce cardiac output.

Causes and risk factors Congenital pulmonary valve/outflow narrowing may occur alone or with other heart abnormalities and can run in families. What changes in the body The right ventricle works against a narrowed outlet; critical obstruction can greatly limit pulmonary blood flow.

Causes and risk factors TOF is a congenital combination sometimes associated with genetic syndromes, including 22q11.2 deletion. What changes in the body VSD, overriding aorta, right-ventricular outflow obstruction and RV hypertrophy create anatomy-dependent right-to-left flow and reduced pulmonary flow.

Causes and risk factors The great arteries connect to the wrong ventricles during fetal development; maternal diabetes is one associated risk factor. What changes in the body Aorta from RV and pulmonary artery from LV create parallel circulations, so survival depends on adequate mixing through atrial/ventricular or ductal connections.

Causes and risk factors Absent tricuspid-valve formation produces a hypoplastic right ventricle, often with associated septal or outflow abnormalities. What changes in the body Systemic venous blood must cross an atrial communication and mix; pulmonary flow depends on associated anatomy and may be too low or too high. Diagnostic evaluation Echocardiography defines the missing valve and connections; saturation and selected catheter studies help evaluate flow. Clinical findings Cyanosis, feeding difficulty, poor grow

Causes and risk factors Kawasaki disease has an incompletely understood trigger in susceptible children, usually under five, and is not spread person to person. What changes in the body Systemic vasculitis can injure coronary arteries, producing dilation/aneurysm and later thrombosis or ischemia. Diagnostic evaluation Diagnosis is clinical using fever and characteristic features, with inflammatory tests and echocardiography to assess coronary involvement; incomplete presentations also require evaluation. Causes and risk factors Acute rheumatic fever follows a group A streptococcal infection in susceptible children; recurrence is more likely after another GAS infection. What changes in the body An abnormal immune response causes inflammation involving joints, heart, brain and skin; valve injury can lead to chronic rheumatic heart disease. Chronic hyperglycemia injures retinal microvessels; leakage causes edema and ischemia can drive fragile new vessels. Early disease may be silent. Blurred vision, floaters or sudden vision loss require eye assessment. Dilated retinal examination detects disease; OCT/angiography guide selected cases. Glucose/BP management and scheduled eye follow-up reduce risk. Treatment may include anti-VEGF injections, laser or surgery according to stage. Support accessible diabetes self-care when vision is impaired. Sources: NEI

Impaction causes fullness, otalgia, tinnitus or conductive loss, or prevents needed examination. Confirm with otoscopy and ask about perforation/tubes, prior ear surgery, infection, diabetes, anticoagulation and immune suppression. Clinician-selected options include softening agents, irrigation or removal under direct vision. Do not irrigate a known/suspected perforated drum; avoid cotton swabs or inserted objects. Reassess symptoms and canal after treatment; persistent hearing loss needs further evaluation. Source

Contrast acute painful infection with chronic/recurrent drainage, tympanic damage and conductive hearing loss. Persistent foul drainage or a suspected cholesteatoma needs ENT evaluation because adjacent structures may be damaged. Otoscopy and audiometry assess damage. Tympanoplasty repairs the drum; ossiculoplasty reconstructs the sound-conducting bones; mastoidectomy removes diseased mastoid tissue. entries.h: 🚨 The drug trap that shows up every year
entries.t: Never give anticholinergics or atropine to a patient with closed-angle glaucoma. They dilate the pupil, which jams the drainage angle shut and spikes the pressure. Watch for this hidden inside antihistamines, TCAs, scopolamine and pre-op orders.

A painless curtain or shadow moving across vision, often after floaters and flashes of light. It is the one condition that gets face-down positioning after repair, so the gas bubble presses the retina back.
A clouded lens , not a pressure problem. Painless, gradual, cloudy or yellowed vision, glare at night. Surgery is elective and done one eye at a time .

entries.h: 👂 Conductive vs sensorineural, in one line each
entries.t: Conductive — sound cannot get in . Wax, fluid, perforation, otosclerosis. Often fixable. Sensorineural — the hair cells or nerve are damaged. Noise, age, ototoxic drugs. Usually permanent. Ototoxic offenders: aminoglycosides loop diuretics high-dose aspirin cisplatin
Vertigo + tinnitus + fluctuating hearing loss. Caused by too much endolymph in the inner ear. Nursing priority is safety — the vertigo causes falls. Low-sodium diet and diuretics reduce the fluid.

entries.h: ⭐ Meniere’s — three symptoms, one disease · more
entries.t: Open-angle glaucoma is gradual and painless and takes peripheral vision first; lifelong beta-blocker drops. Closed-angle is sudden severe pain + halos + N/V and is a surgical emergency . Cataract is a clouded lens , not a pressure problem. Surgery only, non-urgent, one eye at a time. Retinal detachment = painless curtain across the vision. Emergency. The only one that gets face-down (prone) positioning post-op, about 2 weeks . Macular degeneration takes central vision and spares peripheral. Amsler grid at home catc

entries.h: ⭐ Meniere’s — three symptoms, one disease · more · more
entries.t: Eye drops: 5–10 min between different drops; occlude the inner canthus 2 min to block systemic absorption. Meniere's : low sodium, low caffeine and alcohol to cut inner-ear fluid ( not for blood pressure). Meclizine + a diuretic, and fall precautions during vertigo. External otitis hurts when you move the tragus or pinna — that is what separates it from otitis media. Ruptured tympanic membrane: the pain suddenly relieves . Keep the ear dry, no swimming or flying, usually heals on its own. Ototoxic drugs : furosemid

entries.h: ⭐ Meniere’s — three symptoms, one disease · more · more · more
entries.t: New hearing loss teaching: face her, cut background noise, get her attention first, and rephrase rather than repeat louder.
What the faculty actually said in the review session for this week — their numbers, their worked calculations, their priority rulings. On an exam, this beats the textbook.

Newly blind (diabetic retinopathy): the priority is keep frequently used items in consistent locations . The cue word is recently — someone blind twenty years can be left to ask for help, someone blind three weeks cannot. Perimetry is just formal visual field testing. If she will not fixate, coach her to hold the center light — do not cancel the test and do not medicate her. Wanting to look at the moving thing is normal, not an inability to complete the test. Hold the timolol the morning of tonometry so the pressur

entries.h: 🎧 From the exam-prep recording · more · more
entries.t: Acute closed-angle presents as fixed dilated pupil + hazy cornea + severe pain with vomiting , coming on over minutes to an hour. The pupil is fixed because the pressure has paralyzed the nerve; the cornea is hazy because fluid is being forced into it. Their glaucoma risk list: family history, over 60, diabetes, hypertension, corticosteroid use , thin central cornea , high myopia. They explicitly said not risks: corrective lenses, vitamin A, sunglasses — sunglasses actually prevent cataracts and retinal injury. Ant

entries.h: 🎧 From the exam-prep recording · more · more · more
entries.t: Weber louder in one ear tells you only that the two ears are unequal. The next step is the Rinne test — not charting a type of loss, not calling the provider. Their tuning-fork positions: Weber on the forehead , heard equally in both ears when normal. Rinne on the mastoid , then in front of the ear — normal is air conduction outlasting bone conduction . Swimming class + severe ear pain + purulent discharge = otitis externa , swimmer's ear. Otitis media is behind the eardrum, so it only drains once the tympanic memb

entries.h: 🎧 From the exam-prep recording · more · more · more · more
entries.t: On a priority question, all four options can be correct actions — you cannot eliminate on accuracy, only on order. Their words: "I actually am going to do all four of these things." Calc: 2,500 mL over 12 h = 208.3 mL/hr — but the item asked in liters , so the answer is 2.5 L and there is no calculation at all. The faculty themselves went to mL/hr on the recording and had to back up. Read the units, and round only at the very end.

Glaucoma is a pressure problem; cataract is a lens problem. Different answer every time. Retinal detachment being painless does not make it less of an emergency. Sensorineural loss is usually permanent; conductive loss is often fixable.

entries.h: 🧪 What confirms it — every test, all thirteen
entries.t: The thing to know first: almost nothing here is a blood test. Eyes and ears are diagnosed by looking and by measuring — a chart, a pressure, a tuning fork, a scope. Blood work shows up in only two places: a culture when something is infected and draining, and the routine pre-op panel before surgery. If a question offers you a serum level for glaucoma or Meniere, it is the wrong answer. Eye disorder What confirms it What it shows Vision impairment & blindness Snellen chart (distance), Rosenbaum or Jaeger card (near)

entries.h: ⚠️ What it turns into — the complication for each one
entries.t: This is the section the cards above do not have, and it is the one the exam likes, because it is where “so what?” lives. Two patterns carry most of it: an untreated eye disorder costs sight permanently , and an untreated ear infection spreads inward — to the mastoid, the labyrinth, and in the worst case the meninges. Disorder What it turns into Vision impairment & blindness Falls and fractures , medication errors from misread labels, depression and social withdrawal, loss of driving and independence Glaucoma Perman

entries.h: 🪂 After middle ear surgery — the discharge teaching
entries.t: Stapedectomy, tympanoplasty, mastoidectomy, grommets. The page describes these procedures but this is the part that gets examined: what she may and may not do afterwards . One idea runs through all of it — anything that raises pressure in the middle ear can shift the graft or the prosthesis , so for several weeks she has to stop doing those things. Teach Why No bending from the waist, no heavy lifting, no straining for several weeks — and move and turn the head slowly All of it raises middle-ear pressure and can di

Her numbers and her wording, taken from the Monday recording. Where a figure here differs from the textbook, hers is the one on your exam — and she said outright that everything covered Monday and Tuesday is on the sensory quiz.

Normal IOP: 12–20, teetering to 21. Over 22 is suspicious. Her number. The textbook range you will also see is 10–21 — if an option sits at 22 or above, it is abnormal either way. Legal blindness is 20/200 , and she wants you able to explain it: at 20 feet the client sees what a normal eye sees at 200 feet . Astigmatism is a misshapen cornea — football-shaped, not round. Corrected with a specially shaped lens. Myopia is nearsighted, hyperopia is farsighted, emmetropia is normal. Multiple eye drops: wait 5 to 10 min

entries.h: 👁️ The seven optic disorders, section by section
entries.t: Every disorder below is laid out in the same six sections, in the same order, so you can go straight to the one you want. They stay closed until you open them.

entries.h: ▸ 👁️ Vision Impairment and Blindness Open Close
entries.t: 🖼️ See the picture: Changes inside the retina 🖼️ See the picture: BPPV and the Dix–Hallpike test

Reduced visual function that glasses, contact lenses or surgery cannot fully correct. Legal blindness in the United States is a best-corrected acuity of 20/200 or worse in the better eye, or a visual field of 20° or less. Low vision is functional impairment short of that — she can still use what sight she has, with help.

Age is the largest factor. The four leading causes in adults are cataract, glaucoma, macular degeneration and diabetic retinopathy . Also uncorrected refractive error, trauma, stroke, retinopathy of prematurity, and the two chronic diseases underneath so much of it — diabetes and hypertension .

Reduced acuity, loss of visual field, trouble reading, driving or recognizing faces, bumping into things, falls , squinting or turning the head to use a better part of the field, and withdrawal from company because conversation has become hard work.

Snellen or tumbling-E acuity, visual fields by confrontation or formal perimetry, ophthalmoscopy, tonometry, and a functional assessment — what she can and cannot do at home. Assess fall risk every time.

Treat the cause where there is one. Refractive correction, then low-vision aids: magnifiers, large print, high contrast, screen readers, talking devices. Orientation and mobility training and referral to vision rehabilitation.

Say who you are when you come in, and say when you are leaving — do not let her discover she is talking to an empty room. Sighted guide: she takes your arm just above the elbow and walks half a step behind ; you never grab or steer her. Orient her to the room and then do not move her belongings or the furniture . Clock-face positions for the meal tray. Good non-glare lighting. Announce steps, curbs and doorways before you reach them. Encourage independence — doing it for her is not kindness.

entries.h: ▸ 💧 Glaucoma Closed-angle is an emergency Open Close
entries.t: 🖼️ See the picture: Red eyes, side by side 🖼️ Infographics Glaucoma

An optic neuropathy caused by raised intraocular pressure damaging the optic nerve. The vision it takes does not come back . Two forms behave completely differently: open-angle is chronic and silent; closed-angle is sudden and a surgical emergency.

Age over 40, family history, diabetes, hypertension, severe myopia, eye trauma and long-term corticosteroids . African ancestry raises open-angle risk; Asian ancestry raises closed-angle risk. Anticholinergics and mydriatics can precipitate an acute closed-angle attack — that is why the drug history matters.

Open-angle: painless, gradual, takes peripheral vision first — the “tunnel” — and is often symptomless until a great deal is already gone. Closed-angle: sudden severe eye pain and headache, halos around lights , blurred vision, nausea and vomiting , a red eye, a fixed mid-dilated pupil and a globe that feels hard.

Tonometry — normal intraocular pressure is 10–21 mmHg . Ophthalmoscopy for cupping of the optic disc . Visual field testing (perimetry) maps what has been lost. Gonioscopy looks at the angle itself; OCT measures the nerve fiber layer.

Open-angle — lifelong topical drops: prostaglandin analogues (latanoprost), beta blockers (timolol), alpha agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors; then laser trabeculoplasty or trabeculectomy. Closed-angle — emergency: systemic acetazolamide, osmotic mannitol and miotic pilocarpine to break the attack, then laser peripheral iridotomy .

The drops are for life and they are not for symptoms. She will feel no different on them — that is the point, and it is why people stop and lose their sight. Occlude the inner canthus 1–2 min to cut systemic absorption, and leave 5–10 min between different drops. Timolol is a beta blocker even in the eye: watch for bradycardia and bronchospasm , and never stop it abruptly. Avoid anticholinergics and mydriatics in anyone at risk of closed-angle. Sudden pain with halos and vomiting is an emergency — same day, not nex
📄 Glaucoma 📄 PDF · Opens in Drive →

A clouding of the normally clear lens . Painless, gradual, and the commonest cause of reversible blindness in the world. Note the distinction the exam leans on: a cataract is a lens problem, not a pressure problem.

Ageing accounts for most. Then UV exposure, smoking, diabetes, long-term corticosteroids , blunt or penetrating trauma, previous intraocular surgery or inflammation, and congenital causes such as maternal rubella.

Painless gradual blurring; glare and halos, worst at night and when driving ; colors look faded or yellowed; double vision in the one eye; needing a new spectacle prescription repeatedly; a diminished or absent red reflex , and late on a visibly cloudy gray-white pupil.

Visual acuity, then ophthalmoscopy for the red reflex — reduced or absent is the finding. Slit-lamp examination confirms and grades it; glare testing shows the functional problem the acuity chart can miss.

No drug, drop or diet reverses a cataract. Surgery is the only treatment — phacoemulsification with an intraocular lens implant, as a day case under local anesthetic, one eye at a time . It is not urgent : it is done when the cataract stops her doing what she wants to do.

After surgery: eye shield, especially at night, and dark glasses for glare. No bending at the waist, no straining, no lifting over about 10 lb / 4.5 kg , and avoid coughing, sneezing or vomiting if you can — anything that raises intraocular pressure. Mild itching and a little morning discharge are expected. Report sudden pain, decreasing vision, flashes or new floaters, or increasing drainage — those are bleeding, infection and detachment. Antibiotic and steroid drops as prescribed; vision sharpens over days to wee
🖼️ See the picture: Changes inside the retina 🖼️ Infographics Retinal Detachment
The retina — the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye — separates from the tissue beneath it. A detached retina cannot function , and the loss becomes permanent if it is not treated promptly.
Ageing and shrinkage of the vitreous, high myopia , previous cataract surgery, blunt or penetrating trauma , diabetic retinopathy, family history, and a previous detachment in the other eye.

A sudden increase in floaters ; flashes of light ; and then a dark curtain or shadow drawn across the field of vision that grows. It does not hurt — painlessness is what makes people wait, and waiting is what costs the sight.

Retinal examination after pupil dilation, indirect ophthalmoscopy with scleral depression , and B-scan ultrasound when blood or cataract blocks the view. Acuity and visual fields document what has already gone.
Reattach the retina: laser photocoagulation , cryopexy (freezing), pneumatic retinopexy with a gas bubble, scleral buckle , or vitrectomy .

This is time-critical — the same day. After a gas bubble the positioning is the whole treatment: she may need face-down (prone) positioning for around two weeks so the bubble presses the retina back into place. No air travel and no high altitude while the bubble is there — it expands and the pressure rises dangerously. Eye shield, no straining or bending, report pain or falling vision, and keep every follow-up appointment.
🖼️ Retinal Detachment Exam 1 · Study page →
↗ New tab 📄 Retinal Detachment 📄 PDF · Opens in Drive →

Degeneration of the macula , the central retina. It takes central vision and spares the periphery — the mirror image of glaucoma. The leading cause of irreversible central vision loss over 60. Dry (atrophic) is 90% and gradual; wet (neovascular) is 10%, sudden and far more damaging.
Age over 60, and smoking — much the biggest thing she can change . Then family history, white ancestry, light-colored irises, hypertension, obesity, a high-fat diet and UV exposure.

Blurred or darkened central vision; a central blind spot (scotoma); straight lines look wavy or bent (metamorphopsia); difficulty reading and recognizing faces. Peripheral vision stays, so she can still walk about safely — which is worth saying to her, because the diagnosis sounds like total blindness.

The Amsler grid , which she also uses at home to monitor herself. Visual acuity, dilated fundus examination showing drusen , fluorescein angiography and OCT to find and follow the neovascular membrane.

Dry — no cure; AREDS2 antioxidants (vitamins C and E, lutein, zeaxanthin, zinc, copper) may slow it. Wet — intravitreal anti-VEGF injections (ranibizumab, aflibercept, bevacizumab), and photodynamic or laser therapy.

Stopping smoking is the single most useful thing she can do. Teach daily Amsler grid use and to report new waviness, blur or a new blank patch at once — wet AMD is treatable if it is caught early. Magnifiers, large print, high-contrast, strong lighting and audiobooks. Dark leafy greens and oily fish. Reassure her that peripheral vision remains, so independent mobility is preserved.
🖼️ Macular Degeneration Exam 1 · Study page →
↗ New tab 🖼️ Macular degeneration — central vision 🖼️ Infographic · With the notes →
↗ New tab 📄 Macular Degeneration 📄 PDF · Opens in Drive →

Inflammation of the conjunctiva — “pink eye”. Bacterial, viral, allergic or irritant. Very common, and the infectious forms are highly contagious . Vision itself stays normal; severe pain or lost vision means it is something else .

Bacteria (staphylococci, streptococci, H. influenzae ; gonococcal or chlamydial in the newborn), viruses ( adenovirus most often), allergens such as pollen and animal dander, and irritants like chlorine and smoke. Contact lens wear and poor hand hygiene run through most of it.

Redness, itching or a gritty “sand in the eye” feeling, tearing, discharge. Bacterial — thick yellow-green purulent discharge, lids stuck together in the morning . Viral — watery discharge, often with a cold, usually starts in one eye. Allergic — both eyes, itching dominates , watery stringy discharge.

Usually clinical: inspect the discharge, the lids and the preauricular nodes (tender in viral). Culture if it is severe, recurrent, or in a newborn. Fluorescein staining if a corneal abrasion or ulcer is suspected.

Bacterial — topical antibiotic drops or ointment. Viral — supportive only: cool compresses and artificial tears; antibiotics do nothing . Allergic — topical antihistamine or mast-cell stabilizer, cool compresses, avoid the allergen. Neonatal gonococcal infection is an emergency and needs systemic treatment.

Hand hygiene is the whole battle. Do not share towels, flannels, pillows or eye make-up, and throw away the make-up she was using . No contact lenses until cleared, and discard the current pair and case. Wipe from the inner to the outer canthus , a clean surface each time, a separate cloth for each eye . Stay off work or school while there is discharge. Never let the dropper tip touch the eye or lashes.
📄 Conjunctivitis 📄 PDF · Opens in Drive →

Surgical removal of the whole eyeball, leaving the optic nerve stump, the extraocular muscles and the rest of the orbital contents. It is done when an eye is beyond saving, or when keeping it endangers the other one.

Intraocular malignancy (melanoma, retinoblastoma), severe trauma with no useful vision remaining, a painful blind eye , endophthalmitis that will not settle — and to prevent sympathetic ophthalmia , an autoimmune inflammation that can blind the remaining good eye after a penetrating injury to the other.

Depends on why it is being done: pain in a blind eye, no light perception, a mass found on imaging, or an infection that is not responding. The point to hold on to is that the presentation is the underlying disease, not the surgery.
Acuity and light perception in both eyes, ultrasound, CT or MRI of the orbit, and histology for tumor. Assess the fellow eye carefully — from here on, it is her only eye and it is the priority.

Enucleation with an orbital implant placed at the same operation, a pressure dressing for the first 24–48 hours, antibiotics and analgesia. A custom ocular prosthesis is fitted about 4–6 weeks later, once the swelling has settled.

Expect the pressure dressing at first. Report bright red bleeding, fever, or pain that is increasing rather than settling — that is hemorrhage or infection. Teach prosthesis handling: wash hands, remove, clean and reinsert as taught, and do not let it dry out. Protect the remaining eye absolutely — polycarbonate safety glasses, always. With one eye there is no depth perception : warn her about steps and curbs, pouring hot drinks, and driving. Grief and body image are part of this care, not an afterthought — she has

entries.h: 👂 Weber and Rinne — which test tells you what
entries.t: Two tuning-fork tests that answer two different questions. Weber tells you the side. Rinne tells you the type. Neither one alone gives you a diagnosis, and that is exactly what the exam tests.

entries.h: 👂 The six otic disorders, section by section
entries.t: Same six sections, same order. Ear problems split into outer, middle and inner — and where the problem sits tells you most of the answer.

Reduced ability to detect sound. Conductive — something in the outer or middle ear blocks conduction. Sensorineural — the cochlea or cranial nerve VIII is damaged. Mixed — both. Presbycusis is the age-related sensorineural loss, and it takes the high frequencies first — which is why consonants disappear before vowels do.

Conductive: cerumen impaction, foreign body, otitis media or effusion, perforated tympanic membrane, otosclerosis. Sensorineural: ageing, noise exposure , ototoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, loop diuretics, high-dose salicylates, cisplatin, vancomycin), Meniere's, acoustic neuroma, congenital causes and infection.

Asking for things to be repeated, turning the volume up, struggling with consonants and in noisy rooms, tinnitus , withdrawing from conversation, and being thought confused when she simply cannot hear. Speaking too loudly suggests sensorineural loss; speaking too softly suggests conductive, because she hears her own voice through bone.

Otoscopy first — is it just wax? Then the whisper test, and the tuning-fork pair: Weber lateralizes to the bad ear in conductive loss and to the good ear in sensorineural ; Rinne is air > bone normally and in sensorineural, and bone > air in conductive . Then audiometry and tympanometry.

Remove the cause: cerumen removal, treat the infection, myringotomy and tubes, stapedectomy for otosclerosis. Hearing aids for sensorineural loss, cochlear implant for profound loss, assistive listening devices — and stop the ototoxic drug wherever that is possible.

Do not shout. Shouting raises your pitch , and the high frequencies are exactly what she has lost — it distorts the consonants further. Instead: get her attention first, face her with the light on your face so she can lip-read, speak at normal volume slightly slower, lower your pitch , cut the background noise, and rephrase rather than repeat the same words louder. Hearing aid care: turn it off with the battery door open , in a dry container away from heat; clean with a dry cloth; whistling means a poor fit or wax.
🖼️ Ear anatomy & hearing loss 📈 Infographic · Full-size image →

entries.h: 🖼️ What an ear examination may show

entries.t: Inflammation or infection of the external auditory canal — “swimmer's ear”. The infection sits outside the tympanic membrane, which is what separates it from otitis media.

Water sitting in the canal after swimming, trauma from cotton buds , hearing aids or earbuds, humid weather, eczema or dermatitis, and either too much or too little cerumen. In diabetes and immunocompromise, watch for malignant otitis externa — a Pseudomonas infection that can invade the skull base.

Ear pain that is markedly worse when the pinna or tragus is moved or pressed — that is the giveaway. Itching, a red swollen canal, discharge, and conductive hearing loss if the canal swells shut. Usually no fever .

Otoscopy shows a swollen erythematous canal with debris; the examination itself hurts. Pain on pinna traction distinguishes it from otitis media. Culture the discharge if it is severe or not responding, and in a diabetic assess specifically for the malignant form.

Topical antibiotic drops with or without a corticosteroid (ciprofloxacin, or neomycin/polymyxin/hydrocortisone). A wick if the canal is too swollen to admit drops. Analgesia, and keep the ear dry. Systemic antibiotics only for spreading infection or in diabetes and immunocompromise.

Nothing smaller than your elbow goes in your ear — no cotton buds, ever. Keep the ear dry: earplugs or a shower cap, no swimming until cleared, dry the ear after washing. Warm the drops in your hand first — cold drops in the ear cause vertigo. Straighten the canal to instil: adult, pull the pinna UP and BACK; child under 3, DOWN and BACK . Then lie with that ear uppermost for a few minutes. Finish the whole course.
🖼️ See the picture: What an ear examination may show

Acute infection of the middle ear , with fluid trapped behind an intact tympanic membrane. Overwhelmingly a disease of small children, because their eustachian tube is shorter, wider and more horizontal , so it drains badly and organisms travel up it easily.

It follows an upper respiratory infection. S. pneumoniae , H. influenzae , M. catarrhalis . Risk rises with age 6–24 months , daycare, bottle-feeding lying flat , passive smoke, pacifier use, cleft palate, Down syndrome and allergy. Breastfeeding protects.

Ear pain, fever, irritability, pulling or tugging at the ear in an infant who cannot tell you, poor feeding, trouble sleeping and hearing loss. If the drum perforates, the pain suddenly eases and purulent drainage appears — relief, not improvement.

Otoscopy: a red, bulging, opaque tympanic membrane, loss of the light reflex , and reduced mobility on pneumatic otoscopy. Tympanometry confirms effusion. Always check for mastoid tenderness behind the ear.

Analgesia always. Many resolve alone, so watchful waiting for 48–72 hours is reasonable in a well child over two. Amoxicillin is first-line when antibiotics are indicated. Myringotomy with tympanostomy tubes for recurrent infection or persistent effusion.

Finish the entire antibiotic course even though the pain stops in a day or two. Feed infants upright — never propped with a bottle lying flat. No passive smoke. Keep pneumococcal and influenza immunisations current. With tubes in place, report a tube that falls out or drainage that persists. Report high fever, pain or swelling behind the ear, or a stiff neck — mastoiditis and meningitis are the complications worth catching.
🖼️ See the picture: What an ear examination may show
A tear or perforation of the tympanic membrane, from pressure, infection or direct injury. Most heal on their own within weeks.

Acute otitis media with pus building up behind the drum, barotrauma from flying or diving, a blow to the ear or head, blast injury, a foreign body or cotton bud , skull fracture, and sudden very loud noise.

Sudden sharp ear pain that then eases abruptly , drainage that may be clear, purulent or bloody, conductive hearing loss, tinnitus and sometimes vertigo. Clear watery drainage after head trauma may be cerebrospinal fluid — that is an emergency, not an ear problem.
Otoscopy shows the perforation and its size. Hearing assessment with Weber and Rinne, then audiometry; tympanometry. If CSF is suspected, the halo or ring test and beta-2 transferrin; CT for trauma.
Most need nothing but time and a dry ear. Antibiotics only if it is infected; analgesia as needed. Tympanoplasty or myringoplasty if it fails to heal or the hearing loss is significant.

Keep the ear completely dry — no swimming, and cotton wool coated in petroleum jelly for showering. No diving or flying until cleared. Do not instil anything into the ear unless it is prescribed — with a hole there, drops reach the middle ear. Do not blow the nose forcefully; sneeze with the mouth open. Report fever, increasing pain or foul-smelling discharge. Reassure her that the hearing usually returns as it heals.

entries.h: ▸ 🎪 Meniere Disease Falls risk Open Close
entries.t: 🖼️ See the picture: Hearing and inner-ear disorders 🖼️ Infographics Meniere's Disease

A disorder of the inner ear caused by excess endolymph (endolymphatic hydrops). It is chronic and it attacks without warning , which is what makes it so disabling — not the attack itself but never knowing when the next one comes.

The cause is unknown. Associations include autoimmune disease, viral infection, head trauma, family history, allergy and migraine. Attacks are triggered by salt, caffeine, alcohol, nicotine and stress .

The classic triad — vertigo (severe, rotational, minutes to hours, with nausea and vomiting), fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss , and tinnitus — plus a sensation of fullness or pressure in the ear. Usually one ear. Between attacks she may be entirely well, which makes others doubt her.

The history makes the diagnosis. Audiometry shows a low-frequency sensorineural loss. Weber and Rinne, electronystagmography and caloric testing assess the vestibular side, and MRI is done to exclude an acoustic neuroma .

Acute attack — antihistamines (meclizine), antiemetics, benzodiazepines, bed rest. Maintenance — low-sodium diet , diuretics, betahistine, and avoiding caffeine, alcohol and nicotine. Refractory — intratympanic gentamicin or steroids, endolymphatic sac decompression, or labyrinthectomy, which destroys the hearing on that side.

Safety comes first — the vertigo causes falls. During an attack: lie still in a quiet darkened room, no sudden head movements, side rails up, and call for help before getting up. Do not drive, operate machinery, climb ladders or swim alone — the attacks give no warning. The low-sodium diet is the single biggest lever she controls . Keep a diary of attacks and what preceded them; that is how the triggers get found.
🖼️ Meniere's Disease Exam 1 · Study page →
↗ New tab 📄 Meniere's Disease 📄 PDF · Opens in Drive →
🖼️ See the picture: Hearing and inner-ear disorders
The disorders of the cochlea and the vestibular apparatus, affecting hearing, balance or both: labyrinthitis , vestibular neuritis , BPPV , ototoxicity and acoustic neuroma .

Viral or bacterial infection — labyrinthitis often follows a cold or an otitis media. Displaced otoliths cause BPPV. Ototoxic drugs : aminoglycosides, loop diuretics, high-dose salicylates, cisplatin, vancomycin. Head trauma, ageing, and a benign tumor of cranial nerve VIII in acoustic neuroma.

Vertigo, nystagmus , nausea and vomiting, imbalance and falls, sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus. The pattern separates them: BPPV — brief seconds-long vertigo triggered by a change of head position, no hearing loss . Labyrinthitis — vertigo with hearing loss. Vestibular neuritis — vertigo without hearing loss. Acoustic neuroma — one-sided progressive hearing loss and tinnitus, later facial numbness.

Romberg and gait, the Dix-Hallpike maneuver for BPPV, audiometry, electronystagmography and caloric testing, MRI with contrast if an acoustic neuroma is suspected — and a careful medication review for ototoxicity, which is the cause most often missed.

Vestibular suppressants short-term only (meclizine, antiemetics). Corticosteroids, and antivirals or antibiotics for labyrinthitis. Epley canalith repositioning for BPPV, which often works in a single session. Vestibular rehabilitation exercises . Stop the ototoxic drug. Surgery or stereotactic radiosurgery for acoustic neuroma.

Fall prevention runs through all of it. Move slowly and change position in stages — sit on the edge of the bed before standing. Good lighting, rugs and clutter gone, a stick or frame if she is unsteady. No driving while the vertigo is active. Report new one-sided hearing loss or tinnitus — that is the acoustic neuroma pattern and it needs imaging. On ototoxic drugs, report tinnitus, any change in hearing or new dizziness immediately : the damage can be permanent, but it is often reversible if the drug is stopped ea
One per disorder, built from the structure of your ATI chapter.

AMD risk increases with smoking, hypertension, high cholesterol, and obesity. AMD risk rises after age 60, with family history, or light-colored eyes. Cataracts risk increases with advanced age, diabetes, heredity, and smoking. Cataracts risk rises with eye trauma, heavy sun exposure, and steroid use.

AMD : distorted objects, blurred vision, loss of central vision. AMD : poor depth perception; can progress to blindness. Cataracts : gradual painless vision loss, blurred vision, visible lens opacity. Cataracts : absent red reflex; reduced night vision and color perception.

Ophthalmoscopy examines the fundus: retina, optic disc, macula, and vessels. Visual acuity testing uses Snellen and Rosenbaum eye charts. Fluorescein angiography checks blood flow adequacy to the retina. Cataracts are confirmed by viewing the lens with an ophthalmoscope.

This chapter covers three major eye disorders: age-related macular degeneration (dry vs wet), cataracts (lens clouding from aging, trauma, or steroid use), and glaucoma (optic nerve damage from elevated pressure), including risk factors, diagnostics, medications, and surgical care.
Wear sunglasses outdoors and protective eyewear for sports or hazardous work. Get annual eye exams, especially after age 40. Learn early glaucoma warning signs: reduced vision and mild eye pain.

AMD risk increases with smoking, hypertension, high cholesterol, and obesity. AMD risk rises after age 60, with family history, or light-colored eyes. Cataracts risk increases with advanced age, diabetes, heredity, and smoking. Cataracts risk rises with eye trauma, heavy sun exposure, and steroid use. Glaucoma risk increases with age, race, genetic predisposition, and hypertension. Glaucoma risk also rises with diabetes, severe myopia, and retinal detachment. Glaucoma can also stem from eye trauma, tumors, or infec

AMD : distorted objects, blurred vision, loss of central vision. AMD : poor depth perception; can progress to blindness. Cataracts : gradual painless vision loss, blurred vision, visible lens opacity. Cataracts : absent red reflex; reduced night vision and color perception. POAG : often asymptomatic early; headache and mild eye pain. POAG : gradual peripheral vision loss; halos seen around lights. POAG : IOP rises above 20 mm Hg , typically 22 to 32 mm Hg . Angle-closure glaucoma : sudden IOP spike to 30 mm Hg or h

From this module — built from the notes above on this page, not a section of the ATI chapter. Few eye disorders are diagnosed by blood test — assessment is visual and structural. Blood glucose and HbA1c for diabetic retinopathy risk. Inflammatory markers and autoantibodies for uveitis and scleritis. ESR and CRP urgently for suspected giant cell arteritis with visual loss — treatment starts before the biopsy. Lipids and blood pressure, since vascular disease drives retinal vein and artery occlusion.

Ophthalmoscopy examines the fundus: retina, optic disc, macula, and vessels. Visual acuity testing uses Snellen and Rosenbaum eye charts. Fluorescein angiography checks blood flow adequacy to the retina. Cataracts are confirmed by viewing the lens with an ophthalmoscope. Tonometry measures IOP; normal range is 11 to 21 mm Hg .

Wet AMD : laser therapy seals the leaking blood vessels. Wet AMD : ocular injections of bevacizumab or ranibizumab block vessel growth. Cataracts: check visual acuity with the Snellen chart regularly. Cataracts: increase room lighting and provide magnifiers or large-print materials. Cataracts: assess how reduced vision affects the client's daily function. Postop cataract care: prevent elevated IOP and prevent infection. Postop cataract care: give ophthalmic meds, control pain, teach fall prevention. Glaucoma: monit
Atropine 1% ophthalmic dilates the pupil and relaxes eye muscles preop. Atropine has a fast onset but a long duration of action. Medication therapy is the priority treatment for glaucoma.

Cataract surgery removes the lens and inserts a replacement intraocular lens. Replacement lenses can correct refractive errors and improve vision. Glaucoma surgery options include laser trabeculectomy, iridotomy, or shunt placement. Educate glaucoma surgery clients on adhering to their medication schedule.

AMD: eat antioxidant-rich foods with vitamin E and B12 as advised. AMD: use community resources for transportation and low-vision aids. Cataracts: atropine effects last 7 to 12 days ; wear sunglasses for light sensitivity. Cataracts: avoid activities that raise IOP, like bending, straining, or coughing. Cataracts: report sudden vision change, floaters, or pain with nausea and vomiting. Glaucoma: space different eye drops 5 to 10 min apart. Glaucoma: apply gentle pressure to the inner eye corner after drops.
Consult an ophthalmologist for cataract surgery evaluation and care. Refer to an ophthalmologist when glaucoma surgery becomes necessary.

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from NEI, 2025 . Glaucoma damages the optic nerve and can cause peripheral vision loss progressing to complete blindness if untreated. Vision already lost to glaucoma cannot be restored; treatment can only stop further damage from occurring. Because early glaucoma often has no symptoms, damage can progress silently before it is caught on screening. National Eye Institute (NIH) · Glaucoma · open the source →

Covers middle ear conditions like otitis media and inner ear disorders like vertigo, Meniere's disease, and labyrinthitis — anatomy, hearing loss types, risk factors, diagnostics, nursing care, medications, procedures, and teaching.

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from NIDCD, 2025 . Sound at or below about 70 A-weighted decibels is unlikely to damage hearing even with long exposure. Repeated or prolonged exposure to sound at 85 dBA or higher can cause hearing damage, with louder sounds causing harm faster. Wearing earplugs or other hearing protection during loud activities is a key way to prevent noise-induced hearing loss. Noise-induced hearing loss is described as the only type of hearing loss that is completely preventable. NIDCD (NIH) · N
Middle ear risk: recurrent colds/otitis media, enlarged adenoids, trauma, air pressure changes (diving, flying) Inner ear risk: viral or bacterial infection, damage from ototoxic medications

Middle ear : hearing loss, ear fullness or pain, red inflamed canal, bulging tympanic membrane, fever Middle ear : fluid or bubbles behind the TM, and a diffuse or absent light reflex Inner ear : hearing loss, tinnitus, dizziness or vertigo, vomiting, nystagmus, balance changes

Usually none — diagnosis is by examination and audiometry. Culture of ear discharge in persistent or resistant otitis externa or media. Drug levels for ototoxic medicines — aminoglycosides, high-dose loop diuretics, some chemotherapy. Autoimmune and syphilis serology in sudden sensorineural hearing loss. Glucose and lipids, since vascular disease contributes to inner ear ischemia.

Audiometry is a noninvasive hearing test measuring frequency, pitch, and intensity Tympanogram measures TM and middle-ear mobility; useful for diagnosing middle ear disease Weber and Rinne tuning-fork exams determine whether hearing loss is present Otoscopy examines the external canal, tympanic membrane, and malleus

Pull the auricle up/back in adults, down/back in children to straighten the ear canal A normal TM is pearly gray and intact, with a visible anterior light reflex Bulging TM with a diffuse or absent light reflex signals middle-ear fluid or infection Avoid touching the ear canal lining — it is painful and sensitive ENG : ask simple questions to keep client alert; keep NPO and on bedrest until vertigo resolves Monitor ototoxic drug levels: gentamicin, furosemide, aspirin/NSAIDs, and cisplatin can damage hearing Routin

Meclizine (antihistamine/anticholinergic) treats vertigo from inner ear disorders Ondansetron treats nausea and vomiting from vertigo; avoid in certain cardiac rhythm disorders Diphenhydramine and dimenhydrinate (antihistamines) treat vertigo and nausea from inner ear disease

Myringotomy incises the TM to drain middle-ear fluid and prevent perforation A pressure-equalizing tube (grommet) replaces Eustachian tube function for 6-18 months Stapedectomy removes the stapes and replaces it with a prosthesis, done via the ear canal Stapedectomy treats otosclerosis, a cause of conductive hearing loss in older adults

Fast immediately before ENG/caloric testing; avoid caffeine, alcohol, sedatives, antihistamines for several days prior ENG is not performed on clients with a pacemaker — signals interfere with results During vertigo, rest in a quiet, darkened room and move the head slowly Avoid caffeine and alcohol; space fluid intake evenly and reduce salt to control vertigo Take a diuretic, if prescribed, to reduce fluid in the semicircular canals After ear surgery, avoid rapid movements and bending from the waist for weeks After
Vestibular rehab combines biofeedback, physical therapy, and stress management for frequent vertigo Postural training teaches positions to avoid and exercises that can stop a vertigo attack

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2023 . Acute mastoiditis is most often a complication of an untreated or inadequately treated middle ear infection. Infection erodes through the bony walls of the mastoid air cells, which can lead to pus collecting behind the ear. Adults with mastoiditis typically present with severe ear pain, fever, and headache along with redness and swelling behind the ear. Untreated mastoiditis can spread inward to cause meningitis, a brain abscess, or venous sinus thrombosis, c

Additional lecture and study notes. Perimetry is just formal visual field testing. If she will not fixate, coach her to hold the center light — do not cancel the test and do not medicate her. Acute closed-angle presents as fixed dilated pupil + hazy cornea + pain with vomiting . Chronic open-angle eats peripheral vision first. Their glaucoma risk list: family history, over 60, diabetes, hypertension, corticosteroid use , thin central cornea , high myopia. They explicitly said not risks: corrective lenses, vitamin A

Assess age, nutrition/protein intake, chronic illness, recurrent infection, immunization history, medications/chemotherapy, surgery and exposures, stress/sleep and family history. Leukopenia means reduced total WBC; leukocytosis means elevated total WBC and is not proof of bacterial infection. Neutropenia concerns neutrophils specifically: interpret CBC with differential/ANC and trend, not WBC alone. Connect low defenses to infection surveillance, skin/oral integrity and immediate reporting of fever. Brunner & Sudd

Organism → reservoir → exit → transmission → entry → susceptible host. Pair links with practical interruptions: appropriate antimicrobial treatment/source control; environmental cleaning; covering coughs/containing drainage; hand hygiene/PPE; aseptic catheter/wound care; immunization and nutrition. Distinguish colonization from symptomatic infection. Brunner & Suddarth and the supplied ATI adult medical-surgical/nutrition texts, reconciled with the current guidance linked here.

For every device, confirm indication daily and remove promptly when unnecessary. CLABSI: hand hygiene, maximal sterile insertion barriers, appropriate skin antisepsis, hub disinfection and intact dressing care. CAUTI: aseptic insertion, closed drainage, unobstructed flow and bag below bladder/off floor. VAP: head elevation 30–45° when appropriate, oral care including toothbrushing, sedation/liberation protocols and mobility. Routine oral chlorhexidine and stress-ulcer drugs are not VAP prevention measures. Sources:

Diarrhea: assess stool frequency/blood, travel/food/water/antibiotics, immune status, fluid balance and electrolytes. Oral rehydration solution treats mild–moderate dehydration; severe dehydration/shock or inability to tolerate oral therapy requires urgent evaluation and IV treatment. Diagnostic testing is guided by severity/exposure. Teach safe water/food, handwashing and warning signs. Immunizations: review record, immune status, prior reactions and current CDC schedule before administration. Emerging infections:
📚 Reading: Hinkle ch. 32 & 66

HIV is a CD4 disease. The virus destroys helper T cells, and every complication follows from how few are left. Learn the CD4 ladder and the opportunistic infections fall into place. CD4 count — what it predicts cells/mm³ <200 AIDS — PCP, toxo 200–499 early symptoms 500–1500 normal

CD4 < 200 That is the diagnostic threshold, regardless of how well the patient looks. Below it, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) becomes the classic killer — and prophylaxis with Bactrim starts at that same number. Precaution Room You wear Classic examples Airborne Negative pressure, door shut N95 M easles, T B, V aricella Droplet Private, door may be open Surgical mask Influenza, pertussis, meningitis , mumps Contact Private Gown + gloves C. diff , MRSA, VRE, scabies

entries.h: ⭐ Two mnemonics that carry the table
entries.t: Airborne = “My Tiny Vampire” — Measles, TB, Varicella. C. diff needs soap. Alcohol gel does not kill C. diff spores. Wash with soap and water, and use bleach to clean the room.

Adherence is the whole treatment. Missed doses breed resistance faster than any other drug class. Therapy is lifelong , continues in pregnancy (it prevents transmission to the baby), and an undetectable viral load means untransmittable sexually.

entries.h: ✅ Antiretroviral teaching, in one card · more
entries.t: CD4 is the monitoring lab , not WBC. CD4 <200 or an AIDS-defining condition = AIDS. Viral load tracks how well ART is working. HIV testing sequence: antigen/antibody combination screen first, then a confirmatory differentiation assay. PEP : start as soon as possible, ideally within hours, never beyond 72 hours . Continue 28 days . Assess immune risk using the CBC differential/ANC, its trend and the clinical context. Infection-protection measures follow the patient’s risk and local policy. A positive-pressure HEPA P

Earlier study notes, retained for comparison with the guidance above. These notes may reflect a book edition or lecture convention; check the assigned source for exam wording. Neutropenic precautions : private room, reverse isolation/positive pressure, no fresh flowers or plants, limited visitors, daily cleaning, dedicated equipment. The sign goes up at ANC ≤1,000 — but a client can be neutropenic above that. Use Standard Precautions for every patient and add the organism-specific transmission precautions. TB and m

Earlier study notes, retained for comparison with the guidance above. These notes may reflect a book edition or lecture convention; check the assigned source for exam wording. Airborne (TB, measles, varicella) = negative pressure, door closed , N95. Droplet (flu, bacterial meningitis, pertussis) and contact (C. diff, MRSA, VRE) = door may stay open.

Doff gown and gloves inside the room and do hand hygiene before you leave, not in the hall. One exception: an N95 comes off after you step out and close the door — then hand hygiene again. C. diff : bleach cleaning, contact precautions. Priority problem is dehydration , then electrolytes. HAI prevention: pull lines and catheters the moment they are not needed, scrub the hub 15 sec with friction, chlorhexidine 30 sec at dressing changes ( 2 min only on a moist site — groin or femoral) and let it dry , dressings q7 d
What the faculty actually said in the review session for this week — their numbers, their worked calculations, their priority rulings. On an exam, this beats the textbook.

For both CLABSI and CAUTI the most effective action is do not place the device unless it is necessary . Sterile insertion is the runner-up — the question asks for most effective, and several options are effective. Femoral central lines infect far more than subclavian. Prophylactic antibiotics are never the answer for a line or a catheter. Antibiotics are for a known infection. After a needlestick, wash the site with soap and water, report immediately and obtain urgent exposure assessment. Start indicated post-expos

Earlier study notes, retained for comparison with the guidance above. These notes may reflect a book edition or lecture convention; check the assigned source for exam wording. Needlestick from an HIV-positive source: wash with soap and water first — express the blood if it was deep — then report, PEP, baseline draw. All four are correct actions; only the order is being tested. Prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia with appropriate head elevation, oral care including toothbrushing, and protocols that minimize seda

Earlier study notes, retained for comparison with the guidance above. These notes may reflect a book edition or lecture convention; check the assigned source for exam wording. VAP prevention is HOB at least 30° , semi-Fowler's, so stomach contents cannot be aspirated. Scheduled q2h suctioning is the wrong answer — suction on need, or you traumatize the trachea. Add chlorhexidine oral care and a PPI for stress-ulcer prophylaxis. MRSA home teaching: keep the area covered with a clean, dry dressing . No petroleum jell

ART goals, their SATA: it lowers viral load (target undetectable), raises CD4 — not lowers — and prevents opportunistic infections . It does not cure, and it does not prevent transmission — it reduces it. Their warning: never tell a client with HIV they cannot transmit it. Poor ART adherence leads to drug resistance and treatment failure . Not "immediate" opportunistic infections, not "complete loss within days", not "rapid" progression — those take years. Watch the absolute words. Their fewest-steps heuristic: whe

Earlier study notes, retained for comparison with the guidance above. These notes may reflect a book edition or lecture convention; check the assigned source for exam wording. The bow-tie: CD4 180 is AIDS by definition — nothing else drops CD4 that far — and bilateral infiltrates mean pneumonia. Priorities: patent airway, medication adherence, nutrition . Complications: respiratory failure, sepsis, malnutrition . They ruled out TB (no night sweats, no hemoptysis) and asthma (no wheeze). Be very careful ever choosin

Varicella is airborne and contact. It spreads through the air and from the lesions, so gown and gloves go on with the N95 until every lesion has crusted. From that same question: influenza is droplet ; HIV and hepatitis B are standard precautions — you do not catch them by standing in front of someone. The physical difference: a droplet is larger and falls faster ; airborne particles are tiny and travel further . That is the whole distinction. Know the precautions themselves too — N95 fit, door closed — not just wh

Select-all-that-apply is plus/minus scored — a correct pick earns a point, a wrong pick loses one. Their strategy: pick only what you are confident about. Better to leave a point on the table than lose one. Same for every next-generation item where you may pick many. Psychosocial items: throw out what is never therapeutic first — "avoid emotional concerns", "your feelings are irrational" — then choose between what is left. Their point: the diagnosis is usually not what is being tested, the feelings are. Calc: aceta

Drawing blood from a central line does not itself cause CLABSI — bad technique does. An incontinent VRE client transmits far more than one with a closed Foley system. Viral infections get supportive care, not antibiotics.
