Rising ICP What you see EARLIEST Change in LOC — restless, confused, harder to rouse Then Headache, vomiting (often projectile ), pupil changes LATE — Cushing’s triad ↑ systolic with widening pulse pressure · ↓ heart rate · irregular respirations 🖼️ The focused neurologi

entries.h: 🚨 Cushing’s triad is a late, ominous sign
entries.t: By the time the triad appears, herniation is close. It is never the answer to "earliest sign". Positioning: head of bed 30° , head midline , no neck flexion, no hip flexion. Avoid coughing, straining and suctioning longer than 10 seconds.

Ischemic and hemorrhagic strokes look identical at the bedside, and the treatment for one is fatal in the other. CT exists to rule out bleeding before giving tPA. BE-FAST: B alance · E yes · F ace droop · A rm drift · S peech · T ime — note the last known well time.
Right-sided weakness. Aphasia — language is on the left. Slow, cautious, anxious. Aware of the deficit, so depression is common.
Left-sided weakness. Left-sided neglect — ignores that half of the world. Impulsive, poor judgment, unaware of the deficit — so a major fall risk .

entries.h: ⭐ The one intervention that prevents the common killer
entries.t: Swallow screen before anything by mouth. Aspiration pneumonia is the leading cause of death after stroke. Nothing by mouth - not even water or medications - until swallowing is formally assessed.

entries.h: ⭐ The one intervention that prevents the common killer · more
entries.t: Normal ICP 10–15 mmHg ; normal CPP >50 mmHg ; CPP = MAP − ICP . Rising ICP drops CPP and starves the brain. A change in LOC is the earliest sign of rising ICP. Cushing's triad — rising systolic with widened pulse pressure, bradycardia, irregular/Cheyne-Stokes respirations — is a late herniation sign. Mannitol and 3% saline pull fluid off the brain; confirm mannitol is working by increased urine output . Never Trendelenburg with raised ICP. GCS : eye 1–4, verbal 1–5, motor 1–6. Max 15, min 3. GCS ≤8 → intubate. Deco

entries.h: ⭐ The one intervention that prevents the common killer · more · more
entries.t: Non-contrast CT within 25 minutes of arrival decides ischemic vs hemorrhagic and t-PA candidacy. CT first acutely; MRI is better detail but too slow for the emergency. A patient who is not eligible for thrombolysis still needs urgent stroke-team evaluation for thrombectomy eligibility and the appropriate antithrombotic plan. A heparin infusion is not a routine substitute for reperfusion treatment.

Earlier study notes, retained for comparison with the guidance above. These notes may reflect a book edition or lecture convention; check the assigned source for exam wording. Ischemic stroke ~ 87% , hemorrhagic ~ 13% . t-PA window 3–4.5 hr from symptom onset. Contraindicated with anticoagulants, SBP >180, recent bleed or surgery, age under 18, or abnormal glucose. Not a candidate → heparin drip. Hemorrhagic: "worst headache of my life." No t-PA ever. Lower the BP, check and reverse coags, then surgical evacuation.

Seizures : protect the airway, turn her to the side, time it, pad the head. Never restrain, never put anything in the mouth. Status epilepticus (> 5 min , or repeated without recovery) → IV lorazepam first , then fosphenytoin or levetiracetam. Migraine POUND : Pulsating, One-day duration ( 4–72 hr ), Unilateral, Nausea, Disabling. Triptans/NSAIDs acutely, beta blockers to prevent. A TIA resolves fully with no infarct on imaging — but it gets the same urgency of workup as a stroke.
What the faculty actually said in the review session for this week — their numbers, their worked calculations, their priority rulings. On an exam, this beats the textbook.

Posturing scores on the GCS motor scale: decorticate = 3, decerebrate = 2 . The scale runs 3–15 — "you get 3 points just for showing up." Eye 4, verbal 5, motor 6. 8 or less: sedate and intubate. Posturing means the brainstem is being compressed. With posturing and high ICP, elevate the HOB to 30° first. It takes seconds and gravity does the work; mannitol has to be fetched and mixed . That is the whole reason it beats the drug. Their ICP mechanism table, worth learning as cause → effect: head elevation → venous ou

Earlier study notes, retained for comparison with the guidance above. These notes may reflect a book edition or lecture convention; check the assigned source for exam wording. Mannitol and 3% saline are either/or, never both — together they pull too much fluid. Treat them as interchangeable when you see them as options. ICP hyperventilation target: PaCO₂ 30–35 (normal 35–45) → cerebral vasoconstriction → less volume in the skull. Reducing ICP, their SATA: HOB 30°, mannitol, quiet and dimly lit room. Not coughing an

Hematoma pattern recognition — Epidural: arterial, a blow to the temple (the thinnest bone), brief LOC → lucid interval → decline , needs burr holes urgently. Subdural: venous, crescent-shaped, elderly / alcohol / anticoagulated, confusion and unsteadiness over 3–5 days , may recall a bump a week ago. Subarachnoid: berry aneurysm (~1% of people), thunderclap "worst headache of my life" , photophobia, no trauma; calcium channel blockers for vasospasm. Intracerebral: elderly, chronic hypertension, sudden severe heada

Seizure priority is protect the client from injury — turn them side-lying so vomit does not go into the lungs. The benzodiazepine and the documentation both come after. Never restrain a seizing client — it injures muscle and can stop their breathing — and never put anything in the mouth. Post-ictal: do very little. The brain is exhausted. Raise the head slightly, monitor vitals, and let them wake on their own — do not overstimulate them to rouse them. Head-injury room setup, their SATA: bed in the lowest position,

entries.h: Original course wording · more · more · more
entries.t: Their stroke matrix — TIA: resolves within 24 h, usually within an hour; painless; antiplatelets or anticoagulants; the only one that may get a carotid endarterectomy to prevent a future stroke. Ischemic: a clot; painless; CT before thrombolytics; rapid neuro assessment for eligibility; alteplase within 4.5 h . Hemorrhagic: sudden severe headache, nausea, photophobia; may need surgical evacuation. Headache may occur with either ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke. Sudden neurologic deficits require the stroke pathway an

Earlier study notes, retained for comparison with the guidance above. These notes may reflect a book edition or lecture convention; check the assigned source for exam wording. Ischemic strokes and TIAs do not hurt. A severe headache means a rupture. Their shorthand: a stroke is either a blocked artery or a broken one . Stroke screening is BEFAST — balance, eyes, face, arms, speech, time. NIHSS runs 0–42 : 0 is no damage, 42 is severe. Suspected stroke with airway and breathing already confirmed: next is a rapid neu

t-PA dissolves the clot, endovascular therapy removes it, a stent opens the artery, endarterectomy removes plaque . Four different answers. The early ICP change is a subtle LOC change, not Cushing's triad. If the triad is there, you are late.

entries.h: ⚠️ What it turns into — the complication for each one
entries.t: The disorder cards below run definition, causes, signs, diagnostics, management and nursing. This is the part they do not have, and it is where the exam lives: so what happens if this is missed or left? Everything here is about the space inside a rigid skull: a bleed, a clot or swelling all end in the same place if nothing is done. Disorder What it turns into Ischemic stroke Hemorrhagic transformation , particularly after thrombolysis. Cerebral edema peaking at 48–72 hours. Aspiration pneumonia from dysphagia — whi

Stroke, raised intracranial pressure, seizures, myasthenia gravis, Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, Guillain-Barré syndrome, and Huntington’s disease. Each disorder has six core sections with relevant infographics beside the notes.

entries.h: ▸ 🧠 Ischemic Stroke Time is brain Open Close

entries.t: Sudden loss of brain function because a vessel is blocked and the tissue it feeds is starved of oxygen . It accounts for about 85% of strokes. Thrombotic strokes build on atherosclerotic plaque and often come on over hours, sometimes during sleep; embolic strokes arrive suddenly from elsewhere, most often from a heart in atrial fibrillation. The dead core cannot be saved; the surrounding penumbra can, and only for a few hours — which is the whole reason for the urgency.

Hypertension is the single biggest modifiable risk factor , then atrial fibrillation , diabetes, hyperlipidaemia, smoking, obesity, physical inactivity, heavy alcohol use, obstructive sleep apnea, carotid stenosis and previous TIA or stroke. Non-modifiable: age, male sex, Black ancestry, and family history. Oral contraceptives combined with smoking in women.

Sudden onset of: one-sided weakness or numbness of the face, arm or leg; confusion; trouble speaking or understanding; visual loss; dizziness or loss of balance; or a severe headache . Deficits follow the vessel: a left-hemisphere stroke gives right-sided weakness and aphasia ; a right-hemisphere stroke gives left-sided weakness, unilateral neglect and impulsiveness . Also dysphagia, homonymous hemianopsia, emotional lability and incontinence. A transient ischemic attack resolves completely within 24 hours, and it

Non-contrast CT of the head immediately — the first job is to rule out hemorrhage, because the treatment for the two is opposite. Establish the last known well time , which decides eligibility for treatment more than anything else. NIH Stroke Scale, blood glucose (hypoglycemia mimics stroke), ECG for atrial fibrillation, coagulation studies, CBC, electrolytes and troponin. Then CT angiography or MRI, carotid ultrasound and echocardiography to find the source. A swallow screen before anything by mouth — including me

Intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase or tenecteplase within 4.5 hours of the last known well time , once hemorrhage is excluded and the exclusion criteria are checked. Mechanical thrombectomy for a large-vessel occlusion, up to 24 hours in selected clients. Then aspirin, or dual antiplatelet therapy for minor stroke, and anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation . Statin, blood pressure control, glucose control, and carotid endarterectomy for significant stenosis. Early rehabilitation.

Ask when the client was last seen normal and make sure that time is documented and handed over — it is the number the whole treatment decision rests on. Nil by mouth until the swallow screen is passed , then thickened fluids and upright positioning as directed by speech and language therapy. During and after thrombolysis: neurological checks and vital signs on the protocol schedule, no invasive lines, injections or urinary catheters for 24 hours, and report any headache, vomiting or deterioration at once — that is
Everything the practice quiz your course linked asks about, in one place. The same questions are in the NUR 258 Mega Quiz.

Embolic: a clot forms elsewhere — classically in the heart in atrial fibrillation — and travels to the brain. Thrombotic: a clot forms on a narrowed, atherosclerotic artery in the neck or brain. Hemorrhagic: uncontrolled hypertension , aneurysm, anticoagulants, older fragile vessels. TIA: symptoms last minutes to hours and resolve fully — but it is a warning and always needs urgent medical work-up . Modifiable risks: smoking, obesity, inactivity, hypertension, diabetes, high cholesterol, atrial fibrillation, heavy

entries.h: 🧠 What each part of the brain does
entries.t: Frontal: personality, judgment, voluntary movement, Broca’s area (speaking). Parietal: sensation and spatial awareness. Temporal: hearing, memory and learning, emotion , Wernicke’s area (understanding). Occipital: vision . Cerebellum: balance and coordination . Brainstem: breathing, heart rate, swallowing, consciousness. Left brain: right-sided weakness, aphasia, agraphia, alexia, impaired math, right visual field loss, slow and cautious, aware of deficits so often depressed or frustrated . Right brain: left-sided

Receptive aphasia (Wernicke): cannot understand. Expressive aphasia (Broca): understands but cannot get the words out — ask yes/no questions, use a communication board, give time, do not finish their sentences. Dysarthria = slurred speech from weak muscles. Apraxia = cannot perform a purposeful movement despite strength. Agnosia = cannot recognize objects. Agraphia = cannot write. Alexia = cannot read. Hemianopia: half the visual field is lost — teach the client to turn the head and scan ; place items in the seen f

Ischemic stroke An artery is blocked and tissue loses blood supply. Hemorrhagic stroke A vessel leaks blood into or around the brain. Time-sensitive care Urgent imaging determines the treatment pathway. Recognize Sudden face, arm, speech, vision, balance or other focal changes. Act Activate emergency stroke assessment and establish the last-known-well time. Protect Assess airway, glucose and swallowing safety; follow the stroke protocol.

entries.h: ▸ 🚨 Hemorrhagic Stroke and Cerebral Aneurysm Worst headache of my life Open Close

entries.t: Bleeding into or around the brain. Intracerebral hemorrhage is bleeding into the brain tissue itself, usually from long-standing hypertension. Subarachnoid hemorrhage is bleeding into the space around the brain, usually from a ruptured berry aneurysm . Only about 15% of strokes are hemorrhagic, but they carry much higher mortality, because blood in the skull raises pressure in a box that cannot expand.

Uncontrolled hypertension above all. Then aneurysms and arteriovenous malformations, anticoagulant and antiplatelet therapy , thrombolysis, trauma, cocaine and amphetamine use, bleeding disorders, and cerebral amyloid angiopathy in older adults. Aneurysm rupture is more common in women, with smoking, heavy alcohol use, family history and polycystic kidney disease.

Sudden, severe headache — classically described as 'the worst headache of my life' — with nausea and vomiting, neck stiffness and photophobia in subarachnoid hemorrhage, and rapid deterioration in level of consciousness. Focal deficits, seizures, and signs of rising intracranial pressure: a falling level of consciousness is the earliest and most sensitive sign, long before the late Cushing triad of rising blood pressure with a widening pulse pressure, bradycardia and irregular breathing — by then herniation is immi

Non-contrast CT immediately , which shows blood. If CT is negative and suspicion remains, lumbar puncture looking for blood or xanthochromia — but never before imaging, because a lumbar puncture with raised pressure can cause herniation . CT angiography or cerebral angiography to find the aneurysm. Frequent neurological checks with the Glasgow Coma Scale and pupil assessment , blood pressure, coagulation studies, and intracranial pressure monitoring in severe cases.

Control the blood pressure — here it is lowered, the opposite of ischemic stroke — usually with a titratable intravenous agent. Reverse anticoagulation urgently if the client is on it. Manage raised intracranial pressure with head elevation, osmotic therapy (mannitol or hypertonic saline), sedation and sometimes an external ventricular drain. Secure the aneurysm early by surgical clipping or endovascular coiling . Nimodipine for 21 days after subarachnoid hemorrhage to reduce vasospasm , which typically peaks days

Neurological checks are the intervention — changes here are the client's only warning. Report any decline in level of consciousness, new pupil asymmetry, worsening headache or vomiting immediately. Aneurysm precautions : quiet, dimly lit room, head of bed elevated 30 degrees with the head midline and the neck not flexed or rotated , limited visitors, no bright lights or loud noise, and clustering of care. Avoid anything that raises intracranial pressure: straining at stool, coughing, vomiting, hip flexion, suctioni

entries.h: ▸ 🧠 Increased Intracranial Pressure LOC first Open Close
entries.t: 🖼️ Infographics Increased Intracranial Pressure Increased ICP 1 Increased ICP 2

The skull is a fixed box holding brain tissue, blood and cerebrospinal fluid . If any one increases, another must decrease or the pressure rises — that is the Monro–Kellie doctrine. Normal intracranial pressure is 10–15 mmHg ; pressure above 20 compromises perfusion and, untreated, ends in herniation . Cerebral perfusion pressure = mean arterial pressure − intracranial pressure , and it needs to stay above 50 mmHg ( 60–70 is ideal).

Fixed space Brain tissue, blood and CSF share the adult skull. Compensation Some blood or CSF displacement initially limits pressure. Rising pressure Further expansion can reduce cerebral perfusion. Early concern A declining level of consciousness or new neurologic change needs prompt assessment. Position and care Keep the head and neck aligned; use ordered positioning, oxygenation and sedation strategies. Late danger Abnormal posturing or the Cushing response signals severe deterioration. Do not wait for these fin

Anything that adds volume: traumatic brain injury, hemorrhage, stroke with edema, tumor, abscess, meningitis and encephalitis, hydrocephalus , and metabolic causes such as hepatic encephalopathy. Made worse by hypoxia, hypercapnia, fever, seizures, pain and agitation — all of which increase cerebral blood flow or metabolic demand.

A change in level of consciousness is the earliest and most sensitive sign — restlessness, irritability, confusion, drowsiness — and it appears long before anything dramatic. Then headache worse in the morning and with coughing, projectile vomiting without nausea, pupil changes (sluggish, then unequal, then fixed and dilated on the side of the lesion), papilledema, weakness and posturing — decorticate (arms flexed inward) is less ominous than decerebrate (arms extended). The Cushing triad — rising systolic pressure

Serial neurological assessment: Glasgow Coma Scale, pupils, motor response and vital signs, at the ordered frequency and compared with the previous set. CT or MRI for the cause. Intracranial pressure monitoring by external ventricular drain, which both measures and treats, or an intraparenchymal monitor; calculate cerebral perfusion pressure. ABGs, electrolytes and osmolality, temperature, and glucose.

Mental status and speech Assess alertness, orientation, attention and speech. Describe the actual responses. Consider hearing, language, sedation and other factors that affect testing. Pupils and cranial functions Assess pupil size, equality and light response. Examine eye movement, facial symmetry, hearing and other cranial functions as indicated. Motor and sensory function Compare right and left movement, strength and sensation. Assess coordination, reflexes and gait when appropriate and safe. Document focal find

Head of bed elevated 30 degrees with the head midline to promote venous drainage. Osmotic therapy — mannitol or hypertonic saline — to pull fluid out of the brain. Sedation and analgesia; neuromuscular blockade in severe cases. Cerebrospinal fluid drainage via the ventricular drain. Controlled ventilation to maintain normal carbon dioxide; brief hyperventilation only as a rescue measure, because sustained hypocapnia causes ischemia . Treat fever and seizures aggressively. Corticosteroids for tumor-related edema, bu

Assess neurologically and report the trend, not just the number — a client who is a little harder to rouse than an hour ago is the finding that matters. Position: head of bed 30 degrees, head midline, neck neutral, hips not flexed more than 90 degrees. Avoid everything that raises pressure: clustering painful care together, suctioning for more than 10–15 seconds or without pre-oxygenation, straining, coughing, vomiting, and Valsalva. Space out interventions and give stool softeners, antiemetics and analgesia rather

Three things in the skull: brain, blood and CSF (Monro-Kellie). The body compensates by shifting CSF to the spinal canal, making less CSF and constricting cerebral vessels ; vasodilation and protein leaking into tissue (edema) push ICP up. Maintain the prescribed oxygenation and ventilation targets. Routine prophylactic hyperventilation can reduce cerebral blood flow; brief controlled hyperventilation is reserved for a prescribed emergency temporizing measure in selected patients while definitive treatment is arran

Earlier study notes, retained for comparison with the guidance above. These notes may reflect a book edition or lecture convention; check the assigned source for exam wording. PaCO2: CO2 dilates cerebral vessels — a PaCO2 above 45 raises ICP. Ventilate to 30–35 . Your course numbers: normal ICP 10–15 mmHg , report above 20 ; CPP goal above 50, ideally 60–70 . (Other sources quote ICP 5–15 and CPP 60–100.) MAP = (systolic + 2 × diastolic) ÷ 3; CPP = MAP − ICP. Example: BP 130/88 → MAP 102; ICP 12 → CPP 90. External

Earliest: change in level of consciousness — restlessness, confusion, irritability. Late: pupil changes, one-sided weakness, decorticate posturing ( flexion , arms to the core) then decerebrate ( extension , worse), Cheyne-Stokes or irregular breathing. Cushing’s triad: rising systolic with widening pulse pressure , bradycardia , slow irregular respirations — herniation is close. Doll’s eyes: eyes moving opposite to the head turn is normal; eyes fixed midline, moving with the head = brainstem damage . Unconscious (

Avoid: coughing, sneezing, straining (Valsalva), vomiting, hip flexion , neck flexion — give stool softeners and antiemetics early. HOB 30°, head midline. Fever raises ICP: antipyretic as prescribed, remove blankets, cool the room or bath — prevent shivering . Mannitol: an osmotic diuretic that blocks water and sodium reabsorption so they leave in the urine. Watch for fluid overload first (crackles, pulmonary edema) , then dehydration and electrolyte loss; not for anuria; thirst and dry mouth are expected.

entries.h: ▸ ⚡ Seizures and Status Epilepticus Open Close
entries.t: 🖼️ Infographics Seizures 2 Seizures 1

A seizure is a sudden episode of abnormal electrical activity in the brain. Epilepsy involves a persistent tendency to unprovoked seizures. Focal seizures begin in a network on one side; generalized seizures involve bilateral networks. Some are of unknown onset or unclassified. A convulsive seizure lasting 5 minutes or repeated seizures without recovery is an emergency. Simple Nursing · Seizures 1 · types and phases · Open original PDF ↗ Classification note: An aura can itself be a focal seizure; it does not occur

Simple Nursing · Seizures 2 · care and emergencies · Open original PDF ↗ Current safety guidance: A convulsive seizure reaching 5 minutes, or repeated seizures without recovery, needs urgent treatment—do not wait 30 minutes. EEG preparation follows the testing team’s instructions; do not stop antiseizure medicines or deprive sleep on your own. AES · status epilepticus · NHS · EEG preparation

Idiopathic in many people. Otherwise: head injury, stroke, brain tumor, infection (meningitis, encephalitis), hypoxia, congenital malformation, and metabolic causes — hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, hypocalcemia, uremia and liver failure . Common triggers in a person with known epilepsy: missed medication (the single commonest cause of status epilepticus), sleep deprivation, alcohol or its withdrawal, illness and fever, flashing lights, and stress .

Often an aura first — a smell, taste, visual change or rising sensation — which is itself a focal seizure and a useful warning. Tonic-clonic: loss of consciousness, stiffening then rhythmic jerking, tongue biting, incontinence, and cyanosis, followed by a postictal phase of confusion, headache, deep sleep and muscle soreness that can last hours. Focal seizures with impaired awareness show as staring with automatisms — lip smacking, picking at clothes — and are often mistaken for daydreaming or intoxication. A posti

Record onset, duration, initial body part involved, awareness, movements, eye deviation, and recovery. Check bedside glucose, oxygenation, electrolytes and possible causes; EEG and brain imaging help evaluation. Drug levels are useful for selected medicines when indicated. A normal routine EEG does not exclude epilepsy. Follow the testing team’s medication and sleep instructions.

Long-term antiseizure medicines depend on seizure type and individual risks. For convulsive status epilepticus , activate the emergency response, support airway/breathing, check glucose and treat hypoglycemia, and give a benzodiazepine per protocol (for example IV lorazepam or IM midazolam when IV access is unavailable). Persistent seizures require a second-line medicine such as levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, or valproate, with specialist escalation and monitoring. Do not delay rescue treatment while obtaining tests.

During a seizure: stay with the client, turn them on their side, protect the head, loosen tight clothing, clear the area, and time it. Never put anything in the mouth, never restrain the limbs, and never try to stop the movements — you will cause injury and you will not shorten the seizure. Afterwards, keep them on their side, suction if needed, reorient gently, allow them to sleep, and document everything you observed. Seizure precautions : bed in the lowest position with rails padded and up, suction and oxygen at

entries.h: ⚠️ What not to do during a seizure (picture)
⚡ What drives a seizure, and what sets one off
entries.t: Glutamate excites, GABA inhibits. A seizure is too much excitation or too little inhibition. Benzodiazepines and phenobarbital work by strengthening GABA. Who is at risk: hypoglycemia and other metabolic or electrolyte problems, fever, CNS infection such as meningitis, stroke, head injury, brain tumor, and alcohol or drug withdrawal. Triggers to teach: avoid alcohol (it lowers the seizure threshold), sleep loss, dehydration and heat, hormone shifts (menstruation, ovulation, pregnancy), flashing lights if photosensi

Focal aware (simple partial): stays aware and remembers it — a brief sensory change such as vision changes or tingling. Focal impaired awareness (complex partial): blank stare plus automatisms (lip smacking, hand rubbing, picking) that the client does not remember. Absence: a few seconds of staring that looks like daydreaming, mostly in children, with immediate recovery. Atonic (drop attack): sudden loss of tone and a fall, often head first — a helmet protects the head. Tonic-clonic = generalized: aura → stiffening

Phenytoin 10–20 mcg/mL. Below 10 the client is unprotected: seizure precautions and report. Above 20 is toxicity (nystagmus, unsteady gait, slurred speech). Phenytoin teaching: no antacids within 2 hours (less absorption), report any rash (Stevens-Johnson), report sore throat or easy bruising (low blood counts), meticulous oral care for gum overgrowth, regular blood levels. Tube feeding: continuous enteral feeding binds phenytoin and lowers absorption . Hold the feeding 1–2 hours before and after each dose (per pol

Focal onset Begins in a network within one hemisphere. Generalized onset Involves bilateral networks from the start. After the event Assess recovery, breathing and injury. Observe Time the event; describe movement, awareness, eye deviation and recovery rather than guessing a subtype. Protect Clear hazards, cushion the head and position on the side when feasible. Stay with the person and call for help. Avoid harm Do not restrain movements or put objects, food, drink or medication into the mouth during convulsions.

Start the clock Protect the person and summon assistance. Assess breathing Support airway and oxygenation; check glucose per protocol. Escalate promptly Use the prescribed rescue pathway for a prolonged seizure. Five-minute threshold A convulsive seizure lasting 5 minutes is a treatment emergency; do not wait 30 minutes. Medication sequence A benzodiazepine is commonly first-line, followed by a longer-acting antiseizure drug when needed. Afterward Reassess breathing and consciousness. Document duration, features, i

Neuronal excitability Drug mechanisms reduce seizure susceptibility. Steady exposure Consistent dosing supports seizure control. Safety monitoring Adverse effects and interactions vary by medicine. Carbamazepine Monitor serious rash, blood-count effects, sodium and interactions as indicated. Valproate Monitor liver, platelet and pregnancy-related risks; it has major fetal risks. Teaching Do not stop abruptly; follow the individualized monitoring and pregnancy-prevention counseling plan.

entries.h: ▸ Myasthenia Gravis (MG) Weakness worsens with use Open Close

entries.t: Autoantibodies disrupt communication at the neuromuscular junction , often involving acetylcholine receptors. Muscles become weak with repeated use and improve with rest. MG = fatigable muscle weakness ; sensation is usually preserved. Simple Nursing · Myasthenia gravis · Open original PDF ↗ Read with this correction: MG impairs nerve-to-muscle signaling; it is not a whole-body acetylcholine deficiency or a “dry body” disorder. Antibody and electrical testing are central; the older Tensilon test is rarely used. Dia

MG is autoimmune and can be associated with thymus abnormalities. Infection, surgery, exhaustion, and certain medicines can worsen weakness. Check new prescriptions with the prescriber/pharmacist for MG precautions.

Ptosis, diplopia, tiring while chewing, dysphagia, nasal/slurred speech, and neck or limb weakness. The pattern varies; eye symptoms do not have to progress in a fixed downward sequence. Weak cough, difficulty managing secretions, or new breathing/swallowing difficulty needs urgent escalation.

Antibody testing, repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fiber EMG support diagnosis; chest imaging assesses the thymus. In worsening disease, assess respiratory effort, cough, swallowing, and serial vital capacity/inspiratory strength as ordered. Normal oxygen saturation does not rule out dangerous respiratory muscle weakness. MGFA · respiratory assessment

Pyridostigmine improves neuromuscular transmission. Corticosteroids or other immune therapies control disease; selected patients undergo thymectomy. Myasthenic crisis requires airway/ventilatory support and specialist treatment, often IVIG or plasma exchange. Cholinergic excess can also cause weakness with diarrhea, sweating, secretions, or bradycardia; do not guess the cause or independently increase medicine. NHS · MG treatment

Give medicines at the prescribed times. Coordinate meals with the pyridostigmine plan, assess swallowing, and arrange rest before meals and activity. Use aspiration precautions and individualized food textures. Escalate promptly if oral medicines cannot be taken safely. Priority: breathing and swallowing before activity tolerance. MG in acute care · Symptoms and overview

entries.h: ▸ Parkinson’s Disease Movement + medication timing Open Close

entries.t: Progressive loss of dopamine-producing neurons affects movement circuits. Bradykinesia is central; resting tremor and rigidity are common. Treatment supports function and symptoms but does not cure the disease. Simple Nursing · Parkinson’s disease · Open original PDF ↗ Meal and swallowing update: Do not eliminate dietary protein. If protein affects levodopa response, individualize dose/meal timing with the care team. Food texture and thickened liquids depend on a swallowing assessment. Levodopa and meals
Risk increases with age; genetic and environmental factors contribute. Review medicines because dopamine-blocking drugs can cause or worsen parkinsonism.

Look for slow movement, resting tremor, rigidity, short shuffling steps, reduced arm swing, freezing, and balance problems . Dysphagia, constipation, orthostatic hypotension, sleep changes, depression, and cognitive changes may also occur. Not everyone has every feature. NHS · Parkinson’s symptoms

Diagnosis is mainly clinical: history, neurologic examination, and response to treatment. Imaging may help exclude other causes; a routine CT does not confirm Parkinson’s. Assess gait/falls, orthostatic symptoms, swallowing, nutrition, bowel function, cognition, and “on/off” changes. Parkinson’s overview

Carbidopa/levodopa replaces dopamine through levodopa while carbidopa reduces its peripheral breakdown. Other options include dopamine agonists, MAO-B inhibitors, and COMT inhibitors; selected patients benefit from deep brain stimulation. Monitor for dyskinesia, hallucinations, hypotension, and wearing-off. Dopamine agonists can cause sudden sleep or impulse-control problems. NHS · Parkinson’s treatment

Give the exact formulation on the patient’s individual schedule. Do not abruptly stop therapy; urgently arrange an alternative if swallowing or NPO status prevents dosing. Encourage safe movement, deliberate steps/cues, fall prevention, upright meals, and swallowing support. Plan fluids/fiber and bowel care as appropriate. Preserve independence and allow time to respond. Time-critical medicines and swallowing

entries.h: ▸ Multiple Sclerosis (MS) CNS myelin + variable deficits Open Close

entries.t: Immune-mediated injury damages myelin and nerve fibers in the central nervous system : brain, spinal cord, and optic pathways. Symptoms reflect the affected areas. MS may follow a relapsing or progressive course; it is not always relapsing-remitting. Simple Nursing · Multiple sclerosis · Open original PDF ↗ Treatment update: Use the current treatment categories below: disease-modifying therapy, short-course relapse treatment, and symptom management. Cyclosporine is not a universal first-choice MS drug, and IVIG is

The cause is multifactorial. Family history, Epstein–Barr virus exposure, and smoking are associated with risk; women are affected more often. Infection or overheating can temporarily worsen existing symptoms.

Fatigue, visual disturbance/optic neuritis, numbness, weakness, spasticity, poor balance, bladder problems, and cognitive changes. Findings vary with lesion location. Heat can worsen previous symptoms temporarily (Uhthoff phenomenon); this alone does not prove a new relapse. MS Trust · heat sensitivity

Neurologic assessment and MRI of the brain/spinal cord are key; CSF findings and other tests can support diagnosis and exclude mimics. There is no single definitive screening test. Compare new symptoms with baseline and assess for fever, infection, and other causes before labeling deterioration a relapse. NHS · diagnosis and symptoms

Disease-modifying therapies reduce inflammatory disease activity and are selected for the MS type and individual risks. A short course of high-dose corticosteroids can speed recovery from a function-limiting relapse; this is different from long-term disease control. Symptom treatment may include baclofen for spasticity and bladder/pain therapies. MS Trust · relapse treatment

Balance activity with planned rest; use cooling strategies and avoid overheating. Support safe exercise, mobility aids when needed, skin protection, bowel/bladder care, and independent self-care. Monitor treatment-specific infection risks and labs. Report persistent new deficits; sudden stroke-like symptoms need emergency assessment rather than assuming MS. NHS · treatment and support

entries.h: ▸ Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) Peripheral nerves · breathing first Open Close

entries.t: An acute immune-mediated disorder of the peripheral nerves , affecting myelin and sometimes axons. Rapidly increasing weakness can compromise breathing and swallowing. Suspected GBS requires hospital assessment and close monitoring. Simple Nursing · Guillain-Barré syndrome · Open original PDF ↗ Read with this clarification: GBS can threaten breathing and autonomic function, but death is not inevitable; most people recover. The pattern is often ascending, with variants possible. WHO · GBS
Often follows a respiratory or gastrointestinal infection. Campylobacter is a common trigger. The immune response attacks peripheral nerves; GBS is not a contagious infection itself. WHO · GBS

Bilateral weakness, often beginning in the legs and ascending, with reduced or absent deep-tendon reflexes. Tingling and nerve pain may occur. Facial/bulbar weakness can impair speech, cough and swallowing. Autonomic involvement can cause dangerous heart-rate or blood-pressure changes. WHO · GBS

Trend strength, reflexes, cough, swallowing and respiratory function, including vital capacity as ordered. Monitor heart rhythm and blood pressure. Nerve-conduction studies/EMG and lumbar puncture support the diagnosis; testing must not delay treatment of deterioration. WHO · GBS · NHS · GBS

IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) or plasma exchange treats the immune process. Severe respiratory weakness may require ventilation. Provide prescribed pain treatment, clot prevention and rehabilitation. Recovery can take months; persistent weakness or fatigue is possible. NHS · GBS

Priority: breathing, swallowing and autonomic stability. Escalate a weakening cough, trouble managing secretions, new dyspnea or unstable vital signs promptly. Prevent aspiration, pressure injury and immobility complications; support nutrition, communication and gradual rehabilitation. Explain that profound weakness does not mean the patient cannot understand you. NHS · GBS

entries.h: ▸ Huntington’s Disease (HD) Inherited · movement, thinking and mood Open Close

entries.t: A progressive inherited brain disorder caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the HTT gene . It affects movement, cognition and behavior. Huntington’s is distinct from Parkinson’s and from immune-mediated demyelinating disorders. MedlinePlus · Huntington’s genetics

Autosomal dominant inheritance: a child of a parent carrying one disease-causing copy has a 50% chance of inheriting that copy in each pregnancy. Having one affected parent does not mean every child inherits it. Offer genetic counseling for testing and family planning. NHS · Huntington’s · MedlinePlus · Huntington’s genetics

Chorea means involuntary, irregular movements. Difficulty planning, impaired judgment, depression or irritability may accompany movement changes. Later problems can include dysarthria, dysphagia, weight loss and dependence in daily activities. Presentation varies; juvenile disease can feature rigidity rather than prominent chorea. MedlinePlus · Huntington’s genetics

Review the family history and neurologic findings; genetic testing can identify the HTT expansion. Predictive testing is a personal choice supported by counseling and informed consent. Assess gait, swallowing, weight, communication, cognition, mood and caregiver needs. NHS · Huntington’s

There is no established cure. Specialist treatment targets chorea, mood and behavioral symptoms. Physical, occupational and speech/swallowing therapies help maintain function. Coordinate care and future planning with the patient and family. NHS · Huntington’s

Protect swallowing and nutrition: use the individualized swallowing plan, upright meals, adequate time and dietitian support; monitor intake and weight. Reduce fall hazards and use appropriate mobility assistance. Allow time to communicate, offer simple choices and maintain predictable routines. Assess mental health and support caregivers without assuming involuntary movements are intentional behavior. HDSA · nutrition, swallowing and communication

This chapter reviews neuro diagnostics: cerebral angiography, CT, EEG, the Glasgow Coma Scale, ICP monitoring, lumbar puncture, MRI, PET/SPECT, and x-ray, covering purpose, informed consent, prep, and nursing care before, during, and after each test.

From this module — built from the notes above on this page, not a section of the ATI chapter. Explain the procedure fully — neurological tests are frightening and much of the distress is avoidable. Screen for metal implants, pacemakers and pregnancy before MRI ; the scanner magnet is always on. Check renal function and contrast allergy before contrast studies. Check anticoagulation and platelets before lumbar puncture. Establish a neurological baseline before the procedure, so any change afterwards is interpretable

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2025 . About 10 to 40 percent of patients get a headache after a lumbar puncture, usually within two to three days. Choosing a small, non-cutting spinal needle of 24 gauge or smaller lowers that headache risk to roughly 2 percent. The headache is positional, easing when the patient lies flat and returning within minutes of sitting up. Most cases resolve on their own within one to two weeks with rest, fluids, and caffeine. StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf) · Postdural Punc

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from MedlinePlus, 2025 . Normal cerebrospinal fluid is clear and essentially free of cells, protein, and toxins. Cloudy or abnormal fluid can point to an infection, an autoimmune condition, or another disease of the brain or spinal cord. MedlinePlus (National Library of Medicine) · Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) Analysis · open the source →

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from MedlinePlus, 2025 . CSF analysis checks fluid drawn by spinal tap for infections such as meningitis and encephalitis, plus autoimmune disease, bleeding, or tumors. Collecting the sample during the lumbar puncture takes about five minutes, and the patient needs to stay still throughout. Providers usually order more tests to confirm a diagnosis rather than relying on the CSF result alone.

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from NINDS, 2026 . EEG records the brain's electrical activity through scalp electrodes and usually takes about an hour to complete. A longer, sleep-based EEG of about four hours may be needed to capture a seizure that a routine study misses. Cerebral angiography injects dye into blood vessels to show aneurysms, malformations, and areas of narrowing or blockage in the brain. NINDS (NIH) · Neurological Diagnostic Tests and Procedures · open the source →

Have the client avoid food and fluids for at least 6 hr before angiography. Assess allergy history; a contrast allergy may need pretreatment with a steroid or antihistamine. Bleeding disorders or anticoagulant use call for extra monitoring for post-procedure clotting. Check BUN and creatinine to confirm the kidneys can clear the contrast dye. A mild sedative may be given; monitor vital signs continuously during the procedure. After the procedure, closely watch the insertion site to confirm clotting occurs. Restrict

Sedation or anxiolysis for MRI in claustrophobia, with proper monitoring. Hold antiepileptics before EEG only if specifically instructed ; usually they are continued. Avoid caffeine before EEG; sleep deprivation may be requested deliberately. Contrast agents — check allergy and renal function; hold metformin per policy. Analgesia for post-lumbar-puncture headache; a blood patch if it persists.

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from NINDS, 2026 . For a lumbar puncture the patient lies curled on one side or leans forward so a needle can pass between two vertebrae. A local anesthetic numbs the lower back before the needle is inserted to withdraw roughly three teaspoons of spinal fluid. The sample can help detect brain bleeding, infection, multiple sclerosis, metabolic disease, or other neurologic conditions. NINDS (NIH) · Neurological Diagnostic Tests and Procedures · open the source →

The head will be immobilized; the client must stay still throughout the procedure. Void immediately before the cerebral angiography procedure begins. Expect a metallic taste and a warm sensation right after dye injection. A catheter goes into a groin or neck artery to inject dye and take x-rays. After imaging, the catheter is removed and pressure or a closure device seals the artery.

Neurologist and neuroradiologist for selection and interpretation. Radiology technologist for safety screening and positioning. Anesthesia where sedation is needed. Pharmacist for contrast interactions and antiepileptic timing. Rehabilitation team alerted early where results suggest a deficit.

Cerebral angiography risks bleeding or hematoma at the arterial entry site. After angiography, check the site and distal pulses, color, and refill; apply pressure and notify the provider for bleeding. Before contrast or sedated CT, hold food and fluids 4 hr ; shellfish allergy alone doesn't rule out iodine contrast. Remove all metal objects before CT or MRI; the client wears a hospital gown. EEG recording runs 45 to 120 min ; wash hair first and skip caffeine, stimulants, or sedatives as directed. Total GCS score e

Sensory input Peripheral nerves carry information toward the CNS. Integration Brain and spinal cord process information. Motor output Peripheral pathways carry signals to muscles and organs. Central nervous system Brain and spinal cord: processing, coordination and many reflex pathways. Peripheral nervous system Nerves outside the CNS include sensory, somatic motor and autonomic pathways. Localize the problem Distribution, reflexes, strength and sensation help identify which pathways may be affected.

ATI Active Learning Template — System Disorder Pain Management Filled from ATI chapter 5 , row by row from that chapter’s own sections — 12 of 12 rows have content. 8 rows came from outside your ATI chapter — 2 cite a source, 6 are built from this page’s own notes. Each one is labeled.

Chapter covers holistic pain management: nurses' duty to assess and treat pain using self-report as the gold standard, nociceptive versus neuropathic physiology, acute versus chronic patterns, and a focused assessment covering location, quality, intensity, timing, and aggravating or relieving factors.

Pain is what the client says it is. Believe the report; disbelief is the commonest barrier to treating it. Prevent rather than chase — scheduled analgesia for predictable pain, and premedication before painful procedures. Start a bowel regimen the same day an opioid starts. Screen for the beliefs that drive under-treatment: fear of addiction, of being a nuisance, and of masking a diagnosis. Multimodal analgesia lowers opioid requirement and side effects.

Undertreatment risk factors: cultural attitudes, lack of knowledge, fear of addiction, and exaggerated fear of respiratory depression. Infants, children, older adults, and clients with substance use disorder face the highest risk of undertreated pain. Common pain causes include trauma, surgery, cancer, arthritis, fibromyalgia, and neuropathy. Cancer pain can stem from tumor invasion, nerve compression, bone metastases, infection, or immobility. Diagnostic or treatment procedures, such as injections, intubation, or

Nonverbal cues can supplement self-report: facial grimacing, restlessness, pacing, or guarding. Moaning, crying, and a shortened attention span can signal pain in nonverbal clients. Vital signs may rise briefly with acute pain but normalize even as pain continues. Because vital signs stabilize over time, they aren't a reliable long-term pain measure.

No laboratory test measures pain. Renal and hepatic function, since both change opioid and NSAID dosing. Acetaminophen level in suspected overdose; watch the total daily dose across combination products. CBC before NSAIDs where bleeding risk or low platelets are a concern. Urine drug screening where a monitoring agreement is in place — used to support care, never as a punishment.

Structured assessment: site, quality, severity, timing, aggravating and relieving factors, and functional effect. A consistent scale used the same way each time; a behavioral tool where the client cannot self-report. Reassess after every intervention and document it. Distinguish nociceptive from neuropathic pain — burning, shooting and electric pain needs an adjuvant, not more opioid. Function is the better outcome: sleeping, walking, eating, and getting out of the chair.

Parenteral opioids suit immediate, short-term acute pain; oral suits stable chronic pain. Nonpharmacologic options, such as yoga, meditation, distraction, heat or cold, and TENS, can lower medication needs. The WHO analgesic ladder starts with nonopioids and progresses through weak to strong opioids as needed. Oral opioid dosing needs a higher dose than IV because less medication reaches the bloodstream. Acetaminophen must not exceed 4 g per day for clients 50 kg (110 lb) or more. Acetaminophen can be safely combin

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2023 . Mild pain is treated first with a non-opioid such as an NSAID or acetaminophen, with or without an adjuvant drug. Moderate pain adds a weaker opioid like hydrocodone, codeine, or tramadol, often paired with a non-opioid agent. Severe pain calls for a stronger opioid such as morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl, or methadone. Adjuvant drugs such as antidepressants, anticonvulsants, topical anesthetics, and corticosteroids can boost pain control alongside the primary

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2023 . Patient-controlled analgesia lets the patient self-dose IV pain medication within limits set by the prescriber. A lockout interval blocks another dose for a set time after each button press, even if the patient tries again sooner. One- and four-hour dose caps alert staff when a patient's pain is not being controlled within the ordered limits. Nurses should reassess pain and sedation level every one to two hours for the first day or two of therapy. Only the pa

Report pain early — it is easier to control before it is severe. Explain that addiction is uncommon when opioids treat real pain , and what tolerance and physical dependence actually mean. Constipation is expected with opioids and is prevented, not waited for. No alcohol or unprescribed sedatives with opioids; do not drive until the effect is known. Store opioids locked and dispose of leftovers properly — most misused prescription opioids come from a friend or relative’s cabinet.

Pain service or anesthesia for regional blocks and patient-controlled analgesia. Pharmacist for opioid rotation and equianalgesic conversion. Physiotherapy and occupational therapy — function and pain move together. Psychology for cognitive behavioral therapy, which has good evidence in chronic pain. Palliative care for complex pain, whatever the prognosis.

Undertreated pain can worsen anxiety with acute cases or fuel depression with chronic pain. Opioid overdose can cause sedation, respiratory depression, and coma. Identify clients at high risk for over-sedation, such as older adults. Titrate opioid doses carefully while closely monitoring respiratory status. Hold the opioid and give naloxone if breathing drops under 8/min , is shallow, or the client won't wake. Monitor closely after giving naloxone; the opioid can outlast it, requiring repeat doses. ATI Active Learning Template — System Disorder Meningitis Filled from ATI chapter 6 , row by row from that chapter’s own sections — 12 of 12 rows have content. 4 rows came from outside your ATI chapter — 4 cite a source, 0 are built from this page’s own notes. Each one is labeled.

Meningitis inflames the meninges protecting the brain and spinal cord. Viral meningitis is common and self-limiting; fungal affects immunocompromised clients; bacterial meningitis is highly contagious with high mortality, requiring rapid diagnosis and vaccination-based prevention.

Hib vaccine: 4-dose series starting at 2 months , final dose at 12-15 months PPSV targets respiratory infection but also lowers CNS infection risk Vaccinate immunocompromised adults, those with chronic disease, smokers, and LTC residents Give one PPSV dose to unvaccinated adults over 65 with no prior disease MCV4 covers Neisseria meningitidis; give it before college dorm living Immunize other communal-living groups too, such as military recruits

Viral meningitis follows viral illness (mumps, measles, herpes, West Nile); no vaccine exists Fungal meningitis (Cryptococcus neoformans) is a severe sinus-based infection Bacterial meningitis often follows infections like otitis media, pneumonia, or sinusitis Bacterial organisms: Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae A weakened immune system (immunosuppression) raises meningitis risk considerably Direct spinal fluid contamination is a risk factor Invasive procedures, skull fractu

Severe constant headache, nuchal rigidity, and photophobia are classic subjective complaints Fever, chills, nausea, and vomiting are common objective findings Altered consciousness ranges from confusion to lethargy, difficulty arousing, or coma Positive Kernig's sign: leg extension from flexed hip causes pain/resistance Positive Brudzinski's sign: neck flexion causes involuntary hip and knee flexion Hyperactive deep tendon reflexes and tachycardia can occur Seizures and marked restlessness or irritability may also
Culture/sensitivity of urine, throat, nose, blood guides antibiotic choice, not diagnostic alone CBC typically shows an elevated white blood cell count

Lumbar puncture with CSF exam is the top test confirming meningitis Bacterial CSF: cloudy, high WBC/protein, low glucose, high pressure Viral meningitis CSF typically appears clear rather than cloudy CIE on CSF distinguishes viral from protozoal cause, especially if antibiotics were given first CT or MRI can reveal increased ICP or a brain abscess

Isolate the client right away once meningitis is suspected; start droplet precautions Continue droplet precautions until 24 hr of antibiotics and secretions clear Report meningococcal cases to the public health department promptly Keep a quiet, dim environment with minimal stimuli; raise HOB to 30° Have the client avoid coughing or sneezing, which raise ICP; use seizure precautions Replace fluids and electrolytes per lab results; older adults risk secondary pneumonia Watch vital signs for septic shock and monitor f

Ceftriaxone or cefotaxime plus vancomycin covers bacterial meningitis until cultures return Antifungals treat fungal meningitis; antivirals treat viral meningitis Phenytoin is given for rising ICP or an active seizure Acetaminophen or ibuprofen treat headache and fever; avoid opioids that mask consciousness Ciprofloxacin, rifampin, or ceftriaxone are given prophylactically to close contacts Dexamethasone or prednisone corticosteroids are given to reduce inflammation

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2023 . Anyone suspected of having bacterial meningitis should get a lumbar puncture to collect CSF for gram stain, culture, cell count, glucose, and protein. Bacterial meningitis typically shows low glucose, high protein, and a high neutrophil count on the CSF sample. A gram stain or positive culture from the CSF confirms the diagnosis and guides antibiotic choice. StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf) · Bacterial Meningitis · open the source →

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from CDC, 2026 . Routine meningococcal conjugate vaccination is recommended for all preteens and teens as part of the standard immunization schedule. A meningococcal B vaccine series is also available and may be recommended for certain higher-risk patients. Vaccination greatly lowers risk but cannot prevent every case, so patients should still seek care promptly for fever, headache, or stiff neck. Mild, temporary side effects such as soreness lasting one to five days are common afte

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from CDC, 2024 . Patients with known or suspected meningococcal meningitis are placed on droplet precautions until they have had 24 hours of effective antibiotics. Staff who were within about three feet of the patient for more than eight hours need preventive antibiotics regardless of vaccination status. Preventive antibiotics such as rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone are most effective when started within 24 hours of exposure. Infectious disease specialists, emergency physici

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2023 . Roughly one in four people with meningococcal disease develops a lasting complication. Documented after-effects include seizures, hearing loss, vision loss, and problems with memory, balance, coordination, or speech. Bacterial meningitis carries a mortality rate of about 10 to 15 percent. Delayed treatment can let intracranial pressure rise and reduce blood flow to the brain, which can be fatal. StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf) · Bacterial Meningitis · open the so

ATI Active Learning Template — System Disorder Seizures and Epilepsy Filled from ATI chapter 7 , row by row from that chapter’s own sections — 12 of 12 rows have content. 2 rows came from outside your ATI chapter — 2 cite a source, 0 are built from this page’s own notes. Each one is labeled.

Seizures are sudden abnormal brain electrical discharges causing altered consciousness or motor/sensory changes; epilepsy means recurrent unprovoked seizures. This chapter covers seizure types, triggers, safety care, medications, surgical options, and status epilepticus.

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from CDC, 2024 . Preventing head injury lowers epilepsy risk — using seat belts, car seats, helmets, and fall precautions all help. Managing stroke risk through a healthy diet, activity, not smoking, and limiting alcohol also lowers epilepsy risk since stroke can trigger it. Cysticercosis, a preventable parasitic infection, is the leading cause of epilepsy worldwide and is avoided through handwashing and safe food and water. Staying current on recommended vaccines helps prevent infe

Genetic predisposition raises absence-seizure risk, especially in children Acute fever, head trauma, cerebral edema, and stroke (first 24 hr ) can trigger seizures Abrupt AED discontinuation can cause rebound seizure activity Infection, metabolic imbalance, toxin exposure, and hypoxia are common causes Brain tumors and fluid or electrolyte imbalances can also trigger seizures In older adults, cerebrovascular disease raises seizure risk considerably Hormonal shifts with menses or pregnancy can change seizure pattern

Generalized seizures affect both cerebral hemispheres; some start with an aura Tonic-clonic: brief muscle stiffening and loss of consciousness, then 1-2 min of rhythmic jerking Breathing can stop in the tonic phase and turn irregular, causing cyanosis A postictal period of confusion and sleepiness follows tonic-clonic seizures Tonic seizures: sudden loss of consciousness with increased muscle tone only Myoclonic seizures: brief, symmetric or asymmetric jerking or stiffening of limbs Atonic/akinetic seizures: second
Check alcohol and illicit substance levels, HIV status, and toxin screening if indicated CBC, electrolytes, BUN, and glucose help rule out other causes
EEG records brain electrical activity to pinpoint seizure origin MRI, CT/CAT, PET, CSF analysis, or skull x-ray can identify the cause

Shield the client from onlookers while a seizure runs; dignity is part of seizure care. Position for a patent airway; suction secretions and turn the client onto their side Loosen tight clothing; never restrain the client or force the jaw open Never insert padded tongue blades or any object into the mouth Document seizure onset, duration, consciousness, apnea, cyanosis, motor activity, and incontinence Postictal: keep the client side-lying, check vitals, assess injuries, do neuro checks Ask about an aura afterward

AEDs like phenytoin aim to control seizures using one medication first If one AED fails, the dose is raised or another drug added Routine blood tests confirm therapeutic AED levels and medication adherence

Vagal nerve stimulation treats focal seizures unresponsive to medication therapy The device implants in the left chest wall, wired to the left vagus nerve It delivers programmed intermittent brain stimulation tailored to the client's needs

Take AEDs at the same time daily to boost their effectiveness Tolerance or age-related sensitivity may need more frequent level checks and dose changes Watch for drug-specific side effects and food or drug interactions Some AEDs cause gum overgrowth — stress routine oral hygiene and dental visits Phenytoin lowers oral contraceptive effectiveness — advise backup birth control Several AEDs reduce warfarin absorption and speed its metabolism, weakening anticoagulation Antiseizure drugs raise birth-defect risk — pregna
Refer clients to community resources like the Epilepsy Foundation For school-age children, involve the disability office to arrange an IEP

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from CDC, 2024 . Sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP) affects about 1 in 1,000 adults with epilepsy each year, and about 1 in 4,500 children. The strongest risk factors are generalized seizures and seizures that are frequent or poorly controlled. SUDEP most often occurs during sleep, from a combination of breathing pauses and dangerous heart rhythm changes during a seizure. Taking antiseizure medication consistently is described as the most important step a patient can take t

ATI Active Learning Template — System Disorder Headaches Filled from ATI chapter 12 , row by row from that chapter’s own sections — 12 of 12 rows have content. 3 rows came from outside your ATI chapter — 1 cite a source, 2 are built from this page’s own notes. Each one is labeled.

Headaches range from primary (migraine, tension, cluster — no organic cause) to secondary (tumor, aneurysm — needs workup). This chapter details migraine and cluster headache patterns, triggers, diagnostics, pain management, medications, and prevention.

Teach stress-management strategies and how to recognize headache triggers A headache diary helps track type and response to treatment Hand hygiene helps prevent viral illness that mimics cold symptoms Review OTC medications and herbal remedy options for pain control Common triggers: alcohol, allergies, strong odors, bright light, medication overuse Other triggers: fatigue, sleep loss, depression, stress, anxiety, hormone shifts
Cluster headaches tend to peak during spring and fall Cluster headaches are more common in males aged 20-50

Migraines bring photophobia, phonophobia, nausea or vomiting, and unilateral pain behind the eye Migraine symptoms usually stay consistent and disrupt ADLs for 4-72 hr Classic migraine (with aura): prodrome of irritability, cravings, or GI change beforehand Aura stage brings numbness, tingling, confusion, and visual flashes over minutes to an hour Second stage: severe throbbing pain with nausea, vomiting, drowsiness, and vertigo over hours Common migraine (no aura): unilateral pulsating pain worsened by activity fo

No routine bloods — primary headache is a clinical diagnosis. ESR and CRP in anyone over 50 with a new headache — giant cell arteritis. Lumbar puncture where subarachnoid hemorrhage or meningitis is suspected and imaging is normal. Electrolytes, glucose and toxicology for headache with confusion. A sudden, worst-ever, thunderclap headache is imaged and investigated, never treated as migraine.
Neuroimaging is warranted for neuro findings or new headaches after age 50

Pain management is the main focus of care during a headache episode Keep the environment cool, dark, and quiet; raise the head of bed to 30° Give prescribed analgesics and antiemetics as ordered by the provider

Abortive therapy works best during the aura or right after headache onset For mild migraine: NSAIDs, acetaminophen, or OTC migraine-formula anti-inflammatories Metoclopramide, an antiemetic, relieves migraine-related nausea and vomiting For severe migraine: triptans like zolmitriptan, sumatriptan, or eletriptan cause vasoconstriction Ergotamine combined with caffeine narrows blood vessels and reduces inflammation Isometheptene combination drugs are used when other options fail Preventive therapy: NSAID plus a beta-
Home oxygen at 12 L/min for 15-20 min can relieve cluster pain within 15 min

Keep a headache diary of patterns and triggers; report new neuro changes Stay in a cool, dark, quiet room and elevate the head of bed Women over age 50 face higher cardiovascular and stroke risk Avoid tyramine foods like pickles, caffeine, beer, wine, aged cheese, processed meats Estrogen, nitroglycerin, and nifedipine are medications that can trigger migraines Manage anger and conflict, get enough sleep, and avoid light glare Track your menstrual cycle — hormone shifts around menses can trigger migraines

Neurologist for refractory or atypical headache and for preventive therapy. Pharmacist — medication overuse headache is common and is caused by the treatment. Psychology for cognitive behavioral therapy and biofeedback, which have real evidence. Physiotherapy for cervicogenic headache. Ophthalmology where visual symptoms or raised intracranial pressure are suspected.

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from StatPearls, 2025 . Using simple pain relievers or NSAIDs on 15 or more days a month can itself trigger medication overuse headache. Using combination analgesics, triptans, ergots, or opioids on just 10 or more days a month carries the same risk. The pattern is diagnosed when headaches occur 15 or more days a month for over three months in someone with an existing headache disorder. Complete withdrawal of the overused medication gives the best outcome, though about half of patie

ATI Active Learning Template — System Disorder Stroke Filled from ATI chapter 16 , row by row from that chapter’s own sections — 12 of 12 rows have content. 3 rows came from outside your ATI chapter — 3 cite a source, 0 are built from this page’s own notes. Each one is labeled.

Covers stroke pathophysiology, hemorrhagic vs. ischemic types, risk factors, and FAST recognition, plus emergency nursing priorities, thrombolytic and anticoagulant therapy, surgical options, and rehabilitation needs for post-stroke deficits like aphasia and neglect.

Hypertension, diabetes, and smoking raise stroke risk — treat early to reduce it. Control blood pressure, keep glucose in target range, and quit smoking to lower risk. Maintain a healthy weight and exercise regularly to reduce stroke risk. Use FAST to screen for stroke: face drooping, arm drift, slurred speech, time to call 911.

Cerebral aneurysm or AV malformation increases hemorrhagic stroke risk. Higher stroke risk in Black American, Hispanic, Indigenous, and Alaska Native populations. A family history of stroke raises a person's overall risk. Age over 65 years raises ischemic stroke risk. Diabetes mellitus and obesity are both modifiable risk factors. Untreated sleep apnea also contributes to stroke risk. Hypertension, atherosclerosis, and hyperlipidemia are major vascular risk factors. Hypercoagulable states such as sickle cell diseas

Sudden stroke signs: severe headache, dizziness, gait or vision changes, confusion, slurred speech, unilateral numbness. TIA causes brief neuro deficits from focal ischemia without permanent damage. TIA symptoms resolve within 1-24 hours with no lasting deficits. Deficits are contralateral to the damaged hemisphere — left damage causes right-sided weakness. Aphasia types: expressive (cannot speak) and receptive (cannot understand language). Agnosia is failure to recognize familiar objects; alexia is trouble reading

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from AHA/ASA, 2023 . Stroke workup includes blood tests along with the medical history and neurologic exam, though the page does not name a specific required panel. Results from laboratory testing are combined with imaging findings rather than used alone to confirm a stroke diagnosis. American Stroke Association · Common Diagnosis Methods · open the source →

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from AHA/ASA, 2023 . CT and MRI scans are the primary imaging tools used to diagnose stroke. MRI gives a sharper, more detailed picture of brain injury than CT. Electrical tests such as EEG and evoked response testing, plus blood-flow tests like ultrasound and angiography, may add further diagnostic detail. American Stroke Association · Common Diagnosis Methods · open the source →

Priority: assess LOC, airway patency, vital signs, and circulation first. Check VS every 15 min to 2 hr ; report BP over 185/110 mm Hg . Give oxygen to keep saturation above 94% or if LOC drops. Place on a cardiac monitor and obtain a 12-lead ECG for dysrhythmias. Watch for rising ICP signs like decreasing level of consciousness. Check glucose; hyperglycemia is linked to worse neurologic outcomes. Elevate head of bed to 30° and keep neck midline to lower ICP. Start seizure precautions and perform frequent neurologi

Alteplase (tPA) dissolves clots; give within 3 to 4.5 hr of symptom onset. Alteplase goal: administer within 45 minutes of ED arrival. Alteplase is contraindicated with active bleeding; hold antiplatelets or anticoagulants 24 hrs . Watch for alteplase adverse effects: hypotension, intracranial bleeding, bruising. Warfarin targets INR 2 to 3 for atrial fibrillation-related stroke prevention. Anticoagulant therapy is avoided for clients with hemorrhagic stroke. DOACs (dabigatran, apixaban, rivaroxaban) are alternativ

Thrombolytic therapy must start within 6 hr of symptom onset. Thrombolytics are contraindicated in hemorrhagic stroke or high bleeding risk. MRI rules out hemorrhage before starting thrombolytic therapy. Thrombectomy to remove the clot can be mechanical, endovascular, or intra-arterial. Carotid angioplasty with stenting places a stent via femoral catheter access. Stenting causes less blood loss and a shorter hospital stay than endarterectomy.

Follow prescribed liquid and food consistency levels to reduce choking risk. Sit upright and tuck chin forward when swallowing to lower aspiration risk. Unilateral neglect means the client can't see, feel, or move the affected side. Neglect raises injury risk and creates a self-care deficit on that side. Dress and care for the affected side of the body first each time. Pull the affected limb to midline to protect it from the wheelchair. Periodically look toward the affected side to stay aware of it.

Stroke team includes neurologist, social worker, rehab coordinators, psychologist, PT/OT, SLP, dietitian, pharmacist. SLP provides language therapy and helps manage swallowing difficulties. PT rebuilds ambulation using canes, walkers, or wheelchair adaptations. OT restores hand and arm function; recommends massage or gloves if it doesn't return. Social services arrange rehab placement and evaluate home safety needs before discharge.

Not in your ATI chapter — filled from AHA/ASA, 2023 . Reduced mobility and swallowing trouble after stroke can let material enter the lungs and cause pneumonia. Immobility after stroke raises the risk of deep vein thrombosis from blood pooling in the leg veins. Seizures are described as common after larger strokes because of abnormal electrical activity in the injured brain tissue. Post-stroke depression is a treatable complication that can be more severe in patients with a prior history of depression. Prolonged pr

Additional lecture and study notes. Posturing scores on GCS motor: decorticate = 3, decerebrate = 2. Scale runs 3–15 — "an object gets 3." Eye 4, verbal 5, motor 6. ≤8: sedate and intubate. A drop from 14 to 10 is the reportable event. With posturing and high ICP, elevate the HOB to 30° first — it takes seconds, and mannitol has to be fetched and mixed. Mannitol and 3% saline are interchangeable as osmotic options on their items. Hematoma pattern recognition — Epidural : arterial, temple blow, brief LOC then lucid

entries.h: Concussion, contusion and diffuse axonal injury
entries.t: A concussion is a traumatic disturbance of brain function. Headache, dizziness, confusion, amnesia, nausea and difficulty concentrating can occur even when routine imaging shows no structural injury. A contusion is a focal area of bruised or bleeding brain tissue. Injury may occur beneath the impact or on the opposite side as the brain moves within the skull—coup and contrecoup injury. Diffuse axonal injury results from forces that stretch and shear nerve fibers across multiple brain regions. Severe injury can caus

entries.h: Brain death is different from coma
entries.t: Death by neurologic criteria means permanent loss of function of the brain as a whole, including the brainstem. Coma, a low Glasgow Coma Scale score, sedation or a single test result does not establish this diagnosis. Qualified clinicians determine whether the injury is permanent and whether the required prerequisites have been met. The assessment includes coma, absence of brainstem reflexes and absence of spontaneous breathing during a formal apnea test. Confounding medicines, hypothermia and major metabolic distu

entries.h: Degenerative disc disease and nerve compression
entries.t: Intervertebral discs cushion the vertebrae. With degeneration, a disc loses water and structural strength; herniated disc material can press on a nerve root or the spinal cord. Root compression may cause pain radiating along an arm or leg, tingling, reduced sensation, weakness and altered reflexes. The location of the compressed nerve helps explain the pattern. Assessment includes pain, gait, strength, sensation, reflexes and bowel or bladder changes. MRI may identify disc or nerve compression when indicated. Many

Use pillows and supported alignment to reduce strain. New bladder or bowel changes, saddle numbness or worsening leg weakness needs urgent assessment. Read the steps and sources Open full-size image Original Study Hub nursing illustration.

entries.h: Bell palsy: protect the eye and assess the whole patient
entries.t: Bell palsy causes acute peripheral facial-nerve dysfunction, usually affecting facial movement on one side. Weakness may involve the forehead, eyelid and mouth, with altered taste, ear discomfort or difficulty keeping food in the cheek. The diagnosis follows clinical assessment and exclusion of other causes. Forehead movement alone cannot safely rule out stroke; new facial weakness with other acute neurologic findings needs an emergency stroke assessment. Early prescribed corticosteroid treatment can improve recove

entries.h: ALS: plan support before a crisis
entries.t: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis involves progressive loss of upper and lower motor neurons. Weakness, muscle wasting, fasciculations, stiffness and changes in speech or swallowing may occur. Clinical assessment and electrodiagnostic testing help establish the diagnosis and exclude mimics. Sensation is often relatively preserved, but cognitive or behavioral changes can occur. Specialist treatment may slow progression or treat symptoms, while rehabilitation and assistive technology support function. Assess breathing, c

entries.h: Brain abscess: focal infection with mass effect
entries.t: A brain abscess is a localized collection of infection within brain tissue. Organisms may spread from an ear, sinus or dental infection, enter after trauma or surgery, or reach the brain through the bloodstream. Immunosuppression increases risk. Headache, focal weakness or language change, seizure and declining consciousness can occur; fever may be absent. Contrast-enhanced brain imaging identifies the lesion and surrounding edema. Blood cultures and, when obtained, aspiration material help identify the organism. T
