📚 Outline: Module 8 — Part 1 Endocrinology · Part 3 Endocrine Disorders

Nearly every endocrine disease is one gland doing too much or too little, and the two are mirror images. Learn one side properly and you get the other for free. Negative feedback: the product switches off its own signal. If the product is high and the signal is also high, the problem is the gland giving the signal.

Hypothalamus → pituitary → target gland → hormone. The hormone then feeds back and turns the top of the chain off. Primary problem = the target gland itself. Hormone low, and the pituitary signal (TSH, ACTH) is high because it is shouting at a gland that cannot answer. Secondary problem = the pituitary . Hormone low and the signal is low too. Both numbers low → the problem is upstream. One low, one high → the problem is the gland.

Hypothyroid Hyperthyroid Everything is Slow and cold Fast and hot Signs Fatigue, weight gain , cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, hair loss, bradycardia, depression, menorrhagia Weight loss with good appetite, heat intolerance, diarrhea, tremor, tachycardia, anxiety, insomnia, exophthalmos in Graves TSH (primary) High Low T3 / T4 Low High Crisis Myxedema coma — hypothermia, hypotension, bradycardia, unresponsive Thyroid storm — fever >38.5 , tachycardia, agitation, delirium TSH moves opposite to the thyroid

PTH raises serum calcium — it pulls it from bone, reabsorbs it in the kidney, and activates vitamin D to absorb it from the gut. Phosphate moves the opposite way. Hyperparathyroid → high calcium → stones, bones, groans and moans : renal calculi, bone pain and fractures, constipation and abdominal pain, lethargy and confusion. Reflexes are depressed . Hypoparathyroid → low calcium → irritable everything : tetany, perioral tingling, muscle cramps, Chvostek and Trousseau signs, and the one that kills — laryngospasm .

Cushing (too much cortisol) Addison (too little) Body Central obesity, moon face , buffalo hump , thin limbs, purple striae, thin skin, bruising Weight loss , fatigue, anorexia, bronze hyperpigmentation Sodium / water Retained — hypertension, edema Lost — hypotension, dehydration Potassium Low High Glucose High Low Immunity Suppressed — infection risk, poor healing — Addisonian crisis — profound hypotension, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia and shock, often triggered by stress, infection, or abruptly stopping steroids .

Type 1 Type 2 Problem No insulin — autoimmune beta-cell destruction Insulin resistance plus relative deficiency Onset Usually young, abrupt Usually adult, gradual Ketones Yes — DKA Rarely — HHS instead The three Ps: polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia. Glucose spills into the urine and drags water with it. entries.h: ▸ M9 Anemia · Blood Disorders · Hypertension Week 9
entries.t: 📚 Outline: Module 9 — Part 1 Anemia · Part 2 RBC and Platelet Disorders · Part 3 The Healthy Heart · Part 4 Hypertension · Part 5 Cardiac Disorders (pt 1)

Every anemia, whatever its cause, ends in the same place: not enough oxygen reaching tissue. That is why they all share fatigue, pallor, tachycardia and breathlessness — and why the cause is what makes them different, not the symptoms. Classify by cell size first: small, normal, or large. That one number narrows it immediately.

MCV Type Causes Clue Low microcytic Small, pale cells Iron deficiency (commonest of all), thalassemia, chronic disease Pica , spoon nails (koilonychia), low ferritin Normal normocytic Normal size, too few Acute blood loss , hemolysis, chronic kidney disease, aplastic anemia In CKD the problem is erythropoietin , not iron High macrocytic Large, immature cells B12 deficiency, folate deficiency B12 causes neurological signs — numbness, tingling, gait and balance problems. Folate does not. Pernicious anemia is B12 defi

Sickle cell is autosomal recessive . Under stress — hypoxia, dehydration, infection, cold, acidosis, high altitude — hemoglobin S polymerizes, the cell stiffens into a sickle, and it jams small vessels. Vaso-occlusive crisis — severe pain, most often in bones, chest and abdomen. Treatment is hydration, oxygen, analgesia (opioids are appropriate) and warmth. Acute chest syndrome — chest pain, fever, hypoxia and a new infiltrate. A leading cause of death. Functional asplenia — repeated infarction destroys the spleen,

Disorder What happens Key point Thrombocytopenia <150,000 Too few platelets — petechiae, purpura, bleeding gums Spontaneous bleeding risk rises sharply below 20,000 ITP Autoimmune destruction of platelets Otherwise well patient with a low count DIC Clotting and bleeding at the same time. Widespread microthrombi consume the clotting factors and platelets, so the patient then bleeds from everywhere. Low platelets, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer , prolonged PT/aPTT. Triggered by sepsis, trauma, obstetric emergency, mali

entries.h: ❤️ The healthy heart, in one card
entries.t: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume. Stroke volume depends on three things: Preload — how full the ventricle is before it contracts. Volume. Afterload — the resistance it must push against. Mostly blood pressure. Contractility — how hard the muscle squeezes. Frank–Starling: more stretch gives a stronger contraction — up to a point. Past that point the fibers are overstretched and output falls . That failure point is heart failure. Ejection fraction normal 55–70% . Below 40% is systolic failure.

Category Systolic Diastolic Normal <120 and <80 Elevated 120–129 and <80 Stage 1 130–139 or 80–89 Stage 2 ≥140 or ≥90 Crisis >180 and/or >120 Primary (essential) hypertension is ~90–95% — no single identifiable cause. Secondary has one: renal disease, renal artery stenosis, hyperaldosteronism, phaeochromocytoma, sleep apnea, oral contraceptives. It is called silent because it damages arteries for years without a single symptom. Headache and nosebleed are late, not early. End-organ damage: heart (LVH, failure, MI),

Erikson, Piaget, play and fear for all five stages, and the milestones that actually get asked. Almost every stage question is really asking what this age is afraid of — match the intervention to the fear and it answers itself.
One table answers a third of this course.

Physical growth Track serial measurements on appropriate growth charts. Developmental skills Motor, language, social and adaptive abilities emerge. Support and screening Family context and validated screening guide follow-up. Variation Children develop at different rates; patterns and loss of skills matter. Theories Piaget and Erikson offer frameworks, not diagnostic tests or rigid deadlines. Family teaching Use age-appropriate safety, play, communication and anticipatory guidance.

entries.h: 👶 What each stage needs from you
entries.t: Infant — keep the parent present, respond promptly. Trust is built by needs being met consistently . Toddler — offer two acceptable choices , never an open question. “Pink cup or blue cup?”, not “Will you take your medicine?” Preschooler — a simple honest explanation, and let them handle the equipment. School age — give tasks and choices, explain the equipment, respect privacy. Adolescent — privacy and confidentiality , involve them in decisions, allow peer visits.

Sensorimotor (0–2) — learns through senses and movement. Object permanence at 9–10 months . Preoperational (2–7) — magical thinking, animism, egocentrism, centration. Concrete operational (7–11) — conservation, classification, logic about concrete things. Formal operational (11+) — abstract and hypothetical thinking. Concrete versus formal decides how you teach a procedure, not just what you say.
Four motor milestones, three growth numbers.
Up to 10% of birth weight lost in the first 3–4 days Weight doubles by 6 months , triples by 12 months Length up 50% at one year
Posterior closes 6–8 weeks Anterior closes 12–18 months Bulging at rest = raised ICP. Sunken = dehydration.
Stepping — ~6 wk Tonic neck — 3–4 mo Rooting, palmar, extrusion — ~4 mo Moro — ~6 mo Plantar — 8–9 mo Babinski — ~1 yr A reflex that persists past its date is the finding, not the reflex itself.

Back to sleep, every sleep. Firm bare crib, no co-sleeping. Rear-facing car seat, back seat, until at least 2 years No honey before 12 months — infant botulism No cow's milk before 12 months Choking: no nuts, grapes, hot dogs, popcorn

Breast milk or formula only for about 6 months . Both are 20 kcal/oz . Breast milk needs vitamin D and runs out of iron by 4–6 months . Then iron-fortified cereal first, then one new food at a time so an allergy can be spotted.

The posterior closes first. That is the one people reverse. Posterior — closes about 1 to 2 months Anterior — the big diamond, closes 12 to 18 months Normal is flat and soft , and a pulsation is expected — it is an artery under a membrane, and it shows more when the baby cries. Sunken → dehydration , fluid volume deficit Bulging → raised intracranial pressure , alongside a high-pitched cry and a widening head circumference Judge a bulge on a calm, upright baby. A fontanelle can bulge while a baby screams or lies fl

entries.h: 😭 Crying, and the one cry that is not normal
entries.t: A well infant cries 1 to 3 hours a day. It is the only vocabulary they have: hungry, thirsty, tired, wet, too hot, too cold, hurting, or done with being handled. When a parent says “she cries all the time”, assess before you act — ask for the pattern, frequency and quality . Without that, calling the provider gives them nothing to work with, and calling it normal dismisses her. Rhythmic, builds, settles with feeding or holding — ordinary Inconsolable, drawing the legs up, worse after feeds — think colic or reflux H
Toddlers need control. Preschoolers need explanation.

15 months — walks alone, 3–5 words 2 years — runs, 2-word phrases, ~50% intelligible 3 years — tricycle, 3-word sentences, ~75% intelligible 4 years — hops, dresses self, ~100% intelligible 5 years — skips, ties laces, prints name Rough rule: words per phrase roughly matches age in years at 2 and 3.

Readiness is the child's, not the calendar's. Physiologic control arrives around 18 to 24 months , and pushing before the signs are there makes it take longer. Sits on the toilet 5 to 8 minutes without getting up or crying Stays dry about 2 hours , and recognizes the urge Walks to the bathroom and knows which room it is Follows a simple direction — “go sit on the potty” Pulls clothing up and down Shows interest, and wants to please Not required: dressing herself completely, or climbing onto the seat unaided — help

At 4 to 6, the answer is usually scissors. Preschoolers can hold and use them correctly, and cutting is the classic activity a nurse recommends to parents who ask how to build the skill. 3 years — copies a circle, builds a tower of 9–10 blocks 4 years — uses scissors , copies a square, draws a person with 3 parts , cuts food with a table knife 5 years — prints their name, ties laces, draws a person with body parts Watch the distractors on this one. Dolls and action figures are imaginative play, not fine motor. A ho

entries.h: 🚨 The leading cause of death in toddlers
entries.t: Unintentional injury — and every bit of it is preventable teaching. Drowning — never alone near water, including buckets and baths Poisoning — locked cupboards; toddlers explore by mouth Falls — stair gates, window guards Burns — pot handles turned in, water heater turned down
Anemia — 15 and 30 months Lead and autism — 18 and 24 months Vision — from 3 years Lead above 5 mcg/dL is abnormal: find and remove the source and recheck. Chelation is for 45 mcg/dL or higher.

Cow's milk capped at 16–24 oz/day — calcium blocks iron absorption Whole milk until 2 , then low-fat Physiologic anorexia — the appetite drop is expected, not pathology Choking foods: hot dogs, whole grapes, raw carrots

entries.h: ⭐ The two answers that keep reappearing
entries.t: Toddler tantrum → ignore the behavior, keep them safe. Attention reinforces it. Toddler resisting care → offer two acceptable choices. Time-out is one minute per year of age . And preschoolers think illness is punishment — say plainly that it is nobody's fault.
One needs to achieve. The other needs to belong.

The mirror of the 6-year-old question: which finding in a 12-month-old needs reporting? Expected at 12 months is walking, a pincer grasp , babbling with a few real words, and a birth weight that has tripled . Report anything below. No babbling , and no attempt to imitate sounds No pincer grasp — still raking with the whole hand Cannot bear weight or pull to stand with support Anterior fontanel still wide open — it normally closes by about 12–18 months . A late one raises hypothyroidism, rickets, raised ICP and chro

entries.h: 🚨 Pubic hair in a 6-year-old — report it
entries.t: The question is usually written as “which finding should the nurse report?” in a 6-year-old, and this is the one. Earlier than expected means before 8 in girls or 9 in boys . Pubic hair on its own may be premature adrenarche — early adrenal hormones — and not true precocious puberty It is assessed to rule out early puberty, a hormone exposure or an endocrine disorder . True early puberty speeds bone maturation and can reduce adult height The clinician checks growth rate, progression and other puberty signs ; hormon

Industry vs inferiority — they need to do things well Cooperative play, team games, collecting Growth slows to about 5 lb and 2 in a year Scoliosis screening in early adolescence, at the growth spurt — forward bend test Fears loss of control and being left out

Identity vs role confusion — they need to fit in Adolescence delivers 20–25% of adult height Vaccines at 11–12 : Tdap (then every 10 y), HPV 2 doses 6–12 mo apart, meningococcal with a booster at 16 Commonly deficient in calcium, iron and zinc Fears being different ; body image is the adherence problem

Girls start with breast budding , and menarche comes last , roughly two years later. Growth stops 2–2.5 years after menarche. Boys start with testicular enlargement . Girls start about two years earlier, which is why the growth spurts do not line up.

Unintentional injury — mainly motor vehicle crashes — then suicide and homicide. Risk-taking peaks because the reward system matures before the judgment system does . Ask about mood and self-harm directly, and in private. Asking does not plant the idea.

School age wants facts and control; adolescents want privacy and peers. The wrong intervention for the wrong stage is the classic distractor. Preschoolers read a procedure as punishment — the answer is reassurance , not just distraction. Regression under stress is normal. Normalize it to the parents; do not treat it. Separation anxiety and stranger anxiety overlap in age — read which behavior is described, not the months. Ear assessment flips to up and back after age 3 . Where this came from. Built from your NUR 23

entries.h: 🩺 Vital signs, pain & assessment by age
entries.t: A child is not a small adult. They compensate brilliantly and then crash suddenly, and blood pressure is the last thing to fall . The ranges matter, but the pattern matters more.
Two directions and one exception.
A child compensates by raising the heart rate , and keeps compensating until they cannot. Blood pressure falls last. A normal blood pressure never rules out shock.

Age decides the route. History can rule one out. Axillary — works at any age , and is the safe default Oral — not until the child can hold their mouth closed, about 5 to 6 years . Avoid it with vomiting or respiratory distress . Rectal — mostly reserved for infants, and used at any age only when it is genuinely needed 🚨 When not to go rectal. Two mechanisms, and every contraindication is one of them. Vagal stimulation → a cardiac condition . The probe can trigger a vagal response and slow the heart. Breaching the m

entries.h: 🥋 How to take them, and in what order
entries.t: Least invasive first, or the numbers are about your handling, not the child. Respirations first — they need nothing but your eyes Then apical heart rate , then blood pressure, then temperature Leave the child in the parent's arms or whatever position comforts them Save anything frightening — the otoscope, the throat — for last A crying toddler's respiratory rate is not his respiratory rate. Every invasive step you take first contaminates every number after it. Two technique points the exam keeps asking: Watch the a

entries.h: 🟨 When the number and the child disagree
entries.t: Believe the child first. A pulse oximeter cannot read a pulse it cannot feel. Cold hands and feet, a cool room, an undressed baby, shivering, movement, poor perfusion — any of them and the saturation it prints is a guess. The check that settles it: does the heart rate on the oximeter match the heart rate you counted ? If the two disagree, the probe is not tracking the pulse and the saturation means nothing. Warm the child — blankets, cover the head, close the door Look at colour and warmth , and at how the child is
In order, earliest first.

entries.h: 🚨 Early signs, in the order they appear
entries.t: 1 · Tachycardia — the very first compensation 2 · Tachypnea , then nasal flaring, grunting, retractions 3 · Irritability, then lethargy — a change in behavior is a vital sign 4 · Poor feeding in an infant — often the parent's first complaint 5 · Falling blood pressure — late, and ominous If the stem gives you a quiet, floppy child after a period of crying, that is not settling. That is decompensation.
Infant — 1–3 mL/kg/hr Child — 0.5 mL/kg/hr Adolescent / adult — 40–80 mL/hr

entries.h: 👀 Findings that are normal, and findings that are not
entries.t: Circumoral cyanosis can be benign; central cyanosis of the lips and tongue is always abnormal A protuberant abdomen is normal; a firm distended one is not Petechiae after delivery are normal; generalized petechiae are not Innocent murmurs are common in school age as the heart outgrows the chest

entries.h: 😭 Pain, by what they can do
entries.t: Pick the scale by whether the child can self-report — not by how much pain you think there is. 0–3 years FLACC Behavioral. Five items scored 0–2, max 10. You observe it. 3 years and up Wong-Baker FACES The child points. They pick the face, you do not pick it for them. 3 years and up Poker Chip Tool Four red chips, each a “piece of hurt”. The child picks how many they have, 1 to 4. They must be able to count to 4. 3 to 13 years Oucher Six photos of a child’s face beside a 0–100 scale. The child points to the photo,

1 a little hurt 2 3 4 the most hurt Line up four red poker chips in front of the child. Say: “These are pieces of hurt. One is a little bit of hurt and four is the most hurt you could ever have. How many pieces of hurt do you have right now?” Write down how many chips the child picks. If the child has no hurt , the score is 0 . Then ask about the hurt (where it is, what it feels like) in the child’s own words. It is a self-report tool, like FACES: the child chooses, not you. It suits preschoolers who can count to 4

A poster with six photographs of a child’s face , from no hurt at the bottom to the biggest hurt at the top, beside a 0–100 number scale. Versions show children of different backgrounds, so the child can pick the one that looks like them. A child who can’t count to 100 points to a photo; one who can uses the numbers. For ages 3 to 13 . A 3-year-old after surgery: FACES, the Poker Chip Tool and the Oucher all work, because each lets the child report the hurt without numbers up to 10. Numeric 0–10 and the visual anal

entries.h: 🧭 The order you do things in

entries.t: Auscultate the apical pulse a full minute — and do it before you disturb the infant Respirations and heart rate before anything that makes them cry Invasive and frightening things last Specimen collection moves least invasive to most invasive . A urine culture needs a sterile cath specimen; a 24-hour collection discards the first void. Do procedures in a treatment room, never in the child's bed — the bed has to stay a safe place Where this came from. Built from your NUR 235 module pages — the high-yield cards, exam

Everything in peds is per kilogram , and the margin for error is a fraction of an adult’s. The exam tests three things: is this dose safe, is this route right for this age, and is this volume too much for this muscle.
The single most common calculation in this course.

1. Convert the weight to kilograms — divide pounds by 2.2 2. Multiply by the safe range from the reference: mg/kg/day 3. Compare the ordered dose to that range — and if it is outside it, the answer is hold and call the provider , never give it and monitor. Watch the units. A range given per day and an order written per dose is the classic trap — divide the daily range by the number of doses first.

A child weighs 33 lb . The safe range is 20–40 mg/kg/day divided into 3 doses. The order reads 150 mg every 8 hours . 33 ÷ 2.2 = 15 kg 15 × 20 = 300 mg/day · 15 × 40 = 600 mg/day Per dose: 100–200 mg 150 mg sits inside that — safe to give

Using pounds as kilograms — a 2.2× overdose Comparing a per-dose order to a per- day range Rounding a pediatric dose the way you would an adult's Giving a dose outside the safe range because it is “only slightly” over

The muscle has to be big enough for what you are putting in it. Age IM site Rough volume ceiling Infant Vastus lateralis 0.5–1 mL Toddler / child Vastus lateralis or deltoid once walking up to 2 mL Adolescent Deltoid or ventrogluteal adult volumes

Vastus lateralis is the infant site — the gluteal muscle is not developed until they have been walking about a year Two nurses check high-alert drugs and any weight-based dose Give the injection in a treatment room , and let a parent comfort afterwards Never say it will not hurt — say how long it will last

entries.h: 💊 Routes, and what only peds does

entries.t: Rotavirus — PO MMR and varicella — SQ Everything else — IM
Only normal saline and lactated Ringer's are appropriate Infuse slowly , on a pump, with strict intake and output Watch for overload: crackles, rising heart rate and blood pressure

Never call medicine candy or a treat Never mix a dose into a full bottle or a whole meal — if they do not finish it, you do not know what they got Offer a choice about how , never about whether Iron tablets look like candy and are a classic pediatric poisoning
Acetaminophen overdose → N-acetylcysteine Lead above 5 mcg/dL → chelation Never induce vomiting after a corrosive ingestion

Under 3 — pull the pinna down and back Over 3 — pull the pinna up and back Then massage the tragus , and warm refrigerated drops in your hand first — cold drops in the ear cause vertigo. The same up-and-back rule reappears in the preschool ear assessment. It is the same fact asked twice. Where this came from. Built from your NUR 235 module pages — the high-yield cards, exam traps and briefs for modules 1 to 4. The numbers here are the numbers your course teaches. 🧩 Peds

A child holds a far larger share of their body weight as water and turns it over far faster, so they dehydrate in hours rather than days. Weight is the measurement that matters — not what the parents think they drank.
The calculation this course asks for by name.
A child weighs 26 kg . First 10 kg → 1000 mL Next 10 kg → 10 × 50 = 500 mL Remaining 6 kg → 6 × 20 = 120 mL Total 1620 mL/day , which is 67.5 mL/hr
Infant — 1–3 mL/kg/hr Child — 0.5 mL/kg/hr Adolescent / adult — 40–80 mL/hr Output below this is the earliest hard number you get that a child is dry.
Weight is the truth. Everything else is a clue.

entries.h: ⭐ Percent lost = percent of body weight lost
entries.t: A child who was 10 kg last week and is 9.5 kg now has lost 500 g , which is 5% — and in a child, 1 kg lost is 1 liter of fluid . Mild · about 5% Thirsty Alert, moist-ish mouth, normal or slightly raised heart rate, urine still passing. Moderate · about 10% Dry & tachycardic Dry mucous membranes, sunken fontanelle, reduced skin turgor, fewer wet diapers, irritable. Severe · 15% or more Shock Lethargy, marked tachycardia, cool mottled skin, no tears, minimal urine. Blood pressure falls last.

entries.h: 🚨 The findings that matter most in an infant
entries.t: Sunken fontanelle — and remember bulging means the opposite problem, raised ICP Fewer wet diapers — ask how many today versus a normal day No tears when crying A change in behavior is a vital sign. Irritable, then lethargic, is the direction of travel. 🧒 Dehydration Picture, memory hook and nursing care →

entries.h: ✅ Oral rehydration first, when they can take it
entries.t: An oral rehydration solution — not water, not juice, not soda Small amounts, often : a teaspoon every few minutes beats a cup they will vomit Keep going through the vomiting — slow and small, do not stop Resume a normal diet as soon as they will take it; the old “rest the gut” advice is out

entries.h: 🚨 When it has to be IV
entries.t: Severe dehydration, shock, or a child who cannot keep anything down Only normal saline or lactated Ringer's Bolus by weight, then reassess — heart rate, mental state, urine output Strict intake and output, and daily weights on the same scale

entries.h: 💡 What tells you it is working
entries.t: In order: heart rate settles , then the child brightens up , then urine output rises , then weight climbs. If the heart rate has not come down, nothing else you see is reassurance.

entries.h: 🚨 A child can be given too much just as easily
entries.t: Crackles , rising heart rate and rising blood pressure Puffy eyelids, new peripheral edema, a sudden weight gain Always on a pump , never by gravity, and never a free-flowing bag Fluid is a drug in pediatrics. It is calculated, checked by two nurses, and pumped. Where this came from. Built from your NUR 235 module pages — the high-yield cards, exam traps and briefs for modules 1 to 4. The numbers here are the numbers your course teaches. 🧩 Peds
Preparation, play and consent, matched to the age. What frightens a child changes completely between three and thirteen , and the exam answer follows the fear, not the procedure.

How long before, and in what words. Age How far ahead What actually helps Infant Just before Keep the parent present; comfort and swaddle after Toddler Minutes before Very short words. Two choices , never an open question Preschool An hour or so before Simple honest words; let them handle the equipment; say it is not a punishment School age Days before Explain how it works, give them a job, respect modesty Adolescent As early as possible Full explanation, privacy , and a say in decisions

entries.h: 🚨 The words that get you marked wrong
entries.t: Never promise it will not hurt. Say how long it will last and what they can do. Never call medicine candy or a treat. Do not use words that sound like something else to a literal thinker — a preschooler hears “dye” , “put you to sleep” and “take your vitals” exactly as they sound. Procedures happen in the treatment room . The bed stays a safe place.

entries.h: 💕 Separation, and what it looks like
😕 The three stages of separation anxiety
entries.t: 1 · Protest — crying, clinging, refusing the nurse. Loud, and the healthiest of the three. 2 · Despair — quiet, withdrawn, stops crying. Looks like settling. 3 · Detachment — cheerful with anyone, indifferent to the parent. The most worrying, and the easiest to mistake for adjustment. A quiet child is not necessarily a settled child. Despair is often mistaken for improvement — that is the trap.

Rooming in , and encouraging the parents to stay Keep home routines — bedtime, the same comfort object, the same words Consistent staff, so it is not a new face each time Say when you will be back, and come back when you said
A toilet-trained toddler who wets again, a school-age child who wants a bottle — this is normal under stress . Normalize it to the parents and do not treat it. It resolves at home.

entries.h: 🎯 Who reacts worst — the risk factors
entries.t: Asked which child is most at risk of a stress reaction , you are being asked to pick out these. They stack: the more that are true, the harder the admission. 👶 Age about 6 months to 3–4 years — old enough to miss the parent, too young to understand why. This is the peak-vulnerability window 🏥 A first hospitalization , and one that was unplanned or emergent — no preparation, no rehearsal, no warning 😕 An anxious parent. A young child reads the caregiver and mirrors them. Calming the parent is an intervention for the

Infant — solitary. Mobiles, rattles, faces. Toddler — parallel. Beside another child, not with them. Preschool — associative. Together but loosely organized. School age — cooperative. Rules, teams, collecting. Adolescent — the peer group itself.

Let a preschooler give the injection to a doll, handle the stethoscope, put the mask on the teddy first. It gives back control , which is exactly what the hospital takes away. For a school-age child, a job does the same work: hold the tape, count to ten, pick which arm.

entries.h: 📍 The position is decided by where the provider needs to reach
entries.t: Femoral venipuncture — supine, legs in a frog position Lumbar puncture — side-lying knees-to-chest, or flexed sitting Gavage / tube feeding — semi-recumbent , head and chest up 30–45° NG tube insertion — upright, chin forward , never tilted back Over-flexing an infant’s neck for a lumbar puncture presses on the diaphragm and compromises the airway. Round the back, not the neck. All six procedures, the reason behind each position, and two plates are on the NUR 235 Module 1 page .

The provider obtains consent — explains the procedure, risks and alternatives The parent or guardian signs it The nurse witnesses the signature and verifies understanding by teach-back If the parent cannot explain it back, the nurse stops and calls the provider. Witnessing a signature is not the same as obtaining consent. An adolescent should be asked for assent even where they cannot legally consent — and adolescents get confidentiality and a conversation without the parent in the room. Where this came from. Built

entries.h: NCLEX Drugs 1 · NG-043 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Pharmacology · NCLEX Drug Review Series

Opioid Analgesics · Anticonvulsants · Benzodiazepines · Antidepressants & Anxiolytics NG-043 PHARM Series: NCLEX Drug Review 1 of 5 ADHD-friendly visual edition Four CNS drug families, one study map: class (what family?) → action (what does it change?) → watch (safety & teaching). These are the drugs that show up over and over on NCLEX — learn the brand/generic pairs cold , then hang one mechanism and one trap on each. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

💊 Opioids ↑ pain threshold by altering perception — resp depression is the #1 danger, naloxone reverses. ⚡ Anticonvulsants ↑ the interval between seizures — Dilantin, Tegretol & Depakote need blood level monitoring. 😴 Benzos "-pam/-lam" Enhance GABA (inhibitory) — flumazenil reverses. 🧠 SSRI/SNRI/TCA Boost serotonin (± norepinephrine) — never combine with an MAOI. 🗺️

STEP 2 · CLASS → MECHANISM → TRAP One card per class: what it is, how it works, the one nursing point that matters most, and the trap NCLEX loves to hide.

entries.h: 💊 Opioid Analgesics Demerol · Dilaudid · Duragesic/Sublimaze · Morphine · Vicodin/Norco
entries.t: Mechanism: ↑ pain threshold by altering pain perception in the CNS (bind mu-opioid receptors). ⭐ Key nursing point: Assess respiratory rate and sedation level before every dose — hold and notify the provider for significant respiratory depression or oversedation. Pair with a scheduled bowel regimen (opioids slow peristalsis → constipation is universal, not occasional).

Verify the order Patient, drug, indication, dose, route and timing. Check suitability Allergies, assessment, labs, contraindications and interactions. Evaluate response Document administration and reassess effects. Drug knowledge Know the purpose, mechanism, major adverse effects and required monitoring. Calculation Use correct units and an independent check when required; confirm unusual doses. Teach back Ask the patient to explain purpose, schedule and important symptoms to report. Trap 1: Meperidine (Demerol) bu

Mechanism: ↑ the interval between seizures / raise the seizure threshold so neurons fire less easily. ⭐ Key nursing point: Monitor blood levels for phenytoin (Dilantin), carbamazepine (Tegretol), and valproic acid (Depakote) — narrow therapeutic windows. Gabapentin (Neurontin) is also frequently prescribed off-label for chronic neuropathic pain. 🚨 NCLEX trap: Phenytoin causes gingival hyperplasia (teach meticulous oral hygiene); Tegretol can suppress bone marrow (watch CBC for infection/bleeding signs); Depakote is

Mechanism: enhance/facilitate GABA, the brain's main inhibitory neurotransmitter — opens the chloride channel more often, calming neuron firing. ⭐ Key nursing point: monitor sedation, respiratory status, and fall risk. Versed (midazolam) is commonly used for short procedural sedation. Never discontinue abruptly after regular use — withdrawal can include seizures. 🚨 NCLEX trap: Antidote = flumazenil . Benzo + opioid together is a black-box respiratory-depression combo — extra vigilance, not routine co-administration

entries.h: 🧠 SSRIs Celexa · Lexapro · Paxil · Prozac · Zoloft
entries.t: Mechanism: inhibit serotonin reuptake in the CNS, leaving more serotonin available at the synapse. ⭐ Key nursing point: full antidepressant effect takes about 2–4 weeks — teach patients not to expect immediate relief and not to stop early because "it isn't working yet." Watch closely for worsening mood or suicidal ideation early in treatment, especially in adolescents/young adults. 🚨 NCLEX trap: Combining an SSRI with another serotonergic drug (MAOI, tramadol, triptans, St. John's Wort) risks serotonin syndrome — a

Mechanism: Effexor (SNRI) blocks reuptake of both norepinephrine and serotonin at nerve endings. Elavil (TCA, older class) works similarly but also blocks histamine/cholinergic/alpha receptors, giving it more side effects. ⭐ Key nursing point: TCAs are cardiotoxic in overdose (widened QRS, dysrhythmias) — narrow therapeutic index, teach strict adherence and safe storage, especially with a depressed or at-risk patient. 🚨 NCLEX trap: Elavil's anticholinergic effects — dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, con

Mechanism: exact mechanism not fully defined; thought to act by changing serotonin activity in certain brain regions. ⭐ Key nursing point: Buspar is not a PRN anxiety drug — it takes about 2–4 weeks of scheduled dosing to reach full effect, has minimal sedation, and carries no significant abuse/dependence potential, unlike the benzodiazepines above. 🚨 NCLEX trap: A student may confuse Buspar with a benzodiazepine because both treat anxiety — but Buspar will not help an acute panic attack right now, and it is not cr
STEP 3 · SAFETY & PATIENT TEACHING What to say at the bedside, and the one table that keeps benzos and SSRIs from blurring together.

💧 Start a bowel regimen with any scheduled opioid — do not wait for constipation to happen 🚗 No driving/operating machinery until effects on alertness are known 🍷 Avoid alcohol — additive CNS/respiratory depression 🩸 Anticonvulsants: report rash, sore throat, unusual bruising (possible marrow suppression) and keep lab-draw appointments for drug levels

🚫 Never stop a benzodiazepine or an SSRI/SNRI/TCA abruptly — taper under provider guidance ⏳ Antidepressants need 2–4 weeks for full effect — keep taking it even if symptoms haven't shifted yet 🍷 Avoid alcohol with any of these classes 🆘 Report worsening mood, agitation, or suicidal thoughts immediately, especially in the first weeks

entries.h: 📊 Don't mix them up: Benzodiazepine vs. SSRI
entries.t: Benzodiazepine SSRI Onset: fast — can relieve acute anxiety same-day Onset: slow — 2–4 weeks for full effect Mechanism: enhances GABA (inhibitory) Mechanism: blocks serotonin reuptake Dependence/abuse potential: higher , taper to stop Dependence/abuse potential: low, but taper to avoid discontinuation syndrome Antidote available: flumazenil No specific antidote — treat serotonin syndrome supportively 🧠 "Benzo = right now, SSRI = weeks from now." If the NCLEX question needs relief today, it's not describing an SSRI.

SAY IT OUT LOUD 💊 Opioids Check RR & sedation first — naloxone reverses ⚡ Anticonvulsants Dilantin/Tegretol/Depakote → drug levels 😴 Benzos "-pam/-lam" · GABA · flumazenil reverses 🧠 SSRI/SNRI/TCA Never combine with an MAOI — serotonin syndrome

Q1: Before giving a scheduled opioid, what must the nurse assess first? Show answer Respiratory rate and level of sedation — hold and notify the provider if depression/oversedation is present. Q2: Which three anticonvulsants need periodic blood level monitoring? Show answer Phenytoin (Dilantin), carbamazepine (Tegretol), and valproic acid (Depakote). Q3: What is the antidote for a benzodiazepine overdose? Show answer Flumazenil (Romazicon). Q4: Why is combining an SSRI with an MAOI dangerous? Show answer Risk of se

& Safe Medication Administration NG-087 Pharmacology ADHD-friendly visual edition Drug cards feel like an overwhelming wall of facts. They aren't — every drug you'll ever study fits into the same 5-field template . Learn the template once, then plug in any drug for the rest of the program. This is the study method every other drug page assumes you already know. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🗂️ The Fab 5 Name · Class · Mechanism → Indication · Side effects · Contraindications. ⚠️ Adverse ≠ side effect Side effect = expected. Adverse = severe & unexpected. 🧪 NCLEX = generic names Not brand names — learn the generic first. 🤰 Pregnancy A→X A = safest studies · X = proven fetal harm, never give. 🗂️
STEP 1 · THE FAB 5 Every drug card, no matter the class, answers the same 5 questions in the same order.

entries.h: 🧾 The Fab 5 — filled in for a real drug (Lisinopril)

entries.t: Verify the order Patient, drug, indication, dose, route and timing. Check suitability Allergies, assessment, labs, contraindications and interactions. Evaluate response Document administration and reassess effects. Drug knowledge Know the purpose, mechanism, major adverse effects and required monitoring. Calculation Use correct units and an independent check when required; confirm unusual doses. Teach back Ask the patient to explain purpose, schedule and important symptoms to report. 🧠 "Name it, Class it, Explain i

entries.h: ①② Name & Class — the ID tags
entries.t: Every drug has 1 generic name but can have multiple brand/trade names EXAM TIP NCLEX tests generic names only, never brand names Class = the drug family — often told by its suffix (see the Drug Suffixes reference page) Generic Brand Warfarin Coumadin Ibuprofen Advil, Motrin Acetaminophen Tylenol 🧠 1 drug, 1 generic, many nicknames. Learn the generic first — that's the one that shows up on the exam.

entries.h: ③ Mechanism → Indication — the "why it works"
entries.t: Mechanism of action = how the drug works at the cellular/chemical level. Indication = what it's used for — the two are always connected by a chain of logic. Penicillin breaks down the bacterial cell wall → kills bacteria → treats infection Heparin/Warfarin block clotting factors → prevents clots → treats DVT/PE/AFib Labetalol blocks alpha & beta receptors → vessels relax, heart slows → treats hypertension 🧠 "Mechanism is the verb, indication is the reason." If you can explain the mechanism in one sentence, the indi

entries.h: ④⑤ Side Effects & Contraindications — the "watch for"
entries.t: Side effects = expected, usually tolerable. Contraindications = reasons to never give this drug to this client. Antibiotics for ear/GI/skin infections often cause nausea & vomiting (side effect) Acetaminophen + liver disease = contraindication (hepatotoxicity risk) 🧠 A side effect you monitor; a contraindication you don't even start. 📖
STEP 2 · EFFECT VOCABULARY These 4 words get mixed up constantly on exams — the difference is severity and predictability.

entries.h: 📊 Therapeutic → Side → Adverse → Toxic: one severity ladder
entries.t: 🧠 "Therapeutic is the goal, side is a shrug, adverse is an alarm, toxic is a buildup." Toxic effect specifically means the drug is accumulating — think renal failure or elderly clients who can't clear it.

entries.h: 🔗 Synergistic vs. ❌ Antagonistic vs. ➕ Additive interactions
entries.t: Interaction What happens Additive Combined effect = same as the sum of each drug alone Synergistic Combined effect is greater than expected — e.g. opioids + alcohol → dangerous CNS depression Antagonistic One drug blocks another — e.g. naloxone reverses opioids 🧠 Synergy stacks, antagonism blocks. Naloxone is the antagonist superhero of every opioid overdose question.

entries.h: 🤰 Pregnancy categories — safest to most dangerous
entries.t: A safest B C D X never A = well-controlled studies show no risk . X = studies show proven fetal harm — never given in pregnancy . 🧠 "A is Awesome, X marks eXit." Alphabetical order = risk order.

entries.h: 🚫 Contraindication vs. ⚠️ Caution — know which one stops you cold
entries.t: Contraindication = a reason never to give the drug to this client at all — e.g. acetaminophen in severe liver disease , pain medication + active alcohol use , caffeine-containing stimulants + Adderall . These aren't side effects to monitor — they're reasons to hold the drug and call the prescriber before it's ever given. 🧠 A side effect is something you watch . A contraindication is something you stop . 🛡️
STEP 3 · APPLY THE TEMPLATE SAFELY Knowing the card means nothing if the med doesn't reach the right client safely — this is where the 5 Rights page picks up.

entries.h: ✅ From card to bedside — the full loop
entries.t: 🗂️ Study the Fab 5 for this drug (name · class · mechanism → indication · side fx · contraindications) ▼ 🧾 Verify the order against the MAR — 3 checks: med room, order, bedside ▼ ✅ Confirm the 5 Rights — patient · drug · dose · route · time ▼ 📝 Document immediately & evaluate the response 🧠 Knowledge (the card) + Process (the rights) = safety. One without the other still causes errors.

entries.h: 🧪 Toxic effect — a Fab-5 red flag to watch
entries.t: Accumulation happens fastest when the client can't eliminate the drug — think renal failure , hepatic impairment , or the elderly with reduced clearance. 🧠 If a drug card doesn't mention how it's cleared, ask — renal vs. hepatic clearance changes your monitoring plan.

entries.h: 🎓 Client education is part of the card
entries.t: A complete drug card always ends with: what should the client watch for and report? That single question turns memorized facts into real teaching. 🧠 "If you can't teach it back, you don't know the card yet."

Adverse effect = unexpected and severe, like an allergic reaction with hives or respiratory distress. Q3: Naloxone reversing an opioid overdose is what kind of drug interaction? entries.h: Adrenergic Blockers · NG-095 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Pharmacology · Adrenergic Drug Classes

Adrenergic Antagonists — the umbrella term for alpha- & beta-blockers NG-095 PHARM ADHD-friendly visual edition "Adrenergic antagonist" just means a drug that blocks a receptor the sympathetic nervous system uses. There are two families — alpha-blockers and beta-blockers — and some drugs (carvedilol, labetalol) block both at once . This page is the overview and the alpha side; beta-blockers get their own deep dive. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🚫 Antagonist = blocker Sits on the receptor and stops norepinephrine/epinephrine from working there. 🩸 Alpha blocked = vessels relax Vasodilation → BP drops → orthostatic hypotension is the #1 safety issue. 🫀 Beta blocked = heart slows Full mechanism, drug list & asthma warning live on NG-176 Beta Blockers — cross-reference, don't re-learn it here. 🚨 Epi is contraindicated In an alpha-blocker hypotensive crisis, epinephrine can drop BP further — give norepinephrine instead. 💊
STEP 1 · THE MECHANISM Norepinephrine and epinephrine turn receptors ON — an adrenergic blocker's whole job is to sit on that same receptor and turn it back OFF.

entries.h: 🔒 Agonist turns it on · Antagonist blocks it
entries.t: EXAM TIP Block alpha receptors → vasodilation by relaxing the smooth muscle of blood vessels. In ophthalmic preps, alpha blockade also relaxes the iris dilator muscle, which is why alpha-blocker use is linked to intraoperative floppy iris syndrome during cataract surgery.

Sympathetic signal Norepinephrine acts at receptors in target tissues. Central suppression Clonidine reduces sympathetic outflow. Peripheral blockade Alpha blockers reduce receptor-mediated vasoconstriction. Monitor Orthostatic symptoms, blood pressure, falls and relevant pulse changes. Clonidine Sedation and dry mouth can occur; abrupt withdrawal can cause rebound hypertension. Alpha blockers First-dose hypotension is important; some are used for urinary symptoms. 🧠 "Antagonist = anti-agonist." The blocker doesn't

Alpha-1 — blood vessels, bladder neck/prostate smooth muscle, iris dilator Alpha-2 — mostly presynaptic (brakes on further NE release); clonidine stimulates this one centrally — see NG-243 Clonidine Beta-1 — heart (rate & contractility) Beta-2 — bronchioles & vessels (bronchodilation, vasodilation) 🧠 "1 is the one right next to it." Beta- 1 = heart, right in your chest. Beta- 2 = the other two letters away — lungs.

Alpha-blockers Beta-blockers Block vascular & prostate/bladder-neck smooth muscle receptors Block cardiac (β1) ± bronchial/vascular (β2) receptors Main effect: vasodilation → BP drops Main effect: HR & contractility drop #1 safety issue: orthostatic hypotension #1 safety issue: bradycardia / never stop abruptly Deep dive: NG-141 Alpha Blockers Deep dive: NG-176 Beta Blockers (Cardio batch) 🧠 "Alpha drops the pipes, Beta drops the pump." Alpha-blockers relax the pipes (vessels); beta-blockers slow the pump (heart).

entries.h: 💊 The dual blockers — carvedilol & labetalol block BOTH
entries.t: A few drugs don't pick a side — they block alpha-1 AND beta receptors at the same time, giving both vasodilation and a slower heart rate in one pill. Generic Trade Use Dose / route Carvedilol Coreg, Coreg CR Essential HTN; HF — reduces disease progression 6.25 mg PO twice daily (starting dose) Labetalol Trandate HTN — usually an add-on to a diuretic 100 mg PO twice daily; also IV Wean, don't crash: in uncompensated HF needing IV inotropes, those must be tapered off before starting carvedilol — starting a beta-block
STEP 2 · THE DANGER LIST One drug class, a body-wide adverse effect list — group it by system instead of memorizing a wall of words.

System What to watch CNS 🧠 Dizziness, fatigue, weakness, anxiety, depression, drowsiness, insomnia, memory loss, mental status changes, nervousness, nightmares EENT 👁️ Blurred vision, dry eyes, intraoperative floppy iris syndrome , nasal stuffiness Resp 🫁 Bronchospasm, wheezing CV ❤️ Bradycardia , heart failure, pulmonary edema GI 🍽️ Diarrhea, constipation, nausea GU 🚻 Erectile dysfunction, decreased libido Derm 🩹 Stevens-Johnson syndrome , toxic epidermal necrolysis, itching, rashes, urticaria Endo 🍬 Hyperglycemia

History of serious hypersensitivity reaction Pulmonary edema or cardiogenic shock Bradycardia , heart block, or sick sinus syndrome Uncompensated HF needing IV inotropes — wean first Severe hepatic impairment Asthma or other bronchospastic disorders 🧠 "Slow heart, tight lungs, sick liver — say no."

Antidepressants → tremors Cimetidine → increased adrenergic-blocker effect Clonidine → increases clonidine's effect (two BP-lowering drugs stacking) Digoxin → digoxin toxicity risk 🧠 "Cimetidine slows the liver, so the blocker builds up." Same logic shows up with lots of H2-blocker drug interactions.

entries.h: 🚨 Hypotensive crisis on IV therapy — why epinephrine is the wrong answer
entries.t: Monitor BP, pulse, and ECG every 2 minutes until stable during IV administration. If a hypotensive crisis occurs, epinephrine is contraindicated — because alpha is blocked, epi's unopposed beta-2 effect can push BP down further ("epinephrine reversal"). Norepinephrine may be used instead — it's a much weaker beta-2 agonist, so its alpha-mediated vasoconstriction still wins. Instruct the client to change positions slowly to minimize orthostatic hypotension, and to notify the HCP if chest pain occurs during the IV in
STEP 3 · WHAT THE CLIENT NEEDS TO HEAR If it's an adrenergic blocker of any kind, orthostatic precautions and "never stop cold turkey" apply.

entries.h: ✅ Universal teaching for any adrenergic blocker
entries.t: 1 🪑 Rise slowly — sit, pause, then stand 2 🩺 Check BP/pulse before dosing per parameters 3 ❌ Never stop abruptly — taper under provider guidance 4 📞 Report chest pain, fainting, or new SOB right away 🧠 "Blocked receptors, gradual changes." Whatever adrenergic receptor is blocked, the body needs time to adapt — both starting the drug (slow position changes) and stopping it (taper).

NG-141 Adrenergic Alpha Blockers — tamsulosin, doxazosin, prazosin; first-dose orthostatic hypotension NG-160 Prostate – BPH — alpha blockers as first-line BPH therapy NG-260 Peripherally Acting Antiadrenergics — reserpine/guanethidine-class, an older mechanism NG-176 Beta Blockers (Cardio batch) — full cardioselective vs nonselective deep dive NG-243 Clonidine — a central alpha-2 agonist , not a blocker; easy to mix up on exams 🧠 "Antagonist blocks, agonist activates." Adrenergic blockers ≠ clonidine. Say it every

Adrenergic antagonist (this page) Adrenergic agonist Blocks the receptor — turns the signal off Stimulates the receptor — turns the signal on Alpha-blockers, beta-blockers, carvedilol, labetalol Epinephrine, norepinephrine, albuterol (β2 agonist), clonidine (central α2 agonist) Net effect on BP: usually lowers it Net effect on BP: usually raises it (except clonidine, which lowers it centrally) 🧠 "-onist just means 'acts on it' — the prefix tells you the direction." Ant agonist = ant i, against, blocks. Ag onist = g

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🚫 Antagonist = blocks the receptor, stops NE/epi from acting there 🩸 Alpha blocked = vessels relax = orthostatic hypotension risk 🫀 Beta blocked = HR/contractility drop — full detail on NG-176 🚨 Crisis? No epi Give norepinephrine — epi can drop BP further

Q1: What does "adrenergic antagonist" mean? Show answer A drug that blocks an adrenergic (alpha or beta) receptor, preventing norepinephrine/epinephrine from acting there — the opposite of an agonist. Q2: Why is epinephrine contraindicated during an alpha-blocker hypotensive crisis? Show answer With alpha blocked, epinephrine's unopposed beta-2 vasodilation can drop BP even further ("epinephrine reversal"). Norepinephrine is used instead because it has minimal beta-2 effect. Q3: Name two drugs that block BOTH alpha

entries.h: Anti-inflammatory Agents · NG-100 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Pharmacology · Pain & Anti-Inflammatory Unit — Group Map

The Overview Page — NSAIDs · Acetaminophen · Corticosteroids · DMARDs NG-100 PHARMACOLOGY ADHD-friendly visual edition Every anti-inflammatory drug interrupts the same fire — the body's inflammatory cascade — just at a different spot and a different speed . This page is the map for the whole pain & anti-inflammatory unit: compare the 4 big families here, then go deep on NSAIDs ( NG-256 ) , Acetaminophen ( NG-232 ) , and the DMARD Sulfasalazine ( NG-175 ) on their own pages. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Driv

🗂️ 4 families, 1 goal NSAIDs, Acetaminophen, Corticosteroids & DMARDs all fight pain/inflammation — different mechanism, different speed. 💊 Steroids = slow & broad "-sone / -lone" suffix. Days to work. NOT a rescue drug for an acute attack. 🐢 DMARDs = disease-modifying Weeks–months onset. Used for RA and IBD (sulfasalazine does both). 🚨 The 2 must-knows NSAID "triple whammy" nephrotoxicity + Tylenol max-dose liver toxicity — the two highest-yield NCLEX traps in this unit. 🗂️
STEP 1 · MEET THE FIRE One inflammatory cascade, four different places to jump in and shut it down.

entries.h: 🔥 The inflammation cascade — where each family blocks it
entries.t: BIG PICTURE Tissue injury releases arachidonic acid from cell membranes. The enzyme COX (cyclooxygenase) turns it into prostaglandins — the chemicals that cause pain, fever, and swelling . Every drug on this page interrupts that chain somewhere.

Acetaminophen Primarily reduces pain and fever. NSAIDs Reduce prostaglandin-mediated pain and inflammation. Patient factors Liver, kidney, bleeding and cardiovascular risks guide choice. Acetaminophen safety Check all combination products to avoid duplicate exposure; excess can injure the liver. NSAID safety Monitor GI bleeding, kidney function, pressure and interacting anticoagulants. Teaching Use the prescribed dose and duration and report concerning symptoms. 🧠 "Steroids block early, NSAIDs block the middle, Tyl

GROUP MAP The single most-tested contrast: which one hurts the stomach/kidneys, which one hurts the liver, which one hurts the immune system. Class Example drugs Mechanism Best for Key risk NSAIDs 🔥 Ibuprofen, Naproxen, Ketorolac (Toradol), Indomethacin, Aspirin Block COX-1 & COX-2 → ↓prostaglandins Pain, fever, inflammation, gout, RA/OA GI bleed · renal injury · CV risk Acetaminophen 🧠 Tylenol Central COX inhibition — antipyretic/analgesic, weak peripheral anti-inflammatory Fever/pain when NSAIDs are risky (PUD, b

-sone / -lone = corticosteroid (methylprednisolone, fluticasone, beclomethasone) -profen / -oxicam / -fenac = NSAID (ibuprofen, meloxicam, diclofenac) -lukast = leukotriene inhibitor (montelukast, zafirlukast) Acetaminophen has no shared suffix — it's chemically its own thing (a para-aminophenol derivative), which is exactly why it doesn't act like an NSAID. 🧠 If the drug name ends in -sone/-lone , assume slow, broad, sugar-raising before you even read the question stem. 💊
STEP 2 · THE BROAD BLOCKER Powerful and slow — a maintenance drug that gets mistaken for a rescue drug on exams.

Drug Route Use Beclomethasone Inhaled Asthma maintenance / prevention Fluticasone Inhaled (also nasal) Asthma maintenance, allergic rhinitis Methylprednisolone (brand: Solu-Medrol) IV / PO — systemic Acute flares, after the rescue inhaler in an attack Slow onset — corticosteroids work over hours to days, not minutes. They calm swelling and inflammation broadly, but they are NOT the first drug given for the first sign of an acute attack . 🧠 "AIM" for an acute asthma attack, in order: A lbuterol 1st → I pratropium 2n

🍬 Hyperglycemia — monitor blood glucose, especially in diabetics 🦠 Oral thrush (Candida) — inhaled route; mouth sores/white patches 🧬 Immunosuppression / infection risk — systemic, long-term use 🦴 Osteoporosis — long-term systemic use ⛔ Never stop abruptly after long-term systemic use — adrenal insufficiency/crisis risk; taper down 🧠 Blood sugar UP, immune system DOWN. Picture a "-sone" pill sitting on a sugar cube while an immune cell falls asleep.

🔄 Use a spacer to improve delivery and cut mouth deposition 🚿 Rinse mouth after each use — spit, don't swallow the water ⏱️ Take on a scheduled, daily basis — not PRN ❌ Never use for the first sign of an acute attack — reach for the rescue inhaler (albuterol) instead 🧠 Rinse & spit, never for the fit. "Fit" = acute attack. Steroids don't touch an attack already happening. 🫁
STEP 3 · PREVENT, DON'T RESCUE Two more anti-inflammatory classes that only work if taken before the trigger — never during.
Montelukast , Zafirlukast (brand: Singulair) . 🧠 "Luke likes to SING (airway open)." Monte lukast keeps the airway singing — but only if taken every day, not as a rescue drug during an attack .

Blocks mast cell degranulation → prevents the release of histamine and inflammatory mediators before they start. 🧠 Cromolyn = the sunscreen of asthma drugs. Sunscreen only works if applied before sun exposure — cromolyn only works if taken before exercise.

🚑 Rescue — during an attack 🛡️ Preventer — before it starts Albuterol — fast-acting bronchodilator, first drug given Inhaled corticosteroids, leukotriene inhibitors, mast cell stabilizers — daily or pre-exposure only Works in minutes Works over hours to weeks — will not stop an attack already happening 🧠 If the NCLEX stem says "first sign of an acute attack" — the answer is always the rescue drug, never a "-sone," "-lukast," or Cromolyn. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🗂️ 4 families NSAIDs · Acetaminophen · Corticosteroids · DMARDs — each blocks the fire at a different point 💊 "-sone/-lone" = corticosteroid = slow, broad, sugar-raising, NOT a rescue drug 🛡️ Preventers only work BEFORE Leukotriene inhibitors + mast cell stabilizers — never during an attack 🚨 Deep dives next NSAIDs, Acetaminophen & Sulfasalazine each get their own page in this unit

Q1: Which anti-inflammatory family has the slowest onset and works "upstream" in the inflammatory cascade? Show answer Corticosteroids ("-sone/-lone") — they block inflammation broadly and take hours-to-days to work; never the first drug for an acute attack. Q2: A client is having their first sign of an acute asthma attack. What order do drugs get given? Show answer AIM — Albuterol 1st, Ipratropium 2nd, Methylprednisolone (Solu-Medrol) last. Q3: Which drug family is dosed specifically to prevent exercise-induced br

entries.h: Erectile Dysfunction Drugs · NG-115 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Pharmacology · Genitourinary Drug Class

PDE5 Inhibitors — sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil NG-115 PHARM ADHD-friendly visual edition Phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5) inhibitors are oral drugs that block the enzyme (PDE5) that normally breaks down cGMP in the penis. More cGMP hanging around means more smooth muscle relaxation, more blood flow in, and an erection — but only with sexual stimulation . One interaction on this page is ABSOLUTE and can kill : nitrates. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🔗 Related page: the nitrate contraindication on this page is the same drug class covered in depth on NG-216 · Nitrates — read that page for the full nitric-oxide/preload mechanism of nitrates themselves. ⛽ Blocks PDE5 More cGMP stays around → vessel relaxation → blood flow in → erection, only with stimulation. 🚫 Nitrates = ABSOLUTE no Combined vasodilation → severe, possibly fatal hypotension. ⏱️ Timing differs by drug Sildenafil/vardenafil ≈ 4 hr window; tadalafil up to 36 hr — "the weekend pill." 🚨 Erection > 4 h
STEP 1 · THE MECHANISM One enzyme, one pathway — PDE5 inhibitors don't create arousal, they just let the body's own erection signal last longer.

EXAM TIP Sexual stimulation releases nitric oxide (NO) in the penis, which raises cGMP and relaxes smooth muscle, letting blood flow in. The enzyme PDE5 normally breaks cGMP back down, ending the erection. PDE5 inhibitors block that breakdown — cGMP lasts longer, so the erection lasts longer.

Alpha blockade Relaxes smooth muscle around the prostate and outlet. Hormonal treatment Some medicines gradually reduce prostate volume. PDE-5 inhibition Supports nitric-oxide-mediated vascular relaxation. BPH care Monitor urinary symptoms, retention and orthostatic effects. ED medicines Review nitrate use and cardiovascular suitability. Urgent symptoms Prolonged painful erection or acute inability to void needs prompt care. 🧠 "No stimulation, no show." Sildenafil has no effect without sexual stimulation — it doesn

Phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5) inhibitors Oral drugs, taken before planned sexual activity Sildenafil (as Revatio) is also used for pulmonary arterial hypertension Tadalafil, low daily dose, is also used for BPH 🧠 "5 for 5." PDE- 5 inhibitor. If you see -afil at the end of a drug name, think PDE5 inhibitor.

Allows blood flow into the penis, resulting in an erection — used for erectile dysfunction . Determine that ED is present before starting therapy. 🧠 The drug enables the physical mechanism; it does not create desire or arousal on its own.

Generic Trade Use Typical dose & timing Sildenafil Viagra (Revatio for PAH) Erectile dysfunction 25–100 mg PO, 30–60 min before sexual activity; not more than once/day Tadalafil Cialis ED, BPH 5–20 mg PO; daily low-dose for BPH, or as needed — effective up to 36 hr before activity Vardenafil Levitra, Staxyn Erectile dysfunction 5–20 mg PO, ~60 min before activity; window ≈ 4 hr ⚠️
STEP 2 · THE DANGER LIST One contraindication is absolute, one complication is a urologic emergency, and two symptoms mean stop and call.

PDE5 inhibitors and nitrates both raise cGMP / nitric oxide-driven vasodilation . Given together, the two vasodilating effects stack — the result can be severe, life-threatening hypotension and cardiovascular collapse . Always ask about ED medication use before giving a nitrate, and never give a PDE5 inhibitor to a patient on nitrate therapy. 🧠 "Blue pill, red flag." Any ED drug question that also mentions chest pain / nitroglycerin use is testing this exact interaction. See NG-216 · Nitrates for the nitrate side o

Do not take concurrently with alpha-adrenergic blockers (e.g., drugs for BPH) unless the patient is on a stable dose — both classes drop BP, and together they raise the risk of symptomatic hypotension . 🧠 Two vasodilators, two chances to fall — orthostatic teaching applies here too.
🧠 "4 is the floor." Any erection lasting longer than 4 hours is a urologic emergency, not something to "wait out."

👁️ Sudden vision loss one or both eyes 👂 Sudden hearing loss or decrease 🔔 Ringing in the ears tinnitus 💫 Dizziness with any of the above Also expect and teach: headache, flushing, GI upset, nausea, nasal congestion/runny nose as common (non-emergency) adverse reactions. 🧠 "Eyes, ears, and erections — all reported." Vision loss, hearing loss/ringing, priapism, and chest pain during sexual activity are the four "call now" symptoms for this drug class. 🗣️
STEP 3 · WHAT THE CLIENT NEEDS TO HEAR Timing, honesty with every provider about ED med use, and what this drug does not protect against.

1 ⏱️ Take as directed — timing before activity varies by drug 2 ❌ Not more than once per day for sildenafil 3 💬 Tell every provider and dentist you take an ED drug — before any nitrate is ever prescribed 4 🚨 Chest pain during sex → seek immediate medical attention , do not take a nitrate first 5 🛡️ No STI protection — this drug offers none; discuss protection separately 🧠 "If chest pain hits, don't reach for nitro." A patient on sildenafil who develops chest pain during intercourse must get emergency care — nitrogl

Antiretrovirals (e.g., protease inhibitors) — increase PDE5-inhibitor blood levels/effectiveness → higher side-effect risk Antihypertensives — increase the antihypertensive's effect → additive hypotension Nitrates — absolute contraindication , see above Alpha blockers — caution unless on a stable dose 🧠 Always screen the full med list, OTC drugs, and herbal products before giving these agents — several categories stack with the same vasodilation.

entries.h: 🆚 Not for women, not a cure, not stimulation
entries.t: Myth Reality "It creates arousal" No — it only sustains an erection once sexual stimulation has already started. No stimulation, no effect. "Women can take it too" Not indicated for use in women. "It's fine with my nitro spray" Absolute contraindication — risk of severe hypotension. "It protects against STIs" It does not — counsel on protection separately. 🧠 "Wingman, not magic." The drug supports a signal that's already there — it doesn't create desire, doesn't replace protection, and doesn't mix with nitrates. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD ⛽ Blocks PDE5 cGMP stays up, erection sustained — only with stimulation 🚫 Nitrates = ABSOLUTE no severe/fatal hypotension risk — see NG-216 ⏱️ Sildenafil/vardenafil ≈4h Tadalafil up to 36h — "weekend pill" 🚨 >4hr erection priapism — emergency

Q1: How do PDE5 inhibitors work? Show answer They block the enzyme PDE5, which normally breaks down cGMP — cGMP stays elevated, smooth muscle stays relaxed, and blood flow into the penis is sustained. They require sexual stimulation to have any effect. Q2: What is the one absolute contraindication, and why? Show answer Nitrates — both drug classes vasodilate through the same nitric-oxide/cGMP pathway, and combined they can cause severe, life-threatening hypotension and cardiovascular collapse. entries.h: NCLEX Drugs 2 · NG-124 · Nursing Field Notes
