Fungal skin infection — ringworm, athlete's foot, jock itch & fungal nails NG-067 INTEGUMENTARY · FUNGAL ADHD-friendly visual edition Tinea is a superficial fungal infection of keratin — skin, hair or nails — caused by dermatophytes . It is highly contagious and is named for where it lands : capitis, corporis, cruris, pedis, unguium. The classic lesion is a round, itchy, scaly patch with a raised active edge and a clearing center . Treatment is an antifungal — topical for skin, but oral for hair and nails because a

🍄 A fungus, not a worm Dermatophytes eat keratin , so they live in the dead top layer , plus hair and nails . "Ringworm" is a shape, not an animal. 📍 Named by the address capitis scalp · corporis body · cruris groin · pedis feet · unguium nails. 💊 Fungus → antifungal Skin = topical "-azole" or terbinafine. Hair or nail = ORAL , for weeks to months. 🚨 Teach: do not share HIGHLY contagious. No sharing brushes, hats, towels, clothes. Keep skin dry. 🧬
STEP 0 · LEARN THIS ONCE Same skin drawing as every page in this set — this time with fungal filaments living in the dead surface layer.

entries.h: 🔬 Skin cutaway — tinea is the SHALLOWEST of all
entries.t: DEPTH = THE ANSWER Dermatophytes need keratin to eat, and the only fully keratinized, dead tissue is the stratum corneum — plus hair shafts and nail plates . That is the whole disease in one sentence: fungus lives in dead keratin; the redness and itch are your immune system reacting from below .

Barrier breach or exposure Organisms reach vulnerable tissue. Local infection Inflammation affects the skin or underlying layers. Spread risk Some infections can progress beyond the local site. Impetigo Superficial bacterial infection often produces crusted lesions. Cellulitis Deeper infection causes spreading warmth, redness, swelling and pain. Tinea Dermatophyte infection requires antifungal treatment rather than antibacterial therapy. 🧠 "Fungus is a surface squatter." It never invades living tissue in a healthy

entries.h: 📖 Lesion vocabulary — tinea is a SCALE disease
entries.t: Tinea produces an erythematous scaly plaque with an annular (ring) shape. "Annular + scaly + clearing center" is exam code for tinea. 🧠 Scale = keratin. Fungus eats keratin, so fungus makes scale. Follow the flakes. 🍄
STEP 1 · WHY IT HAPPENS Warm + damp + contact with fungus = tinea. Get any of those three away and it struggles.

Tinea is a superficial fungal infection of keratinized tissue — skin, hair or nails — caused by dermatophytes (genera Trichophyton , Microsporum , Epidermophyton ). It is highly contagious . "Ringworm" is a misnomer — there is no worm. The name describes the expanding ring-shaped lesion. 🧠 "Ringworm has no worm, and tinea has no location — until you add the second word."

Fungal spores land on skin — person, animal, soil or object ▼ Warm + moist + a small break = they germinate ▼ Hyphae digest keratin and spread OUTWARD through the stratum corneum ▼ The immune system reacts from the dermis below ▼ Raised, red, scaly ACTIVE edge + itch ▼ The center clears as the fungus moves on = the RING 🧠 The ring is a footprint. The edge is where the fungus is now; the middle is where it used to be.

Person to person — direct skin contact, contact sports Animal to person — puppies, kittens, calves, guinea pigs (often the more inflamed lesions) Object to person — brushes, combs, hats, towels, clothing, bedding, gym mats, shared shoes Soil to person — gardening without gloves Self-spread — scratching the groin after touching the feet 🧠 "Pedis first, cruris second." Teach patients to put socks on before underwear so they do not carry the fungus from foot to groin.

entries.h: 🌡️ Risk factors — what makes skin friendly to fungus
entries.t: Heat and humidity ; sweating; occlusive shoes and synthetic clothing Moist skin folds — groin, under the breasts, between the toes Communal wet floors — showers, changing rooms, pool decks Diabetes , obesity, immunosuppression , peripheral vascular disease Contact sports — wrestling ("tinea gladiatorum"), rugby Existing tinea pedis — the reservoir for nail and groin infection 🧠 "Fungus loves a warm wet cave." Dry it out and you have already started treatment.

entries.h: 🧪 Bug → drug: the rule that runs this whole set
entries.t: 🧠 Fungus → antifungal. Look for "-azole" or terbinafine . An antibiotic will do absolutely nothing for tinea — and a steroid will make it worse. 🔎
STEP 2 · WHAT YOU SEE Itchy, scaly, and shaped like a ring — then find out which body part it landed on.

Circular / annular rash — an expanding ring Scaly , with a raised, more active outer border and a clearer center Pruritus — itching, sometimes intense Plus: mild redness; occasionally small pustules or vesicles along the edge Not usually painful; the patient is systemically well 🧠 "Round · Rough · Restless." Round shape, rough scale, restless itching.

entries.h: 📍 Name it by where it is
entries.t: Tinea capitis — scalp (children); patchy hair loss, black dots, scale, possible kerion Tinea corporis — trunk, arms, legs = the classic ringworm Tinea cruris — groin = jock itch ; usually spares the scrotum Tinea pedis — feet = athlete's foot Tinea manuum — hand (often just one, with tinea pedis on both feet) Tinea unguium — nails = onychomycosis Tinea barbae / faciei — beard area / face Tinea versicolor is a different yeast (Malassezia) — patchy pigment change, not a ring 🧠 "CAP-COR-CRU-PED-UNG" — head, body, groi
🧠 If a question names a Latin body part you do not recognize, translate it — the answer is usually just "which body part is this?"

entries.h: 💍 The ring, explained — and the trap that ruins it
entries.t: 🧠 Scrape the edge, not the middle. And if the rash "got better on steroid cream then spread," think tinea incognito.

entries.h: 🔬 Confirming it — KOH prep & Wood's lamp
entries.t: 🧠 KOH dissolves you, not the fungus. Skin cells melt away; branching septate hyphae stay behind.
🧠 "Thick, yellow, crumbly, lifting." Four adjectives = fungal nail = oral therapy = months, not weeks.

entries.h: ⭐ Scalp & feet — the two that behave differently
entries.t: 🧠 Scalp needs a tablet. Feet need a towel. 🩺
STEP 3 · WHAT YOU DO Kill the fungus, dry the environment, and above all — stop it spreading.

entries.h: 💊 Cream or tablet? One question decides it
entries.t: 🧠 "Hair and nails need a tablet." A cream cannot get inside a hair shaft or under a nail plate.

entries.h: ⭐ PRIORITY: teach how to stop the spread
entries.t: On this topic the highest-priority nursing action is almost always education to prevent transmission . Do NOT share brushes, combs, hats, towels, bed linen, clothing, shoes or sports gear Wash towels, linen and clothing in hot water; hot-wash or replace hair brushes Cover lesions during contact sport; no wrestling/swimming until treated per policy Wear thongs/flip-flops in communal showers and changing rooms Wash hands after applying cream and after touching the lesion Check the household — and the pets. Take an it

entries.h: 💨 Keep it DRY — the environmental half of treatment
entries.t: Dry thoroughly after washing — especially between the toes and in skin folds Pat, do not rub; dry the groin before the feet so you do not carry fungus upward Change socks daily (more often if sweaty); cotton or moisture-wicking Alternate shoes so each pair dries out for 24 h; avoid occlusive plastic shoes Loose cotton underwear ; avoid sitting around in damp gym or swim gear Absorbent powder may help in folds — but it does not replace the antifungal 🧠 "Dry between the toes" — small sentence, big exam points, and it

Absorbed BEST with a high-FAT meal — take it with whole milk, peanut butter or ice cream Takes weeks to months — a scalp course typically runs many weeks Do NOT stop when the itching stops. Itch settles long before the fungus is gone — stopping early is the number-one cause of relapse May cause photosensitivity — teach sun protection May cause headache, GI upset, rash; report a sore throat, fever or jaundice Interacts with warfarin and can reduce the effectiveness of oral contraceptives ; avoid alcohol Derived from

Topical "-azoles" — clotrimazole, miconazole, ketoconazole. Apply to the lesion plus ~2 cm of normal skin around it Terbinafine — topical cream, or oral for nails and scalp Itraconazole / fluconazole — other oral options Ketoconazole or selenium sulfide shampoo may be used as an adjunct in tinea capitis to reduce shedding — it does not replace the oral drug Oral agents may need liver function monitoring ; check interactions before giving An antihistamine may be prescribed for the itch — it treats the symptom, not t

Gloves for direct contact with lesions; hand hygiene before and after Assess and document the lesion : site, size, shape, border, scale, satellite lesions Keep nails short and discourage scratching — scratching spreads and can cause secondary bacterial infection Cool compresses and loose clothing for comfort Watch for secondary bacterial infection : increasing pain, warmth, pus, fever Reassure — it is treatable and, in most sites, does not scar 🧠 Scratching turns a fungal problem into a bacterial one.

Never treat a suspected fungal rash with a topical steroid alone. Never stop the antifungal because the itching or the redness has gone. Never let the patient share brushes, hats, towels or bed linen. Never expect a cream to cure a scalp or nail infection. Never give griseofulvin on an empty stomach — it needs fat to be absorbed. 🧠 Don't steroid it, don't stop it, don't share it. 🔀
STEP 4 · THE REAL EXAM SKILL A ring with a clear center is a fungus until proven otherwise.
🧠 Rings anywhere warm and damp = tinea. Same body, five patterns.

CONDITION HOW IT DIFFERS FROM TINEA Psoriasis Silvery, thick scale on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees), well-demarcated but no central clearing . Autoimmune, not infectious. Responds to steroids — tinea does not. Nummular eczema Coin-shaped, but solid — itchy, weeping or crusted, with no clear center and no raised scaly ring. Impetigo Honey-colored crust , no ring, bacterial → needs an antibiotic . Cellulitis Hot, painful, spreading, often febrile, no scale . Bacterial and deep. Pityriasis rosea A single "herald p

The priority for tinea is nearly always teaching to prevent spread . Griseofulvin with a high-fat meal — do not pick "on an empty stomach." Do not stop when the itching stops — courses run weeks to months. Scalp and nail infections need ORAL therapy; a cream is the wrong answer. Scrape the active border , not the cleared center, for the KOH prep. Recurrent groin tinea? Look at the feet — that is usually the reservoir. Tinea is not a reason for isolation, but it is a reason to stop sharing personal items. 🧠 If an an

Tinea vs psoriasis — clearing center vs solid silvery plaque Tinea vs eczema — ring vs ill-defined itchy patch Tinea vs impetigo — scale vs honey crust Tinea capitis vs alopecia areata — scaly with broken hairs vs smooth bald patch Tinea vs cellulitis — itchy and scaly vs hot and painful Tinea versicolor vs corporis — pigment patches vs an expanding ring 🧠 Scaly ring, smooth patch, honey crust, hot leg. Four pictures, four diagnoses. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 💍 Ring with a clear center Raised scaly ACTIVE edge. Itchy. No worm. 📍 capitis · corporis · cruris · pedis · unguium Scalp · body · groin · feet · nails. 💊 Hair or nail = ORAL Skin = topical -azole or terbinafine. Griseofulvin with a HIGH-FAT meal. 🚨 Do not share · keep dry Highest-priority teaching. Don't stop when the itch stops.

Q1: What actually causes ringworm? Show answer A dermatophyte fungus that digests keratin — not a worm. It lives in the dead stratum corneum, hair shafts and nail plates. Q2: Describe the classic lesion. Show answer A round, itchy, scaly patch with a raised, more active outer border and a clearing center — the ring. Q3: Name the tinea of the scalp, body, groin, feet and nails. Show answer Capitis (scalp), corporis (body/ringworm), cruris (groin/jock itch), pedis (feet/athlete's foot), unguium (nails/onychomycosis).

How wounds close · the healing phases · assessment · dressings · drains · dehiscence & evisceration NG-080 FUNDAMENTALS · SKILL ADHD-friendly visual edition Wound care is four questions asked in order: how is this wound closing? what phase is it in? what does the bed look like? what does the bed need? Answer those and the dressing chooses itself. 🧵 3 intentions Primary = edges together · Secondary = fills from the bottom · Tertiary = left open, closed later. ⏱️ 4 phases Hemostasis → Inflammatory → Proliferative → Maturation. 🔴🟡⚫ RED · YELLOW · BLACK Red = protect · Yellow = cleanse · Black = debride. 🚨 Evisceration Sterile saline-moist gauze · low Fowler's, knees bent · NEVER push it back in · call surgery. 🧬
STEP 1 · THE BIOLOGY Two frameworks. Intention = how the edges come together. Phase = where the wound is in time.

Intact barrier Skin limits fluid loss and protects against injury. Disruption Pressure, trauma, moisture or disease damages tissue. Repair response Healing depends on perfusion, nutrition and the cause. Assess Location, size, tissue, exudate, surrounding skin, pain and infection signs. Care Cleanse and dress according to wound type; protect surrounding skin. Support healing Address pressure, circulation, nutrition, glucose and other modifiable factors. 🧠 1 = zip it now. 2 = it fills itself. 3 = wait, then zip it. I

entries.h: ⏱️ The four phases — with the tissue drawn at each stage
entries.t: 🧠 "Stop · Clean · Build · Polish." Stop the bleeding (hemostasis), clean the site (inflammatory), build new tissue (proliferative), polish the scar (maturation).

entries.h: 🍽️ What speeds healing up — and what stalls it
entries.t: Helps ✅ Hurts ❌ Adequate protein (collagen is protein) Malnutrition, low albumin <3.5 g/dL Vitamin C — needed to cross-link collagen; zinc and vitamin A support repair Deficiency states, alcohol misuse Good perfusion and oxygenation Smoking (vasoconstriction + carbon monoxide), PVD, anemia, shock Glycemic control Hyperglycemia — impairs white cells and feeds bacteria Moist, protected wound bed Drying out, repeated trauma from dressings, infection, foreign body Young, healthy immune system Corticosteroids , chemothe

entries.h: ⭐ Why "moist wound healing" beats a dry scab
entries.t: Cells cannot migrate across a dry crust — they have to burrow underneath it. A moist wound bed with dry, intact surrounding skin heals faster and hurts less. Too dry → cells die, scab forms, epithelium is slowed, dressing removal rips new tissue. Too wet → the wound edges macerate (soggy, white), the wound gets bigger, and bacteria thrive. The dressing's job is to balance : add moisture to a dry wound, absorb from a wet one. 🧠 "Moist in the middle, dry at the edges." Goldilocks rule for every dressing decision on t
STEP 2 · LOOK Every dressing change is an assessment opportunity. Look before you cover it back up.

entries.h: 🔴🟡⚫ The wound bed — red, yellow, black
entries.t: 🧠 Traffic light, backwards. Black = stop everything and debride. Yellow = slow down and clean. Red = go, just protect it.

Also chart the amount (scant / small / moderate / large, or the number of saturated gauze pads, or milliliters from a drain) and odor after cleansing. A sudden increase in serosanguineous drainage from a surgical incision around post-op day 3–14 is the classic warning sign of impending dehiscence — see the Complications section. 🧠 Sero = serum (clear). Sangui = blood (red). Pus = purulent. Put the two together and you get "serosanguineous" — pale pink.

Location and wound type/etiology Size — length × width × depth in cm ; undermining and tunnelling by the clock (12:00 = head) Wound bed — % red granulation / yellow slough / black eschar; is there epithelium at the edges? Exudate — type, amount, odor (assess after cleansing) Wound edges — approximated? rolled? undermined? macerated? Periwound skin — erythema, warmth, induration, maceration, excoriation Pain — before, during and after the dressing change Signs of infection , and whether the wound is progressing or s

entries.h: 🧪 Culturing a wound — the technique that gets a valid result
entries.t: Cleanse the wound with sterile normal saline FIRST. Culturing before cleansing just grows the surface junk. Never swab pus, exudate, eschar or slough — those give you colonizing organisms, not the pathogen. Swab clean, viable granulation tissue : rotate the swab over about 1 cm² for several seconds with enough pressure to express fluid from the tissue (Levine technique). Label, bag, and send promptly; note antibiotics already given. If both aerobic and anaerobic cultures are ordered, follow lab requirements for the
STEP 3 · DO IT Pick the dressing from what the wound needs, not from what's in the cupboard.

entries.h: 🩹 Dressing types, drawn — matched to the wound
entries.t: Two more you should be able to name: antimicrobial dressings (silver, iodine, medical-grade honey) for infected or heavily colonized wounds, and negative-pressure wound therapy ("wound vac") — a sealed foam dressing under suction that removes exudate, reduces edema and pulls the wound edges together; monitor the seal, the canister output and for bleeding. 🧠 Dry wound → add water (hydroGEL). Wet wound → soak it up (foam, ALGinate). "Gel gives, alginate absorbs."

entries.h: ✅ Wet-to-dry dressing change — the ordered skill, step by step
entries.t: 1 Prepare Check the order. Assess pain and give analgesia 30–45 minutes before the change. Ask about latex, adhesive and iodine allergies . Explain the procedure, provide privacy, position the patient. ▼ 2 Set up Hand hygiene → gather supplies → open sterile field and pour sterile saline into the sterile container → place gauze/packing to soak. Have a plastic waste bag within reach. ▼ 3 Remove the old dressing Clean gloves. Loosen tape gently toward the wound, supporting the skin. If the gauze is stuck, moisten it

entries.h: 🚿 Cleaning direction — the picture that answers the question
entries.t: Irrigation: use warmed sterile normal saline, hold the syringe about 2.5 cm (1 in) above the wound, and irrigate from the cleanest area toward the dirtiest until the return runs clear. Standard teaching for a safe irrigation pressure is a 35 mL syringe with a 19-gauge angiocatheter (about 8 psi ). Wear a gown, mask and eye protection — irrigation splashes. 🧠 One swab, one stroke, one direction — then bin it. Never go back over a clean area with a used swab.

entries.h: 🔪 Debridement — five ways to remove dead tissue
entries.t: Type How it works Mechanical Physical removal — wet-to-dry gauze, hydrotherapy/whirlpool, irrigation, gentle scrubbing. Fast but non-selective (takes healthy tissue too), painful, can bleed. Enzymatic (chemical) A prescribed topical enzyme ointment applied directly to the necrotic tissue only. Selective , slower, painless. Protect the surrounding skin. Autolytic The body's own enzymes do it, under a moisture-retentive dressing (film, hydrocolloid, hydrogel). Most selective and least painful — but the slowest. Not f

Record each drain separately — label them (JP #1, JP #2), chart output in mL , color and consistency. Empty when ½ to ⅔ full and re-establish the vacuum every time (a bulb that has re-expanded is not draining). Secure the tubing so it doesn't pull, and keep the reservoir below the wound . Report: a sudden increase in output, output that stops abruptly, a change back to bright red bloody drainage, purulence or foul odor, or a dislodged drain. Expect the drainage to progress from sanguineous → serosanguineous → serou
STEP 4 · EMERGENCIES Two words to know cold: dehiscence and evisceration. One of them is a surgical emergency.

entries.h: 🚨 Dehiscence vs evisceration — and exactly what you do
entries.t: 🧠 "Cover, curl, call — never cram." Cover with sterile saline-moist gauze, curl the patient into low Fowler's with knees bent, call the surgeon, and never push anything back inside.

Timing: classically around post-op day 3–14 , when the inflammatory phase ends and the new collagen is still weak. The warning sign: a sudden increase in serosanguineous drainage from a previously drying incision. The patient may describe a "popping" or "giving way" sensation, often while coughing, vomiting, straining or getting up. Risk factors: obesity, malnutrition/low protein, infection, diabetes, corticosteroids, smoking, chronic cough, vomiting, straining, abdominal distension, poor surgical closure. Preventi

Infection — increasing erythema, warmth, edema, induration, purulent drainage, odor, increasing pain, fever, leukocytosis, delayed healing. Wound infections typically declare themselves around post-op day 3–6 . Hemorrhage — frank bleeding, a rapidly saturating dressing, a hematoma (swollen bluish bulge under the incision). Apply pressure, mark the drainage border with the time, and escalate. Fistula — an abnormal tract between the wound and another organ or the skin; look for unexpected drainage such as stool or ur

Hand hygiene before and after touching the wound; clean technique for most home dressing changes. Splint the incision with a pillow when coughing, sneezing, laughing, vomiting or standing up. Ask for pain medicine early — before the pain becomes unbearable, and ideally 30–45 minutes before a dressing change. Signs to report: increasing redness/swelling/warmth, thick or foul drainage, fever ≥ 38 °C (100.4 °F) , increasing pain, wound edges pulling apart, or any sudden increase in drainage. Eat the protein , stay hyd

Q1: A deep pressure ulcer is left open to granulate in. Which type of healing is that? Show answer Secondary intention — the edges are not approximated, so the wound fills in from the base with granulation tissue, contracts, and heals with a large scar over weeks to months. Q2: On post-op day 2 the incision is red, warm, slightly swollen and tender. Is this infection? Show answer Not necessarily — this is the expected inflammatory phase (days 1 to about 4 or 5). It becomes concerning if it is increasing after day 5

entries.h: Why major burns affect the whole body
entries.t: Follow the tissue injury, fluid shifts and changes in oxygen delivery. One idea at a time Untimed learning 🧬 Tissue Locate the injured skin layers. 💧 Fluid shift Leaky capillaries move fluid into tissue. 🫁 Oxygen Assess airway and inhalation injury. 🧪 Reassess Interpret changing labs with the whole patient.
Epidermis Dermis Subcutaneous fat Fascia / muscle

Epidermis: surface barrier without its own blood vessels; some sensory endings extend into it. Dermis: vessels, nerves, follicles and glands. Injury here affects healing and sensation. Subcutaneous fat: insulation and cushioning; deeper structures include fascia and muscle. Read more: NSW ACI: Foundations of burn patient care (2025)
Epidermis · injured Dermis Subcutaneous fat Fascia / muscle Dry, red and blanching. Usually painful. Limited to the epidermis. Part of the dermis

Epidermis · injured Dermis · partly injured Subcutaneous fat Fascia / muscle Some dermis remains. Blisters, moisture and pain are common; deeper injury may look pale and feel less sensitive. Through the dermis
Epidermis · injured Dermis · injured Subcutaneous fat Fascia / muscle Entire dermis is destroyed. Often dry or leathery; sensation may be reduced centrally. Edges can still hurt. Beyond skin

Epidermis · injured Dermis · injured Subcutaneous fat · injured Fascia / muscle · injured Extends beyond skin into structures such as fat, fascia, muscle or bone. Urgent specialist evaluation is needed. Hatched areas show injury. Pain alone does not measure severity. Depth may be mixed and change over time. Read more: NSW ACI: Burn depth · American Burn Association: Referral guidance
Vessel walls help maintain the balance between blood and tissue fluid.

Fluid leaves the circulation. Tissue edema increases while perfusion can fall. Blue marks represent fluid/protein movement; red shapes represent red cells. This is a mechanism diagram, not a volume measurement. Excess resuscitation can also worsen edema. Read more: NSW ACI: Foundations of burn patient care (2025) · ABA: Burn shock resuscitation guideline (2024) Inflammatory injury Vascular permeability rises and fluid distribution changes. Less effective circulating volume Reduced preload and altered cardiac functi

1 · Coagulation: greatest injury; tissue is nonviable. 2 · Stasis: impaired perfusion; tissue may recover or deteriorate. 3 · Hyperemia: increased flow; tissue generally recovers. Protect perfusion, warmth and the wound. Reassess depth because tissue in the zone of stasis can deteriorate. Read more: NSW ACI: Foundations of burn patient care (2025)

entries.h: Electrical injury can be deeper than it looks
entries.t: Assess the mechanism and associated falls or trauma. Deep muscle injury can release potassium and myoglobin; monitor rhythm, renal function and urine findings. Fluid and urine-output targets may differ from a routine thermal-burn plan.

Shock can reduce gut perfusion; assess distention, vomiting and feeding tolerance. Major burns increase energy demands and protein breakdown. Start nutrition support when clinically appropriate; bowel sounds alone do not determine readiness. Use stress-ulcer prevention when indicated by the patient’s risk and protocol. Read more: Vanderbilt: Adult burn nutrition (document revised July 2023) · Vanderbilt Burn Center: Clinical protocols
Leak and edema develop over hours. Perfusion, oxygenation and fluid response guide care. Stabilization → wound healing
Permeability improves and fluid may be mobilized. Wound care, nutrition and infection assessment remain central. Across recovery

Movement and function begin early and continue through scar remodeling. There is no universal moment when every patient “flips.” Review current findings instead of assuming an exact 18–24-hour peak or mandatory diuresis at a fixed hour. Read more: ABA: Burn shock resuscitation guideline (2024) · NSW ACI: Burn physiotherapy and occupational therapy (2025)
Urgent assessment

Voice change, stridor, respiratory distress, soot or an enclosed-space exposure warrant urgent evaluation. Singed hair alone does not automatically decide intubation. Anticipate airway support based on the whole assessment. Read more: NSW ACI: Adult burn emergency assessment

A conventional pulse oximeter cannot reliably exclude carbon monoxide poisoning. In a compatible exposure, give oxygen and obtain urgent evaluation with co-oximetry according to protocol. Neurologic symptoms or loss of consciousness are concerning even with a “normal” saturation. Read more: CDC: Clinical guidance for carbon monoxide poisoning
Cell injury can raise K⁺ early. Later losses can lower it, but either direction is possible.
May fall or rise as water balance and treatment change. Interpret the measured value and symptoms.
Plasma loss may cause hemoconcentration. Hemodilution, bleeding or cell destruction may lower values later.

Trend renal function, acid–base status and lactate with the bedside assessment. A hematocrit of 60% is not required. K⁺ over a single cutoff is not a complete severity assessment; consider the level, rate of change, ECG, symptoms and renal function. Read more: Vanderbilt Burn Center: Clinical protocols

A normal-looking ECG does not rule out serious hyperkalemia. Report significant potassium abnormalities or new rhythm changes promptly and follow the emergency treatment plan. Read more: Vanderbilt Burn Center: Clinical protocols

The local cold injury — tissue that literally freezes NG-116 INTEGUMENTARY · EMERGENCY ADHD-friendly visual edition Frostbite is tissue that actually freezes : ice crystals form in and around the cells while the vessels clamp down, so the part is starved of blood at the same time as it is being torn apart from the inside. Frostbite is the LOCAL injury; hypothermia (NG-041) is the SYSTEMIC one — and the two arrive together far more often than not. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →

🧊 Cells become snowballs Ice crystals + vasoconstriction + vascular stasis = frozen, starved tissue. 🔥 Rapid rewarming = PRIORITY Circulating warm water 37–39 °C (about 98.6–102 °F) until the part is pliable and red-purple. ❌ Never rub. Never dry heat. Rubbing shears the ice crystals through the tissue. Numb skin cannot feel a burn. 🚫 Don't thaw if it may refreeze Freeze → thaw → refreeze is far more destructive than staying frozen. 🧊
STEP 1 · PATHO Two injuries happening at once: ice inside the tissue, and no blood getting to it.

entries.h: 🧊 Normal tissue vs frozen tissue — the cutaway

entries.t: Cold exposure Heat loss exceeds heat production. Hypothermia Core temperature falls and organ function slows. Frostbite Tissue freezes and develops local injury. Hypothermia care Handle gently, prevent further heat loss and use the appropriate rewarming pathway. Frostbite care Protect tissue, avoid rubbing and prevent refreezing after thawing. Assess Mental status, breathing, circulation and the extent of injury. 🧠 "Every cell becomes a little snowball." Two things are killing the tissue: the ice (direct cell damag

entries.h: 🧨 The cascade — why the damage keeps going after you warm it
entries.t: Cold exposure → skin vessels vasoconstrict to protect the core ▼ Blood flow to fingers, toes, ears, nose falls → vascular stasis ▼ Tissue temperature drops below freezing → ice crystals form outside then inside cells ▼ Water pulled out of cells → cellular dehydration , electrolyte shifts, membrane rupture ▼ Rewarming → blood floods back → reperfusion injury : inflammation, edema, more microthrombi ▼ Progressive dermal ischemia over hours to days → blistering, then necrosis / gangrene The final tissue loss is decide

entries.h: 📍 Where frostbite happens — the far corners
entries.t: 🧠 "The body sacrifices the edges to save the middle." Vasoconstriction protects the core and abandons the periphery — so the periphery is what freezes.

🍺 Alcohol vasodilates + kills judgment 🚬 Nicotine vasoconstricts 🏚️ Homelessness prolonged exposure 💧 Wet clothing heat loss ×25 vs dry 🥾 Tight boots/gloves constrict flow 🌬️ Wind chill strips warmth fast 🫀 PVD / diabetes already poor flow 👵👶 Very old / very young poor thermoregulation 🧠 ↓ LOC or mental illness can't self-rescue ❄️ Previous frostbite permanently cold-sensitive 🧠 "Wet, windy, drunk, and tight." Four things that turn a cold day into a frostbite injury. 🔎
STEP 2 · CLUES Same depth language as every other wound page — this time the injury came from cold.

You may also see it split simply into two: superficial frostbite (skin blue, mottled or waxy yellow; clear blisters; skin still moves over the tissue below) and deep frostbite (skin white, hard as wood, blood-filled blisters, progressing to gangrene). The true depth cannot be judged until after rewarming — and often not for days. 🧠 Blister color = depth. Clear blister = superficial and likely to recover. Blood-filled blister = deep and likely to lose tissue. Exactly the same rule as pressure injuries on NG-044 .

entries.h: 🔎 What you assess — before and after rewarming
entries.t: Color — white / waxy yellow / mottled blue / gray; after thawing, does it turn red-purple (good) or stay pale (bad)? Texture — soft and pliable (superficial) vs hard, wooden, non-indentable (deep). Sensation — numbness is universal at first; return of sensation and pain after rewarming is a good sign. Blisters — present? clear or hemorrhagic? when did they appear? Perfusion — capillary refill, pulses (may need Doppler), warmth. Edema — expect it to increase for 24–48 h after thawing; check for tight compartments. C

entries.h: ⭐ Frostbite vs hypothermia — local vs systemic
entries.t: Frostbite (this page) Hypothermia (NG-041) LOCAL tissue freezing SYSTEMIC drop in core temperature Fingers, toes, ears, nose, cheeks The whole body; core temp < 35 °C (95 °F) Threatens the limb Threatens the life — cold myocardium → V-fib Treat with rapid rewarming of the part in warm water Treat with core rewarming , gentle handling, cardiac monitoring Damage keeps declaring itself for weeks Danger is immediate — arrhythmia, afterdrop If the patient has both, the core comes first. Stabilize airway, breathing, circ
STEP 3 · CARE One correct method, and a list of tempting wrong ones.
🧠 "Warm water, no rubbing, no fire, no pressure." The frozen part is full of microscopic glass — rubbing drags it through the tissue, and anesthetic skin cannot tell you it is being burned.

1 ABCs and core temperature first Get the patient out of the cold. Treat systemic hypothermia before or alongside the limb, and handle gently — the cold heart is irritable. ▼ 2 Remove wet and constrictive things Wet clothing, boots, gloves, rings, watches and jewelry — before the swelling starts. Dry the patient, insulate the rest of the body. ▼ 3 Decide: is refreezing possible? If the part could refreeze before definitive care, do NOT thaw it. Protect and transport frozen. Freeze–thaw–refreeze causes far more tiss

entries.h: 🚨 The refreezing rule — the highest-yield trap
entries.t: Do not begin rewarming unless the part can be kept thawed. 🧠 "Better frozen than half-thawed." A second freeze makes bigger ice crystals in tissue that is already injured.

entries.h: 💧 Blisters, dressings and the little details
entries.t: Dressings: loose, bulky, dry, non-adherent . Place gauze between every finger and toe so they don't macerate against each other. No occlusive dressings and nothing circumferential/tight — swelling after thawing can turn a snug wrap into a tourniquet. Elevate the part after rewarming; keep the patient on bed rest if the feet are involved. Blisters: practice varies. Many protocols debride or aspirate clear blisters and leave hemorrhagic blisters intact; some leave all blisters intact. Follow the provider's order and
STEP 4 · WATCH & TEACH The wound that follows behaves like any other wound — see NG-080 — but the timeline is unusually slow.

entries.h: 📅 What it looks like over time
entries.t: Surgery is not rushed. Except for infection or compartment syndrome, amputation decisions wait for a clear line of demarcation — classically summarized as "frostbite in January, amputate in July." Early appearance badly over-predicts tissue loss. 🧠 Frostbite lies on day one. A black finger in week two may still have a viable base — which is why nobody cuts early.

Infection / cellulitis — the dead tissue is a culture medium. Fever, spreading redness, purulence, worsening pain. Compartment syndrome — post-thaw edema in a closed space. Pain out of proportion , pain on passive stretch, tense compartment, paraesthesia. Escalate immediately; pulselessness is a late sign. Gangrene and auto-amputation — dry gangrene mummifies and may separate on its own. Rhabdomyolysis and AKI in extensive deep injury. Long-term sequelae: permanent cold sensitivity, chronic neuropathic pain, numbne

You are now permanently cold-sensitive in that area — dress in layers, cover the ears, nose and hands, and change wet gloves and socks immediately. Stop smoking — nicotine constricts the exact vessels the healing tissue depends on. Avoid alcohol in the cold. Loose, layered, dry clothing ; mittens beat gloves; boots that are not tight. Protect the injured part — no direct heat, no soaking without instruction, no picking at blisters or eschar. Report: fever, increasing pain, spreading redness, foul drainage, or any n

entries.h: 🗺️ Where this page sits in the set
entries.t: NG-051 — Skin : the layers and the partial- vs full-thickness rule that this page's degrees map onto exactly. NG-044 — Pressure Injuries : same depth logic, different cause. Blister color means the same thing on both pages. NG-080 — Wound Care : how the frostbite wound is dressed, debrided and documented once it declares. NG-041 — Hypothermia : the systemic partner. Local vs systemic; limb vs life. 🧠 Cold hurts twice: once to the whole body ( NG-041 ) and once to the corners (this page). ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧊 Ice + stasis Crystals wreck the cells; vasoconstriction starves them. 🔥 37–39 °C water Circulating warm water, 20–30 min, until pliable and red-purple. Analgesia first. ❌ No rub · no fire · no pressure And never thaw if it can refreeze. 🩸 Blister color = depth Clear = superficial. Blood-filled = deep.

Q1: In one sentence, what is happening to the tissue in frostbite? Show answer Ice crystals form in and around the cells, pulling water out and rupturing membranes, while cold-induced vasoconstriction causes vascular stasis and microthrombi, so the tissue is simultaneously frozen and starved of blood. Q2: What is the priority treatment, and at what temperature? Show answer Rapid rewarming by immersing the part in circulating warm water at about 37 to 39 degrees Celsius (about 98.6 to 102 degrees Fahrenheit), typica

Prepared wound receives the graft. Meshing can expand coverage and permit drainage. Prevent shear and follow the surgeon’s dressing and movement restrictions. Clean hands before and after care. Use aseptic technique and dedicated or cleaned equipment.
Select PPE for anticipated exposure and transmission precautions. Follow the burn unit’s environmental rules.

Watch for changing wound findings and systemic deterioration. Obtain ordered cultures; antimicrobial treatment follows the clinical plan. CDC recommends excluding flowers and potted plants from areas for immunosuppressed patients. Why: Pseudomonas aeruginosa lives in standing water and soil, such as vase water and potting soil, and is a classic burn-wound infection. An N95 is for airborne organisms such as TB, not this. Do not turn this into a universal rule that every burn requires the same isolation setup. Read m
Titrated IV analgesia is commonly used because poor perfusion can make IM or subcutaneous absorption unreliable.

Use the prescribed multimodal plan. Time medication for procedures and monitor sedation, breathing and relief. Explain the plan and offer pauses, positioning and other comfort strategies. A deep burn can have a numb center while other injured areas remain painful. Read more: NSW ACI: Burn pain

Follow measured electrolyte, renal and perfusion trends; do not expect every patient to have identical abnormalities. Assess tetanus protection and use prescribed prevention for thrombosis and stress ulcers when indicated. Routine systemic antibiotics for every burn are not a substitute for wound care and infection assessment. Suspected infection or sepsis requires timely treatment.

Burns III · TBSA estimation & the Parkland fluid calculation — the math page NG-146 INTEGUMENTARY · CALCULATION ADHD-friendly visual edition The Rule of 9's is a fast way to estimate the percentage of the body burned — the Total Body Surface Area (TBSA) . You need that number for one reason: it is the input to the fluid-resuscitation formula. Once you have TBSA, the Parkland formula tells you how many milliliters of Lactated Ringer's to give in the first 24 hours — and the urine output tells you whether that number

entries.h: 🧭 This page vs. its sibling — they are NOT the same page
entries.t: NG-146 (this page) = the NUMBERS. Rule of 9's, the palm rule, Lund–Browder, pediatric proportions, the Parkland formula, the 8-hour/16-hour split, and worked practice problems. NG-164 = the REHABILITATION PHASE. What happens after the wounds close: contracture prevention, positioning and splinting, pressure garments, water-based lotion, daily exercise, scar maturation, itch, sun protection, nutrition and psychosocial recovery. Both come from the same source infographic, so they share a title — but do not study them
STEP 1 · GET THE PERCENTAGE Divide the adult body into chunks of 9% (plus one 1% chunk). Front and back are counted separately.

entries.h: 🧍 Adult Rule of 9's — anterior & posterior, fully labeled
entries.t: EXAM TIP A whole arm or leg includes front and back. Front of one arm = 4.5% ; whole arm = 9% . Count the perineum’s 1% only once.

entries.h: 📐 Nines Navigator — Rule of Nines Practice
entries.t: Practice adult burn percentages with a front-and-back body map, 40 cases, six-question rounds, hints, and worked answers. No timer. Practice calculating TBSA →

Region Front Back Whole Head & neck 4.5% 4.5% 9% Each arm (with the hand) 4.5% 4.5% 9% Trunk 18% (chest 9 + abdomen 9) 18% (upper back 9 + lower back & buttocks 9) 36% Each leg (with the foot) 9% 9% 18% Perineum — — 1% (count once) Whole-body check: head & neck 9 + both arms 18 + trunk 36 + both legs 36 + perineum 1 = 100% . Worked example: entire front of the trunk + one whole arm = 18% + 9% = 27% TBSA (assuming those whole surfaces are partial- or full-thickness). Which burns count: superficial partial-thickness,

entries.h: ⭐ The three habits that stop Rule-of-Nines mistakes
entries.t: ↔️ FRONT ≠ BACK always ask which side 1️⃣ ADD THE 1% perineum is easy to forget 🚫 SKIP 1° BURNS superficial is not counted 🧍 WHOLE LIMB? arm 9 · leg 18 ➗ HALF IT one surface = half the region ✅ SUM CHECK can't exceed 100 Only partial-thickness (2°) and full-thickness (3°/4°) burns are included in TBSA. A superficial (1°) sunburn is NOT counted — it does not leak the way deeper burns do, so counting it would over-estimate the fluid. 🧠 “First degree doesn't count.” If the stem says “reddened, painful, no blisters, bl

entries.t: Answer first: a child's head is proportionally much bigger and the legs proportionally smaller . Using the adult chart on an infant badly under-estimates the burn.

STEP 2 · WHEN 9's WON'T WORK Rule of 9's is fast but blunt. Use the palm rule for scattered burns and Lund–Browder when accuracy matters.

Answer first: the patient's own palm including the fingers is roughly 1% of their TBSA. Use it for patchy, scattered or irregular burns that don't fill a whole 9% region. 🧠 “One hand, one percent.” Count palms for splash and spatter burns; count nines for whole-region burns.

A printed chart that assigns a percentage to each small body segment and adjusts the head/thigh/leg values by exact age band . Most accurate method, and the standard in burn centers Essential in children , where Rule of 9's is crudest Slower — you shade a diagram and add up small numbers Rule of 9's is the rapid field/ED estimate ; Lund–Browder is the definitive one done later 🧠 “Nines for now, Lund–Browder for later.” Fast first, accurate second.

Counting a whole leg (18%) when only the front was burned ( 9% ) Counting the 1° sunburn region into TBSA Forgetting the perineum's 1% when the stem specifically mentions it Using adult percentages on a toddler Adding to more than 100% Using the nurse's palm instead of the patient's 🧠 Read the stem twice: “anterior”, “posterior”, “entire”, “circumferential”. Those four words change the answer. 🧮
STEP 3 · TURN % INTO mL Three numbers multiplied together. The hard part is not the multiplication — it is knowing what each number means.

The commonly taught version of the consensus (Parkland) formula for the first 24 hours after a major burn, given as Lactated Ringer's . 4 mL × body weight (kg) × %TBSA = total LR in the first 24 h → ½ over the first 8 h · ½ over the next 16 h 🧠 “ 4 for the 4 -alarm fire · half in 8 .” Four milliliters, weight, burn percent — then cut it in half and put the first half in the first eight hours.

entries.h: ⏳ The clock starts at the TIME OF INJURY — not arrival
entries.t: This is the highest-yield trap in the whole topic. If a patient is burned at 08:00 and reaches you at 10:00, you have 6 hours left to deliver the first half — so the rate has to be higher, not the same. 🧠 “The burn started the stopwatch, not the ambulance.” Always ask what time did this happen?

entries.h: ➗ Turning the total into an hourly rate
entries.t: Exam questions often want the mL/hr , not just the total. Two divisions: first 8 h rate = (total ÷ 2) ÷ 8 next 16 h rate = (total ÷ 2) ÷ 16 The first-8-hour rate is always double the next-16-hour rate If hours have already been lost, divide by the hours remaining in that block Weight in pounds? ÷ 2.2 to get kilograms first 🧠 “Front-load it.” The leak is worst early, so the fluid goes in fastest early.

The capillary leak begins to seal, so the plan changes. Crystalloid volume is reduced and titrated down as urine output allows Colloid (e.g. albumin) is often added in the second 24 hours in many protocols, once capillaries are less leaky, to hold fluid in the vessels Maintenance fluid (often with dextrose) replaces evaporative loss Electrolytes flip: potassium falls , H&H falls with hemodilution — see NG-107 Watch hard for the swing to fluid overload during diuresis: crackles, JVD, dyspnea, sudden weight gain 🧠 “D
STEP 4 · DO THE MATH Cover the answer, work it on paper, then check. Three of these are lifted straight from the classic question banks.

entries.h: 🎓 Example 1 — full-thickness burns to ALL posterior surfaces
entries.t: A client has full-thickness burns to all posterior body surfaces . Using the Rule of 9's, calculate the % TBSA affected. back of head & neck …… 4.5% entire back (upper 9 + lower 9) …… 18% back of both arms (4.5 × 2) …… 9% back of both legs (9 × 2) …… 18% 4.5 + 18 + 9 + 18 = 49.5% TBSA Why students miss it: they use whole-limb values (9% per arm, 18% per leg) instead of halving for the posterior surface only. 🧠 “All the back = just under half the body.” 49.5% — remember it as “about 50%.”

A client has partial-thickness burns to the anterior legs and the perineum . Calculate the % TBSA. front of right leg …… 9% front of left leg …… 9% perineum …… 1% 9 + 9 + 1 = 19% TBSA Why students miss it: they forget the perineum's 1% and answer 18%, or they count whole legs and answer 37%. 🧠 “18 + the little 1.” When the stem says perineum , it is because that 1% is the point of the question.

entries.h: 🎓 Example 3 — now turn it into milliliters
entries.t: The client above weighs 100 kg with 19% TBSA . Calculate the Lactated Ringer's fluid resuscitation needed. 4 mL × 100 kg × 19 %TBSA = 7,600 mL in the first 24 hours ½ = 3,800 mL in the first 8 hours → 475 mL/hr ½ = 3,800 mL over the next 16 hours → 237.5 mL/hr 🧠 “Same halves, different speeds.” Equal volumes, but the first one has to go in twice as fast.

entries.h: Practice A · 70 kg adult, burns to the entire front of the trunk and the whole right arm
entries.t: TBSA? Show answer Anterior trunk 18% + whole right arm 9% = 27% TBSA . Parkland total and first-8-hour rate? Show answer 4 × 70 × 27 = 7,560 mL in 24 h. Half = 3,780 mL in the first 8 h → 472.5 mL/hr ; then 3,780 mL over 16 h → 236.25 mL/hr .

entries.h: Practice B · 80 kg adult, burns to the head and neck (all round), anterior trunk, and both anterior legs
entries.t: TBSA? Show answer Head and neck all round 9% + anterior trunk 18% + anterior legs 9 + 9 = 45% TBSA . Parkland total? Show answer 4 × 80 × 45 = 14,400 mL in 24 h. First 8 h: 7,200 mL → 900 mL/hr . Next 16 h: 7,200 mL → 450 mL/hr . (A burn this size also needs an airway assessment first — head and neck burns.)

entries.h: Practice C · 154 lb adult, posterior trunk and the back of both legs, burned 3 hours before arrival
entries.t: Weight in kg and TBSA? Show answer 154 ÷ 2.2 = 70 kg . Posterior trunk 18% + posterior legs 9 + 9 = 36% TBSA . Total, and the rate for the remainder of the first 8-hour block? Show answer 4 × 70 × 36 = 10,080 mL total. Half = 5,040 mL must be in by 8 hours after the injury . Three hours are already gone, so it has to run over the remaining 5 hours → 5,040 ÷ 5 = 1,008 mL/hr . Then 5,040 mL over the next 16 h → 315 mL/hr . Titrate to urine output throughout. 🧠 Do these on paper, out loud, three days in a row. Burn ma

SAY IT OUT LOUD 9 · 9 · 18 · 18 · 18 · 1 Head · each arm · front trunk · back trunk · each leg · perineum = 100% . 🖐️ 1 palm = 1% Patient's palm + fingers. Use it for scattered burns. 🧮 4 × kg × % Parkland total of LR for 24 h. Half in 8 h, half in 16 h, clock from injury . 🚽 Urine rules the rate ≥30 mL/hr, BP ≥90, HR <120. The formula only starts the infusion.

Deep bacterial skin infection — spot it, mark it, escalate it NG-147 INTEGUMENTARY · INFECTION ADHD-friendly visual edition Cellulitis is an acute bacterial infection of the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue , usually Staph aureus or Group A Strep , that gets in through a break in the skin — most often on a lower leg . Because it is deep, the redness has no crisp border ; it spreads. The exam answer is almost always the same three moves: mark and date the margin, elevate the limb, give the antibiotic on time — an

🦠 Deep bacterial infection Staph aureus or Strep pyogenes in the deep dermis + subcutaneous fat . Deep = the border is fuzzy . 🔥 Red · Hot · Swollen · Tender Usually ONE lower leg . Poorly-defined spreading erythema — not a sharp-edged patch. 🖊️ Mark the margin Outline the redness, write the date & time on the skin . That single line tells the next nurse if it is winning or losing. 💊 Bacteria → antibiotics Plus elevate the limb, treat pain, and find the portal of entry (often athlete's foot). 🧬
STEP 0 · LEARN THIS ONCE Every page in this set uses this exact drawing. Learn the layers once and each disease becomes "the same picture, with something different happening in it."

entries.h: 🔬 Skin cutaway — where cellulitis actually lives
entries.t: DEPTH = THE ANSWER Impetigo sits in the top of the epidermis . Tinea sits in the dead keratin . Cellulitis is the deep one: deep dermis and subcutaneous fat — and because the infection is deep, the redness you see on the surface has no crisp edge .

Barrier breach or exposure Organisms reach vulnerable tissue. Local infection Inflammation affects the skin or underlying layers. Spread risk Some infections can progress beyond the local site. Impetigo Superficial bacterial infection often produces crusted lesions. Cellulitis Deeper infection causes spreading warmth, redness, swelling and pain. Tinea Dermatophyte infection requires antifungal treatment rather than antibacterial therapy. 🧠 "Deep = diffuse." The deeper the infection, the blurrier the border. Superfi

entries.h: 📖 Lesion vocabulary — you need this for all five pages
entries.t: Exam questions describe lesions instead of naming them. Learn the eight words and the description tells you the disease. 🧠 "Flat, Firm, Fluid, Foul, Flake." Macule is flat · papule/plaque are firm · vesicle/bulla are fluid · pustule is foul (pus) · crust and scale are the flakes left behind. 🦠
STEP 1 · WHY IT HAPPENS A break in the barrier + bacteria on the skin + a host who cannot fight back = cellulitis.

Cellulitis is an acute bacterial infection of the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue , most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Group A Streptococcus , classically in a lower limb (over the shin/tibia). 🧠 "CELLulitis = the CELLar." It lives in the basement of the skin — the deep layers — not the attic.

Break in the skin barrier ▼ Staph / Strep get into the deep dermis ▼ Bacterial enzymes + toxins spread through tissue planes ▼ Inflammation: vessels dilate & leak ▼ Redness · warmth · swelling · pain — spreading outward ▼ Untreated → abscess · lymphangitis · bacteremia 🧠 Strep makes enzymes that dissolve tissue planes, which is exactly why the redness spreads instead of staying in a neat circle.

entries.h: 🚪 Portals of entry — always look for the front door
entries.t: 🧠 "No door, no cellulitis." If you cannot find a break, look harder — between the toes, under a dressing, in a skin fold, at an old IV site.

Trauma / any wound — the doorway Diabetes — poor perfusion, neuropathy, impaired white cells Tinea pedis (athlete's foot) — cracks between the toes Lymphedema — stagnant lymph cannot clear bacteria Venous insufficiency — sluggish flow, fragile skin Obesity — moist skin folds, poorer perfusion Previous cellulitis — damaged lymphatics recur Immunosuppression — steroids, chemo, HIV 🧠 "Damp, damaged, diabetic." Wet skin, broken skin, and bad sugar control — the three setups.

Each episode scars the lymphatics . Damaged lymphatics → more swelling → less clearance of bacteria → the next episode is easier to get . Breaking that cycle is nursing work: treat the athlete's foot , moisturize dry cracked skin, manage edema (compression once infection is controlled and arterial flow is adequate), and control blood glucose. 🧠 Vicious circle: swelling → infection → scarring → more swelling.

entries.h: 🧪 Bug → drug: the rule that runs this whole set
entries.t: 🧠 Name the organism and the drug class names itself. Bacteria → antibiotic. Fungus → "-azole"/terbinafine. Virus → "-cyclovir". Autoimmune → calm the immune system down. 🔎
STEP 2 · WHAT YOU SEE Think infection: the four cardinal signs plus a body that is starting to react systemically.

Erythema — red, with a poorly-defined spreading border Warmth — compare with the other limb using the back of your hand Edema — tight, shiny, sometimes peau d'orange dimpling Pain / tenderness — and it hurts more than it looks like it should Fever , malaise, sometimes chills 🧠 "RHOP" — R ed, H ot, O edematous, P ainful. If all four are on ONE limb, think cellulitis.

Red streaks running up the limb ( lymphangitis ) + tender nodes Fever > 38 °C / 100.4 °F , rigors, tachycardia, hypotension, confusion Fluctuance — a soft, boggy pocket = abscess , needs drainage Pain out of proportion , dusky/purple skin, bullae, crepitus , rapid progression Redness clearly past the marked line despite 48 h of antibiotics Never assume "it just needs more time" when the redness is racing past the line and the patient is febrile. 🧠 "Streaks + spikes = speak up." Red streaks or a fever spike means es

entries.h: 📈 How bad is this? The escalation ladder
entries.t: 🧠 Pain out of proportion is the necrotizing fasciitis flag. The skin can look almost normal while the patient is in agony — that mismatch is the whole point.

entries.h: ⭐ Deep vs superficial — cellulitis vs erysipelas
entries.t: 🧠 "Erysipelas = Edge you can feel." Both start with E. Cellulitis fades; erysipelas has a step you can run your finger over.

WBC ↑ with a left shift (normal adult 4.5–11.0 × 10⁹/L ) CRP / ESR ↑ — inflammation markers, useful for trending Blood cultures if febrile/systemically unwell — before the first antibiotic dose Wound or abscess culture if there is drainable pus Blood glucose / HbA1c — undiagnosed diabetes shows up this way Imaging (ultrasound) if abscess or DVT is suspected 🧠 Cultures before antibiotics — once the drug is in, the culture may grow nothing and you lose the answer.

Measure the erythema (cm) and compare with the marked outline Limb circumference at a marked point — same spot, same tape, every time Temperature , pulse, BP, respiratory rate, mental status Pain score — a rising score with a shrinking rash is a red flag Distal pulses, capillary refill, sensation — is perfusion intact? Photograph per facility policy (with consent) alongside the marked line 🧠 Same spot, same tape, same time. Trends only mean something if you measure the same way twice. 🩺
STEP 3 · WHAT YOU DO Kill the bacteria, drain the pus if there is any, drop the swelling, and prove it is getting better.

entries.h: 🖊️ THE nursing intervention: mark and date the margin
entries.t: 🧠 "Draw it, date it, watch it." If the exam offers "outline the border of the erythema with a skin marker and note the date/time," that is almost always the answer.

Choice is prescriber-driven and depends on severity and local resistance patterns, but the families you should recognize: Penicillins — e.g. dicloxacillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate Cephalosporins — e.g. cephalexin (oral), cefazolin (IV) Clindamycin — an option in penicillin allergy If MRSA is suspected or there is purulence: doxycycline, TMP-SMX, or IV vancomycin Nursing: ask about allergies first, give doses on time to keep blood levels steady, and teach finish the whole course . 🧠 Purulent = think MRSA. Non-purule

entries.h: ⬆️ Elevate the limb — free and effective
entries.t: Raise the affected limb above the level of the heart whenever the patient is resting. Gravity drains the edema, which lowers pressure, improves perfusion and speeds antibiotic delivery to the tissue. Pair it with a bed cradle or pillows so the linen is not pressing on tender skin. 🧠 "Toes above the nose" is the memorable version — heart level is the real target.

Analgesia before dressing changes and repositioning Cool compresses for comfort — never ice directly on the skin Hydration and antipyretics for fever Skin care: moisturize the surrounding skin, treat any tinea pedis Glucose control in diabetes — hyperglycemia stalls healing Mobility when able, plus VTE prevention for the swollen immobile limb Hand hygiene and standard precautions; contact precautions if there is draining pus per facility policy 🧠 ELEVATE: E levate · L abs · E rythema marked · V itals · A ntibiotics

Never massage or vigorously rub a cellulitic limb — you push bacteria along tissue planes. Never apply a hot pack to numb, neuropathic or poorly-perfused skin — burns are silent. Never squeeze or "pop" an abscess at the bedside — drainage is a provider procedure. Never stop antibiotics because the redness improved — relapse and resistance follow. Never apply tight compression before infection and arterial flow have been assessed. 🧠 Don't rub, don't pop, don't stop.

entries.h: 🗣️ Patient teaching — what they take home
entries.t: Finish every dose , even after it looks better Elevate the limb at home; keep moving to prevent clots Come back for: fever, red streaks, spreading past the line, new pus, worsening pain, vomiting the antibiotic Wash and cover every cut; keep skin moisturized so it does not crack Dry between the toes and treat athlete's foot — that is the recurrence prevention step Diabetes: check your feet daily , including between the toes and with a mirror 🧠 "Finish · Elevate · Return." Three sentences the patient can repeat back
STEP 4 · THE REAL EXAM SKILL Five skin conditions, five patterns. Distribution and appearance narrow it before you read a single lab value.
🧠 One leg = cellulitis. One band = shingles. Around the mouth = impetigo. Rings = tinea. Elbows & knees with silver = psoriasis.

entries.h: 📊 Red leg differential — the three that get confused
entries.t: CELLULITIS STASIS DERMATITIS DVT Sides One leg Usually both One leg Onset Days Months–years Hours–days Skin Hot, red, tender, spreading Brown staining, scaly, itchy Swollen, may be pale or dusky Fever Common No No (usually) Itch vs pain Pain Itch Ache / tightness Treatment Antibiotics Emollients, compression, topical steroid Anticoagulation 🧠 "Both legs itch = it is not an infection." Bilateral, itchy, chronic → stasis dermatitis, and it gets misdiagnosed as cellulitis constantly.

Cellulitis vs erysipelas — fuzzy border vs sharp raised border Cellulitis vs abscess — diffuse firmness vs a fluctuant pocket (needs drainage) Cellulitis vs necrotizing fasciitis — pain that fits vs pain out of all proportion Cellulitis vs contact dermatitis — painful + febrile vs itchy with a shape that matches an exposure Cellulitis vs gout — spreading limb redness vs an exquisitely tender single joint (classically the great toe) 🧠 Pain says infection. Itch says inflammation or allergy. That single question sorts

The rash spread past the line → notify the provider , do not simply re-mark it and wait. Blood cultures come before the first antibiotic dose, not after. "Cellulitis of both lower legs" in an afebrile, itchy patient → question the diagnosis. Elevation is the answer more often than students expect. Recurrent cellulitis → the missed intervention is usually treating tinea pedis . Cellulitis itself is not spread person-to-person like impetigo — but draining pus is infectious material. 🧠 If an option says "mark and date

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🦠 Deep dermis + fat Staph or Strep. Deep = fuzzy border. 🔥 Red · Hot · Swollen · Tender Usually ONE lower leg, often febrile. 🖊️ Mark + date the margin Then elevate above the heart. 🚨 Red streaks = escalate Streaking, fever, fluctuance, pain out of proportion.

Because it is deep, the erythema has a poorly-defined, fading border rather than a sharp edge. Q2: Name the two usual organisms. Show answer Staphylococcus aureus and Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes). Q3: What is the classic bedside nursing intervention for tracking progress? 01 / Recovery timeline
Phase labels help organize care; recovery activities overlap. 1 · Emergent / resuscitation
Airway + circulation From injury through initial stabilization, often about 48–72 hours. 2 · Acute wound care
Wounds + nutrition Ongoing wound care, infection prevention and support for healing. 3 · Longer-term rehabilitation

Movement + daily life Scar care, independence and emotional recovery continue for months or longer. Rehabilitation starts early. Positioning, movement and participation begin when clinically appropriate. They do not wait for every wound to close. Sources: NSW ACI: Burn physiotherapy and occupational therapy (2025) · MSKTC: Exercise after burn injury
02 / Movement
A scar across the front of the elbow can shorten and limit straightening. Uninjured elbow
Flexible skin allows the elbow to move through its available range. Flexion contracture

Thermal or other injury Energy damages skin and sometimes deeper tissue. Barrier and capillary effects Fluid loss, edema and infection risk increase. Whole-patient response Large burns can cause shock and organ dysfunction. Depth Superficial, partial-thickness and full-thickness describe tissue involvement. Extent Estimate total body surface area using an age-appropriate method. Priorities Airway, breathing, perfusion, pain and temperature; follow burn-center and resuscitation guidance.

Wound closure Dressings, grafts or other care support healing. Scar development Tissue remodeling can limit movement. Rehabilitation Positioning, range of motion and daily function need ongoing attention. Nutrition Energy and protein needs can increase; follow the nutrition plan. Mobility Use prescribed exercises and splints while protecting healing tissue. Psychosocial care Body-image changes, pain, sleep and family support affect recovery. 1 · Shortened scar: tight tissue across the inner elbow can restrict exten

Match the position to the burn location, graft precautions and therapist’s plan. 1 Anterior neck Extension as prescribed; avoid a posture that keeps the front of the neck shortened. 2 Axilla / shoulder Abduction and rotation are set by the therapist for the burned surface. 3 Front of elbow Extension may protect range; forearm position follows the treatment plan. 4 Hand and wrist Use a fitted, burn-specific splint. Palm and back-of-hand burns may need different positions. 5 Hip and knee Avoid sustained shortening ac

entries.h: W · W · E — three care habits
entries.t: Use the routine your burn team prescribes. Macho Man’s WWE memory cue Water-based moisturizer. Wear prescribed garments. Exercise as prescribed. AI-generated fan illustration for a study mnemonic. No affiliation or endorsement. W
Apply to healed skin. Choose a fragrance-free product advised by the team. W
Follow the fitted garment’s schedule. Inspect skin and report fit problems. E

Practice movement and daily activities. Follow graft and wound restrictions. Individual plan, consistent routine. Product choice, garment wear time and exercises are not identical for every burn survivor. Sources: MSKTC: Scar management · MSKTC: Exercise after burn injury
05 / Skin function

entries.h: A deep burn can change how skin works
entries.t: Scar appearance, sensation and gland function depend on the depth of injury and healing. Uninjured skin
Oil and sweat glands support skin function. Sensory nerves detect touch and temperature. Deep-burn scar · example

Damaged glands can contribute to dryness or less sweating. Sensation and pigment can change. Care follows function: moisturize healed skin, protect it from sun and heat, and check areas with reduced sensation. Simplified cross-sections, not to scale. Not every scar is raised or has the same loss of structures. Sources: MSKTC: Temperature sensitivity · MSKTC: Sun protection
06 / Change over time
These are common patterns, not a promised recovery schedule. Newly healed
The area may be sensitive, dry or a different color. More active scarring
Some scars become thicker, tighter or itchier. Remodeling
Many gradually soften, flatten and fade. Longer-term

Texture, pigment or movement changes can persist. Follow progress, not a deadline. Ask the burn team about increasing tightness, skin breakdown or symptoms that interfere with daily life. Color swatches are illustrations of one skin tone, not a diagnostic scale. Sources: MSKTC: Scar management
07 / Nutrition
Nutrition changes with wound healing, activity, body size and overall health.
Include protein foods to support healing and muscle.
Needs may be higher during healing and decrease as recovery progresses.
Choose varied foods. Use vitamin or mineral supplements only as advised.

Follow the fluid plan, including any medical restrictions. Review with the dietitian: intake, weight trend, healing, strength and activity. A high-calorie diet is not a permanent requirement for every survivor. Sources: MSKTC: Healthy eating after burn injury

entries.h: Skin protection and life after discharge
entries.t: Protect healed skin from ultraviolet exposure with clothing, shade and the burn team’s sunscreen guidance. Pigment may return unevenly. Reduced sensation or altered sweating can change temperature tolerance. Check skin and plan breaks from heat or cold. Include sleep, body image, work or school, and emotional support in the recovery plan. Ask the person which activity matters most.

New skin breakdown, drainage, spreading redness or systemic illness. Increasing tightness or loss of movement. A garment or splint causing numbness, color change, persistent pressure or worsening pain.

entries.h: Eczema · Atopic vs Contact Dermatitis · NG-182 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Skin & Wound · Dermatitis · Pathophysiology Course 🩹 SKIN & WOUND SET NG-051 Skin (foundation) NG-044 Pressure Injuries NG-080 Wound Care NG-116 Frostbite NG-182 Dermatitis NG-225 Psoriasis NG-204 Skin Cancer

Atopic vs Contact Dermatitis — two itchy rashes with completely different stories NG-182 INTEGUMENTARY · IMMUNE ADHD-friendly visual edition Both look like an angry, itchy rash. The difference is where it came from . Atopic dermatitis is inside-out : an inherited leaky skin barrier plus an over-reactive immune system, flaring for years in the bends of the joints . Contact dermatitis is outside-in : something touched the skin, and the rash is shaped exactly like whatever touched it . 📄 Simple Nursing original — open

🧬 Atopic = inside-out Genetic · chronic · flares & remits · flexural (elbow & knee creases). 🧪 Contact = outside-in Something touched it · sharply demarcated to the contact area. 🤝 Atopic TRIAD Eczema + asthma + allergic rhinitis — ask about all three. 🩹 Moisturize, don't just medicate Emollients are the treatment, not an afterthought. Break the itch–scratch cycle. 🧬
SIDE A · INSIDE-OUT A chronic, relapsing, inherited condition — the skin's brick wall is leaky and the immune system is trigger-happy.

entries.h: 🧬 Why atopic skin flares — the barrier cutaway

entries.t: Immune or irritant response Inflammation disrupts the skin barrier. Itch and lesions Appearance depends on the condition and site. Barrier cycle Scratching and dryness can worsen inflammation. Atopic dermatitis Chronic itch and barrier dysfunction with an atopic tendency. Contact dermatitis A local reaction to an irritant or allergen. Psoriasis Immune-mediated inflammation commonly produces well-defined scaly plaques. 🧠 Atopic skin is a wall with crumbling mortar. Water leaks out (dry, itchy) and irritants get in (

entries.h: 🤝 The atopic triad — always ask about all three
entries.t: 🌿 Atopic dermatitis the skin 🫁 Asthma the lungs 🤧 Allergic rhinitis the nose These three travel together and often appear in that order through childhood — the "atopic march." A family history of any of them raises the odds of the others. Serum IgE is often elevated and eosinophils may be raised, but the diagnosis is clinical. 🧠 "Skin, sneeze, wheeze." If a child has bad eczema, ask about night cough, wheeze and a permanently runny nose — you may be the first person to connect them.

entries.h: ⚠️ Cardinal feature: the itch comes first
entries.t: Atopic dermatitis is "the itch that rashes," not the rash that itches. Pruritus is the defining symptom — it is often worst at night and wrecks sleep for the child and the parents. Acute flare: erythematous papules and vesicles, weeping serous exudate , crusting. Subacute: drier, scaly, red plaques. Chronic: lichenification (thick, leathery skin with exaggerated skin lines), excoriations, pigment change, fissures. Always: dry skin (xerosis) between flares. The skin is never truly "normal." 🧠 Wet → dry → leather. Ac

entries.h: 🔬 Acute → subacute → chronic — the same eczema, three faces
entries.t: 🧠 Wet → flaky → leathery. Acute needs drying and calming, subacute needs greasing, chronic needs the scratching stopped.

entries.h: 🗺️ Where it shows up — and it MOVES with age
entries.t: This single contrast answers the classic exam confusion. Eczema hides in the creases ; psoriasis sits on the points . Full detail on the psoriasis side: NG-225 — Psoriasis . 🧠 "Eczema bends, psoriasis extends." Infants are the exception — babies get it on the cheeks and the outsides of the limbs, and the rash migrates into the creases as they grow.

🧼 Harsh soap strips the lipid mortar 🧴 Fragrance perfumed products 🧥 Wool & synthetics scratchy fabric 🥵 Heat & sweat overheating, hot showers 🏜️ Dry air winter, indoor heating 🐈 Aeroallergens dust mites, dander, pollen 😰 Stress a real, documented trigger 🦠 Infection often S. aureus Food allergy triggers eczema in a minority of infants and young children — do not restrict a child's diet on your own ; that needs an allergy evaluation. 🧠 Hot, dry, scratchy, stressed. Four words that cover most flares — and all four a

entries.h: 🚨 Complications — the two you must recognize
entries.t: Secondary bacterial infection (usually Staphylococcus aureus ): honey-colored crusting , pustules, worsening redness and pain, fever. Broken, scratched, weeping skin is an open door. Eczema herpeticum — herpes simplex spreading across eczematous skin. Clusters of monomorphic "punched-out" vesicles and erosions, rapidly spreading, with fever and a sick-looking child. This is a dermatological emergency — escalate urgently for antiviral treatment. Sleep deprivation and its knock-on effects on school, work, mood and fa
SIDE B · OUTSIDE-IN Something touched the skin. The rash is a photograph of whatever it was .

entries.h: 🧪 Irritant vs allergic — two different mechanisms
entries.t: 🧠 Irritant = a burn. Allergic = a grudge. An irritant damages anybody's skin the first time; an allergen only reacts in someone the immune system has already met it in — and it takes a day or three to show up.

entries.h: 🔎 The rash is shaped like the culprit
entries.t: Common culprits to know: irritants — soaps, detergents, solvents, bleach, alcohol gel, frequent hand-washing, saliva (lip-lickers), urine and stool. Allergens — urushiol (poison ivy/oak/sumac), nickel (jewelry, snaps, watch backs, belt buckles), fragrance, preservatives, neomycin , hair dye (PPD) and rubber accelerators in gloves. 🧠 "If the rash has a straight edge, a human-made object made it." Ask: what touches your skin at work, at home, in your hobby, and what is new in the last 3 days?

entries.h: 🌿 Poison ivy — the myths you have to correct
entries.t: Blister fluid does NOT spread the rash. New patches appear later because thinner skin reacts later, or because there was more urushiol there. The rash is not contagious person-to-person. But urushiol on clothing, boots, tools, gloves and pet fur absolutely re-exposes you — wash all of it. Wash the skin with soap and cool water as soon as possible after exposure — ideally within minutes. Once it is bound, washing no longer prevents the reaction. The rash appears hours to a few days after exposure and typically lasts

entries.h: ⚠️ Latex — know which reaction you are being asked about
entries.t: Irritant contact dermatitis — dry, cracked hands from glove occlusion, powder and hand-washing. Not an allergy at all. Type IV allergic contact dermatitis — delayed, itchy, eczematous, usually to rubber accelerator chemicals ; appears 24–72 h after wearing gloves. Type I latex allergy — IgE-mediated, immediate : urticaria, angioedema, wheeze, anaphylaxis . This is the life-threatening one. Cross-reactive foods ("latex–fruit syndrome"): banana, avocado, kiwi, chestnut. Ask about them. High-risk groups: healthcare wo
STEP 3 · COMPARE The table the exam question is written from.

entries.h: ⭐ Atopic vs Irritant contact vs Allergic contact
entries.t: Feature Atopic dermatitis Irritant contact Allergic contact Cause Inside-out : inherited barrier defect + over-reactive immune response Outside-in : direct chemical/physical damage to the barrier Outside-in : Type IV delayed hypersensitivity (T-cell mediated) Immune memory? Yes — chronic immune dysregulation, ↑ IgE No — anyone gets it with enough exposure Yes — needs prior sensitization First exposure? N/A — lifelong tendency Reacts on the first exposure No reaction the first time; reacts on re-exposure Timing Chro

entries.h: ⚖️ Eczema vs psoriasis — the other classic mix-up
entries.t: Eczema (atopic dermatitis) Psoriasis FLEXURAL — inside the elbows and behind the knees EXTENSOR — outside of elbows, front of knees, scalp, lower back Itch is severe and the dominant symptom Itch is variable; may burn or sting instead Ill-defined edges; weeping and crusting in flares Sharply demarcated , thick plaques with silvery-white scale Lichenification, excoriations, dry skin between flares Scraping the scale can cause pinpoint bleeding (Auspitz sign); Koebner phenomenon — new plaques at sites of injury Usual

entries.h: 🔁 The itch–scratch cycle — why it never just settles
entries.t: 🧠 Scratching feels like treatment and behaves like fuel. Every intervention on the next section exists to break this loop. 🩺
STEP 4 · MANAGE Most of this is teaching — and most of the teaching is about moisturizer.

entries.h: ✅ Atopic dermatitis — the daily routine that actually works
entries.t: 1 Bathe smart Short (5–10 min), lukewarm bath or shower once daily. Fragrance-free, non-soap cleanser — no bubble bath, no scrubbing, no washcloths on inflamed skin. Pat dry, don't rub. ▼ 2 "Soak and seal" Apply emollient within about 3 minutes of getting out, while the skin is still damp. Thick ointments and creams beat lotions. Apply liberally, at least twice a day and every time after washing hands — even when the skin looks fine. ▼ 3 Treat the inflammation Topical corticosteroids to active areas, at the lowest

entries.h: 💊 Topical steroid potency by body region — thin skin needs weak steroid
entries.t: 🧠 "Weak where the skin is thin." Face, eyelids, armpits and groin get the gentlest preparation; palms and soles can take the strongest.

entries.h: ✅ Contact dermatitis — the treatment is detective work
entries.t: Identify and remove the agent. Nothing else works if the exposure continues. Take a full history: occupation, hobbies, new products, jewelry, cosmetics, topical medicines, plants, gloves. Wash the area with mild soap and cool water as soon as possible after exposure; wash contaminated clothing, tools and pets. Cool compresses and colloidal oatmeal baths for weeping, itchy skin; calamine for symptom relief. Topical corticosteroids for localized disease; systemic corticosteroids for severe or widespread reactions (cl

entries.h: 👨‍👩‍👧 Teach the family — the sentences that land
entries.t: "This is not contagious and it is not your fault." Say it out loud, especially to parents and to school-age children. "Moisturizer is medicine." Every day, forever — not only when it flares. "Use the steroid properly and you'll use less of it." Under-treating a flare from steroid fear leads to longer, worse flares. Use as prescribed, on the areas prescribed. "Short nails, cotton clothes, cool room." Call for: honey-colored crusting, pus, fever, rapidly spreading painful blisters/punched-out sores (possible eczema h

NG-225 — Psoriasis : the extensor-surface, silvery-scale counterpart. Learn the two together or you will mix them up. Allergic = 12–72 h later, itches (Type IV). 🚨 Punched-out vesicles + fever Eczema herpeticum — escalate now.

Q2: Where is atopic dermatitis found in an infant, and where in an older child? Show answer Infants: cheeks, scalp, trunk and the extensor surfaces of the limbs, typically sparing the diaper area.
