entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Integumentary · Skin Infections & Inflammatory Conditions · Pathophysiology Course 🩹 SKIN INFECTION & INFLAMMATION SET NG-147 Cellulitis NG-209 Impetigo NG-067 Tinea NG-202 HSV & Shingles NG-225 Psoriasis

Herpes simplex & herpes zoster — the viruses that live in your nerves NG-202 INTEGUMENTARY · VIRAL ADHD-friendly visual edition Shingles is reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus — chickenpox that has been asleep in a nerve ganglion for decades. When immunity dips it travels back down the nerve and blisters the skin that nerve supplies: one dermatome, one side, stopping at the midline , with burning pain 2–3 days before the rash. Herpes simplex does the same trick on the lip or genitals. All of them are treated

⚡ ONE band · ONE side Shingles follows a single dermatome and stops at the midline . That is the whole diagnosis in one glance. 😣 Pain comes FIRST Burning, tingling or stabbing 2–3 days before any rash — the nerve is inflamed before the skin is. ⏱️ Antiviral within 72 h Acyclovir · valacyclovir · famciclovir — start as early as possible after the rash appears. 🦠 You catch CHICKENPOX Not shingles. A person without varicella immunity exposed to the blister fluid develops chickenpox . 🧬
STEP 0 · LEARN THIS ONCE Same skin drawing as every page in this set — this time the disease arrives down the nerve instead of through the surface.

entries.h: 🔬 Skin cutaway — the only one that comes from the INSIDE
entries.t: DEPTH = THE ANSWER Bacteria and fungi come in from outside. This virus lives in a sensory nerve ganglion and travels down the axon into the epidermis it supplies. That is why the rash is banded, one-sided and painful before it is visible .

Viral infection Herpes viruses can establish latency. Reactivation Virus may become active again. Skin and nerve findings Patterns depend on the virus and site. HSV Recurrent grouped vesicles or ulcers can occur at oral, genital or other sites. Shingles Varicella-zoster reactivation commonly causes painful unilateral dermatomal lesions. Care Antivirals when indicated, pain control and precautions based on site, extent and immune status. 🧠 "Grouped vesicles on a red base" is the sentence that means herpes family — c

entries.h: 📖 Lesion vocabulary — this is a vesicle disease
entries.t: Vesicle → pustule → crust, all in a band. Highlighted below. 🧠 Scattered = chickenpox. Clustered in a band = shingles. Clustered on the lip = cold sore. 🦠
STEP 1 · WHY IT HAPPENS An old virus, a tired immune system, and a nerve that remembers exactly where it goes.

Shingles (herpes zoster) is reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus — the virus that caused chickenpox — from a sensory nerve ganglion, producing a painful blistering rash in the dermatome that nerve supplies. Herpes simplex (HSV-1 / HSV-2) behaves the same way: it hides in ganglia and reactivates as grouped vesicles in the same spot each time. 🧠 "Chickenpox once, shingles later." No chickenpox (or vaccine virus) = no shingles.

Chickenpox in childhood ▼ Virus travels UP sensory nerves and goes dormant in the dorsal root ganglia ▼ Years later, cell-mediated immunity drops ▼ Virus reactivates and travels DOWN the axon ▼ Nerve inflammation = burning pain FIRST ▼ Grouped vesicles appear in that ONE dermatome 🧠 It is an "opportunistic" reactivation — the virus waits until your defenses are down before it attacks.

entries.h: 🧬 Where it comes from — chickenpox that never left
entries.t: 🧠 The ganglion is the hotel. The virus checks in after chickenpox and checks out when your immune system stops watching the door.

Age — risk rises sharply after 50 , as VZV-specific immunity wanes Immunosuppressive drugs — corticosteroids, chemotherapy, transplant drugs, biologics Cancer , especially hematological; HIV ; other immunodeficiency Another active infection (e.g. pneumonia) occupying the immune system Major physical or emotional stress , fatigue, poor nutrition Surgery, trauma, radiation 🧠 "Old, ill, stressed, suppressed." Four words, all the risk factors.

entries.h: 🧪 Bug → drug: the rule that runs this whole set
entries.t: 🧠 Virus → "-cyclovir". Antivirals suppress , they do not cure — the virus stays in the ganglion for life. 🔎
STEP 2 · WHAT YOU SEE Pain first, then a one-sided band of grouped blisters that refuses to cross the midline.

Prodrome: burning, tingling, itching, numbness or stabbing pain in one strip of skin, 2–3 days before the rash Rash: red papules → grouped vesicles on an erythematous base → pustules → crusts Unilateral , following one dermatome , most often the trunk (thoracic) — it stops at the midline Paraesthesia — burning, numbness, tingling, hypersensitivity to touch Low-grade fever < 38 °C / 100.4 °F , headache, malaise, fatigue Itching as it crusts 🧠 "Pain, then band, then blisters." In that order, every time.

Clinical — the dermatomal pattern plus grouped vesicles is usually enough PCR / viral swab of vesicle fluid if the picture is unclear or the patient is immunocompromised A direct fluorescent antibody test may be used where available Consider testing for immunosuppression (including HIV) in a young patient with shingles Ophthalmology review without delay if the eye or nose tip is involved 🧠 Shingles in a young adult is a question, not just a diagnosis — why are their defenses down?

entries.h: 🗺️ Dermatomes — why the rash stops at the midline
entries.t: 🧠 T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus. Two landmarks that show up in exams over and over.

entries.h: ⏱️ The timeline — and the two clocks you are watching
entries.t: 🧠 Clock 1 = 72 hours for the drug. Clock 2 = crusted over for the contagion.

entries.h: 🚨 Shingles on the face — the two emergencies
entries.t: 🧠 "Nose tip = eye trip." Lesions on the tip of the nose (Hutchinson's sign) mean the eye is at high risk — urgent ophthalmology.
🧠 The rash is temporary; the nerve damage may not be. Treat the pain aggressively and early — that is the prevention. 🩺
STEP 3 · WHAT YOU DO Antiviral early, pain controlled properly, and everyone around the patient protected.

entries.h: 🦠 Who can catch what — the rule everyone gets wrong
entries.t: 🧠 Shingles gives chickenpox, not shingles. Say that sentence out loud until it sticks.

Acyclovir · valacyclovir · famciclovir Start as early as possible , ideally within 72 h of the rash appearing They shorten the illness and reduce the risk of postherpetic neuralgia — they do not eradicate the virus Encourage fluids — adequate hydration matters, especially with IV acyclovir, which can affect the kidneys Give doses on time ; monitor renal function as prescribed For HSV, the same drugs are used episodically or as daily suppression 🧠 "-cyclovir = virus." And early beats perfect — a dose today is worth

Localized shingles in an immunocompetent patient: standard + contact precautions ; cover the lesions with a dressing Disseminated zoster , or zoster in an immunocompromised patient: airborne + contact precautions — negative-pressure room until lesions are crusted Chickenpox (varicella) : always airborne + contact Staff and visitors must be immune — non-immune, pregnant or immunocompromised people should not care for or visit the patient Keep away from newborns , pregnant people without immunity , and the immunosupp

entries.h: 😖 Pain — treat it like nerve pain, not a scrape
entries.t: Assess it properly and regularly — this pain is frequently under-treated Neuropathic agents : gabapentin or pregabalin, tricyclic antidepressants Topical : lidocaine patch or gel; capsaicin (only on intact, healed skin) Analgesics as prescribed; opioids may be needed short-term for severe acute pain Cool compresses , calamine, colloidal oatmeal baths for comfort Loose cotton clothing — even fabric can hurt (allodynia); a bed cradle keeps sheets off the skin 🧠 Plain acetaminophen/NSAIDs alone rarely touch nerve pain

Keep lesions clean, dry and COVERED with a non-adherent dressing Do not rupture the blisters — the fluid is infectious and the skin is a barrier Keep nails short ; discourage scratching (secondary bacterial infection risk) Watch for secondary infection : increasing pain, spreading redness, pus, fever Hand hygiene before and after all contact; gloves for lesion care Support rest, nutrition and fluids — the immune system needs them Acknowledge the emotional load : the pain is exhausting and often invisible to others

Recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) — 2 doses, recommended for adults 50 years and older , and for immunocompromised adults 19+ per current guidance It is recommended even if the person has already had shingles or does not remember having chickenpox It is not a live vaccine; expect a sore arm, tiredness or aches for a day or two — that is a normal response Varicella (chickenpox) vaccine in childhood prevents the primary infection in the first place Vaccination is the most reliable way to lower the risk of shingle

Never let a non-immune, pregnant or immunocompromised person care for or visit the patient. Never break the blisters — the fluid is loaded with live virus. Never treat facial shingles as routine; ask about the eye every time. Never delay the antiviral waiting for a test result. Never tell a patient shingles is "caught" from someone else's shingles — it comes from their own dormant virus. 🧠 Don't pop it, don't delay it, don't expose the vulnerable. 🔀
STEP 4 · THE REAL EXAM SKILL One band that stops at the midline is shingles. Everything else is something else.
🧠 One band, one side, stops at the midline. No other rash on this page does that.

HSV-1 HSV-2 VZV (shingles) Classic site Lip border, mouth Genital area One dermatome, often trunk Pattern Small recurring cluster Painful grouped ulcers Unilateral band, stops at midline Latent in Trigeminal ganglion Sacral ganglia Dorsal root ganglia Recurs? Often, same spot Often, decreasing over time Usually once, can recur Treatment All three: the "-cyclovir" family — acyclovir, valacyclovir, famciclovir 🧠 Same family, same drugs, different postcode.

SHINGLES CHICKENPOX Which event Reactivation First infection Spread One dermatome, one side All over the body Age Usually older adults Usually children Pain Severe, comes first Itch > pain Precautions Contact (airborne if disseminated / immunocompromised) Airborne + contact 🧠 Same virus, two chapters.

A contact does not "get shingles" — a non-immune contact gets chickenpox . The patient is contagious until every lesion is crusted , not until the pain stops. Antiviral within 72 h of rash onset — do not pick "wait for the culture." Localized, covered shingles in a well patient = contact precautions; disseminated or immunocompromised = airborne . Pain before a rash in one strip of skin is shingles until proven otherwise. Lesions on the nose tip → the eye is at risk → urgent referral. Shingles pain is neuropathic —

Shingles vs cellulitis — blistered band with burning nerve pain vs diffuse hot red swelling Shingles vs contact dermatitis — dermatomal vs shaped like whatever touched the skin Shingles vs impetigo — clustered vesicles on a red base vs honey crust Shingles vs tinea — painful band vs itchy ring HSV vs impetigo — recurs in the same spot after tingling vs new golden crusts anywhere 🧠 Burning band = virus. Hot swelling = bacteria. Itchy ring = fungus. 🖼️
PHOTO GUIDE Panel 3 is shingles. Look at where it stops.

SAY IT OUT LOUD ⚡ One dermatome, one side Stops at the midline. Grouped vesicles on a red base. 😣 Pain 2–3 days first Burning/tingling before any rash. Treat as NEUROPATHIC pain. ⏱️ "-cyclovir" within 72 h Shortens it and lowers postherpetic neuralgia risk. 🦠 Contagious till crusted A non-immune contact gets CHICKENPOX. Cover the lesions.

Q1: What causes shingles? Show answer Reactivation of varicella-zoster virus — the chickenpox virus — from a sensory nerve ganglion where it has been dormant since the childhood infection. Q2: Describe the rash in one sentence. Show answer Grouped vesicles on an erythematous base, unilateral, following a single dermatome, and stopping at the midline. Q3: What comes before the rash, and why does it matter? Show answer Burning, tingling, itching or stabbing pain in that strip of skin, 2–3 days earlier, because the ne

entries.t: Nursing Field Notes / Skin & Wound · Skin Cancer · Pathophysiology Course 🩹 SKIN & WOUND SET NG-051 Skin (foundation) NG-044 Pressure Injuries NG-080 Wound Care NG-116 Frostbite NG-182 Dermatitis NG-225 Psoriasis NG-204 Skin Cancer

Basal cell · Squamous cell · Melanoma — and the ABCDE that catches the deadly one NG-204 INTEGUMENTARY · ONCOLOGY ADHD-friendly visual edition Skin cancer is uncontrolled growth of skin cells after their DNA has been damaged — nearly always by ultraviolet light . Which cell mutates decides which cancer you get: the basal layer → basal cell carcinoma, the keratinocytes above it → squamous cell carcinoma, the melanocytes → melanoma. The layers are drawn on NG-051 ; this page shows what happens when each one goes wron

🔤 A B C D E Asymmetry · Border irregular · Color varied · Diameter >6 mm · Evolving . 🔬 3 cells, 3 cancers Basal → BCC (most common) · keratinocyte → SCC · melanocyte → melanoma (deadliest) . 🚨 Biopsy decides Nothing is diagnosed by looking. Tissue biopsy is definitive. ☀️ SPF 30+, 15 min before, q2h Avoid 10 am–4 pm · never tanning beds · burns happen on cloudy days. 🧨
STEP 1 · CAUSE Ultraviolet light breaks DNA. Enough breaks in the wrong genes and the cell stops obeying the "stop dividing" signal.

entries.h: ☀️ UVA vs UVB — how deep the damage goes

entries.t: Cell damage UV exposure and other factors can damage skin cells. Abnormal growth A lesion develops or changes. Evaluation Examination and biopsy establish the diagnosis. Melanoma clues Asymmetry, irregular border, varied color and evolution; size alone is not decisive. Other clues A nonhealing sore, recurrent bleeding or a changing raised lesion needs review. Prevention Sun protection and avoiding tanning devices reduce UV exposure. UVB is mostly absorbed in the epidermis — it causes sunburn and directly damages ke

☀️ UV exposure frequent sunburns 🛏️ Tanning beds never safe 👷 Outdoor occupation cumulative dose 🧑‍🦰 Fair skin light skin, blond/red hair, freckles 👪 Family history parent with melanoma 🔵 Many moles >50 nevi or atypical nevi 💊 Immunosuppressants transplant & HIV meds 🩹 Prior skin cancer or chronic wound/scar 👴 Older age lifetime UV adds up ☢️ Radiation / arsenic occupational Darker skin does not mean immunity. Skin cancer is less common in deeply pigmented skin but is more often found late — and it favors the palms

entries.h: 📖 Key terms you get tested on
entries.t: Nevus / nevi = mole(s). Melanocytic = made of pigment cells. Neoplasm = tumor = a new abnormal growth. Benign = stays put, well-defined, grows slowly, doesn't invade. Malignant = invades locally and can metastasize. Actinic (solar) keratosis = premalignant rough, dry, "sandpaper" scaly patch on sun-damaged skin — a precursor to squamous cell carcinoma. Treat it. Dysplastic / atypical nevus = irregular mole; a marker of increased melanoma risk. Metastasis = spread to distant sites via lymph or blood. Breslow depth =
STEP 2 · WHICH CELL? Find the cell of origin on the cross-section and everything else about the cancer follows.

entries.h: 🔬 Three cells, three cancers — the origin cutaway
entries.t: 🧠 Bottom, middle, pigment. B asal cell starts at the b ottom of the epidermis. S quamous starts in the s quamous cells above it. Melanoma starts in the melanocytes — and it is the one that digs downward .

entries.h: 👁️ What they look like on the skin
entries.t: 🧠 Pearly = basal. Scaly & crusty = squamous. Multicolored & changing = melanoma. Three words, three cancers.

Feature Basal cell (BCC) Squamous cell (SCC) Melanoma Cell of origin Basal layer keratinocytes Keratinocytes above the basal layer Melanocytes How common Most common skin cancer Second most common Least common of the three How dangerous Locally destructive; rarely metastasizes Can metastasize — higher risk on the lip, ear, and in immunosuppressed patients Most deadly ; metastasizes early and widely Classic look Pearly/waxy papule, rolled translucent border, telangiectasias, central ulcer that bleeds and re-scabs Fi

entries.h: 🧪 Diagnosis — nothing is decided by looking
entries.t: Full-body skin examination in good light, including scalp, between toes, soles, nails, genital area — and the "ugly duckling" check: the mole that doesn't look like the patient's other moles. Dermoscopy to magnify surface patterns. Tissue biopsy is required for definitive diagnosis — but only for lesions that are genuinely suspicious (irregular, uneven, changing). Normal moles are not biopsied. For suspected melanoma, a full-thickness (excisional) biopsy is preferred so the pathologist can measure Breslow depth ; s

entries.h: 🚨 Melanoma in darker skin — the pattern that gets missed
entries.t: People with darker skin get melanoma less often but die of it more often , largely because it is found late. Look at the palms, soles, between the toes, nail beds, mucous membranes and the eyes — not just sun-exposed areas. A new, widening, irregular dark band in a nail , especially with pigment spilling onto the surrounding skin ( Hutchinson sign ), needs referral — not "wait and see." Teach sun protection to everyone. Pigment reduces risk; it does not remove it. 🧠 "Check the soles and the nails." The single most
STEP 3 · SCREEN Five letters. Benign on the left, suspicious on the right, every time.

entries.h: 🔤 The ABCDE plate — benign vs suspicious, side by side
entries.t: E is the most important letter. A lesion that is abrupt, sudden or rapidly changing in color, size or shape gets referred even if the other letters look reassuring. Add the "ugly duckling" sign : the mole that looks different from all of that person's other moles. 🧠 A symmetry · B order · C olour · D iameter · E volving. Chant it in that order, and remember "Irregular is BAD, and change is worse."

A sore that will not heal , or heals and reopens repeatedly. A lesion that bleeds, oozes, crusts or itches without an obvious cause. New pain, tenderness or numbness in a mole. Redness or swelling extending beyond the border of a mole. Spread of pigment from a mole into the surrounding skin. A new pigmented lesion in an adult — most moles appear before about age 30. Any lesion in a chronic wound, burn scar or old radiation site (Marjolin ulcer → SCC). 🧠 "Won't heal, won't stop bleeding, won't stay the same." Any on

entries.h: ✅ How to teach a monthly self-skin exam
entries.t: Once a month, in good light , after a bath or shower. Use a full-length mirror plus a hand mirror ; ask a partner or family member for the back and scalp. Work in a fixed order: face → ears → neck → chest → abdomen → arms and hands ( including palms, between fingers and nail beds ) → back and buttocks → legs → soles and between the toes → scalp (part the hair) → genital area. Take photos or draw a body map so change is obvious next month. Report anything meeting ABCDE, anything that doesn't heal, or any "ugly duckl
STEP 4 · TEACH This is where nursing actually changes the outcome — and it is heavily tested.
🧠 "30, 15, 2." SPF 30+ , applied 15 minutes before, reapplied every 2 hours (and after water). Three numbers, most of the teaching questions.

entries.h: 👨‍👩‍👧 Everything else the patient needs to hear
entries.t: Shade and clothing beat sunscreen. Sunscreen is the last line, not the first. Infants under 6 months should be kept out of direct sun and covered with clothing/shade; use sunscreen on babies only as advised by their provider. Some medicines cause photosensitivity — you burn much faster. Common examples include tetracyclines, sulfonamides, some diuretics, amiodarone, some psychiatric medicines, and isotretinoin (see NG-051 ). Ask, and teach strict sun protection. Radiation-therapy skin and old burn scars stay sun-se

Before: confirm consent and site marking, review anticoagulants and allergies, explain what a biopsy or Mohs day actually involves (long day, staged excisions, repeated waiting). After a surgical excision: keep the dressing clean and dry per order, watch for bleeding, infection and dehiscence, teach wound care and suture-removal timing — see NG-080 . Topical chemotherapy (for superficial lesions/actinic keratoses): warn that the treated area is meant to become red, crusted and sore before it heals; apply with glove

NG-080 — Wound Care : post-excision wound care, and the chronic wound that can turn into an SCC. NG-182 — Dermatitis and NG-225 — Psoriasis : benign inflammatory rashes you must not mistake for cancer — and vice versa. A "patch of eczema" that never clears in one fixed spot deserves a second look. 🧠 One stubborn spot that behaves differently from everything around it i

The honey-crusted rash — highly contagious, mostly in children NG-209 INTEGUMENTARY · PEDS INFECTION ADHD-friendly visual edition Impetigo is a very common, highly contagious superficial bacterial skin infection of infants and children, caused by Staph aureus and/or Group A Strep . Itchy red sores around the nose and mouth burst and dry into the unmistakable honey-colored crust — and that crusting stage is when it spreads fastest, by hands, towels, linen and toys. Nursing care is half skin care and half stopping th

🍯 Honey-colored crust The single most recognizable sign in dermatology. Golden, stuck-on crust around the nose and mouth of a child. 🚨 HIGHLY contagious Direct contact and objects — towels, linen, toys, clothes. The crusting stage is the most contagious . 🦠 Staph or Strep Superficial — top of the epidermis only , so it heals without scarring (except the deep form, ecthyma). 🏫 Home from school Off school/daycare, hand hygiene, separate laundry in hot water, short nails, gently soak crusts off. 🧬
STEP 0 · LEARN THIS ONCE Same skin drawing as every page in this set — this time with a shallow blister forming right under the surface.

entries.h: 🔬 Skin cutaway — impetigo is the SHALLOW one
entries.t: DEPTH = THE ANSWER The blister forms under the stratum corneum , so its roof is paper-thin. It ruptures almost immediately, and the fluid dries into the honey-colored crust . Because it never reaches the dermis, ordinary impetigo does not scar .

Barrier breach or exposure Organisms reach vulnerable tissue. Local infection Inflammation affects the skin or underlying layers. Spread risk Some infections can progress beyond the local site. Impetigo Superficial bacterial infection often produces crusted lesions. Cellulitis Deeper infection causes spreading warmth, redness, swelling and pain. Tinea Dermatophyte infection requires antifungal treatment rather than antibacterial therapy. 🧠 "Impetigo is a roof problem." The infection is in the roof of the skin, so i

entries.h: 📖 Lesion vocabulary — impetigo uses four of these words
entries.t: Impetigo is a vesicle → pustule → crust story, and the bullous form adds the bulla . Highlighted below. 🧠 Vesicle is small, bulla is big. "B" for BIG bulla. 🦠
STEP 1 · WHY IT HAPPENS Common bacteria + a child's skin + a scratch = the most contagious rash on the ward.

Impetigo is a very common, highly contagious superficial bacterial skin infection caused by Staphylococcus aureus and/or Group A Streptococcus , affecting mostly infants and young children . It lives in the top of the epidermis — that is why it crusts rather than swells, and why it usually heals without a scar. 🧠 "Impetigo — infant-igo." The name itself tells you the age group.

Bacteria colonize the nose & skin surface ▼ A tiny break — scratch, bite, eczema, cut ▼ Bacteria multiply just under the stratum corneum ▼ A thin-walled vesicle fills with pus ▼ It ruptures → oozes → dries into HONEY-COLORED CRUST ▼ The child scratches → new lesions + other children 🧠 Itch is the engine. Scratching is what seeds the next lesion and the next child — which is why short nails is a real intervention, not a nicety.

entries.h: ⭐ Who gets it & what makes it worse
entries.t: Age 2–5 years is the classic peak; can occur at any age Crowding — daycare, school, siblings, sports teams Warm, humid weather and summer months Broken skin — eczema, insect bites, chickenpox, scabies, minor trauma Poor hygiene or limited access to washing facilities Skin-to-skin contact sports — wrestling, rugby 🧠 "Hot, crowded, scratched." Those three words cover nearly every risk factor.

entries.h: 🚨 How it travels — and the five places you break the chain
entries.t: 🧠 Fomite = an object that carries the bug. Towel, toy, doorknob, wrestling mat. Impetigo spreads by contact , not by air.

entries.h: 🧪 Bug → drug: the rule that runs this whole set
entries.t: 🧠 Bacteria → antibiotic. The only extra decision in impetigo is topical or oral — and that is decided by how much skin is involved. 🔎
STEP 2 · WHAT YOU SEE A child, itchy sores around the nose and mouth, and a crust the color of dried honey.
🧠 "Golden crust on a small face." If the stem says honey-colored or golden-yellow crust in a child, the answer is impetigo — every time.

Itchy red sores , classically around the nose and mouth ; also hands, feet, arms and legs Sores burst and dry into a stuck-on, honey/golden crust Lesions at different stages at the same time — new ones keep appearing Regional lymph nodes may be swollen and tender Usually little or no fever and the child is otherwise well Itch, not pain — pain suggests the deeper form (ecthyma) or cellulitis 🧠 Itchy + crusty + a well child = impetigo. Painful + hot + an unwell child = think cellulitis.

Mostly clinical — the appearance is the diagnosis Swab for culture & sensitivity if it is widespread, recurrent, not responding, or MRSA is suspected Consider checking for an underlying cause: eczema, scabies, head lice, chickenpox If PSGN is suspected later: urinalysis (blood + protein), BP , and renal function 🧠 Swab before starting the antibiotic if a swab is being taken at all.

entries.h: 📈 How one sore evolves — and its most contagious moment
entries.t: 🧠 The crust is not the "healed" stage. Students lose marks here: a crusted lesion is still shedding bacteria.

entries.h: 🔬 Three forms — non-bullous vs bullous vs ecthyma
entries.t: NON-BULLOUS BULLOUS ECTHYMA Depth Superficial epidermis Superficial epidermis Into the dermis Lesion Small vesicles → honey crust Large flaccid bullae > 1 cm Punched-out ulcer, thick crust Where Face, around nose/mouth Trunk, arms, diaper area Legs, buttocks Pain Itchy Itchy, may be tender Painful Scars? No No Yes Treatment Topical, or oral if extensive Usually oral antibiotic Oral antibiotic 🧠 "Ecthyma etches." Only the deep one leaves a mark.
🧠 "Throat → heart. Skin → kidney." Strep throat can lead to rheumatic fever; strep skin infection is the one linked to glomerulonephritis. 🩺
STEP 3 · WHAT YOU DO Treat the skin, and stop it reaching the rest of the class.

entries.h: ✅ Stop the spread — the five teaching points
entries.t: 🧠 "School · Soap · Separate · Short nails · Soak." Five S's, in the order you would teach them.

entries.h: 💊 Topical or oral? The decision rule
entries.t: TOPICAL — for a few localized lesions : mupirocin ointment applied to the lesions after gently removing crust. (Retapamulin and ozenoxacin are alternatives where available.) ORAL — when it is widespread , bullous , ecthyma , involves multiple household members, or has failed topical therapy: a cephalosporin (cephalexin) or an anti-staph penicillin; clindamycin or TMP-SMX / doxycycline if MRSA is suspected. 🧠 "A few = cream. A lot = pill."

Gloves on. Standard + contact precautions for draining lesions Soak with warm soapy water or a saline compress to soften the crust Gently lift the softened crust — do not scrub or pick at dry crust Pat dry, then apply the ointment to clean skin — ointment on top of crust does not reach the bacteria Cover loosely with a non-adherent dressing to stop scratching and shedding Dispose of dressings as infectious waste; hand hygiene after removing gloves 🧠 Soften, lift, treat, cover. Ointment on crust is wasted ointment.

entries.h: 🗣️ Family teaching — say it exactly like this
entries.t: "It is very catching — mostly by touch and by shared things." "Keep them home from school/daycare until the treatment has been in for 24–48 h and the sores are drying up." " Wash your hands before and after touching the sores or putting on the cream." " Their own towel, their own bedding — washed separately in hot water." " Nails short and filed , and try to keep the sores covered ." " Finish the whole course , even when it looks better." "Come back if the sores spread , get painful , or the child develops fever ,

Never let the child share towels, bedding, washcloths or clothing. Never scrub or forcibly pick dry crusts — soften them first. Never send the child back to school just because the sores look drier. Never apply ointment on top of a thick crust and call it treated. Never skip hand hygiene between lesion care and any other patient contact. 🧠 Don't share, don't scrub, don't send back early.

24–48 h: no new lesions appearing; existing sores start drying 3–5 days: crusts loosening and falling away, redness fading 7–10 days: skin healed, usually with no scar (temporary pink or pale patches are normal) Not improving in 48 h? — reassess: wrong depth (ecthyma), resistant organism, poor adherence, or an untreated underlying condition such as scabies or eczema 🧠 "48 hours is the checkpoint." No improvement by then means something else is going on. 🔀
STEP 4 · THE REAL EXAM SKILL Crusty and around the mouth is impetigo. Learn what it is NOT.
🧠 Around the mouth + golden crust = impetigo. Same body, five patterns — distribution answers the question first.

CONDITION HOW IT DIFFERS FROM IMPETIGO Cold sore (HSV-1) A tight cluster of small vesicles on the lip border , preceded by tingling; recurs in the same spot. Impetigo is more scattered, oozier, and crusts golden. Cellulitis Painful , hot, swollen, spreading, often febrile , deep. Impetigo is itchy, superficial and crusty in a well child. Eczema (atopic dermatitis) Chronic, dry, itchy, flexural . Watch out: eczema is a common portal of entry , so a child can have both — a suddenly weeping, crusted eczema patch is us

The crusting stage is the MOST contagious , not the least. School exclusion is tied to treatment started + lesions drying , not to how the sores look alone. Teaching must include separate laundry in hot water — a frequently-chosen wrong-if-omitted option. The renal complication follows strep skin infection; rheumatic fever follows strep throat . Ointment goes on clean skin after the crust is soaked off. A painful, punched-out ulcer that scars is ecthyma — it needs an oral antibiotic. 🧠 If the option mentions hot wa

Impetigo vs cellulitis — crusty & itchy vs hot & painful Impetigo vs HSV — golden crust vs grouped vesicles that recur in one spot Impetigo vs tinea — crust vs ring with a clear center Non-bullous vs bullous — tiny vesicles vs big floppy blisters Impetigo vs ecthyma — heals clean vs punches into the dermis and scars 🧠 Crust, cluster, ring, ulcer. Four words, four diagnoses. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🍯 Honey-colored crust Child · around nose & mouth · itchy. 🚨 Crusting = most contagious Contact + fomites: towels, linen, toys. 💊 Few = cream · Lots = pill Mupirocin topically; oral for widespread, bullous or ecthyma. 🏫 5 S's School out · Soap · Separate laundry · Short nails · Soak the crust.

Q1: Which organisms cause impetigo? Show answer Staphylococcus aureus and Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) — alone or together. Q2: Describe the classic lesion and where it appears. Show answer Itchy red sores that burst and dry into a stuck-on, honey-colored (golden) crust, classically around the nose and mouth of a young child; also hands and feet. Autoimmune skin — silvery plaques, and the one word patients need to hear NG-225 INTEGUMENTARY · AUTOIMMUNE ADHD-friendly visual edition Psoriasis is a chronic autoimmune disease in which the body attacks its own skin, pushing keratinocyte turnover from about 30 days down to 3–5 days . Immature cells pile up as well-demarcated red plaques topped with thick silvery scale on extensor surfaces — elbows, knees, scalp, sacrum and nails. There is no organism , so it is not contagious — that sentence is the single most im

⚡ Skin in a hurry Autoimmune T cells drive keratinocyte turnover from ~30 days to 3–5 days . Cells pile up unfinished. 🩹 Silvery scale, sharp edge Well-demarcated red plaques with silvery-white scale on EXTENSOR surfaces — elbows, knees, scalp, sacrum. 🚫 NOT contagious No bug is involved. This is the single most important thing you will ever teach a psoriasis patient. 🦴 Ask about joints Up to a third develop psoriatic arthritis . Morning stiffness > 30 min → refer early. 🧬
STEP 0 · LEARN THIS ONCE Same skin drawing as every page in this set — but look closely: there is no organism anywhere in it.

entries.h: 🔬 Skin cutaway — normal on the left, psoriatic plaque on the right
entries.t: NO ORGANISM Cellulitis, impetigo, tinea and shingles all have something living in the picture. Psoriasis does not. The immune system is the pathogen — which is why it is treated by calming immunity down, and why it can never be caught from another person.

Immune or irritant response Inflammation disrupts the skin barrier. Itch and lesions Appearance depends on the condition and site. Barrier cycle Scratching and dryness can worsen inflammation. Atopic dermatitis Chronic itch and barrier dysfunction with an atopic tendency. Contact dermatitis A local reaction to an irritant or allergen. Psoriasis Immune-mediated inflammation commonly produces well-defined scaly plaques. ① THICK SILVERY SCALE — keratinocytes shed before they mature (parakeratosis: they still carry the

entries.h: 📖 Lesion vocabulary — psoriasis is the PLAQUE + SCALE disease
entries.t: A plaque is a raised, flat-topped lesion larger than 1 cm . Add silvery scale and you have psoriasis. 🧠 Plaque = a papule that grew up. Bigger than 1 cm and flat on top. 🔥
STEP 1 · WHY IT HAPPENS An immune system that attacks its own skin, plus a trigger that sets it off.

Psoriasis is a chronic autoimmune inflammatory disease in which immune cells attack healthy skin, causing massively accelerated division of epidermal cells . The immature cells pile up on the surface as thick, silvery, scaly plaques . It is lifelong , comes in flares and remissions , and is not curable — but it is very controllable. 🧠 "Psoriasis = skin in a hurry." Nothing is invading; the factory is just running far too fast.

Genetic predisposition + a trigger ▼ T lymphocytes are wrongly activated in the skin ▼ They release cytokines (TNF-α, IL-17, IL-23) ▼ Keratinocytes divide ~ 10× too fast — 3–5 days instead of ~30 ▼ Immature cells stack up + capillaries dilate and grow ▼ Raised red plaque with silvery scale 🧠 The cytokines in that box are exactly what the biologic drugs block — TNF, IL-17, IL-23.

entries.h: ⏩ The speed problem — 30 days vs 4 days
entries.t: 🧠 The scale IS the cells. Silvery flakes are keratinocytes that were rushed to the surface before they finished.

entries.h: 🎯 Triggers — and the one that is NOT a trigger
entries.t: 🧠 "S · S · S — Stress, Sickness, Sepsis." And the trap: SUN IS GOOD , not a trigger. Sunburn is bad because it is trauma .

entries.h: 🧪 Cause → treatment class: the rule that runs this whole set
entries.t: 🧠 No organism → no antibiotic, no antifungal, no antiviral. You calm the immune system instead. 🔎
STEP 2 · WHAT YOU SEE Sharp-edged red plaques with silvery scale, on the outside of joints, in a patient who feels well.

Well-demarcated plaques — you can trace the edge with a finger Raised and flat-topped , deep red or salmon-pink underneath Thick, loose, SILVERY-WHITE scale on the surface Symmetrical and on EXTENSOR surfaces — elbows, knees, scalp, sacrum Itching, burning or soreness ; plaques may crack and bleed Nail changes — pitting, oil-drop discoloration, lifting, thickening The patient is systemically well — no fever, no pus, no spreading redness 🧠 "Sharp · Silver · Symmetrical · Stretched-out (extensor)." Four S's.

Plaque (vulgaris) — by far the commonest; the classic silvery plaques Guttate — sudden crop of small "raindrop" spots on the trunk, often after strep throat , common in children and young adults Inverse (flexural) — smooth, shiny, red patches in the skin folds with little scale Pustular — sterile pustules; generalized pustular psoriasis is a medical emergency Erythrodermic — widespread redness and shedding; emergency (fluid loss, temperature instability, infection risk) Nail and scalp psoriasis often accompany any

entries.h: ⭐ Two signs with names — Auspitz & Koebner
entries.t: 🧠 Auspitz = A for After you lift the scale (bleeding). Koebner = K for Knock/injury makes new plaques.

entries.h: 🗺️ Extensor vs flexural — plus the nails
entries.t: 🧠 Psoriasis is on the OUTSIDE of the joint. Eczema is on the INSIDE. That one line sorts most stems.

entries.h: 🦴 Psoriatic arthritis — psoriasis is not only skin-deep
entries.t: 🧠 "Skin first, joints later." Ask about morning stiffness at every visit — early referral prevents permanent damage. 🩺
STEP 3 · WHAT YOU DO Moisturize relentlessly, calm the immune system as far as you need to, and treat the person, not just the plaque.
🧠 Every rung sits on emollient. If "apply moisturizer regularly" is an option, it is rarely wrong.

entries.h: 🧴 THE two NCLEX answers: moisturize & sunlight
entries.t: 1. Moisturize frequently. Apply a thick emollient immediately after bathing, onto damp skin , to trap water in. Use lukewarm (not hot) water, a mild non-soap cleanser, and pat dry — never rub. 2. Sunlight in moderation is GOOD. Controlled UV light slows the overactive skin cells. Do not tell a psoriasis patient to avoid the sun — but do teach them to avoid sunburn , which is trauma and can trigger Koebner. 🧠 Students answer "avoid sunlight" and lose the mark. Sun helps. Sunburn hurts.

Emollients — the foundation, used every day forever Topical corticosteroids — the mainstay for flares; use the lowest effective potency for the shortest time , and only mild preparations on the face and folds (skin thinning, striae) Vitamin D analogues (calcipotriene/calcipotriol) — often paired with a steroid Coal tar — effective; warn about staining and smell Salicylic acid — lifts thick scale so other treatments can get in Calcineurin inhibitors — steroid-sparing option for the face and folds Apply thin , rub in

Methotrexate is dosed WEEKLY, never daily. Daily dosing is a fatal medication error. Folic acid is usually prescribed alongside it Methotrexate is teratogenic — it must be stopped and effective contraception used; check pregnancy status. Monitor FBC, LFTs, renal function ; avoid alcohol Biologics (infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept; IL-17/IL-23 inhibitors) — screen for latent TB and hepatitis first ; hold for active infection; teach infection precautions and injection technique Live vaccines are generally avoided o

entries.h: 🗣️ Teaching — start with the sentence that matters most
entries.t: "You cannot give this to anyone. It is not an infection." Say it first, and say it to the family too Moisturize daily , especially after bathing; lukewarm water, gentle cleanser, pat dry Protect the skin — avoid scratching, picking scale, tight clothing and sunburn (Koebner) Use treatments as prescribed , even when the skin looks better; flares will come and go Stop smoking, moderate alcohol , manage weight, manage stress Report : joint pain or morning stiffness, widespread redness, pustules, fever, or signs of inf

Never imply psoriasis is contagious, or use isolation precautions for it. Never give methotrexate daily — it is a weekly dose. Never scrub, pick or forcibly remove the scale — that is trauma and Koebnerizes. Never use potent topical steroids on the face or skin folds without a specific order. Never tell the patient to stay out of the sun. Never start a biologic without checking TB/hepatitis screening and for active infection. 🧠 Don't isolate, don't scrub, don't dose it daily, don't ban the sun.

Erythrodermic psoriasis — widespread redness and shedding over most of the body. The skin barrier fails: fluid and protein loss, hypothermia, high-output heart failure, sepsis risk Generalized pustular psoriasis — sheets of sterile pustules with fever and feeling very unwell Often triggered by abrupt withdrawal of systemic steroids , severe infection or drug reactions Nursing: monitor temperature, fluid balance and vital signs; warm environment; meticulous skin care; IV fluids as prescribed; urgent dermatology revi
STEP 4 · THE REAL EXAM SKILL Silvery scale on the outside of joints, in a well patient, with no organism.

entries.h: 🗺️ Where each one shows up — the whole set, plus eczema
entries.t: 🧠 Psoriasis = extensor. Eczema = flexural. The two most confused rashes, separated by one word.

NO NO YES Steroid response Improves Improves Worsens (tinea incognito) 🧠 If a steroid ma

Sunlight is GOOD. The most-missed question on this topic. Psoriasis is NOT contagious — no isolation, no gloves-for-fear, and say so to the family. Methotrexate is WEEKLY. Check the frequency on every order. Moisturize after bathing on damp skin — not "avoid moisturizer because it is greasy." Do not pick or scrub the scale — Koebner makes new plaques. New small "raindrop" spots after a sore throat = guttate psoriasis. Widespread redness + shedding = erythrodermic = emergency, treat like a barrier failure. Joint pai

Psoriasis vs tinea — solid silvery plaque vs a ring with a clear center Psoriasis vs eczema — extensor & sharply edged vs flexural & ill-defined Psoriasis vs cellulitis — chronic, scaly, well patient vs acute, hot, febrile patient Psoriasis vs seborrhoeic dermatitis — thick silvery scale vs greasy yellowish scale on the scalp and nose folds Nail psoriasis vs fungal nail — pitting and oil-drop vs thick crumbly yellow-brown; test if unsure Psoriatic arthritis vs rheumatoid — DIP joints and sausage digits vs MCP/PIP a
PHOTO GUIDE Panel 4 is plaque psoriasis — on the same sheet as the eczema it gets mixed up with.

SAY IT OUT LOUD ⚡ 30 days → 3–5 days Autoimmune acceleration of keratinocyte turnover. 🩹 Silvery plaques, EXTENSOR Sharp edges. Elbows, knees, scalp, sacrum, nails. 🚫 NOT contagious · ☀️ sun helps Moisturize daily. Avoid sunburn (Koebner). 🦴 Ask about joints Psoriatic arthritis hits the DIP joints. Methotrexate is WEEKLY.

Q1: What is happening in the skin in psoriasis? Show answer Autoimmune T-cell activation drives keratinocytes to divide far too fast — turnover falls from about 28–30 days to 3–5 days — so immature cells pile up as thick silvery scale on a red, thickened plaque. Q2: Describe the classic lesion and where it appears. Show answer Well-demarcated, raised, flat-topped red plaques with thick silvery-white scale, symmetrically on extensor surfaces — elbows, knees, scalp and hairline, lower back/sacrum — plus nail changes.
The arm on the operative side changes the rules for the rest of that patient’s life. Positioning, lymphedema and what to teach.

Surgery Breast and sometimes lymphatic tissue is removed. Early recovery Wound, drain, pain and circulation checks guide care. Long-term function Shoulder mobility, body image and swelling surveillance matter. Wound and drains Monitor output and signs of bleeding or infection; teach care before discharge. Movement Follow the surgical team’s progressive range-of-motion and activity plan. Lymphedema Assess persistent swelling and use individualized prevention and treatment advice. Procedure Removes Lumpectomy The tum
Semi-Fowler’s with the affected arm elevated on a pillow — above the level of the heart, to drain lymph by gravity Turn on the back or unaffected side , never the operative side

No blood pressure cuff on that arm No venipuncture, no injections, no IV lines, no finger sticks No tight jewelry, watches or sleeves No heavy lifting — typically nothing over 5–10 lb initially Protect from cuts, burns and sunburn; wear gloves for gardening and washing up Use an electric razor for the underarm Put a sign above the bed. Every clinician who walks in needs to know which arm.

Jackson-Pratt or Hemovac , usually for 1–3 weeks Teach the patient to empty, measure and record output Recompress the bulb to restore suction after emptying Drains usually come out when output falls below about 30 mL/day Report sudden increase, bright red bleeding, or foul odor

Start early: hand, wrist and elbow movement, ball squeezing — usually within 24 hours Wait for shoulder exercises until the surgeon clears them — typically after drains are out, to protect the suture line Then progress to wall climbing with the fingers , hair brushing, rope turning Full shoulder range too early disrupts the incision. Too late causes a frozen shoulder. Follow the surgeon's schedule.

Lymphedema is swelling of the arm because lymph has nowhere to drain. It can appear months or years later, and once established it is managed rather than cured. Report: heaviness, tightness, rings or sleeves getting tight, visible swelling, or any redness, warmth or fever — that is cellulitis and needs antibiotics urgently. Infection in a lymphedematous arm spreads fast because the immune drainage is gone. Never treat a red, warm arm as minor.

Keep the arm elevated when resting Skin care — moisturize, treat every scratch promptly Compression sleeve as prescribed, including for air travel Maintain a healthy weight; gentle regular exercise helps drainage

entries.h: 💐 The part that is not physical
entries.t: Body image, sexuality and fear of recurrence are central, not peripheral. Look for readiness cues — whether the patient looks at the incision is the classic indicator of beginning acceptance. Offer, but do not push, information about prostheses, reconstruction and support groups. Let the patient set the pace and the topic.

No BP, no needles, no constriction on the affected arm — for life Elevate the arm; turn to back or unaffected side Hand and elbow exercises early; shoulder exercises only when cleared Redness and warmth in that arm = infection , treat urgently Looking at the incision signals psychological readiness Sources. M easles · T uberculosis · V aricella — negative pressure room, door closed, N95 . Everything else on that table is droplet or contact.

Never give aspirin to a child with a viral illness - Reye syndrome. Acetaminophen or ibuprofen instead. Reye syndrome causes acute encephalopathy and liver failure, and it is associated with aspirin during varicella or influenza. This is why pediatric aspirin all but disappeared. Untreated strep throat can become rheumatic fever and permanently damage heart valves. The whole antibiotic course must be finished, even once the child feels well. Strep can also cause acute glomerulonephritis 1–3 weeks later — tea-colore

Keep fingernails short ; mittens for infants — scratching causes scarring and secondary infection Cool baths with oatmeal or baking soda; calamine lotion Antihistamines for itch; acetaminophen for fever Contagious from 1–2 days before the rash until all lesions have crusted

Treat for comfort , not for the number Light clothing, cool room, fluids No cold baths, no alcohol rubs - both cause shivering, which raises temperature Febrile seizures come from a rapid rise in temperature, not from how high it gets

entries.h: 💉 When to worry about a rash
entries.t: A purpuric or petechial rash with fever is meningococcal until proven otherwise. Emergency. A rash that does not blanch when pressed Rash with difficulty breathing, swelling of the face or tongue — anaphylaxis Rash with a stiff neck, severe headache or photophobia

Koplik spots = measles. All stages at once = varicella Roseola: fever breaks, THEN the rash My Tiny Vampire for airborne No aspirin — Reye syndrome Finish the strep antibiotics — rheumatic fever Non-blanching rash + fever = emergency Sources. The pilosebaceous unit · Three factors · Isotretinoin safety NG-393 Skin & Wound ADHD-friendly visual edition Acne is a chronic inflammatory condition of the pilosebaceous unit — the hair follicle and its oil gland. Three things have to line up: too much sebum , a follicle that plugs itself , and bacteria multiplying in the plugged space. Most of what people blame — chocolate, greasy food, poor hygiene — is not on the list. The unit Pilosebaceous — hair follicle plus oil gland Does NOT cause it Chocolate, greasy fo

Naming the lesions Comedones — the plugged follicle. Open = blackhead (dark from oxidized keratin, not dirt). Closed = whitehead . Papule — small, raised, red, solid. Pustule — the same with visible pus. Nodules and cysts — deep, painful, and the ones that scar. Distribution follows the oil glands: face, neck, chest, upper back and shoulders. Grading it Mild = comedones only. Moderate = papules and pustules. Severe = nodulocystic, and that one gets systemic treatment early because scarring is permanent . The part t

Teaching that actually works Wash gently twice a day with a mild cleanser. Do not scrub, and do not wash more often — both worsen it. Do not pick or squeeze. That is how a lesion becomes a scar. Water-based, non-comedogenic cosmetics; remove make-up before bed. Improvement takes 6 to 8 weeks . Stopping early because “it is not working” is the commonest failure. Benzoyl peroxide bleaches towels and clothing — warn her. The drugs, stepwise Benzoyl peroxide — antibacterial, first line, expect dryness. Topical retinoid

The unit Pilosebaceous — hair follicle plus oil gland Does NOT cause it Chocolate, greasy food, poor hygiene Does aggravate it Corticosteroids, stress, high-carb diet, oil-based cosmetics The dangerous drug Isotretinoin — a teratogen, two forms of contraception Does chocolate cause acne? Show answer No. Their false list was chocolate, greasy food, hygiene and water-based cosmetics. Open comedone or closed — which is the blackhead? Show answer Open. Three collections of pus in three places you would not otherwise put together. They turn up on the same exam because each has one signature symptom that gives the location away — and the question is testing whether you know which one.

Location plus signature symptom. You are not being asked to diagnose. You are being asked to hear one odd detail — a voice, a mealtime, a place on the body — and name where the problem is. And one of the three has an airway attached to it. That is the one that turns from a sore throat into an emergency.

👅 Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) Beside a tonsil, usually on one side only Muffled “hot potato” voice Pus collects between the tonsil and the wall of the throat. Look for severe one-sided sore throat , trismus (she cannot open her mouth widely), drooling , and the uvula pushed away from the swollen side . It usually follows tonsillitis, and it is treated by drainage plus antibiotics — antibiotics alone do not empty a collection. Drooling, stridor or difficulty breathing is an airway emergency. entries.h: ✅ What is the same in all three
entries.t: A collection of pus has to be drained. Antibiotics help the surrounding tissue; they do not empty a cavity. Warm compresses for comfort and to encourage drainage — except where an airway is involved, where assessment comes first. Pain control before care , not after. Dressing changes on an open pilonidal wound hurt. Watch for spread : rising fever, expanding redness, tachycardia, feeling generally unwell. Finish the antibiotic course even once it feels better, and return if it worsens. The one that is different: on

🏠 Study Hub 🧠 Mega Quiz 14-week plan · NUR 234 · 235 · 258

Three courses. One to two hours a day. A fixed weekly rhythm so you never have to decide what to study, an exam overlay for the weeks that matter, and a way back in when you miss days. 🤰 NUR 234 🧒 NUR 235 🩺 NUR 258

entries.h: ⭐ The whole plan in six lines
entries.t: One course a day , not three. Mon 258 · Tue 234 · Wed 235. Thursday is quiz day — all three courses mixed together. Friday goes to whatever you got wrong on Thursday. Saturday is the long block: patho, A&P, and next week's preview. Sunday off. Actually off. When an exam is within 7 days, the exam overlay replaces Friday and Saturday. The single most important rule on this page. Never try to catch up. If you miss three days, you do not do four days' work on Thursday. You rejoin the plan at today and let the missed d

Why one course a day and not a bit of each. Switching subjects costs you the first ten minutes every time you do it. Three switches a day is thirty minutes of your hour gone before you learn anything. One course a day means one switch. You get your whole hour. MON 🩺 NUR 258 — this week's module Open the module page, One bite mode, work through the bites. Then its quiz. TUE 🤰 NUR 234 — this week's module Same shape. One bite, then the quiz at the bottom. WED 🧒 NUR 235 — this week's module Same shape again. By Wednes

entries.h: ⏱️ What one hour actually looks like
entries.t: The hour has a fixed shape so you never spend any of it deciding. Same four blocks every single day. 0–10 Recall Yesterday's three cards. Say the answers out loud before you look. Getting it wrong here is the point — that is what makes it stick. 10–35 Learn Today's module in One bite . One bite, then Next. Do not scroll ahead to see how many are left. 35–50 Test That module's quiz. Answer first, then check. Read the rationale even when you got it right — it explains the wrong answers too. 50–60 Capture Write three

Do not stretch all four blocks. Repeat the middle: Recall, Learn, Test, Learn, Test, Capture. Two modules, or one module plus one ATI template. Recall and Capture stay at ten minutes no matter how long the session is.

entries.h: ✅ Why it starts with a test and ends with writing
entries.t: Starting with recall means the hour opens with your brain producing instead of consuming — that is the difference between recognizing a fact and being able to retrieve it under exam pressure. Ending with three lines gives the hour a finish line you can see. There is a card on the desk that was not there an hour ago.

With three courses you will almost always have an exam within seven days. So this is not the exception — it is most weeks. When it happens, Friday and Saturday switch over to the exam. Monday to Thursday do not change. Do not stop the other two courses to cram for one. That is how you win an exam this week and lose the next two. T−3 ⭐ Spotlight only Open every module page for that exam and hit Exam spotlight . Only the high-yield card. No reading anything else. That is 6–14 facts per module and it is the right amou

entries.h: ⚠️ Two exams in the same week
entries.t: It happens roughly four times this semester — see the map below. When it does: the earlier exam gets T−3 and T−2. The later one gets the day between them. Do not split each day in half; you will do neither properly.

Built from the exam groupings already on your three course pages. Exams usually land at the end of their week range , so treat this as the shape of the semester, not the dates — pencil in the real ones when your syllabus lands. Reading the map. A cell in your course color is one exam that week . A red cell marked ⚠️ is a collision — two exams in the same week. The pale gray rows are the weeks with nothing due. Week 🩺 NUR 258 🤰 NUR 234 🧒 NUR 235 What it means 1 Sensory Contraception Peds care Build the habit. Nothin

NUR 258 sits one week ahead of the other two, nearly all semester. Its exam lands the week before 234 and 235 collide. That gap is the plan's shock absorber. Weeks 5, 9 and 11 are your genuinely light weeks — use them to get ahead, not to rest twice.

Three finals and a unit exam in one week cannot be revised in that week. NUR 234's final is comprehensive over all fourteen weeks. So from week 11 , Saturday's second hour becomes final review — oldest material first, because week 1 is the part you have not seen since week 1.

entries.h: 📚 The review layer — content mastery & NCLEX
entries.t: Older material does not get its own study day — there isn't one to give. It gets attached to the new material instead. Three rules, and they cost almost no extra time.

entries.h: 💊 Rule 1 — drugs get learned the day they appear
entries.t: When a drug turns up in any course, open its card in the Drug Guide that same day. Two minutes. Pharmacology is heavily weighted on NCLEX and it is the subject that decays fastest when studied alone. Learned attached to a patient, it stays.

entries.h: 🧬 Rule 2 — patho and A&P are the fallback, not a subject
entries.t: You do not study pathophysiology on a schedule. You study it the moment something will not make sense . When a mechanism will not stick — why estrogen causes clots, why the right lower lobe aspirates, why insulin needs collapse after birth — that is Saturday hour 1. Go to Physiology or Pharmacology and fix that one thing. A mechanism you understand needs revising once. A fact you memorized needs revising five times.

entries.h: 🧠 Rule 3 — Thursday carries the old courses
entries.t: The Super Mega Quiz holds everything — NUR 125, 175, 198 and all three current courses. Shuffled, unfiltered. That is not a shortcut, it is the whole point: NCLEX does not tell you which course a question came from. Practicing retrieval without the label is the skill the exam actually tests. Once a month, make Thursday NUR 198 / 175 / 125 only . That is your content mastery insurance. What you want Where it lives When Drugs Drug Guide · Pharmacology The day the drug appears Mechanisms Physiology · patho pages Satur
It will go wrong. Fourteen weeks, three courses, a job and a life. A plan that only works on good days is not a plan.

Do Recall and Test only . Skip Learn entirely. Fifteen minutes of retrieval beats sixty minutes of reading, and it beats zero by more than you would think. Never skip a day because you cannot do the whole hour.

Rejoin at today. If today is Wednesday, you do Wednesday. The missed material comes back on Thursday in the quiz anyway — that is what the mixed quiz is for . It finds your gaps without you having to remember where they are. Do not build a catch-up backlog. Backlogs are what make people quit in week 6.

Open the module page, press One bite , and read one bite . Then you are allowed to stop. You almost certainly will not stop — but the deal has to be real, or it stops working. The hard part is starting, not continuing.

entries.h: 👀 You read it and nothing went in
entries.t: That is reading, not studying, and it is the commonest way to waste an hour. Close the page and try to say the last chunk out loud. If you cannot, that is your signal — go back and do that chunk as a quiz instead of a read. If you could, you did not need to re-read it anyway.

Let it be the one whose exam is furthest away — deliberately, and on purpose, not by accident. Then use the next light week (5, 9 or 11) to bring it back. Choosing what to drop is a plan. Dropping whatever you happen to run out of time for is not.

entries.h: ✅ Before week 1 — a short setup list
entries.t: You have about a week and a half. Do not study ahead. Do these instead — they are worth more than a head start on week 1 content. Get the three syllabi and write the real exam dates onto the map above. Pick your hour — the same hour every day. Which hour matters far less than it being the same one. Buy index cards. Physical ones. The Capture block needs something your hands do, away from a screen. Do one practice day now on any module, so week 1 is not also the week you learn the routine. Tell someone the plan. Out

Ctrl + P prints it flat on white with the colors removed, so it works on paper and does not drink your ink. Stick the default week and the collision map somewhere you will see them. Last thing. This plan asks for about ten hours a week and assumes you will miss some of them. It is built to survive being followed imperfectly — that is the only kind worth having.

Modules 1–3

Compare the patient’s report with what you observe. Match the response to the phase of the therapeutic relationship. The therapeutic relationship, recovery goals and the least restrictive safe setting guide care. Psychotropic medicines act on neurotransmitter systems and often need time to show their full benefit. CBT examines automatic thoughts. Behavioral approaches reinforce a specific behavior. Inpatient care provides structure when safety cannot be maintained in the community. Orientation establishes roles and
boundaries. The working phase addresses goals. Termination reviews progress and prepares for the relationship to end.

entries.h: Which follow-up question helps distinguish benefit from an adverse effect?
entries.t: Think… “What symptoms have improved, and how alert do you feel during the day?” links the treatment goal to everyday function.

entries.h: What would a CBT nurse explore first when a client avoids group?
entries.t: Think… Ask what went through the client’s mind just before deciding to stay away.

entries.h: A patient asks what you would do about a personal decision. Which response supports autonomy?
entries.t: Think… Ask what matters most to them and explore their options together.

Orientation establishes the agreement. Working addresses the goal. Termination reviews progress. A patient’s account is subjective. Observed behavior is objective.

entries.h: A patient says, “My medicine helps the voices, but I feel unsteady when I stand.” What comes first?
entries.t: Assess standing tolerance, sedation and fall risk. Advise stopping all medications permanently. Wait for the next routine visit.
A. Assess standing tolerance, sedation and fall risk. The symptom could increase immediate risk of injury. Assess it and communicate findings so the regimen can be reviewed.

entries.h: During the working phase a client avoids group because they expect rejection. What would help?
entries.t: Decide for the client. Explore the thought and agree on one manageable action. Reassure them everyone will like them.
B. Explore the thought and agree on one manageable action. Exploring the prediction and trying a small action connects the thought, emotion and behavior.

entries.h: A patient says “I feel empty” while smiling. How would you chart the two findings?

entries.h: A grieving patient cries and asks you to sit quietly. What therapeutic response fits?
entries.t: Think… Stay if they wish. Follow their lead and allow silence.

entries.h: A patient is pacing and shouting. Where should you stand when approaching?

entries.h: Module 5 · Legal and ethical care, grief and loss
entries.t: Autonomy includes participating in decisions. Grief varies across people and cultures and does not follow a fixed timetable. A family requests private details. A grieving patient wants time alone. Examine consent, safety and the patient’s preferences in each situation.

entries.h: Module 6 · Anger, aggression, abuse and violence

Pacing, a clenched jaw and a rising voice can signal escalation. A private disclosure of abuse calls for an immediate safety assessment.

Trauma-informed care emphasizes safety, choice and permission. Intrusive memories, avoidance and hyperarousal can follow trauma. During severe anxiety, attention narrows and complex instructions become difficult. Flashbacks may make a past threat feel present.
At panic-level anxiety, use short, concrete directions. Return to teaching when attention improves. Separate the feeling of anger from a behavior that threatens safety.

entries.h: A patient in a panic is overwhelmed by several people giving advice. Which approach fits?

C. Have one calm nurse stay nearby and use brief directions. Severe anxiety limits attention. A calm presence and simple instructions support orientation while medical causes are assessed.

entries.h: A relative asks for details about a competent adult patient. What should the nurse check first?

A. What the patient has authorized the team to share. Consent and applicable confidentiality rules guide disclosure.

Depression can reduce energy and pleasure. Assess suicide risk directly whenever cues raise concern. Positive symptoms include hallucinations and delusions. Negative symptoms include reduced emotional expression, motivation and speech. Use consistent boundaries with the team. Assess intake and compensatory behaviors without judgment. Alcohol

entries.h: A patient discloses current suicidal intent. What takes priority?
entries.t: Think… Stay with the patient, summon the clinical team and initiate the appropriate observation and safety measures.

entries.t: Think… Ask what it is telling them to do and whether they feel likely to act on it.

entries.h: Why does a history of purging matter when the patient describes palpitations?
entries.t: Think… Electrolyte losses can disturb cardiac conduction and warrant urgent assessment.

First action Ask about suicidal thoughts, intent, plan and access to means. For immediate danger, stay with the patient, obtain help and initiate safety precautions. Look for a response Reassess safety, sleep, intake and impulsive behavior. Document what changed after intervention.

First action Ask what the voices are saying, whether the person feels able to resist and whether anyone is in danger. Respond calmly and acknowledge distress. Look for a response Check that the patient can seek staff support and identify a way to reduce distress.

entries.h: Personality, eating and substance use disorders
entries.t: First action Assess circulation, mental status and immediate physiological risk. Report concerning rhythm, dehydration or withdrawal findings and follow the ordered protocol. Look for a response Trend vital signs, electrolytes or withdrawal assessments as indicated and check engagement with the care plan.

entries.h: Module 8 · Mood disorders and suicide safety
entries.t: Mania can threaten rest, hydration and judgment. Depression can reduce energy and pleasure. Assess suicide risk directly whenever cues raise concern. Little sleep with sustained energy, impulsivity and pressured speech suggests mania. Hopelessness or giving away possessions warrants direct safety questions.

Positive symptoms include hallucinations and delusions. Negative symptoms include reduced emotional expression, motivation and speech. A hallucination is a sensory experience. A delusion is a fixed belief. The patient’s distress can be real in either case.

entries.h: Module 10 · Personality, eating and substance use disorders
entries.t: Use consistent boundaries with the team. Assess intake and compensatory behaviors without judgment. Alcohol withdrawal can progress to seizures or delirium. Purging can cause potassium loss and dysrhythmias. Tremor, sweating and agitation after stopping alcohol can indicate withdrawal.

Ask directly about suicidal thoughts and current intent when warning signs are present. Hallucination describes perception. Delusion describes a belief. Withdrawal risk depends in part on time since last use.

entries.h: A patient says a voice is ordering them to do something frightening. Which question comes first?
entries.t: How long ago were you diagnosed? What is the voice saying, and do you feel you might act on it? Why do you believe it?
B. What is the voice saying, and do you feel you might act on it? The content and the patient’s ability to resist guide immediate safety precautions.

entries.h: A patient who has been purging reports palpitations and feels faint. What is the priority?
entries.t: Start a long discussion about self-image. Encourage unsupervised exercise. Assess circulation and obtain prompt evaluation of rhythm and electrolytes.
C. Assess circulation and obtain prompt evaluation of rhythm and electrolytes. Purging can disturb electrolytes and cardiac conduction.

entries.h: How can the nurse prepare an autistic patient for a change in routine?
entries.t: Think… Use the patient’s preferred communication method and preview one step at a time.

entries.h: A patient with dementia suddenly cannot attend to a conversation. What is the priority?
entries.t: Think… Assess for superimposed delirium and a reversible medical cause.

entries.h: Which combination after an antipsychotic dose change warrants immediate escalation?

entries.h: Module 11 · Somatic symptoms and neurodevelopmental disorders
entries.t: For somatic distress, acknowledge the symptoms and assess new changes. For autism or ADHD, match communication and routines to the individual’s strengths. Sensory overload or a disrupted routine can precipitate distress in autism. ADHD affects attention, activity or impulse control across settings.

entries.h: Module 12 · Disruptive behavior and cognitive disorders
entries.t: For disruptive behaviors, describe the behavior and use consistent, predictable limits. Sudden confusion in someone with dementia still needs assessment. A sudden change in attention, awareness or behavior suggests delirium. A gradual decline over months or years is more typical of dementia.

Compare neuroleptic malignant syndrome with serotonin toxicity, which often involves hyperreflexia or clonus. Review recent changes and combinations. Fever, marked rigidity and altered mental status after an antipsychotic are an emergency. Tremor with GI symptoms and unsteady gait can signal lithium toxicity.

The therapeutic relationship, recovery goals and the least restrictive safe setting guide care. Psychotropic medicines act on neurotransmitter systems and often need time to show their full benefit. Sudden inattention suggests delirium. Progressive loss of function suggests dementia. Fever and marked rigidity after an antipsychotic require urgent assessment. Review medication changes and the time symptoms began.

entries.h: An older patient who usually knows the staff suddenly cannot follow a conversation. Which action fits?
entries.t: Investigate acute delirium and possible medical causes. Assume the dementia has progressed. Defer assessment until tomorrow.
A. Investigate acute delirium and possible medical causes. The rapid change in attention differs from the patient’s baseline.

entries.h: After starting an antipsychotic, a patient develops high fever, marked stiffness and confusion. What comes first?
entries.t: Offer reassurance and wait. Escalate for urgent evaluation of neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Schedule a routine review.
B. Escalate for urgent evaluation of neuroleptic malignant syndrome. This cluster can indicate a life-threatening medication reaction.

Modules 1–3

Connect a change in mentation or breathing to the patient’s baseline, recent medicines and fluid status. Falls, medication effects, sensory loss and functional changes often interact. Verify hearing aids, glasses, mobility aids and usual assistance. Compare pH first, then PaCO₂ and bicarbonate. Typical arterial ranges are pH 7.35–7.45, PaCO₂ 35–45 mmHg and HCO₃⁻ 22–26 mEq/L. Before surgery, verify identity, consent and required checks. After surgery, assess airway, pain, circulation, wound and mobility.

entries.h: An older adult is newly confused after surgery. Which history matters most immediately?
entries.t: Think… Establish when the change began and what attention and function were like before surgery.

entries.h: When pH falls and PaCO₂ rises, which primary process does that pattern suggest?
entries.t: Think… Respiratory acidosis. Assess ventilation and the cause of CO₂ retention.

entries.h: Which assessment belongs with a postoperative pain score after an opioid?
entries.t: Think… Assess respiratory rate, depth and level of sedation.

entries.h: Older adults, chronic illness and disability
entries.t: First action Assess airway, breathing and vital signs, then investigate new confusion and reversible causes with the team. Look for a response Look for return toward baseline attention and safer transfers. Recheck after interventions.

First action Assess the patient’s breathing, mental status, fluid balance and recent losses. Address the immediate problem and review the trend. Look for a response Recheck breathing, intake and output, weight and relevant labs after treatment.

entries.h: Perioperative care, pain and skin integrity
entries.t: First action For shallow breathing, assess responsiveness and ventilation, summon help and support the airway per protocol. Reposition and protect vulnerable skin. Look for a response Reassess sedation and respiratory effort after analgesia. Check skin during position changes.

entries.h: Module 1 · Older adults, chronic illness and disability
entries.t: Falls, medication effects, sensory loss and functional changes often interact. Verify hearing aids, glasses, mobility aids and usual assistance. New inattention that varies over hours suggests delirium. Ask someone who knows the patient when the change began.

entries.h: Module 2 · Fluid, electrolytes and acid–base balance
entries.t: Compare pH first, then PaCO₂ and bicarbonate. Typical arterial ranges are pH 7.35–7.45, PaCO₂ 35–45 mmHg and HCO₃⁻ 22–26 mEq/L. Slow, shallow breathing can retain CO₂ and lower pH. Loss of gastric acid through prolonged vomiting favors metabolic alkalosis.

entries.h: Module 3 · Perioperative care, pain and skin integrity
entries.t: Before surgery, verify identity, consent and required checks. After surgery, assess airway, pain, circulation, wound and mobility. Increasing sedation with shallow breathing after an opioid is an urgent cue. Nonblanchable redness over a pressure point needs offloading.

Typical adult serum potassium is 3.5–5.0 mEq/L. Both low and high levels can alter cardiac conduction. Typical arterial pH is 7.35–7.45, PaCO₂ 35–45 mmHg and bicarbonate 22–26 mEq/L. Read these together.

entries.h: A postoperative patient is difficult to awaken and breathing shallowly after an opioid. Which action takes priority?
entries.t: Offer more analgesia. Assess and support breathing and call for assistance. Begin discharge teaching.
B. Assess and support breathing and call for assistance. Increasing sedation with shallow breathing can signal impaired ventilation.

entries.h: An older adult becomes confused over a few hours. Which question best guides your assessment?
entries.t: How many birthdays have they celebrated? Have they ever needed glasses? When were they last at their usual level of attention?
C. When were they last at their usual level of attention? Time of onset helps identify an acute change that needs evaluation.

Modules 4–6

Separate an upper-airway sound from a lower-airway sound and notice when the effort to breathe increases despite less noise. Differentiate upper-airway noise from lower-airway wheeze. Assess voice, ability to handle secretions and work of breathing. Check breath sounds, respiratory effort, oxygenation and drainage trends. Keep chest tubing unobstructed and avoid routine clamping. Distinguish rescue bronchodilators from maintenance therapy. An exacerbation is a change from the usual pattern of dyspnea, cough or
sputum.

entries.h: Which needs faster escalation, new stridor at rest or isolated nasal congestion?
entries.t: Think… New stridor can signal a threatened airway.

entries.h: A chest-drain patient suddenly becomes breathless. What should you assess first?
entries.t: Think… Assess the patient’s airway and breathing, then evaluate the drainage system while obtaining help.

entries.h: In severe asthma, wheezing gets quieter while the patient becomes exhausted. What does this suggest?
entries.t: Think… Airflow may be falling dangerously. Obtain urgent respiratory support.

First action Stay with the patient, activate urgent airway support and provide oxygen and positioning per protocol. Look for a response Monitor effort, air movement, oxygenation and responsiveness while help arrives.

entries.h: Lower respiratory disorders and chest care
entries.t: First action Assess the patient and summon urgent help for sudden respiratory distress. Inspect the system for disconnection or kinks per policy. Look for a response Recheck breath sounds, oxygenation and comfort after intervention.

First action Position upright, assess effort and give prescribed oxygen or bronchodilator therapy to the ordered target. Escalate exhaustion, confusion or worsening airflow. Look for a response Reassess air movement, ability to speak, respiratory effort and oxygenation after treatment.

Differentiate upper-airway noise from lower-airway wheeze. Assess voice, ability to handle secretions and work of breathing. A harsh inspiratory sound over the neck suggests stridor. Drooling, retractions or difficulty speaking increase urgency.

entries.h: Module 5 · Lower respiratory disorders and chest care
entries.t: Check breath sounds, respiratory effort, oxygenation and drainage trends. Keep chest tubing unobstructed and avoid routine clamping. Sudden dyspnea with unequal breath sounds after chest trauma raises concern for pneumothorax. Fever, cough and focal crackles suggest infection.

Distinguish rescue bronchodilators from maintenance therapy. An exacerbation is a change from the usual pattern of dyspnea, cough or sputum. A prolonged expiratory phase and increased work of breathing may occur in COPD. In severe asthma, dwindling air movement despite distress can signal deterioration.

Stridor suggests upper-airway narrowing. Wheezing usually arises in the lower airways. Compare oxygen saturation with the ordered target and the patient’s baseline. Assess work of breathing even when the number looks reassuring.

entries.h: A patient develops new stridor and cannot speak comfortably. Which action has priority?
entries.t: Activate urgent airway support and assess breathing. Offer a drink. Wait for morning rounds.
A. Activate urgent airway support and assess breathing. Stridor and difficulty speaking can indicate a threatened upper airway.

entries.h: A patient with severe asthma becomes drowsy and little air movement is audible. Which interpretation fits?
entries.t: The attack has resolved. The patient can go home. Ventilation may be failing and help is needed urgently.
C. Ventilation may be failing and help is needed urgently. Quiet breath sounds with drowsiness can reflect fatigue and dangerously limited airflow.
