Stop the infusion; summon help and support breathing.
Turn off oxytocin and initiate the ordered response.
Call for help and lift the presenting part off the cord.
Call for help; assist with McRoberts and suprapubic pressure.
Sit her up.
Left side, oxygen, large-bore IV access and urgent evaluation.
Assess bleeding and fetal heart tones; no digital vaginal examination.
Prompt assessment and antihypertensive treatment per protocol.
Early feeding and glucose checks per neonatal protocol.
Emergency surgical response.
Empty the bladder.
Assess fetal heart tones before and after.
VS often; lung sounds (crackles); dyspnea/orthopnea; edema; daily weight. Highest strain 28–32 wks and right after placenta delivery.
Rest (2 periods/day + full night); low sodium; meds exactly as prescribed; HOB up + left tilt; epidural; assisted vaginal delivery; continuous FHR; SCDs; stool softeners.
Never supine in labor. Watch for cardiac collapse/HF right after the placenta delivers (fluid shift). Left-sided failure is worse for the fetus.
Left = lungs (crackles, orthopnea); JVD/ascites are RIGHT-sided. Constipation and nausea at 8 wks are normal; 4 lb in a week is not. HF drugs aren't tested.
Unilateral calf swelling, warmth, redness, tenderness; compare calf diameters. Ultrasound, PTT/INR.
Ambulate (best), hydrate, SCDs, prophylactic anticoagulant for high-risk post-cesarean.
Bleeding on anticoagulants; delivery may be timed with the drug stopped ~24 h before.
Anticoagulants do NOT dissolve the clot. D-dimer is unreliable in pregnancy.
Urine dip every visit (nitrites, WBC, glucose, protein). Pyelo: flank pain on tapping over kidney, fever, uterine irritability.
Pyelo = inpatient IV antibiotics, fetal monitoring, stay until afebrile and not contracting. Teach: wipe front to back, void after sex, fluids, cotton, no bubble baths.
Asymptomatic UTI can become pyelo, sepsis, and preterm labor.
Back labor is rhythmic, back- to-front; pyelo pain is over the kidney and reproduced by tapping. "Holding urine" and bubble baths are wrong answers.
Screen everyone 24–28 wks (earlier if high risk). 1-h > 140 → 3-h test; 2 abnormal values = GDM. Newborn: heel-stick glucose; jittery, lethargic, poor feeding.
Carb control (complex carbs), ~30 min exercise daily, glucose diary, insulin adjustments in 2nd/3rd trimester, growth US, NSTs, kick counts.
Newborn hypoglycemia: feed within 30 min of birth. Macrosomia → shoulder dystocia risk. GDM → higher lifetime type 2 risk.
Insulin does NOT cross the placenta (glucose does). One abnormal value ≠ GDM. Type 1/2 clients don't get a GTT. Values are given; don't memorize the chart.
Gestational age; amount (count pads), color, clots, tissue; pain; Rh type; shock signs (↓BP, ↑HR, pale, clammy).
"Come in to be examined and save any tissue." Sort SAB by tissue lost. RhoGAM if Rh- negative.
Missed abortion/retained stillbirth → infection, septic shock, DIC.
Bed rest, a tampon, or "spotting is harmless" are wrong. Threatened = closed cervix, FHT present (most hopeful).
Sudden one-sided lower abdominal pain + shock signs (case: BP 95/58, HR 132).
Ruptured → surgery. Unruptured → methotrexate: stop prenatal vitamins/folic acid, no alcohol, serial hCG, wait months to conceive.
Ruptured ectopic = hemorrhage emergency. RhoGAM if Rh-negative.
IUD, PID, tubal ligation, endometriosis are risk factors. Methotrexate is only for UNruptured.
Very high hCG, uterus larger than dates, dark brown "sludgy" bleeding, grape-like tissue, early preeclampsia signs.
D&C with suction; serial hCG follow-up.
Delay pregnancy 6 months–1 year; retained tissue can regrow (choriocarcinoma).
A rising hCG during follow-up can't be told apart from a new pregnancy, which is why she must wait.
Painless dilation history; signs of labor or ROM.
Nothing in the vagina, no tub soaks, take it easy.
Remove at 37 wks, or early if labor or ROM (or the cervix tears). Abdominal cerclage → cesarean.
Cerclage is for painless dilation, not labor.
Previa: painless bright red, soft uterus. Abruption: painful dark red, board-like uterus, FHR drifting down → bradycardia.
Previa: assess bleeding + FHT, CBC, T&S. Abruption: left side, O2, 2nd large-bore IV, CBC/T&S/coags, emergent delivery.
NO vaginal exams with previa. Abruption can be concealed; DIC risk.
A slowly falling FHR baseline with bloody show can be an early abruption. Complete previa = cesarean.
Petechiae, purpura, oozing IV sites, gum/nose bleeding. Labs: platelets ↓, fibrinogen ↓, PT/PTT ↑.
Volume expanders, blood products, keep warm, ICU care.
Confirm type & screen, CBC, coags are actually drawn before procedures.
Fibrinogen is LOW, not high. D-dimer isn't reliable in pregnancy.
Regular contractions, pelvic pressure, cervical change, nitrites (infection). fFN, UA, cultures.
Hydrate, treat infection. Terbutaline subcut (buys time). Betamethasone IM before 34 wks (2 doses, 24 h apart).
Hold terbutaline if maternal HR > 120 (cardiac boxed warning).
Terbutaline doesn't mature lungs; betamethasone does. A positive fFN does NOT mean she will deliver.

entries.h: Clinical side note · Positive-pressure rooms are not routine for every low WBC count
entries.t: CDC protective-environment recommendations specifically address allogeneic stem-cell transplant recipients. Other patients need individualized infection precautions; an airborne infection can change room requirements. Source
BP, headache not relieved by Tylenol, vision changes, epigastric pain, brisk DTRs/clonus, urine output, RR, LOC. HELLP: AST/ALT ↑, platelets ↓.
BP ≥ 160/110 → antihypertensive within ~30 min. Mag: low stimulation, IV fluids ≤ 125 mL/h, VS q30 min, strict I&O, continuous FHR.
Mag toxicity: STOP infusion → mag level → calcium gluconate → provider. PPH risk after birth. Platelets < 100,000 = no epidural.
Warm and flushed is EXPECTED on mag, not toxicity. The first action is stopping the drip, not giving calcium.

entries.h: Clinical side note · Magnesium toxicity: do not wait for the lab result
entries.t: Stop magnesium and summon urgent help. Support breathing and give calcium gluconate as ordered or per emergency protocol. Draw ordered labs without delaying emergency treatment. Source
Maternal Rh type and Coombs. Oligo < 300 mL (renal); poly > 2000 mL (GI).
RhoGAM at 28 wks, within 72 h of birth if baby Rh+, and any time blood may mix.
Fluid problems raise cord prolapse, PPH, and prolonged labor risk.
RhoGAM protects FUTURE pregnancies. Identical twins share a placenta (higher risk).
GBS status from ~36-wk swab (sooner in preterm labor).
Penicillin in labor every 4 h; ≥ 2 doses before birth = covered.
Not covered → increased newborn surveillance for infection.
GBS is NOT an STI. Swab even if a cesarean is planned.
Contraction frequency, duration, resting tone; bladder; dilation (stage 1) vs descent (stage 2).
Hypotonic: empty bladder, oxytocin, amniotomy. Hypertonic: stop oxytocin, fluids, reposition, terbutaline if it persists.
Full bladder blocks descent, weakens contractions, raises hemorrhage risk. Goal: q2–3 min with ≥ 60 s rest.
Stage 1 problem = dilation; stage 2 problem = descent. Arrest = halted despite everything.
Before oxytocin: head engaged, vertex, ripe cervix (Bishop ≥ 8), category I/II strip, no CPD. Contractions and FHR q30 min.
Own pump, LR main line, port closest to the client. Titrate up if q5 min; leave if q2–3 min. Prostaglandin first if Bishop is low.
Stop for > 5 contractions/10 min, a contraction > 2 min, or a bad strip. Remove Cervidil (tape) for tachysystole/distress. Watch water intoxication.
Never piggyback oxytocin. "It is not a race." Apply the Bishop chart, don't memorize it.
Rupture: sudden excruciating pain (prior cesarean scar). Inversion: excessive bleeding. AFE: sudden dyspnea, cyanosis, arrest, DIC.
Rupture → OR, O2, fluids, blood. Inversion → provider replaces uterus. AFE → emergency response, DIC care.
Avoid excess fundal pressure and pulling on the cord (inversion).
Inversion is never normal. Sudden acute pain in labor is never normal.
Sudden FHR drop after ROM; cord felt or seen. Risk: high station at ROM, preterm, polyhydramnios, transverse.
Lift presenting part off the cord and hold; call for help; O2; prepare emergency cesarean; saline-soaked towel on exposed cord.
Don't get her up if ruptured with a high station.
Knee-chest is NOT the first action; it's a temporary band- aid. Don't let go until the OR.
Risk: GDM, macrosomia > 4000 g, post-dates. After birth: arm movement (Erb's), clavicle crepitus.
Call for help + NICU; McRoberts; suprapubic pressure when directed; record head and body times.
~5 min before serious hypoxia; be ready to resuscitate.
NEVER fundal pressure.

entries.h: Clinical side note · Shoulder dystocia: correct the picture labels
entries.t: McRoberts means sharply flexing the mother’s hips, with knees toward the chest. Suprapubic pressure is a separate maneuver. Never use fundal pressure. Evaluate whether episiotomy is needed for access; it does not release the bony obstruction itself. Call for help immediately. Source
Position (OP, breech, transverse, face/brow); pelvimetry for inlet/outlet contraction.
ECV: empty bladder, US in room, FHT, terbutaline, towel under right hip. Trial of labor if CPD borderline.
ECV needs ≥ 37 wks, adequate fluid, single fetus, reactive NST. Transverse lie → cord prolapse risk.
ECV is scheduled, not done in labor. Breech, transverse, face/brow usually → cesarean; OP can deliver vaginally.
Full dilation and effacement, ROM, head engaged, bladder empty.
Empty bladder before the device; assess newborn for bruising, cephalohematoma.
Max 3 vacuum pop-offs. Only a skilled provider uses them.
9 cm is NOT enough (a 9 cm forceps case hemorrhaged).
Vasa previa: red blood with ROM + sudden bradycardia. Two-vessel cord at delivery.
Vasa previa: surveillance, scheduled cesarean. Two-vessel cord: work up for cardiac/renal anomalies.
Accreta spectrum → major hemorrhage; percreta may need hysterectomy.
Vasa previa blood is FETAL. Accreta = endometrium, increta = myometrium, percreta = through.

entries.h: Amniotomy / internal monitoring / scalp stim · guide 10.13–10.15

entries.t: FHT before and after AROM; fluid color, odor, amount, time. FSE/IUPC need ROM + ≥ 3 cm.
Be ready for meconium. IUPC allows amnioinfusion.
AROM → cord prolapse, AFE. Internal devices → infection, limited mobility.
Most important AROM step = FHT. Scalp stim: an acceleration is reassuring.
Indications: scheduled (CPD, malpresentation, HSV, prior classical), emergency (distress, abruption, prolapse, arrest).
NPO after midnight, teaching, IV, prep; SCDs; early ambulation.
Hemorrhage, infection, organ injury; newborn respiratory issues and cold stress.
Classical incision = no vaginal birth later (rupture risk).

Choosing a normal pregnancy change (nausea, constipation, frequency, foot edema) as the "abnormal" finding. Treating the monitor instead of the patient. Mixing up left (lungs) and right (body) heart failure. Thinking insulin crosses the placenta. Diagnosing GDM from one abnormal GTT value. Telling a possible miscarriage to stay home on bed rest instead of coming in. Doing a vaginal exam on a client with placenta previa. Calling warmth/flushing on magnesium a sign of toxicity. Giving calcium gluconate before

stopping the magnesium. Giving terbutaline with maternal HR over 120. Expecting terbutaline (not betamethasone) to mature fetal lungs. Reading a positive fFN as "she will deliver." entries.h: A provider prescribes oxytocin at 3 milliunits/min for labor augmentation. The pharmacy supplies 20 units of oxytocin in 1,000 mL of lactated Ringer's. How many mL/hr does the n...
entries.t: A provider prescribes oxytocin at 3 milliunits/min for labor augmentation. The pharmacy supplies 20 units of oxytocin in 1,000 mL of lactated Ringer's. How many mL/hr does the nurse set on the pump? 3 mL/hr 9 mL/hr 15 mL/hr 30 mL/hr

9 mL/hr 20 units = 20,000 milliunits in 1,000 mL, so the bag is 20 milliunits/mL . Then 3 milliunits/min divided by 20 milliunits/mL = 0.15 mL/min, and 0.15 x 60 = 9 mL/hr . Skipping that final x60 leaves 0.15 and is the single most commonly missed step.

entries.t: Massage the fundus vigorously Inspect the perineum, vagina and cervix for a laceration Encourage her to void and reassess Document the finding as normal lochia rubra

Inspect the perineum, vagina and cervix for a laceration A firm fundus with continued bleeding means the uterus is not the source , so look for a laceration or hematoma, classically a bright red continuous trickle without clots. Massage will not help a uterus that is already contracted, and this is not normal lochia.

entries.h: A newborn has a scalp swelling that crosses the suture lines and was present at birth. How does the nurse document this finding?
entries.t: Cephalohematoma, which raises the risk of jaundice Caput succedaneum, which resolves in a few days Molding, which requires no documentation A subgaleal hemorrhage requiring immediate surgery

Caput succedaneum, which resolves in a few days Caput succedaneum crosses suture lines and resolves within days; a cephalohematoma is bounded by sutures, does not cross them, and carries a higher jaundice risk as the blood breaks down. Whether it crosses the suture line is the entire discrimination.

entries.h: A newborn born at 28 weeks is receiving gavage feedings. On day 6 the abdomen is distended, a feeding is returned undigested, and the diaper contains bloody stool. Which action ...
entries.t: A newborn born at 28 weeks is receiving gavage feedings. On day 6 the abdomen is distended, a feeding is returned undigested, and the diaper contains bloody stool. Which action does the nurse take first? Stop all feedings and report the findings Give the next feeding more slowly over a longer time Place the newborn prone and reassess the abdomen in 2 hours Change the newborn from gavage feedings to nipple feedings

Stop all feedings and report the findings A distended abdomen, bloody stool and feeding intolerance point to NEC , so all feeds are stopped immediately and reported — feeding a hypoxic gut makes the ischemia worse. Slowing the feeding or changing the route is still feeding, so it does not protect the gut.

entries.h: A client is pregnant. She has one child born at 39 weeks, one child born at 34 weeks, and a pregnancy loss at 10 weeks. Both children are living. What is her GTPAL?

entries.t: 4-1-1-1-2 Gravida counts all pregnancies including the current one , giving 4. Term (37 weeks or more) is 1, preterm (20 to under 37 weeks) is 1, abortions (under 20 weeks) is 1, and living children is 2.

entries.h: A laboring client on oxytocin has repetitive decelerations that begin after each contraction peaks and return to baseline after the contraction ends. Which action does the nurse...
entries.t: A laboring client on oxytocin has repetitive decelerations that begin after each contraction peaks and return to baseline after the contraction ends. Which action does the nurse take first? Position the client on her left side Increase the oxytocin to strengthen contractions Document the finding and continue monitoring Perform a cervical examination to check dilation

Position the client on her left side Decelerations that begin after the peak and recover after the contraction are late decelerations from uteroplacental insufficiency , and of these options repositioning is the intrauterine resuscitation measure - alongside stopping the oxytocin, an IV bolus and early notification, matched to the cause rather than run in a fixed order. Oxygen is not routine; it is for maternal hypoxia. Increasing oxytocin worsens it and documentation alone is never sufficient.

Cluster care and keep the lights dim Swaddle the newborn snugly Offer small, frequent, high-calorie feedings NAS care is the opposite of stimulation : cluster care, dim lights, low noise, swaddling, non-nutritive sucking, and small frequent high-calorie feedings with the head elevated. Bright light and vigorous stimulation worsen the hyperirritability and tremors.

entries.h: A nurse observes a parent settle a 2-month-old for a nap prone on a soft quilt with crib bumpers in place. Which action should the nurse take first?
entries.t: Document the observation in the record Reposition the infant supine on a bare, firm mattress Ask the parent why she prefers the prone position Plan to teach safe sleep at the discharge visit

Reposition the infant supine on a bare, firm mattress Safe sleep is supine in a bare, firm crib with no co-sleeping, and an unsafe sleep surface is an active airway risk — remove it now, then teach. Teaching later does not protect the infant currently in the crib.

entries.h: A nurse is counseling a 16-year-old who has just been licensed to drive. Which instruction is the priority?
entries.t: Keep an emergency kit with flares and a blanket in the trunk Verify that his insurance card is in the glove compartment Never drive after using alcohol or drugs, and never ride with a driver who has Install a GPS app so his parents can locate the car

Never drive after using alcohol or drugs, and never ride with a driver who has Unintentional injury — motor vehicle crashes above all — is the leading cause of adolescent death , with alcohol and drugs a major contributor. Emergency kits, insurance and GPS are reasonable, but none of them prevents the crash.

entries.h: A nurse receives report on four children. Which child should the nurse assess first?
entries.t: An 8-year-old with sickle cell disease who has sudden chest pain, fever and dyspnea A 3-year-old with iron deficiency anemia who is pale and tired A 6-year-old with hemophilia who has mild knee swelling after bumping a table A 15-year-old with mononucleosis who reports a sore throat

An 8-year-old with sickle cell disease who has sudden chest pain, fever and dyspnea Chest pain with fever and dyspnea in sickle cell disease is acute chest syndrome , a life-threatening emergency. The other three are expected findings for their diagnoses — pallor in iron deficiency, a minor bleed in hemophilia, and pharyngitis in mono.

entries.h: A 7-year-old at a school event develops hives, lip swelling and audible stridor minutes after eating a cookie containing peanuts. Which action should the school nurse take first?
entries.t: Administer oral diphenhydramine Administer intramuscular epinephrine Apply high-flow oxygen by mask Call the parents for permission to treat

Administer intramuscular epinephrine IM epinephrine is the first action in anaphylaxis — it is the only agent that reverses airway edema and vasodilation. Antihistamines are adjuncts, oxygen supports but does not treat the cause, and calling for permission delays a life-saving drug.

entries.h: A 5-year-old is being observed after a fall from a playground structure. Which finding should the nurse report as the priority?
entries.t: The child reports a headache The child, previously alert and chatty, is now confused and difficult to arouse The child vomited once shortly after the fall The heart rate has drifted from 96 to 88

The child, previously alert and chatty, is now confused and difficult to arouse A change in level of consciousness is the earliest sign of neurologic deterioration and outranks the others. Cushing's triad — rising BP, falling HR, falling RR — is a late finding, so waiting for the heart rate to drop meaningfully means waiting too long.

entries.t: A 3-year-old arrives with a temperature of 39.5 C, drooling, a muffled voice, and is sitting forward on his hands refusing to lie back. He has no cough. Which action should the nurse take first? Inspect the throat with a tongue blade for exudate Obtain a throat culture Keep the child upright with the parent and ensure emergency airway equipment is at the bedside Position the child supine for a chest x-ray

Keep the child upright with the parent and ensure emergency airway equipment is at the bedside High fever, drooling, muffled voice, tripod posture and no cough is epiglottitis — never use a tongue blade or inspect the throat, because it can trigger complete airway obstruction. Croup is the look-alike, but croup brings a barking cough with a low-grade fever.

entries.h: An infant with tetralogy of Fallot has a hypercyanotic (tet) spell. What is the nurse's first action?
entries.t: Place the infant in a knee-chest position Lay the infant flat and stimulate vigorously Give a rapid IV fluid bolus first Withhold oxygen to avoid closing the duct

Place the infant in a knee-chest position Knee-chest raises systemic vascular resistance, which pushes blood back through the pulmonary circulation instead of shunting right to left. Older children squat instinctively for the same reason. Then calm the child, give oxygen and morphine as prescribed.

Which action should the nurse take first? Perform a neurovascular check and notify the provider immediately Pain that analgesia does not touch is compartment syndrome , not an inadequate dose, and pallor with paresthesia adds two more of the 6 Ps. His diaper contains stool mixed with blood and mucus. Which action is the priority? Notify the provider immediately; the findings suggest intussusception Episodic severe pain with knees drawn up, currant jelly stool and a sausage-shaped mass is intussusception, which needs air or barium enema reduction. The pain-free intervals make the child look completely well — that is the trap , and it is why this gets mistaken for colic.

entries.h: A child with nephrotic syndrome is admitted. Which findings does the nurse expect? Select all that apply.
entries.t: Massive proteinuria Generalized edema including periorbital swelling Hypoalbuminemia Grossly bloody urine Hyperlipidemia

Massive proteinuria Generalized edema including periorbital swelling Hypoalbuminemia Hyperlipidemia Nephrotic syndrome leaks protein : heavy proteinuria, low albumin, edema as oncotic pressure falls, and a compensatory rise in lipids. Gross hematuria points to glomerulonephritis instead - that is the pair these questions separate. Periorbital swelling on waking is often the first thing a parent notices.

entries.h: A child is admitted with a suspected Wilms tumor. Which nursing action is essential?
entries.t: Palpate the abdominal mass each shift to track its size Post a sign at the bedside not to palpate the abdomen Encourage vigorous activity Place the child prone for comfort

Post a sign at the bedside not to palpate the abdomen Do not palpate the abdomen. Handling a Wilms tumor can rupture the capsule and seed malignant cells across the abdomen. A sign goes above the bed so no one does it out of habit - one of the few nursing interventions that is entirely about not doing something.

entries.t: Think… Think inhalation injury. Airway edema can progress quickly.

entries.h: After pituitary surgery a patient has very large amounts of dilute urine, marked thirst and high sodium.
entries.t: Think… Diabetes insipidus causes loss of free water. SIADH usually causes water retention and low sodium.

entries.h: An insulin-treated patient is shaky and sweaty but awake and able to swallow safely.
entries.t: Think… Low glucose can impair brain function. Oral carbohydrate is appropriate only when swallowing is safe.

First action Get urgent airway support, administer high-concentration oxygen per protocol and prepare for airway management. Look for a response Reassess voice, air movement, work of breathing and perfusion.
First action Measure output, assess volume status and report findings for ordered fluid and hormone therapy. Look for a response Trend intake, output, sodium and neurologic status.

First action Check glucose. If below 70 mg/dL, give fast-acting carbohydrate per protocol. If unable to swallow, use protocol-directed IV dextrose or glucagon. Look for a response Recheck glucose after 15 minutes for oral treatment and repeat per protocol until corrected.

What percentage is one entire adult leg? 18 percent What does the adult posterior trunk include? The back totaling 18 percent When does the Parkland clock begin? At the time of injury Which burn is red and dry without blisters? A superficial burn What are the emergent phase priorities? Airway and circulation support What combination raises concern for inhalation injury? Facial burns, soot and hoarseness

What mineralocorticoid can also be deficient in Addison’s disease? Aldosterone What skin finding can accompany primary Addison’s disease? Hyperpigmentation What skin changes can occur with Cushing’s syndrome? Easy bruising and purple striae What urine pattern fits SIADH? Concentrated urine with high specific gravity What medication replaces ADH activity in central DI? Desmopressin What blocker class is used before adrenal surgery for pheochromocytoma? An alpha blocker

Which pancreatic cells make glucagon? Alpha cells What process underlies type 2 diabetes? Insulin resistance with declining secretion When is glucose rechecked after initial oral treatment? After 15 minutes What key laboratory feature is essential to assessing HHS? Hyperosmolarity What does the current module teach for DKA with potassium 3.1 mmol/L? Typical adult serum potassium: 3.5–5.0 mmol/L. Replace potassium and delay insulin under protocol What tool helps inspect the soles of the feet? A mirror

Typical adult serum sodium reference range is 135–145 mEq/L. DI tends toward high sodium with dilute urine. SIADH tends toward low sodium with concentrated urine. For an awake adult able to swallow with glucose below 70 mg/dL, the usual 15–15 rule is 15 g of fast carbohydrate and a glucose recheck in 15 minutes. Typical fasting glucose is 70–99 mg/dL.
Clear lungs do not clear a burn airway. Likewise, a glucose number alone does not distinguish DKA from HHS: look for ketones, acidosis, dehydration and mental-status change.

entries.h: A client with burns to the face and anterior neck is hoarse and has singed nasal hair and carbonaceous sputum. What is the priority action?
entries.t: Calculate the TBSA using the rule of nines Obtain intubation equipment now Start lactated Ringer's by the Parkland formula Apply silver sulfadiazine to the facial burns

Obtain intubation equipment now Inhalation cues mean the airway will swell shut within 1 to 2 hours , so intubation equipment comes before TBSA estimation or fluids. Face, neck or chest burns make airway the priority; only waist-down burns put fluids first.

entries.h: A client has 6 L of pale urine in 24 hours, urine specific gravity 1.002, serum sodium 152 and BP 88/54. Which condition does the nurse suspect?
entries.t: Typical adult references: serum sodium 135–145 mEq/L; urine specific gravity about 1.005–1.030. Diabetes insipidus SIADH Cushing's syndrome Thyroid storm

Diabetes insipidus Dilute high-volume urine with low specific gravity and high serum sodium is DI - dry inside, too little ADH. SIADH is the mirror: scant concentrated urine, high specific gravity, overload and low sodium.

entries.h: Neurologic change, stroke and spinal cord injury
entries.t: Start with time of onset and neurologic baseline. Compare movement, level of consciousness, swallowing and breathing before choosing the priority. ▣ Course PowerPoint library Browse all Exam 3 decks All study guides NUR 258 · Exam 3 course outline
Sudden focal changes start the stroke clock. Hypertension and headache after a high spinal cord injury are urgent.

entries.h: A patient suddenly has facial droop, arm weakness and difficulty speaking.
entries.t: Think… Suspect acute stroke. Symptoms alone cannot tell ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke.

entries.h: A person with a T4 injury has a pounding headache, sweating above the lesion and a sudden rise in blood pressure.
entries.t: Think… Think autonomic dysreflexia. Bladder distention is a common trigger.

First action Activate the stroke pathway, establish last known well and check glucose. Prepare for urgent brain imaging. Look for a response Repeat neurologic assessments and keep the patient NPO until swallowing safety is assessed.

First action Sit upright, loosen constrictive items, recheck BP frequently and inspect the catheter or bladder first. Follow the emergency protocol. Look for a response Confirm blood pressure moves back toward the patient's baseline as the trigger is relieved.

What is Cushing’s triad? Bradycardia, irregular breathing and widened pulse pressure What is the highest eye-opening score on the GCS? 4 points What does decorticate posturing look like? Abnormal arm flexion toward the core What communication problem may occur with a left-hemisphere stroke? Aphasia What does the B in BE FAST represent? Balance changes What does the A in BE FAST represent? Arm weakness

Blood between dura and arachnoid? Subdural hematoma Temporary loss of reflexes below a spinal injury? Spinal shock What turning method preserves spinal alignment? Log rolling Central nervous system demyelinating disease? Multiple sclerosis Tremor, rigidity and bradykinesia suggest what? Parkinson disease Chronic progressive cognitive decline? Dementia

Fluctuating double vision, drooping lids or weakness that worsens with use Think myasthenia gravis. A weak cough, difficulty swallowing or shallow breathing calls for urgent respiratory assessment. Episodes of neurologic deficits separated in time Consider multiple sclerosis. Compare function with baseline and review infection or overheating when symptoms worsen. Slowness, rigidity and a resting tremor Think Parkinson disease. Assess fall and swallowing risks and keep prescribed medications on schedule. New

confusion, pupillary change or a falling Glasgow Coma Scale score after head trauma Escalate immediately, support airway and oxygenation, and protect spinal alignment. Reassess the individual eye, verbal and motor responses.

Glasgow Coma Scale: eyes 1–4, verbal 1–5 and motor 1–6. Report individual components and the trend, and document any untestable component. With suspected acute stroke, last known well is the last time the patient was at neurologic baseline, even if the deficit was first noticed later.
A sudden severe BP rise after spinal cord injury suggests autonomic dysreflexia. Lower pressure in neurogenic shock is a different pattern.

entries.h: Which assessment finding is the earliest indicator of rising intracranial pressure?
entries.t: A subtle change in level of consciousness Widening pulse pressure with bradycardia Cheyne-Stokes respirations Fixed dilated pupils

A subtle change in level of consciousness A change in LOC is the earliest sign ; Cushing's triad - rising systolic with widened pulse pressure, bradycardia and irregular respirations - is a late herniation sign . If the triad is present, you are already late.

entries.h: A client with a T4 spinal cord injury has BP 208/112, HR 48, a pounding headache and flushing above the injury. What does the nurse do first?
entries.t: Administer the prescribed antihypertensive Sit the client upright Check for a fecal impaction Lay the client flat and elevate the legs

Sit the client upright In autonomic dysreflexia the first action is to sit her up , which uses gravity to drop the blood pressure immediately, then find and remove the trigger - check the bladder before the bowel. Antihypertensives are an adjunct, not the first move, and lying flat worsens the hypertension.

entries.t: “Fluids first,” “infection always first,” and “never give calcium” are not universal rules. Assess airway, breathing, circulation, active bleeding, fluid status and orders. A low hemoglobin does not by itself authorize a transfusion. Do not delay urgent treatment while deciding which exam mnemonic fits.
