entries.h: 2. Where the professor adds to or differs from the student's guide
entries.t: When they conflict, go with the professor, since she writes the test. DIC priorities: The student's guide says to give heparin "only if clotting is the dominant problem." Halecka taught the order as (1) treat the underlying cause (antibiotics for sepsis) → (2) airway/O2, IV fluids, vasopressors, and start the heparin drip at the same time as the fluids → (3) blood products (platelets, FFP, cryo, PRBCs) last. Heparin stops new clots; it doesn't dissolve existing ones.

entries.h: Clinical side note · DIC: the sequence depends on bleeding and thrombosis
entries.t: Treat the cause promptly. Heparin is considered when thrombosis predominates; it is not a universal step before blood products. Active bleeding may require urgent platelets, plasma or fibrinogen replacement while the cause is treated. Source Polycythemia vera is a cancer (blood cancer). Aplastic anemia is NOT a cancer. Hemophilia labs: platelets normal , PTT ↑ , INR normal . Give clotting factors before and after procedures. Do not transfuse before a procedure (only after, if they bleed). Hemophilia joint bleed

entries.h: Clinical side note · DIC: the sequence depends on bleeding and thrombosis
entries.t: (RICE): if the area is now an open, bleeding wound, Compression is the priority. HIT vs. a high PTT: a PTT of 106–110 on a heparin drip → titrate per protocol (hold about 1 hr and decrease); don't panic. Platelets dropping on heparin (e.g., 250K → 80K) = HIT → stop the drip and call the provider (likely protamine sulfate and a switch to a different anticoagulant). Check platelets at least once a shift on a drip.

entries.h: Clinical side note · HIT is a clotting emergency
entries.t: Suspected immune HIT requires stopping all heparin and prompt evaluation for a non-heparin anticoagulant. Protamine reverses heparin anticoagulation; it does not treat the immune process of HIT. Source Iron timing: take it between meals (empty stomach → N/V and noncompliance; with food → absorption drops ~50%). Liquid iron stains teeth → use a straw and rinse after. Recheck labs every 2–3 months. Transfusion is a "band-aid," not the treatment for iron deficiency, aplastic anemia, sickle cell, or DIC. Treat the

entries.h: Clinical side note · HIT is a clotting emergency
entries.t: cause. Infection kills first: in pancytopenia, infection/sepsis is the priority unless the patient is actively bleeding right now. Neutropenic fever: notifying the provider for antibiotics/cultures comes before putting the sign on the door ("the sign doesn't stop germs"). Leukemia subtypes: "Do not panic." Questions may name AML/CLL/etc., but answer with general leukemia care. Sickle cell crisis: fluids are the priority (dilute the blood, stop clumping), then pain meds. Bed rest during crisis (Hgb ~5, dizzy,

entries.h: Clinical side note · HIT is a clotting emergency
entries.t: hypotensive → fall risk and ↓ O2 demand). Prevent clots with SCDs, SubQ heparin, and range of motion instead of walking. Splenomegaly is an EXPECTED finding in sickle cell, polycythemia vera, and leukemia. A ruptured spleen is an emergency: hypotension, bleeding, left shoulder pain . Neutropenic room = POSITIVE pressure (not negative, no N95 needed). Mask the patient during transport.

entries.h: Clinical side note · Positive-pressure rooms are not routine for every low WBC count
entries.t: CDC protective-environment recommendations specifically address allogeneic stem-cell transplant recipients. Other patients need individualized infection precautions; an airborne infection can change room requirements. Source Hospice: O2 at about 2 L is for comfort only. Usually no antibiotics. Dyspnea is managed with morphine and anxiolytics. Only the hospice physician and nurse follow the patient.

entries.h: Clinical side note · Hospice is an interdisciplinary service
entries.t: The team includes nursing, medical, social and spiritual support. Treatments are chosen for the person’s comfort goals; hospice is not limited to a physician and nurse, and antibiotics are not universally prohibited. Source
Definition The process of making blood cells; one stem cell splits into the myeloid and lymphoid lines
Definition RBCs (O2), platelets/megakaryocytes (clotting), neutrophils (bacteria), eosinophils (parasites/allergy), basophils (histamine), monocytes → macrophages, mast cells
Definition T cells (kill infected cells), B cells (make antibodies), plasma cells (release antibodies), NK cells (kill virus-infected and cancer cells)
Definition Protein in RBCs that carries O2
Definition % of blood volume made up of RBCs
Definition RBC size . Microcytic (<80) = iron deficiency. Normocytic = chronic/kidney disease. Macrocytic (>100) = B12/folate deficiency or alcohol. You don't need to memorize the numbers.
Definition Amount of Hgb per RBC; hypochromic (low) = iron deficiency
Definition Stored iron. ↓ = iron deficiency ; ↑ = overload/inflammation. The lab to monitor for iron deficiency.
Definition Total iron-binding capacity: ↑ in iron deficiency , ↓ in overload/chronic disease
Definition Immature RBCs; measures bone marrow activity
Definition Confirms sickle cell disease
Definition Diagnoses aplastic anemia and leukemia. Site: posterior iliac crest . Afterward, hold pressure (the concern is low platelets).
Definition Breaks down WBC types; shows immature cells (blasts) in leukemia

entries.h: Clinical side note · ALL also occurs in adults
entries.t: ALL is common in childhood but is not restricted to children. Acute leukemias involve immature cells; chronic leukemias differ. WBC counts can be low, normal or high. Source
Definition All three cell lines low: RBCs (anemia), WBCs (infection), platelets (bleeding)
Definition Low neutrophils → infection risk
Definition Absolute neutrophil count; guides neutropenic precautions
Definition Low platelets → bleeding risk
Definition Tiny red/purple pinpoint dots (superficial bleeding)
Definition Larger purple patches; deeper, worse than petechiae
Definition Nosebleed
Definition Black, tarry stool (upper GI bleed)
Definition Blood / hemoglobin in the urine

Definition & key points ↓ Hgb, ↓ Hct, ↓ RBCs → less O2 to tissues. General S/S: fatigue, weakness, pallor, SOB, tachycardia, dizziness/syncope, cold intolerance, brittle nails, poor wound healing (from low tissue O2).
Definition & key points Not making enough RBCs (iron/B12/folate deficiency, bone marrow suppression, chemo)
Definition & key points RBCs destroyed early (e.g., sickle cell)
Definition & key points Craving non-food items (ice, dirt, clay); a sign of iron deficiency
Definition & key points Red, cracked sores at the corners of the mouth; a classic anemia sign
Definition & key points Iron, B12, or folate deficiency ("red is red")

Definition & key points Most common anemia. Causes: GI bleed (#1), heavy periods, pregnancy, poor diet, alcohol, IBD, long-term NSAIDs/aspirin. Labs: ↓ ferritin, ↑ TIBC, microcytic/hypochromic. Treatment: PO iron + vitamin C (orange juice) , between meals. Avoid taking it with milk, calcium, antacids, or tea/coffee. IV iron infusion if PO fails. Expected: dark/black stools and constipation. Diet: red meat, seafood, beans, leafy greens, dried fruit.

Definition & key points Bone marrow stem cell failure → pancytopenia . Not cancer. Causes: chemo/radiation, drugs/chemicals, viruses, idiopathic. Treatment: stem cell transplant (best cure) + immunosuppressants, plus RBC/platelet transfusions as needed. Supplements do nothing. Patient may be on neutropenic and bleeding precautions.
Definition & key points Large RBCs (↑ MCV) from impaired DNA synthesis. Two types: B12 deficiency and folate deficiency . Large cells clump and get damaged leaving the marrow.
Definition & key points B12 deficiency from lack of intrinsic factor . On the test, megaloblastic = B12 = pernicious.
Definition & key points Protein made in the stomach, needed to absorb B12. Lost with gastric surgery/bypass, stomach cancer, Crohn's, or genetics.

Definition & key points Anemia S/S plus neuro symptoms : paresthesia, balance/gait/proprioception problems, confusion, memory loss (B12 protects the myelin sheath). Treatment: lifelong IM/SubQ injections , never switched to oral. At risk: gastric surgery, Crohn's, vegans, alcoholics.
Definition & key points Causes: poor diet, alcoholism, pregnancy. No neuro symptoms. Treatment: PO folic acid and leafy greens, beans, citrus.
Definition & key points Yellow IV fluid with added vitamins (B12, folate, thiamine) given to alcoholic patients
Definition & key points Autosomal recessive hemolytic anemia. Crescent-shaped RBCs clump → vaso-occlusive crisis , severe pain, hypoxia. Pain and jaundice are unique to sickle cell among the anemias.
Definition & key points Sickled cells block vessels → ischemic pain, possible tissue necrosis
Definition & key points D ehydration (#1, especially in summer), I nfection, S tress/cold, ↓ O2/high altitude
Definition & key points IV fluids (priority, NS) , IV opioids, O2, treat the cause (antibiotics if fever/infection), transfusion if Hgb < 7, and a heparin drip if a clot is present
Definition & key points Sickling/clot in the lungs; an emergency
Definition & key points ↑ fetal hemoglobin (HbF) → ↓ sickling and crises (long-term prevention)
Definition & key points Swollen hands/feet in children with sickle cell
Definition & key points Spleen destroyed by repeated sickling/infarcts
Definition & key points Hydrate, avoid cold/high altitude/smoking/flying high, keep vaccines current, low-dose aspirin to prevent clots, seek care for fever or chest pain

Definition & key points Cancer : marrow overproduces RBCs → thick, viscous blood → clots (stroke, MI, DVT). S/S: ruddy (red) face , HTN, headache, dizziness, blurred vision, splenomegaly, itching after a hot shower , possible jaundice. Treatment: therapeutic phlebotomy (first-line; the blood is discarded, not donated), fluids , low-dose aspirin, hydroxyurea/interferon. Priority: prevent clots (range of motion, fluids). No iron and no warm compresses.
Definition & key points Burning pain and redness of the hands/feet (polycythemia vera)
Definition & key points Removing blood to ↓ RBC count; like old-fashioned "bloodletting"

Definition & key points Cancer of the bone marrow: overproduction of immature WBCs (blasts) . WBC count looks high but is functionally low , and crowding causes pancytopenia . Diagnose with CBC w/ diff + bone marrow biopsy. Risks: chemicals/pesticides, smoking, prior chemo, genetics.
Definition & key points Acute = fast and aggressive, treated aggressively (often a 4–6 week hospital stay for induction chemo). Chronic = slow, sometimes "watch and wait," but can turn acute.
Definition & key points The letter M or L tells you which cell line is affected: AML/CML = myeloid, ALL/CLL = lymphoid
Definition & key points Acute myeloid leukemia; blasts on biopsy; older adults
Definition & key points Chronic myeloid leukemia; Philadelphia chromosome ; treated with TKIs (imatinib/Gleevec). Phases: chronic → accelerated → blast crisis
Definition & key points Late CML phase that behaves like acute leukemia

Definition & key points Acute lymphocytic leukemia; most common childhood leukemia (peak ~age 4), good prognosis. Kids present with bruising, bone pain, frequent infections, fatigue. Also needs CNS chemo.
Definition & key points Chronic lymphocytic leukemia; older adults (~70); often found on routine labs; lymphocytosis; "watch and wait"
Definition & key points Fever + night sweats + weight loss
Definition & key points Cancer of the lymphatic system/lymph nodes → immunocompromised patient

Definition & key points Reed-Sternberg cells (cells with two nuclei). Younger adults (15–34) and again after 60. Painless swollen cervical (neck) node first; spreads in an orderly , predictable node-to-node pattern. Goal = cure (~92–94% cure rate). Chemo + radiation. Risk factor: Epstein-Barr virus.

Definition & key points Older adults, more often men; B or T cells; spreads randomly , so it is usually found late (stage 3–4). Worse S/S (B symptoms, nodes in many areas). Goal = remission. Watch for tumor lysis syndrome after chemo.

Definition & key points Cancer of plasma cells (B cells) in the marrow; older adults (" old CRAB "). Malignant plasma cells make M protein → kidney damage. Classic presentation: older patient with excruciating bone pain + high calcium . No cure. Treatment: chemo/radiation, immunotherapy, HSCT, bisphosphonates (e.g., alendronate/Fosamax), calcitonin , IV fluids , pain control, fall/fracture precautions , dialysis if kidneys fail. Never give calcium supplements.
Definition & key points C alcium ↑ (confusion, constipation, weakness, kidney stones), R enal failure, A nemia, B one lesions/pain/fractures
Definition & key points Abnormal antibody made by myeloma cells; found in blood/urine; clogs the kidneys
Definition & key points "Punched-out," hollow-looking holes in bone on X-ray (myeloma)
Definition & key points A bone breaks easily from disease, not trauma
Definition & key points Painful sores/inflammation of the mouth and GI lining from cancer treatment
Definition & key points ↓ production (marrow problems, leukemia, chemo), ↑ destruction (ITP), ↑ consumption (DIC)
Definition & key points Electric R azor, A void aspirin/NSAIDs/heparin, small N eedles, D ecrease sticks/IM injections, protect from I njury

Definition & key points Soft toothbrush, no flossing , no rectal temps, no enemas or suppositories , stool softeners (no straining), minimize BP cuff use and suctioning, keep lips moist, avoid unnecessary Foleys, no crunchy foods, cluster lab draws into one stick, hold pressure 5–10 min. IM injections are worse than SubQ; question IM orders when platelets are low.

Definition & key points X-linked (mostly males), genetic; missing a clotting factor → can't form a stable clot. Hemophilia A = Factor VIII; B (Christmas disease) = Factor IX. Deep bleeds: hemarthrosis (joints), intracranial, GI; any head bump → ER for a head CT. Treatment: replace the factor (often self-injected through a port), no aspirin, RICE, no contact sports (swimming is OK).
Definition & key points Bleeding into a joint; ~75% of hemophilia bleeds
Definition & key points Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation; Compression is the priority if actively bleeding

Definition & key points Most common inherited bleeding disorder; affects men and women equally. Missing vWF , which helps platelets stick and activates Factor VIII. Superficial/mucosal bleeding: nosebleeds, gums, heavy periods, easy bruising; often diagnosed later in life. Treatment: desmopressin (DDAVP) before procedures, vWF replacement.
Definition & key points Synthetic ADH (also used for diabetes insipidus); temporarily ↑ vWF/Factor VIII

Definition & key points Disseminated intravascular coagulation: "clot everywhere, then bleed everywhere." Always secondary to something else: sepsis (#1) , trauma, burns, shock, OB emergencies (abruption, amniotic fluid embolism), cancer. Microclots use up platelets and factors → bleeding from IV sites, gums, nose, GI/GU; organ ischemia. Mortality is >80% if missed.
Definition & key points ↓ platelets, ↓ fibrinogen, ↓ H&H (if bleeding). ↑ PT, ↑ PTT, ↑ INR, ↑ D-dimer, ↑ FDPs, schistocytes present

Definition & key points Treat the cause → O2/airway, fluids, vasopressors + heparin drip → platelets/FFP/cryo/PRBCs. Avoid unnecessary sticks, monitor I&O, no warm compresses (vasodilation → more bleeding), no aspirin .
Definition & key points Breakdown products of clots; ↑ when clots form and break down (DIC)
Definition & key points Clotting protein; consumed in DIC; replaced with cryoprecipitate
Definition & key points Blood product rich in fibrinogen
Definition & key points Immune thrombocytopenic purpura: autoimmune antibodies destroy platelets. Treatment: corticosteroids or splenectomy.
Definition & key points Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura: clots form in the capillaries → AKI, MI, stroke
Definition & key points Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia: immune reaction to heparin → platelets drop while on heparin , causing clotting. Stop heparin and notify the provider.

Definition & key points IV drip for active clots (DVT, PE, MI, ischemic stroke not eligible for tPA, new A-fib); SubQ for prevention. Baseline labs: CBC (platelets, H&H), PT/PTT/INR. Monitor aPTT (therapeutic 60–80) . Antidote: protamine sulfate . Prevents new clots; doesn't dissolve old ones.
Definition & key points PO, long-term (DVT, PE, A-fib, mechanical valve); bridged from heparin. Monitor INR (2–3) . Antidote: vitamin K .
Definition & key points INR monitors warfarin ; aPTT monitors heparin
Definition & key points Blood from a donor
Definition & key points Your own blood, donated ahead of a planned surgery
Definition & key points The patient's own blood suctioned during surgery, filtered, and reinfused
Definition & key points Universal donor (used in a true emergency)
Definition & key points Universal recipient
Definition & key points Required before PRBCs
Definition & key points Should only get Rh-negative blood. Rh-positive blood can make them form antibodies, which matters most in women of childbearing age.
Definition & key points Use within 24 hours of thawing; infuse within 4 hours once started. ABO type must still be compatible.
Definition & key points Use special platelet tubing; infuse each unit over about 15–30 minutes; keep at room temperature (never refrigerate) and agitate gently. ABO type is still checked.
Definition & key points Packed red cells; ↑ O2-carrying capacity

ABO compatibility chart: which FFP or red cells can this patient receive? ↗ Definition & key points Plasma: a volume expander + clotting factors (↓ INR). Used in DIC, massive transfusion, and warfarin reversal.
Definition & key points Yellowish product; infused quickly (15–30 min); don't refrigerate

Definition & key points Order and consent → good IV (18–20 g) → baseline vitals before the tech picks up the blood → Y-tubing with filter → prime with 0.9% NS only → clamp the saline and open the blood → stay 15 min and recheck vitals → finish within 4 hr → flush the remaining blood in the tubing with NS. Two licensed nurses verify at the bedside.
Definition & key points Keep a 1 L NS bag on new primary tubing in the room for reactions. Don't open the Y-tubing saline (that pushes more blood in).

Definition & key points Stop the transfusion , run NS on new tubing , stay with the patient and take vitals, call provider/rapid response and the blood bank, send the bag, tubing, blood, and urine to the lab, document

Definition & key points ABO incompatibility; the most serious. Classic and unique signs: flank/low back pain, hemoglobinuria, feeling of impending doom ; also fever, chills, hypotension, tachycardia, ↑ BUN/creatinine. Never restart.

entries.h: Clinical side note · A transfusion reaction needs clinical review
entries.t: Stop the transfusion and assess airway, breathing and circulation. Notify the provider and blood bank. Do not automatically restart for fever or hives: serious causes must be excluded and restart authorized under local policy. Source

Definition & key points Most common; reaction to donor WBCs. Temp rises ≥1°F (0.5°C) over baseline; no flank pain, hemoglobinuria, or doom, and normal BUN/creatinine . Stop, call provider, Tylenol; may restart slowly (still within 4 hr of the original start).
Definition & key points Hives, itching, flushing. Common after many transfusions; may premedicate with Benadryl + Tylenol . Mild: may restart slowly. Severe/anaphylaxis: epinephrine.
Definition & key points Transfusion-associated circulatory overload (too fast or too much). HTN , SOB, crackles, JVD, edema. No saline! Sit upright, O2, diuretics (sometimes morphine), KVO line.

entries.h: Clinical side note · TACO: avoid adding a fluid load
entries.t: Stop the transfusion, sit the patient upright, support oxygenation and administer prescribed diuretics. Maintain necessary IV access according to policy; “no saline” is not an instruction to remove IV access. Source
Definition & key points "Keep vein open": very slow rate (~5 mL/hr) to keep IV access

Definition & key points Transfusion-related acute lung injury (donor antibodies in the lungs). Sudden respiratory distress within 6 hr, SpO2 < 90%, hypotension , infiltrates on X-ray , no fluid overload signs . O2/intubation, possibly fluids/pressors. Never restart.

entries.h: Clinical side note · TRALI also causes wet lungs
entries.t: TRALI causes noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. Crackles or pulmonary edema do not by themselves distinguish it from TACO. Respiratory support is central; routine diuresis is not the treatment for TRALI. Source
Definition & key points Contaminated product: high fever, chills, hypotension, shock. Stop, blood cultures , antibiotics , IV fluids. Never restart.
Definition & key points Hemolytic, TRALI, bacterial

Definition & key points Kidney hormone (given SubQ) that stimulates the marrow to make RBCs. For chronic anemia (CKD, chemo, patients who refuse blood). Not for an acute bleed. Monitor CBC/Hgb (don't rise too fast) and BP (HTN, clot risk); needs adequate iron.
Definition & key points Abnormal growth of cells
Definition & key points Stays in one place and doesn't spread (e.g., basal cell skin cancer is often just removed)
Definition & key points Invades tissue and can spread
Definition & key points Spread to distant organs (bone and brain are often the "final stop")
Definition & key points Cancer-causing substance ("anything can cause cancer")
Definition & key points Lung cancer (men and women; vaping counts)
Definition & key points Men: lung, prostate, colorectal. Women: lung, breast, colorectal.

Definition & key points Warning signs: C hange in bowel/bladder, A sore that doesn't heal, U nusual bleeding/discharge, T hickening/lump, I ndigestion/trouble swallowing, O bvious change in a wart/mole, N agging cough/hoarseness, U nexplained weight LOSS (not gain), P ernicious anemia (new B12 deficiency → think GI cancer)

Definition & key points T cells, B cells, NK cells, and lymphokines find and kill malignant cells. Fails through loss of recognition (self vs. non-self), cancer cells hiding, or suppressor T cells turning the response down.
Definition & key points Cancer of epithelial tissue: skin, GI lining, lung, breast, prostate
Definition & key points Cancer of connective/supportive tissue: bone, cartilage, muscle
Definition & key points Bone marrow / lymphocytes / plasma cells

Definition & key points Prevent cancer from developing: avoid carcinogens, sunscreen, diet/exercise, no smoking/drinking, immunizations (HPV vaccine) , chemoprevention (aspirin/celecoxib → colon; vitamin D/tamoxifen → breast)
Definition & key points Using drugs/substances to block cancer from developing
Definition & key points Screening to catch cancer early: Pap (21+, every 3 yr), mammogram (~40–45+), colonoscopy (~45+), prostate exam/PSA (~50+), annual fecal occult blood test, self-exams
Definition & key points Already have cancer: prevent metastasis /complications
Definition & key points Blood tests suggesting some cancers (PSA = prostate-specific antigen)
Definition & key points Tissue sample to confirm cancer and determine stage and grade

Definition & key points The provider delivers a diagnosis or scan results; refer the patient to them. Routine lab trends (e.g., WBC during pneumonia) are OK to share. Treatment starts only after diagnosis, staging, and grading.
Definition & key points How far it has spread. T = tumor size, N = lymph Node involvement, M = Metastasis. Stage 0 (in situ) to 4 (metastatic); higher is worse.
Definition & key points Stage 0: non-invasive, still in place
Definition & key points What the cells look like under a microscope (differentiation), Grade 1–4. Higher is worse.
Definition & key points How much tumor cells still look and act like their tissue of origin
Definition & key points Resembles normal tissue (Grade 1); better
Definition & key points Doesn't resemble normal tissue (Grade 3–4); fast spread, poor prognosis
Definition & key points Complete eradication
Definition & key points Prolong survival and contain spread (remission)
Definition & key points Relieve symptoms and improve quality of life; not seeking a cure
Definition & key points Cancer signs reduced or gone (may return)
Definition & key points The most frequently used, "ideal" cancer treatment
Definition & key points Skin sample / part of the tumor / whole tumor / aspiration of a tumor near the surface
Definition & key points Mass + small margin vs. tumor + surrounding tissue (to get all the "roots")
Definition & key points Removing high-risk tissue before cancer develops (e.g., mastectomy with family history)
Definition & key points Relieve symptoms, not cure (e.g., remove a tumor pressing on the lungs to ease SOB)
Definition & key points Restore function or appearance (e.g., breast implants)
Definition & key points Treatment given before the main treatment to shrink the tumor
Definition & key points Radiation affects only tissue in the treatment field
Definition & key points Most common; daily doses over weeks. The patient is NOT radioactive. The skin is marked with a tattoo; don't wash it off. Avoid sun 10 am–3 pm.

Definition & key points Seeds/implant placed in or next to the tumor (cervical, uterine, prostate, breast). The patient and body fluids ARE radioactive. Temporary = stays in the hospital for a few days, then the implant is removed. Permanent = goes home; radioactivity fades over months.

Definition & key points Radiation sign, private room with the door closed, lead apron + thyroid shield , dosimeter badge (on the outside of the apron), cluster care , rotate caregivers , no pregnant nurses , encourage self-care, patient stays in the room, linens and dressings stay in the room until discharge. Dislodged implant: don't touch it — use long-handled tongs to put it in a lead container. Visitors: 30 min max, 6 ft away, no pregnant visitors or kids.
Definition & key points Badge that measures a worker's radiation exposure (read about monthly)

Definition & key points Flush twice with the lid down, strain urine 7–10 days , sleep apart, no sex, wash laundry separately (then run an empty cycle), don't share utensils, no heavy lifting or straining (can push seeds out)

Definition & key points Usually localized and starts within about 2 weeks ; mimics chemo effects (fatigue, mouth sores, alopecia, cracked lips, pancytopenia, N/V/D) plus skin burns → impaired wound healing → infection

Definition & key points Drugs that kill rapidly dividing cells (cancer and healthy cells). Universal effect: pancytopenia . Most often IV through a central line or port. Methotrexate is a chemo drug also used for autoimmune disease. Requires a chemo-certified nurse.
Definition & key points Check the platelets on the CBC
Definition & key points Surgically placed central access; accessed with a Huber needle at 90°
Definition & key points Always pull back for blood return before and during chemo through a central line or port
Definition & key points Leakage of the drug from the vein into surrounding tissue
Definition & key points Drug that causes tissue damage and necrosis if it leaks; never give peripherally
Definition & key points Stop the infusion → notify the provider → give the antidote SubQ/intradermally at the site (if one exists). Prevention: check patency.

Definition & key points Purple chemo gloves , long-sleeved disposable gown, face shield , chemo waste containers, chemo sign. Patient waste is hazardous too (wear PPE when emptying a Foley). Staff exposure → N/V, skin/eye irritation, nasal ulcers, reproductive problems .
Definition & key points Some drugs (e.g., doxorubicin) have a maximum lifetime dose; exceeding it → cardiopulmonary toxicity

Definition & key points Chemo-induced nausea/vomiting: the most common side effect. Antiemetics (ondansetron/Zofran) before and after, bland diet, small frequent meals, stop fluids 1 hr before treatment , cold or room-temperature foods (avoid odors), high protein, plastic utensils for metallic taste, food diary
Definition & key points Megestrol (Megace) ; steroids are a last resort

Definition & key points Inflamed, painful, cracked, bleeding mouth sores (swollen gums/tongue/lips = stomatitis, not anaphylaxis). Care: frequent mouth checks; non-alcohol rinses ( magic mouthwash = lidocaine + diphenhydramine, salt water/0.9% NaCl, baking soda); no lemon-glycerin swabs ; topical anesthetic before meals; soft, bland, cool foods; avoid salty, spicy, acidic, or crunchy food; straw ; 2 L water/day; moist lips; gentle brushing, no flossing

Definition & key points Hair loss ~7–10 days after starting; regrows ~1 month after treatment. Cold cap constricts follicles so less chemo reaches the scalp ( contraindicated in brain cancer ). Use a hat or sunscreen on the scalp.
Definition & key points Pancytopenia from chemo

Definition & key points The most significant adverse effect (infection kills first). Precautions at ANC ≤ 1,000: private positive-pressure room, hand hygiene, dedicated equipment, limit/screen visitors, no fresh flowers/plants/fresh fruit , mask during transport, daily dressing changes, clean room, clean toothbrush daily (dishwasher), no rectal temps, temp checks, report fever immediately
Definition & key points Platelets < 50,000 → bleeding precautions; assess petechiae/purpura, epistaxis, stool for occult blood ; stool softeners
Definition & key points Monitor fatigue and Hgb/Hct, assess dizziness and orthostatic hypotension , O2, rest, EPO or transfusion (Hgb < 7)

Definition & key points Infection words → neutropenia. Bleeding words → thrombocytopenia. Fatigue/dizziness/Hgb → anemia. Minimizing IV sticks applies to both neutropenia and thrombocytopenia; limiting visitors and dedicated equipment apply to neutropenia and brachytherapy.
Definition & key points Cognitive impairment: trouble concentrating, learning, and remembering. Teach puzzles, reading, repeating challenging tasks; avoid alcohol/drugs.
Definition & key points Monitor EF with an echo (healthy 50–70%); watch for HF (SOB, crackles = left-sided; edema = right-sided) and pneumonia
Definition & key points Possible sterility; use birth control during chemo; consider freezing eggs/sperm beforehand

Definition & key points Chemo-induced peripheral neuropathy: numbness/tingling ( early sign ), burning, starts in fingers and toes and moves up symmetrically; orthostatic hypotension. Teach daily foot checks , supportive closed-toe shoes, protect from burns.
Definition & key points Not relieved by rest. Alternate rest and activity, light exercise (walking) , don't stay in bed all day , good nutrition.
Definition & key points Pain → anxiety → fear → more pain (the pain cycle). Give meds on a schedule (opioids for moderate/severe, nonopioids for mild); add non-drug methods.
Definition & key points Hgb/WBC/platelets rising to normal, better energy and appetite, fewer sores, fewer bleeding episodes
Definition & key points Replaces diseased marrow with healthy stem cells by IV (after chemo wipes out the marrow). Used in leukemia, aplastic anemia, myeloma, and some lymphomas. Does NOT mean cured.
Definition & key points Patient's own stem cells
Definition & key points Donor stem cells (often family)
Definition & key points Identical twin donor

Definition & key points ~ 8–10 days after transplant while the new cells "take"; the most critical time. Highest risk of sepsis and bleeding ; patients need antibiotics, transfusions, immunosuppressants.
Definition & key points Donor cells attack the recipient ; happens with allogeneic transplants; acute or chronic; morbidity/mortality in 30–50%; treated with steroids/immunosuppressants
Definition & key points The recipient's body attacks the graft; prevented with immunosuppressants (↑ infection risk)
Definition & key points Uses the immune system to fight cancer (stimulates or suppresses it), e.g., monoclonal antibodies
Definition & key points Hits specific cancer cells while sparing normal cells → fewer side effects (e.g., monoclonal antibodies, TKIs)
Definition & key points e.g., the HPV vaccine prevents cervical and other HPV cancers

Definition & key points Tumor (lung/breast) compresses the SVC → blood backs up in the head and upper body. S/S: facial/neck edema, purple/red face, JVD, distended chest veins , dyspnea, epistaxis , cerebral edema if severe; systemic BP low . Order of care: sit up (High-Fowler's) → O2 (prepare for intubation) → high-dose IV steroids → one-time high-dose radiation → surgery if that fails.

Definition & key points Chemo rapidly kills cells, which burst and dump their contents → AKI and dysrhythmias . Labs: ↑ K⁺, ↑ phosphorus, ↑ uric acid, ↓ calcium ("3 up, 1 down"). S/S: flank pain, ↑ BUN/creatinine, muscle cramps/weakness, seizures , mental status changes (from low Ca), GI distress, gout. Priority: IV fluids (prehydrate before chemo). Then allopurinol , diuretics, for high K⁺: IV insulin + D50 (fast) or sodium polystyrene (Kayexalate); dialysis if severe; cardiac monitor.

Definition & key points Metastatic tumor presses on the cord. Back pain first , then weakness, numbness/tingling, ↓ DTRs, bowel/bladder incontinence → paralysis. Care: high-dose corticosteroids → emergency radiation → surgery ; frequent neuro checks.

Definition & key points Bone metastasis or myeloma; tumors release a PTH-like hormone → ↑ Ca. " Bones (pain, fractures), stones (kidney), groans (N/V, constipation, ileus), psychiatric overtones (confusion, lethargy, depression)." Treatment: fluids 2–4 L/day, IV NS, loop diuretics, steroids, calcitonin/bisphosphonates.

Definition & key points Specialty focused on comfort and quality of life (symptoms plus psychosocial and spiritual needs). Can be given alongside curative treatment or within hospice; inpatient, outpatient, or home. Goal: prevent and relieve suffering. Doesn't replace treatment.

Definition & key points End-of-life comfort, not cure . Requires a terminal illness and a physician certifying ≤ 6 months to live. Living longer doesn't mean discharge; eligibility is re-evaluated (about every 90 days) and extended. The patient can leave anytime and restart treatment. Patient + family = the unit of care (includes bereavement support). Settings: home, hospital, hospice facility, nursing home, assisted living.

Definition & key points Maintenance meds stopped; only the hospice MD and nurse follow the patient. Morphine/fentanyl for pain; morphine + anxiolytics (lorazepam/Ativan, Xanax) for dyspnea. O2 at ~2 L for comfort only. Generally no antibiotics for pneumonia. Comfort-focused chemo or radiation can still be used to relieve symptoms.
Definition & key points Do not resuscitate; the patient's wishes guide care (family conflict is common)

DISC — sickle cell crisis triggers: Dehydration, Infection, Stress/cold, ↓ O2/altitude RANDI — bleeding precautions: Razor, Avoid ASA/NSAIDs, Needles small, Decrease sticks, Injury (Old) CRAB — multiple myeloma: Calcium ↑, Renal failure, Anemia, Bone lesions B symptoms — fever, night sweats, weight loss CAUTION UP — cancer warning signs TNM — Tumor size, Nodes, Metastasis TLS: 3 up, 1 down — K⁺, phosphorus, uric acid ↑; calcium ↓ Bones, stones, groans, psychiatric overtones — hypercalcemia RICE — Rest, Ice,

Compression (priority if bleeding), Elevation Never restart: hemolytic, TRALI, bacterial. No saline: TACO. NCJMM steps — Recognize cues → Analyze cues → Prioritize hypotheses → Generate solutions → Take action → Evaluate outcomes
The same mnemonics, plus the abbreviations used in this guide, with each letter spelled out.

TACO = fluid overload from a transfusion T = Transfusion A = Associated C = Circulatory O = Overload In plain words: too much blood went in too fast, so fluid backs up into the lungs. BP goes UP → give diuretics, no saline. TRALI = lung injury from a transfusion T = Transfusion R = Related A = Acute (sudden) L = Lung I = Injury In plain words: antibodies in the donor's blood attack the patient's lungs. BP goes DOWN → airway support; never restart. Never restart: hemolytic, TRALI, bacterial. No saline: TACO.

DISC = what triggers a sickle cell crisis D = Dehydration I = Infection S = Stress C = Cold Also: low oxygen / high altitude (the student's guide lists it with DISC) RANDI = bleeding precautions when platelets are low R = electric Razor only A = Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs (ibuprofen-type pain meds) N = small Needles D = Decrease needle sticks and IM shots I = protect from Injury RICE = for a hemophilia joint bleed R = Rest I = Ice C = Compression (the priority if it's actively bleeding) E = Elevation DIC = clotting,

then bleeding, everywhere D = Disseminated (spread all over the body) I = Intravascular (inside the blood vessels) C = Coagulation (clotting) HIT = heparin destroying platelets H = Heparin I = Induced (caused by) T = Thrombocytopenia (low platelets) ANC = how many infection-fighting cells the patient has A = Absolute N = Neutrophil C = Count

(Old) CRAB = multiple myeloma (usually an older person) C = Calcium is high (it leaks out of the bones) R = Renal failure (renal = kidney) A = Anemia B = Bone pain and bone lesions (holes in the bones) ALL = the childhood leukemia A = Acute (comes on fast) L = Lymphocytic (affects lymphocytes, a type of WBC) L = Leukemia B symptoms = 3 signs seen in lymphoma and leukemia (not an acronym; just remember the 3) Fever Night sweats Weight loss

CAUTION UP = cancer warning signs C = Change in bowel or bladder habits A = A sore that doesn't heal U = Unusual bleeding or discharge T = Thickening or a lump (breast, testicle, anywhere) I = Indigestion or trouble swallowing O = Obvious change in a wart or mole N = Nagging cough or hoarseness U = Unexplained weight LOSS P = Pernicious anemia (new B12 deficiency, which can mean a GI cancer) TNM = how cancer is staged (how far it has spread) T = Tumor size N = lymph Nodes involved M = Metastasis (spread to other
organs)

SVC syndrome = a tumor squeezing the big vein S = Superior (upper) V = Vena C = Cava (together: the big vein bringing blood from the head and arms back to the heart) TLS = tumor lysis syndrome (cancer cells bursting after chemo) T = Tumor L = Lysis (bursting) S = Syndrome Labs: 3 up, 1 down . Potassium ↑, phosphorus ↑, uric acid ↑; calcium ↓. Bones, stones, groans, psychiatric overtones = high calcium Bones = bone pain, fractures Stones = kidney stones Groans = stomach pain, nausea, constipation Psychiatric
overtones = confusion, tiredness, depression

GVHD = a stem cell transplant complication G = Graft (the donor cells) V = Versus (attacking) H = Host (the patient) D = Disease Time, Distance, Shielding = brachytherapy (radioactive seed) safety Time = spend as little time in the room as possible (cluster care, 30-min visits, rotate nurses) Distance = stay 6 ft away Shielding = lead apron, thyroid shield, dosimeter badge NCJMM = the clinical judgment model your exam questions follow N = Nursing C = Clinical J = Judgment M = Measurement M = Model Its 6 steps, in
order: Recognize cues Analyze cues Prioritize hypotheses Generate solutions Take action Evaluate outcomes
Professor Halecka told you twice to chart these side by side, because most of the symptoms overlap. Focus on the column that sets each one apart.

What's wrong Not enough iron (GI bleed #1) Key labs ↓ ferritin, ↑ TIBC, microcytic Sets it apart Pica, angular cheilitis; black stools on iron are expected Treatment PO iron + vitamin C between meals ; IV iron if PO fails Wrong-answer trap Transfusion is not the fix

What's wrong No intrinsic factor → can't absorb B12 Key labs Macrocytic (↑ MCV), ↓ B12 Sets it apart Neuro symptoms (paresthesia, gait, confusion) Treatment Lifelong injections Wrong-answer trap Never switch to pills; iron is irrelevant
What's wrong Poor diet, alcohol, pregnancy Key labs Macrocytic , ↓ folate Sets it apart No neuro symptoms Treatment PO folic acid Wrong-answer trap —

What's wrong Marrow stem cells fail; not cancer Key labs Pancytopenia , empty marrow on biopsy Sets it apart Infections + bleeding + anemia Treatment Stem cell transplant + immunosuppressants Wrong-answer trap Supplements do nothing

What's wrong Genetic; RBCs sickle and clump Key labs Hgb electrophoresis Sets it apart Pain + jaundice (no other anemia has these) Treatment Fluids first , pain meds, O2, treat the cause; hydroxyurea long-term Wrong-answer trap Don't ambulate in crisis; no iron/B12

What's wrong Cancer ; too MANY RBCs Key labs ↑ Hgb/Hct/RBCs Sets it apart Ruddy face , itching after a hot shower, HTN, clots Treatment Phlebotomy , fluids, aspirin Wrong-answer trap No iron; no warm compresses

Cells Immature WBCs crowd the marrow Who ALL = kids; others = older adults Sets it apart WBC high but doesn't work → pancytopenia ; diagnose with bone marrow biopsy Goal / treatment Chemo → stem cell transplant. Answer generally; don't panic over subtypes.
Cells Lymphocytes Who Young adults (and >60) Sets it apart Reed-Sternberg cells , painless neck node, orderly spread Goal / treatment Cure (~92–94%)
Cells B/T cells Who Older adults, men Sets it apart Random spread, found late, B symptoms Goal / treatment Remission ; watch for TLS

Cells Plasma cells Who Older adults Sets it apart Bone pain + ↑ calcium , lytic lesions, kidney failure ( CRAB ) Goal / treatment No cure; fluids, bisphosphonates, calcitonin, fall precautions; no calcium

Problem Missing Factor VIII (A) or IX (B); X-linked Platelets Normal Other labs ↑ PTT , normal INR Bleeding pattern Deep : joints, head Priority Replace the factor before and after procedures; compression if bleeding
Problem Missing vWF; men and women Platelets Normal Other labs — Bleeding pattern Superficial : nose, gums, heavy periods Priority Desmopressin (DDAVP) / vWF

Problem Secondary to sepsis, trauma, OB Platelets ↓ Other labs ↓ fibrinogen; ↑ PT/PTT/INR, ↑ D-dimer Bleeding pattern Clots and bleeds everywhere Priority Treat the cause → fluids + heparin → blood products
Problem Autoimmune destruction of platelets Platelets ↓ Other labs — Bleeding pattern Petechiae, bruising Priority Steroids or splenectomy
Problem Immune reaction to heparin Platelets ↓ while on heparin Other labs — Bleeding pattern Clotting Priority Stop heparin , call the provider
Clue that sets it apart Flank pain, hemoglobinuria, impending doom , ↑ BUN/Cr BP ↓ Action Stop; NS on new tubing; rapid response; send blood + urine Restart? Never
Clue that sets it apart Fever ≥1°F above baseline only ; normal BUN/Cr BP ~Normal Action Stop, call provider, Tylenol Restart? Yes, slowly (within 4 hr of the original start)
Clue that sets it apart Hives, itching , flushing BP Normal (↓ if anaphylaxis) Action Benadryl (epinephrine if severe); premedicate next time Restart? Yes, slowly, if mild
Clue that sets it apart Crackles, JVD, edema , SOB BP ↑ Action Sit up, O2, diuretics , NO saline Restart? Not specified in lecture
Clue that sets it apart Sudden respiratory distress, infiltrates on X-ray, NO fluid overload BP ↓ Action O2, intubation Restart? Never
Clue that sets it apart High fever, chills, shock BP ↓ Action Blood cultures , antibiotics, fluids Restart? Never

entries.h: Pancytopenia: which low cell line is the question about?

entries.t: Risk Infection (kills first) Sign on door / treat Neutropenic at ANC < 2,000; sign at ≤ 1,000 Nursing actions that match Positive-pressure private room, no fresh flowers/fruit, limit visitors, dedicated equipment, mask during transport, daily dressing changes, clean room, report fever → antibiotics

Risk Bleeding Sign on door / treat Sign at < 50,000 ; transfuse ~20,000 Nursing actions that match RANDI, no IM injections/rectal temps/enemas, stool softeners, check stool for occult blood, watch for epistaxis, petechiae/purpura, pressure 5–10 min

Risk ↓ O2 Sign on door / treat Transfuse at Hgb < 7 Nursing actions that match Monitor fatigue, check Hgb/Hct, dizziness/orthostatic hypotension , O2, rest, EPO Minimizing IV sticks applies to both WBC and platelets. Limiting visitors and dedicated equipment apply to both neutropenia and brachytherapy.
Cause Tumor presses on the SVC (lung/breast) Key S/S Purple, swollen face/neck, JVD , epistaxis, dyspnea; systemic BP ↓ Order of care Sit up O2/airway IV steroids one-time radiation surgery

Cause Cells burst after chemo Key S/S ↑ K, ↑ phos, ↑ uric acid, ↓ Ca ; flank pain, cramps, seizures, AKI, dysrhythmias Order of care IV fluids first allopurinol, diuretics, insulin + D50 for K dialysis
Cause Metastasis presses on the cord Key S/S Back pain first → weakness, numbness, bowel/bladder loss Order of care Steroids radiation surgery neuro checks
Cause Bone metastasis / myeloma Key S/S Bones, stones, groans, psychiatric overtones Order of care Fluids, IV NS, loop diuretics, steroids, calcitonin/bisphosphonates
External radiation No Brachytherapy (internal) Yes , including body fluids Chemo Drug in their waste
External radiation None needed Brachytherapy (internal) Lead apron + thyroid shield + dosimeter , cluster care, rotate staff, no pregnant nurses Chemo Purple gloves, gown, face shield
External radiation — Brachytherapy (internal) Radiation sign Chemo Chemo sign

External radiation Don't wash off the tattoo; no sun 10 am–3 pm Brachytherapy (internal) Tongs if a seed falls out; strain urine 7–10 days; no heavy lifting Chemo Check blood return; extravasation → stop, antidote SubQ at the site

Professor Halecka's exams are about spotting what's going on and choosing what to do first . This section pulls those answers together in plain English. Medical terms and abbreviations have their meaning in parentheses. To study it, cover the right-hand column, say the answer out loud, then check.

entries.h: The 7 rules that answer most questions
entries.t: Treat the cause first. A transfusion (giving blood) is just a band-aid. For example, DIC (the body clotting and then bleeding everywhere) caused by sepsis (an overwhelming infection in the blood) → give antibiotics. A sickle cell crisis triggered by an infection → give antibiotics. Infection kills first. When all the blood counts are low, infection is more dangerous than bleeding or anemia (low red blood cells), unless the patient is actively bleeding right now. A fever in a cancer patient or a patient with low

entries.h: The 7 rules that answer most questions
entries.t: WBCs (white blood cells, which fight infection) = call the provider for antibiotics. Not Tylenol. Not putting the precautions sign on the door. When in doubt, fluids. Sickle cell crisis, polycythemia vera (too many red blood cells), tumor lysis syndrome (cancer cells bursting after chemo), high calcium, multiple myeloma (a bone marrow cancer): fluids are the first move. The one exception: TACO (fluid overload from a transfusion) gets diuretics (water pills that make you pee out fluid), NOT saline. Low platelets

entries.h: The 7 rules that answer most questions
entries.t: (the cells that plug leaks and stop bleeding) = nothing that pokes, scrapes, or strains. No IM shots (injections into the muscle), no rectal temps, no razors, no flossing, no straining on the toilet. Expected vs. emergency. An enlarged spleen (the organ under your left ribs that filters old blood cells) is expected in sickle cell, polycythemia vera, and leukemia. A ruptured spleen (BP, or blood pressure, dropping; pain in the left shoulder) is the emergency. Read what the question is actually asking. Several

entries.h: The 7 rules that answer most questions
entries.t: answers may be true. Pick the one that answers this question.

entries.h: If you see THIS → think THAT
Craving ice or dirt (pica), cracked corners of the mouth
entries.t: Think… Iron deficiency
Think… B12 (pernicious) anemia

entries.h: Gastric bypass, stomach surgery, Crohn's (an inflammatory bowel disease), vegan
entries.t: Think… B12 deficiency (the gut can't absorb B12, or the diet doesn't have it)

entries.h: Anemia + pain + jaundice (yellow skin/eyes from broken-down red cells)
entries.t: Think… Sickle cell

entries.h: Red face, itchy after a hot shower, high Hgb (hemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying part of red cells), clots
entries.t: Think… Polycythemia vera

entries.h: All counts low, not cancer, bone marrow "empty"
entries.t: Think… Aplastic anemia

entries.h: WBC count high, but frequent infections + bruising
entries.t: Think… Leukemia

entries.h: Child with bruising, bone pain, always sick
entries.t: Think… ALL (acute lymphocytic leukemia, the childhood leukemia)

entries.h: Painless lump in the neck, young adult, "Reed-Sternberg cells" (abnormal cells with two nuclei seen on biopsy)
entries.t: Think… Hodgkin lymphoma

entries.h: Older adult, bone pain + high calcium
entries.t: Think… Multiple myeloma

entries.h: Male, deep bleeding into joints, platelets normal, PTT high (PTT = a test of how long blood takes to clot)
entries.t: Think… Hemophilia

entries.h: Nosebleeds, bleeding gums, heavy periods; men or women
entries.t: Think… von Willebrand disease

entries.h: Bleeding from IV sites + clotting at the same time, patient is septic (has sepsis)
entries.t: Think… DIC

entries.h: Platelets dropping while on heparin (an IV blood thinner)
entries.t: Think… HIT (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia: the heparin is destroying platelets) → stop heparin

entries.h: PTT of 106 on a heparin drip, platelets fine
entries.t: Reference range: Platelets: 150,000–400,000/µL. aPTT: approximately 25–35 seconds without anticoagulation; treatment targets follow the ordered protocol. Use the laboratory’s stated range. Think… Just adjust the drip per protocol; not an emergency

entries.h: During a transfusion: flank pain (pain in the side/back over the kidneys), blood in the urine, "I feel like I'm dying"
entries.t: Think… Hemolytic reaction (wrong blood type; the patient's body bursts the donor red cells)
Think… Febrile reaction (febrile = fever)
Think… Allergic reaction

entries.h: During a transfusion: high BP, crackles in the lungs, JVD (jugular vein distention: bulging neck veins)
entries.t: Think… TACO (transfusion-associated circulatory overload: too much fluid)

entries.h: During a transfusion: can't breathe, low BP, infiltrates on X-ray (white, cloudy areas in the lungs), no fluid overload
entries.t: Think… TRALI (transfusion-related acute lung injury: donor antibodies attack the lungs)

entries.h: During a transfusion: high fever + shock
entries.t: Think… Bacterial (septic) reaction (the blood bag was contaminated)

entries.h: Purple, swollen face and neck, JVD, nosebleed in a lung or breast cancer patient
entries.t: Think… SVC syndrome (a tumor squeezes the superior vena cava, the big vein that drains the head and arms)

entries.h: Right after chemo: high K (potassium), high phos (phosphorus), high uric acid, low Ca (calcium), flank pain
entries.t: Think… Tumor lysis syndrome

entries.h: Cancer patient, new back pain → weak legs, incontinence (can't control bladder/bowels)

entries.h: Part 1: The 7 rules that answer most questions
entries.t: Treat the cause first. A transfusion (giving blood) is just a band-aid. For example, DIC (the body clotting and then bleeding everywhere) caused by sepsis (an overwhelming infection in the blood) → give antibiotics. A sickle cell crisis triggered by an infection → give antibiotics. ABO compatibility chart: which FFP or red cells can this patient receive? ↗ Infection kills first. When all the blood counts are low, infection is more dangerous than bleeding or anemia (low red blood cells), unless the patient is

entries.h: Part 4: Every topic in plain words
entries.t: Each topic answers three questions: What is it? (in everyday words) · Remember it by (a hook) · Do this (the nursing action).

Your blood has 3 kinds of cells, each with one job. RBCs (red blood cells) carry oxygen. Hgb (hemoglobin) is the part that actually holds the oxygen. WBCs (white blood cells) fight infection. Neutrophils are the main infection-fighting WBC. Platelets plug leaks so you stop bleeding. They're all made in the bone marrow (the soft "factory" inside your bones). Pancytopenia = all 3 are low. So think: tired (RBCs), infections (WBCs), bleeding (platelets). Anemia = not enough working RBCs or Hgb → tired, pale, short of

breath, dizzy. Thrombocytopenia = low platelets. Neutropenia = low neutrophils. ANC (absolute neutrophil count) = how many infection fighters the patient actually has. MCV = the size of the red cells. Small = iron problem. Big = B12/folate problem. (" Mega loblastic" = mega = big.) Ferritin = your iron savings account. Low ferritin = iron deficiency. Petechiae = tiny red pinpoint dots under the skin (small bleeds). Purpura = bigger purple patches (worse bleeding).

What is it? Not enough iron to build red cells; usually from slow bleeding (GI tract, heavy periods) Remember it by "Pica and the cracked mouth" : craving ice or dirt, cracks at the corners of the mouth Do this Iron pills between meals + orange juice (vitamin C helps absorption); no milk/antacids with it; black stools are normal

What is it? The stomach is missing intrinsic factor (a protein the stomach makes so the gut can absorb B12) Remember it by B12 = Brain. It's the only anemia with nerve symptoms (tingling, balance problems, confusion). Do this Shots for life. Pills won't work because the gut can't absorb them.
What is it? Not enough folate, a B vitamin (from poor diet, alcohol, pregnancy) Remember it by Like B12 but no nerve symptoms Do this Folic acid pills

What is it? The bone marrow "factory" shuts down. Not cancer. Remember it by A-plastic = no factory. All 3 counts drop. Do this Stem cell transplant (new marrow cells from a donor); protect from infection and bleeding

What is it? Genetic; red cells bend into crescent shapes, jam the blood vessels, and break apart early Remember it by The only anemia with pain + jaundice (yellow skin) Do this Fluids first (thin the blood so cells stop jamming), then pain meds, O2, bed rest; avoid cold, dehydration, high altitude Polycythemia vera is the opposite of anemia: the marrow makes too many red cells, so the blood gets thick like syrup → clots. It is a cancer. Hook: red face, itchy after a hot shower. Do: take blood out (phlebotomy, like
donating blood, but it's thrown away), fluids, aspirin.

Leukemia = the marrow floods with baby (immature) WBCs that don't work. The WBC count looks high, but the patient keeps getting infections, because the cells are useless and they crowd out the RBCs and platelets. Treat it like pancytopenia. On the test, don't worry about which letters (AML, CLL…); answer the general way. ALL (acute lymphocytic leukemia) is the kids' leukemia , with a good prognosis (expected outcome). Lymphoma = cancer of the lymph nodes (the infection-filtering glands in your neck, armpits, and

groin). Hodgkin = the "good" one: young people, painless neck lump, spreads in order from one node to the next, curable , Reed-Sternberg cells on biopsy. Non-Hodgkin = the messy one: older people, spreads randomly, found late, aim for remission (cancer under control, though it may come back). Multiple myeloma = cancer of plasma cells (antibody-making cells) that eats bone. Calcium leaks out of the bones into the blood and clogs the kidneys. Hook: "Old CRAB" : older person with high C alcium, R enal (kidney)
failure, A nemia, B one pain. Do: fluids, fall precautions (bones break easily), bone meds. Never give calcium.

Low platelets (thrombocytopenia): bruises and petechiae. Bleeding precautions sign at < 50,000 . Hook: RANDI (electric Razor, Avoid aspirin, small Needles, Decrease sticks, protect from Injury). Hemophilia = missing a clotting factor (one of the proteins the blood needs to form a clot). Boys, genetic. Platelets are normal . Bleeds go deep (into joints, the head). Do: give the missing factor; any head bump = CT scan; no contact sports. von Willebrand disease = hemophilia's milder cousin: men and women, surface

bleeding (nose, gums, heavy periods). Do: desmopressin (DDAVP, a medication that boosts the missing clotting protein). DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation) = "clot everywhere, then bleed everywhere." The name breaks down as: disseminated = all over the body, intravascular = inside the blood vessels, coagulation = clotting. What happens, step by step: Something huge triggers it, usually sepsis (an overwhelming infection in the bloodstream). Trauma, burns, shock, and childbirth emergencies can also do it. The

body goes into emergency mode and flips the "clot" switch everywhere at once, so tiny clots form in vessels all over the body. Those tiny clots block blood flow, and organs like the kidneys, brain, and lungs start getting damaged. Making all those clots uses up the platelets and clotting proteins (like fibrinogen). Nothing is left to stop bleeding, so the patient bleeds from everywhere : IV sites, gums, nose, urine, stool, internally. Analogy: a town has a limited supply of sandbags. A false alarm makes everyone

dump sandbags on every street. The roads get blocked (clots cut off the organs), and when a real leak happens, there are no sandbags left (bleeding). Labs: platelets and fibrinogen down (used up). PT, PTT, INR up (these measure how long blood takes to clot, and it takes longer because the supplies are gone). D-dimer up (clot breakdown pieces). Do: fix the cause first (antibiotics for sepsis) → fluids + heparin (stops new clots from using up even more supplies) → blood products last (to restock the supplies). HIT

(heparin-induced thrombocytopenia) = the heparin is wrecking the platelets. The body has an immune reaction to heparin that destroys platelets. Platelets drop while on heparin → stop the heparin. Heparin vs. warfarin (two blood thinners): H eparin (IV or shot, works fast) → check PT T (therapeutic, or target, range 60–80 seconds) → antidote P rotamine. Hook: "HPTT-P." W arfarin (Coumadin, a pill for long-term use) → check INR (therapeutic 2–3) → antidote vitamin K . Hook: "Warfarin and K go together."

Setup: take vitals before the blood arrives → Y-tubing (tubing shaped like a Y so saline and blood share one line) with normal saline only → stay with the patient for the first 15 min (most reactions happen then) → finish within 4 hr . Every reaction starts the same way: STOP the blood , run saline on new tubing (the old tubing still has blood in it), stay with the patient, call for help.

entries.h: Then tell the reactions apart by their one clue:
entries.t: Hemolytic (wrong blood type; the body bursts the donor's red cells): flank pain + blood in the urine + "I'm going to die" → never restart Febrile (a reaction to the donor's white cells): just a fever → Tylenol; can restart slowly

entries.h: Clinical side note · A transfusion reaction needs clinical review
entries.t: Stop the transfusion and assess airway, breathing and circulation. Notify the provider and blood bank. Do not automatically restart for fever or hives: serious causes must be excluded and restart authorized under local policy. Source Allergic: itchy hives → Benadryl; can restart slowly if mild TACO (too much fluid, too fast; the heart can't keep up): high BP + wet lungs (crackles) → diuretics, no saline TRALI (donor antibodies injure the lungs): can't breathe + low BP , but the lungs aren't "wet" with fluid →

entries.h: Clinical side note · A transfusion reaction needs clinical review
entries.t: airway support; never restart Bacterial (the blood bag was contaminated): high fever + shock → blood cultures (tests to find bacteria in the blood) + antibiotics; never restart EPO (erythropoietin, a hormone shot that tells the marrow to make more red cells) works slowly. It's for long-term anemia (kidney disease, chemo), not an emergency bleed. Watch BP and Hgb.
Benign = stays put, doesn't spread. Malignant = invades and spreads. Metastasis = cancer that has spread to other organs.
Primary = don't get it (sunscreen, vaccines, no smoking) Secondary = screen for it to catch it early (Pap smear, mammogram, colonoscopy) Tertiary = already have it; stop it from spreading

Staging = how far it has SPREAD. TNM: Tumor size, lymph Nodes involved, Metastasis. Stages 0–4. Grading = how WEIRD the cells look under the microscope (1 = still look normal, 4 = unrecognizable). Higher is worse for both. Warning signs: CAUTION UP. The big one: unexplained weight LOSS , not gain. Scope of practice: the provider tells the patient about cancer results, not you.

Prophylactic (preventive) = remove it before cancer develops (e.g., mastectomy with a strong family history) Palliative (for comfort) = remove it to ease symptoms, not to cure (e.g., a tumor making it hard to breathe) Reconstructive = rebuild afterward (e.g., breast implants)

External radiation (a beam aimed from outside the body): the patient is NOT radioactive . Don't wash off the skin tattoo (it marks where to aim the beam); avoid sun 10 am–3 pm. Brachytherapy (radioactive seeds placed inside the body, next to the tumor): the patient IS radioactive . Hook: "Time, Distance, Shielding." Time: cluster care (do everything in one visit), 30-min visitor limit, rotate nurses Distance: visitors stay 6 ft away; no pregnant visitors or kids Shielding: lead apron + thyroid shield (protects the

neck) + dosimeter badge (measures how much radiation you've been exposed to) Seed falls out → don't touch it, use tongs . At home: strain urine for 7–10 days (to catch seeds), no heavy lifting (straining can push seeds out), sleep apart.

Chemo kills all fast-growing cells: cancer, plus hair, mouth lining, gut, and bone marrow. That explains almost every side effect: Hair → alopecia (hair loss) Mouth → stomatitis (painful mouth sores): magic mouthwash (a numbing rinse) or salt water, a straw, soft cold foods, no alcohol mouthwash Gut → nausea/vomiting (the most common): Zofran (an anti-nausea med), small bland meals, no fluids 1 hr before treatment Marrow → pancytopenia (low WBCs are the most dangerous) Before giving it: check for blood return (pull

back on the syringe and see blood, which proves you're in the vein). Swelling or burning at the site → stop (extravasation). Port = a small device implanted under the chest skin for giving IV meds long-term. Protect yourself: purple chemo gloves, gown, face shield. The patient's urine and stool are hazardous too. Which low count is the question about? Infection words (fever, visitors, fresh flowers, positive-pressure room, which pushes air out so germs can't drift in) → low WBCs

entries.h: Clinical side note · Positive-pressure rooms are not routine for every low WBC count
entries.t: CDC protective-environment recommendations specifically address allogeneic stem-cell transplant recipients. Other patients need individualized infection precautions; an airborne infection can change room requirements. Source Bleeding words (nosebleed, petechiae, stool softener, occult blood, meaning hidden blood in the stool) → low platelets Tired/dizzy words (fatigue, orthostatic BP, meaning BP drops when standing up; Hgb) → low RBCs Stem cell transplant (replacing damaged bone marrow with healthy cells) ≠ cured.

entries.h: Clinical side note · Positive-pressure rooms are not routine for every low WBC count
entries.t: The first 8–10 days are the most dangerous (infection and bleeding) while the new cells "take." GVHD (graft-versus-host disease) = the donor's cells attack the patient's body.

entries.h: Oncologic emergencies (the "call for help now" four)

entries.t: What's happening, in plain words A tumor squeezes the superior vena cava (the big vein draining the head and arms), so blood backs up into the face and neck Hook "Purple balloon head" First move Sit up, O2

What's happening, in plain words Chemo pops cancer cells all at once; their insides flood the blood and hit the kidneys and heart Hook "3 up, 1 down" (potassium, phosphorus, uric acid ↑; calcium ↓) First move IV fluids (flush it out)
What's happening, in plain words A tumor presses on the spinal cord Hook Back pain first , then the legs and bladder stop working First move Steroids

What's happening, in plain words Calcium leaks out of the bones into the blood Hook Bones, stones, groans, psych overtones (bone pain, kidney stones, stomach pain/constipation, confusion) First move Fluids
Palliative care = comfort care that can happen ALONGSIDE treatment.

entries.h: Hospice = comfort care INSTEAD of a cure:
entries.t: Expected to live ≤ 6 months Can leave anytime; isn't kicked out for living longer The family is part of the care O2 is just for comfort; morphine treats pain and breathlessness; usually no antibiotics

entries.h: Part 6: Mnemonics & abbreviations, letter by letter

entries.t: TACO = fluid overload from a transfusion T = Transfusion A = Associated C = Circulatory O = Overload In plain words: too much blood went in too fast, so fluid backs up into the lungs. BP goes UP → give diuretics, no saline. TRALI = lung injury from a transfusion T = Transfusion R = Related A = Acute (sudden) L = Lung I = Injury In plain words: antibodies in the donor's blood attack the patient's lungs. BP goes DOWN → airway support; never restart. Never restart: hemolytic, TRALI, bacterial. No saline: TACO.

DISC = what triggers a sickle cell crisis D = Dehydration I = Infection S = Stress C = Cold Also: low oxygen / high altitude (the student's guide lists it with DISC) RANDI = bleeding precautions when platelets are low R = electric Razor only A = Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs (ibuprofen-type pain meds) N = small Needles D = Decrease needle sticks and IM shots I = protect from Injury RICE = for a hemophilia joint bleed R = Rest I = Ice C = Compression (the priority if it's actively bleeding) E = Elevation DIC = clotting,

then bleeding, everywhere D = Disseminated (spread all over the body) I = Intravascular (inside the blood vessels) C = Coagulation (clotting) HIT = heparin destroying platelets H = Heparin I = Induced (caused by) T = Thrombocytopenia (low platelets) ANC = how many infection-fighting cells the patient has A = Absolute N = Neutrophil C = Count

(Old) CRAB = multiple myeloma (usually an older person) C = Calcium is high (it leaks out of the bones) R = Renal failure (renal = kidney) A = Anemia B = Bone pain and bone lesions (holes in the bones) ALL = the childhood leukemia A = Acute (comes on fast) L = Lymphocytic (affects lymphocytes, a type of WBC) L = Leukemia B symptoms = 3 signs seen in lymphoma and leukemia (not an acronym; just remember the 3) Fever Night sweats Weight loss

CAUTION UP = cancer warning signs C = Change in bowel or bladder habits A = A sore that doesn't heal U = Unusual bleeding or discharge T = Thickening or a lump (breast, testicle, anywhere) I = Indigestion or trouble swallowing O = Obvious change in a wart or mole N = Nagging cough or hoarseness U = Unexplained weight LOSS P = Pernicious anemia (new B12 deficiency, which can mean a GI cancer) TNM = how cancer is staged (how far it has spread) T = Tumor size N = lymph Nodes involved M = Metastasis (spread to other
organs)

SVC syndrome = a tumor squeezing the big vein S = Superior (upper) V = Vena C = Cava (together: the big vein bringing blood from the head and arms back to the heart) TLS = tumor lysis syndrome (cancer cells bursting after chemo) T = Tumor L = Lysis (bursting) S = Syndrome Labs: 3 up, 1 down . entries.h: A nurse is calculating intake and output for a client with continuous bladder irrigation. Which is correct?
entries.t: Count the irrigant as intake and all drainage as output Subtract the irrigant volume so it is not counted in intake or output Count only half the irrigant as intake Count the irrigant as output only

Subtract the irrigant volume so it is not counted in intake or output The irrigant is not counted in I&O - it goes in and comes right back out, so including it invents both intake and urine that never existed. Subtract the irrigation volume from total drainage to get true urine output.

entries.h: A client rescued from a house fire has headache and dizziness, and SpO2 reads 98 percent on room air. What does the nurse do?
entries.t: Document the normal saturation and continue monitoring Apply 100 percent oxygen by non-rebreather and obtain a carboxyhemoglobin level Apply 2 L by nasal cannula and recheck in an hour Prepare for immediate intubation

Apply 100 percent oxygen by non-rebreather and obtain a carboxyhemoglobin level In carbon monoxide poisoning the pulse oximeter is worthless - the probe cannot distinguish oxyhemoglobin from carboxyhemoglobin, so it reads 98 percent on a poisoned client. Treatment is 100 percent oxygen by non-rebreather plus a blood carboxyhemoglobin level; symptoms are mostly neurologic.

entries.h: A foot blister is painless in a person with neuropathy. What does that imply?
entries.t: It still needs prompt attention It is safe to ignore A heating pad will speed healing
It still needs prompt attention Reduced sensation can hide injury. Prompt assessment helps prevent worsening wounds.

entries.h: A client with a T4 spinal cord injury has BP 208/112, HR 48, a pounding headache and flushing above the injury. What does the nurse do first?
entries.t: Administer the prescribed antihypertensive Sit the client upright Check for a fecal impaction Lay the client flat and elevate the legs

Sit the client upright In autonomic dysreflexia the first action is to sit her up , which uses gravity to drop the blood pressure immediately, then find and remove the trigger - check the bladder before the bowel. Antihypertensives are an adjunct, not the first move, and lying flat worsens the hypertension.

entries.h: Fifteen minutes into a transfusion a client has chills, fever and flank pain. What does the nurse do first?
entries.t: Notify the provider Stop the transfusion Slow the rate and reassess in 15 minutes Administer the prescribed antipyretic

Stop the transfusion For any suspected reaction the sequence is stop the transfusion, keep the line open with 0.9 percent NS on new tubing, stay with the client, then notify . Slowing the rate keeps incompatible blood going in, and notifying first delays the one action that stops the exposure.

entries.h: A drip is ordered at 5 mcg/kg/min for a client weighing 154 lb. The bag contains 400 mg in 250 mL. What rate does the nurse program?
entries.t: 8.2 mL/hr 13.1 mL/hr 21 mL/hr 26.3 mL/hr

13.1 mL/hr 154 divided by 2.2 = 70 kg; 70 x 5 = 350 mcg/min = 21,000 mcg/hr = 21 mg/hr; the bag is 1.6 mg/mL, so 21 divided by 1.6 = 13.1 mL/hr . Answering 21 means stopping at mg/hr and never converting to volume - round only at the very end.

entries.h: Acute respiratory acidosis · Recognize CO₂ retention
Follow the changes in breathing, blood gases and mental status
entries.t: Breathing becomes inadequate Too little alveolar ventilation leaves carbon dioxide in the bloodstream. ↓ PaCO₂ rises → pH falls Usual arterial ranges are PaCO₂ 35–45 mmHg and pH 7.35–7.45. In acute respiratory acidosis, PaCO₂ is high and pH is low. ↓ The bedside clues Headache, confusion and drowsiness point to rising CO₂. Perioral tingling and carpal spasm after rapid breathing fit respiratory alkalosis.

entries.h: Why the other answers do not fit
entries.t: Tingling around the mouth with carpal spasm Rapid breathing lowers CO₂. Tingling around the mouth and carpal spasm fit respiratory alkalosis. Kussmaul respirations with fruity-smelling breath Deep Kussmaul breathing is compensation for metabolic acidosis. Fruity breath points toward ketones, as in diabetic ketoacidosis. Muscle cramps and a pH of 7.50 after days of vomiting Vomiting causes gastric acid loss. A pH of 7.50 is alkalemic and fits metabolic alkalosis in this setting.

entries.h: A nurse is preparing to perform endotracheal suctioning of a client who has a tracheostomy and coarse gurgling respirations. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? (Select all that apply.)
entries.t: Answers Hyperoxygenate the client with 100% oxygen for 30 to 60 seconds before suctioning Apply suction intermittently only while withdrawing the catheter Limit each suction pass to 10 to 15 seconds Perform no more than three suction passes, allowing at least 1 minute between passes ↓ Reasoning SUCTIONING REMOVES OXYGEN ALONG WITH SECRETIONS, so the nurse hyperoxygenates first, suctions ONLY ON WITHDRAWAL FOR NO MORE THAN 10 TO 15 SECONDS PER PASS, limits passes, and rests the client between passes using sterile technique. entries.h: Mrs. Lewis is a 39-year-old with a long history of IBS: alternating constipation and diarrhea, cramping relieved after a bowel movement, symptoms worse with stress, and a normal colonoscopy and labs. entries.t: Answer These are red flags that the problem is no longer consistent with IBS and require further evaluation ↓ Reasoning NEW BLOODY STOOLS AND UNEXPLAINED WEIGHT LOSS ARE NEVER IBS. Clinical detail As the instructor framed it, IBS hurts but it doesn't harm — IBS is irritated but structurally normal, with a normal colonoscopy and normal labs, while IBD is inflamed and damaged, and inflamed bowel tissue bleeds easily. Stress does trigger IBS, but it does not cause bleeding or weight loss. Alternating constipation and diarrhea is classic IBS; blood and weight loss are not, and once you have evidence the bowel is injured or inflamed you go IBD over IBS. entries.h: Match each clinical picture in an older adult to the state it best fits.
entries.t: What the finding means Delirium arrives in hours to days, fluctuates through the day, and takes attention and arousal with it, while dementia takes months to years and leaves attention intact until late. Clinical detail Any abrupt change on top of established dementia is delirium until proven otherwise, and urinary infection is a common trigger in this age group. Slower word finding with no loss of function is ordinary aging, not disease, and it is the item most often over-called. entries.h: A nurse caring for a patient receiving TPN through a central line meets resistance when attempting to flush and notes the infusion has become sluggish; the external catheter length appears longer than documented. What should the nurse do?

entries.h: Four hours after a laparoscopy for endometriosis, a client reports sharp right shoulder pain. What should the nurse do?
entries.t: Answer Reassure her this is referred pain from the CO₂ and encourage ambulation ↓ Reasoning Shoulder and neck pain after laparoscopy is referred pain from the carbon dioxide used to inflate the abdomen. Clinical detail It is expected. Walking , a heating pad and lying on the left side move it along, and it clears in a day or two. What is not expected is severe or worsening abdominal pain, a rigid abdomen, fever or heavy bleeding — that is bleeding or an injured bowel or bladder until someone proves otherwise. What is not expected is severe or worsening abdominal pain, a rigid abdomen, fever or heavy bleeding — that is bleeding or an injured bowel or bladder until someone proves otherwise. Original Study Hub illustration · Endometriosis: tissue outside the uterus. A female pelvic anatomy diagram labels normal endometrium inside the uterine cavity and endometriosis lesions on the outer uterine surface, an ovary, the pelvic lining and the fallopian tube, with an ovarian endometrioma labelled as a chocolate cyst and an adhesion. Symptoms listed: painful periods, chronic pelvic pain, deep pain with sex, bowel and bladder pain especially during periods, fatigue and possible fertility difficulty, and that some people have very few symptoms. Assessment: pain and menstrual history, pelvic examination and imaging such as ultrasound or MRI, normal imaging does not exclude endometriosis, and a clinical diagnosis can guide treatment while laparoscopy may be appropriate in selected cases. Treatment depends on symptoms and fertility goals: pain relief, hormonal suppression, surgery, with supportive symptom tracking and pelvic floor or pain care. Key distinctions: endometriosis occurs outside the uterus, adenomyosis occurs within the uterine muscle, pregnancy and hysterectomy are not guaranteed cures, and pain severity does not reliably match lesion extent. entries.h: At a well-child visit a mother says her 2-month-old “cries all the time.” Which action should the nurse take first?
entries.t: Answer Ask the mother to describe the pattern, frequency and quality of the crying ↓ Reasoning Assess before you act. Clinical detail A healthy infant cries 1 to 3 hours a day — it is how they say hungry, thirsty, tired, wet or hurting — so “all the time” means nothing until you know the pattern, frequency and quality . Calling the provider first skips the data that would make the call useful. Carrying on with the check-in dismisses a parent's concern for the sake of the schedule , and calling it normal without asking is the same dismissal in kinder words. What the quality tells you: a high-pitched, shrill cry is a neurologic sign — raised intracranial pressure until proven otherwise — and that one is reported straight away. Which is exactly why the nurse asks first. entries.h: A 74-year-old man started a new blood pressure medication yesterday and felt lightheaded when he stood up this morning. Supine after five minutes: blood pressure 128/76, heart rate 72. At one minute standing: blood pressure 104/62, heart rate 92. He denies chest pain. Capillary glucose 104 mg/dL, temperature 36.8 degrees C, oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air.
entries.t: What the finding means Consensus criteria define orthostatic hypotension as a sustained fall of at least 20 mm Hg systolic or 10 mm Hg diastolic within three minutes of standing, and his drop is 24 and 14. Clinical detail Rising in stages and supervised walking prevent the fall this sets up, and repeating positional vitals alongside his symptom reports shows whether it is controlled. Hypoglycemia is the tempting alternative, but a capillary glucose of 104 mg/dL rules it out. His heart rate did rise with standing, which argues against a purely neurogenic cause. entries.h: Which findings indicate that oxytocin is needed after birth? Select all that apply.
entries.t: Answers Excessive vaginal bleeding A fundus above the expected level A flaccid, boggy uterus ↓ Reasoning Oxytocin makes the uterus contract , which is how postpartum bleeding is controlled - the muscle clamps down on the open vessels where the placenta was. Clinical detail So it is indicated when the uterus is boggy, high, displaced or bleeding . A firm fundus at the umbilicus is the goal , not an indication. A fundus deviated to one side is not one of them: it usually means a full bladder is pushing the uterus aside, so the first step is to help her empty her bladder , then reassess.
