entries.h: Match each presentation to the type of shock it indicates.
entries.t: What the finding means Neurogenic shock is the one that cannot compensate, so the pulse is slow and the skin warm and dry, which is the opposite of every other type. Clinical detail Hypovolemic shock empties the tank, so neck veins are flat. Cardiogenic shock backs fluid up, so neck veins distend and the lungs crackle. Septic shock is warm and vasodilated early with a rising lactate. Anaphylaxis is defined by the airway and skin signs appearing within minutes of exposure. entries.h: A nurse is monitoring a client in the acute phase of a major burn for infection. Why is fever an unreliable indicator?
entries.t: Answer Burn clients often run an inflammatory, hypermetabolic fever that does not mean infection ↓ Reasoning Inflammation and hypermetabolism can keep a low-grade temperature up for weeks after a burn, so fever on its own does not equal infection. Clinical detail Look instead for a change in pattern : worsening wound appearance, altered drainage or odor, mental status change, hemodynamic instability, worsening glucose control, or culture and laboratory evidence. Early on the opposite problem applies — loss of intact skin means loss of thermoregulation, so clients tend to be hypothermic . entries.h: A 24-year-old reports painful periods that have worsened over several years, deep pain with intercourse, and painful bowel movements during her period. Which condition should the nurse suspect?
entries.t: Answer Endometriosis ↓ Reasoning This is the classic triad of endometriosis : dysmenorrhea that is secondary and progressive, dyspareunia that is deep, and dyschezia that tracks the period. Clinical detail Endometritis is an infection of the uterine lining, almost always postpartum, and comes with fever and foul lochia. PID brings fever, discharge and cervical motion tenderness. Primary dysmenorrhea starts at menarche and does not worsen year on year. Original Study Hub review graphic · based on the quiz explanation Why the other answers do not fit Endometritis Endometritis is an infection of the uterine lining, almost always postpartum, and comes with fever and foul lochia. Pelvic inflammatory disease Primary dysmenorrhea Primary dysmenorrhea starts at menarche and does not worsen year on year. Shared reasoning for choices without a separate note: This is the classic triad of endometriosis : dysmenorrhea that is secondary and progressive, dyspareunia that is deep, and dyschezia that tracks the period. Endometritis is an infection of the uterine lining, almost always postpartum, and comes with fever and foul lochia. PID brings fever, discharge and cervical motion tenderness. Primary dysmenorrhea starts at menarche and does not worsen year on year. Original Study Hub illustration · Endometriosis: tissue outside the uterus. A female pelvic anatomy diagram labels normal endometrium inside the uterine cavity and endometriosis lesions on the outer uterine surface, an ovary, the pelvic lining and the fallopian tube, with an ovarian endometrioma labelled as a chocolate cyst and an adhesion. Symptoms listed: painful periods, chronic pelvic pain, deep pain with sex, bowel and bladder pain especially during periods, fatigue and possible fertility difficulty, and that some people have very few symptoms. Assessment: pain and menstrual history, pelvic examination and imaging such as ultrasound or MRI, normal imaging does not exclude endometriosis, and a clinical diagnosis can guide treatment while laparoscopy may be appropriate in selected cases. Treatment depends on symptoms and fertility goals: pain relief, hormonal suppression, surgery, with supportive symptom tracking and pelvic floor or pain care. Key distinctions: endometriosis occurs outside the uterus, adenomyosis occurs within the uterine muscle, pregnancy and hysterectomy are not guaranteed cures, and pain severity does not reliably match lesion extent. Educational illustration, sources ACOG and WHO. entries.h: Which behavior by the spouse of a client with alcohol use disorder is an example of enabling?
entries.t: Answer Calling her husband's employer to report he has the flu after a night of drinking ↓ Reasoning Enabling means shielding the person from the consequences of using — lying to the employer removes the very consequence that could motivate change. entries.h: According to Maslow's hierarchy of needs, which of the following client actions would be considered most basic?
entries.t: Answer A client seeks shelter at a center for battered women. ↓ Reasoning Seeking shelter addresses physiological and safety needs — the most basic levels of Maslow's hierarchy. Clinical detail Safety needs (freedom from fear/order = answer A) come next, then love/belonging (answer B), then esteem (answer D), and finally self-actualization (answer C). entries.h: A 10-month-old hospitalized for observation is in the playroom eating a teething biscuit when the caregiver calls out. The infant is clutching at his throat, has a weak, ineffective cough, makes no sound, and his lips are turning dusky. HR 150/min SpO2 88%
entries.t: What the finding means A weak, ineffective cough with no sound and clutching at the throat is the universal choking sign of a complete foreign body airway obstruction, not anaphylaxis, a breath-holding spell, or epiglottitis, none of which present this way. entries.h: Which statements are true about the fontanelles of a 1-month-old? Select all that apply.
entries.t: Answers Both fontanelles should be flat, soft and open Crying can make the fontanelles pulsate A sunken fontanelle can mean dehydration or fluid volume deficit A bulging fontanelle can mean raised intracranial pressure ↓ Reasoning At 1 month both are still open — and the closing order is the one people reverse. Clinical detail The posterior closes first, at about 1 to 2 months ; the anterior is the big one and takes 12 to 18 months . So “anterior closed, posterior open” is backwards, and nothing is closed at 4 weeks. Normal is flat and soft , and a pulsation is fine — you are watching an artery under a membrane, and it shows more when the baby cries. Sunken points to dehydration . Bulging points to raised intracranial pressure . Judge a bulge on a calm, upright baby , though — a fontanelle can bulge transiently while a baby screams or lies flat, and that alone is not the emergency. entries.h: Which instruction should the nurse give the client just before the needle is inserted for a thoracentesis?

entries.h: A week ago this toddler was seen for difficulty passing stool and sent home on an over-the-counter stool softener with advice on fluids and fruit. This is the return visit. Select the findings that need following up.
entries.t: What the finding means Put together, these say the constipation has got worse, not better , and that this is not ordinary constipation. Clinical detail Lethargy and refusing food , a distended abdomen with hypoactive bowel sounds and a palpable faecal mass , ribbon-like foul-smelling stools and a raised blood pressure together point to Hirschsprung disease - a segment of bowel with no nerve cells, so it never relaxes and stool cannot get past. The ribbon-like stool is the giveaway: it is being squeezed through a segment that will not open. This child needs evaluation, not a stronger laxative. A female pelvic anatomy diagram labels normal endometrium inside the uterine cavity and endometriosis lesions on the outer uterine surface, an ovary, the pelvic lining and the fallopian tube, with an ovarian endometrioma labelled as a chocolate cyst and an adhesion. Symptoms listed: painful periods, chronic pelvic pain, deep pain with sex, bowel and bladder pain especially during periods, fatigue and possible fertility difficulty, and that some people have very few symptoms. Assessment: pain and menstrual history, pelvic examination and imaging such as ultrasound or MRI, normal imaging does not exclude endometriosis, and a clinical diagnosis can guide treatment while laparoscopy may be appropriate in selected cases. Treatment depends on symptoms and fertility goals: pain relief, hormonal suppression, surgery, with supportive symptom tracking and pelvic floor or pain care. Key distinctions: endometriosis occurs outside the uterus, adenomyosis occurs within the uterine muscle, pregnancy and hysterectomy are not guaranteed cures, and pain severity does not reliably match lesion extent. entries.h: A client on lithium develops vomiting and diarrhea from gastroenteritis, then a coarse tremor, ataxia, and confusion. Which mechanism explains the rising lithium level?

entries.h: A nurse is planning care for a 7-month-old infant who has non-organic failure to thrive. Which of the following actions should the nurse take first?
entries.t: Answer Observe the caregiver through an entire feeding ↓ Reasoning Assessment comes before intervention. entries.h: After a TURP, continuous bladder irrigation is draining freely. Which finding should the nurse report promptly to the surgical team?
entries.t: Correct answer New thick, bright-red drainage with repeated clots Why New thick, bright-red drainage with repeated clots suggests significant bleeding. Assess the patient and catheter flow, report the change promptly, and follow the prescribed irrigation protocol. Color alone cannot identify the bleeding vessel. Why the other answers do not fit Over the last hour, 1,250 mL drained after 1,200 mL of irrigant was infused The collection bag contains both urine and returned irrigant. Here, 1,250 − 1,200 = 50 mL of urine in one hour. These volumes alone do not show heavy bleeding. A brief bladder spasm that resolved with prescribed medication A catheter can irritate the bladder. A brief spasm that settles with medication is less concerning here. Persistent pain, leakage or reduced drainage warrants a patency check. Light pink drainage that is getting clearer Light pink drainage that becomes clearer suggests bleeding is decreasing. The concerning change is newly dense, bright-red drainage with repeated clots. entries.h: A nurse is caring for an older adult client who is incontinent. Which effects of aging might contribute to urinary alterations? Select all that apply.

entries.h: The client has soaked a full pad in 10 minutes. The fundus is soft, boggy, and 2 cm above the umbilicus, displaced to the right . Lochia is bright red with small clots.

entries.h: A client who has taken a first-generation antipsychotic for eight years develops slow, writhing tongue and lip movements that persist even after the drug is reduced. Which mechanism explains this, and how does it differ from acute dystonia?
entries.t: Answer Chronic D2 blockade causes postsynaptic receptor upregulation and supersensitivity; acute dystonia is an early, reversible dopamine-acetylcholine imbalance ↓ Reasoning Tardive dyskinesia arises after months to years when sustained D2 blockade drives receptor upregulation and supersensitivity , producing late, often irreversible choreoathetoid movements that can worsen on dose reduction and are treated with VMAT2 inhibitors such as valbenazine. entries.h: A client whose mother and aunt have schizophrenia developed psychosis at 19 after heavy cannabis use and a traumatic assault. Which model best explains this?
entries.t: Answer Stress-diathesis model: inherited vulnerability expressed when environmental stressors exceed a threshold ↓ Reasoning The stress-diathesis model holds that a genetic or neurodevelopmental diathesis sets a vulnerability threshold, and illness emerges when stressors such as substance use, trauma, or sleep loss exceed it, which explains why concordance in identical twins is high but far below 100 percent. Clinical detail Pure genetic and pure environmental explanations both fail that data, and kindling describes progressive episode sensitization in mood and seizure disorders. Clinically this means the nurse targets the modifiable side of the equation: substances, sleep, stress, and support. entries.h: A 9-year-old with known asthma arrives with a severe exacerbation. He can only speak in short, broken phrases and sits in a tripod position with retractions. His SpO2 is falling, and the wheezing that was loud on arrival has become inaudible.
entries.t: What the finding means Short, broken speech, tripod positioning, retractions, a falling SpO2, and a change from loud wheezing to a silent chest signal impending respiratory failure, because an inaudible chest in this context means airflow has dropped too low to generate sound, not that the attack is resolving. Clinical detail This is a true respiratory emergency rather than a resolving exacerbation, anxiety, or aspiration, none of which would include progressive hypoxia with a silent chest. The nurse should prepare for continuous bronchodilator therapy and provider notification and establish IV access in case intubation is needed, rather than reassuring the family, using a long-acting agent that has no role in acute attacks, or delaying oxygen; air movement and oxygen saturation are the parameters that most directly show whether the obstruction is worsening or responding. entries.h: A 91-year-old man is in the last days of life. At 0200 the nurse turned him onto his side, gave mouth care, stopped the maintenance intravenous fluid as ordered, and taught his daughter about the gurgling sound. At 0400 the gurgling is quieter, his face is relaxed, and his daughter is sitting with him holding his hand.
entries.t: What the finding means National Cancer Institute guidance says repositioning often helps noisy terminal secretions and that limiting intravenous hydration in the final days reduces them. Clinical detail A quieter sound with a relaxed face and a settled family are the outcomes that matter in comfort care; an oxygen saturation is not a goal here and is the tempting wrong choice for a student used to numbers. entries.h: A 38-year-old client with peritonitis is admitted to a med-surg unit. entries.t: Answer The client’s condition is worsening — intervention is required ↓ Reasoning Every single trend is moving the wrong way: rising HR, rising RR, FALLING SpO₂ (94 → 86%), climbing fever, pain going from 4/10 localized to 10/10 generalized and radiating, and a WBC climbing 12k → 16k. Clinical detail A near-normal blood pressure does not reassure you when everything else is deteriorating. The peritoneum is a STERILE lining — like sterile plastic wrap around the abdominal contents — so bacteria there (from a perforated ulcer or a leaking diverticulum) is a SURGICAL EMERGENCY. On trend items, don’t judge single values; read each row left to right. entries.t: Answer Chronic inhalation of indoor toxins can cause lung damage. ↓ Reasoning Environmental risk factors for COPD include prolonged and intense exposure to occupational dusts and chemicals, indoor air pollution, and outdoor air pollution. entries.h: A client being treated for diverticulitis reports that stool and gas are now draining from an abnormal opening between the bowel and the bladder. The nurse recognizes this as which complication?
entries.t: Answer Fistula ↓ Reasoning A FISTULA IS AN ABNORMAL TUNNEL THAT DEVELOPS BETWEEN ORGANS, which is exactly what stool draining from bowel into bladder describes. Clinical detail An abscess is infection walled off and trapped inside the pouch; an obstruction happens when the inflammation swells enough to stop things from flowing through; and perforation is the pouch actually popping, which spills bowel contents into the abdomen and produces peritonitis with a rigid board-like abdomen - the client here is not describing that. Abscess, fistula, obstruction, bleeding, and perforation are the five complications that come from pouches that pop. entries.h: A nurse is planning preoperative teaching for a client scheduled for an open abdominal procedure. Which outcome is most appropriate?

entries.h: A client with agoraphobia has not left home in a year and says staying in is the only thing that keeps her calm. Which mechanism explains why avoidance perpetuates her anxiety?
entries.t: Answer Avoidance is negatively reinforced by immediate relief and prevents extinction learning ↓ Reasoning Escaping the feared situation produces instant anxiety relief, which negatively reinforces the avoidance, and because the client never stays long enough to learn the feared outcome does not occur, extinction of the conditioned fear cannot occur. Clinical detail The other options misapply mechanisms belonging to GABA pharmacology, memory anatomy, and tardive dyskinesia. This is the rationale for graded exposure, and the nurse prepares the client for anxiety to rise before it falls. entries.h: The safe dose range for a medication is 15 to 40 mg/kg/day PO divided every 6 hr. A child weighs 22 lb. What is the maximum safe amount the nurse may give in a single dose?
entries.t: Answer 100 mg ↓ Reasoning STEP 1, convert weight: 22 lb divided by 2.2 = 10 kg. Clinical detail STEP 2, maximum daily dose: 10 kg x 40 mg/kg/day = 400 mg/day. STEP 3, DIVIDE BY DOSES PER DAY: every 6 hr = 4 DOSES, so 400 divided by 4 = 100 mg MAXIMUM PER DOSE. Answering 400 mg is the classic error of reporting the daily maximum as a single dose, which would give the child four times the safe amount in 24 hr. Answering 40 mg comes from multiplying 40 mg/kg by 1 kg instead of 10 kg. entries.t: ABO compatibility for blood products · Choose the recipient’s type, then the FFP, pRBC, platelet or cryoprecipitate column. entries.h: A 62-year-old man on the medical unit has had eight watery stools since midnight. A stool sample is positive for Clostridioides difficile toxin. He is in a private room. He has no cough, no rash, and no fever.

entries.h: A nurse in the emergency department is caring for a 12-year-old child who has ingested bleach. Which of the following statements by the nurse indicates an understanding of this ingestion?
entries.t: Answer "Injury by a corrosive liquid is more extensive than by a corrosive solid." ↓ Reasoning A liquid corrosive does not stick, so more is swallowed and it coats as it goes — larger area of contact, more extensive esophageal and often gastric injury. Clinical detail A solid or granule adheres to the mouth and upper esophagus, which hurts at once and tends to limit how much goes down. The other three are the classic traps: a clean mouth proves nothing , because oral and pharyngeal burns do not reliably accompany esophageal ones — children who looked fine have had severe injury on endoscopy. Neutralizing is never done : a weak acid on an alkali is an exothermic reaction, adding a thermal burn to the chemical one. And activated charcoal is contraindicated for corrosives — it does not bind them and it coats the mucosa so the damage cannot be seen on endoscopy. Airway first, keep them NPO, endoscopy stages the burn. entries.h: While assessing an acutely ill client's respiratory rate, the nurse assesses four normal breaths followed by an episode of apnea lasting 20 seconds. How should the nurse document this finding?
entries.t: Answer Biot respiration ↓ Reasoning The nurse will document that the client is demonstrating a Biot respiration pattern. Clinical detail Biot respiration is characterized by periods of normal breathing (three to four breaths) followed by varying periods of apnea (usually 10 seconds to 1 minute). Cheyne-Stokes is a similar respiratory pattern, but it involves a regular cycle where the rate and depth of breathing increase and then decrease until apnea occurs. Biot respiration is not characterized by the increase and decrease in the rate and depth, as characterized by Cheyne–Stokes. Eupnea is a normal breathing pattern of 12 to 18 breaths per minute. entries.h: A nurse is providing teaching to the parent of a school-age child who is starting methylphenidate. Which of the following instructions should the nurse include?

entries.h: A client falls to the floor and begins a tonic-clonic seizure. After calling for help, which action should the nurse take?
entries.t: Answer Turn the client onto her side and loosen anything tight around the neck ↓ Reasoning During the seizure the job is protect, do not restrain . entries.h: A 3-year-old is admitted with a fever of unknown source, and the provider orders a urine culture. Which action should the nurse take to obtain the specimen?

entries.h: An 8-year-old has a serum calcium of 7.4 mg/dL. When the nurse taps the cheek over the facial nerve, the cheek twitches. Which additional finding should the nurse expect?

entries.h: A 72-year-old man with small cell lung cancer has had two days of confusion and headache. He has no edema and his mucous membranes are moist. He also reports constipation and mild low back pain. Sodium 118 mEq/L, serum osmolality 258 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 62 mEq/L.
entries.t: What the finding means Constipation and back pain are genuine problems, but a sodium of 118 mEq/L with confusion and headache is symptomatic hyponatremia that can progress to seizures. Clinical detail The pattern fits SIADH, which is common in small cell lung cancer: normal volume status, serum osmolality below 275 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality above 100 mOsm/kg, and urine sodium above 40 mEq/L. Dehydration is the tempting choice, but moist membranes with concentrated, sodium-rich urine is the opposite of a volume-depleted kidney. Correction is deliberately slow, generally no more than about 8 mEq/L in 24 hours, to avoid osmotic demyelination. entries.h: A client with septic shock for 2 days develops oozing from IV sites and gums, petechiae across the chest, and dark, cyanotic fingertips. Labs show platelets 68,000/mm3, fibrinogen 140 mg/dL, a prolonged PT, and an elevated D-dimer.
entries.t: What the finding means DIC uniquely produces simultaneous bleeding (oozing IV sites, petechiae) and clotting (cyanotic nail beds from microemboli), triggered here by sepsis, along with low platelets, low fibrinogen, a prolonged PT, and an elevated D-dimer, a pattern not seen together in ITP, HIT, or TTP alone. Clinical detail The priority actions are treating the underlying sepsis and replacing consumed clotting factors and platelets; NSAIDs and Valsalva maneuvers both raise bleeding and hemorrhage risk and should be avoided, and withholding fluids would worsen perfusion. Trending fibrinogen and platelet counts is the most direct way to monitor the worsening or improving consumptive coagulopathy, unlike uric acid, rheumatoid factor, or A1c, which are unrelated to DIC. entries.h: Highlight the findings that are NOT expected changes of aging and need follow-up.
entries.t: What the finding means Gradual hearing loss, needing reading glasses, thinner less elastic skin and an earlier wake time are expected age-related changes, so they act as distractors here. Confusion is the tempting one to write off as dementia, but a change over two days is acute and must be worked up. entries.h: A hemodialysis client develops headache, nausea, and confusion during treatment. This suggests:
entries.t: Published infographic · AJKD Blog / NephMadness 2026 Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome: how rapid solute removal can affect the brain. Look for the water shift and the neurologic clues. Open the publisher’s infographic full size ↗ · Publisher and credits Original NUR 198 hemodialysis review: Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome: signs and first actions · Open full-size picture Answer Disequilibrium syndrome ↓ Reasoning During or shortly after hemodialysis, urea may fall faster in blood than in the brain. Water shifts into brain tissue. New restlessness, headache, nausea, or confusion warrants immediate assessment and notification of the dialysis team; escalate severe neurologic changes as an emergency. Original Study Hub review graphic · based on the quiz explanation Why the other answers do not fit Air embolism Air entering the circulation typically raises concern for abrupt dyspnea, chest pain, or hypotension. The headache, nausea, and confusion during solute removal fit DDS more closely. Hypoglycemia Low glucose can also cause confusion. Check a bedside glucose; symptoms alone do not establish hypoglycemia. The timing and cluster of neurologic symptoms during dialysis point toward DDS. Infection A dialysis access infection more often raises concern with fever, chills, or redness or drainage at the access. It is a less direct explanation for new neurologic changes during treatment. entries.h: A nurse reviews the CBC of a client with long-standing COPD and finds an elevated hematocrit. How should the nurse interpret this result?
entries.t: Answer It is a compensatory response to chronic hypoxemia ↓ Reasoning Chronic hypoxemia stimulates erythropoietin, so the body makes more red cells — secondary polycythemia, which raises the hematocrit. Clinical detail Students often expect a low hematocrit; in COPD the value is elevated, and it reflects long-term low oxygen, not infection. entries.h: A nurse is reviewing RIPE therapy with a client newly diagnosed with active TB. Which of the following statements by the client indicate correct understanding? Select all that apply.
entries.t: Answers I will have blood drawn to check my liver during treatment I will take vitamin B6 with my isoniazid I will report any changes in my vision right away I will take all four medications for at least six months ↓ Reasoning RIPE runs 6-12 months with serial liver function monitoring, prompt reporting of vision changes (ethambutol), and B6 alongside isoniazid. Clinical detail Stopping when symptoms resolve is the classic adherence failure — symptoms improve long before the organism is eradicated, and stopping early breeds resistance. entries.h: A client is in the oliguric phase of AKI. The cardiac monitor shows tall, peaked T waves. Which action should the nurse take first?

entries.h: A client with a femur fracture is in skeletal traction. Which finding indicates the traction is achieving its purpose?
entries.t: Answer The client reports fewer muscle spasms and the leg is in neutral alignment ↓ Reasoning Traction is applied to reduce and immobilize the fracture, and relief of muscle spasm with the limb held in alignment shows the counterpull is working. entries.h: A nurse obtains a pulse oximetry reading of 84% on a client who is alert, conversing in full sentences, and has pink mucous membranes and unlabored respirations. Which of the following factors could account for an inaccurate reading? (Select all that apply.)

Clinical detail The earlobe is an acceptable alternate sensor site and does not cause error, and a low-grade fever does not invalidate the reading. entries.h: A nurse is caring for a client who had a stroke and has dysphagia. Which of the following actions should the nurse take to reduce the risk of aspiration? (Select all that apply.)
entries.t: Answers Position the client in an upright 90-degree sitting position for meals Instruct the client to tuck the chin toward the chest when swallowing Provide thickened liquids as prescribed Keep the client upright for 30 to 60 minutes after the meal ↓ Reasoning UPRIGHT 90-DEGREE POSITIONING, A CHIN-TUCK THAT NARROWS THE AIRWAY ENTRANCE, THICKENED LIQUIDS THAT MOVE MORE SLOWLY AND ARE EASIER TO CONTROL, AND REMAINING UPRIGHT AFTER MEALS ALL REDUCE ASPIRATION RISK. Clinical detail STRAWS ARE AVOIDED IN DYSPHAGIA because they deliver a fast bolus to the back of the throat before the client can control it. Tilting the head back opens the airway and markedly increases aspiration risk, which is the opposite of the protective chin-tuck maneuver. entries.h: A nurse is teaching a client who has chronic constipation about lifestyle changes. Which of the following instructions should the nurse include? (Select all that apply.)
entries.t: Answers Gradually increase dietary fiber to 25 to 30 g per day Drink about 2 to 3 liters of fluid daily unless contraindicated Respond to the urge to defecate rather than delaying Increase physical activity such as walking as tolerated ↓ Reasoning FIBER, FLUID, ACTIVITY, AND HONORING THE DEFECATION URGE ARE THE CORE NONPHARMACOLOGIC MEASURES FOR CONSTIPATION, along with a regular toileting time that uses the gastrocolic reflex after a meal. Clinical detail FIBER MUST BE INCREASED GRADUALLY AND ALWAYS WITH ADEQUATE FLUID, or it can worsen constipation or cause obstruction. Daily stimulant laxatives cause laxative dependence and loss of bowel tone, and lying flat is incorrect because an upright, squatting-type position uses gravity and abdominal pressure to ease defecation. entries.h: A nurse is caring for a client on postoperative day 3 following an abdominal hysterectomy. The client has a distended abdomen, absent bowel sounds, no passage of flatus, and has vomited 300 mL of green fluid. Which of the following actions should the nurse take first?

Clinical detail Giving oral fluids to a client who is vomiting with an obstructed gut risks ASPIRATION. Opioids further slow peristalsis and worsen ileus, and a warm compress delays needed treatment. Early ambulation prevents ileus but does not treat established ileus with vomiting. entries.h: Which problem is most likely driving the delirium and should be treated first?
entries.t: Answer A urinary tract infection ↓ Reasoning Constipation, untreated pain and sleep disruption all precipitate delirium and all need attention, but a fever with a white count of 14.2 and a cloudy urinalysis points to an active infection driving this episode. A positive urinalysis alone in an older adult without symptoms is asymptomatic bacteriuria, which CDC says should not be routinely screened for or treated. entries.h: Match each nursing activity to the level of prevention it represents.
entries.t: What the finding means Primary prevention acts before disease exists, and immunization is its clearest example. Clinical detail Secondary prevention finds disease early in people who feel well, which is what screening does, while tertiary prevention limits disability once disease is established. Primordial prevention changes the conditions that create risk factors in the first place, such as building an environment where walking is possible, and it is the level most often mislabeled as primary. entries.h: A 2-month-old in the cardiology clinic is wearing only a diaper after a weight check. He is in no visible distress. BP 76/52 mm Hg, HR 146/min, respirations 34/min, temperature 36.3°C (97.4°F), SpO₂ 66% on room air. Which nursing actions are the priority? Select all that apply.
entries.t: Answers Wrap the baby in warm blankets or blankets from home Check the colour and warmth of the infant's skin Compare the heart rate on the oximeter to his actual heart rate, and reposition the probe ↓ Reasoning Everything else is normal, and the baby looks well. Clinical detail BP, heart rate, respirations and temperature all sit in range for a 2-month-old — so a saturation of 66% in a child with no visible distress is a bad reading until proven otherwise. A truly hypoxic infant at 66% would be mottled, grunting, retracting and frantic. He has been undressed in a cool room . Cold hands and feet mean poor peripheral perfusion, and a pulse oximeter cannot read a pulse it cannot feel. So: warm him , look at his colour and warmth , and check whether the oximeter's heart rate matches his real one — if the numbers disagree, the machine is not tracking his pulse and the saturation it prints is meaningless. Move the probe and recheck on another extremity. Treat the equipment before you treat the number. The Broselow cart, oxygen and an urgent call to the provider are all responses to a child who is actually in trouble; using them here frightens the parent and treats an artefact. If the reading stays low once he is warm and the probe is tracking, then it is real — escalate then. entries.h: A patient's TPN bag is nearly empty and the replacement bag has not yet arrived from pharmacy. Which action by the nurse is correct?
entries.t: Answer Notify the provider and pharmacy and follow the order to hang a dextrose-containing solution until the new bag arrives ↓ Reasoning NEVER ABRUPTLY STOP TPN — STOPPING ALL OF THAT SUGAR AT ONCE CAUSES REBOUND HYPOGLYCEMIA, so a dextrose-containing solution is hung to bridge the gap until the patient's own bag arrives. Clinical detail Hanging another patient's bag is a MED ERROR: every TPN bag is mixed in pharmacy for one specific patient with that patient's name on it, which is also why a second nurse must verify the bag before it is hung. entries.h: At 1000 this patient had a Glasgow Coma Scale of 9, a sluggish right pupil, heart rate 52, blood pressure 178/70, and an intracranial pressure of 26 mm Hg. Mannitol was given. Highlight the findings in the 1100 note that show the therapy is working.

Clinical detail A better level of consciousness, a briskly reactive pupil, and a pressure back near the normal range say the mannitol worked. Normal adult intracranial pressure is usually cited as roughly 5 to 15 mm Hg, sources differ slightly, and values above about 20 to 25 mm Hg prompt treatment. Head-of-bed elevation and a midline neck are interventions being maintained, not signs of improvement. entries.h: A client who drinks a liter of vodka daily is admitted after a fall. The nurse recognizes that alcohol withdrawal can be fatal because of which mechanism?
entries.t: Answer Chronic alcohol downregulates GABA receptors and upregulates glutamate, so abrupt cessation produces unopposed CNS excitation ↓ Reasoning Alcohol is a GABA agonist and NMDA antagonist, so the brain adapts by downregulating GABA receptors and upregulating glutamate/NMDA activity; when alcohol is removed, inhibition is deficient and excitation is excessive, producing withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens that can be lethal. Clinical detail Benzodiazepine withdrawal is dangerous for the same reason, whereas opioid withdrawal is a noradrenergic rebound that is miserable but rarely fatal in a healthy adult. entries.h: A nurse is caring for a client receiving total parenteral nutrition (TPN) through a central line. Which nursing interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
entries.t: Answers Verify the TPN bag label and prescription with a second nurse Monitor daily weights and intake/output Monitor blood glucose levels every 4 hours Have 10–20% dextrose available if the next TPN bag is delayed ↓ Reasoning Independent double-check applies to high-alert therapies — yes. Clinical detail Daily weights and I&O track fluid and nutritional response — yes. Glucose q4h — yes, because TPN delivers a heavy carbohydrate load and causes HYPERglycemia. Keeping dextrose available — yes: if TPN stops abruptly the client’s already-elevated insulin keeps working and they crash into HYPOglycemia. The wrong ones: TPN needs a DEDICATED lumen (a central line has several — just don’t share the TPN one). Flushing before and after “use” only applies to intermittent (usually home) TPN — standard hospital TPN runs continuously, so there is no before or after. Dr. Karagessian’s advice on that last one: if you’ve never heard of it, leave it unselected. entries.h: A 45-year-old woman on a telemetry unit has a narrow-complex tachycardia at 190 beats per minute with a pulse and stable blood pressure. The provider orders adenosine 6 mg IV. Which action by the nurse is correct?
entries.t: Answer Give it as a rapid IV push into a port closest to the heart, followed immediately by a rapid saline flush. ↓ Reasoning Adenosine has a half-life of only a few seconds, so it must be pushed fast into the IV port nearest the heart and chased immediately with a rapid saline flush or it will never reach the AV node. Clinical detail A slow push, a distal site, or a piggyback wastes the drug. entries.h: A nurse is planning care for a hospitalized child with autism spectrum disorder who becomes highly distressed by changes. Which approach best addresses this child's needs?
entries.t: Answer Maintain a consistent daily routine and use the child's usual communication method and comfort object ↓ Reasoning Predictable routine, the child's established communication system, and familiar transitional objects reduce sensory and social overload and prevent behavioral escalation. entries.h: A client with Parkinson's disease started carbidopa-levodopa with entacapone 3 weeks ago. Before therapy the client needed help to eat because of tremor and froze repeatedly while walking the hall. Today the client feeds self, walks the hall with one pause, and has dark brown urine. About an hour after each dose the client has new writhing, twisting movements of both arms.
entries.t: What the finding means Evaluating this therapy means comparing function before and after: eating without help and walking with almost no freezing shows the dopamine replacement is doing its job. Clinical detail The writhing, twisting movements after each dose are dyskinesia, a dose-related effect of levodopa that entacapone can intensify, so the provider needs to know and adjust the dose or timing. Dark urine from entacapone looks alarming but is harmless and expected. A masklike face and monotone speech are baseline Parkinson's findings, not proof of drug failure or drug harm. entries.h: Time BP 0800 168/112 mm Hg 0830 166/114 mm Hg The client reports a persistent headache and right upper quadrant pain. Deep tendon reflexes are 3+ , and urine protein is 3+ on dipstick. Normal: urine protein negative to trace
entries.t: What the finding means A blood pressure of 168/112 and 166/114 mm Hg on two readings, both at or above the 160/110 mm Hg severe-range threshold, combined with a severe headache, right upper quadrant pain, hyperreflexia, and heavy proteinuria meets criteria for preeclampsia with severe features rather than gestational hypertension (no severe findings) or chronic hypertension (predates 20 weeks); HELLP is a lab diagnosis, not confirmed by these findings alone. Clinical detail A quiet, dark environment reduces seizure-triggering stimuli, and magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice to prevent eclamptic seizures, while methylergonovine is contraindicated with hypertension and ambulation or aggressive fluids raise seizure and pulmonary edema risk. entries.h: A 4-month-old girl with a large ventricular septal defect and a harsh, loud murmur heard along the left side of the sternum is seen for follow-up. Her mother says she sweats and gets breathless after about 2 oz of formula and needs 40 minutes to finish a bottle . She has gained only 110 g (about 4 oz) in the past month. Respiratory rate 68/min, heart rate 172/min, liver edge felt 3 cm below the right costal margin.
entries.t: What the finding means A VSD shunts blood left to right, floods the lungs, and produces exactly this picture: tachypnea, tachycardia, sweating with feeds, an enlarged liver, and poor weight gain. Clinical detail The plan targets the two problems at once. Feedings are kept short and frequent because feeding is hard work for a failing heart, and the calories are concentrated so she grows on less volume. Knee-to-chest treats a Tet spell in a cyanotic defect, not this one; holding the diuretic would worsen congestion; arm-to-leg blood pressure gaps point to coarctation, which is not her defect. Daily weight and work of breathing during feeds are the two measures that show whether the plan is working. entries.h: A nurse is reviewing assessment findings for four clients with sensory disorders. Match each finding to the condition it best represents.

entries.h: A provider prescribes levothyroxine 0.088 mg PO daily. The pharmacy supplies levothyroxine 44 mcg tablets. How many tablets should the nurse administer per dose?
entries.t: Answer 2 tablets ↓ Reasoning STEP 1, make units match: 1 mg = 1,000 mcg, SO 0.088 mg x 1,000 = 88 mcg (move the decimal 3 places RIGHT when going from mg to mcg). Clinical detail STEP 2, apply DESIRED divided by HAVE x QUANTITY: 88 mcg divided by 44 mcg x 1 tablet = 2 tablets. A common wrong answer is 0.5 tablet, which happens when the student moves the decimal the wrong direction and treats 0.088 mg as smaller than the tablet strength. Always convert before calculating, never compare mg to mcg directly. entries.h: A 5-year-old fell from playground equipment and hit his head. On arrival his exam was normal. Over the past hour he has become increasingly drowsy, vomited once, and now has a sluggish left pupil.
entries.t: What the finding means A child with a head injury who was initially normal but becomes increasingly drowsy, vomits, and develops a sluggish pupil is showing a classic epidural hematoma pattern, a lucid interval followed by rapid deterioration from arterial bleeding and rising intracranial pressure, which is a neurosurgical emergency and not an expected concussion course, seizure disorder, or anxiety reaction. Clinical detail The nurse must notify the provider immediately for emergent imaging and trend level of consciousness and pupil response frequently, because a falling score or a new pupil change signals brain compression that can progress to herniation within minutes to hours. Letting the child sleep undisturbed, keeping him flat, or resuming normal activity right away would delay detection of deterioration; bowel sounds, deep tendon reflexes, red reflex, and phenylalanine are not relevant to this acute neurologic emergency. Growth tracking along the curve, a closed and flat anterior fontanel at this age, brisk capillary refill, physiologic bowlegged stance in a toddler, and normal symmetric reflexes are all expected findings that do not need referral. entries.h: A client is burned at 0800 and arrives at the hospital at 1000. Parkland gives a 24-hour total of 16,200 mL. At what rate should the first half be infused?
entries.t: Answer 1,350 mL/hr ↓ Reasoning The clock starts at the time of the burn, not at arrival. entries.h: A client with a severe exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease requires reliable and precise oxygen delivery. Which mask will the nurse expect the health care provider to prescribe?
entries.t: Answer Venturi mask ↓ Reasoning The Venturi mask is the most reliable and accurate method for delivering precise concentrations of oxygen through noninvasive means. Clinical detail It is used primarily for clients with COPD because it can accurately provide appropriate levels of supplemental oxygen, thus avoiding the risk of suppressing the hypoxic drive. The Venturi mask uses the Bernoulli principle of air entrainment (trapping the air like a vacuum), which provides a high airflow with controlled oxygen enrichment. For each liter of oxygen that passes through a jet orifice, a fixed proportion of room air is entrained. Varying the size of the jet orifice and adjusting the flow of oxygen can deliver a precise volume of oxygen. The other methods of oxygen delivery listed, the nonrebreathing mask, tracheostomy collar, and face tent, do not use the Bernoulli principle and thus lack the precision of a Venturi mask. Original Study Hub review graphic · based on the quiz explanation Why the other answers do not fit Nonrebreathing mask The other methods of oxygen delivery listed, the nonrebreathing mask, tracheostomy collar, and face tent, do not use the Bernoulli principle and thus lack the precision of a Venturi mask. entries.h: Which feature distinguishes this presentation from hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS)?

entries.h: An 11-year-old girl was admitted in diabetic ketoacidosis with a blood glucose of 486 mg/dL, venous pH 7.18, bicarbonate 10 mEq/L, and large urine ketones. She has had 6 hr of IV isotonic fluid and a continuous regular insulin infusion. Highlight the findings that show the ketoacidosis is resolving.
entries.t: What the finding means DKA is diagnosed by hyperglycemia, ketones, and acidosis, so resolution is judged on those same three things, not on the glucose alone. Clinical detail The pH has climbed above 7.30 and the bicarbonate above 15 mEq/L, the ketones are clearing, the deep rapid Kussmaul breathing and fruity odor are gone, and the glucose is down. Temperature, blood pressure, sore fingertips, and a clean IV site are normal findings that say nothing about the acidosis. One caution: at a glucose near 250 mg/dL dextrose is usually added to the IV fluid so the insulin infusion can keep running until the ketones fully clear, and potassium is watched closely as insulin drives it back into the cells. entries.h: the course asks the class, 'If you delay the priority intervention, what complication are you allowing to happen?' Which complication chains are correct? Select all that apply.
entries.t: Answers Appendicitis → rupture → peritonitis → sepsis Diverticulitis → perforation → peritonitis → sepsis Crohn's disease → fistulas → abscess → sepsis Ulcerative colitis → toxic megacolon → ulceration/perforation → sepsis ↓ Reasoning DIFFERENT DISEASES, SAME ENDING — SOMETHING RUPTURES OR PERFORATES, GI CONTENTS LEAK WHERE THEY DO NOT BELONG, AND THE PATIENT GOES TO PERITONITIS AND THEN SEPSIS. Clinical detail Appendicitis and diverticulitis both perforate; Crohn's tunnels into fistulas that abscess; ulcerative colitis dilates into toxic megacolon that ulcerates and perforates; colorectal cancer obstructs and then perforates or metastasizes. IBS does NOT belong on this list — IBS hurts but does not harm, the bowel is structurally normal, and it does not perforate. Celiac disease damages the villi of the small intestine and causes malabsorption, not toxic megacolon. entries.h: Which nonpharmacological measure should the nurse recommend for engorgement in a client who is breastfeeding?
entries.t: Answer Cold compresses or chilled cabbage leaves after feeds, for short periods ↓ Reasoning For a client who wants to keep feeding : warmth before a feed to help the milk flow, cold after for comfort, and cabbage leaves used briefly and stopped once she is comfortable . entries.h: The nurse is planning care for the 22-year-old client newly diagnosed with Crohn's disease. Which complications should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
entries.t: Answers Bowel obstruction from strictures and narrowed bowel Malnutrition with continued weight loss Fistula formation Dehydration with electrolyte loss ↓ Reasoning CROHN'S COMPLICATIONS ARE BLOCK, STARVE, TUNNEL, DRY OUT - obstruction, malnutrition, fistulas, and dehydration. Clinical detail Look at that swollen, narrowed bowel and ask whether stool can pass easily; it cannot, so it blocks. The damaged small intestine cannot absorb, so the client starves, the transmural inflammation tunnels into fistulas, and daily diarrhea dries the client out. Surgery repairs a fistula or a stricture but does NOT cure Crohn's, because it can come back anywhere from mouth to anus, and continuous rectal-to-colon inflammation is ulcerative colitis, not Crohn's skip lesions. entries.h: A nurse is teaching a client about barrier contraceptive methods. Which instructions should the nurse include?
entries.t: Answers Remove the diaphragm within 24 hours of insertion. Leave the contraceptive sponge in place no longer than 30 hours total. Use spermicide no more than twice a day to lower the risk of mucosal irritation. Have the diaphragm refitted after a weight change of about 10 lb (4.5 kg). ↓ Reasoning A diaphragm may go in as much as 6 hours ahead of intercourse, and has to come out by the 24-hour mark, and the contraceptive sponge should not stay in longer than 30 hours total because toxic shock syndrome risk rises after 24 hours. Clinical detail Spermicide used more than twice daily raises the risk of mucosal lesions, and a 4.5 kg weight change means the diaphragm needs refitting for a proper seal. entries.h: A nurse is assessing a client who has heart failure for edema. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

entries.h: A nurse is caring for a client who has left-sided unilateral neglect following a right-hemisphere stroke. The client shaves only the right side of the face and eats only the food on the right side of the tray. Which interventions should the nurse include in the plan of care?

entries.h: West Nile virus · Which sample shows nervous-system involvement?

entries.t: Serum · blood West Nile virus–specific IgM supports recent infection. Blood alone cannot tell you whether the central nervous system is involved. CSF · spinal fluid In a patient with meningitis or encephalitis, West Nile virus–specific IgM in CSF supports neuroinvasive disease. ↓ Why the sample matters IgM ordinarily crosses an intact blood–brain barrier poorly. Interpret the result with the symptoms and sample quality. Blood contamination, barrier damage and cross-reacting antibodies can affect interpretation.

entries.h: Why the other answers do not fit
entries.t: A positive blood culture A routine positive blood culture supports a bloodstream infection. It does not identify West Nile virus in the central nervous system. Raised white cell count Leukocytosis is a nonspecific inflammatory response. It identifies neither the virus nor where the infection is occurring. A chest x-ray infiltrate An infiltrate is a lung finding. It cannot establish infection of the brain or meninges.

A globin-chain production problem. Severity and treatment vary by type. Open full-size infographic Read the study notes Textbook notes for children (NUR 235)

Inherited changes reduce alpha- or beta-globin production, depending on the type. Ineffective red-cell production and early red-cell destruction cause anemia. Severity varies from a carrier state or trait with little or no anemia to severe disease needing ongoing specialist care. Trait does not simply progress into severe disease.

The normal red cell is compared with smaller, paler red cells (microcytic, hypochromic). Target cells have a red central area, a pale surrounding ring and a red outer rim. They may occur in thalassemia, but are not diagnostic by themselves. Confirmation can involve CBC, iron studies, hemoglobin analysis and genetic testing. Alpha-thalassemia trait may not be evident on routine hemoglobin electrophoresis.
Fatigue, pallor, weakness and reduced exercise tolerance can reflect anemia. More severe disease may involve jaundice, an enlarged spleen and impaired growth.

Trend CBC, symptoms, growth in children and activity tolerance. Follow the individualized transfusion plan; assess for transfusion reactions. Review red cell compatibility Track prescribed iron-overload monitoring, including ferritin trends and organ iron assessment when ordered. Iron overload can also occur through increased absorption in some non-transfusion-dependent forms. Support adherence, assess treatment side effects and help families keep follow-up appointments.

Trait may require no treatment. Transfusions and iron chelation are used when indicated. Chelation removes excess iron; it is not iron replacement. Stem-cell transplantation or gene therapy may be options for selected patients after specialist assessment. Eligibility depends on type, severity and the treatment.

Do not assume microcytosis means iron deficiency. Take iron only when deficiency is confirmed and treatment is prescribed. Keep hematology, transfusion, chelation and monitoring appointments as applicable. Discuss genetic counseling and family or partner testing with the care team. Seek urgent care for severe breathing difficulty, chest pain or fainting. Report fever promptly, especially after splenectomy or during treatments that increase infection risk.

entries.h: 🗝 Memory hook — chain shortage → target cells → watch iron
entries.t: Short supply of chain parts = reduced alpha- OR beta-globin production. Target painted on a red cell = target cells may be seen; the picture is a schematic, not a diagnostic smear. Robot magnet collecting Fe = chelation removes excess iron. The magnet is only a memory symbol. Small cells do not automatically mean iron deficiency.
Does a low MCV automatically mean the patient should take iron?
No. Thalassemia can cause small red cells without iron deficiency. Confirm iron status and follow the prescribed plan.

Your Maternal & Child textbook's version for children — Cooley anemia, signs after about 6 months, frontal bossing, transfusions every 3–4 weeks, deferoxamine over 8–12 hours, and never iron — is on the Sickle Cell, Thalassemia, G6PD & Hemophilia page .

entries.t: Skip to study content ABSN / STUDY HUB Visual library Module 7 NUR 258 · EXAM 3 · CPP · MODULE 7

Understand the subtraction, practice the calculation, and see why rising intracranial pressure can reduce perfusion. Understand the formula Try a calculation CPP = MAP − ICP The pressure difference, expressed in mmHg. ICP rises → CPP falls When mean arterial pressure stays unchanged. MAP falls → CPP falls When intracranial pressure stays unchanged. Larger text Hide graphic for recall Print 01
CPP = mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure.
Mean arterial pressure contributes to the pressure driving blood toward the brain.
Intracranial pressure acts against cerebral perfusion. If MAP stays fixed and ICP rises, CPP falls.

Cerebral perfusion pressure: MAP − ICP Subtract the opposing intracranial pressure from mean arterial pressure. MAP 70 mmHg ICP 22 mmHg CPP 48 mmHg − = If ICP rises by 5 while MAP stays the same: 70 − 27 = 43 mmHg CPP falls when ICP rises or MAP falls. The pressure difference helps assess perfusion; it is not a direct measurement of brain blood flow. 02

Change one pressure and observe how CPP responds. MAP (mmHg) ICP (mmHg) 70 − 22 = 48 mmHg Reset example Practice calculation only. This tool does not set treatment targets or measure brain blood flow.

entries.h: Recall question: MAP stays at 70 and ICP rises from 22 to 27. What happens?
entries.t: CPP falls from 48 to 43 mmHg. The 5 mmHg increase in ICP produces a 5 mmHg decrease in CPP when MAP is unchanged. 03

entries.h: Keep course numbers and clinical goals clear
entries.t: Interpret the calculated value in context.
The current course page states CPP above 50 mmHg, ideally 60–70. The 48 mmHg example is below the course threshold. Return to the assigned Module 7 material

Brain Trauma Foundation guidance recommends a CPP target of 60–70 mmHg for adult severe traumatic brain injury. Use the prescribed patient-specific target and monitoring plan. Escalate new neurologic deterioration promptly. CPP is a pressure difference; oxygenation, vascular resistance and autoregulation also affect cerebral perfusion.

entries.h: Newborn circumcision care: Gomco, Mogen and Plastibell | ABSN Study Hub
entries.t: NUR 234 · Newborn care and discharge teaching
Gomco and Mogen clamps come off at the end of the procedure. A Plastibell ring stays on. Knowing which device was used tells you what to teach at the next diaper change.

Lifted bell. A metal bell shields the glans (the head of the penis). The clinician removes the bell and clamp when the procedure ends. Diaper care. Apply petroleum jelly as directed to prevent sticking. Use petroleum gauze if ordered.
Lifted clip. A flat metal clamp holds the foreskin. When the clinician removes it, no device remains. Diaper care. Follow the same petroleum jelly and dressing instructions as for Gomco.

Resting ring. A ligature holds the foreskin against a plastic ring. The ring separates on its own. Never pull or twist it. Diaper care. The course teaches warm-water care without petroleum jelly while the ring is on. At home, follow the procedural clinician’s instructions about ointment.

Verify parental consent, vitamin K administration, prior void per nursery policy and the pain-control plan. Local anesthetic treats procedural pain. Swaddling and sucrose provide additional comfort. Suspected hypospadias? Defer circumcision and notify the clinician. The foreskin may be needed for repair. Review hypospadias

entries.h: Diaper changes, first void and normal healing
entries.t: Clean gently. Wash hands, rinse away stool with warm water and fasten the diaper loosely. Avoid rubbing, alcohol wipes and tub baths until healed. Expect mild swelling, tenderness and a thin yellow film. Leave the film in place. A few small blood spots can occur. Recheck for ongoing bleeding. Document the first wet diaper. The course uses a 6–8 hour window after circumcision. Follow your facility’s earlier notification threshold. Seek urgent care if there is no urine by 8 hours or only dribbling. Ring timing. NUR 2

Active bleeding: Apply gentle direct pressure with sterile gauze and notify the clinician. More than a few drops or persistent bleeding needs urgent assessment. Heavy blood loss with pallor, cold skin or weakness is an emergency. Call emergency services. Seek urgent care for no urine by 8 hours, a ring slipping onto the shaft, a dark blue or black glans, marked swelling, spreading redness, pus, or a newborn rectal temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher.

Parent Education for Newborn Care & Circumcision Care. The handout’s petroleum-gauze teaching applies to clamp care in this course. For a Plastibell, use the ring instructions above. Its coin-sized bleeding example is an exam cue. Clinically, seek help for ongoing bleeding or more than a few drops.

entries.h: A nurse is caring for a client who has bipolar disorder with psychotic features and a history of obesity and type 2 diabetes. Which of the following antipsychotics should the nurse expect the provider to select as most weight-neutral?
entries.t: Ziprasidone and aripiprazole are the most weight-neutral second-generation antipsychotics, making ziprasidone appropriate for a client with obesity and diabetes. Olanzapine and clozapine carry the highest risk of weight gain and new-onset diabetes, and quetiapine also causes substantial weight gain and sedation. Olanzapine Quetiapine Ziprasidone Clozapine Olanzapine and clozapine carry the highest risk of weight gain and new-onset diabetes, and quetiapine also causes substantial weight gain and sedation. entries.h: A client with bipolar disorder is starting lithium. Which outcomes should the nurse include in the plan of care?
entries.t: Recognizing toxicity, steady hydration, adherence to level monitoring, and reporting fluid losses all protect against the narrow therapeutic window of lithium . Sodium restriction is the tempting distractor because reducing salt is standard advice in many conditions, but low sodium causes the kidney to retain lithium and raises the level toward toxicity. A fine tremor is a common, expected effect, and self-discontinuation risks relapse. The client will describe the early signs of lithium toxicity before discharge The client will maintain a fluid intake of 2 to 3 L per day The client will keep scheduled appointments for serum lithium levels The client will restrict dietary sodium to prevent fluid retention The client will stop the medication if a fine hand tremor develops The client will report vomiting or diarrhea to the provider promptly A fine tremor is a common, expected effect, and self-discontinuation risks relapse.

entries.h: A nurse is caring for a client 18 hr after a lumbar puncture. Which of the following findings should the nurse report to the provider immediately?
entries.t: Fever with NUCHAL RIGIDITY and photophobia points to MENINGITIS, an infectious complication of the puncture. Mild site tenderness, generous fluid intake, and lying flat afterward are all expected findings. Also report CLOUDY CSF (a sign of infection) and any new numbness or weakness in the legs, which suggests a spinal hematoma. The client reports mild tenderness at the puncture site The client has taken in 2,000 mL of oral fluid since the procedure Temperature of 38.8 C (101.8 F) with nuchal rigidity and photophobia The client remained flat in bed for the first 4 hr after the procedure Mild site tenderness, generous fluid intake, and lying flat afterward are all expected findings.

entries.t: For salmeterol (LABA), the type / action is: long-acting beta-2 agonist methylxanthine; relaxes bronchial smooth muscle anticholinergic; blocks ACh, ↓ secretions short-acting beta-2 agonist; relaxes airway smooth muscle long-acting beta-2 agonist The course lists this feature under theophylline (methylxanthine). entries.h: Which nursing intervention is appropriate during meals for a hospitalized client with bulimia nervosa?
entries.t: Observation during and after meals prevents purging and hiding food. Post-meal privacy enables purging, and praising weight or appearance can be distressing. Allow the client privacy immediately after eating Observe the client during and for about one hour after meals Praise the client for gaining weight Permit the client to weigh and record their own intake

entries.h: Which set of findings best fits a client in respiratory acidosis?
entries.t: Respiratory acidosis is the not-breathing picture: CO2 climbs, and high CO2 causes CNS depression, so the client is sleepy, confused and headachy while breathing too little. Perioral tingling and carpal spasm are the classic respiratory alkalosis findings from breathing too fast, which is the easiest set to mix up with this one. Drowsy, confused, headache, with a rising CO2 Tingling around the mouth with carpal spasm Kussmaul respirations with fruity-smelling breath Muscle cramps and a pH of 7.50 after days of vomiting Rapid breathing lowers CO₂. Tingling around the mouth and carpal spasm fit respiratory alkalosis. Deep Kussmaul breathing is compensation for metabolic acidosis. Fruity breath points toward ketones, as in diabetic ketoacidosis. Vomiting causes gastric acid loss. A pH of 7.50 is alkalemic and fits metabolic alkalosis in this setting.

entries.h: A nurse is discussing relapse prevention with a client who has bipolar disorder. Which of the following information should the nurse include?
entries.t: Sleep disturbances and anhedonia can indicate relapse; psychotherapy helps prevent relapse. The client should limit caffeine and take medications consistently to prevent relapse. Use caffeine in moderation to prevent relapse. Difficulty sleeping can indicate a relapse. Begin taking your medications as soon as a relapse begins. Participating in psychotherapy can help prevent a relapse. Anhedonia is a clinical manifestation of a depressive relapse. The client should limit caffeine and take medications consistently to prevent relapse. The client should limit caffeine and take medications consistently to prevent relapse.

entries.h: Which finding after a lumbar puncture should the nurse report to the provider immediately?
entries.t: New numbness, tingling, or weakness in the lower extremities suggests nerve irritation or compression such as a hematoma and requires immediate provider notification. A headache relieved by lying flat is the expected spinal headache and is managed with positioning and fluids rather than an urgent call. Mild soreness at the insertion site New numbness and weakness in both legs Headache that is relieved by lying flat Urine output of 60 mL per hour A headache relieved by lying flat is the expected spinal headache and is managed with positioning and fluids rather than an urgent call.

entries.h: Three hours after a lumbar puncture, a client reports a throbbing headache that worsens when sitting up. Which action should the nurse take first?
entries.t: A postural headache after a lumbar puncture is a common spinal headache from cerebrospinal fluid loss, and it is treated first with flat positioning and fluids. Meningitis is tempting because headache is a symptom, but meningitis presents with fever and nuchal rigidity rather than a headache that improves when lying down. Assist the client to lie flat and encourage oral fluid intake Prepare the client for an emergency computed tomography scan Notify the provider that the client is showing signs of meningitis Have the client sit up straight and take slow deep breaths

entries.h: A client who has bipolar disorder reports 3 days of diarrhea, upset stomach, irritability, confusion, and a new right-hand tremor. Which of the following 6 items require immediate follow-up?
entries.t: The findings suggest lithium toxicity : check the lithium level and dosage , sodium (hyponatremia raises lithium levels), BUN (renal excretion), and TSH/levothyroxine (lithium causes hypothyroidism, and thyroid status affects presentation). Lithium level Acetaminophen Sodium level Lithium dosage BUN level TSH level Levothyroxine dosage White blood cell count Blood pressure

entries.h: A client who has bipolar disorder has been taking lithium for 3 weeks and reports nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and a coarse hand tremor. Which action should the nurse take?
entries.t: Coarse tremor + GI upset = early lithium toxicity (1.5–2.0 mEq/L). A fine tremor is expected; a coarse tremor is not. Hold, notify, draw a level. A low-sodium diet raises the lithium level — that is the opposite of what you want. Teach a consistent sodium intake and 2–3 L of fluid daily . Reassure the client these are expected initial effects Hold the lithium and notify the provider; obtain a lithium level Encourage a low-sodium diet to reduce fluid retention Administer the next dose with food A low-sodium diet raises the lithium level — that is the opposite of what you want.

entries.h: Which findings are typical of a panic attack? Select all that apply.
entries.t: Panic attacks come on abruptly with cardiac-looking symptoms — chest pain, palpitations, dyspnea, dizziness, trembling, diaphoresis, and a sense of doom — which is exactly why they are mistaken for an MI. Bradycardia and a slow build over days do not fit the sympathetic surge of panic. Chest pain and palpitations Shortness of breath Bradycardia and hypotension Dizziness and trembling Sweating with a sense of impending doom Gradual onset over several days Bradycardia and a slow build over days do not fit the sympathetic surge of panic.

entries.h: A nurse is preparing a 58-year-old client for a lumbar puncture on a medical unit. Which of the following actions should the nurse take before the procedure?
entries.t: BLEEDING RISK is the reason to check coagulation studies and confirm anticoagulants were held; an epidural or spinal hematoma can compress the cord. An EMPTY BLADDER keeps the client comfortable while curled in the flexed position for a prolonged time. A 12 hr NPO order is not standard because there is no general anesthesia, and shaving the entire back is unnecessary; only the site is prepped. Verify that the client's coagulation studies are on the chart Ask the client to empty the bladder Maintain the client NPO for 12 hr before the procedure Confirm that prescribed anticoagulants were held as ordered Shave the client's entire back from the shoulders to the sacrum A 12 hr NPO order is not standard because there is no general anesthesia, and shaving the entire back is unnecessary A 12 hr NPO order is not standard because there is no general anesthesia, and shaving the entire back is unnecessary

entries.h: A nurse is caring for a client who is experiencing a panic attack. Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
entries.t: Assisting with deep-breathing exercises helps the client regain control and reduce anxiety during a panic attack. Assist the client with deep-breathing exercises. Discuss new relaxation techniques. Show the client how to change the behavior. Distract the client with a television show.

entries.h: Which of the following actions should the nurse include in the care of a client after a lumbar puncture?
entries.t: Flat positioning, extra fluids, site inspection, and neurologic checks of the legs address the two main risks after the procedure, which are spinal headache and nerve or bleeding complications. Hourly ambulation defeats the purpose of flat positioning, and there is no reason to withhold ordered analgesics. Keep the client flat for the prescribed period Withhold all analgesics for 24 hours Encourage increased oral fluid intake Inspect the puncture site for drainage or swelling Ambulate the client in the hallway every hour Check movement and sensation in the lower extremities Hourly ambulation defeats the purpose of flat positioning, and there is no reason to withhold ordered analgesics.

entries.h: A client with endometriosis asks why she has pain. What is the nurse's best explanation?
entries.t: Endometrial-like tissue outside the uterus responds to the same hormones and bleeds each cycle , causing inflammation, adhesions and pain, classically before and during menstruation and with intercourse. It is a common cause of infertility, and it is not an infection or a malignancy. “Tissue like the uterine lining grows outside the uterus and bleeds with each cycle, with nowhere to drain.” “The uterus is infected.” “It is caused by using tampons.” “It is a form of cancer.”

entries.h: An infant who has tetralogy of Fallot has a hypercyanotic spell. Which position should the nurse use?
entries.t: Knee-chest - it keeps desaturated blood from the legs out of circulation and raises systemic vascular resistance , pushing blood through the pulmonary artery instead of across the defect. An older child squats for the same reason. The four defects: pulmonary stenosis, right ventricular hypertrophy, VSD and an overriding aorta . Prone with the head flat Sitting fully upright Supine with the legs elevated Knee-chest

entries.h: Which heart defects make up tetralogy of Fallot? (Select all that apply.)
entries.t: Tetralogy of Fallot is four defects. Remember PROV : P ulmonary stenosis, R ight ventricular hypertrophy, O verriding aorta, V entricular septal defect. The narrowing is on the pulmonary side, not the aortic side: blood struggles to get out to the lungs, so the right ventricle works harder and thickens, and oxygen-poor blood crosses the VSD into the aorta that sits over it. That mixing is why these children are cyanotic. Aortic stenosis and mitral valve prolapse are separate conditions, not part of the four. Pulmonary stenosis Aortic stenosis Ventricular septal defect (VSD) Mitral valve prolapse Overriding aorta Right ventricular hypertrophy Aortic stenosis and mitral valve prolapse are separate conditions, not part of the four. Aortic stenosis and mitral valve prolapse are separate conditions, not part of the four.

entries.h: A nurse is caring for a client who has bipolar disorder. The client states, "I am very rich, and I feel I must give my money to you." Which of the following responses should the nurse make?
entries.t: This matter-of-fact, concise response is therapeutic. Option a is a "why" question, c does not recognize poor judgment, d offers disapproval. entries.h: Which client statement about bipolar disorder indicates a need for further teaching?
entries.t: Bipolar disorder is lifelong — stopping the mood stabilizer when stable is the number-one cause of relapse and rehospitalization. The other three are correct: sleep loss is the biggest relapse trigger, labs continue indefinitely, and alcohol and stimulants destabilize mood. “I'll keep a regular sleep schedule because losing sleep can trigger an episode.” “Once I feel stable for a few months I can stop the mood stabilizer.” “I'll keep my lab appointments even when I feel fine.” “I'll avoid alcohol because it can destabilize my mood.” The other three are correct: sleep loss is the biggest relapse trigger, labs continue indefinitely, and alcohol and stimulants destabilize mood.

entries.h: Which result confirms neuroinvasive West Nile virus?
entries.t: IgM in the CSF is confirmatory because IgM does not cross the blood-brain barrier - finding it there means it was made there. Serum IgM shows infection but not nervous-system involvement. IgM antibody in the cerebrospinal fluid A positive blood culture Raised white cell count A chest x-ray infiltrate A routine positive blood culture supports a bloodstream infection. It does not identify West Nile virus in the central nervous system. Leukocytosis is a nonspecific inflammatory response. It identifies neither the virus nor where the infection is occurring. An infiltrate is a lung finding. It cannot establish infection of the brain or meninges.
